content.title: How can Sweden become a leader in AI and digital skills?
content.description: Sweden's competitiveness depends on a skilled workforce with strong digital and AI skills. What does Sweden need to do to prepare tomorrow's workers?
content.extendedDescription:
AI is expected to transform the economy and working life in the coming years. For Sweden to strengthen its competitiveness, it needs widespread digital skills, cutting-edge AI expertise and an education system that prepares people for a new era. But are today's policies, governance and division of responsibilities sufficient to meet these developments?
This seminar brings together representatives from business and politics to discuss how Sweden can take the lead in developing digital and AI-related skills. What choices are needed to prepare pupils, students and working professionals? How do we improve the interaction between education and the labour market? And what do decision-makers need to do now to stop Sweden falling behind?
content.subject: Employment/labour market
speakerTitles: Chair of the Municipal Executive Board
Head of the skills supply unit

content.title: From scrolling to offending – digital misogyny and rape of normal degree
content.description: How are boys' views of women, sex and boundaries shaped in a digital world characterised by algorithms, pornography and misogynistic online environments?
content.extendedDescription: Boys today encounter pornography, violent ideals and misogynistic messages at ever younger ages. Social media algorithms and digital communities help shape norms around masculinity, sex and power, influencing young people's views of women, consent and boundaries. Meanwhile, researchers, youth clinics and schools report changing norms around sexual relationships and growing uncertainty about what is expected of boys and girls. Drawing on Tankesmedjan Tiden's new report From Scroller to Perpetrator, we discuss how to understand boys' digital radicalisation, why this development is a gender equality issue and what political measures are needed to prevent men's violence against women.
content.subject: Gender equality

content.title: How to increase productivity in healthcare
content.description: Over time, healthcare spending as a share of GDP in Sweden has increased. Today it is around 10 per cent. Productivity developments in the sector therefore matter greatly, both for healthcare and for the economy as a whole.
content.extendedDescription:
Produktivitetskommissionen's final report presents a range of proposals for making healthcare more efficient. How they are taken forward will have a major impact on future care.

One proposal identified by the commission as an important measure for increasing healthcare productivity is stronger primary care. During the seminar, we discuss how productivity should be measured and which reforms are most important to pursue to improve care.

Welcome to a seminar where we discuss how productivity should be measured in healthcare and which of the commission's proposals matter most for developing care.

content.title: How can Sweden attract more and larger industrial investments?
content.description: Ireland's systematic efforts have made it a global pharmaceutical powerhouse. Can Sweden copy the recipe and attract more cash?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden has a strong identity as an industrial nation and has long been an attractive location for investment in production. But the trend is declining – both the number and the share of foreign investments in Swedish industry are shrinking.

The dwindling number of industrial investments in Sweden and the EU is a problem with major risks as the renewal of know-how and related services contracts. To meet increasingly fierce global competition, industry must develop and grow. Other countries are doing better. What can Sweden do to become more attractive to investment? Welcome to an engaging seminar with an international outlook and concrete examples of what is needed!
content.subject: Economy
speakerTitles: Head of Public Affairs and Communications

content.title: Healthcare's working environment at rock bottom – political action is needed now
content.description: Warnings about the working environment in healthcare are frequent. Before the turn of the year, Arbetsmiljöverket published the results of an extensive inspection of healthcare. The review identified shortcomings at 320 of 437 workplaces. What measures are needed to improve the working environment in healthcare?
content.extendedDescription: Despite recurring warnings about shortcomings in healthcare's working environment, nothing changes. Läkarförbundet's working environment surveys show that poor conditions jeopardise quality of care, employees' health and the ability to recruit and retain staff in the future. The seminar brings together, among others, the Chair of Läkarförbundet and the Director-General of Arbetsmiljöverket to discuss the importance of political action and long-term solutions that can ensure a good working environment in healthcare.

content.title: Secure, clear and sustainable leadership – what is needed now?
content.description: Safety-critical government agencies operate under intense pressure, with complex mandates and high demands for accountability, legal certainty and trust. Leadership then becomes crucial to the working environment, culture and long-term capacity. What kind of leadership is needed for employees to want, and feel able, to stay?
content.extendedDescription: A panel discussion on the importance of leadership in agencies with society-critical mandates. Organisations with high demands and long-term missions need managers who can provide clarity, trust and security even under pressure. The discussion focuses on the relationship between leadership and the working environment, how conflicts, harassment and cultures of silence can be prevented and addressed, and what support managers need to succeed. The question is how agencies build trust, follow up problems and create organisations where people can develop and contribute over time.
content.subject: Security/defence
speakerTitles: Rear Admiral (Lower Half) and Director of Communications

content.title: How desperate are the party leaders' pick-up attempts?
content.description: Who swipes right and who swipes left in Swedish politics? Cooperation across party and bloc boundaries is fundamental to gaining government power in today's Sweden. With only a few months until the election, there are both established partnerships and unwritten coalitions.
content.extendedDescription:
Finding common issues to pursue is central for party leaders, but how eager are their representatives? What are the winning formulas and pitfalls of political courtship? Druid & Zimmerman show presents a live podcast before an audience. David Druid and Katherine Zimmerman explore the week's political events with Ekot political reporter Lova Olsson and satirist Moa Wallin. Expect:

Sharp analysis and unexpected perspectives
Humour, satire – and perhaps a little scandal thrown in

It will be an evening that both entertains and offers fresh insights – and might even make your choice in 2026 a little easier.

content.title: Children's and young people's health – how we build a strong Sweden
content.description: Children's and young people's health affects both quality of life and society's long-term development. Ill health entails major costs and difficulties entering working life. At the same time, responsibility falls between schools and employers. How do we take shared responsibility, and what does failing to do so cost?
content.extendedDescription: The seminar examines the connection between children's and young people's health, opportunities and education in preparation for the working life of the future, with a particular focus on the economic consequences of failing to invest early in their health and development. Researchers come together to discuss how different parts of society can take more coordinated responsibility for young people's opportunities to thrive – and the consequences if we fail. The discussion highlights transitions between preschool, school and working life, where responsibility for the overall picture is often lacking.

content.title: What role can sewage sludge in agriculture play in a resilient food supply?
content.description: Sweden needs to strengthen food preparedness, reduce dependence on imported mineral fertilisers and protect soil, water and human health. Quality-assured and certified sewage sludge is often highlighted as part of the solution – but also raises questions about risks.
content.extendedDescription: Quality-assured and certified sewage sludge is often highlighted as part of the solution – but also raises questions about risks associated with heavy metals, micropollutants and trust in the food chain. In this panel discussion, food companies, agriculture, the water and wastewater sector and experts come together to discuss how risks can be managed through upstream work such as REVAQ, responsible handling and processing, certification and full traceability – and how nutrients can be returned in a way that is safe, accepted and sustainable in the long term.

content.title: Racism and hate in public debate – who takes responsibility?
content.description: What responsibility do those in power, government agencies and opinion leaders have for the tone of debate? How can we together contribute to respectful, democratic debate? And to a society free from discrimination?
content.extendedDescription:
People in our society are subjected to hate and threats, and the UN Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination has called on Sweden to counter racist hate in public debate. Meanwhile, negative attitudes towards minority groups are increasing, not least among young people.

The words we use matter – in politics, the media and public discourse. Who is responsible for combating and responding to hate and racism when it spreads?

The opening of Torget för mänskliga rättigheter och demokrati features Lars Arrhenius, Equality Ombudsman, Fredrik Malmberg, Director-General of Institutet för mänskliga rättigheter, and Petra Mårselius, Director-General of Forum för levande historia.

content.title: The medicines system has reached the end of the road – what can we do here and now?
content.description: Medical advances are creating new opportunities to treat diseases and improve patients' quality of life. At the same time, Sweden's medicines system faces significant challenges. The minister responsible has described the system as having reached the end of the road.

The government has now appointed an inquiry into medicines to review the system fundamentally. This is an important step towards a more sustainable long-term solution. But inquiries take time – and patients cannot wait.
So what can be done right now? What improvements are possible within today's system? And what concrete measures can be implemented without waiting for a larger reform?

content.title: The police – more than blue lights
content.description: What does it mean to have civilian employees at Polismyndigheten, and why is it so important?
content.extendedDescription:
Polismyndigheten is Sweden's largest government agency, with just over 41,000 employees, a significant proportion of whom – around 16,000 – are civilian staff. Without us, Polismyndigheten comes to a halt!
For many people, the police are still synonymous with uniforms and flashing blue lights.
Once the patrol has left the crime scene, it is often civilian colleagues who continue working on cases.
Members of ST inom Polisen are also often the people you meet when you contact the police.
Together with other civilian employees and colleagues with police expertise, we contribute to Polismyndigheten's important public mission in fighting crime and interacting with citizens, and work towards a safer society.
The event takes the form of a seminar/panel debate.

content.title: How defence investments affect the whole of society
content.description: Major defence investments affect the whole of society – from business and the economy to the public sector and civil society. What opportunities, challenges and choices follow from the new security situation and the expansion of total defence?
content.extendedDescription:
Extensive investments in defence and preparedness affect not only Sweden's security, but also business, government agencies, the economy and civil society. How does society change when defence capabilities are expanded rapidly? What new demands, opportunities and challenges emerge in the changed security situation?

The seminar examines the business, security policy, economic, cultural and organisational implications of the investments now being made in total defence. It focuses on how the public sector, business and civil society are affected – and which choices will be decisive going forward.
content.subject: Security/defence

content.title: When crisis strikes, Sweden's most experienced nurses are ready to step forward
content.description: Changing geopolitical conditions and the risk of new pandemics are increasing concern. Sweden faces new threats – we must be able to mobilise experienced nurses when crisis strikes. Senior nurses can play a decisive role, but how can Sweden find them without registers?
content.extendedDescription: Sweden has more than 40,000 retired nurses with invaluable experience. A new study shows that many want to contribute during crises and disasters. This opens up a powerful, previously untapped resource that could strengthen Sweden's preparedness and also support normal operations, as Sweden already faces difficulties securing the skills it needs. What strategies does Sweden have for making use of senior and specialist-trained nurses?

content.title: Implementing EU legislation across the country – from cities to rural areas
content.description: Municipalities must put extensive EU rules into practice, but conditions differ greatly between large and small municipalities, rural areas and islands. How is Sweden addressing these challenges, and how do we create workable local solutions from the perspective of small municipalities?
content.extendedDescription: It sounds technical – but it is profoundly political, practical and local. The EU's new requirements for waste management in a circular economy involve a systemic shift: more sorting, greater producer responsibility and higher recycling targets. For Sweden's municipalities, the question is not whether but how to implement this. And conditions vary widely – from the complex logistics of big cities to seasonal variations in archipelagos and long distances in rural areas. This seminar focuses specifically on implementation: what does it take to make the EU's ambitions work in practice – throughout the country?
content.subject: Climate/environment

content.title: The Brain Capital Momentum: is human capacity the most important investment of our time?
content.description: As AI and global changes reshape working life and decision-making, are investments in human capacity, resilience and confidence in the future as crucial as investments in technology and physical infrastructure? What does Sweden need to strengthen its Brain Capital?
content.extendedDescription:
We are at a historic moment when the ability to learn, create and manage change is becoming crucial to long-term competitiveness. The concept of Brain Capital places human capacity – health, motivation, cognition and confidence in the future – at the centre of investment in society.
In this discussion, leaders from business, research and investment explore why, what and how Sweden can make human capacity its most important infrastructure. The event is a moderated discussion in a Hot Seat or Fireside Chat format.

content.title: An industrial platform for sustainability innovation
content.description: How can collaboration between business, innovation and technology help Swedish industry achieve its climate targets?

BridgeHouse™, a national innovation platform from AstraZeneca, Scania and RISE, will be launched during Almedalsveckan. Its aim is to promote innovation, competitiveness and sustainable technology to help Swedish industry reach its climate targets. The initiative is supported by the government and co-funded by Vinnova.
On the Tech Arena stage, Per Alfredsson, CEO of AstraZeneca AB, Christian Levin, CEO of Scania, and Malin Frenning, CEO of RISE, present the vision behind the initiative. They explain why leading players from different parts of Swedish business are choosing to collaborate across traditional sector boundaries, and what role innovation can play in meeting climate targets for 2030, 2045 and beyond.
The discussion is moderated by Magnus Björsne, CEO of BioVentureHub and Head of BioVenture Innovation Unit, AstraZeneca.

content.title: Together for a good life for everyone – the path to Sweden's most prestigious quality award
content.description: The public sector faces a growing challenge: delivering high quality over time while demands increase and resources are limited. How do we make quality an integral part of governance and management, rather than just a separate goal?
content.extendedDescription:
Region Jönköpings län is making history. For the first time, Utmärkelsen Svensk Kvalitet is being awarded to a Swedish region. The citation highlights our long-term work with quality as a strategy and sound resource management – an approach that delivers results in national comparisons and a balanced budget.

Welcome to a discussion about how we use follow-up, evaluation and shared learning to develop our operations – and how quality as a strategy and sound resource management can create sustainable results in practice and contribute to a county where people want to live, grow up and stay.

content.title: Can I swim? How do we secure knowledge of what is happening in the sea?
content.description: Effective environmental monitoring is essential for detecting changes in the environment that affect marine life, people along the coast and at sea, and businesses, in both the short and long term.
content.extendedDescription:
Those working in environmental monitoring currently need to cut the frequency of sampling, the number of samples and the types of samples taken. Several marine infrastructures – field stations, vessels and laboratories – essential for data collection and analysis face an uncertain future. This risks leaving many gaps in the picture we build, allowing changes in the marine environment to go undetected.

In this session, we want to:
• Explain why environmental monitoring matters.
• Give examples of when environmental monitoring has contributed to successful measures for a better marine environment.
• Discuss what needs to be done to safeguard existing time series and develop environmental monitoring for future challenges.
content.subject: Animals/nature

content.title: From research strength to innovation capacity: what does Europe need to avoid falling behind?
content.description: Europe faces a widening innovation gap with the USA and China. How do we create better conditions for research at Swedish and European higher education institutions to lead to sustainable growth, new companies and technological independence?
content.extendedDescription: Europe is at a decisive moment. Although universities and research institutes generate strong research, only a fraction of research innovations reach the market – and even fewer underpin companies that succeed in scaling internationally. At the same time, the climate crisis, geopolitical uncertainty and the digital transition demand greater European self-sufficiency in technology, skills and critical innovations. At a time when the pace of innovation is increasing globally, we need to strengthen our ability to move from research lab to market and create innovation systems that work in practice, not just on paper.
content.subject: Innovation

content.title: How to solve the skills crisis – time for a ministry for skills provision?
content.description: Skills shortages are among businesses' greatest obstacles to growth. Yet responsibility for education, the labour market and business is split between different ministries and government agencies. This hampers coordination and implementation.
content.extendedDescription:
Many companies find their contact with education inadequate, regardless of the level of the education system involved. As a result, recruitment opportunities are missed, students lack links to working life, and reskilling courses stand empty.

It is time to connect education more closely to labour market needs in earnest. Could a ministry for skills provision be a solution?

Welcome to a discussion about educational provision, young people's opportunities and how we create an education system designed around business needs. For real.
content.subject: Business

content.title: How do young politicians view the media policy of the future?
content.description: The media's business model and role in building society are being challenged by new technology, new competition and a multifaceted communications landscape. Traditional media compete with influencers and social media accounts for young people's attention. How do young politicians view developments in the media?
content.extendedDescription:
Sveriges Tidskrifter has produced an election manifesto setting out the most important political issues from a media perspective. Two representatives from our young board – Next Gen Board – challenge politicians from the youth parties on the basis of the manifesto. How do tomorrow's media policymakers view developments in the media, and how would future media policy be shaped if they could decide?
A number of representatives from political youth organisations will attend to share their views on the media and media policy.

content.title: What do children do in prison?
content.description: The issue that has attracted the most attention in criminal justice debate and among the public is lowering the age of criminal responsibility so that fourteen-year-old children can be remanded in custody and imprisoned. But what will children do in prison, and what happens when they leave?
content.extendedDescription:
How can the agency carry out this task while maintaining a children's rights perspective? Under the Convention on the Rights of the Child, children have a right to development – even if they are held on remand for a long time and sentenced to prison. Children must attend school and have meaningful leisure time, and ultimately their development should enable them to leave Kriminalvården rehabilitated and safe for themselves and society.

We are now bringing together a number of people to discuss how to do the best we can for these children. When the worst has happened, we all need to help.
content.subject: Justice/crime
speakerTitles: Remand Prison Chaplain who meets children in custody

content.title: European copyright – how do we protect what we create?
content.description: Visual art, music, literature and journalism are pillars of our society. You encounter copyrighted material every day, so what happens if that protection is weakened?
content.extendedDescription:
This year, the European Commission is evaluating the effects of the new copyright law that came into force in Sweden in 2023. It is based on an EU directive intended, among other things, to strengthen protection for authors and performing artists.

During this discussion, we present the results of a new survey mapping how sectors have responded to implementation – has protection become stronger in practice? We also discuss what we can expect from the evaluation. Does current copyright protection need to be strengthened at European level?

Politics, culture, academia and law meet in an engaging discussion about how we should protect what we create.
content.subject: Culture
speakerTitles: Legal Adviser, IT and Media Law

content.title: A national cultural guarantee – opportunities and challenges for the performing arts
content.description: There are proposals to introduce a national cultural guarantee for children and young people. What opportunities and challenges would such a model bring? What matters for the conditions of the independent performing arts sector in a reform?
content.extendedDescription:
Teatercentrum invites you to a breakfast discussion about national cultural guarantees and the future of cultural policy. From the perspective of the independent performing arts sector, we discuss how a cultural guarantee could affect access to culture, artistic freedom and the ability to reach audiences throughout the country.

The event begins with a short presentation followed by an open discussion in which participants are invited to contribute their perspectives and experiences. The discussion is aimed at people in the cultural sector, politics and civil society, and others who want to discuss culture's role in society and the cultural policy of the future.

Coffee and sandwiches will be provided. The programme will not be livestreamed.

content.title: Behind the walls and at the heart of society's development
content.description: Political reforms involving longer sentences and a faster criminal justice process mean Kriminalvården faces a historic expansion, requiring thousands of new employees and construction at record speed. How do we manage this together from a national perspective? Is there enough funding, and where do we find the staff?
content.extendedDescription: A panel discussion on challenges and opportunities for municipalities, the property sector and the labour market. Kriminalvården faces a historic expansion as the agency triples the number of places in prisons and remand centres. Today, we have more than 50 ongoing construction projects across the country, while staff numbers must also double. Kriminalvården is a central actor in society – we reduce reoffending while also driving growth and hiring thousands of new employees. But do supply and demand match?
content.subject: Infrastructure/transport

content.title: From law to reality: why is nicotine reaching minors?
content.description: Despite clear legislation, minors can widely obtain nicotine products. Use among young people is increasing and, in many cases, the products are far too easy to obtain. Supervisory responsibility is divided between several levels, but outcomes point to significant shortcomings in compliance and oversight.
content.extendedDescription: How can it be so easy for minors to obtain nicotine despite legal requirements and supervision? The seminar presents a new survey of municipalities' test purchases, showing how the rules work in practice. We examine the chain of responsibility from legislation to local supervision and hear how key players view the issue: retailers, industry organisations, municipalities, county administrative boards and Folkhälsomyndigheten. The focus is on where the system fails and what concrete measures are needed to stop children's access to nicotine within the foreseeable future.
content.subject: Justice/crime
speakerTitles: Deputy Chair of the Municipal Executive Board

content.title: Why a centre for men's health is needed
content.description: Women rate their health more poorly than men do. Could one explanation be that the men around them seek too little help, consume too much alcohol and die by suicide more often than women? Some diseases are specific to men but are insufficiently detected by healthcare.
content.extendedDescription:
By following Australia's example of a publicly funded centre for men's health, Sweden could also improve its broad approach to men's health. This ranges from earlier detection of treatable diseases such as cancer and cardiovascular disease to involving both partners in sexological problems and treating fertility problems.

We want to discuss how men and healthcare can take more responsibility for men's health, and how this would benefit society as a whole.
content.subject: Health and social care

content.title: Industrial biotechnology: the key to Sweden's green industrial transition?
content.description: Industrial biotechnology offers new bio-based solutions for transforming the production of everything from fuels and chemicals to materials and food. Sweden has unique conditions for taking a leading role in the biotechnology revolution.
content.extendedDescription: With abundant raw materials and a strong research tradition, the foundations exist for making industrial biotechnology a central part of Sweden's industrial strategy. But what is needed for the next step in Sweden's and Europe's development? This seminar discusses how Sweden can take a leading position in developing industrial biotechnology. Given Sweden's favourable conditions in this field, prioritising it could have a powerful impact on Swedish competitiveness.

content.title: How do we build competitiveness through net zero?
content.description: Swedish manufacturing is crucial to welfare and growth. The industry's own emissions are falling, and Swedish green technology is a global success. Where are the opportunities for further emissions reductions, and how can efforts towards net zero strengthen competitiveness in an increasingly uncertain world?
content.extendedDescription:
Net Zero Industry has produced new statistics on manufacturing and invites you to a discussion about why work towards net zero is a crucial success factor for stronger competitiveness, particularly in an increasingly turbulent global situation. How important is an innovation programme in enabling the industrial ecosystem to take rapid steps towards more resilient and competitive manufacturing with net-zero greenhouse gas emissions?

The discussion is led by Sofia Wieselfors, Programme Director, Net Zero Industry.

content.title: Work must pay – including for the most vulnerable
content.description: People experiencing harmful substance use and homelessness have no incentive to start working when their wages are offset against income support. The Danish social exemption card model allows them to keep the money. Stockholm's governing politicians have recently relaxed the rules. Could this be a first step in Sweden?
content.extendedDescription:
Welcome to a panel discussion on an issue that should be highly relevant in the election campaign. Learn about the Danish exemption card, listen to those who have led the way in this direction in Sweden and, above all, hear experiences from people who have lived with homelessness and harmful substance use. Dom Fläckfria, a band formed by staff and residents at an emergency shelter, will play music on the theme, and Irina Bagley will sing.
The event is part of the Förnya det sociala reportaget project, funded by Allmänna arvsfonden.

content.title: Researcher mobility in focus – are we moving in the right direction?
content.description: How does mobility affect quality in higher education and research?
content.extendedDescription: Mobility among research and teaching staff is a prerequisite for quality in higher education and research. However, there is considerable variation across the higher education sector, for example in the proportion of internationally recruited researchers and teachers. Many internationally recruited researchers also leave Swedish higher education after a few years. Mobility between higher education and other sectors has a clear direction – the flow out of higher education is much greater than the flow in. UKÄ has published several reports on mobility and doctoral education that will form the basis of a short presentation and panel discussion. Welcome to UKÄ's seminar, where we highlight current higher education policy issues and discuss responsibilities and the way forward.

content.title: A race to the bottom or a national backbone? Municipalities' dilemma as AI data centres arrive
content.description: AI data centres are now being established in Sweden at record speed. Global hyperscale operators are looking for land and power, but the ability to set requirements for local benefits, waste heat and societal impacts is uneven. Meanwhile, competition between municipalities is driving a race to the bottom.
content.extendedDescription:
AI data centres are now being established in Sweden at record speed. Municipalities are on the front line as global hyperscale operators look for land and power – but their ability to set requirements for local benefits, waste heat and societal impacts is uneven. Meanwhile, competition between municipalities is driving a race to the bottom.
Decisions involving hundreds of megawatts risk being made faster than analysis, regulation and planning can keep up.
What do municipalities need from central government, grid owners and government agencies to avoid losing control of developments?

content.title: Stop wasting – make the most of what we already have
content.description: The construction and transport sectors currently account for around half of Sweden's climate emissions and consume significant financial and material resources.
content.extendedDescription:
The construction and transport sectors currently account for around half of Sweden's climate emissions and consume significant financial and material resources. But Sweden can become a world leader in resource-efficient development of the built environment with a low climate footprint if we move from resource-intensive new construction projects to circular business models that create value in what already exists. This requires us to stop measuring success solely in new construction or kilometres of newly laid asphalt, and instead focus on meeting needs and providing accessibility.

We highlight concrete examples of solutions and present work to transform Sweden's built environment sector. A warm welcome to the presentation and discussion!

content.title: Have we fished out our seas – and what is needed to reverse the trend?
content.description: Fish stocks in Skagerrak and Kattegatt have collapsed despite extensive regulation and good data availability. What does this development tell us about Sweden's fisheries management – and what political choices are needed to strengthen marine biodiversity and our future food supply?
content.extendedDescription: New research based on 75 years of fisheries data from Skagerrak and Kattegatt shows that commercial landings have fallen by more than 90 per cent since the mid-1900s. Species such as cod, herring and mackerel have declined sharply, and catches can now only be made of shellfish and certain flatfish. The seminar discusses how a lack of a holistic approach jeopardises our food supply and functioning ecosystems. What political decisions and measures are needed to reverse the trend for fish in Västerhavet?

In this session, decision-makers and representatives from the public and private sectors discuss challenges in building civil defence and how both sectors can jointly contribute to a more robust and effective total defence.

Discover insights from Bonava's new survey of what people actually prioritise in their homes – and how that knowledge is already being put into practice. Drawing on Sweden, the Baltic countries, Germany and Finland – new forms of housing, large-scale initiatives and smart, market-adapted solutions – we discuss how different models, collaborations and business arrangements contribute to feasibility, long-term thinking and benefits for local communities. We offer concrete European experiences and new perspectives on how innovation and collaboration can create stable, sought-after housing.

content.title: How much change can a municipality handle as development accelerates?
content.description: Swedish municipalities face major, rapid changes linked to industrial investments. These affect housing, skills provision, infrastructure and local attractiveness. content.extendedDescription:
But what happens when investments move faster than society can keep up? How do we build communities that endure – not just for new industrial establishments, but for the people who live there?

The seminar highlights different municipal and regional perspectives. It focuses not on individual establishments, but on the bigger question: how small communities build capacity, trust and confidence in the future when the pace of change is high and many interests must be accommodated at once.

content.title: Design, hospitality and a sense of home – staff housing in the green transition
content.description: Housing is a strategic key to the industrial transition in northern Sweden. How do we create accommodation that can be put in place quickly, lasts over time and supports everyday life far from home?
content.extendedDescription: As northern Sweden transitions to fossil-free industry, housing becomes a strategic issue. Using Aurora Village in Luleå as an example, we discuss how modular construction, permanent housing standards, social spaces, hospitality and community can create staff accommodation that works over time. At Aurora Village in Luleå, modular construction to permanent housing standards has put people at the centre. Through collaboration between the municipality, architects, operations and construction, and a focus on thoughtful design, social spaces, community building and shared activities, staff accommodation has been created that is more a home than a temporary solution.

content.title: The infinite building – how we can design for a sustainable future
content.description: In recent years, the construction sector has focused heavily on minimising the climate impact of materials incorporated into new buildings. But what happens during operation and at the end of a building's lifespan? Can we design buildings so that they can be adapted and taken apart?
content.extendedDescription: In this lecture, we explore how buildings can be designed to last longer and how we can take care of their constituent materials at the end of their lifespan. These two aspects could significantly reduce buildings' environmental impact and, with the right design, they could look like ordinary buildings. We draw on a number of architectural examples designed to last longer and to be dismantled and partly rebuilt in other forms. A new way of building can start now – who is coming along?

content.description: How is the transition of shipping and ferry services on Gotland progressing, and can collaboration between academia, society and industry drive development forward?
content.extendedDescription:
The first Gotland ferry prepared for hydrogen operation is now being built. A technical solution based on gas turbines creates a multi-fuel solution that lowers the barriers to switching to fossil-free fuels. The seminar presents the current status of construction and ongoing research at Uppsala universitet on hydrogen as a fuel for the Gotland ferry and other shipping.
A subsequent panel discussion explores the value of collaboration between academia, society and industry. What opportunities, challenges and difficulties does collaboration involve? How can we jointly drive development forward?

content.title: Assessing asylum claims based on sexual orientation, gender identity and gender expression
content.description: How are cases assessed in Sweden when people cite sexual orientation, gender identity and gender expression – LGBTQI – as grounds for asylum?
content.extendedDescription: Asylum grounds linked to sexual orientation, gender identity and gender expression form a distinct category in asylum assessment because they are based on internal processes rather than external events. Assessing these grounds involves evaluating not only the credibility of a person's actions, but also their sexual orientation and identity. Applicants may therefore experience the investigations as intrusive and traumatising. The event will discuss Delmi's latest policy brief, written by Thomas Wimark. The brief examines how the likelihood of being granted asylum varies between different grounds for asylum and which factors influence approval rates.

content.title: Water, sanitation and hygiene: the prerequisite for effective investments in climate and health
content.description: The global water crisis is deepening as climate change puts pressure on already weak water, sanitation and hygiene services. This leads to recurring crises and reduces the impact of investments in health and climate adaptation. Should Sweden give water, sanitation and hygiene a clear priority of their own?
content.extendedDescription:
Safe access to water, sanitation and hygiene is fundamental to functioning societies, and therefore also determines whether investments in areas such as climate adaptation, health and economic stability have an impact. When water services fail, risks turn into recurring crises with growing long-term costs; when they work, they strengthen public health and make other investments more effective.

content.title: How can properties become key players in our future energy system?
content.description: Properties could play a much greater role in the energy system. But what steps are needed to get there, what can we learn from current projects and innovations, and what benefits would success bring to society?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden's combined property stock holds enormous, largely untapped potential. Through local energy production, energy storage and energy sharing, properties can become a central resource in meeting today's and tomorrow's capacity challenges. There is also potential to increase society's resilience and preparedness – something more urgent today than ever.

In an engaging on-stage discussion, we explore important energy initiatives that could pave the way for closer integration between the property sector and the energy system in the future.

content.title: Sweden as an engine of innovation – who takes responsibility for the next leap?
content.description: How do we make the most of the favourable conditions for innovation and entrepreneurship that many believe exist in Sweden today? What can we solve at home, where is deeper cooperation within the EU needed – and what role can Sweden play in that development?
content.extendedDescription: Sweden is sometimes highlighted as one of Europe's, and the world's, most innovative countries. Yet business competitiveness faces challenges. Many companies struggle to find the right skills, particularly in tech and AI, and some choose to scale abroad. How do we persuade companies to stay and grow in Sweden? What needs to be done in regulation, capital markets, research, development and higher education to create better conditions for innovation and entrepreneurship? What can we solve at home, where is deeper cooperation within the EU needed – and what role can Sweden play in that development?
content.subject: Innovation

content.title: Why is Sweden choosing unemployment?
content.description: Political leaders have gradually abandoned the goal of full employment. Entirely unnecessarily. The truth is that we can eliminate involuntary unemployment – if we want to. But do politicians really want that?
content.extendedDescription:
Welcome to Almedalen's only real economics seminar!

Drawing on Jakob Segerlind's essay Unnecessary Unemployment, some of Sweden's sharpest minds discuss why Sweden has chosen high unemployment when the USA has repeatedly shown that it does not have to be this way. Instead, we are constrained by pessimistic, outdated calculations of so-called equilibrium unemployment. Unemployment has become a religion.

The focus needs to shift to what actually matters: macroeconomic policy.

Together with a spirited group, that is what we will do from the stage at Donners Eventhall. Come and hear about the policies and solutions that usually become Socialdemokraterna's five years later.
content.subject: Employment/labour market

content.title: From quarterly reports to a quarter-century – what will get more people dreaming big?
content.description: Most strategic business plans cover 3–5 years and often assume that the future is an extension of the present. But how are we affected by getting stuck in short-term thinking – and what happens if we dare to look towards the really big questions?
content.extendedDescription:
In an election year, reflecting on the future we want to create – for business, society and ourselves – is more important than ever. Everything we take for granted today began as someone's vision. What dreams and ideas could shape tomorrow's society?
In this session, you will meet visionaries sharing their thoughts on the future of business and society. What will their headlines say during Almedalsveckan 2040? And what will encourage more people to think big again?
Welcome to a discussion about long-term thinking, dreams and the courage to look beyond the next quarterly report.

content.title: When protection is not enough – for safety today and less exclusion tomorrow
content.description: How can we create long-term safety after a child has been protected? Stockholm will be the first in Sweden to implement an evidence-based treatment model for families where children have experienced violence or serious neglect.
content.extendedDescription:
How can we create long-term safety after a child has been protected? During the seminar, we discuss how coordinated, evidence-based interventions can increase children's safety, promote healing and create conditions for lasting change in families where violence and neglect have occurred.

Why is Stockholms stad the first municipality in Sweden to invest in MST-CAN? We explore how the model can help break destructive patterns, reduce the need for placements and create better long-term outcomes for children and families – while using society's resources more effectively.

content.title: How prepared are Nordic telecom networks for growing Russian hybrid threats?

And how should we plan ahead as rules, processes and municipal interpretations change?

During Almedalsveckan, we invite you to an open discussion about the future of construction and how the new rules could affect individuals, landowners, architects, municipalities and developers.

We believe more people need to come together to discuss how to create better conditions for small-scale, sustainable construction while safeguarding quality, architecture and long-term thinking.

Drop by, share perspectives and join us and others interested in construction, community development and architecture for a discussion.

content.title: The boundaries of community
content.description: Are Swedes nationalists? And what do Swedes consider important for being seen as part of the national community? A new study takes a closer look at this and its connections to different forms of trust, willingness to defend the country and party sympathies.
content.extendedDescription: The latest edition of Gemenskapsbarometern – a national survey with a local focus on 50 municipalities – asked respondents about their views of Sweden, Swedes, Swedish citizenship and what matters for being considered Swedish. The seminar presents how Swedish nationalism varies by geography and individual factors, and what national identity and community are primarily based on: ethnicity, culture or citizenship. We also discuss their significance for willingness to defend the country and different forms of trust, what distinguishes the parties' voters, and whether the national community has boundaries.
content.subject: Research
content.organizationType: Collaboration between different types of organisation

content.title: Access to healthcare – why are more resources not enough to shorten waiting lists?
content.description: Swedish healthcare receives more resources than before, yet access has not improved at the expected pace. Waiting lists for specialist care have grown, more people wait longer than the care guarantee allows, and many patients find it difficult to contact healthcare services.
content.extendedDescription: Kunskapsverket's report How Is Healthcare Doing?, for which Sirona supported the analysis, shows that the regions' healthcare costs per resident increased by 18 per cent between 2010 and 2022, while the number of healthcare contacts per resident rose by only 2 per cent. During the seminar, we discuss what is actually preventing better access: a lack of resources, governance, administration, skills provision or how healthcare capacity is used? The aim is to move beyond the question of ‘more money’ and discuss which changes can actually give patients faster, closer and more coordinated care.
content.subject: Regional issues

content.title: How to build a resilient heating system in an uncertain world
content.description: The climate transition, geopolitics and electrification are changing the energy system. How do we ensure a robust heat supply? What roles do district heating, heat pumps and new solutions play – and how should policy guide development?
content.extendedDescription:
The energy system faces major changes. Climate requirements, increased electrification and a more uncertain global situation place new demands on robustness and flexibility.

District heating, heat pumps and hybrid solutions have different strengths – but how do we optimise the whole system?

The seminar brings together participants from across the value chain to discuss the heating system of the future. How is energy security affected? How can flexibility contribute to stability? And what policy decisions are needed?

The focus is on a systems perspective, resilience and the interaction between technologies.
content.subject: Sustainability
content.accessibility: Hearing loop, wheelchair-accessible entrance and venue
speakerTitles: Team Manager and Head of District Heating
Head of Southern and Western Sweden

content.title: What is needed to strengthen Sweden's competitiveness in healthcare, research and innovation?
content.description: Swedish university healthcare is a world leader in many fields, but it needs to take the next step to strengthen Sweden in global competition in healthcare, research and innovation.
content.extendedDescription: A year ago, the Swedish University Hospital Alliance, SUHA, was formed to unite and strengthen Swedish university healthcare nationally and internationally. The alliance has prioritised six focus areas in which university hospitals drive development together. This year, hospital directors and representatives of the different workstreams come together on stage to discuss with Minister for Health Care Elisabeth Lann what Sweden needs to keep developing world-class healthcare, research and education – benefiting patients throughout the country.
content.subject: Health and social care
speakerTitles: Director of Health and Medical Care
Acting Director of Health and Medical Care
Director of Research, Development and Education

content.title: Hottest in Almedalen – high-temperature incineration of hazardous waste, an essential service
content.description: In an increasingly uncertain world, Europe and the Nordic region need greater self-reliance. Countries able to recycle, treat and reuse resources are less exposed to geopolitical risks and raw material shortages when supply chains are disrupted.
content.extendedDescription:
The Nordic region has the capacity to manage hazardous waste, safeguarding society's functioning, industry and the economy, and protecting our ecosystems. Other European countries also benefit from these operations, and the market for highly specialised environmental services is being harmonised. But some proposals threaten these activities. How important is a harmonised EU market for more complex environmental services? How can the Nordic region take a stronger position in Europe's circular economy? What are the biggest challenges ahead for the waste and environmental technology sector?

Tags: Self-sufficiency, sustainability, resilience, economy, circularity
content.subject: Sustainability

content.title: Swedish wool – the textile of the future
content.description: Swedish wool is a local, renewable, high-quality resource that can be used in everything from clothing and furniture to building materials and protective equipment. Despite its unique properties, much of the wool goes to waste because collecting, sorting and delivering it is currently expensive and cumbersome for sheep owners.
content.extendedDescription:
How can we build a profitable, traceable Swedish wool value chain that creates circular jobs, strengthens rural areas and reduces dependence on imports?

Arena Svensk Ull presents concrete policy and practical recommendations to strengthen the Swedish wool value chain, increase demand for sustainable and circular materials, and make Swedish wool a strategic resource for rural development, resilience and sustainable competitiveness. The discussion brings together participants from industry, politics, academia and business to show how Swedish wool can be part of future sustainable textiles and benefit society.
content.subject: Sustainability
content.organizationType: Collaboration between different types of organisation

content.title: How do the real economy, the green economy and the media war work?
content.description: Sweden's economy is praised in the USA and we top the EU's economic growth rankings, while the opposition argues that economic policy has failed. What is the actual state of Sweden's economy, and how does the new media landscape affect it?

We welcome you to our media stage.

content.title: The social contract in 2035: duties, digitalisation, preparedness and residents' influence
content.description: What trends are shaping the social contract of the future, and what does this mean for everyone who needs to develop legitimate and effective public services?
content.extendedDescription:
For the third time, Kairos Future is exploring Sweden's social contract. How do the country's residents view rights and duties, democracy, trust and cohesion? Particular attention is given to views on the digitalisation of welfare services, new preparedness efforts and residents' influence over all the rapid changes.

Trends and data from the study will be presented, of great interest to all organisations developing public services and therefore dependent on the premises of the social contract. As an audience member, you can also contribute your thoughts – the panel will reflect on them through Mentimeter.

Participating from Kairos Future are Cecilia Löfgreen, Director Public, and moderator Maarja Edman, alongside panellists.
content.subject: Democracy

content.title: PISA 2029 will measure AI literacy – are Swedish schools ready?
content.description: In three years, PISA will begin measuring young people's AI literacy. Meanwhile, the proposed new compulsory school curricula call for restrictive use of digital learning materials and tools. How do these fit together?
content.extendedDescription:
When PISA 2029 takes place, Swedish compulsory school pupils' AI literacy will be measured for the first time. This raises new questions about schools' mission: what knowledge and skills do pupils need to develop to be prepared for the future? And how does this fit with Swedish education policy emphasising restraint in the use of digital tools and learning materials?

This seminar brings together different professional perspectives to discuss what AI literacy means in practice. What consequences do today's choices have for pupils' learning? How are equity and future results affected?
What should school authorities, school leaders and teachers be doing now to prepare themselves and their pupils for PISA 2029?
content.subject: Education

content.title: How to stop labour-related crime in construction
content.description: The construction sector is central to Sweden's competitiveness and societal development. But today we see unscrupulous operators exploiting weaknesses in the system, circumventing regulations and creating unfair competition. This affects the whole built environment sector.
content.extendedDescription:
Labour-related crime and unscrupulous operators distort competition in construction and civil engineering, undermine conditions and put both quality and safety at risk. At the same time, historically large investments are underway in Sweden.
Welcome to a discussion about what is required of the built environment sector to stop labour-related crime: what effect do limits on subcontracting tiers actually have, what responsibility do politicians and government agencies bear, and how do we ensure that the right operators win – and that legitimate businesses are not driven out?
content.subject: Construction
content.organizationType: Collaboration between different types of organisation
speakerTitles: Member of the Committee on the Labour Market

content.title: Can chess break exclusion and strengthen reintegration?
content.description: How can chess contribute to better school results and stronger reintegration after crime? How can cognitive and social skills such as concentration, problem-solving and impulse control be developed through structured interventions, thereby promoting inclusion and social sustainability?
content.extendedDescription:
The seminar explores chess as an educational and social tool in schools and correctional services. It focuses on how the game can strengthen individuals' cognitive abilities, self-regulation and sense of responsibility, and help break destructive patterns of behaviour.

Drawing on examples and experience, we discuss how accessible interventions can create new opportunities for learning, inclusion and reintegration. Cooperation between schools, civil society and correctional services is also highlighted as a central factor in long-term impact.

The seminar is a moderated discussion with space for reflection and questions from participants. No preparation is required.
content.subject: Education

content.title: Electric cars as an energy resource – how do we make the most of new technology to strengthen the electricity system?
content.description: Five million little cash cows travelling the roads and easing the load on the grid whenever they stop. It sounds a little too good to be true, but electric cars could soon become both financial successes and electricity system heroes. How do we make it happen?
content.extendedDescription: The technology is called vehicle-to-x and is about maximising the use of electric car batteries. If we can connect the batteries to the grid, they provide both power and system benefits. This helps the electricity system while generating income for car owners and accelerating electrification – a win-win-win. In this seminar, we join the sector's leading experts to get to the bottom of how to accelerate the technology. What is needed to make both charging infrastructure and cars ready for a large-scale introduction of ‘V2X’? And how can individuals and companies benefit? What is the actual scale of the potential?
content.subject: Sustainability
content.accessibility: Wheelchair-accessible toilet, wheelchair-accessible entrance and venue
speakerTitles: Professor of Industrial Electrical Engineering and Automation
Head of the Resource-Efficient Society Department

content.title: How do the new deportation rules affect young people and those subjected to honour-related violence and oppression?
content.description: Today, young people who have lived in Sweden for a long time can be deported at the age of 21. Those who fail to find work paying at least SEK 33,390 a month are not allowed to stay either. What impact could these rules have on young people?
content.extendedDescription:
What impact could prison sentences have on girls around fourteen years old as they develop into independent individuals? Do such young girls who are also subjected to honour-related violence and oppression – which may itself be a factor in the offending – need to be treated in a particular way to support their self-esteem and independence?
What consequences could the new deportation rules have for young people who see no safety in their former home country? How can we take responsibility for ensuring they are not subjected to abuse or discrimination after deportation?
content.subject: Children/young people

content.title: Red flags at work – where are the boundaries?
content.description: Where is the line for what is acceptable at work when pay cannot be discussed, demands increase and criticism is seen as disloyalty? What behaviours build a sustainable working life – and which threaten security, rights and influence?
content.extendedDescription:
How should we think about situations where pay cannot be discussed? When the working environment is strained? Or when criticism is interpreted as disloyalty rather than engagement? What behaviours build a sustainable working life – and which should never be accepted?

Political youth organisations discuss power, responsibility and the conditions shaping the working life of the future. We start with concrete workplace situations and talk about what feels reasonable – and what does not. Through short exercises, the youth organisations use green and red flags to show where the boundaries lie.

Welcome to a discussion about fair conditions and workplace culture with those shaping the politics of the future.
content.subject: Employment/labour market

speakerTitles: Head of Press and Advocacy / moderator

content.title: How do we build the world's leading mining nation? The instructions and materials are ready – who dares assemble it?
content.description: Sweden needs metals and minerals for the transition, preparedness and growth. But investment is held back by lengthy permitting processes, uncertain energy access and conflicting land-use objectives. How do we create rules that combine competitiveness, sustainability and local support?
content.extendedDescription: Sweden has the bedrock, knowledge and conditions to build a strong mining nation. But assembling the whole also requires stable, long-term political rules. Today, investment is held back by lengthy and unpredictable permitting processes, uncertain energy access and political changes of direction on mining and land use. Meanwhile, the need for metals and minerals is increasing with electrification, new industry and a more uncertain world. How do we create the conditions to actually build the world's leading mining nation, rather than merely talk about it?
content.subject: Business

content.title: How do we strengthen efforts to improve public transport's passage through traffic?
content.description: Work to improve public transport's passage through traffic must be continuous; otherwise punctuality worsens, journey times increase and drivers' working conditions deteriorate. What are the success factors?
content.extendedDescription: In this seminar, Västtrafik shares experiences from its work in the Gothenburg area, where congestion, space and competition for street space place particular demands. We hear how it developed its traffic accessibility report, and how data, journey-time comparisons and spatial analyses are combined with a structured dialogue with Göteborgs Stad. The seminar focuses on the working approach: how issues of street space, public transport flow and opportunities for more sustainable travel have been prioritised, visualised and anchored with stakeholders. The seminar offers practical insights into building a long-term, constructive process for improving public transport flow. It concludes with a reflective panel discussion.
content.subject: Infrastructure/transport

content.title: Women's health in socioeconomically disadvantaged areas – a vital issue
content.description: Creating space for all girls and women to have their voices heard is a central democratic issue. We want to focus on the importance of amplifying the voices of girls and women in socioeconomically disadvantaged areas and raising issues that matter to them. Health is one such important issue.
content.extendedDescription: Women and girls in socioeconomically disadvantaged areas are often affected by unequal living conditions that can lead to poorer physical and mental health. Factors such as financial insecurity, limited access to healthcare and heavy everyday burdens increase the risk of deteriorating health, while opportunities to influence these conditions are often limited. What challenges do girls and women in disadvantaged areas face in achieving good health, and what can and must be done to address them?
content.subject: Gender equality
speakerTitles: Community Police Officer, Järva, and Board Member, Sveriges Kvinnoorganisationer

content.title: Sweden's economy – four years ahead
content.description: Sweden's economy is marked by uncertainty, with inflation, interest rates, growth and scope for reform shaped by global risks and geopolitical tensions. The coming years will be decisive. What is the outlook, and what choices and risks lie ahead for fiscal policy?
content.extendedDescription:
The macroeconomics seminar brings together leading political and financial decision-makers for an in-depth discussion of Sweden's economic development over the next four years. Starting from the current economic situation, it explores conditions for growth, investment and the need for reform amid continued global uncertainty.
The focus is on how international risks affect Sweden's economy, how fiscal policy can balance stability and room for action, and what structural reforms are needed to strengthen investment, competitiveness and long-term growth. A strategic discussion of the choices shaping Sweden's economy, now and over the next few years.
content.subject: Economy

content.title: Beyond the opinion polls – what determines voters' trust?
content.description: When trust in political parties is tested, understanding what drives voter support becomes central to the development of democracy and the direction of the election campaign.
content.extendedDescription: Opinion polls show voter support but rarely capture the underlying factors that shape citizens' trust. Ahead of the 2026 election, this raises questions about which attributes, leadership factors and views of society actually affect parties' legitimacy. The seminar presents a new survey of Swedish parties' reputations and analyses which dimensions most strongly influence voter support. Through current data and a subsequent discussion, it explores how political parties build or lose trust, how this affects the democratic process and which factors could matter most in the final stages of the election.

content.title: How do we develop the next generation of experts when AI takes over junior roles?
content.description: As AI automates tasks that have traditionally provided an entry point into working life, we risk breaking the natural chain of skills transfer. How do we meet future skills needs in the AI era?
content.extendedDescription: The discussion explores how AI and future skills provision are viewed from different perspectives, from the public sector to private business. The panel examines challenges unique to each sector as well as common ground. A central question is how we use and develop junior talent at a time when AI is rapidly changing tasks and entry-level roles. How do we build tomorrow's senior expertise if we do not also create room for juniors to grow today? And are there similar obstacles and opportunities across sectors despite their different missions?
content.subject: Digitalisation

speakerTitles: Director of Education and Labour Market Services

content.title: Popular education – why and for whom?
content.description: How should society respond to disinformation and widening knowledge gaps? The question concerns the role popular education should play in strengthening democracy and how public resources for lifelong learning should be allocated.
content.extendedDescription: Nine out of ten Swedes consider disinformation a threat to democracy. Just as many believe education can be part of the solution. This is shown by Knowledge in Decline?, a new report from Folkbildningsrådet and Folkuniversitetet based on data from SOM-institutet. Can popular education help us reach greater consensus and equip ourselves against disinformation? The discussion addresses the survey's findings: who should benefit from public resources for lifelong learning? Which groups should be prioritised in publicly funded education initiatives? Do disinformation and influence operations threaten our democracy?
content.subject: Culture
speakerTitles: Secretary-General, Folkuniversitetet, and Chair, Studieförbunden i samverkan

content.title: Together for a good life for everyone – focusing on residents' needs
content.description: How do we create a county where people want to live and stay, with equal opportunities for a good life? Residents' needs do not follow our organisational boundaries. We therefore need to meet people as one coherent system. What does it take to change and work from residents' perspectives?
content.extendedDescription:
In Jönköpings län, we are tackling this challenge together. Starting with the question ‘What is best for Esther?’, we are developing collaboration between the region, the county's 13 municipalities, Jönköping University, Länsstyrelsen and other stakeholders. Through initiatives such as the senior leadership programme, we are strengthening leadership that takes responsibility for the whole. Municipal dialogues and new ways of working provide insights that we put into practice while learning along the way.

Welcome to a discussion about how we can strengthen our ability to collaborate and develop as one system – and realise the ambition of supporting a good life for everyone.
content.subject: Regional issues
content.accessibility: Wheelchair-accessible entrance and venue
speakerTitles: Chair of the Regional Executive Board
Chair of the Municipal Executive Board

content.title: Multigenerational prevention – parenting support as a crime prevention measure
content.description: Children of parents involved in crime are at increased risk of becoming involved in crime themselves. For mothers facing multiple difficulties, a lack of trust in government agencies makes it harder to access support. How can relationship-based parenting support strengthen families and prevent vulnerability across generations?
content.extendedDescription:
Qrut meets mothers facing multiple difficulties: substance abuse, crime and exposure to violence, often combined with trauma, mental ill health and neurodevelopmental conditions. When trust in government agencies is absent, the path to support and change becomes long, sometimes almost non-existent.

We explore how civil society and government agencies can work together to make crime prevention interventions better targeted, more accessible and more lasting. Parenting support is not just care; it is also a crime prevention investment in the future. We share Qrut's unique working method and findings from current research on parenting support.
content.subject: Human rights
content.accessibility: The event is captioned

content.title: We can cure the incurable, so why aren't we?
content.description: Previously incurable diseases can now be cured by addressing their root causes with gene and cell therapies. But society needs to adapt healthcare, economics and policy to make these curative treatments available. What are we waiting for – and how do we ensure the treatments reach patients?
content.extendedDescription:
We are facing a medical breakthrough in which previously incurable diseases can now be cured by addressing their root causes with gene and cell therapies. The question is not whether the technology works, but how society should adapt healthcare, economics and policy to make these curative treatments available. What are we waiting for – and how do we ensure these opportunities benefit patients and society?

The event is part of Life Science-dagen, an initiative by the Medicon
Village research park.
content.subject: Research
speakerTitles: Professor of Developmental Biology and Director of LU ATMP Centrum
Moderator and Dean, Faculty of Medicine

content.title: Sustainable heart care in primary care
content.description: How can a national heart plan make a real difference to patients? Late detection, unequal follow-up and a lack of a holistic approach mean many people do not receive the right preventive care in time, especially when cardiovascular disease, COPD and kidney disease occur together.
content.extendedDescription: The seminar explores how prevention, early detection and a more coordinated approach in primary care can benefit patients and make healthcare more sustainable. The government has tasked Socialstyrelsen with developing a national heart plan to prevent and treat cardiovascular disease. The assignment covers everything from preventive measures that reduce the risk of disease to updated guidelines and greater patient involvement. We discuss the importance of secondary prevention and systematic risk assessments, as well as understanding patients with multiple chronic conditions and building sustainable primary care.
