content.title: Crime prevention – what actually works here and now?
content.description: Crime affects people's sense of safety, the business climate and local communities' development. Yet knowledge of which interventions actually prevent crime is fragmented. What works, and how should responsibility be shared between central government, municipalities, civil society and business?
content.extendedDescription:
Safety is fundamental to growth, investment and social cohesion. Repressive measures dominate debate during the election year, but recognition of the importance of crime prevention is also growing.

What does research say about effective interventions to solve problems here and now? What are municipalities' and police experiences? And what role can business play in strengthening local communities and reducing risks before crimes occur?

Länsförsäkringar operates locally throughout Sweden and sees how insecurity affects households and businesses. We bring together a range of societal actors for an evidence-based discussion of what actually works.
content.subject: Justice/crime
content.accessibility: Wheelchair-accessible entrance and venue
speakerTitles: Head of Operations, nattvandrare.nu, former Police Officer

content.title: Where do we find the capital for Europe's and Sweden's growing challenges?
content.description: Amid increasing geopolitical tensions, Europe faces significant challenges and investment needs, particularly in security and defence, energy supply, digitalisation, the climate transition and strategic autonomy.
content.extendedDescription: This will require enormous amounts of capital, including substantial private-sector funding. Although the EU has launched the Savings and Investments Union to strengthen Europe's capital markets and mobilise European savings, Europe will remain dependent on banks and other financial institutions for these capital needs for a long time. What are businesses' investment and financing needs today? How can we ensure banks can finance a larger share of the necessary investments? What role can pension capital play? What incentives and changes, for example to regulations, are needed to meet these investment needs?
content.subject: Economy
content.accessibility: Wheelchair-accessible entrance and venue

content.title: Government agencies' role in jobs and investment throughout the food chain
content.description: In practice, government agencies' inspections and decisions affect whether businesses dare to invest, develop and hire. When application of the rules feels unpredictable, small and medium-sized operators are particularly affected.
content.extendedDescription:
A panel discussion with business, government agency and political representatives.

How do agencies' working methods affect businesses' willingness to invest, grow and hire in practice?
We start from concrete examples from businesses across the food chain, from primary production to processing, using them as a starting point for a forward-looking discussion.

Participants:
Christina Nordin, Director-General, Livsmedelsverket
Magnus Oscarsson, Member of Parliament (KD), who led the inquiry into more equivalent and effective controls throughout the food chain
Business owners from dairy production and food processing

The discussion focuses on working methods, application and dialogue in practice, and what could make a difference to businesses' willingness to invest and develop.
content.subject: Business

content.title: 30 years of Facken inom industrin – how has it shaped wage formation?
content.description: Facken inom industrin has been a cornerstone of Swedish wage formation for 30 years. Joint negotiations by unions representing blue-collar workers, white-collar employees and university-educated professionals have shaped the model and Sweden's labour market. How important is this cooperation to future stability, competitiveness and real wages?
content.extendedDescription:
On 1 June 1996, the chairs of major industrial unions wrote an article in DN Debatt. This began a collaboration between blue-collar workers, white-collar employees and university-educated professionals that celebrates its 30th anniversary this year. We want to celebrate with coffee and cake!

The celebration begins with a short discussion with the chairs of the unions comprising Facken inom industrin:
- Peter Hellberg, Chair of Unionen
- Marie Nilsson, Chair of IF Metall
- Ulrika Lindstrand, Chair of Sveriges Ingenjörer
- Madelene Engman, Chair of GS-facket
- Nataša Stojković, Chair of Livsmedelsarbetareförbundet

A warm welcome!
content.subject: Employment/labour market

content.title: Young people want to work – but who gives them their first chance?
content.description: Increasing mandatory requirements in the labour market risk excluding more people than they include. Young people with criminal records face particular difficulty, often rejected before receiving a first chance. Meanwhile, solutions are sought to skills shortages and growing exclusion. Who will open the door?
content.extendedDescription: In this seminar on risk, responsibility and opportunities in today's labour market, we discuss barriers, missing support structures and how more young people can get a real chance to work and establish themselves. The discussion challenges current views of employability and highlights concrete ways to reduce exclusion and create a more inclusive labour market. What conditions do more employers need to hire young people with criminal records or other barriers, such as lacking an upper secondary qualification?

content.title: How can Swedish associations and businesses jointly improve public health in Sweden?
content.description: By combining the power of sport with business resources, we can improve public health and lower barriers to an active life. How can cross-country skiing encourage healthy habits, more movement and societal benefits?
content.extendedDescription:
With the national team bus at its centre, a health hub is created focusing on movement, inspiration and discussions about a healthier Sweden.

Visit our national team bus and we promise to inspire you and teach you everything you need to know about this fantastic sport, or even motivate you to take the next step in your development.
Discussions throughout the week cover public health, prevention and sport's role in society.
Morning training at 7:00 and afternoon training at 16:30 on Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday. Meet at the bus!
You can also test your capacity on a ski ergometer – challenge skiing legend Anders Södergren or compare your performance with active national cross-country team members.

Together, we make Almedalen healthier!

content.description: By combining the power of sport with business resources, we can improve public health and lower barriers to an active life. How can cross-country skiing encourage healthy habits, more movement and societal benefits?
content.extendedDescription:
With the national team bus at its centre, a health hub is created focusing on movement, inspiration and discussions about a healthier Sweden.

Visit our national team bus and we promise to inspire you and teach you everything you need to know about this fantastic sport, or even motivate you to take the next step in your development.

Morning training at 7:00 and afternoon training at 16:30 on Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday. Meet at the bus!
You can also test your capacity on a ski ergometer – challenge skiing legend Anders Södergren or compare your performance with active national cross-country team members.

content.title: How can the EU promote democratisation and human rights when autocratization is the trend?
content.description: As democracy erodes in the EU’s neighbourhood, the effects spill across borders. In Türkiye and Georgia, human rights defenders are pushed back, and elections lose credibility. What does this mean for the EU’s responsibility and ability to act?
content.extendedDescription:
Democracy is sliding backwards in several EU neighbouring countries, which is both a threat to the human rights of the citizens in these countries and creates security concerns for the EU. 
In both Turkiye and Georgia, the human rights situation has deteriorated rapidly in recent years: human rights defenders face considerable repression, and elections in both countries are losing credibility. 
In this session, Kajsa Ollongren, EU Special Representative for Human Rights, will discuss with two prominent human rights defenders from Turkiye and Georgia what the EU can do to promote democratisation when everything is moving in the other direction.
content.subject: EU
content.accessibility: Hearing loop, wheelchair-accessible toilet, wheelchair-accessible entrance and venue
speakerTitles: EU Special Representative for Human Rights

content.title: Communication choices in the final stretch – how do parties think when it matters most?
content.description: The election is approaching and parties will soon finalise plans for the crucial last weeks. How do they approach strategic communication choices? What determines decisions about announcements, resource allocation and voter groups?
content.extendedDescription:
The election is approaching and parties will soon finalise plans for the crucial last weeks. How do party leaders approach strategic communication choices? What determines decisions about announcements, resource allocation and voter groups?

New restrictions on political advertising on social media force parties to find new ways to reach people. Will door-knocking and physical presence in streets and squares increase, or are there new routes? How does AI change text production and audience analysis? And how are financial resources weighed when allocating budgets for the final stretch?

The seminar offers a unique look behind the scenes with those actually steering the campaigns.
content.subject: Communication/information
speakerTitles: Campaign Director and Deputy Party Secretary

content.title: When election promises must become action
content.description: Opinion polls come thick and fast in election years. Parties do what they can to influence public opinion. What do we know about election promises' influence on opinion and campaigns – do they matter? What will happen to promises made in the 2026 campaign? Can the fate of earlier promises tell us anything?
content.extendedDescription:
Politics has recently become both more engaging and more polarising. Seminar participants discuss how to turn visions into reality and exert influence in practice, and how political reforms should be designed and implemented to become reality.

How do politicians react to opinion polls? How do you develop proposals that align with public opinion or, ideally, influence it? Can proposals such as a cap on childcare fees win elections – what do an experienced domestic affairs reporter and a former state secretary say? How important are opinion polls to political craftsmanship, to ‘Politics for Real’?
content.subject: Other
content.organizationType: Collaboration between different types of organisation
content.accessibility: Hearing loop, wheelchair-accessible toilet, wheelchair-accessible entrance and venue
speakerTitles: PhD in Political Science and Head

content.title: A rich life – how on earth do you achieve it?
content.description: Amid higher living costs, economic uncertainty and increasing personal responsibility for pensions and financial security, many face the same question: how do you actually create a rich life? How do you build genuine financial stability?
content.extendedDescription: What does a rich life mean, and how on earth do you get there? How should we think about risk, security and the long term? How do we build financial confidence and spread practical insights into how everyday finances and long-term saving can enrich life in both money and opportunities? Together with people bringing different experiences of entrepreneurship, investment, careers and life choices, we hold a practical, down-to-earth discussion about personal finances. The focus is on what makes a difference in practice: getting started with saving and investing, building financial stability over time and making decisions that last through different life stages, even when circumstances change.
content.subject: Economy
content.accessibility: Hearing loop, wheelchair-accessible entrance and venue

content.title: How do we build stronger local communities rooted in living forests?
content.description: How do we build communities where forests, local processing, the economy and people strengthen each other within the same value chain?
content.extendedDescription:
Today's construction often involves standardised solutions, long material flows, intensive timber processing and weak links between raw material origins and finished buildings. Meanwhile, demands for climate benefits, biodiversity, traceability and local resilience are increasing. Supported by the practice-oriented research project Levande skog Levande samhälle, the Rotväven building has been developed as a concrete example of how buildings can be understood as part of a larger system.
We discuss how construction can become part of a coherent system in which forests, industry, local processing and design work together. The focus is on moving from individual projects to structural change.

A short introductory film about Rotväven is followed by a panel and discussion.
content.subject: Construction

content.title: As many as possible, for as long as possible – sport and the future
content.description: Sport and associations create community and health, but access is unequal. In disadvantaged areas, many young people lack money, facilities and functioning clubs, leading them to leave sport early. How do we open pathways for more people and achieve the goal: as many as possible, for as long as possible?
content.extendedDescription: Sport has a unique ability to create community, participation and hope for the future. How do finances, a lack of pitches and facilities, and pressure on associations affect children's and young people's opportunities to participate? How do we remove barriers, which solutions work in practice and how can they be scaled up? What does sport need to become a sustainable, inclusive place that children and young people can both join and stay in? The seminar highlights concrete examples and ways forward to make sport accessible to more people where needs are greatest, and its positive role in society.
content.subject: Children/young people
content.accessibility: Hearing loop, wheelchair-accessible entrance and venue

content.title: Can media and information literacy in schools strengthen democracy?
content.description: Participation in our societies and media and information literacy are intended to strengthen democracies and protect them from external threats. But how should this work in everyday school practice?
content.extendedDescription: Finland's 2045 vision for comprehensive school, developed by the government with an external delegation, states: ‘The global crisis of democracy and participation is a major educational challenge in Finnish society too. Trust in institutions has deteriorated in many countries, disinformation spreads rapidly and young people feel detached from societal influence and decision-making.’ As a remedy, Finnish policy documents for comprehensive and upper secondary schools propose media education. Corresponding Swedish documents call it media and information literacy. Both countries emphasise these skills as essential to participation in society.
content.subject: Democracy
content.organizationType: Collaboration between different types of organisation
content.accessibility: Wheelchair-accessible toilet
speakerTitles: Programme Manager, Higher Education and Research

content.title: Customer insights as a competitive advantage
content.description: How do companies use AI to turn customer insights into action that actually drives growth for Swedish businesses?
content.extendedDescription:
Organisations hold more customer data than ever, but does this automatically lead to better decisions? Despite extensive investments in customer experience, research shows that almost 80 per cent of organisations believe they meet customers' expectations, while only 20 per cent of customers agree. This Experience Gap offers the greatest opportunities for growth and competitive advantage.

How do you move from data to action? How can AI and modern analytical tools help organisations understand what customers actually need? During the seminar, we share concrete examples and methods for making customer insights a strategic asset, and examine how to break down organisational silos, make insights available to more people and ensure the customer's voice becomes a natural part of decision-making.

The seminar also takes place on 24/6 at 11.00.
content.subject: Digitalisation

content.title: From pilot project to new standard – how do we scale up circular construction?
content.description: Several construction projects now show that reuse and circular working methods can reduce construction's climate impact. Solutions exist, but how do we move from individual pioneering projects to construction in which circularity and resource efficiency are a natural part of everyday practice?
content.extendedDescription:
What roles do clients, contractors and policymakers play in expanding reuse, circular methods and resource-efficient solutions in construction? What requirements, incentives and forms of collaboration are needed? And what will ensure these solutions become a natural part of future construction rather than remaining isolated good examples?

Welcome to a discussion with representatives from politics, property and construction about translating experience from today's projects into widespread practice, and taking circular construction from pilot project to new standard.
content.subject: Climate/environment

content.title: Women's health: a crucial issue for Swedish growth
content.description: Mental ill health accounts for almost half of long-term sick leave and is increasing fastest among women. This should be seen as one of the Swedish labour market's greatest failures and a threat to both skills provision and growth. How do we create sustainable workplaces for women?
content.extendedDescription:
Women's mental health is developing in a worrying direction, with women reporting increased stress, pressure and ill health linked to work and living conditions. Meanwhile, the labour market is changing rapidly through digitalisation, AI development and new demands for flexibility and availability.

Drawing on the report How Are Things, Sweden 2026?, we discuss mental health, working environments and living conditions, particularly women's situation. The report's findings underpin a discussion about leadership, workplace flexibility, psychosocial working environments and how society can create better conditions for wellbeing and working capacity over time.
content.subject: Economy
content.accessibility: Hearing loop, wheelchair-accessible entrance and venue

content.title: The importance of the youth movement's voice and influence
content.description: There are few places created by young people for young people and their allies to meet and hang out! Beyond formal meetings, we want to create a networking space offering opportunities for young people to collaborate, meet new actors or simply have fun.
content.extendedDescription:
Join LSU's popular annual event: the youth movement networking gathering in Almedalen! Meet us and each other for open conversations, discussions and exchanges of experience about conditions for young people and the youth movement, the election and issues important to you.
Meet politicians, young people, non-profit organisations and others who want young people represented and heard in political debate. Catch up with old acquaintances, make new friends or simply relax at a gathering designed for you, whether you are young or not.
Welcome to Almedalen's place for and by young people. Spend Thursday evening hanging out and debriefing after a week in one of Swedish politics' most important meeting places.
content.subject: Children/young people

content.title: Renovating residential buildings with low environmental impact – practical examples from rental housing
content.description: Investment in renovation has been on a par with new construction in 2013–2026. Construction and property account for just over 20% of climate emissions. Renovation needs are substantial, and new EU requirements are being added.
content.extendedDescription:
How can renovation reduce environmental impact through reuse, resource-efficient material choices, energy efficiency and reduced construction needs? We discuss measures offering the greatest climate and environmental benefits from a lifecycle perspective, from materials and transport to energy use and waste.
The discussion also addresses how property owners can respond to new societal requirements and forthcoming EU energy efficiency requirements. Practical examples show how existing homes can become an important part of the climate and environmental transition.
Participants share examples from work in which solutions and materials are weighed against cost and feasibility, including fossil-free paints, kitchen solutions offering the industry's most extensive sustainability solution, and clay plaster on bathroom ceilings.
content.detail: Tent by the guest harbour near the Strandgatan — Kaserngatan junction
content.subject: Construction
content.accessibility: Wheelchair-accessible toilet, wheelchair-accessible entrance and venue

content.title: Sweden is transitioning – what would sustainability experts propose if they were in government?
content.description: Sweden has ambitious climate targets and wants to become one of the world's first fossil-free welfare nations. Proposals for the necessary measures are now being presented.
content.extendedDescription:
Ahead of the 2026 election, Aktuell Hållbarhet launches Solskensregeringen, tasked with identifying the measures Sweden needs for the transition. Seven ‘ministers’, all leading experts in their fields, present proposals for making Sweden more sustainable. Topics include green jobs that counter exclusion, tax shifts, cities and nature's role, infrastructure and energy sovereignty.
Markus Wråke – Minister for Energy
Stefan Krook – Minister for Finance
Evin Cetin – Minister for Social Sustainability
Nina Ekelund – Minister for Enterprise
Olga Kordas – Minister for Urban Development
Mattias Goldmann – Minister for Infrastructure and Mobility
Linda Burenius – Minister for Nature and the Environment
content.subject: Sustainability
content.accessibility: Wheelchair-accessible toilet, wheelchair-accessible entrance and venue
speakerTitles: Entrepreneur, Founder of God El among other ventures

content.title: Bingebydalen – one area, many voices, but who gets to shape tomorrow's society?
content.description: Can an area have strong engagement despite socioeconomic challenges? How do we create safety, strengthen residents' voices and give more people opportunities to influence societal development throughout life?
content.extendedDescription:
Bingebydalen – the people's alternative during Almedalsveckan
Welcome to Bingebydalen, a vibrant meeting place in the heart of Bingeby, where engagement flourishes despite socioeconomic challenges. During Almedalsveckan, we invite you to something quite different from political speeches and receptions: here it is about neighbourhoods, community and sustainability!

Music, refreshments and grilled sausages
During the day, we offer local music, home-baked refreshments and grilled sausages to everyone who drops by. It is free, accessible and open to all, regardless of background or finances.

Why Bingebydalen? We believe change starts small: in the neighbourhood, in conversations and in action. Bingebydalen is our way of showing that inclusion and sustainability are more than words.
content.subject: Democracy
content.accessibility: Wheelchair-accessible toilet, wheelchair-accessible entrance and venue

content.title: How to win tomorrow's energy customer
content.description: The energy market is changing rapidly while customer expectations rise. What happens when the energy sector stops complicating things and starts truly listening to customers? How can it become genuinely customer-centred and strengthen competitiveness?
content.extendedDescription:
Today, customers expect energy companies not only to supply electricity but also to help them understand and manage energy issues. Yet the industry remains stuck in a technology-led mindset that does not fully match customers' actual needs.

The seminar features two energy companies representing both transformation and innovation: international energy company E.ON, on a journey towards stronger customer focus, and new company Buddy Energy, which has built its offering around customer needs from the outset.

Together, we discuss what energy customers actually want, share insights from EY's industry survey and explore how energy companies can change to create customer value in an increasingly complex market.
content.subject: Energy

content.title: When business benefits meet global health – measurable value in partnerships
content.description: How is business value created in collaborations that also deliver real societal benefits? What makes partnerships with civil society strategic, measurable and long-term? How can clear reporting, practical cases and measurable results make partnerships concrete? How is Collective Impact achieved?
content.extendedDescription: The discussion highlights examples showing how investments in global health strengthen care pathways in emerging markets while opening new business opportunities. We discuss how organisations such as Operation Smile can offer companies new opportunities through Collective Impact strategies. We explore how companies such as Mölnlycke Health Care can collaborate with NGOs as part of their business strategy, for example by increasing Access to Care and reaching more people needing healthcare and good medical equipment. We also discuss funders' role: how can development aid and philanthropy play a strategic part in social transformation in collaboration with others?
content.subject: Health and social care

content.title: Only a fraction of children in families affected by addiction receive support – how can we do better?
content.description: 15 per cent of children in Sweden are negatively affected by a parent's excessive drinking. The consequences can be substantial both now and in adulthood. Yet only a fraction receive support. What do successful municipalities and others do?
content.extendedDescription:
Movendi has examined the support municipalities provide to children growing up in families affected by harmful substance use and addiction. The findings are presented in a report showing that support reaches only a fraction of vulnerable children. But action is possible. The report highlights examples of strengthening protective factors such as school, associations and safe adults to create a society where more children and young people enjoy safe, fulfilling childhoods.
Solutions often involve clear structures, a broad perspective, networks with associations and concrete interventions. Measures to learn from and be inspired by!

Welcome! Breakfast is served from 8.00.
content.subject: Children/young people
content.accessibility: Hearing loop, wheelchair-accessible toilet, wheelchair-accessible entrance and venue

content.title: Two universities and philanthropists collaborating on societal challenges
content.description: How can universities collaborate with each other and philanthropists to respond faster to societal challenges despite their long-term structures, strengthening their contribution to society?
content.extendedDescription: Universities have four tasks: research, teaching, innovation and service to society. When new challenges emerge, universities, built around long-term work, sometimes struggle to act quickly enough to offer the best possible support. Collaboration between universities can help by creating greater critical mass and a broader range of specialist knowledge and capabilities. If philanthropists can also be engaged, the potential contribution to society can be substantial. We discuss these issues and give two examples of Göteborgs universitet and Chalmers working with two philanthropists to address a health issue and an urgent educational initiative in refugee camps.
content.subject: Education
content.accessibility: Wheelchair-accessible entrance and venue

content.title: AI Governance for Sweden: How do we get the right results for business transformation and people?
content.description: As AI takes on a growing role in decisions that affect citizens' lives, good intentions aren't enough. This session explores what it actually takes to build trustworthy AI in the public sector — from governance and accountability to security and EU regulatory compliance.
content.extendedDescription: December 2027 is the deadline for the EU AI Act's key obligations. This will fundamentally transform how public authorities govern AI and establish standards that private sector organisations providing or deploying AI must comply with. This panel cuts through the complexity: what's actually coming? What must your organisation do now? How do you implement these changes in practice? We explore what governments worldwide are already debating and implementing, share international best practices, and look at real examples from countries around the world and from Sweden
content.subject: Digitalisation
content.accessibility: Hearing loop, wheelchair-accessible entrance and venue
speakerTitles: Vice President, Head of global government

content.title: When simplicity meets security – balancing business freedom and crime prevention
content.description: The balance between making entrepreneurship easy and combating financial crime.
content.extendedDescription:
Many politicians talk about making it easier to start and run businesses. But have we missed the point? Perhaps it is more about making life harder for criminals and more profitable for those following the rules. The seminar explores the balance between making entrepreneurship easy and combating financial crime.

What tensions arise when combining simplicity for entrepreneurs with protection against fraud and financial crime? Can digitalisation create systems that make doing the right thing natural and wrongdoing difficult, and how can we prevent complex legacy systems from being easy to manipulate?

How far can and should we go in pursuing criminals without stifling entrepreneurship? And how can smart digital solutions increase security while simplifying everyday life for business owners?
content.subject: Justice/crime

content.title: From obstacles to action – creating a more resource-efficient built environment
content.description: Sweden faces major investments in important built-environment projects. Meanwhile, construction faces a dual pressure: we must increase the pace while reducing climate impact.
content.extendedDescription:
To meet society's needs, the sector must use resources more intelligently. What needs doing is often clear, but our ability to use natural resources is frequently limited by regulation, conflicting objectives and unclear permitting processes. How can we accelerate the transition together?

By bringing together politics, business, government agencies and built-environment professionals, we aim to show how collaboration, simpler rules and more predictable permitting can unlock our shared ambitions. The seminar seeks constructive discussion of how to create better conditions for sustainable development, greater resilience and faster delivery of important projects.
content.subject: Construction

content.title: We know they are going to die – but do we act as though they are alive?
content.description: About priorities and decisions following an incurable diagnosis. How do care goals change depending on whether disease is curable? What do patients and loved ones need when it cannot be cured? How can a palliative approach provide security? What is dying like in a system built to cure?
content.extendedDescription:
Regardless of diagnosis, patients with terminal, incurable illness and their loved ones need access to a palliative approach and palliative care. Reviews have shown shortcomings in many regions and a need for improvements. The seminar brings together patients, relatives, politicians and experts to discuss care today and how it should develop.

Cancer, Alzheimer's, dementia, cognitive disorders, Lewy body disease, ALS, common diseases.

The event is a seminar structured as a discussion between panellists. Participants need no preparation.
content.subject: Health and social care
speakerTitles: Programme Director, Palliative Care and Eldercare

content.title: Increased production, high sustainability ambitions and tighter requirements – how can it work in practice?
content.description: Sweden needs to increase food production and meet sustainability targets while transparency and credibility requirements tighten. How can new requirements and expectations be managed to strengthen Swedish food production instead of increasing bureaucracy, costs and uncertainty?
content.extendedDescription: The seminar explores how to combine increased food production with high sustainability ambitions in practice. Starting from producers' realities and the food chain's shared responsibility, we seek a solutions-focused discussion about smarter use of certification, regulation and market requirements to simplify compliance, reduce administrative burdens and strengthen the competitiveness of Swedish food production. It focuses on the conditions, working methods and partnerships needed for regulations, market requirements and credible systems to strengthen both sustainability and competitiveness in practice.
content.subject: Food
content.organizationType: Collaboration between different types of organisation

content.title: From skills shortages to a flow of skills – learning centres as the key
content.description: Industry is held back by growing skills shortages while education fails to match needs. How do we secure skills provision? This is central to competitiveness and regional development but requires new collaboration models between education and working life.
content.extendedDescription:
What challenges and needs does Swedish industry face today?
To help address them, we are creating Industrins tekniska lärcentrum (ITLC) together with partners.

Industrial skills shortages are a growing societal challenge affecting growth, innovation and the green transition. Meanwhile, a gap remains between education and labour market needs.
The seminar explores how to strengthen practical knowledge, make industry more attractive through modern, representative environments and create more APL and LIA work-based learning placements. It focuses on solutions, barriers and new collaboration models for sustainable skills provision.
content.subject: Education
content.accessibility: Wheelchair-accessible entrance and venue

content.title: How do capital markets affect Sweden's municipalities and regions?
content.description: How should municipalities approach borrowing amid higher interest rates and greater local and geopolitical uncertainty, and should municipalities and regions allow more room for financial risks in their planning?
content.extendedDescription:
This seminar explores how global and Swedish capital markets work and their connection to municipal and regional finances amid geopolitical turbulence. How are Sweden's municipalities and regions affected by capital market fluctuations? What happens locally when interest rates and risk appetite change globally? How should municipalities approach borrowing amid higher interest rates and greater local and geopolitical uncertainty, and should they and regions allow more room for financial risks in planning? How do capital markets affect opportunities for major investments in infrastructure, climate and welfare?

Coffee and pastries are served before the seminar, between 15.10 and 15.40.
content.subject: Economy
content.accessibility: Wheelchair-accessible entrance and venue

content.title: Electricity's Gordian knot: can the state unlock offshore wind investment?
content.description: Offshore wind can be expanded at industrial scale to meet growing electricity demand driven by industrial transition and more AI centres. Yet a gap separates industry's electricity price expectations from the cost of investing in new generation. How do we untie this Gordian knot?
content.extendedDescription:
Low electricity prices are essential to Swedish industry's electrification and competitiveness. Yet all new generation comes at a price that cannot be compared with old, fully depreciated generating assets.

The discrepancy between expectations of future electricity prices and conditions for investors in new generation is a Gordian knot that must be untied to accelerate electrification. Perhaps Sweden needs an electrification leap in which new production enables electricity use to expand? What might that look like? What roles must market actors play, and where must policymakers intervene?
content.subject: Energy
content.accessibility: Wheelchair-accessible toilet, wheelchair-accessible entrance and venue

content.title: The future of district heating – which bioenergy should be used?
content.description: District heating is central to the energy system – but which bioenergy will be sufficient in future?
content.extendedDescription:
District heating plays an important role in Sweden's energy system and the transition towards a more robust, electrified society. It provides half of heating and a tenth of electricity generation. Meanwhile, the sector faces crucial questions about long-term competitiveness and access to sustainable bioenergy.
Demand for forest raw materials is growing from several directions, particularly forestry and chemicals industries, while new EU regulations and national interpretations affect which fuels are feasible and profitable. Energimyndigheten's scenarios also indicate changing conditions for both bioenergy and district heating's future role.
How do we secure a sustainable long-term bioenergy supply? What is the relationship between the energy sector and the forest industry?
content.subject: Energy

content.title: Tomorrow's critical infrastructure – digital preparedness for Sweden and Europe
content.description: Cloud services and AI now underpin the critical infrastructure on which civil defence relies. But who actually controls digital infrastructure, and what happens when geopolitical rules change?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden is currently heavily dependent on a few American cloud providers. This practical choice worked well for a long time but now poses real risks to national security, total defence and freedom of action. The question is no longer whether we need change, but what it should look like and how to achieve it.
The panel discusses concrete steps: how the public sector, defence sector and business can set smarter requirements, build a competitive European cloud sector and combine security with innovation. The goal is not isolation. It is an ecosystem where Europe sets the terms of its own digital future.
content.subject: Digitalisation
speakerTitles: Deputy CEO and Chief of Staff
State Secretary to Minister for Civil Defence Carl-Oskar Bohlin
Vice President, Head of Business Area Secure Business

content.title: What healthcare do we want – and how much can it cost?
content.description: What is healthcare's ultimate purpose: to prolong life, reduce suffering or support people through life's end? And what happens to our view of humanity when medical possibilities lack clear limits?
content.extendedDescription:
This discussion brings together physician and author Fanny Nilsson and Cecilia Strömberg Wallin, host of Filosofiska rummet on Sveriges radio. Drawing on ‘Go to A&E – How Much Healthcare Can We Afford?’, awarded Natur & Kultur's prize for a debate book, they examine healthcare's ethical foundations: responsibility, dignity, continuity and boundaries.

As more conditions can be treated through specialist care, but fewer people have coordinated, continuous contact with healthcare, fundamental questions come to the fore. And why have we not embraced the most cost-effective, secure and humane part of medical science, which delivers better health outcomes, longer lives and lower healthcare costs?
content.subject: Health and social care
content.accessibility: The event is captioned, Hearing loop, Wheelchair-accessible toilet, Wheelchair-accessible entrance and venue

content.title: Ask the Finance Minister: how can Sweden become the richest country in the EU?
content.description: Moderaterna's goal is for Sweden to have the EU's highest prosperity in 10 years. A family on ordinary wages should be able to buy a house in a safe area and enjoy a good life. This requires policies that grow the economy, enable more jobs and make effort pay. How do we get there?
content.extendedDescription:
Welcome to an entirely new kind of economics seminar. Instead of academic discussions, the Finance Minister invites you to an open questioning session where you can ask anything about economic policy's direction. How will growth and employment increase? Is the work-first approach really necessary? Is it time to shorten working hours? Should Sweden borrow more or less? What trade-offs underpin economic policy this parliamentary term, and what is on the to-do list for the next ten years?

The Finance Minister is joined by three experts with very different political starting points and perspectives. Come ready with questions and expect lively, fast-paced debate.
content.subject: Other
content.accessibility: Wheelchair-accessible entrance and venue

content.title: Europe's most interesting combination – renewable energy, rapid establishment and a strategic position
content.description: The green transition and a new security situation are redrawing Sweden's growth map. With renewable energy, strong basic industries and new business opportunities linked to defence and preparedness, the region's role in tomorrow's economy is growing.
content.extendedDescription:
Session 1 – Strategic position: the hub of northern Europe
Proximity to raw materials and markets. Infrastructure as the backbone. The strategic role in a new geopolitical landscape.

Session 2 – Energy: the foundation of everything
Fossil-free, competitively priced energy is crucial to business location decisions. How do we ensure energy is not just produced but used where it creates the most value?

Session 3 – Rapid establishment: lead time as currency
In today's investment climate, time is often as important as capital. How do we create faster processes, better coordination and a shorter path from decision to reality?
content.subject: Business
speakerTitles: Chair of the Regional Development Committee

content.title: From vacancy to value – can Sweden lead Europe's property transition?
content.description: AI, EU directives and urban transformation are changing construction and property. How can Sweden attract investment, create appealing cities and become a model for Europe's future?
content.extendedDescription:
Four panels. Four motions. An audience that votes.
During the morning, PropTech Sweden brings together politicians, property owners, tech companies, investors and built-environment professionals in a new debate format where the audience not only listens but takes a position.

We discuss how AI, EU directives and urban transformation affect construction and property, and whether Sweden can become a leading model for Europe's biggest transition.

Themes running through the discussions:
The EU sets the rules – Sweden attracts the investment.
Sweden as a model for the future.
Urban infrastructure as democracy's everyday setting.
The property owner – problem or solution?

Come with an opinion. Leave with a new one.
content.subject: Construction
content.accessibility: Wheelchair-accessible entrance and venue
speakerTitles: Entrepreneur and former Minister for Energy and Digitalisation

content.title: Geopolitics in your electricity bill
content.description: Geopolitics increasingly appears in electricity bills. What happens when oil and gas markets are shaken, and how should customers and businesses in Sweden respond? What is the global situation and the extent of fossil dependence, and how do we act amid rapid change?
content.extendedDescription:
We live in a time when global conditions change rapidly, sometimes so quickly that analyses need date stamps. Energy markets respond immediately to geopolitical turmoil, and even in Sweden, with relatively low fossil dependence, households and businesses clearly feel the fluctuations.
How should we understand and respond to this? What does it mean when fossil resources increasingly become geopolitical tools in war, peace and the times in between?

We bring together perspectives from consumers, research and the energy sector. We discuss the latest geopolitical and energy market developments, Swedish electricity customers' experiences, and the role energy companies can and should play in providing security and guidance in an increasingly complex world.
content.subject: Energy
content.organizationType: Collaboration between different types of organisation
content.accessibility: Wheelchair-accessible toilet, wheelchair-accessible entrance and venue
speakerTitles: Head of Security and Defence Policy

content.title: How can we protect essential services together?
content.description: How do we protect critical infrastructure in an increasingly complex, interconnected society? Examples from Stockholm and Malmö's ports show the importance of responsibility, priorities and collaboration between municipal, regional and national levels in strengthening Sweden's civil defence.
content.extendedDescription: How do we protect critical infrastructure as essential societal functions become increasingly interconnected and interdependent? As operations, ownership and responsibility are divided between municipalities, companies and private actors, complexity and vulnerability increase. The seminar discusses how different levels of society can work together to strengthen protection of strategically important geographical areas and infrastructure. Examples from Stockholm and Malmö's ports raise questions about priorities, the division of responsibilities and how Sweden can develop more robust civil defence amid growing security challenges.
content.subject: Security/defence
speakerTitles: Former Director of Sustainability and Safety

content.title: Climate policy in the EU and Sweden – between ambition and setbacks
content.description: The EU has strengthened climate policy, but calls for lower ambitions are growing. Meanwhile, emissions are rising in several member states, including Sweden. Amid tensions between higher ambitions and setbacks, and between EU and national policy, how can science-based policy packages meet the challenge?
content.extendedDescription:
The EU has substantially strengthened climate policy through the Green Deal and new legislation, but several member states are moving in the opposite direction. Calls to lower ambitions are growing while emissions increase, including in Sweden. This jeopardises climate targets and creates tensions between EU and national policy.
The seminar examines how to understand and manage climate policy tensions through science-based measures. The programme also includes an overview of EU climate policy and discussion of Sweden's challenges in meeting EU targets after the 2026 election.

The seminar is part of Uppsala universitet's climate days.
content.subject: Climate/environment

content.title: How does the changed security situation affect Sweden's property market?
content.description: Which municipalities perform best in property? How do submarkets and property actors fare in the changed security and preparedness situation? What challenges and opportunities do they face?
content.extendedDescription: A presentation of analyses and insights from this year's report Svensk Fastighetsmarknad 2026. Svefa's courtyard, Fastighetshubben, at Adelsgatan 25 is the meeting place in Almedalen where public and private sectors can meet, exchange experiences and discuss property-related issues focusing on urban development, the built environment and sustainable society. On stage, we organise seminars, panel debates and networking receptions focusing on strategic urban development, the property market and sustainability. Meet property specialists from every part of the sector. Find the full Almedalen programme at www.svefa.se
content.subject: Economy
content.accessibility: Wheelchair-accessible entrance and venue
speakerTitles: Head of Valuation and Analysis Business Area
Head of Transaction Advisory Business Area

content.title: What role does the financial sector play in future sustainability issues?
content.description: What role should banks, pension providers and insurers actually play in societal development, and which issues will shape the sustainability agenda ahead?
content.extendedDescription: Länsförsäkringar invites you to Almedalen's major sustainability round with Sweden's leading financial-sector sustainability executives. Geopolitical turmoil, AI as both enabler and threat, rising greenhouse gas emissions, growing climate adaptation needs, biodiversity loss, total defence development and the EU's Omnibus package simplifying sustainability rules shape the world around us. How do these affect financial actors' sustainability work? What issues are crucial to long-term business and societal benefits but may not even feature on management's agenda today? For 45 minutes, we discuss risks, opportunities and how finance can support positive development and future-proof society. Welcome to a duel featuring some of the country's most influential sustainability leaders.
content.subject: Sustainability
content.accessibility: Wheelchair-accessible entrance and venue
speakerTitles: General Counsel and Head of Sustainability

content.title: The current situation – the world right now
content.description: Amid a barrage of headlines about the economy, health, climate and growing conflicts, we try to understand our times. Behind major challenges there are also advances, innovations and positive trends. What might they tell us about the direction of the future?
content.extendedDescription:
A programme of short segments featuring different experts, moderated by Karl Rydå, Political Editor-in-Chief of Upsala Nya Tidning. The aim is to provide perspective, build understanding, contribute to more nuanced discussion of issues shaping our times and inspire hope for the future.

Anders Hagfeldt – Vice-Chancellor, Uppsala universitet
Kristoffer Schjött- Quist – Entrepreneur and Speaker
Lina Emilsson – Senior Lecturer in Game Design, Uppsala universitet
Henrik Wiman – Psychologist, Author and Speaker, Wiman Psykologi
Sara Jansson – CEO, Prohelia Företagshälsa
Magnus Öberg – Senior Lecturer in Peace and Conflict Research, Uppsala universitet
Elin Bjarnegård – Professor of Political Science, Uppsala universitet

The session is divided into three blocks with breaks between them.
content.subject: Democracy

content.title: Why are we vulnerable to information influence?
content.description: A changing information landscape, technological development and our cognition interact, making it difficult to resist information influence. When foreign threat actors exploit these vulnerabilities, they can harm society.
content.extendedDescription: Our media landscape is increasingly made up of images. Visual disinformation appears in our feeds, and generative AI and new technology make it easy to tailor disinformation to different audiences, while our brains cannot always distinguish truth from falsehood. Here you gain insight into the reports Visual Literacy and Preparedness (2026) and The Janus Face (2025), which describe vulnerabilities and ways to reduce them. The seminar includes a presentation and a panel discussion. There will also be opportunities to ask participants further questions afterwards.
content.subject: Democracy

speakerTitles: Professor of Art at Umeå konsthögskola, Umeå universitet, former Vice-Chancellor of Konstfack, Board Member

content.title: Sweden spends hundreds of billions on healthcare, but almost nothing on keeping people healthy
content.description: Can private healthcare providers ensure Sweden shifts to preventive care and becomes a world leader in longevity?
content.extendedDescription:
We spend almost SEK 700 billion annually on healthcare in Sweden, yet we are not becoming healthier. The Swedish system is built to treat disease rather than prevent it. Meanwhile, we know that up to 80 per cent of the healthcare burden comes from lifestyle diseases: conditions we can substantially influence ourselves.
The average Swede spends the last ten years of life in impaired health. Reducing that period offers major societal gains.
With the report ‘From Medical Care to Health Care – How Longevity Strengthens Public Health and the Economy’, we propose shifting from ‘How do we treat disease?’ to ‘How do we keep people healthy for as long as possible?’.
content.detail: Folkhälsodalen, S:t Hans and S:t Per church ruins
content.subject: Health and social care
content.accessibility: Wheelchair-accessible toilet, wheelchair-accessible entrance and venue
speakerTitles: Chair of the Primary Care Committee's Public Health and Dental Care Subcommittee
Physician and Host of Hälsa för ohälsosamma

content.title: Periods: no more taboos
content.description: It is time to talk more about periods. As long as menstruation remains taboo, it affects everything from girls' self-image to how decisions are made and resources allocated in society.
content.extendedDescription:
WaterAid and Lindex are hosting a menstrual health networking event to challenge stigma and highlight why knowledge is key to change.

Silence and stigma affect girls' self-esteem, education and opportunities to participate fully in society. How do we break taboos and make menstruation a natural part of conversations about gender equality, health and development?

During the evening, we share stories and examples of change when more people dare to take the issue seriously. What happens when knowledge spreads in schools, workplaces and politics? How can more people help break taboos?

Meet others who want change, have a drink and continue the conversation in Restaurang Vår Fru's beautiful courtyard in central Visby. It is an excellent opportunity to meet across sectors and put menstruation on the agenda. Clara Klingenström also joins the event to provide music.
content.subject: Gender equality

content.title: Rail's role in jobs, climate and preparedness
content.description: A functioning, modern railway is crucial to Sweden's competitiveness. Investment in Swedish rail can create tens of thousands of jobs, reduce emissions and strengthen preparedness. How do we move from today's small, short-term solutions to the major investments that are needed?
content.extendedDescription:
Unionen wants substantial long-term investments that improve accessibility for both people and freight and build on rail's historically important role in Swedish welfare. Today's investments create tomorrow's jobs and a more competitive Sweden.

The discussion focuses on national priorities needed for more and better jobs, greater transport capacity and a safe, secure labour market.

Welcome to an open, solutions-focused panel discussion about a future-proof railway policy and the investments needed today, tomorrow and beyond.
content.subject: Infrastructure/transport

content.title: Not for young people – with young people
content.description: How do we create settings where young people feel their voices truly matter? What makes them want to participate, stay and engage over the long term?
content.extendedDescription:
Many young people today are expected to contribute, engage and take responsibility, while their perspectives do not always carry equal weight where decisions are made. This creates a gap between responsibility and influence.

There is also uncertainty about how to engage with young people. Communication sometimes becomes stiff and overly formal, and sometimes so simplified it almost feels like a children's party. When are you actually ‘adult’ enough to be taken seriously?

Why do some environments make young people want to stay, contribute and engage long-term while others drive them away?

Drawing on experiences from basketball, civil society and young leadership, we hold an open discussion with young people from Youth Lab about participation, trust, responsibility and why some settings make young people feel their voices really matter.
content.subject: Democracy

content.title: How do we stop losing top international academic talent and start using it?
content.description: Sweden is good at attracting international students and researchers, but less good at retaining them. Swedish higher education institutions welcome around 35–40,000 international talents annually, yet relatively few establish themselves in the Swedish labour market.
content.extendedDescription:
New statistics from SCB show that just under 6 in 10 doctoral graduates remain 3 years after graduation. The corresponding figure for two-year master's graduates is 36%, and for one-year master's graduates just 19 per cent. Meanwhile, Swedish employers are calling out for skills. How can this happen, and what can we do about it?

How can this happen, and what can we do about it?
This panel brings together four perspectives that rarely share a room: international academic talent, higher education institutions, the public sector and business.

Together, we go straight to the core questions:
• Where do barriers arise?
• Who bears responsibility?
• What can change here and now?
content.subject: Employment/labour market
speakerTitles: Dean, Faculty of Science, Technology and Media
Chief Alliance and Innovation Officer/Deputy CEO

content.title: Who gets to speak to those in power?
content.description: WHO wants to limit contact between politicians and companies in the alcohol and food sectors, as has already happened with tobacco. Does this protect decision-making from undue influence, or risk excluding large parts of business from the democratic process?
content.extendedDescription:
EU decision-makers risk making poorer decisions if contact with companies and other affected stakeholders is further restricted. That is the conclusion of EPHI's report Who Gets to Speak to Brussels? The report examines how World Health Organization recommendations affect contacts between EU institutions and actors in the tobacco, food and alcohol sectors. The guidelines aim to protect politics from undue influence, but the practical result is that decision-makers miss important knowledge and experience from the operations affected by regulation.

The discussion is moderated by EPHI CEO Marie Söderqvist together with public commentator Henrik Jönsson.
content.subject: EU

content.title: Sweden is AI-ready – but is it AI-mature?
content.description: AI is changing how companies compete, grow and create value. But the technology determines not just which companies win, but which countries do. How can Sweden strengthen its position in the global AI economy? What must both policymakers and business do to succeed?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden produces world-class AI unicorns and is climbing global rankings. But competitiveness in the AI era means more than billions for the next startup. What matters is what happens across the wider economy: in industry, the public sector and behind the scenes. How do Swedish companies turn AI innovation into real business benefits? What systemic changes are needed for technology to lift all of Sweden, not just Silicon Stockholm? What do Swedish companies need to compete globally? How can government and business jointly create the right conditions?
A discussion bringing together leading voices from politics, business and technology to explore how Sweden can strengthen its position.
content.subject: Business
content.organizationType: Collaboration between different types of organisation

content.title: How to build public-service buildings for greater wellbeing and a smaller climate footprint
content.description:
LSS supported housing provides important public services where vulnerable people spend much time indoors. A healthy indoor climate is crucial to health and quality of life.
It is time to shift from the lowest construction cost to the best performance for wellbeing and low climate impact.
content.extendedDescription:
The seminar shows how public-service buildings such as LSS supported housing can be built for better health and more sustainable investment. Examples from current projects illustrate how material choices and building systems can create more stable indoor climates while reducing both risks and construction's climate impact.
Air quality, temperature, acoustics and humidity affect wellbeing, sleep and concentration. For people with special needs, these factors can matter even more.
The home is also a workplace for staff and a meeting place for relatives. Yet the focus often remains on the lowest construction cost rather than the best indoor environment or meeting climate targets.

content.title: Can Sweden become a voice for peace again?
content.description: Sweden once called itself a nation of peace; now we choose weapons over dialogue. When peace becomes a memory and obedience replaces courage, we lose our soul. Should we build security with cannons or with conscience and diplomacy?
content.extendedDescription:
Amid conflict and geopolitical rivalry, we discuss how diplomacy and international cooperation can contribute to a more peaceful world. In Palmedalen, we explore Sweden's contribution to peace in an increasingly polarised world. We examine geopolitical tensions, the erosion of neutrality and diplomacy's role to develop concrete proposals in Olof Palme's spirit of solidarity.

A podcast conversation on these issues will be recorded on site during this time. It examines Sweden's role in a changing world and different perspectives on how best to create security: through defence capabilities, diplomacy, international cooperation or a combination. The podcast offers space to reflect on peace, security and the choices shaping tomorrow's society.
content.subject: Security/defence

content.title: What will Sweden's future electricity system look like – and how do we get there?
content.description: The electricity system faces major changes, with development partly characterised by uncertainties and conflicting objectives. This requires clear priorities and shared responsibility.
content.extendedDescription:
The seminar explores how planning can progress effectively, who has a role and what conditions enable success.

Questions:
• How can we balance electricity generation and demand in the short and long term?
• Which decisions and investments should be prioritised today to avoid future capacity shortages?
• How can responsibility and collaboration between electricity system actors be strengthened to create a more efficient whole?
• How do spatial planning, environmental considerations and local decisions affect electricity system development?
• What roles should national, regional and local actors play in expanding a robust, sustainable electricity system?
content.subject: Energy

content.title: The Baltic Sea in a new security situation – local infrastructure, national interest
content.description: Transport flows in the Baltic Sea region are central to trade and international connections. As demands for capacity and robustness increase, functioning ports and roads become more important. How can local infrastructure contribute to Sweden's resilience and a more robust transport system?
content.extendedDescription: The changed security situation in the Baltic Sea region has exposed the vulnerability of transport flows and critical infrastructure. Shipping is central to trade, supply preparedness and Sweden's international connections, but also depends on functioning ports, roads and land-based energy systems. What role does local and regional infrastructure play in Sweden's overall resilience? How can long-term, coordinated decisions strengthen transport system robustness in a new security environment?
content.subject: Infrastructure/transport

Head of Communications and Public Affairs
Member of Parliament and Centerpartiet's Parliamentary Group Leader

content.title: Our digital infrastructure – the foundation of modern total defence
content.description: Building Swedish and European digital infrastructure is an investment in total defence that also brings major competitive advantages. In a deteriorating security situation, controlling your own digital infrastructure is not optional; it is fundamental.
content.extendedDescription: In an increasingly difficult and uncertain security situation, controlling your own digital infrastructure is essential to independence and security. Europe and Sweden depend heavily on global actors, creating risks to security, total defence and self-determination. But sovereign digital infrastructure is more than a defence project. It is an innovation journey that gives the region geopolitical independence and greater competitiveness. The discussion highlights the development needed across the public sector, innovation system and business to jointly create conditions for Swedish and European digital infrastructure.
content.detail: Main hall, entrance from Korsgatan opposite Villa Gutebagge
content.subject: Security/defence
speakerTitles: Political Adviser to the Minister for Civil Defence

content.title: What is happening to Sweden's startup and innovation policy?
content.description: There is broad political agreement that innovation matters – but what does that mean in practice? What do parties promise on Vinnova, innovation vouchers, employee stock options and startup visas?
content.extendedDescription:
Innovation is among the most important drivers of Swedish prosperity and job creation, yet innovation policy risks being sidelined during the election campaign.

Sweden's innovation ecosystem is strong, but conditions are deteriorating. International competition for talent and capital is intensifying. Regulatory complexity and tax conditions make starting and scaling companies harder, and national co-financing to secure EU funding is not fully used.

Ahead of the 2026 election, SISP asked all parliamentary parties the same seven questions. Results in Innovationsvalbarometern 2026 reveal clear differences and gaps deserving debate.
The event is a roundtable with eight participants; audience members are welcome to follow the discussion.
content.subject: Innovation
