content.title: Municipalities' biggest challenges ahead of the 2026 election
content.description: Municipalities face pressure from demographics, efficiency demands, digitalisation and preparedness responsibilities. Meanwhile, welfare services must work for everyone despite staffing problems, whistleblowing and unscrupulous providers, and democracy must be protected despite threats and hatred.
content.extendedDescription:
Demographic changes, strained budgets and growing demands on welfare services create new conflicts over responsibility, resources and governance. Explore two examples many municipalities face today.
* When threats enter everyday democracy – a discussion with Erik Pelling (S):
Car fires, death threats and protected personal data. When politicians and public officials are threatened over decisions made in society's service, their roles and circumstances change, as do those of citizens.
* Time for a sewage revolt? Investments the municipality has yet to see materialise – a discussion with Niklas Gunnar:
Swedish municipalities face historically large investments in water and wastewater infrastructure. What needs to be done, and who should pay?

content.title: Organised crime in Swedish sport
content.description: What do we know about organised crime's impact on Swedish sport, and what capacity exists to detect, prevent and address it? What can be done to reverse the trend, and what role do sport, the police and others have in this work?
content.extendedDescription: A new report produced by Stiftelsen Tryggare Sverige on behalf of Riksidrottsförbundet shows that organised crime in Swedish sport is widespread and affects both elite and grassroots clubs, large and small. This particularly concerns criminal infiltration and, to some extent, the recruitment of children and young people into criminal gangs. Nor are the problems confined to football or disadvantaged areas, as public debate can easily suggest. What do we know about organised crime's impact on Swedish sport, and what capacity exists to detect, prevent and address it? What can be done to reverse the trend, and what role do sport, the police and others have in this work?
content.subject: Justice/crime
content.accessibility: Wheelchair-accessible toilet, wheelchair-accessible entrance and venue

content.title: Bioenergy's election – what does the future hold for Sweden's largest energy source?
content.description: Bioenergy accounts for 37 per cent of Sweden's energy use. Most comes from forestry and forest industry residues. However, bioenergy is governed by strict EU and national rules. What do our politicians think? And how are companies affected?
content.extendedDescription:
How can we increase bioenergy's benefits for the climate, security of supply and competitiveness? This is one of the questions we put to our panel of politicians and bioenergy company representatives.

Svebio presents its election manifesto with key issues for bioenergy's future. Politicians and companies will comment on and discuss it.

What does the future hold for Sweden's largest energy source? Can we increase our energy self-sufficiency? Where do conflicts arise? Can policy instruments and taxes become more stable over the long term?

These are questions addressed – is this bioenergy's election?

The seminar has received Kraftkvinnorna's “Gender-balanced seminar” label and has been assessed as gender-balanced in its participant composition.
content.subject: Energy
speakerTitles: Head of the Resource-Efficient Society Department
Member of Parliament and Group Leader

content.title: How can different societal stakeholders work together on voluntary return migration?
content.description: Returning to your country of origin when you hold a Swedish residence permit is a major decision for many people, and a fundamental right. Support is available for those who want it, but getting there requires knowledge, trust and collaboration.
content.extendedDescription:
Migrationsverket and the national coordinator for voluntary return migration invite you to a discussion on how different stakeholders – authorities, municipalities and civil society – can work together to create the right conditions for individuals to make well-informed decisions. The seminar concludes with a question-and-answer session until 16.30.

Some time has passed since efforts intensified. What have we learned? What do the statistics show about the return migration grant increased on 1 January, and how do applicants experience the process? Meet the national coordinator for voluntary return migration and representatives of municipalities and voluntary organisations as they share their perspectives on return migration and the way forward.
content.subject: Democracy
speakerTitles: National Coordinator for Voluntary Return Migration

content.title: AI without a data strategy delivers neither welfare nor democracy
content.description: Sweden's welfare needs are growing faster than its resources, and AI is often presented as the answer. Yet many AI investments fail to deliver benefits to society. The question is what is needed and how decisions can be scrutinised when AI is used in the public sector.
content.extendedDescription:
AI initiatives that deliver value rarely do so because of the technology alone. It is about information management: how knowledge is structured, who manages it and how data quality work is actually carried out.

It is also a question of democracy. When AI makes or supports public-sector decisions, transparency depends on whether the underlying information is managed and traceable.
The seminar presents practical experiences from several years of AI assignments in the public sector, including at Adda, DIGG, Socialstyrelsen, EKN and Linköpings kommun.

We show where the common barriers lie and what is needed to overcome them: information management, ingestion, business rules, context and organisational ownership.

The event is a 40-minute seminar with an introductory presentation followed by questions.
content.subject: Digitalisation

content.title: Does Sweden have racist laws?
content.description: In recent years, Sweden has introduced a series of new laws, reforms and political proposals on migration and integration. On the surface, they may appear neutral and equal for everyone – but are they really?
content.extendedDescription:
We believe the new rules have particularly significant consequences for people of non-European backgrounds and raise questions about fairness, equal treatment and human rights. Sweden has long been seen as a frontrunner in tolerance and the equal worth of all people. At the same time, political developments have moved towards the EU's minimum standards in migration policy.

What does this mean for those affected? How are young people of non-European backgrounds affected in their daily lives, dreams for the future and sense of belonging? Why are these issues so rarely discussed on Almedalsveckan's major stages?

In this discussion, young people from KISAM – Världens ungdomar share their own experiences, stories and perspectives. Their voices offer insight into how today's policies affect individuals and the consequences they may have for Sweden's future.
content.subject: Democracy
content.accessibility: Hearing loop, wheelchair-accessible entrance and venue

content.title: Smart policy for rapid nuclear power expansion
content.description: How can new policies accelerate construction and reduce the costs of new nuclear power to meet the current government's targets?
content.extendedDescription: While the parties supporting the current government have strongly supported new nuclear power, many in society, including other political parties, have reservations about costs, construction timelines and safety. Even with strong government support, considerable uncertainty remains about whether new nuclear power can be built in Sweden on time and on budget to meet the government's 2035 target of at least 2,500 megawatts of new nuclear capacity. Could better policy accelerate such expansion? This roundtable brings together policy experts to discuss and develop a broader range of policy options addressing nuclear power's challenges and opportunities for new construction that is affordable, sustainable, rapid and has genuine public support. We will draw on lessons from new Uppsala universitet research on nuclear construction in other countries, and from renewable energy projects in Sweden and abroad.
content.subject: Energy
content.accessibility: Wheelchair-accessible toilet, wheelchair-accessible entrance and venue

content.title: What will Stockholm's residents eat then?
content.description: Stockholm is one of Europe's fastest-growing metropolitan regions, but also one of the most dependent. We have built a system that is extremely efficient in everyday life but potentially fragile in a crisis. Who is actually responsible for ensuring Stockholm's residents have food on their plates?
content.extendedDescription: The Stockholm region has a clear imbalance: high consumption, low local production and heavy dependence on long national and global supply chains. Meanwhile, pressure on agricultural land grows as the city expands and competition for land, resources and infrastructure intensifies. At its heart, this is also about the relationship between city and countryside: how metropolitan needs, growth and consumption connect to conditions for Swedish production, farming and food supplies nationwide. During the seminar, a panel discusses questions such as: where are the vulnerabilities? Who is responsible? What is needed to create a food system in which city and countryside strengthen one another, and how can responsibility be monitored and rewarded in practice?
content.subject: Food
content.organizationType: Collaboration between different types of organisation
speakerTitles: Centern Group Leader and First Deputy Chair

content.title: A good neighbour in the industrial community 2.0 – how new establishments create local benefits and resilience
content.description: As in Frövi, new establishments can drive long-term development in smaller industrial communities. How can economic investments be combined with social values and local resilience so that development creates real benefits and resilience over time?
content.extendedDescription:
How can future establishments drive long-term development in the industrial community 2.0? This societal issue focuses on combining economic investment with social values, local collaboration and increased resilience. For smaller towns and rural areas, this is essential if development is to create lasting local benefits.
The discussion examines how value can be understood and monitored locally, beyond traditional growth measures. Examples of how industrial symbiosis can develop into urban and social symbiosis inform a discussion of new ways to strengthen robustness and resilience over time, and therefore competitiveness.
The programme takes the form of a moderated discussion at 10.30–11.15, followed by a summary at 11.15–11.30. No preparation is required.
content.subject: Business
content.organizationType: Collaboration between different types of organisation

content.title: Minimum Viable Sweden – what is our baseline for crisis preparedness?
content.description: Sweden currently lacks clearly defined minimum levels for supplies, infrastructure and societal functions during a crisis. What must keep working, who is responsible, and how can preparedness be built before the next crisis arrives?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden faces a new security situation in which supply chains and critical societal functions must work even during prolonged disruptions. Despite this, there is no shared definition of what must actually be maintained for society to keep functioning.

The seminar explores the concept of Minimum Viable Sweden: the minimum level of robustness required for Sweden to cope with a serious crisis.

Which functions are absolutely essential? How should responsibility be shared between the state, authorities and business? What incentives and regulations are needed to strengthen companies' preparedness? And what commitments are politicians willing to make?
content.subject: Security/defence
speakerTitles: Head of National Security & Defence, Technology Strategy
Head of Strategy and Governmental Affairs

content.title: Clinical research – essential to evidence-based care, but are the conditions in place?
content.description: Research in healthcare is crucial to developing treatments and ensuring high-quality care, but clinicians who conduct research often lack the conditions and incentives they need. How can career structures, funding and healthcare organisation be developed to provide sustainable conditions?
content.extendedDescription: Clinical research is crucial to the development of Swedish healthcare. Research generates new knowledge and helps improve the quality and efficiency of care to ensure good healthcare. To succeed, research needs a greater presence throughout healthcare, and the interaction between research and care must work. Research's methodical approach requires long-term provision of funding, time and other resources. The patient perspective is crucial to ensuring that research is relevant and feasible and that its results actually improve quality of life for people living with illness.
content.subject: Research
content.accessibility: The event is captioned, Wheelchair-accessible toilet, Wheelchair-accessible entrance and venue
speakerTitles: Secretary General for Medicine and Health
Director of Research, Development, Education and Innovation

content.title: From data to decisions in minutes – how AI is changing insight work
content.description: Organisations are drowning in data but are not making better decisions.
content.extendedDescription:
Analysts, communicators and decision-makers face the same paradox: more data than ever, but no greater clarity. Reports pile up, presentations circulate, yet real decisions are delayed. The problem is not access to information. It is the ability to turn it quickly into something that actually changes direction. That is the gap AI is now beginning to close.

The seminar presents how Stella Research Engine is used to turn data into sharp, actionable insights in minutes rather than weeks. The tool changes not only speed but what can actually be delivered.

As a practical example, Svenska kyrkan shares its experiences of working with Ester, the church's own version of Stella. One of Sweden's largest organisations, with responsibilities ranging from parish life to national preparedness, shows how AI support works in practice for communication, strategy and collaboration without requiring technical expertise.
content.subject: Digitalisation

content.title: Regional and local level cooperation - Ukrainian experiences on key factor for resilience
content.description: How can the experiences from the war in Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia region inform efforts to build resilience at local, regional, and national levels?
content.extendedDescription:
Welcome to a seminar exploring how regional and local cooperation strengthens resilience – with lessons directly from Ukraine at war.

In a time when preparedness and collaboration are more critical than ever, we invite you to an inspiring and insightful morning seminar on regional and local cooperation – Ukrainian experiences as a key to resilience.

With lessons and firsthand accounts from the Zaporizhzhia region in Ukraine, we will discuss:
•	How to build resilience in times of crisis,
•	How to collaborate nationally, regionally, and locally to strengthen preparedness,
•	And how Sweden can enhance its own crisis readiness.

The seminar will also highlight the new government assignment given to the County Administrative Boards of Värmland and Västernorrland to deepen cooperation with Zaporizhzhia, provide mutual support, and share experiences.
content.subject: Security/defence

content.title: Who takes the risk? Why investments in sustainable aviation fuel stall
content.description: Despite clear EU policy through ReFuelEU Aviation, sustainable aviation fuels (SAF) are struggling to take off. Many European initiatives have been delayed or cancelled entirely. Airlines report a shortage of SAF, while producers say demand is lacking. Why isn't SAF taking flight?
content.extendedDescription: Under ReFuelEU Aviation, 70 per cent of all aviation fuels must be sustainable by 2050. As early as 2030, 6 per cent must be sustainable. Airlines warn that prices are too high, while producers warn that demand is insufficient to increase production. Discussions are under way at EU level to facilitate increased SAF production. Without SAF, the EU will miss its Fit for 55 targets, particularly because alternative fuels for aviation are difficult to find. This seminar examines the real reasons SAF is not taking off. Why are there not more investment decisions? How do we resolve supply and demand? Will we meet the 2030 targets for sustainable aviation fuels?
content.subject: Energy
speakerTitles: Director-General of Trafikanalys and Newly Appointed Director-General of VTI from 1 July

content.title: For democracy, freedom and human rights: building Folkhemmet 2.0
content.description: In a time of distrust and polarisation, we need discussions about peace, freedom and government by the people. Democracy is not a given: it requires open dialogue and shared responsibility. How do we preserve the trust that holds society together?
content.extendedDescription:
In a time of increasing polarisation and declining trust, Palmedalen becomes an important meeting place for reflection on the values shaping our society. Here, discussions about peace, freedom, public health, democracy, popular education and people's finances take place in the spirit of Olof Palme, reminding us of democracy's vulnerability and the need to nurture shared trust. Bringing together politics, art, workshops, podcast discussions and quiz walks creates a platform where thoughts, knowledge and feelings meet in new ways. On the quiz walk, participants can test their knowledge of democracy, societal issues and Palmedalen's themes. Everyone who answers all questions correctly enters a prize draw.
Popular education plays a central role by creating space for learning, dialogue and critical thinking. Questions about people's finances are also highlighted: how to build a society in which financial security, equal opportunities and participation benefit more people. Through discussion, knowledge exchange and shared reflection, we strengthen

content.title: Myths and truths about nicotine, smoking and the importance of alternatives
content.description: Sweden has reached the smoke-free target, defined as fewer than five per cent of the population smoking daily. Is this because snus and nicotine pouches are available as substitutes, or because of long-term prevention and public information campaigns?
content.extendedDescription:
A light lunch will be served. Is snus a gateway to smoking or the best way to quit? Do flavours and nicotine strength make it even more appealing? Is using snus as dangerous as smoking? Are nicotine pouches really tobacco-free? How dangerous is nicotine itself? What is the actual difference between nicotine medicines and nicotine pouches?

Nicotine sparks debate. Advocates of a preventive, restrictive approach see a conflict between public health interests and the tobacco industry. On the other side are those who see it as a matter of personal freedom, and those who view it as a contest between ideology and science.
We have invited a panel representing both perspectives from politics, public debate and science to explore what is true and what is myth.
content.subject: Research
speakerTitles: Physician and Professor of Internal Medicine

content.title: The wave of reforms – a boost or a collapse in learning for Swedish schools?
content.description: The government is implementing extensive school reforms. Ambitions are high, but can Swedish schools manage so many changes at once, or could the most important thing of all suffer: pupils' learning?
content.extendedDescription:
The government is pushing through a reform package unprecedented in modern times: new grades, new curricula, new teacher training and a complete overhaul of the independent school system. Ambitions are high and some reforms are necessary. But can Swedish schools implement so many changes? Or will the most important thing of all suffer: pupils' learning?

Critics warn that some reforms risk dismantling successful schools, forcing school providers to close well-functioning operations and creating a system in which political enthusiasm takes precedence over educational reality. Others see an opportunity finally to address longstanding problems.

Are the reforms strengthening Swedish schools, or heading towards a loss of learning for an entire generation?
content.subject: Children/young people

content.title: Do we need a coordinated policy for nature?
content.description: Biodiversity loss threatens Sweden's welfare. Does Sweden need a legal nature policy framework that, like the climate policy framework, supports a societal transition for biodiversity? What do the parliamentary parties think?
content.extendedDescription:
Addressing the nature crisis and meeting Sweden's commitments to protect biodiversity requires a societal transition to which everyone contributes, from citizens to businesses and policymakers.

For almost a decade, a climate policy framework has included a Climate Act, climate targets and a Climate Policy Council. It has helped make climate a central political issue. Is a similar framework needed to counter biodiversity loss and give nature a more central place on the political agenda?

The seminar presents a proposed legal nature policy framework and what it could mean. The presentation forms the basis for a discussion between representatives of several parliamentary parties.

The seminar is part of Uppsala universitet's climate days.
content.subject: Climate/environment

content.title: Sweden lived in safety for 200 years – do we understand what Ukraine always knew?
content.description: The Russian invasion has changed the world order. Sweden rearmed. But have we understood what Ukrainians have always known: that safety is not a state but a choice you must make every day?
content.extendedDescription:
This is not a seminar. It is an open invitation.

The founders and guests in SPSU's tent answer one question at a time, asked by anyone in the room. No agenda. No prepared answers. If you have always wondered what Ukrainians really think about Sweden, the war, the future or you, this is your opportunity.

Behind the conversation lies a serious question: Ukrainian and Swedish values have been shaped by very different histories. Sweden has not experienced occupation, attempted annihilation or war at home for 200 years. Ukraine has never had that luxury. How does this affect how we understand one another, and what happens when these world views are forced to coexist?

The unsettling thought: perhaps Ukrainians are not the only ones who need to integrate. Perhaps Sweden needs to integrate into a reality in which the safety we have taken for granted is no longer guaranteed.
content.subject: Integration/diversity
content.organizationType: Collaboration between different types of organisation

content.title: Voters' views on snus, e-cigarettes and nicotine – how do politicians respond?
content.description: We know a great deal about how Swedes use snus, e-cigarettes and nicotine, but less about their knowledge, risk perceptions and attitudes towards these products. Ahead of the election, it is important to understand how well party positions reflect voters' views on public health, individual freedom and EU influence.
content.extendedDescription:
This seminar presents Snusbarometern, a new opinion survey aiming to fill gaps in knowledge about Swedes' attitudes towards snus, e-cigarettes and different nicotine products. The survey examines views on risks, the role of snus in quitting smoking, young people's use and how much power the EU should have over taxes and regulations.

Drawing on the survey, we invite you to a political discussion in which the panel reacts to, is challenged by and reflects on what public opinion actually shows. How can better knowledge of Swedes' views on snus, e-cigarettes and nicotine contribute to better-targeted decisions on public health, individual freedom and Sweden's position in EU negotiations?
content.subject: Democracy
content.organizationType: Collaboration between different types of organisation

content.title: How can science help prepare society for a pandemic?
content.description: The world has reminded us how vulnerable we are to viruses and pandemics. Experiences from Covid-19 show that society cannot afford to be unprepared, making continued research crucial.
content.extendedDescription:
Research is essential both between and during pandemics. Without continuous research, we risk being left helpless when the next pandemic arrives. Between pandemics, we must therefore build knowledge and preparedness. During an ongoing pandemic, rapid, targeted investment in research on the current crisis is needed to develop vaccines, treatments and effective measures, for example.
Ultimately, research is also about solidarity and international responsibility. Viruses do not respect national borders. By collaborating globally and sharing knowledge, we can fight diseases more effectively and fairly. Investment in research is therefore also an investment in a safer, more equal world. Taken together, research into viruses and pandemics is not optional but a necessary investment in a safe and resilient society.

content.title: Threats and violence against essential workers – who takes responsibility?
content.description: Ambulance staff and others on the front line increasingly face threats and violence. What is needed to ensure a safe working environment without compromising rapid help for those who need it?
content.extendedDescription:
When an ambulance service employee lost their life on duty, a difficult but necessary question came into focus: how safe are those tasked with helping others in vulnerable and unpredictable situations?

What happened was not an isolated incident. The investigation shows that something similar could have happened elsewhere. Ambulance staff, healthcare workers and other public employees face threats and violence at work. Many work alone or in small teams, in people's homes, in public places and in situations where risks can change rapidly.

At the same time, their mission is clear: help must arrive quickly when people need it. But is responsibility for employees' safety equally clear?

The seminar addresses the tension between rapid, accessible help and employers' responsibility for a safe working environment. What can be resolved locally, and what requires national decisions?

content.title: What has Sweden not yet done for Ukraine – but must do?
content.description: Sweden supports Ukraine, but is it enough? Four years into the full-scale war, what is missing in politics, civil society and long-term commitment? What is Sweden really prepared to do?
content.extendedDescription:
Civil society support for Ukraine has grown since 2022, but the gap between what is needed and what is delivered remains large. This discussion provides room for an open, honest dialogue about where Sweden can do more.
The conversation takes place in an open-table format, without a stage or prepared speeches. Ukraine's ambassador sits at the same table as politicians, volunteers, Ukrainians and the public. Everyone is welcome to ask questions and contribute. After the moderated discussion, the dialogue continues informally over a networking reception.

The discussion is organised as part of Samarbetsplattformen: Sverige & Ukraina (SPSU), a KlinteVolontär project giving Ukrainian civil society its own voice in Swedish democratic debate and bringing together Swedish and Ukrainian organisations to strengthen long-term cooperation between the countries.

content.title: Young people's voices: this is the Sweden we want
content.description: Today's young people shape tomorrow's society but often lack a voice in decisions affecting their future. Meanwhile, Sweden faces important choices in many areas. How can we take young people's opinions and visions more seriously to better understand and create the Sweden of the future?
content.extendedDescription: The seminar marks the close of Almedalsveckan and connects to the democratic discussion on Almedalen's stage that opened the week. Results from a new Novus survey form the basis for a discussion about young people's values and views of the future, and above all how we can move together towards the society they want. In 2024, Sweden signed the UN Pact for the Future, which includes the Declaration on Future Generations: a commitment to consider future generations' needs in today's decisions. What can we do to make this declaration a reality? We close Almedalen looking ahead: how do we build the Sweden our young people want, together?

content.title: How can cleaning staff free up healthcare resources?
content.description: Healthcare is struggling with both skills shortages and sickness absence. How can it free up more time for direct patient care by having professional providers handle cleaning and service tasks?
content.extendedDescription:
The seminar examines how healthcare's core expertise can be used more effectively by removing tasks that do not require healthcare training. Today, nurses and assistant nurses often perform service tasks such as cleaning, washing dishes, making beds and transporting patients, reducing the time available for direct patient care. By giving professional service providers greater responsibility for these tasks, healthcare staff can spend more time on what they are trained for: medical and nursing care.
We present examples, data and best practice and discuss the potential effects on patient safety, working conditions and access to care. Representatives of the facility management industry and the public sector take part.

content.title: Children's right to a dignified life is not measured in minutes
content.description: Children with disabilities are denied personal assistance to which they are entitled. Today's narrow rules hit the most vulnerable hard. We demand legislative changes so that the child's full needs count.
content.extendedDescription:
Visit RBU's outdoor stand at Almedalen and learn more about the Minuter campaign and why we demand changes to legislation for children and young people with disabilities.
We explain how the current system works in practice and what RBU's legislative proposal involves. You can also sign our petition, which we will deliver to decision-makers.
Take the challenge on site!
Can you manage a day with your basic needs rationed? At the stand, you can experience the time limits many children with disabilities face daily, such as 5 minutes to get dressed and undressed, 3 minutes for communication and 5 minutes per toilet visit. This is not an exaggeration but is based on actual court rulings.
Try it, get involved and share your experience on social media with #rbukampanjminuter.
Read more and sign at rbu.se/minuter, and take the challenge at rbu.se/utmaningen

content.title: Young people and the housing market – how do we lower the barriers?
content.description: More young people are being excluded from the owner-occupied housing market. High prices and a shortage of small homes, especially in major cities, create structural barriers. What is needed to lower those barriers, increase mobility and give more young people a home of their own?
content.extendedDescription:
Young adults today face several simultaneous barriers in the housing market. Small, affordable homes are in short supply. Lending rules, mortgage repayment requirements and large deposits make it difficult to qualify for a mortgage. Meanwhile, market mobility has declined, slowing chains of moves and locking up capital.

The question is not whether these challenges exist, but which reforms can actually make a difference.

This seminar brings together decision-makers, leading researchers and industry representatives for an informed, forward-looking discussion of solutions. How can more small homes be made possible? How do lending rules affect first-time buyers in practice? What is needed to strengthen mobility and create functioning chains of moves? And what political priorities should be set in both the short and long term?
content.subject: Construction

content.title: From populism to national conservatism: the new right in Europe
content.description: Parties usually categorised as populist are now the largest or second-largest in several European countries. Are we witnessing the emergence of a national-conservative party family? How different are these parties? What happens to anti-establishment rhetoric when they enter government?
content.extendedDescription:
Support for so-called right-wing populist parties has increased throughout the 2000s. Today, parties such as Alternativ för Tyskland, Reform UK and France's Nationell samling are the largest or second-largest in almost every European democracy. Ten years after Brexit and Trump's first election victory, no one talks about “peak populism” anymore; instead, it seems obvious that these parties are here to stay.
How substantial are the similarities and differences between them? Is there an ideological consistency that makes it relevant to speak of a national-conservative party family? How does it differ from the old right? How have Trump and Putin influenced these parties' ideology? What happens to anti-establishment rhetoric when they enter government?

content.title: Are we building for the next quarter or the next generation?
content.description: Brick has shaped Swedish cities for hundreds of years, but what role can it play in sustainable construction in the future? What about service life, climate impact, fire safety and how traditional materials evolve through new innovations and smarter use of resources?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden is at a crossroads in construction. We need to build more sustainably, faster and with lower climate impact, while creating communities that endure. Debate often focuses on short-term climate calculations or the pace of construction here and now. Service life, robustness, maintenance and safety over a hundred-year horizon are discussed less often.
This lecture starts with brick as a building material and places it in a wider societal context. What can history teach us about materials that survive generations? How do material choices affect our cities, safety and climate footprints over time? And how do we balance sustainability objectives when building tomorrow's homes and public spaces?
The event is a lecture with opportunities for questions and discussion afterwards.

content.title: Beyond age limits: protecting and supporting children online, where they are
content.description: Following the government inquiry into age limits for social media, what does this mean in practice for children and young people? And how do we move from regulation to real safety in their digital lives?
content.extendedDescription:
Children encounter both risks and opportunities online. They may face harmful content and grooming, but also find community, support and knowledge. Meanwhile, many young people describe a growing divide from the adult world, and we see them increasingly turning to AI for advice and support on sensitive issues.

UNICEF Sverige and Spotify bring together stakeholders from politics, civil society and business to discuss:
- How digital platforms must take responsibility for children's safety and wellbeing regardless of age limits.
- How society needs to reach young people and offer support where they are.
- How we bridge understanding across ages and generations and strengthen young people's resilience as AI becomes more important.

The discussion focuses on how politics, technology and society can together create a safer digital present for children and young people.
content.subject: Children/young people

content.title: Sweden's competitiveness is at stake – how we can win the global race
content.description: China is growing economically, the USA is embracing protectionism and Europe suffers from low growth. As an export-dependent country, Sweden must compete harder, develop faster and strengthen its competitiveness through 2035.
content.extendedDescription:
China is strengthening its position as an economic and industrial powerhouse, the USA is moving towards greater protectionism and Europe is marked by low growth and internal indecision. For Sweden, a small, export-dependent country, there is only one way forward: to compete harder, develop faster and take leading positions in an increasingly tough global arena. What strengths must Sweden build on to secure its competitiveness through 2035?

In this seminar, Per Schlingman speaks with Linda Fagerlund, CEO of Danske Bank Sverige, and Lars Herlitz, Lyten's founder and chair, about Sweden's strategic choices in a new world order. The discussion examines the risks of complacent, uniform political priorities and asks an uncomfortable but necessary question: what is Sweden's long-term plan, really?
content.subject: Economy

content.title: Prioritising migraine – an opportunity for Swedish growth
content.description: Migraine is a common neurological disease and the most disabling disease among people of working age. Beyond considerable personal suffering, it places major strains on private life, employers and society as a whole. Solutions exist for equitable, effective and individualised migraine care.
content.extendedDescription:
Around 1.4 million Swedes suffer from migraine of varying severity. Despite effective treatments and care guidelines, migraine is underdiagnosed, undertreated and underprioritised in Swedish healthcare. Who takes responsibility for those without a diagnosis, those not receiving the care they need and those forced to self-medicate?
We will present a new compilation of data on the societal burden and consequences for the public and private sectors.
The remaining question is who will take responsibility and show the way towards equitable, effective and individualised migraine care that creates value for us all. That is what we will discuss.
content.detail: Life Science arena at restaurant Volare

content.title: Does everyone like the right of public access and kolbullar?
content.description: How do we promote the right of public access in practice? How do we find resources to preserve natural environments as more people want to enjoy nature? And how do we create more sustainable tourism with visitors spread across more places?
content.extendedDescription:
Welcome to STF's campfire in Almedalen. With the sea as a backdrop, coffee brewed over an open fire and freshly cooked kolbullar, we create a relaxed setting for conversations about the right of public access, the future of outdoor recreation and sustainable tourism: no stages, no panels, just a genuine discussion under the open sky.
Those joining us around the fire include Kjell-Arne Ottosson (KD), Åsa Westlund (S), Helena Lindahl (C), Emma Nohrén (MP), Jesper Skalberg Karlsson (M), Anna-Lena Hedberg (SD), Elin Nilsson (L) and Andrea Andersson-Tay (V). We also look forward to visits from Håll Sverige Rent, Svenskt Friluftsliv, SJ and Länsstyrelsen Gotland, among others. Discussions are led by STF's Secretary-General Maria Ros-Hjelm. The campfire is lit at STF Visby Hamn Vandrarhem. The conversations are open to everyone. You will recognise those who attended by the smell of kolbullar :)

content.title: The fashion wardrobe of the future – what reforms are needed now?
content.description: Swedish fashion consumption is unsustainable, while today's system favours new production over reuse, sharing and longevity. What political and economic changes are needed for circular business models to compete on equal terms? How do we create a wardrobe within planetary boundaries?
content.extendedDescription:
Despite growing awareness of the textile industry's climate and environmental impact, consumption of newly produced clothes continues to rise. Consumers are expected to make sustainable choices, but markets and regulations still favour high turnover and constant new purchases.

In this session, Sysav, Fashion Loop and Naturskyddsföreningen invite you to a wardrobe challenge in which we examine our clothing choices and explore smarter ways to consume, use and share our wardrobes. Creating a textile sector within planetary boundaries, however, requires more than changing consumer behaviour. What political priorities, policy instruments and incentives are needed to make circular solutions more accessible, competitive and scalable?

fashion - innovation - sustainability - circularity

content.title: Different perspectives on graduates' role in a changing working life
content.description: The labour market for graduates has become tougher and less predictable. Unemployment has increased, particularly among recent graduates. AI and rapid technological development are fundamentally changing working life. Is this due to the economic downturn, to AI, or are we in the midst of a larger shift?
content.extendedDescription:
Debate is growing about what Sweden really needs: more vocational education, higher education more closely guided by labour market needs, or continued long-term, broad academic education? How do we educate people for jobs and skills whose future form we do not yet know? And does a broad education still have value?

In three in-depth conversations, Saco President Sofia Rydgren Stale meets representatives of three different perspectives on AI, higher education and graduates' role in the labour market of the future.

Drawing on Saco's idea of Slow Politics, the discussions allow space for reflection, different perspectives and more considered debate.

content.title: How do we restore trust when fake is the new normal?
content.description:
Source criticism is being challenged now that false content is often impossible to detect with the naked eye. When technology makes truth difficult to establish, the problem shifts from information to trust: whom can we trust, and why?
At the same time, trust risks replacing critical thinking.
content.extendedDescription:
The seminar starts from a shift in how we view source criticism: from exposing false content to understanding sources, intentions and trust. Drawing on Arbetets museum's “Demokratilabbet”, stakeholders from the social partners, culture and defence – together forming the country's most credible voice – come together to discuss how to strengthen resilience against disinformation in practice.
The conversation highlights different perspectives on the threats, the changing role of trust and what it takes to build and maintain credibility. The focus is on solutions: how organisations can jointly contribute to open discussion, critical thinking and a more resilient democracy, particularly in workplaces where many people meet every day.
content.subject: Democracy

content.title: Obesity care beyond medicines: creating modern, patient-centred treatment in practice
content.description: Swedish obesity care is at a crossroads. Practices differ between regions and knowledge-based governance lags behind, making care unequal and fragmented. When reimbursement issues determine priorities, patients risk falling through the gaps. How can care take the next step?
content.extendedDescription: Swedish obesity care is at a crossroads. Socialstyrelsen's first national evaluation of obesity care shows that hundreds of thousands of patients are not receiving care. Knowledge-based governance lags behind and practices differ between regions, making care unequal and fragmented. Meanwhile, more coordinated, scalable care models are emerging, with long-term support combining medical follow-up, behavioural change and digital tools. When reimbursement issues determine priorities, progress risks slowing and patients fall through the gaps. The seminar discusses how Swedish obesity care can take the next step: separating knowledge-based governance from reimbursement, creating clearer care pathways and strengthening equity in treatment and follow-up.
content.subject: Health and social care
speakerTitles: Chair of Region Skåne's Primary Care Committee

content.title: Can we afford not to invest in water and wastewater infrastructure?
content.description: A recently revised forecast of municipal investment needs in water and wastewater shows that needs through 2040 still amount to hundreds of billions, while municipalities are falling behind the required investment pace. Charges continue to rise.
content.extendedDescription: Swedish municipal water and wastewater organisations need to invest at least SEK 560 billion by 2040, according to the 2023 investment report. An updated report will be presented in spring 2026. Municipalities are not keeping investment in line with needs, for several reasons. Because investments are financed by borrowing and no accumulated funds are available, financing costs are passed on through customer charges to Sweden's property owners, homeowners, housing cooperatives and tenants. Higher charges may make politicians hesitate, but can we really afford not to invest in water and wastewater? And if customers are not to pay for everything, where should the money come from?
content.subject: Economy
speakerTitles: Water Network and Asset Management Strategist

content.title: Strengthening total defence through civil–military innovation
content.description: Sweden faces growing demands for defence capability and robust preparedness nationwide. Through collaboration between industry and the defence sector, civilian solutions are developed and adapted to meet military needs. This enables faster innovation and a more resilient society.
content.extendedDescription:
Demonstration of MSMB 200, a small high-speed motorboat developed to meet Försvarsmakten's needs for transport and support capabilities in maritime environments. The boat was developed jointly by Svekon, Nimbus Group, FMV and Försvarsmakten, adapting and further developing a civilian boat type for military use.

The project includes development, verification and industrialisation of a standardised solution for use in different parts of the country.

During the demonstration, from 14.00-15.00, the boat and the solutions developed to meet Försvarsmakten's requirements will be shown, alongside how a structured, requirements-led approach and close collaboration between industry and defence enabled delivery of a verified operational capability.

The boat will be demonstrated in Visby Gästhamn, berth i1.
content.subject: Security/defence

content.title: Innovation in the built environment – new building approaches for an uncertain future
content.description: How do we build properties that are profitable and attractive not just today, but in 30, 50 or 100 years?
content.extendedDescription:
CREE Buildings invites you to a discussion about developing the next generation of construction.

The technology for building with lower climate impact, greater industrialisation, more flexibility and opportunities for future reuse already exists. In many cases, the challenge is economic and structural rather than technical. Today's investment and valuation models often reward the lowest initial cost over long-term value, reduced risk and future adaptability.

The expert panel explores how new building approaches, business models and partnerships can help develop properties that remain attractive and relevant not just today, but in 30, 50 or 100 years.

As a practical example of how new building approaches can be developed and tested, the seminar also presents MARIEVIK+, a new Vinnova-funded transition lab for circular and adaptive urban environments.
content.subject: Innovation

content.title: How are you doing, Sweden?
content.description: Much has happened in Sweden. Globalisation, technology and migration have fundamentally changed how the country holds together: how we work and live, and what it feels like to be part of society.
content.extendedDescription:
In the gap between the welfare society and the future, documentary filmmaker Lina Maria Mannheimer travelled to smaller communities from north to south and asked the seemingly simple question:

FILM: HUR ÄR LÄGET SVERIGE?

Director: Lina Maria Mannheimer / Short documentary / Sweden / 14 min.
The film consists of 20 stylised portraits and scenes, small everyday vignettes from Swedish homes and workplaces. It was produced as part of Svenska Filminstitutet and Sveriges Television's democracy initiative Mina drömmars land, in co-production with Film i Väst and Mannheimer Produktion.

Tempo Landet runt is a project by Tempo Dokumentärfestival, supported by Svenska Postkodlotteriets Stiftelse and Svenska Filminstitutet.

content.title: Creating robust and efficient infrastructure
content.description: Over the past ten years, Sweden has more than doubled infrastructure funding. Despite this, few are satisfied with the current situation. Rail lines are full, queues stretch along the E6 and a lack of integrated corridor planning means bottlenecks are moved rather than resolved.
content.extendedDescription: Meanwhile, the system is not robust enough. The result is weaker Swedish competitiveness. In this morning discussion, we begin the day in Almedalen by exploring how new organisational models and clearer national priorities can increase both delivery speed and efficiency in building and operating Swedish infrastructure. The goal is simple: to meet growing national freight needs and increasing regional commuting. Participating is Linus Eriksson, CEO of Öresundsbron, who works daily with one of the Nordic region's most important infrastructure links between Copenhagen and Malmö. With extensive experience of transport, regional development and international collaboration, he shares his perspectives on what is needed for infrastructure to be robust, efficient and ready for future needs.

content.title: Can Sweden avoid the multibillion bill for plastic?
content.description: Sweden pays large sums to the EU because we are not meeting plastic packaging recycling targets. What is needed to reverse the trend? Which measures effectively increase recycling?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden pays billions in penalties to the EU because we fail to recycle plastic. Responsibility is spread across producers' design choices, household sorting, municipal collection, recycling facilities and buyers of recycled materials.

The EU is now tightening the rules. Sweden is introducing new waste legislation. Increasing recycling is about reducing climate emissions and making the EU more self-sufficient. How do we move from paying for failure to building a profitable circular economy? How do we reach the target of recycling 55 per cent of plastic packaging?

Recycling organisation Näringslivets Producentansvar (NPA) invites you to a discussion of the political decisions needed to turn a cost into a resource.

Please arrive early enough to have breakfast before the discussion begins.

content.title: Data centres, electricity and preparedness – what is actually possible?
content.description: Data centres are now part of society's basic infrastructure and essential to AI, digital services and preparedness. Yet many plans are moving faster than electricity grids, land, water and permitting processes can accommodate, making the question of what is actually feasible increasingly important.
content.extendedDescription:
WSP invites you to a discussion in Almedalen about feasibility in practice. It starts from key questions:

• How do we obtain a realistic picture of electricity, power capacity, land, water and time that supports both growth and preparedness?

• How can municipalities determine early which data centre projects are feasible, sustainable and compatible with local development and essential services?

• What requirements should be set locally, and how can data centres deliver concrete benefits, such as waste heat, a stronger energy system and greater local robustness?

A discussion about electricity, planning and digital infrastructure now that data centres have become part of societal preparedness.
content.subject: Energy

content.title: Pitch on a Rib – who gets to meet investors?
content.description: Access to investors determines which ideas become reality, but networks and geography often determine who even gets through the door. Do the meeting place and format affect which companies obtain funding? And what is needed for more entrepreneurs to reach capital?
content.extendedDescription:
While the rest of Almedalen sits in seminar rooms, we cast off in a RIB from Visby Hamn. On board: a hand-picked line-up of startups, sharp investors and Gotland's coast as the backdrop.

No spotlights, no slide decks. Just innovative ideas and people who can help bring them to life.

We head out to sea at full speed, pitch in front of one of Gotland's highest and most dramatic cliffs, then return to the harbour. The rest happens on the jetty.

While the RIB is out, the boathouse at the harbour is open for mingling: coffee, sea air and the people building and investing on Gotland. Come ashore and stay for the conversations.

By moving the meeting from the seminar room to the sea, we want to lower the barrier between ideas and capital and show that the best conversations do not always happen where you expect.
content.subject: Innovation

content.title: Theft in grocery stores – has it improved or worsened over the past 4 years?
content.description: Goods equivalent to eighteen fully loaded shopping trolleys are stolen from Swedish grocery stores every hour. Few crimes reported by stores to the police lead to any consequences, and retailers feel deeply discouraged. How does this affect retailers and customers, and what are politicians doing?
content.extendedDescription:
Reported, dismissed, repeated:
Retail is still waiting for action – is there light at the end of the tunnel?
This is the title of Livsmedelshandlarna's new report.

In 2022, Livsmedelshandlarna wrote a report on shoplifting and how Polisen handles it (Projekt Överklaga). Around 20 retailers from north to south, in rural areas and larger cities, contributed to the report. The aim was to examine how Polisen handles shoplifting reports and whether responses differ across the country.

4 years ago, the results were discouraging and showed that Polisen did not prioritise this type of crime. We now ask what has happened over the past 4 years. Has it improved or worsened? We are updating the report and inviting you to a new discussion.
content.subject: Justice/crime

content.title: The state and capital – growth policy for Sweden
content.description: Sweden is a frontrunner with strong industry, cutting-edge research and innovative startups. But we are falling behind. Growth is too low, permitting processes too slow and capital too difficult to mobilise. We risk losing production and business operations while other countries step forward.
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden's investment architecture is insufficient to meet the new reality. How can Sweden better support Swedish companies that want to grow and scale up? How can the state help ensure major investments both come to and remain in Sweden? How can the state become a more active partner in creating long-term, predictable conditions, driving crucial future investments and mobilising capital?

The seminar explores how to lay the foundations for stronger Swedish competitiveness, increase investment and raise growth. This is central to Sweden's economic future. The seminar will discuss Socialdemokraterna's new growth policy, intended to make Sweden richer and put more money in ordinary people's pockets.
content.subject: Economy

content.title: Is healthcare best run as a company? Sweden's most talked-about primary care reform
content.description: Gävleborg is the first in the country to turn publicly operated primary care into a company. What was the result, and what does it mean for the rest of Sweden?
content.extendedDescription:
Swedish primary care is under severe pressure. Access, working conditions and patient safety are recurring challenges. Meanwhile, there is widespread discussion about how care should be governed and organised to meet future needs.

Region Gävleborg has chosen a new path. In one year, 25 health centres and 850 employees moved from public administration into a region-owned company. This is the first time a Swedish region has implemented such a change within its own operations.

The decision has prompted strong reactions. Some see a bold approach to improving conditions for primary care. Others see a risky experiment in an already strained part of healthcare.

What can other regions learn from Gävleborg's choice? Has Region Gävleborg found a new path, or does the change show that primary care cannot develop on its own?
content.subject: Health and social care

content.title: How can the state prevent failure and collapse in medicines policy?
content.description: New medicines can make a real difference, but the system for reimbursement and introduction is increasingly questioned. When treatments for serious common diseases are rejected, the question arises: is the state taking responsibility, and what does this cost patients?
content.extendedDescription: 1.5 million Swedes live with obesity. Hundreds of thousands of families are affected by Alzheimer's disease. These are two of the greatest public health challenges of our time, and we have treatments that can make a real difference. In Sweden, they become trapped in a system that sees them only as a cost, rather than the investment they actually are. TLV has rejected reimbursement for an obesity medicine despite acknowledging that it is unfortunate that no reimbursement solution could be found. And 35 leading researchers and doctors have described NT-rådet's rejection of an Alzheimer's medicine in a DN opinion article as a “shameful betrayal of patients”. The government has appointed an inquiry to reform a medicines system that the responsible minister says has reached “the end of the road”. But what should the state do, and do we have time to wait for an inquiry?
content.subject: Health and social care
speakerTitles: State Secretary to Minister for Social Affairs Jakob Forssmed

content.title: From words to action for more clinical trials in Sweden
content.description: In July 2025, the government commissioned the establishment of a national partnership to strengthen Sweden's role in clinical trials and life sciences. Now it is high time for the partners to unite around that mission. What is needed to make Sweden an attractive location for more clinical trials?
content.extendedDescription:
For Swetrial to become the unifying force that genuinely increases the number of clinical trials, room must be made for trials in everyday healthcare work. Real impact requires regions to take responsibility and, crucially, politicians to issue clear directives with measurable targets. Healthcare often has clear governance, controls and follow-up for production and capacity planning across its services.

With very few exceptions, this is absent for clinical trials, meaning that regions effectively deprioritise them. In other words, how do we move from words to reality?

content.title: Why aren't Meta's scam advertisements being stopped?
content.description: Criminal advertising on Facebook and Instagram exploits Swedish media companies and journalists. Every day, Meta distributes around 15 billion scam advertisements and earns more than SEK 4,000 per second from the fraud. Why do the advertisements keep appearing? What is the Swedish media industry doing?
content.extendedDescription:
These scam advertisements cause financial and psychological suffering for innocent people, while Meta earns large sums by publishing the fraud. The advertisements also undermine the credibility of the media outlets being exploited, making them a democratic problem too.

Publishers' organisation Utgivarna and online marketing organisation IAB Sverige have filed DSA complaints and police reports against Meta and its CEO Mark Zuckerberg for offences including fraud and aiding and abetting fraud. A lawsuit in a Swedish court is also being prepared, and Meta has been expelled from IAB Sverige.

Publishers around the world are now cooperating to force Meta to take responsibility, and Swedish media companies have begun discussions with media intermediaries and advertisers about joint action.

content.title: Does international law have a future?
content.description: Wars, conflicts and global power shifts challenge the foundations of the international legal system. Is international law still relevant, or has it already outlived its role as an international framework for justice and accountability?
content.extendedDescription:
When great powers act outside shared rules, the relevance of international law is questioned, while others argue that it remains an important and resilient foundation for international cooperation. International law rests on states' consent and compliance, making its strength dependent on political will. When states leave agreements such as the Ottawa Convention or breach principles such as non-intervention, they risk eroding norms and legitimising similar behaviour.

This seminar discusses the future of international law at a time when power and norms frequently collide. Has international law weakened, transformed or lost its significance?

The seminar forms part of Folk och Försvar's arena in Almedalen, a meeting place for dialogue, knowledge exchange and new perspectives on Sweden's security. Stakeholders from across society come together to contribute to a safe, free and democratic Sweden.
content.subject: Security/defence

content.title: Algorithms or storytellers – who controls the narrative in an AI-driven economy?
content.description: Those who control the narrative can influence what people perceive as true, right and worth fighting for. Religions, political movements and global brands have all grown from powerful stories about the world and our place in it. But who will shape our thoughts in the future: algorithms or storytellers?
content.extendedDescription: For millennia, storytellers have created the conditions for collective influence. By directing the narrative, they have enabled religions, raised armies and built civilisations. That position is now challenged by humanity's latest innovation, the algorithm, which can map our behaviour, predict our choices and optimise messages on a scale no human storyteller has previously had access to. But what matters most when spreading ideas, products and perspectives: optimisation or meaning? Is it the algorithm that reaches us at exactly the right moment, or the story that makes us understand the message? Who has the greatest influence on the narrative? Let us explore this exciting question about the future together in Almedalen.
content.subject: Communication/information

content.title: Violence, custody and contact – have the legislative changes helped?
content.description: How have recent legislative changes affected whether violent fathers are granted custody and contact with their children? And how are pseudoscientific theories used in custody cases?
content.extendedDescription:
Roks presents a new edition of its report Våld och vårdnad (Eva Diesen, 2026), examining how violence, risk assessments and parental responsibility are handled in Swedish custody disputes. The aim is to highlight how courts apply current law in cases concerning custody, residence and contact where allegations of violence arise, and to analyse the legal and practical consequences for children and parents.

The report has been updated with legislation and case law through 2026.
Particular emphasis is placed on developments following the legislative changes that took effect in 2025, intended to strengthen protection for children and parents exposed to violence.

We ask: has the new legislation had an effect? Is violence considered when deciding custody, residence and contact? And how does the justice system view arguments about parental influence, known as parental alienation?
content.subject: Gender equality

content.title: We want more than we think – why isn't climate commitment turning into action?
content.description: Swedes' commitment to the climate is greater than we think, but is systematically underestimated. This affects both behaviour and political decisions. What happens when decisions rest on a mistaken picture of public opinion, and how can we unlock the hidden scope for action?
content.extendedDescription:
Research and new Swedish data show that we systematically underestimate one another's willingness to contribute to the climate transition. In reality, there is broad support for both individual behavioural changes and political measures, but because we believe others are less committed than they are, we act accordingly.

This kind of social misperception affects not only individual behaviour but also which decisions are seen as politically possible. When decision-makers and citizens start from a mistaken view of public opinion, action may fail to happen despite existing support.

The seminar draws on the Peerpointing initiative's latest study, “Svenskarnas dolda klimatengagemang”, and focuses on the next step: putting this knowledge into practice.
content.subject: Democracy

content.title:
Mental ill-health ➔ Poverty ➔ Loneliness
How do we break involuntary loneliness when welfare fails?
content.description: Mental ill-health and financial vulnerability increase the risk of involuntary loneliness. When benefits do not cover social activities, people are excluded from community and recovery. How can society counter loneliness and create conditions for participation and a good life?
content.extendedDescription: When mental health falters, everything else often collapses. Good care, social connection and financial security improve the chances of recovery and a good life. But instead of offering a way back, today's economic policies and low benefit levels trap people in exclusion. A coffee or a bus ticket to a meeting place becomes an impossible expense. Join a discussion with RSMH, Riksförbundet för Social och Mental Hälsa. We present our report “Mat eller medicin”, make important demands of policymakers and offer solutions we know work. Participants: Hanna Navier, Acting Head of Secretariat at RSMH; Beatrice Ikonen, Head of Education at RSMH; and Jenny Wetterling, Advocacy Policy Spokesperson at RSMH.
content.subject: Human rights

content.title: Climate adaptation in Europe's sparsely populated Arctic areas
content.description: How can we develop, test and spread climate adaptation solutions? The focus is on locally rooted, nature-based, digital and governance-oriented innovations that can strengthen sparsely populated areas' resilience to the effects of climate change.
content.extendedDescription:
The project brings together 26 partners from 15 countries and works directly with ten rural regions across Europe, including Västerbotten in Sweden. Together, we develop, test and spread climate adaptation solutions. The focus is on locally rooted, nature-based, digital and governance-oriented innovations that can strengthen sparsely populated areas' resilience to the effects of climate change.

During the discussion, Camilla Widmark, Sveriges lantbruksuniversitet in Umeå, presents the project's results so far. Join a roundtable on how rural regions in Europe can become drivers of climate adaptation.

The Horizon GRACE project (Growing Climate Resilience in Remote rural Areas through Community Empowerment) is a four-year project under the EU Mission on Adaptation to Climate Change.
