content.title: Labour market entry jobs — can they tackle both skills shortages and exclusion?
content.description: Sweden faces major skills challenges while many people remain far from the labour market. Labour market entry jobs are highlighted as an important reform for integration and skills supply — but why has their impact been limited so far, and what is needed next?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden faces major skills challenges in several sectors, including welfare services, while many people remain far from the labour market. Labour market entry jobs are highlighted as an important reform to create more routes into a first job and strengthen integration, but their impact has so far been limited.

What is needed for labour market entry jobs to work in practice? How do we create more first jobs while ensuring that employers get the right skills and individuals gain a lasting foothold in the labour market?

The seminar brings together representatives from politics, government agencies, trade unions and business to discuss responsibilities, obstacles and practical solutions to strengthen integration and meet Sweden's growing skills needs.
content.subject: Employment/labour market

content.title: The road to equitable cardiovascular care — what must the new plan include?
content.description: Cardiovascular diseases are a leading cause of death and create substantial healthcare needs, while regional differences in access and outcomes persist. The government's forthcoming cardiovascular plan must become an effective tool for prevention, care pathways and equitable care nationwide.
content.extendedDescription: The government has tasked Socialstyrelsen with developing a national action plan to prevent and treat cardiovascular diseases. The seminar discusses what the plan needs to include to meet substantial healthcare needs while reducing regional differences. The focus is on a comprehensive approach spanning prevention and early detection, coordinated care pathways, rehabilitation and long-term follow-up through quality registries. The discussion highlights how implementation should be designed to have a real impact: clear targets and indicators, the division of responsibilities between central government and regions, and the policy tools, incentives and funding solutions needed to ensure equitable access and comparable outcomes nationwide.
content.subject: Health and social care
speakerTitles: Chair of the Regional Executive Board in Region Östergötland and Deputy Chair of SKR's Healthcare Delegation

content.title: How to achieve a nature-positive energy transition
content.description: How can solar parks on agricultural and forest land become nature-positive? Where is solar farming most suitable, how should parks be designed, and what regulations are needed for large-scale solar energy to enhance biodiversity and help meet the EU Nature Restoration Law?
content.extendedDescription:
This panel discussion explores how solar parks on agricultural and forest land can become a practical tool for a nature-positive energy transition. The starting point is that solar farming, when properly located and designed, can enhance biodiversity, create new meadow and wetland habitats and help meet the EU Nature Restoration Law. The discussion examines three areas:

1. Site selection: How do we find locations where solar farming can best coexist with agriculture and forestry while creating new or enhanced ecological value?

2. Design: How can solar parks — including their management, layout and surroundings — be designed to deliver clear benefits for biodiversity and nature restoration?

3. Policy instruments and the EU Nature Restoration Law: How can legislation and policy instruments help steer development towards nature-positive solutions, and what roles do public authorities, businesses and civil society play?
content.subject: Energy

content.title: What does it cost when children stop reading — in knowledge, independence and confidence in the future?
content.description: Reading builds language, knowledge and the ability to find one's way in a complex world. But what happens to schools, working life and democracy if we cease to be a nation of readers — and what is needed to reverse the trend?
content.extendedDescription:
Reading is key to both learning and participation. Yet fewer children and young people are reading, and the consequences are already visible in classrooms, workplaces and public debate. What does this actually cost in knowledge, independence and confidence in the future?

In this seminar, we explore how reading builds language, subject knowledge and critical thinking, while also strengthening independence, judgement and the ability to navigate a complex world. When more people read, opportunities for participation and community increase, and it becomes easier to resist disinformation and polarisation.
We discuss the responsibility different parts of society have to safeguard reading as a foundation for democracy and confidence in the future, and what actually works when we want to reverse the trend.

The seminar takes the form of a discussion between researchers, practitioners and voices from schools.
content.subject: Education
content.accessibility: Hearing loop, wheelchair-accessible toilet, wheelchair-accessible entrance and venue
speakerTitles: Professor, Deputy Vice-Rector for Teacher Education
Head of Quality, Preschool and Compulsory Education

content.title: Cosmic — what happened and what does the future hold?
content.description: The rollout of the Cosmic electronic health record system in many regions has sparked considerable debate. On one hand, technical problems, poor coordination and risks to patient safety; on the other, the need for a shared health record system to improve information sharing and collaboration in healthcare. What happens now?
content.extendedDescription:
The rollout of the Cosmic electronic health record system in many regions has sparked considerable debate and criticism. Many describe it as an integration failure. Technical problems and poor coordination between steering groups and users led to frustration and inefficiency in hospitals. There have been warnings that patient safety has been jeopardised, and critics argue that the rollout should have been halted.

At the same time, some view Cosmic as a long-term investment. A shared health record system can improve information sharing, patient safety and collaboration in healthcare. The question is therefore not only what went wrong, but also what the future should look like. Is better training, more testing and greater influence for healthcare staff needed? We will hear views from users, the supplier and researchers.
content.subject: Health and social care
content.accessibility: Hearing loop, wheelchair-accessible toilet, wheelchair-accessible entrance and venue

content.title: With billions at stake — what leadership does the energy transition require?
content.description: The energy transition is the biggest societal project of our time, with billions at stake. What leadership is needed to bring it to fruition — in business, politics and the energy sector?
content.extendedDescription:
The climate crisis, geopolitical uncertainty and an energy system undergoing major change are forcing businesses and societies to make major, crucial decisions in a short time.

The leadership required must navigate uncertainty and investments, manage risks and drive through changes in a system that has traditionally moved slowly. At the same time, newcomers in new energy are challenging established practices in a sector where investments have long been long-term and the pace of change slow.

How do you lead in a sector where the pace is accelerating rapidly, reality is complex and decisions will shape the energy system, businesses and people's everyday lives for decades to come?

This panel brings together entrepreneurs, industry leaders, investors and decision-makers to discuss the leadership needed as the energy system is reshaped, and what determines who wins and loses in the energy transition.
content.detail: Loops arena för impact, industri och energi
content.subject: Business

content.title: A new world order — how do we equip Swedish SMEs for greater uncertainty?
content.description: What changes are we seeing in the world around us, and what do they mean for Swedish small and medium-sized enterprises?
content.extendedDescription:
Geopolitical tensions, changing trade patterns and a more uncertain economic outlook affect businesses' opportunities to grow and invest. For many companies, it is no longer just about developing the business, but about navigating a more complex and changing reality.

Together with Business Sweden, Almi invites you to a discussion on what is needed to strengthen companies' competitiveness in this situation. We discuss how access to capital, the right networks and partnerships, and relevant knowledge and market insights can help equip businesses for their next step, both in Sweden and internationally.

The discussion will cover, among other things:
• How global uncertainty affects conditions for Swedish businesses.
• The role of capital at a time of greater risk and changing markets.
• What businesses need to strengthen their competitiveness and navigate effectively.
• How cooperation between organisations can provide funding, contacts and knowledge.
content.subject: Business
speakerTitles: Chief Economist and Head of Analysis

content.title: Metal and mineral supply in a changing world
content.description: Metal and mineral supply is affected by a changing world. New regulations, changing market conditions and shifting risks create new circumstances for society and industry. How can stakeholders be mobilised and research and innovation initiatives launched to respond?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden has substantial mineral resources, strong industrial expertise and favourable conditions for contributing to a sustainable supply of metals and minerals. At the same time, the world around us is changing rapidly. New and stricter regulations, increased information and traceability requirements, changing market conditions and an evolving risk landscape affect developments throughout the value chain.

In this context, Swedish Metals & Minerals brings together stakeholders, identifies needs and initiates research and innovation efforts that respond to new challenges and opportunities. The seminar starts from how the programme operates in a changing world and highlights examples of initiatives that strengthen the ability to act as conditions change.
The programme and speakers will be updated.
content.subject: Innovation
content.organizationType: Collaboration between different types of organisation

content.title: Can waste collection close to homes be both simple and efficient?
content.description: Waste collection close to homes is an issue that engages people. Space is tight in cities, while distances are long in rural areas. Yet some municipalities combine high collection rates with satisfied residents. What is the key to successful collection?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden's waste collection landscape is being redrawn. Responsibility for collecting your packaging has shifted from producers to municipalities. A race against time is now under way to ensure that collection also takes place close to homes by 2027.

The question is: will the new system increase collection? To meet recycling targets, Sweden must collect twice as much plastic. And will it be efficient enough? Collection is a hidden cost on your supermarket receipt. Without a smart nationwide system, we all pay the price.

The seminar takes stock of progress with collection close to homes. What is working well? How do municipal waste companies and property owners resolve challenging cases? What can municipalities learn from one another?

Recycling organisation Näringslivets Producentansvar (NPA) invites you to a discussion on the role of collection in the circular economy.

content.title: From niche players to a space cluster — can Sweden become a leading space nation?
content.description: Space is not just an important industry of the future; it is part of Europe's infrastructure, economy, security and climate transition. Satellite communications, navigation and Earth observation are now fundamental to defence, emergency preparedness, digital inclusion and a resilient business sector.
content.extendedDescription: Over many years, Sweden has built a strong ecosystem of expertise in space and satellite systems, from launch capabilities and satellite platforms to ground infrastructure. Swedish companies already play central roles in major international programmes and are well placed to become a strategic space hub. But what is needed to move from several strong niche players to a fully developed industrial cluster that attracts international investment, talent and large-scale contracts? What role should Sweden play in Europe's investments in secure satellite communications and Earth observation — and how do we translate Sweden's space strategy into tangible industrial growth and long-term resilience?
content.subject: Infrastructure/transport
speakerTitles: Member of Parliament and member of the Committee on the Labour Market

content.title: No more guesswork — time for mandatory age verification when buying nicotine?
content.description: Despite a strict age limit of 18, nicotine and tobacco are still sold in shops to minors across the country. After years of training initiatives, shops' actual compliance with age checks remains inadequate. When too few people dare to ask about age, is a change in the law needed?
content.extendedDescription:
A new Ipsos survey shows that minors across the country often succeed in buying nicotine and tobacco products in shops. Years of proactive work involving internal compliance programmes, training and technical solutions have not been enough to reverse the trend.

This seminar brings together representatives from industry, public authorities and politics to jointly identify solutions that can break the trend once and for all. It begins with a presentation of the findings from Ipsos's latest survey of retail sales to minors.

Is it time to move from responsibility at cashier level to statutory, mandatory age verification for nicotine purchases, to reduce hesitation, errors of judgement and social pressure at the checkout?
content.subject: Children/young people
speakerTitles: Deputy Mayor for Social Affairs and Public Safety

content.title: Holodomor — why is it so difficult for Sweden to recognise the genocide of Ukrainians?
content.description: Holodomor — the Soviet famine that killed millions of Ukrainians in 1932–33 — is recognised as genocide by more than twenty countries. Sweden is not one of them. What are the political, diplomatic and historical obstacles — and what is the cost of silence?
content.extendedDescription:
Holodomor is one of the most extensively documented crimes against humanity of the twentieth century. Yet Sweden has not recognised it as genocide — unlike countries such as the USA, Canada, Poland, Estonia and around twenty others. Why?
This debate brings together members of parliament and analysts to examine the obstacles holding back recognition: diplomatic considerations, a lack of historical knowledge, political disagreement and Russia's active opposition to the recognition process in Europe. We also ask: what does Sweden's silence signal to Ukraine and the Ukrainian people?

The discussion is organised within Samarbetsplattformen: Sverige & Ukraina (SPSU), an initiative by KlinteVolontär that gives Ukrainian civil society its own voice in Sweden's democratic debate and brings Swedish and Ukrainian organisations together to strengthen long-term cooperation between the countries.
content.subject: Human rights
content.organizationType: Collaboration between different types of organisation
content.accessibility: Wheelchair-accessible entrance and venue

content.title: The hidden will to defend: Ukraine's outdoor organisations show the way
content.description: How can Sweden harness the strength of the outdoor movement's 7 000 associations and their two million memberships in crisis and war? Lessons from the war in Ukraine show that civil society plays a crucial role and that outdoor recreation is preparedness.
content.extendedDescription:
When Russia invaded Ukraine, it quickly became clear that the country's resilience was not based solely on military strength. It also relied on civil society's exceptional ability to act when the state could no longer meet every need.

In Ukraine, the scouting movement has organised the collection and distribution of food, clothing and medicines, served as local crisis hubs and supported refugees and internally displaced people. Hunting organisations and hunters mobilised early thanks to their local knowledge, outdoor skills and experience with equipment and leadership. Civilian boating organisations have evacuated people, delivered supplies and maintained vital transport when roads and bridges were destroyed.

Together with key figures in Sweden's civil defence and representatives of the Swedish outdoor movement, we discuss how outdoor recreation can contribute to preparedness efforts.
content.subject: Security/defence

content.title: Future of Everything: Sweden's and Europe's place in an AI-dominated world
content.description: AI is changing the foundations of business, culture, democracy and competitiveness. The question is not whether change is coming, but what happens to Sweden and Europe when it does. What choices must we make now to avoid becoming passengers in a future determined by others?
content.extendedDescription:
AI is set to redefine what drives growth, what counts as human creativity, how Europe defends its autonomy and what intelligence means at all. Future of Everything comprises four short stage discussions approaching these questions from different perspectives.

Future of Business: What is needed for Sweden to keep producing world-class companies as AI reshapes value chains?

Future of Europe: What will the European AI stack look like in five years, and what does autonomy mean in practice?

Future of Creativity: What happens to art, copyright and the creative professions when machines become co-creators?

Future of Everything: What will remain of us as humans when machines take over more and more of what previously defined us?
content.subject: Business

content.title: Capital for gender equality — future financing for sustainable development
content.description: How can new financial solutions mobilise capital for women's rights and economic equality?
content.extendedDescription:
Although gender equality is essential to sustainable development, only a small share of the world's capital goes towards women's rights and gender equality. At the same time, interest is growing in impact investing, sustainable financial markets and innovative financial solutions that can generate both social change and long-term economic development.

Gender bonds, gender-lens investing and fintech for financial inclusion are attracting increasing attention in Sweden and internationally. Banks, investors, development aid organisations, international organisations and civil society are exploring how capital markets can be used to strengthen women's economic empowerment and finance gender equality work on a larger scale.

The discussion brings together participants from the public sector, financial sector, international organisations and civil society to discuss how innovative financing models can contribute to gender equality and sustainable development — in Sweden and globally.
content.subject: Gender equality

content.title: Electricity supply in a crisis — where are the limits of Sweden's total defence?
content.description: Storm Johannes was a stress test for Sweden's electricity system and showed that both businesses and public authorities can deliver under intense pressure. At the same time, it made clear that we are close to the limits of our capacity.
content.extendedDescription:
Ellevio's seminar in Almedalen looks ahead: what is needed for electricity supply to withstand not just a single disruption, but several simultaneous crises — or, in the worst case, an armed attack?
The seminar begins with a review of Storm Johannes and key lessons. We then hear perspectives on policy direction and civil defence.

A subsequent panel discusses crucial questions for Sweden's total defence:
• How should preparedness be scaled — and are today's planning assumptions sufficient?
• Where is the boundary between market responsibility and the role of the state?
• How is electricity prioritised when not everything can operate at once?
• What is needed for cooperation to be operational, rather than based solely on goodwill?

Join a discussion about resilience, priorities and the electricity supply of the future in a new security environment.
content.subject: Energy

content.title: The distance between life and death — can the industry unite against railway trespassing?
content.description: Every day, rail traffic in Sweden is affected by people on or near the tracks. The consequences can be serious for the individual, the train driver, passengers and the entire railway system.
content.extendedDescription: Railway trespassing causes more than accidents and near misses. It also leads to disruption, delays and reduced punctuality. Every time trains are stopped or slowed down, thousands of passengers and large parts of the transport system are affected. During Almedalsveckan, Järnvägsbranschens samverkansforum (JBS) brings together leading representatives of the railway sector, public transport and politics to discuss why the issue matters so much, why the industry has chosen to act together and how cooperation can improve safety, punctuality and the resilience of the transport system. This spring, the railway industry has, for the first time, united in a joint national campaign against railway trespassing. The campaign highlights how small the distance can be between a risky decision and a life-changing accident, and how small changes in behaviour can make a big difference.

content.title: We want to help children learn more plant names than brand names
content.description: Who needs wild plants? Plant blindness and biophobia are spreading, widening the distance between us and the ecosystem we are part of. How can we reverse the trend and challenge children to learn our most common plant species, which are also important for our pollinators?
content.extendedDescription:
Programme, 26 June 13.45–14.45
with Anna Lind Lewin and Lotta Fabricius Kristiansen, founders of Pollinera Sverige:
- What are the threats to pollinators?

- How can we counter plant blindness and gaps in knowledge, and reduce our distance from nature?

- Presentation of Pollinera Sverige's survey ‘Have we become plant-blind?’

- Do we need wild plants? In what ways?

- How are pollinators doing on Gotland? Region Gotland is investing in Pollineringsveckan in May.

- How do we increase knowledge of wild flora locally? Does every area of Sweden need its own plant canon?

- How we want to help children learn more plant names than brand names: the school competition ‘Växtblind eller Artsmart’ launches in spring 2027.

- Which plants should feature in our wild plant canon for pollinators? Join in and vote!
content.subject: Animals/nature

content.title: Local politicians' influence and differences in values between politicians and voters
content.description: How much influence do local politicians around the country have, and what differences in values exist between citizens and politicians?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden's democracy is based on representative democracy, but how much influence do local representatives have in practice?

This seminar presents findings from Demoskop's recurring survey of Sweden's municipal and regional politicians — Politikerpanelen. How do local politicians perceive their actual influence, how much power do officials in our municipalities and regions have, and can citizens really influence political developments around the country?

Love Edander Arvefjord, consultant at Demoskop and project manager for Politikerpanelen, presents how Sweden's local politicians answer these questions. Johan Martinsson, Head of Public Opinion at Demoskop, then highlights and discusses differences in values between citizens and politicians, and between urban and rural areas. A panel of representatives from politics, the media and research then comments on and discusses the findings.
content.subject: Democracy
content.accessibility: Wheelchair-accessible entrance and venue

content.title: When AI democratises branding — who is in control?
content.description: Generative AI turns more people into content creators — and brand builders. The opportunities are substantial, but so is the growing risk that a brand will be disseminated and interpreted without a coherent whole. What holds a brand together when more employees, partners and resellers create content?
content.extendedDescription:
Generative AI turns more people within a company into content producers and, consequently, brand builders. The opportunities are enormous, but for large organisations this also brings a new risk: that the brand is disseminated, interpreted and used without anyone truly holding the whole together. This raises the question of what holds a brand together when creation increasingly spreads to employees, partners, resellers and others.

The panel explores the tension between speed and coherence. We highlight examples of what happens when AI relies on outdated guidelines, incorrect input or a weak understanding of the brand. Where is the boundary between healthy decentralisation and dilution of what we want to achieve with the brand? Is ‘control’ even the right ambition, or is it about embedding the brand so deeply that it can withstand being created by many?
content.subject: Digitalisation

content.title: The role of combined heat and power in total defence
content.description: In a more uncertain world, the resilience of the energy system becomes a central part of Sweden's total defence. Combined heat and power can help maintain stable electricity and heat supplies to healthcare, industry and defence even during disruptions. How resilient is Sweden's energy system in a crisis, and what role can combined heat and power play?
content.extendedDescription: This seminar starts from the contribution that combined heat and power makes to society in the face of threats, a possible attack or disruption, what works well today and what needs to be developed. Combined heat and power and district heating have a unique ability to deliver both electricity and heat even when electricity supplies are limited or other parts of the energy system are attacked, such as attacks on substations and transmission lines, or digital control systems being disabled by sabotage or cyberattacks. Lessons from Ukraine show how attacks on electricity grids and heat production quickly affect civilian society's functions, and how local energy production can become crucial. The seminar also uses hypothetical scenarios in a Swedish context to highlight what combined heat and power can do today and how it needs to develop to continue contributing to Swedish preparedness.
content.subject: Energy

content.title: Migration and development aid — how does KD want to shape policy after the next election?
content.description: The link between migration and development aid has gained political importance in Sweden and the EU. Aid is increasingly used to support migration policy objectives, raising questions about effectiveness, priorities and conflicting goals.
content.extendedDescription:
How do the parliamentary parties want to shape policy at the intersection of migration and development aid ahead of the next parliamentary term? In this discussion, Delmi and EBA invite representatives of the parties holding their party day in Almedalen to set out their priorities on an issue that has rapidly risen up the political agenda.

Drawing on current research and European experience, the discussion examines key choices: to what extent aid should be used for migration policy purposes, how different objectives should be balanced and which instruments should take priority. Topics include conditional aid, geographical priorities, deductions from aid budgets and possible departures from OECD-DAC rules.

The discussion aims to clarify the parties' positions and contribute to a more evidence-based debate on a policy area facing important choices.
content.detail: Migration och bistånd - två frågor i ett tält
content.subject: Research

content.title: Obesity — unlike other diseases?
content.description: Modern obesity care with drug treatment offers the prospect of eventually reversing the negative trend of continuous weight gain in the population and reducing serious secondary diseases, including cardiovascular conditions. But who should receive care, who should decide, and who should pay?
content.extendedDescription:
More than half of all Swedes are overweight, and one in six has obesity. The societal challenge is substantial, yet obesity is not treated like other diseases. Access to region-run obesity care is limited, and many people turn to digital healthcare providers specialising in obesity. Increasing numbers are treated with modern GLP-1 medicines and pay out of their own pocket.

How should regions organise obesity care and cooperation with external digital healthcare providers? How should primary care manage patients with obesity who are at high risk of serious illness? How is the clinical encounter affected when the patient pays for treatment? How can care become more equitable across regions and socioeconomic groups?

Breakfast is served from 08:00.

content.title: More generations at work — but are workplaces ready?
content.description: Our labour market has five working generations and a rapidly growing proportion of older workers. More people are pursuing further education and changing careers later in life. This places new demands on how workplaces are designed, operate and are led.
content.extendedDescription:
When more generations share a workplace, questions arise about everything from the physical environment, tasks and ways of working to leadership, communication, culture and attitudes. At the same time, norms and assumptions persist that can limit people when they are considered to have progressed ‘too far’ in their working lives. How do we create workplaces that attract and work for people of different ages? Where several generations can thrive, develop and work together further into later life — without ageism setting limits?

In this discussion, we explore the strengths of multigenerational workplaces, how ageism can be countered in practice and the demands placed on future workplaces, leaders and organisations. How should working life be designed — culturally, spatially and organisationally — so that more people can contribute, develop and work longer?
content.subject: Economy

speakerTitles: All-rounder and Former CEO of TV4

content.title: From ambition to practice — how do we develop public–private cooperation in civil defence?
content.description: Business is crucial to Sweden's security of supply and civil defence. Yet there is still no clear model for how the state and businesses should cooperate in practice. How do we move from ambitions for public–private cooperation to workable models?
content.extendedDescription:
There is broad ambition to strengthen public–private cooperation in civil defence. Yet a clear national model for organising this cooperation in practice is still lacking.

Several inquiries and strategies point to the need for new forms of cooperation, including security-of-supply agreements and other models to secure access to critical resources in crisis and war.

But how do we develop effective cooperation in practice?

This panel discussion takes that question as its starting point and explores how cooperation between the state, public authorities and business can develop in peacetime to strengthen Sweden's resilience. The focus is on practical models, the division of responsibilities and how solutions can be scaled nationally. The discussion is held in cooperation with Krisledningspodden, with Mats Bohman as moderator.
content.subject: Security/defence
speakerTitles: Head of Security and Defence Policy
Lead for Societal Security and Civil Defence

content.title: Can we innovate as if lives were at stake when they are not? Lessons from Ukraine's drone war
content.description: Can we innovate as if lives were at stake when they are not? Driven by necessity, Ukraine has developed inexpensive drones to disable expensive weapons systems. The pace of innovation is exceptionally high. New drone models, for example, can be invented and developed in just a few weeks.
content.extendedDescription:
The military works seamlessly with public authorities, NGOs and startups towards the same goal. Sweden supports Ukraine with money, knowledge and equipment. What can we learn from their experience? How do we create structures for exchanging innovation that work in both everyday life and crisis? How can cooperation in technological innovation become a natural part of our resilience?

Meet representatives from Ukraine whose different perspectives are important to success at the front. Join a powerful discussion about how drone technology and civil society's capacity for innovation enable Ukraine's successes, followed by a dialogue on how Sweden can prepare for war.

For security reasons, the participants from Ukraine will only be named at the discussion.
content.subject: Infrastructure/transport
speakerTitles: Head of Cybersecurity and Secure Communications

content.title: How do we strengthen medicine preparedness throughout Sweden?
content.description: When medicines are unavailable or need to be redistributed, questions arise in everyday healthcare: How do we strengthen regions' ability to prevent and manage shortages? And what national coordination is needed to meet regional challenges?
content.extendedDescription:
The seminar starts from the government's assignment to Läkemedelsverket and Försvarsmakten to analyse how medicines are managed and distributed within Försvarsmakten and in cooperation with other organisations, to enable more appropriate medicine management and better cooperation between civilian and military healthcare.

Alongside this assignment, broader national efforts are under way to secure access to medicines. The inquiry Säkrare tillgång till läkemedel will, among other things, propose measures to prevent and manage supply disruptions and shortages, including antibiotics, review a national coordination and purchasing function, and analyse how the allocation and redistribution of medicines can work better. The government and SKR have also reached an agreement for 2026 on stronger stockholding ahead of new requirements for regions from 2027.
content.subject: Health and social care
speakerTitles: State Secretary to Minister for Health Care Elisabet Lann
Director of Health and Medical Care

content.title: Can your morning swim reduce Gotland's water shortage?
content.description: A shower uses an average of 60 litres of water. When visitor numbers on Gotland peak, pressure increases on an island facing water shortages. Water is vital, both on Gotland and globally. How can we encourage more people to replace their morning shower with a dip in the sea?
content.extendedDescription:
Why shower alone when you can swim together? Every morning during Almedalsveckan, between 8–10, Region Gotland and WaterAid invite you to a shared morning swim at Kallis to highlight Gotland's water shortage and the importance of sustainable water use. WaterAid works in some of the world's most vulnerable areas to ensure that everyone has access to clean water, toilets and hygiene.
During the week, visitors are encouraged to swim and receive a ‘Badborgarmärke’ badge, meet experts who explore water issues from both local and global perspectives, and make the biggest ‘splash’. The organisers provide outdoor soap to borrow and coffee after the swim. Bring your own towel and swimwear.
By taking part, everyone can help reduce water consumption while getting a refreshing start to the day.
But how many Almedalen visitors and local residents will dare to take a dip in the waves?
content.subject: Sustainability
content.accessibility: Wheelchair-accessible entrance and venue

content.title: Can your morning swim reduce Gotland's water shortage?
content.description: A shower uses an average of 60 litres of water. When visitor numbers on Gotland peak, pressure increases on an island facing water shortages. Water is vital, both on Gotland and globally. How can we encourage more people to replace their morning shower with a dip in the sea?
content.extendedDescription:
Why shower alone when you can swim together? Every morning during Almedalsveckan, between 8–10, Region Gotland and WaterAid invite you to a shared morning swim at Kallis to highlight Gotland's water shortage and the importance of sustainable water use. WaterAid works in some of the world's most vulnerable areas to ensure that everyone has access to clean water, toilets and hygiene.
During the week, visitors are encouraged to swim and receive a ‘Badborgarmärke’ badge, meet experts who explore water issues from both local and global perspectives, and make the biggest ‘splash’. The organisers provide outdoor soap to borrow and coffee after the swim. Bring your own towel and swimwear.
By taking part, everyone can help reduce water consumption while getting a refreshing start to the day.
But how many Almedalen visitors and local residents will dare to take a dip in the waves?

content.description: The water beneath our feet — the water that should simply be there, flow from the tap and work. On Gotland, that is not the case. The municipal water has been unfit for consumption, quarrying is lowering groundwater levels and groundwater is not being replenished. What needs to happen?

content.title: Climate targets meet public responsibilities
content.description: How can Sweden build safer and more sustainable public-service buildings? Timber-based building systems for remand centres, prisons and barracks. Timber offers flexible, scalable solutions with a low climate impact, faster processes and maintained security. What is the way forward?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden needs to expand public-service buildings such as remand centres, prisons and barracks. At the same time, climate targets and the security situation, not least the war in Ukraine, demand faster, smarter and more resilient construction. The seminar explores how timber-based building systems can contribute.

We highlight innovation, client requirements and how public-sector organisations can drive progress with climate-smart and flexible solutions. We discuss the needs of total defence and the role of industry, as well as how timber can strengthen preparedness through shorter lead times and domestic production.

The discussion covers carbon storage, prefabrication, circularity and flexible use. We analyse the capacity of the timber value chain and what is needed to scale up. Fire issues are also addressed, with a focus on safety, durability and modern solutions.

Together, we discuss how Sweden can develop robust and climate-smart public-service buildings in timber.
content.subject: Sustainability

content.title: The suburbs, racism and the 2026 election — who gets to define the problems?
content.description: Ahead of the 2026 election, crime, safety and ‘vulnerable areas’ dominate political debate. Problems in the suburbs are often described in simplistic and stigmatising terms. How does this framing affect political priorities and legislation?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden has recently faced sharp criticism in a UN report for shortcomings in its work against racism. The report criticises several political reforms, including the proposed good-conduct requirement and the introduction of so-called security zones. It warns of an increased risk of discriminatory racial profiling, growing exclusion and economic inequality. This panel discussion provides a platform for perspectives, experiences and analyses that are too rarely given space in public debate.

The event takes the form of a moderated panel discussion and addresses, among other things:
- How ‘vulnerable areas’ and crime are framed in the election debate ahead of 2026.
- Consequences for political priorities, legislation and democratic participation.
- Alternative perspectives and solutions that rarely receive space in national debate.
content.subject: Democracy

content.title: Migration and development aid — how do V and M want to shape policy after the next election?
content.description: The link between migration and development aid has gained political importance in Sweden and the EU. Aid is increasingly used to support migration policy objectives, raising questions about effectiveness, priorities and conflicting goals.
content.extendedDescription:
How do the parliamentary parties want to shape policy at the intersection of migration and development aid ahead of the next parliamentary term? In this discussion, Delmi and EBA invite representatives of the parties holding their party day in Almedalen to set out their priorities on an issue that has rapidly risen up the political agenda.

Drawing on current research and European experience, the discussion examines key choices: to what extent aid should be used for migration policy purposes, how different objectives should be balanced and which instruments should take priority. Topics include conditional aid, geographical priorities, deductions from aid budgets and possible departures from OECD-DAC rules.

The discussion aims to clarify the parties' positions and contribute to a more evidence-based debate on a policy area facing important choices.
content.detail: Migration och bistånd - två frågor i ett tält
content.subject: Research
speakerTitles: Member of Parliament and Spokesperson on Development Aid Policy
Member of the Riksdag and Chair of the Committee on Social Insurance

content.title: A pain nurse at every primary care centre
content.description: One in five people lives with persistent pain, but primary care often lacks the right expertise. A pain nurse at every primary care centre could provide early support, create equitable care and reduce sick leave, mental ill health and the need for specialist care. Patients are currently passed around the healthcare system without a clear way forward.
content.extendedDescription:
One in five adults in Sweden lives with persistent pain. That is around 1.7 million people, with many more cases going unrecorded. Many wait years for the right diagnosis and help. Musculoskeletal pain is one of the most common causes of long-term sick leave, second only to mental ill health. The cost to society is estimated at around 2.5 per cent of GDP each year.
Behind the figures are people with fibromyalgia, hypermobility and EDS. The conditions differ, but end up in the same place: primary care, without access to staff with the right expertise in persistent pain. When help is delayed, other problems often follow. Depression, anxiety, exhaustion. Early intervention is not just about relieving pain, but about preventing an entire life from falling apart.
Two patient associations are coming together in Almedalen to move the issue from the waiting room to the decision-making table.
Come and listen to the dialogue with politicians about better care for patients with pain.
content.subject: Health and social care
speakerTitles: Member of Parliament and Centerpartiet's lead member on the Committee on Health and Welfare
Opposition Regional Councillor, Member of the Health and Medical Care Committee

content.title: Sweden should send peace doves — not bombs
content.description: As major powers build up their armed forces and conflicts deepen, the language of peace becomes more important than ever. Diplomacy is not weakness. It is the courage to choose dialogue over confrontation and cooperation over conflict.
content.extendedDescription:
In a time of growing geopolitical tensions, rearmament and armed conflict, we need more spaces where the voice of peace can be heard. In this workshop, participants are invited to fold peace doves and write personal messages about peace, dialogue and international cooperation.

The collected messages will then be compiled and presented to Sweden's Minister for Defence as a symbolic reminder of the importance of safeguarding diplomacy, human security and peaceful solutions to global conflicts.
As the world faces difficult choices, we need to ask ourselves: How do we create conditions for dialogue as divisions grow? How do we ensure that conversation and cooperation have more space than confrontation and mistrust?

Diplomacy is not passivity. It is active work to prevent conflicts and build lasting peace. Through this workshop, we want to give participants the opportunity to contribute their own perspectives and jointly highlight the importance of the language of peace in troubled times.
content.subject: Security/defence

content.title: 92 per cent goes up in smoke — who takes responsibility for plastic?
content.description: Despite ambitious environmental targets and world-leading waste systems, only 8 per cent of all plastic placed on the Swedish market is currently recycled. Meanwhile, more than 75 per cent is incinerated to produce district heating and electricity.
content.extendedDescription:
Plastic incineration accounts for 7 per cent of Sweden's national emissions and almost all of district heating's climate impact. This is a problem for both the climate and competitiveness. Through emissions trading and a fee to the EU, Sweden pays billions every year for these emissions — costs that risk increasing unless the waste system changes.

At the same time, stakeholders across the plastic value chain want to move in the same direction: energy companies need more recycling to reduce emissions and costs, plastic producers need recycled material to meet climate targets and forthcoming quota requirements, and municipalities and consumers expect real circularity.

But plastic is trapped in a system that was not designed for circulation and where responsibility is fragmented. The seminar brings together industry, politicians and municipalities to discuss how policy instruments and incentives can reduce emissions, lower costs and strengthen competitiveness.
content.subject: Sustainability
speakerTitles: Head of Business Development & Public Affairs

content.title: Taxes: an election weapon or a foundation for growth?
content.description: Taxes are crucial to the future of businesses and Sweden as a nation of entrepreneurs. But short-term thinking and bloc politics risk undermining long-term trust. Which tax issues matter most to businesses ahead of the election? And can politicians find common ground that creates stability?
content.extendedDescription:
Taxes affect everything from willingness to invest and entrepreneurship to changes of ownership and generational succession. But are politicians in tune with what Swedish businesses and their owners actually need? And how can Sweden create a more predictable tax policy that extends beyond a single parliamentary term?

The panel takes stock of Sweden's tax climate ahead of the election. Which reforms matter most? Where is the boundary between ideology and reality? And above all: is there a willingness to stop using taxes as a weapon in the election campaign?

In this panel debate during Almedalsveckan, PwC invites representatives of parliamentary parties and business organisations to discuss taxes, entrepreneurship and how Swedish tax policy can become a force for stability and growth.
content.subject: Business
speakerTitles: Member of Parliament and member of the Committee on Taxation

content.title: How can the public sector strengthen its procurement capability for the future?
content.description: Public procurement must contribute to sustainability, preparedness and secure supplies while demands for commercial competence increase. How can the public sector strengthen its skills and capability to meet new societal challenges?
content.extendedDescription:
Public procurement exceeds SEK 1000 billion each year and affects everything from the climate transition and welfare to preparedness, security of supply and efforts to combat welfare fraud. In a more uncertain world, the procurement function has taken on an increasingly strategic role, while demands relating to law, sustainability, commercial competence, digitalisation and AI are rising rapidly.

How can the public sector ensure it has the right skills to meet these demands? Drawing on SOI's updated competency profile, we discuss the skills and ways of working needed to strengthen the profession, improve delivery quality and create public-sector business relationships that are sustainable over the long term.

The discussion brings perspectives on governance, sustainability, preparedness and practical implementation, focusing on how central government, regions and municipalities can equip their organisations for future challenges.
content.subject: Employment/labour market

content.title: The road to a resilient and competitive electricity system — how do we get there?
content.description: Electrification, geopolitical tensions and volatile electricity prices are increasing the demands on Sweden's electricity system. How do we build a system that can withstand crises, enable investment and deliver fossil-free electricity at competitive prices?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden's electricity system needs to become both more resilient and more competitive. It must withstand disruptions and crises, adapt to changing conditions and recover quickly after outages or strains. At the same time, it needs to deliver fossil-free electricity with high reliability, stable prices and predictable investment conditions.

Achieving this requires flexibility in generation, storage and demand, diversified electricity production and robust grid infrastructure with redundancy and reserve capacity. Equally important are available grid capacity, efficient permitting processes and long-term political ground rules that enable profitable investment. How can Sweden build an electricity system that both withstands disruptions and strengthens competitiveness?
content.subject: Energy

content.title: Legislate for defibrillators to be accessible 24-7
content.description: Around 6 000 out-of-hospital cardiac arrests are reported in Sweden each year. Approximately 70 per cent occur in or near the home. Yet most defibrillators are located in workplaces and are often inaccessible when they are needed most. There is now a concrete legislative proposal for round-the-clock access to defibrillators.
content.extendedDescription:
BFHS proposes a legal requirement for defibrillators in residential buildings

Branschrådet för Hjärtstartare i Sverige (BFHS) has developed a concrete legislative proposal to make defibrillators a standard feature of residential buildings. The background is clear: around 6 000 out-of-hospital cardiac arrests are reported in Sweden each year, and approximately 70 per cent occur in or near the home. Despite this, most defibrillators are located in workplaces and are often inaccessible when they are needed most.

The proposal, Lagförslag hjärtstartare 2025_3, aims to increase accessibility, strengthen national preparedness and create a more equitable, life-saving system throughout the country. Clearer responsibilities for property owners could save more lives each year. We want to encourage engagement and give decision-makers a concrete basis for future legislation.
content.subject: Security/defence

content.title: Hydrogen's role for Sweden: industry, the energy system and security of supply
content.description: Hydrogen is less about technology and more about what kind of Sweden we want to be. At a time of growing import dependence, global competition and energy transition, fossil-free hydrogen can strengthen competitiveness, security of supply and the climate transition where alternatives are lacking. What role should it play?
content.extendedDescription:
Please note that the entire hydrogen arena is broadcast via the link above.

In this seminar, we show how and in what form hydrogen can contribute to a more competitive Sweden that is independent of fossil fuels. Topics include hydrogen's role in the energy system, from local initiatives to national development. What role does hydrogen play in the energy system of the future? What synergies are there with district heating? And how can hydrogen contribute to greater flexibility, security of supply and resilience in the electricity system, both locally and nationally? We bring together industry stakeholders and researchers to discuss how hydrogen creates value, from municipal initiatives to large-scale investments. Through concrete examples, we highlight how hydrogen connects electricity, industry and transport, and what is needed for more participants to help realise its potential.
content.subject: Energy

content.title: Building under way — civil defence from planning to robust capacity
content.description: Total defence is being built up rapidly and is largely implemented by municipalities and regions. How can active, structured cooperation work at county level and over time when many stakeholders have a seat at the table?
content.extendedDescription:
The world and Sweden face a difficult security situation. Total defence is now being built up rapidly and will largely be implemented by, and affect, municipalities and regions. These are where people live their lives and where critical welfare functions are maintained around the clock, every day of the year — in everyday life, in crisis and ultimately in war.
The seminar focuses on how active, structured cooperation can work at county level and over time, with many stakeholders at the table and clarity about methods, exercises and dependencies. We discuss with participants:

• How do you move from planning in documents to robust, real capacity?
• What characterises an organisation that ‘has capability’?
• Their best advice for achieving the ability to act together.
content.detail: Kommun- och regionarenan (by the Kruttornet car park/Strandvägen)

content.title: Litter harms animals — both wildlife and pets
content.description: Broken glass injures paws, chocolate and grape leftovers and glycol spills can poison dogs, and picnic leftovers in plastic bags or on cigarette butts can cause animals to eat the plastic too.
content.extendedDescription:
Bring your dog and join our walk against litter! We meet at 16:30 by the Söderport car park, set off towards Almedalen at 17:00 and return to our starting point at 18:00.

The walk is an initiative by Håll Sverige Rent as part of the project ‘Fan-tass-tiska perspektiv’, which approaches litter from the perspective of animals, especially pets. The walk is organised in cooperation with Gotlands kennelklubb. Members of the public, with or without dogs, are welcome to join by registering in advance: https://hallsverigerent.typeform.com/to/W5wAwUQC

The project aims to increase awareness in Sweden of the connection between litter and injuries to pets, and to influence behaviours and attitudes through this new knowledge. The project is funded by Postkodlotteriet. Svedea is also a partner and is analysing litter-related pet injuries to identify where the most important measures can be taken.
content.subject: Animals/nature

content.title: Military defence moves forward — threats, risks, challenges and solutions
content.description: Försvarsmakten faces extensive rearmament, technological development and demands for greater resilience. At the same time, public support, the right skills and effective NATO integration are needed. What challenges does the Supreme Commander face, and how can he address current and future threats?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden's security situation has changed rapidly, placing high demands on Försvarsmakten. Expansion of equipment and personnel must take place alongside a technological shift in weapons systems. Society's resilience also needs to be strengthened more broadly across civilian and military organisations. NATO membership brings new opportunities, but also requirements for interoperability and cooperation. The legitimacy of defence rests on public support and trust, while the right skills and leadership are crucial to success in the current situation.
- How can Försvarsmakten attract and retain the right skills?
- What investment is needed to meet the technological shift?
- How can society's resilience and civil defence be strengthened?
- How can public support and the will to defend be maintained?
- How can effective and rapid NATO integration be ensured?
content.subject: Security/defence

content.title: Popular education 2.0: how do we make AI skills Sweden's new basic competency?
content.description: Sweden has an enormous AI skills gap — most white-collar workers see a need for AI, but only a fraction are offered training. How do we move from a few AI professionals to practical education for everyone?
content.extendedDescription:
For Sweden to be competitive, a handful of experts is not enough; we need broad understanding across the population. Realising AI's potential requires a public education effort on the scale of the introduction of universal schooling or the rollout of broadband.

But today's gap is wide. A large majority of working people see an immediate need for AI skills, but only a fraction are offered training and few employers have a plan to meet this need, creating a major skills gap. In this session, we discuss lessons from and challenges in large-scale continuing education in AI. How do we reach all the way into municipal offices and out to small-business owners? We explore how, together, we can build the national AI literacy that the labour market of the future requires.
content.subject: Digitalisation
content.organizationType: Collaboration between different types of organisation

content.title: From Skåne to Europe: how industrial biotechnology can strengthen Sweden's competitiveness
content.description: Industrial biotechnology is key to Sweden's future competitiveness, preparedness and sustainable growth. Sweden has strong research, innovative companies and good access to raw materials — but risks losing momentum as other parts of the world scale up faster.
content.extendedDescription:
Europe is now mobilising to meet global competition, and European stakeholders are pushing for simpler regulations, strategic investment and more scale-up facilities.

This panel brings together stakeholders and politicians with regional roots to discuss how Sweden can take a clearer role in Europe's biotechnology transition. We identify the conditions needed for innovations to stay, scale up and create value in Sweden, and how we can help shape a Europe that leads in industrial biotechnology.

The discussion is led by Biotech Heights. The innovation hub brings together organisations seeking to develop and advance biotechnology for food and materials. Biotech Heights is based in Lund and is an example of how a strong regional platform can contribute to national and European development.
content.subject: Business
content.organizationType: Collaboration between different types of organisation

content.title: Cheaper or more resilient — how do we build the energy system of the future?
content.description: The electrification of society and industrial expansion require investment in energy infrastructure on an unprecedented scale. At the same time, the energy system must deliver electricity at reasonable and competitive prices. How do we prioritise?
content.extendedDescription:
The electrification of society and industrial expansion require investment in energy infrastructure on an unprecedented scale. At the same time, the energy system must deliver electricity at reasonable and competitive prices. The deteriorating geopolitical situation demands greater preparedness to secure supplies: energy infrastructure must be not only efficient but also robust and resilient to disruption.

Are more power lines the solution — or can we use the energy system more intelligently?
Svenska kraftnät is investing SEK 225 billion in the transmission grid up to 2035. But major challenges remain in regional and local grids, where capacity shortages hinder new industrial development. The gas grid provides flexible energy, for example through gas turbines when demand peaks. This can both ease pressure on the electricity system and strengthen Sweden's security-of-supply preparedness.
So how do we prioritise?
content.subject: Energy

content.title: Trust as Strategy: Communication leadership in building a stronger Nordic future
content.description: In a time of geopolitical uncertainty, growing competition and polarization, can the Nordic region strengthen its collective position through shared values, trust and strategic communication? Could a New Nordic narrative become a strategic advantage?
content.extendedDescription:
Trust is a critical asset for societies, institutions and businesses alike, and communication professionals play a central role in building and maintaining it. Based on Nordic data, this seminar explores whether shared values such as transparency, responsibility and social trust can form the foundation of a stronger pan-Nordic framework.

While national differences shape reputation priorities, significant common ground suggests untapped potential for a unified strategic narrative that strengthens competitiveness, resilience and international influence.

Panelists discuss whether New Nordic can evolve from cultural identity into a practical framework that supports economic growth, democratic stability and geopolitical relevance in an increasingly uncertain world.
content.detail:
Reputation and Trust Analytics

content.subject: Communication/information

content.title: Security and cooperation — how do we create a safer future?
content.description: Security and insecurity are among our biggest societal challenges. What measures, working methods and legislative changes are needed to reverse the trend? How do we strengthen cooperation between public authorities and businesses to increase security?
content.extendedDescription:
Serious organised crime now affects large parts of society, from local communities to businesses and public services. Reversing the trend requires long-term, coordinated work involving multiple stakeholders.

In this session, decision-makers and the organisers of SäkerhetsArenan discuss what is needed in the work ahead to keep our society safe.

New technology creates both opportunities and new risks. How can the public and private sectors work together to counter crime? How can we conduct thorough background checks?

SäkerhetsArenan is organised by SäkerhetsBranschen, Stöldskyddsföreningen, Brandskyddsföreningen, Stiftelsen Tryggare Sverige, Almega Säkerhetsföretagen, Företagsuniversitetet and Säkerhets- och försvarsföretagen (SOFF). Together, we create a shared meeting place for discussions that strengthen Sweden.
content.subject: Security/defence

content.title: Nanoplastics and human health
content.description: Nanoplastics are present in air, water, food and the human body. Research shows that these particles can cross biological barriers and affect the body's organs and systems. What does current research say about health risks, societal impacts and the need for cooperation?
content.extendedDescription:
Nanoplastics consist of extremely small plastic particles that can cross the body's biological barriers, such as the intestinal barrier, the blood–brain barrier and the placenta. Studies show that microplastics and nanoplastics can be found in several organs and tissues, where they can contribute to inflammation, oxidative stress and effects on cell function. Research points to possible links with effects on the nervous system, cardiovascular system, hormonal balance and reproductive health.

During the seminar, Allatra Sweden presents an interdisciplinary view of nanoplastics from a public health perspective. The event takes the form of a seminar with a presentation. No prior knowledge is required.

The aim is to increase knowledge of nanoplastics as a growing societal challenge and create a constructive discussion about the need for further research, preventive measures and international cooperation between researchers, decision-makers and civil society.
content.subject: Climate/environment
content.accessibility: The event is captioned

content.title: Who wins political mudslinging? Civility as a strategy of resistance for democratic dialogue
content.description: Over the past decade, threats and hate have changed political dialogue. This societal development has already had a major impact on our democracy. But what happens to democracy when the tone of debate hardens? Can civility be a strategy of resistance for a better climate of discussion and stronger democracy?
content.extendedDescription:
It is high time we came together to bring about change. Against this background, TCO has launched the report Hövlighetsmissionen. It introduces four principles for a better climate of discussion — principles that can be applied wherever people meet.

Drawing on the report, we bring together politicians, societal stakeholders and journalists to discuss tone, how we treat one another and today's climate of debate. What happens to trust when the tone hardens? Have the rules changed — and if so, how? Is a respectful tone necessary, and how does it affect voters?

Join a discussion about tone and treatment, today's climate of debate and what is needed for change ahead.
content.subject: Democracy

content.title: How well prepared are we to handle sabotage against our drinking water supply?
content.description: Cooperation between organisations to improve understanding of their different roles, identify needs and develop shared ways of working during suspected incidents can be crucial when essential services are sabotaged. Robust preparedness is a vital part of strengthening civil defence.
content.extendedDescription:
When drinking water is threatened: Sweden's first joint sabotage exercise involving water and wastewater operations and the police.

This seminar highlights experience from a completed field exercise. Water and wastewater staff from Region Gotland and the Gotland local police area, supported by Livsmedelsverket, jointly practised a realistic sabotage scenario involving a municipal drinking water facility. The exercise clearly demonstrated the value of cooperation between organisations in improving understanding of roles, identifying needs and developing shared ways of working during suspected incidents. Particular emphasis is placed on the value of field exercises and planning for success. Robust water and wastewater preparedness is a vital part of strengthening civil defence.
content.subject: Security/defence

content.title: A journey through Sweden: diversity, inclusion and what actually works
content.description: Sweden faces both a growing skills shortage and widespread exclusion. Although many people want to and can work, they still encounter barriers to entering working life. Which measures work in practice to make better use of skills and strengthen integration?
content.extendedDescription:
Diversity and inclusion are high on the agenda in most organisations. Yet the gap between intention and reality is well known. What actually makes a difference, and what is mostly about looking good?

Aaron Kroon has travelled around Sweden, meeting leaders and employees across the country. His conversations with people on the ground have given him a picture of integration and inclusion that is rarely seen in public debate: nuanced, sometimes surprising and always rooted in reality.

Christian Horne from Ambea interviews Aaron about what he has seen and learned. Which initiatives deliver real results? What works in workplaces that succeed, and what holds back those that do not? And what should leaders prioritise if they want to do more than tick a box?

The discussion concludes with questions from the audience.
content.subject: Integration/diversity

content.title: From potential to practice: when new technologies such as AI become critical to society
content.description: What requirements must be set for infrastructure, data centres, storage, secure networks, connectivity, data and governance so that new technologies such as AI can be deployed in essential services?
content.extendedDescription:
As society becomes deeply digitalised, at a time of rapid technological development, growing cyber threats and increased demands for resilience, it is no longer enough for each individual component to work on its own. It becomes crucial for the entire digital chain to hold together. Healthcare, energy, finance and other essential services now depend on interconnected infrastructure in which data centres, storage, communications layers such as 5G and secure networks, operations, procurement and next-generation technologies such as AI must work seamlessly together and withstand pressure.

This discussion brings together decision-makers from the public sector, business and politics to consider whether Sweden's digital capability will hold up as new technologies move into the most critical services, and what is needed for every layer of the chain to perform. How do we combine rapid innovation with control, security and long-term societal resilience?
content.subject: Digitalisation

content.title: Taxis as a pillar of society — from everyday life to crisis
content.description: How do we secure taxis as a pillar of society and a preparedness resource across the country — and what political decisions are needed locally, regionally and nationally?
content.extendedDescription:
When society needs passenger transport most — during disruptions, extreme weather, pandemics or heightened alert — the capacity must be there. But emergency preparedness is not built in a vacuum. It relies on genuine taxi services and other lawful operators being available in everyday life to provide safe, traceable, high-quality passenger transport throughout Sweden. At the same time, legitimate businesses are under pressure from unlicensed taxis, illegal taxi operations and labour-related crime, undermining both competition and society's actual transport capacity. The seminar brings together experts and decision-makers to discuss how policy, procurement and requirements can strengthen legality, safety and delivery capability — from everyday life to crisis.

Coffee and cake will be served during the seminar.
content.subject: Infrastructure/transport

content.title: Mandatory but flexible — how does the EU solidarity model affect Sweden?
content.description: The EU's new Pact on Migration and Asylum is based on a solidarity principle intended to distribute responsibility for receiving asylum seekers among member states. What does it mean in practice — and how might it affect Sweden?
content.extendedDescription:
In spring 2024, the EU adopted a new Pact on Migration and Asylum. The pact includes the introduction of a mandatory but flexible solidarity mechanism. Its purpose is to redistribute responsibility away from member states under high migration pressure, mainly at the EU's external border, through mandatory relocations of asylum seekers, financial contributions or support in the form of resources and personnel, with countries choosing how to contribute. The mechanism replaces previous arrangements and is intended to create a more predictable division of responsibility within the EU. At the same time, it raises questions about how the balance between different forms of support will work in practice.

The discussion focuses particularly on what this means for Sweden. How might Sweden use the solidarity mechanism? What political and administrative choices arise, and how might Sweden's role in European cooperation be affected when the system starts to be applied?
content.detail: Migration och bistånd - två frågor i ett tält
content.subject: Research

content.title: General or targeted government grants: what delivers the greatest benefit for patients and taxpayers?
content.description: The government pays tens of billions in healthcare grants to the regions each year, despite the regions having their own responsibilities and taxation powers. Does the money have the intended effects on care, or does it merely fund deficits? And does it matter whether the grants are general or targeted?
content.extendedDescription:
In 2025, the government paid around SEK 70 billion in healthcare grants, a figure that has doubled since 2015. At the same time, the regions are responsible for healthcare and have their own taxation powers. Are government grants needed at all, and do they lead to real change? The answers depend on whom you ask. SKR argues that general grants give regions scope to set the right priorities and reduce unnecessary administration. During its term, the government has reduced targeted grants and increased general grants, while moving billions from SKR to Socialstyrelsen. Critics argue that the money risks disappearing into regional deficits without measurable effect.
In this seminar, we explore which grant model delivers the greatest benefit for patients and taxpayers.
content.subject: Health and social care

content.title: No peace without justice — what can we do about impunity for international crimes in Ukraine?
content.description: Russia's invasion of Ukraine constitutes a serious violation of international law. At the same time, civilians are subjected to indiscriminate attacks. There are also extensive reports of war crimes committed by Russian forces, including torture of prisoners of war, sexual violence against civilians and the deportation of children.
content.extendedDescription:
Join a seminar offering an up-to-date overview of efforts to combat impunity for international crimes in Ukraine: Who has the mandate to investigate war crimes and bring perpetrators to justice? How can evidence be secured in a way that stands up in court? Why is a special tribunal for the crime of aggression needed? And what is being done to ensure compensation for those affected?

During the seminar, we highlight how individuals, civil society organisations and states can contribute to justice. Aggression must not pay. International crimes must not go unpunished. And the harm caused must be recognised and compensated.

Together, we can counter impunity and work towards accountability for Ukraine — because without justice, there is no lasting peace.
content.subject: International affairs
speakerTitles: EU Special Representative for Human Rights

content.title: The Stockholm–Mälar region in the national plan — major benefits but implementation challenges
content.description: The Stockholm–Mälar region accounts for just over half of Sweden's GDP. If Mälardalsrådet's prioritised infrastructure investments are implemented, benefits could reach SEK 222 billion. But this requires projects to be completed on time and skills shortages to be addressed.
content.extendedDescription:
More than four million people live in the Stockholm–Mälar region, which is home to several global corporations. 150 million tonnes of freight are transported to, from and through the region. 850 000 residents commute across one or more municipal boundaries to get to work. 8 out of 10 train journeys in Sweden start or end in Stockholm.

A report from Mälardalsrådet shows that investment in the Stockholm–Mälar region's transport infrastructure delivers benefits of SEK 222 billion through, among other things, shorter journey times, increased freight transport, climate benefits and higher tax revenues. The benefit analysis is based on priorities for roads, railways and shipping lanes agreed by seven regions within Mälardalsrådet's transport policy cooperation En Bättre Sits.

The event is part of Mälardalsarenan, organised by Mälardalsrådet, Mälardalens universitet and Västerås stad.
content.subject: Infrastructure/transport
content.accessibility: Wheelchair-accessible entrance and venue

content.title: Human trafficking in Sweden in 2026 — have we become better at protecting the most vulnerable?
content.description: Human trafficking is one of the most serious human rights violations of our time. Despite legislation, public-authority and international commitments, women, children and men continue to be subjected to sexual exploitation, forced labour, begging and other forms of exploitation. What action is needed, and by whom?
content.extendedDescription:
No single organisation can bear the responsibility for combating human trafficking alone. Effective action requires cooperation between public authorities, the justice system, civil society, churches and international organisations. How can this cooperation be strengthened? What experience do those who meet victims have? And what reforms are needed for Sweden to better prevent human trafficking, protect vulnerable people and hold perpetrators accountable?

Led by Erik Eckerdal, Bishop of Visby Diocese and Svenska kyrkan i utlandet (SKUT), representatives from the government, public authorities, churches and civil society come together to discuss human trafficking, prostitution, digital exploitation and Sweden's responsibility to safeguard the human dignity of the most vulnerable.
content.subject: Human rights

content.title: How can we be more sustainable in health, climate and business?
content.description: How do we address invisible ill health? How can we be optimistic about the climate crisis? How can we benefit from the ambitious talent available in Sweden?
content.extendedDescription:
Discussions in Samtalsträdgården are divided into sessions lasting 45-60 minutes, led by different experts or initiative leaders.

Friday's discussions cover the following topics and are led by the following people:

09.00 - 09.45 ‘When employees suffer in silence — whose responsibility is it?’
An open discussion about what often falls through the cracks: invisible ill health.
Sandra Jönsson and Rebecca Arfwedson, Wellbefy — smarter occupational health!

10.00 - 10.45 ‘Being optimistic about solving the climate crisis — a discussion on the climate transition and what we need to do’
A discussion on the state of the energy transition and how to increase carbon dioxide removal (CDR) through biochar and CCS.
Karsten Deppert, Carbon Collective & Kalle Nilvér, GoClimate

11.00 - 11.45 ‘Challenges in attracting and retaining international talent in business’
How can the public and nonprofit sectors help make Swedish workplaces internationally competitive?
Emelie Andir, Project Manager, Mindpark
