content.title: Can AI strengthen democracy and solve societal problems — for real?
content.description: Can AI be used to lower barriers to democratic participation, increase young people's voter turnout and build trust in society's institutions? How do we move from technology and vision to solving major societal challenges in areas such as climate, health, education, inclusion and humanitarian work?
content.extendedDescription:
How do we take AI from technology and vision to real positive impact in areas such as democracy, climate, health, education, inclusion and humanitarian work?

Can we use AI to strengthen democracy, increase participation and build trust in society's institutions? Drawing, among other things, on our hackathon at Järvaveckan — based on the question of how to motivate more young people to vote in the coming election — we discuss how AI can move from idea to real societal benefit.

The panel brings together different perspectives — technology, ethics, law and societal development — to discuss how we can accelerate both AI adoption and benefits to society. AI is one of the most powerful technologies of our time, but its real value is determined by how, and for what, it is used.
content.subject: Digitalisation

content.title: Disability rights in the digital era
content.description: Not everyone is equal in the information society. While people in Sweden are increasingly dependent on the digital world in everyday life, it remains inaccessible to many. What risks and opportunities does AI present?
content.extendedDescription:
Wikimedia Sverige invites you to breakfast and a discussion about digital accessibility.

Sooner or later, everyone experiences a disability. You may not be able to hear, see, move or speak in the same way as others. As more and more of our lives move into the digital arena, most services and apps are not designed for everyone to use on equal terms.

Sooner or later, most people will therefore find it much harder to use the internet, one of humanity's greatest inventions.

Wikimedia Sverige is the Swedish support association for Wikipedia, and we invite you to breakfast with a short panel discussion on AI, disability rights, accessibility and universal design on the internet. We welcome disability rights organisations, public authorities, politicians and technology companies that want to build a better world.

The event is organised through the project ‘Ett Wikispeech för alla’, funded by Allmänna arvsfonden.
content.subject: Digitalisation

content.title: Is parental insurance equally accessible to all parents?
content.description: Parental insurance is an important tool for promoting gender equality by enabling both women and men to combine family and work. But is it equally accessible to all parents, regardless of background?
content.extendedDescription:
Parental insurance and the right to parental leave are crucial to Sweden's high labour force participation among parents, particularly mothers. At the same time, employment rates differ greatly between groups of parents; for example, foreign-born women have much lower participation than women born in Sweden. How does this relate to differences between groups in the use of parental insurance and leave?

In this discussion, TCO presents a new report examining how the use of parental leave differs between groups according to origin, income and education level. This is followed by a discussion of how to make parental insurance more accessible and ensure that it truly becomes a tool promoting employment and gender equality for all parents, regardless of origin.
content.subject: Gender equality
content.accessibility: Hearing loop, wheelchair-accessible toilet, wheelchair-accessible entrance and venue

content.title: Swedish migration policy today and tomorrow — legally secure and sustainable choices
content.description: Swedish asylum and migration policy is currently undergoing extensive changes. The reforms affect many people and have long-term consequences. How can we shape sustainable migration policy for the future?
content.extendedDescription:
Swedish asylum and migration policy is currently undergoing extensive changes. National reforms and the implementation of the EU Pact on Migration and Asylum mean far-reaching changes to both rules and practice. These decisions will have long-term consequences for legal certainty, integration, sustainable return and Sweden's role in European and global cooperation.
The discussion will address what returning people to crisis-affected countries entails. What role does resettlement play in receiving refugees? What is at stake if the European Convention on Human Rights is reinterpreted, and how is legal certainty affected by so-called ‘safe third countries’ and return hubs?
Act Svenska kyrkan and RESCUE invite you to a discussion with the parties' migration policy spokespersons about legally secure and sustainable choices for the migration policy of the future.
content.subject: Integration/diversity

content.title: Sweden and Ukraine as equal partners — are we there yet?
content.description: Sweden has supported Ukraine — but is it a genuine partnership or symbolic solidarity? How can Ukrainian and Swedish stakeholders meet as equals to build long-term cooperation?
content.extendedDescription:
Samarbetsplattformen: Sverige & Ukraina (SPSU) is a project by KlinteVolontär — a civilian meeting place that gives Ukrainian civil society its own voice in Sweden's democratic debate and brings Swedish and Ukrainian organisations together to strengthen long-term cooperation between the countries.

The tent on Cramérgatan is open to everyone throughout the week. It is a place to pause, take a break from the conference circuit and meet people properly — Ukrainians, volunteers, politicians, researchers and curious citizens. No stage. No name badges determining who gets to speak. Every day, there are seminars and open table discussions about the war, responsibility and the future. The tent also has a photo spot where you can capture the moment and take home a memory of the week.

The week's themes: traditions of remembrance and grief, war crimes and accountability, municipal cooperation, the survival of cultural heritage, civil defence, healthcare in war and Ukraine's path towards the EU.

content.title: The role of foreign trade and shipping in Sweden's supply capacity in crisis and war
content.description: Functioning maritime trade flows in crisis and war are essential to Sweden's security-of-supply preparedness. Strengthening these capabilities requires long-term, deeper cooperation between private and public organisations.
content.extendedDescription: Foreign trade is a central part of Sweden's economy and crucial to access to important goods and raw materials for both businesses and citizens. For the country to withstand disruptions to global trade flows, stable, long-term security-of-supply preparedness and strong military preparedness are necessary. Shipping is a key component: it carries most of Sweden's imports and exports and enables efficient, reliable transport connecting the country with the world. During the seminar, representatives of public authorities and business, together with decision-makers, discuss how Sweden can strengthen the conditions for secure and open maritime foreign trade, robust security-of-supply preparedness and shipping that effectively contributes to the country's resilience and security.
content.subject: Infrastructure/transport
speakerTitles: Deputy Head of Unit and Expert on Foreign Trade and Preparedness
Member of Parliament, Chair of the Committee on Foreign Affairs

content.title: How can Swedish cities win the competition for talent, businesses and residents?
content.description: As competition for skills, investment and the tax base intensifies, cities' attractiveness becomes crucial to long-term growth, sustainability and societal development.
content.extendedDescription:
Swedish cities operate at a time when global competition, demographic change and new working patterns are reshaping the conditions for urban development. The ability to attract and retain residents, businesses and skills has become central to economic vitality, innovation and long-term sustainability. Factors such as safety, the housing market, infrastructure, public services and social cohesion increasingly affect a city's competitiveness.

The seminar highlights the drivers that strengthen Swedish cities' attractiveness, the challenges that risk weakening it and the strategic choices required to secure future growth. Through data, analysis and exchanges of experience, it also discusses how municipal decision-makers work with concrete strategies and experience from their own cities to strengthen attraction, retention and long-term competitiveness.

content.title: The curse of agreements — when political deals become obstacles to action
content.description: Politics is increasingly bound by agreements between parties, providing stability but potentially reducing the ability to act and respond. How is trust in politics affected when agreements take precedence and risk creating deadlock while the world around us changes?
content.extendedDescription:
The Swedish labour market model rests on trust and collective agreements that evolve with working life and society. Politics, by contrast, is moving towards more agreements between parties, from Decemberöverenskommelsen to Januariavtalet and Tidöavtalet. These can create stability, but also risk locking politics into lists of commitments when rapid adaptation is needed.

When room for manoeuvre is constrained in advance, the dialogue that has long enabled effective interaction between politics and the social partners is reduced. This affects the ability of politics to address issues that directly shape working life.

Where is the boundary between necessary stability and lost freedom to act? Unionen brings together a panel to discuss the benefits and limitations of agreements — and how politics can adapt to a changing world without jeopardising parliamentary stability.
content.subject: Democracy

content.title: If war comes — will Sweden's digital backbone hold?
content.description: Communications, command, data and robust infrastructure are now integral to operational capability. As threats intensify, the question becomes urgent: will critical networks, communications links and digital dependencies hold when it really matters?
content.extendedDescription:
After decades of dismantling, responsibilities and cooperation must be rebuilt while pressure from the outside world increases. Can the public sector, Försvarsmakten and companies providing essential services move quickly enough to deliver real operational effect? Who takes responsibility when civilian and military dependencies meet in real time?

At the same time, fragmentation, short-term procurement and unclear responsibilities risk making the digital backbone a weak link. Capability is only as strong as its weakest procurement. How do we prevent governance, processes and decision-making pathways from becoming the bottleneck when the pace must increase?

But the issue is not just about withstanding the first disruption. How do we build a digital defence that can adapt, develop and endure? This requires the ability to repair, restore and strengthen critical systems while pressure continues.
content.subject: Security/defence

content.title: Forests of the future — which decisions today will shape society in 2100?
content.description: Forests' long rotation periods — in Sweden, trees are harvested after an average of 100 years — mean today's political decisions affect the economy, welfare, jobs, climate and biodiversity well into the next century. How should conflicting goals be balanced when future needs meet today's choices?
content.extendedDescription:
What will Sweden look like in 2100 — and what decisions must be made today to get us there? This seminar brings together representatives of political youth organisations to discuss the forests and society of the future. When welfare, rural development, consumption, climate and biodiversity are weighed against each other, what do they choose — and why?

Forests must meet many needs: jobs, exports, the climate transition, biodiversity and thriving rural areas. But when not everything can be prioritised at once, political choices become decisive.

One question is central: how do we make wise decisions about a resource whose consequences will only be felt long after the next election campaign?

This is a discussion about responsibility, direction and confidence in the future — but also about which decisions actually strengthen Sweden's raw material supply, competitiveness and welfare in the long term.
content.subject: Sustainability

content.title: Who takes responsibility for an equitable tech industry — and how do we retain women?
content.description: Women's place in tech is crucial to Sweden's skills supply. What helps women thrive, what makes them hesitate — and whose responsibility is change?
content.extendedDescription:
Minister for Gender Equality Nina Larsson (L) participates as Women in Tech Sweden releases this year's report, State of Women in Tech Sverige 2026 — a snapshot of women's experiences in and around the Swedish tech industry.

The report is based on the association's annual member survey and highlights what makes women thrive and stay in tech, what makes them consider leaving, and the roles of leadership and workplace culture. It also addresses unequal treatment, where members believe responsibility for an equitable industry lies, and what the next generation wants to work with.

Elin Eriksson and Åsa Johansen from Women in Tech Sweden present the report. The panel then discusses what the findings mean for employers, the education system and politics — and for Sweden's skills supply and competitiveness.

The event is free and open to everyone.

Organiser: Women in Tech Sweden.
content.subject: Integration/diversity

content.title: When the lights go out and the heat stops: is Sweden ready?
content.description: The war in Ukraine has shown the world that energy is an instrument of power. When Russian missiles knocked out electricity and heating during winter, parliament went dark and millions were forced to live in darkness and freezing cold. How well equipped is Sweden's total defence to withstand a similar scenario?
content.extendedDescription:
The war in Ukraine has shown the world that energy is an instrument of power. When Russian missiles knocked out electricity and heating during winter, parliament went dark and millions were forced to live in darkness and freezing cold. How well equipped is Sweden's total defence to withstand a similar scenario? Russian cyberattacks on Poland's energy system show that we must be ready today.

How we protect critical infrastructure and ensure a robust energy supply is absolutely crucial to our preparedness in crisis and war. Without electricity, water and heating, all operations stop and the most vital functions in our homes cease to work. We bring together politicians, public-authority representatives and business leaders responsible for keeping Sweden's lights on, even when a crisis becomes reality. Resilience in the energy system is an important form of life insurance.
content.subject: Infrastructure/transport

content.title: How do we strengthen Baltic Sea security through innovation?
content.description: Growing tensions and hybrid threats are changing the security situation around the Baltic Sea, which is central to Sweden's security and supply. Critical infrastructure, sea routes and airspace must be protected. What role do innovation and strategic technology play in Sweden's defence capability?
content.extendedDescription:
A panel discussion on how Sweden can harness skills and expertise from the civilian technology sector to increase resilience and defence capability. Vinnova and Försvarsmakten are running a joint initiative to strengthen the development of innovative defence technology. We fund innovation projects in which civilian organisations and companies in technology, innovation and industry cooperate with military organisations to contribute to a modern defence.

The civil–military innovation programme (CMIP) is carried out by Vinnova and Försvarsmakten on behalf of the government to strengthen Swedish defence capability through synergies between civilian and military research and development. The programme is supported by Försvarshögskolan, Totalförsvarets forskningsinstitut (FOI) and Försvarets materielverk.
content.subject: Innovation
content.accessibility: The event is captioned, Wheelchair-accessible toilet, Wheelchair-accessible entrance and venue

Moderator, Strategic Adviser on Defence Innovation

content.title: Norrbotten — Sweden's Arctic
content.description: As part of the Arctic territory and a substantial part of the Swedish Arctic, Norrbotten differs from the rest of the country. Not only in its climate, but in many issues taken for granted as national election issues.
content.extendedDescription:
Join a roundtable discussion on the Swedish Arctic!

Important trade routes run straight through the Arctic, and many major powers meet in what has now become a geopolitically and strategically highly significant part of the world. This year, the EU and Sweden are presenting new Arctic strategies.

Norrbotten is a substantial part of the Swedish Arctic and, as in the rest of the territory, local communities form the core of what we call the Arctic, whether the issue is strategic raw materials, preparedness, research or tourism.

Are the issues that will shape this year's election campaign equally relevant to Norrbotten and Arctic Sweden, or do they reflect only challenges in Stockholm? For example, there is virtually no unemployment along the Arctic Circle; the sparse population and long distances create difficulties but also offer advantages.
content.subject: Regional issues

content.title: Precision medicine — a healthcare cost or Sweden's next engine of growth?
content.description: Precision medicine is highlighted as a key to the healthcare of the future, with the potential to improve patient outcomes and strengthen Sweden's competitiveness in life sciences. Despite strong research and advanced care, implementation in Swedish healthcare remains slow.
content.extendedDescription:
Precision medicine can both improve patient outcomes and strengthen Sweden's competitiveness in life sciences. Yet implementation in Swedish healthcare remains slow.

What is needed to make better use of these strengths and improve Sweden's position as a country for clinical trials and precision medicine? What decisions are needed to make precision medicine a strategic engine of growth for Sweden, and how can we attract investment and innovation?

Participants from politics, healthcare and industry come together to discuss how implementation can be accelerated and Sweden's position strengthened. Contributors include representatives from Sahlgrenska Universitetssjukhuset, SwedenBIO and AstraZeneca.
content.subject: Business
content.organizationType: Collaboration between different types of organisation
speakerTitles: Senior Director of Science Policy & Relations Europe
Senior Consultant, Associate Professor of Cardiology, Centre for Precision Medicine,

content.title: Is everyone equal in the information society?
content.description: As people in Sweden become increasingly dependent on the digital world in everyday life, it remains inaccessible to many. How can we work together to overcome digital barriers for people with disabilities?
content.extendedDescription:
Sooner or later, everyone experiences a disability. You may not be able to hear, see, move or speak in the same way as others. As more and more of our lives move into the digital arena, most services and apps are not designed for everyone to use on equal terms.

Sooner or later, most people will therefore find it much harder to use the internet, one of humanity's greatest inventions. What can the state, civil society and business do about this? And what risks and opportunities do AI and language models present?

Wikimedia Sverige is the Swedish support association for Wikipedia, and we invite you to a panel discussion on accessibility and universal design on the internet. Listen to disability rights organisations describe everyday life for many people in Sweden and what can be done to improve it.

The event is organised through the project ‘Ett Wikispeech för alla’, funded by Allmänna arvsfonden.
content.subject: Digitalisation

content.title: Businesses have made the transition — but where are the electric cars?
content.description: Swedish businesses have invested billions in electrification, charging infrastructure and new business models to drive the climate transition. Despite this, progress is slow.
content.extendedDescription:
The reason is not a lack of technology or willingness, but changing political conditions. Reduced incentives, unclear ground rules and capacity-based tariffs that undermine profitability are making demand for electric cars hesitant, reducing returns on investment and postponing new initiatives. All this also creates uncertainty among consumers.
Meanwhile, Sweden has been overtaken by its Nordic neighbours. Not only Norway but also Denmark and Finland have a larger share of electric cars thanks to clear policy instruments.
This is also a question of European competitiveness. Industry is shifting production and investment towards electrification to cut emissions and retain jobs in Europe. But without stable political signals to both businesses and consumers, the transition risks losing even more momentum.
This discussion brings together business and politics to explore why the transition is sluggish — and what is needed to regain momentum.
content.subject: Sustainability
content.accessibility: Wheelchair-accessible toilet, wheelchair-accessible entrance and venue
speakerTitles: Deputy CEO and Head of e-Mobility

content.title: Advanced healthcare at home: how can better care be provided at home, and who benefits?
content.description: How can advanced healthcare at home make a difference for patients and their loved ones? Receiving care at home allows many people to remain at home rather than spending their final days in hospital.
content.extendedDescription:
Join us over two days to discuss how advanced healthcare at home (ASIH) can make a difference for patients and their loved ones. ASIH includes both care for acute illnesses from which the patient is expected to recover and care for patients with incurable illnesses, where good palliative care and symptom relief are crucial to quality of life and a sense of security. ASIH allows many patients to receive care at home despite needs that would otherwise require hospital admission.

During the two days, you can meet representatives of patient associations offering support and information to people with different diagnoses and their loved ones. You can also meet Palliativt Kunskapscentrum, which contributes extensive knowledge and experience of care, personal interaction and end-of-life issues.

Hear experiences, ask questions and discuss how home healthcare can develop to meet patients' needs in the best possible way.
content.subject: Health and social care

content.extendedDescription:

content.title: The gap between gut feeling, research and Nutri-Score — whom should you listen to about eating well?
content.description: Every day, we are inundated with fad diets and alarming reports. At the same time, the food system faces an enormous challenge: we need to eat for both our health and the planet. But why is the gap so wide between what we believe is healthy and what science actually says?
content.extendedDescription:
In this seminar, Erik Lundbom from Verian Group will present findings from a brand-new survey of Swedish attitudes to health and fast food, commissioned by MAX Burgers. The figures reveal a clear conflict between our preferences as customers and the reality on our plates.

In Sweden, Nyckelhålet has been our guide for decades, but it is now being challenged by international systems such as Nutri-Score. What happens when businesses move ahead of public authorities? Can an algorithm guide us correctly, or are we simply creating more confusion? Join a discussion on MAX's roof terrace about bridging the gap between unhealthy cravings and planetary health.

Arrive in good time! Before the seminar, we will offer brand-new burgers and samples of the luxury shake available exclusively during Almedalen.
content.detail: MAX Arena, the restaurant's roof terrace
content.subject: Food

content.title: A vibrant city centre is a matter of growth, not just enjoyment
content.description: A vibrant city centre is a matter of growth, not just enjoyment. Strong city centres attract people, skills and investment, creating jobs and a tax base. What is needed to make city centres part of the infrastructure for growth, in line with the government's strategy for vibrant and safe cities?
content.extendedDescription:
The city centre is not a nostalgic postcard. It is the region's engine of growth and hub for commerce, workplaces, investment and attractiveness. Property values, shop openings and hotel rooms indicate whether capital and skills want to stay or move away.

Behaviours and the economy are changing rapidly. E-commerce, hybrid working and demographic changes affect movement, consumption and safety needs. When more people want to live, work, invest and spend time in city centres, synergies emerge that strengthen industries and contribute to long-term development.

The seminar focuses on how to achieve this in practice. What political decisions, policy instruments and local initiatives are needed for lasting effects? The discussion covers mixed uses, mobility, simpler regulations and cooperation between municipalities, property owners, businesses and civil society.
content.subject: Business

content.title: The role of buildings in a future energy system?
content.description: The building stock is an important part of the energy system, but its role is changing. How do major ongoing shifts such as demographic change, electrification, battery technology and EU emissions policy affect Swedish property owners' role in the system?
content.extendedDescription: Sweden is currently implementing the EU's EPBD (Energy Performance in Buildings Directive), which aims to make the building stock more energy-efficient and, eventually, emission-free. At the same time, rapid changes in the surrounding energy system will have a tangible impact in the coming years. Plug-in vehicles are on the verge of dominating the vehicle fleet, and developments in battery chemistries and bidirectional charging could take their role several steps further. Sweden's electricity surplus is attracting well-capitalised data centre operators, further spurred by major AI company stock market listings this summer, and electricity market conditions could change quickly. What overall picture does this paint of the role of buildings and property owners in the new energy system? How does our built environment need to respond and contribute?

content.title: How can we help more young people get their first job?
content.description: Many young people want to work, while employers report difficulty finding the right skills. Yet they fail to connect. Why is this, and what needs to change so that more young people can enter working life?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden has high youth unemployment compared with many other European countries. At the same time, employers in several sectors report skills shortages and difficulty finding the right staff. This points to a clear gap between young people and the labour market.
What causes it? Is it education, employers' requirements or the way systems are designed? And what is needed for more young people to actually get a chance at their first job?
The business community has recently launched a joint initiative to help excluded young people into work, aiming to get 100 000 young people into jobs through 1 000 companies over the next ten years. But what conditions are needed for more employers to recruit? What role does politics play — and what responsibility does business have?

In this discussion, representatives of political youth organisations come together to discuss practical solutions for lowering barriers to the labour market.
content.subject: Employment/labour market

content.title: How can business develop and politics bring about more change?
content.description: We want to discuss vibrant city centres, politics that dares to make changes, retaining international talent and how business in Skåne can improve.
content.extendedDescription:
Discussions in Samtalsträdgården are divided into sessions lasting 45-60 minutes, led by different experts or initiative leaders.

Is politics too timid to tackle the real underlying problems?

Can companies become more sustainable through better owner directives?

content.title: Politics Change, Scholarship Endures: Celebrating Fulbright Sweden Since 1952
content.description: International academic exchange has long strengthened mutual understanding, research cooperation, and democratic resilience. As geopolitical tensions rise and political priorities shift, what role can educational exchange programs play in sustaining strong transatlantic relationships.
content.extendedDescription:
This discussion examines the role of international educational exchange in advancing diplomacy, research collaboration, and democratic engagement between Sweden and the United States. For more than seven decades, Fulbright Sweden has connected students, researchers, educators, and professionals across borders, creating networks that often outlast political administrations and policy cycles.

At a time of increasing geopolitical competition, polarization, and pressure on international cooperation, educational exchange programs raise important questions about how societies build trust, develop future leaders, and maintain strong international partnerships. The conversation will explore the long-term impact of academic mobility on innovation, public policy, higher education, and transatlantic relations.
content.subject: Innovation

content.title: Why are so many children with allergies inadequately treated?
content.description: Pollen allergy is very common among children and young people. It reduces quality of life, lowers school performance and increases the risk of asthma. New data show that more than half of 16-year-olds have uncontrolled disease and only 14% are adequately treated. How can more children get help?
content.extendedDescription:
Is it finally time to address Sweden's most common widespread disease?

One in three people has an allergic disease. A national strategy and national guidelines have now been presented. The strategy emphasises, among other things, that primary care looks after most allergy patients, that access to care varies by socioeconomic status, and that there is a shortage of allergy specialists.

What happens now? Is this the moment when care for what may be Sweden's most common widespread disease takes a step forward, receives resources and becomes a priority?

What do the regions need to do to make primary care governance work, increase fairness and train more allergists? And what is the state doing?

Join an evening of knowledge about allergies, with three themes, from 17-19 in our garden. Hot food and drinks will be available, with opportunities to mingle.
content.subject: Health and social care
speakerTitles: Chair of the Regional Executive Board

content.title: Time to leave the 1980s behind and accelerate electrification
content.description: How do we get electrification moving? Despite high ambitions, electricity use remains at 1980s levels. What measures are needed to accelerate progress? This is crucial to meeting climate targets, securing competitiveness and reducing our need for fossil fuels.
content.extendedDescription: Electrification is too slow. Despite high ambitions, electricity use remains at 1980s levels. Electrification is crucial if we are to meet our climate targets, reduce dependence on imported fossil fuels and secure Sweden's competitiveness. Measures are now needed to make the transition easier for both industry and households. These include taxes, industrial policy, permitting processes and a well-functioning energy system. Today, as in the 1980s, we use around 140 TWh of electricity a year, while still using 140 TWh of fossil fuels. We will describe our dialogues with politicians, public authorities and businesses, as well as the sensible proposals we have collected. We will thank the 1980s for their time, because now it is time for the electricity use of the future!
content.subject: Energy

content.title: Lifelong learning — how do we take responsibility?
content.description: As the labour market changes rapidly through technological development, AI and new skills requirements, lifelong learning becomes crucial. But who is responsible for the transition — central government, regions, employers or individuals?
content.extendedDescription:
The labour market is changing ever faster. Digitalisation, AI and technological development affect both tasks and skills requirements in many professions.
This makes lifelong learning a central issue for individuals, employers and society. Yet the division of responsibility is often unclear. Who should be responsible for enabling people to adapt throughout a long working life?
Should responsibility lie primarily with individuals themselves, employers or society's education system? And how can different organisations cooperate to create effective routes to transition?
The discussion particularly highlights the role of folk high schools and other education providers, opportunities to validate existing skills and the risk of groups being left behind as the labour market changes rapidly. The seminar considers what an effective system for lifelong learning might look like in a time of rapid transition.
content.subject: Education

content.title: Children's summit and student citizens' assembly — engaging children and young people in local democracy
content.description: What does practical work on democracy look like in preschools and schools? We are seeing a trend in which fewer young people regard democracy as the best way to govern a country, while more consider a strong leader or expert a better alternative.
content.extendedDescription:
How can we build strong support for democracy in preschools and schools? By Almedalsveckan, the student citizens' assembly will have met twice. Karlstads kommun was the first municipality in the country to launch a student citizens' assembly for the climate. This democracy project aims to engage children and young people in climate and environmental issues and build confidence in the future and capacity to act by enabling real influence on local democracy.

In autumn 2022, pupils in Karlstads kommun's compulsory schools developed 967 concrete proposals. Of the final 67 proposals submitted to politicians, many have been approved for implementation. One proposal approved by the Children and Youth Committee was to create a permanent student citizens' assembly. This year, we developed the assembly into a children's summit during Barnrättsdagarna, on the theme of social sustainability.
content.subject: Children/young people

content.title: Your shopping basket after the election — the issues shaping food policy in the next parliamentary term
content.description: How will politics affect your shopping basket after the 2026 election? After several years marked by inflation, rising costs and geopolitical uncertainty, attention now turns to the choices that will shape Swedish food policy up to 2030.
content.extendedDescription:
Which political priorities will shape food policy in the next parliamentary term — and what will they mean for the food supply chain and consumers? The seminar discusses competitiveness, preparedness, climate, health and jobs, drawing on Svensk Dagligvaruhandel's election programme and party survey ahead of the 2026 election.

Will Sweden continue to go beyond EU requirements? How do the parties view VAT on food, young people's jobs in retail and companies' role in emergency preparedness? What happens to the shopping basket when politicians weigh regulation against competitiveness and efficiency?

Leading politicians, opinion-makers and industry representatives meet for a forward-looking discussion of the choices that will affect conditions for retail and people's everyday lives during the next parliamentary term.
content.subject: Economy
speakerTitles: Chair of the Committee on Industry and Trade
Head of the Katalys Think Tank

Deputy CEO of the Fores Think Tank

content.title: New paths for neighbourhood development — can we build our way out of segregation?
content.description: Segregation in Sweden persists despite extensive investment. New research shows how neighbourhoods affect life chances and how new construction in disadvantaged areas can change their trajectory.
content.extendedDescription:
Segregation in Sweden is the result of more than a century of housing policy, industrial transformation and migration patterns. In this seminar, we present new research mapping how Swedish segregation developed and which types of urban development have created the most mixed and sustainable neighbourhoods over time.
We also discuss which neighbourhood policies have real potential to improve living conditions in poor districts. Housing policy receives particular attention: can new apartment buildings in disadvantaged areas attract new groups, strengthen local services and benefit existing residents? New Swedish data show that well-designed housing projects can reduce poverty and create opportunities for residents to progress rather than be displaced.
Politics, research and municipal experience come together to discuss which models actually work.
Welcome!

content.title: Skills supply determines Sweden's life sciences position — what is needed now?
content.description: Sweden wants to lead in life sciences, but skills shortages hold back innovation, healthcare development and competitiveness. The strategy points the way but is not enough. Reaching the goals requires political priorities, cooperation and clear responsibility for skills supply.
content.extendedDescription: Securing skills in Swedish life sciences requires political priorities and cooperation between academia, healthcare and business. Needs range from medical and biomedical expertise to AI, data and digital health, as well as healthcare staff who can drive research and innovation — something today's systems do not fully meet. Life sciences and healthcare depend on one another: without the right skills, development stalls; without innovation, quality risks declining. Meeting these needs requires better analysis, future-oriented education, clear career paths, lifelong learning, stronger clinical research and the ability to attract international talent. What political choices are needed, how can cooperation be strengthened and responsibilities clarified? The seminar brings together stakeholders seeking to contribute solutions and strengthen Swedish competitiveness and patient benefit.
content.subject: Research

content.title: Sleepless in the city centre — what tools do municipalities need against reckless driving and traffic disturbances?
content.description: Residents of Swedish cities are affected by nighttime reckless driving, deafening engine noise and aggressive road behaviour, with consequences for safety, the living environment and conditions for business. Municipalities and the police need more tools to tackle recurring traffic disturbances in urban areas.
content.extendedDescription:
Municipalities are already installing noise cameras, introducing nighttime road closures and taking local measures, while the police struggle to prioritise the problem. The technology exists to fine drivers who cause disturbances — but current legislation does not provide sufficient scope.

Meanwhile, other European countries have gone further, and Denmark has introduced stricter rules in recent years, including the possibility of seizing vehicles in cases of serious and disruptive driving.

Swedish municipalities and the police need more tools to tackle recurring traffic disturbances in urban areas. How should safety, privacy and proportionality be balanced? And why is the issue still treated as a local problem when it recurs across the country?
content.subject: Justice/crime
speakerTitles: Head of Local Police Area, Malmö

content.title: Heta stubben: can nature help us find wonder and resilience in a polarised age?
content.description: In a time marked by anxiety, heated debate and widespread mental ill health, many people seek settings that offer calm, meaning and hope. Nature can offer both movement and stillness, but also community and wonder. How can nature, outdoor recreation and spirituality strengthen health and resilience?
content.extendedDescription:
Last year's Almedalen success, Heta stubben, is back. With the sea as a backdrop and the aroma of coffee from the camping stove, Friluftsfrämjandet will speak on several occasions with senior party figures and other decision-makers about their vision for outdoor recreation. 94 per cent of Swedes believe outdoor recreation is good for health and wellbeing. How can it become as natural a part of societal development as it is of our hearts? How can more people be encouraged to be active in nature?
Four in five children are not active enough, and almost half of adults have dangerously poor fitness. The proportion of children spending time in nature every day has fallen from 80 to 50 per cent over 20 years. While evidence of nature's health benefits has become robust, debate about how we manage forests and nature is often polarised.
content.subject: Sustainability

content.title: From requirements to capability — how do we build robust municipal preparedness?
content.description: New requirements for municipalities' and regions' preparedness for crisis and war are about to become reality, but how should they be translated into operational capability? How do we ensure municipalities have the right conditions to fulfil their remit and build robust preparedness?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden's municipalities and regions face stricter requirements for preparedness for crisis and war. The inquiry behind LKRB has now been followed by a bill to parliament, with municipal operational capability at its centre.

But how are these requirements put into practice?

Building robust preparedness involves more than planning. It requires effective leadership, cooperation, technical systems and practical capability even when normal structures come under pressure.

The seminar explores these questions and how operational preparedness can be built in municipalities, as well as the roles that central government, municipalities, business and civil society can play in developing robust, sustained preparedness. The discussion is held in cooperation with Krisledningspodden, with Mats Bohman as moderator.
content.subject: Security/defence
speakerTitles: Deputy Head of the Department for Strategic Direction and Planning
Head of Security of Supply and Risk Analysis
Head of the Department of Finance and Governance

content.title: Important measures for a healthier Baltic Sea
content.description: The Baltic Sea is one of the world's most polluted and overfished seas, but the right measures can reduce eutrophication, strengthen biodiversity and address climate change while enabling people to use the sea and its resources.
content.extendedDescription:
The Baltic Sea is a unique and sensitive ecosystem that has long faced major pressures, from overfishing to pollution, eutrophication and coastal development. Climate change is now adding further pressure. There are therefore calls for better protection and restoration of the marine environment.
At the same time, there is strong pressure to increase use of the sea for shipping, aquaculture, tourism, defence and wind power. Can these different ambitions be reconciled?

Fortunately, history shows that when people around the Baltic Sea come together and make wise decisions, major improvements and benefits can be achieved. Much has been done, but more is needed. At this Baltic Breakfast, researchers from Stockholms universitets Östersjöcentrum present a selection of the most important measures marine researchers have identified for a healthier sea that can also support a sustainable blue economy.
content.subject: Climate/environment
content.organizationType: Collaboration between different types of organisation

content.title: From war to a sustainable labour market — unions, migration and investment in Ukraine
content.description: How can Ukraine build a functioning and fair labour market during and after the war?
content.extendedDescription:
What roles do trade unions, labour mobility and investment play in Ukraine's reconstruction and closer ties with the EU? During the seminar, Union to Union presents a new report on the importance of unions in reconstruction, with concrete recommendations for politics and business. The discussion focuses on how dialogue and cooperation between the social partners can contribute to stability, fair working conditions and long-term development, taking the Swedish model as its starting point.
Migration is central: millions of Ukrainians have left the country amid labour shortages, while new migration flows into Ukraine are emerging, including from Central Asia. The seminar explores the effects on the labour market and the political and institutional responses needed. Perspectives from unions, politics and business are presented, focusing on Sweden's role and how international support can strengthen institutions and enable sustainable investment in Ukraine.

content.title: Can we travel to Almedalen without depleting our carbon budget?
content.description: Almedalsveckan is more than meetings — it drives ideas, relationships and real change. Digital meetings can achieve a great deal, but nothing beats the energy, creativity and decisions that emerge when people meet in person. The question is not whether we should meet, but how to do so without exceeding our carbon budget.
content.extendedDescription:
Many of our most important meeting places require travel. This is a challenge — but also an opportunity. How can we work together to make travel part of the solution rather than the problem? What happens when our travel policies conflict with the need to reach places such as Gotland, which we travel to by plane and ferry?

We invite you to a breakfast networking event focused on these questions. Discover practical, sustainable solutions and hear an exciting presentation showing that air and ferry services can already offer them.

There will be short presentations on stage and a panel discussion led by Maria Stenström, 2030-sekretariatet.

Breakfast is served from 07.00 — conversations among participants begin straight away, and the discussion on stage starts at 07:30.

content.title: How Sweden can succeed in a globally uncertain world
content.description: At a time of geopolitical uncertainty and intensifying global competition, how can Sweden succeed in a globally uncertain world?
content.extendedDescription:
Welcome to Business Sweden's garden! Open seminars and plenty of time to network over coffee.

Business Sweden is tasked by the government and the business community with supporting Swedish exports, attracting international investment to Sweden and contributing to greater competitiveness, sustainable growth and employment nationwide.

In Business Sweden's garden at Ryska Gränd 9, we invite you to an inspiring morning from 08.00–12.00, with open seminars, current perspectives from Swedish and international markets and opportunities to meet new people in a relaxed setting in the heart of Almedalen.
Coffee and refreshments are available throughout the morning.

Programme:

-08.00–09.00 — Breakfast seminar and panel discussion:
How we win the global export battle — 50 000 new industrial jobs are at stake
-09.00–09.25 — Discussion: Team Sweden team players
-09.30–09.50 — Discussion: Geopolitical outlook
-11.00–11.45 — Panel discussion:
How can Sweden secure industrial investments worth billions and jobs amid global competition?

Welcome!

content.title: Digital sovereignty for Sweden and Europe
content.description: Chip development, AI and cloud services are new instruments of power — and Europe is dependent. How do we strengthen our digital sovereignty through smarter procurement?
content.extendedDescription:
We live in a time when hardware, software, AI models and cloud services have become strategic instruments of power. Sweden and Europe depend heavily on a handful of global players, creating risks for innovation, security and self-determination. Critical societal functions need to work and must not be something someone else can switch off.
Digital sovereignty is about resilience and long-term capability, not isolation. The choices we make today shape the future, and we can achieve a great deal without waiting for legislation. The purchasing power of European public authorities and businesses is a powerful tool already available to us.
The seminar brings together those making strategic technology decisions in the public sector and business. We highlight concrete examples from organisations that have moved towards European alternatives, discuss what is required of buyers and suppliers, and identify practical policy implications for Sweden and Europe.
content.detail: Main hall, entrance from Korsgatan opposite Villa Gutebagge
content.subject: Digitalisation

content.title: How do we counter homelessness and vulnerability in society?
content.description: Recently, increasing numbers of younger people, foreign-born people, people with addictions and mental ill health, pensioners and families with children have become homeless. Those on the margins are now also affected by reduced or withdrawn benefits, while violent crime involves ever younger people.
content.extendedDescription:
We revisit questions from Frälsningsarmén's panel discussions on Tuesday and Wednesday:
- Evictions of families with children continue to increase. Why is it so difficult to stop children being evicted?
- What does the new co-occurring disorders legislation mean — is it the solution to the longstanding problem of people with both an addiction and mental ill health falling through the cracks and into homelessness?
- More voices advocate tougher measures against young offenders, including lowering the age of criminal responsibility. Is punishment a solution — or could it make matters worse?
Come and discuss these and other questions about homelessness and addiction care. What is needed to create a society without homelessness and vulnerability?
Representatives of Frälsningsarmén will be present: Per-Johan Fernström, Deputy Head of the Social Division; Maria Olausson, Corps Leader/Operations Lead; and Bodil Nilsson, Head of Operations.
content.subject: Human rights
content.accessibility: Wheelchair-accessible entrance and venue

content.title: What is needed to secure access to vegetables, fruit and berries nationwide in times of crisis?
content.description: What is needed to secure access to vegetables, fruit and berries throughout the country if a crisis comes? Who has responsibility, and who takes it?
content.extendedDescription:
What is on our plates during a crisis or when borders close? Grain storage is currently highlighted as a central element, but a prolonged crisis or serious disruption also requires access to vegetables, fruit and berries. Here, the share of Swedish produce has been declining steadily for a long time. How can access be secured in a crisis? What are the greatest threats? Who is responsible for ensuring these foods are available at all?

In this seminar, we discuss threats to and opportunities for securing access to vegetables, fruit and berries during different crises in Sweden. What does availability look like in different parts of the country? What are the greatest threats relating to cultivation, inputs such as seeds, crop protection, nutrients and water, as well as storage and distribution? What can be done to secure basic availability? What responsibilities lie with central government, municipalities and businesses? And with you?
content.subject: Food
speakerTitles: Member of the Regional Council and Regional Executive Board

content.title: Investment plan for Sweden — how can we secure forthcoming major investments in welfare?
content.description: The coming years require extensive investment in municipalities and regions, including upgrading large parts of the country's water and sewer networks and adapting society to climate change.
content.extendedDescription:
Municipalities and regions invest more than SEK 230 billion annually. These investments are crucial to ensuring equitable welfare nationwide, as well as strengthening Sweden's long-term growth and competitiveness. SKR has developed a consolidated investment plan for municipalities and regions up to 2040 — Investeringsplan för Sverige.

The coming years will require extensive reinvestment, including upgrades to the country's water and sewer networks, much of which were expanded in the 1960s and 1970s. At the same time, investment needs are growing to adapt buildings, roads and other infrastructure to a changing climate.

Investment needs exist nationwide, but conditions vary and risk hitting some municipalities and regions particularly hard. The seminar explores these needs, the available financial conditions and what is required of municipalities, regions

content.title: AI within our own walls — how do we enable secure innovation for faster care and patient safety?
content.description: How do we deliver faster care and greater patient safety without compromising citizens' privacy? How can an in-house AI platform ensure control over data, strengthen digital sovereignty and enable more efficient use of resources?
content.extendedDescription:
Västra Götalandsregionen (VGR) has now taken the next step on its AI journey with a powerful local AI platform, entirely within the region's own walls. This infrastructure provides VGR with the computing power needed to develop and deploy advanced AI solutions for both healthcare and research.

- They can now support projects and initiatives more quickly, promoting better decision support, more efficient care processes and improved research.

- Retain full control over sensitive data, with patient information never leaving their own IT environment, thereby meeting high standards of security, compliance and data protection.

- Create long-term societal value through scalable AI innovation, with the same platform supporting future healthcare needs, research and regional development without having to rebuild from scratch as new uses emerge.

content.title: Electrifying long-distance transport — more than a transition issue
content.description: The electrification of transport needs to accelerate — for the climate, resilience and Sweden's competitiveness. Climate policy, preparedness and industrial policy must be aligned. How do we achieve this?
content.extendedDescription:
Long-distance road transport is now ready to be electrified. The seminar presents findings from the E-Charge project showing how food deliveries can now run on electricity from Helsingborg - Stockholm and how vehicles can use high-power charging (MCS) during the driver's statutory break. The technology is here and we are ready to make the transition, for the climate, industry and perhaps also our preparedness. But long-term ground rules are needed to reduce uncertainty for those investing in vehicles and chargers.

The seminar includes representatives of the vehicle industry, transport buyers, charging operators, haulage companies and politics.
Proposals for policy instruments will be presented and discussed. It is an election year, after all!

content.title: Nobelbanan + Mälarbanan = a perfect match?
content.description: Can a regional route-location study accelerate Sweden's most profitable railway project?
content.extendedDescription:
Is Nobelbanan from Örebro to Karlstad, connecting to Oslo, the next step in Mälarbanan's development? Is Mälarbanan ready for a new national role, and can the regions help develop national planning?

When Mälarbanan was built in the late 1990s, it was Sweden's first major railway investment in many years. It launched the development of regional rail travel in Sweden. The route-location study for Nobelbanan is now nearing completion. Extending Mälarbanan with Nobelbanan is the next step both in expanding functional regions and in building a strong Nordic region.

In 2024, the regions along the Oslo-Stockholm corridor and Trafikverket decided to launch a pilot project involving a route-location study for Nobelbanan. What can we learn from a regionally led route-location study? Can it provide better input for national planning and enable a faster planning process?

content.title: The future of security policy — what does the next generation of leaders think?
content.description: Security policy is shaped today, but young people will live with its consequences tomorrow. As threats change rapidly, how should we address security, NATO and international cooperation?
content.extendedDescription:
We live in a constantly changing world. With new threats, rapid geopolitical shifts and urgent crises, security policy has become one of the defining issues of our time. Sweden now faces the challenge of navigating an uncertain world, and the decisions we make today will shape the world the next generation must live in tomorrow. How do today's choices affect the future? And what do young people think about the decisions being made now?

Utrikespolitiska förbundet (UFS) and Folk och Försvar invite you to an open debate in which political youth organisations can discuss Sweden's security, foreign and defence policy. Together, they will explore how Sweden can best address national security, international cooperation and NATO's role in uncertain times.

The debate is held at Folk och Försvar's arena in Almedalen, a meeting place for dialogue, knowledge exchange and cooperation on Sweden's security.

content.title: Abduction of Ukrainian children: how do we ensure Russia is held accountable?
content.description: Russia has deported thousands of Ukrainian children to Russia and Belarusian territories — a crime under international law. Arrest warrants have been issued. Yet the children are not returning. What is needed for Sweden and Europe to secure real accountability?
content.extendedDescription:
Since 2022, Russia has systematically deported Ukrainian children to Russian families and institutions — a war crime under the Rome Statute. In 2023, the ICC issued arrest warrants for Vladimir Putin and Maria Lvova-Belova. Yet most of the children are still missing. What prevents real accountability?
This discussion brings together members of parliament, children's rights organisations and analysts to examine what Sweden can actually do — in the UN, the EU, bilateral diplomacy and civil society advocacy — to secure the children's return and prosecution of those responsible.

The discussion is organised within Samarbetsplattformen: Sverige & Ukraina (SPSU), a project by KlinteVolontär that gives Ukrainian civil society its own voice in Sweden's democratic debate and brings Swedish and Ukrainian organisations together to strengthen long-term cooperation between the countries.
content.subject: Human rights

content.title: Energy supply under pressure — what decisions are needed now?
content.description: Electrification is driving rapidly growing demand for electricity. Meeting climate targets, strengthening competitiveness and ensuring preparedness require more electricity generation, smarter grids, energy storage and greater energy efficiency. What political decisions are needed now to secure Sweden's long-term energy supply?
content.extendedDescription:
How do we secure electricity as Sweden electrifies rapidly? RISE invites you to a breakfast networking event in Almedalen around four themes:
Energy production in Sweden — dispatchable and renewable electricity for a balanced power system
Energy storage & batteries — the key to stability, flexibility and preparedness
Energy transmission — grids, capacity and smarter use
Energy efficiency — the fastest way to free up electricity for transition and growth

The discussions focus on the political choices needed to enable investment, scale technology and build a robust, flexible and secure electricity system that can meet the demands of the climate transition, industry and national preparedness. RISE contributes independent facts, system analysis and experience from test and demonstration environments used by industry and public organisations.

RISE provides breakfast on a first-come, first-served basis.
content.detail: Main hall, entrance from Korsgatan opposite Villa Gutebagge
content.subject: Research

content.title: Always prepared — together for a better world
content.description: In a time of crises and uncertainty, we need to strengthen society's resilience and safeguard children's and young people's safety, participation and confidence in the future. How can meaningful leisure activities contribute to stronger preparedness, trust and democracy?
content.extendedDescription:
Scouts are always prepared. Prepared for adventures in nature, for challenging situations and for one another. We believe in — and act for — a democratic and peaceful world in which young people have a say. That is building real resilience.

Resilience is not only about handling a crisis. It also involves the broader preparedness built when people help one another, take responsibility, cooperate and trust their own and others' abilities. In Scouterna, children and young people gain both practical skills and the courage to use them — for one another and for society. Resilience also means strengthening what is worth defending: democracy, peace and trust.

Welcome to Scouterna's camp in the middle of Almedalen! Try scouting activities and learn more about how children and young people in Scouterna develop skills for life and the power to make the world better for more people. We also offer popcorn made on a camping stove!
content.subject: Children/young people

content.title: From demolition to a new facade — how can reclaimed bricks become a large-scale industry?
content.description: The construction sector needs to reduce both climate impact and waste. Reusing building materials is often presented as a solution — but how can it work on a larger scale in practice? What systems are needed for collecting, quality-assuring and turning reclaimed materials into products?
content.extendedDescription:
In recent years, reusing facing bricks has grown from a niche into a rapidly expanding part of the construction sector. Reclaimed facing bricks now account for more than ten per cent of Sweden's facing brick market.
The seminar describes how a large-scale reuse system can work in practice, from collecting bricks during demolition, through cleaning and quality assurance, to turning the material into CE-marked construction products.
We discuss the technical, logistical and regulatory conditions needed for reuse to work at scale, and how the industry can develop circular material flows in construction.
The seminar also addresses the ongoing expansion of production capacity in Sweden, where new investments, including support from Klimatklivet, enable more automated and efficient brick reuse facilities.

content.title: When digital society is disrupted — how do municipalities ensure continuity?
content.description: Municipalities now depend heavily on digital systems to deliver essential services, from schools and care to crisis management and safety. At the same time, demands for resilience, redundancy and control are growing amid cyber threats, disruptions to digital infrastructure and a more uncertain world.
content.extendedDescription: How do municipalities ensure that operations continue even when digital systems are affected or disabled? In this breakfast seminar, Helsingborgs stad shares its experience of digital continuity management. Through mapping, staged exercises and analysis of actual dependencies, Helsingborg has exposed technical, organisational and cultural vulnerabilities, moved from insight to systematic change and placed the issue where it belongs — on management's agenda. Together with digital infrastructure organisations, we discuss how municipalities can reduce vulnerabilities, strengthen their digital sovereignty and build more resilient digital public services. Breakfast from 07.30; seminar starts at 08.00. 80 breakfasts have been ordered, first come, first served.

content.description: Every day, municipalities manage external developments and needs in a world challenged by crises, wars and climate disasters. content.title: From vision to reality: accelerating personalised and preventive diabetes care in Sweden
content.description: Nearly 6 million Swedes have a personal connection to diabetes. Smart technology offers enormous untapped potential, yet a recent review shows that the technology struggles to reach people and access is unequal. At the same time, public understanding of the disease and the opportunities offered by technology is limited.
content.extendedDescription:
Modern healthcare involves self-care and digital support. Smart diabetes technology enables solutions that make an immediate difference for both patients and healthcare providers.

For type 2 diabetes alone, the annual cost to society exceeds SEK 20 billion, with 70–80% of direct healthcare costs attributable to complications that can largely be prevented or delayed.

By scaling up the use of medical technology, we can both improve quality of life and achieve better clinical outcomes. There is considerable scope to reverse the trend if we can implement the technology more widely in primary care for people living with type 2 diabetes.

content.title: Medical evacuation in Ukraine - What does it take to save lives?
content.description: Medical evacuation in Ukraine is no longer simply about moving wounded soldiers to safety. Drones, precision strikes and constant surveillance have transformed battlefield conditions, requiring evacuation vehicles to evolve continuously.
content.extendedDescription:
Medical evacuation in Ukraine is no longer simply about transporting wounded soldiers to safety. Drones, precision strikes and constant surveillance have fundamentally changed how evacuation missions are conducted and what vehicles are needed to survive.
As the battlefield evolves, civilian pickups, vans and SUVs are continuously adapted with new protection, evacuation layouts and practical solutions based on frontline experience. What worked a few months ago may no longer be effective today.
In this session, Ukrainian combat medic and Tac Med North instructor Oleksandr will share firsthand insights from helping convert more than 230 vehicles for medical evacuation and frontline support. Through real examples, including projects supported by HUG, participants will learn how battlefield needs drive innovation and how volunteers, engineers and military personnel work together to save lives.
content.subject: International affairs

content.title: Producer responsibility for textiles: seamless or patchwork?
content.description: The EU is introducing extended producer responsibility for textiles, and Sweden must develop a system by 2028. The aim is to drive circularity through better collection, reuse and recycling. Yet uncertainty remains about how the system should be designed in practice and what impact it will actually have.
content.extendedDescription:
As EU regulations are implemented in Sweden, a national system for textile producer responsibility must be designed. This involves the division of responsibilities, funding and how collection and sorting will work in practice. Experience from other markets and existing systems is essential to avoiding inefficient solutions and unnecessary costs.

At the same time, companies are developing their work on circular design, reuse and recycling. How this interacts with the new regulations will determine whether circularity can be scaled up.

The discussion brings together politics and business to consider how producer responsibility can be designed to deliver real results and which priorities are needed going forward.

content.title: Who is responsible for Sweden's resident data?
content.description:
Public-sector digitalisation is moving fast. More and more interactions between residents and public services take place digitally, from applications and decisions to important public information. Large amounts of sensitive data circulate.
Who is responsible for the infrastructure that handles society's resident data?
content.extendedDescription:
This raises a central question: who is responsible for the infrastructure that handles society's resident data?
At a time of growing cyber threats, information influence operations and a more uncertain world, digital trust, transparency and control are becoming increasingly important. The public sector faces a choice: how do we create digital public services that drive innovation while ensuring secure handling of residents' data? The discussion takes a practical and strategic perspective: how municipalities, government agencies and suppliers can work together to build sustainable and secure digital public infrastructure for the long term in Sweden and Europe.
When digital platforms become part of society's basic functions, the issue is no longer just technology, but democracy, responsibility, trust and control.

content.title: Gaza — from emergency relief to reconstruction
content.description: One of the world's most acute humanitarian crises is unfolding in Gaza.
content.extendedDescription:
A recent UN report shows that more than 370 000 homes have been destroyed or damaged, 60 per cent of the population has lost their homes and 1.9 million people are displaced. Children make up roughly half of those forced to flee their homes and seek shelter. While people in Gaza live in humanitarian distress, the country's economy has shrunk by 84 per cent, and reconstruction is estimated to require USD 71 billion.

Sweden is a significant humanitarian donor and has recently increased its support to UN agencies, including UNDP. Among other things, this has enabled the delivery of around 4 000 temporary homes (RHUs), demonstrating how Swedish aid can translate into tangible effects on the ground.

But many challenges remain, and several humanitarian organisations struggle to operate in Gaza because of major restrictions imposed by the authorities and military.

How can Swedish organisations and Swedish aid meet the urgent shelter needs of children and families while laying the foundations for recovery in today's Gaza?

content.title: When electric cars rescue the power system — bidirectional charging in practice
content.description: Sweden's largest pilot project for bidirectional charging of electric cars has recently launched, with 200 participants. How does it work in practice? What are the benefits for individual car owners and electricity customers? What are the benefits for local energy supply and Sweden's entire electricity system?
content.extendedDescription: Bidirectional charging, or vehicle-to-grid (V2G), offers major opportunities for both individual households and Sweden as a country. When the batteries in thousands of electric cars are connected to the electricity system, cars become a pillar of energy balancing and frequency control. Electric cars become a solution for electricity supply, rather than a problem. Sweden's largest pilot project for bidirectional charging has recently launched, with 200 participants. Those responsible for the project and electricity system experts explain the benefits of bidirectional charging for individual car owners and electricity customers. What are the benefits for a municipality's local energy system and Sweden's entire electricity system? How quickly can V2G be rolled out to large numbers of customers?

content.title: Is Sweden wasting its competitiveness through inadequate gender equality?
content.description: Sweden is one of the world's most gender-equal countries, but men still form a clear majority on corporate boards. The research is clear: gender-equal organisations are more profitable and resilient. The question is not whether gender equality matters, but why it is still not a priority.
content.extendedDescription: Sweden has long been at the forefront of gender equality, yet progress on boards and in pay is slow. Why is gender equality still treated as a side issue? For many employers, efforts stop at good intentions because they lack tools for working systematically. But good intentions are not enough. On behalf of the government, Jämställdhetsmyndigheten, Statskontoret and Svenska institutet för standarder will work towards a European standard for effective gender equality work. This would give European organisations a concrete tool to manage and follow up their work properly, as a business-critical activity rather than a side project. The seminar brings together research, politics and business to explore what is needed for gender equality to become a competitive factor, rather than solely a matter of values.
content.subject: Gender equality
speakerTitles: Minister for Gender Equality and Working Life

content.title: Robots, social contact and divorce — conditions and solutions for tomorrow's eldercare
content.description: What kind of later life is possible and desirable at a time when the proportion of older people is growing faster than ever?
content.extendedDescription:
Together with seven organisations in eldercare, we have explored the conditions for later life tomorrow — a life that a rapidly growing share of Swedes should be able to live with dignity, despite acute skills shortages in many welfare professions.

More than 1000 Swedes born in 1945-1954, along with hundreds of relatives and care staff, have answered questions such as:

• What do today's 70-80-year-olds consider the most desirable ways to address the challenges of an ageing population?
• Who is most concerned about older people's perceived loneliness, and how does social contact actually develop after retirement?
• How can older people be encouraged to leave their sought-after homes and move to housing better suited to their long-term needs?
• What potential for automation exists in eldercare, and what do older people themselves think of the technological solutions?

Insights and observations are discussed with a panel comprising:
Daniel Hansson, Head of Health Promotion for Older People in Österåkers kommun.
Marcus Fält, Head of the Care Homes Segment, Attendo

content.title: How have the parties performed on environmental policy, and what are they promising next?
content.description: Which parties have performed best and worst on environmental policy during the parliamentary term? How have the government and parliamentary parties acted on environmental issues in 2022-2026, and what are they promising for the next term?
content.extendedDescription:
Discuss environmental issues with our experts while charging your phone and trying Naturskyddsföreningen's election compass for climate and nature.

Naturskyddsföreningen is a politically independent nonprofit organisation with more than 200 000 members nationwide. We are deeply rooted in research, and our vision is a sustainable future on a healthy, living planet. Since 1985, we have scrutinised environmental policy ahead of parliamentary elections by sending a broad environmental policy questionnaire to the parliamentary parties and evaluating their actions during the preceding term.

We assess political parties in the same way, regardless of party affiliation. We believe that all political parties, wherever they sit on the political spectrum, should naturally work towards a stable climate, healthy ecosystems and a toxin-free environment.

Which issue will determine your vote? Visit our tent on Strandvägen and discuss the election for climate and nature!

content.title: Mum is coming — but is she really?
content.description: Pleasure is a gender equality issue. When the orgasm gap, childbirth injuries and menopausal symptoms are silenced, it shows how women's bodies are still deprioritised. Sexual freedom is about knowledge, care and control over one's own body. What is needed to make sexual freedom a reality?
content.extendedDescription:
‘Yes, yes — Mum is coming!’ Sounds familiar, doesn't it? It is called out from the hallway, the kitchen and amid the daily juggling act. But when the bedroom door closes, or when she seeks healthcare for her most intimate concerns, is Mum really coming?

Welcome to a panel discussion in Almedalen that refuses to look away. We discuss what is often hidden in a drawer or hushed up in the waiting room. Centerkvinnorna knows that sexual freedom is about the right to one's own body, pleasure and equitable health throughout life.

We explore the orgasm gap, childbirth injuries, menopause and gender-equal healthcare. This discussion is for anyone who wants politics that is as incisive as it is caring.

Come and listen, ask questions and join the movement that puts women's bodies and freedom at its centre. It is high time we talked about equality — including where it is felt most deeply.
content.subject: Gender equality

content.title: What responsibility do employers have for sexual harassment?
content.description: Surveys show that more than 150 000 people each year report experiencing sexual harassment at work. Despite legislation and other measures, the problem persists. Why are employers failing to stop and prevent sexual harassment in the workplace?
content.extendedDescription:
Sexual harassment in working life is well known and clearly documented. Employees experience harassment and sexual harassment from managers and colleagues, as well as people who do not work at the same workplace, known as third parties. Women under 30 are the most exposed.

#MeToo clearly showed that employers do not do enough to prevent sexual harassment and often fail to take adequate action.

DO's panel discusses what employers can do to prevent and stop sexual harassment and what the statutory duty to investigate and take action actually means.

The seminar takes place at Torget för mänskliga rättigheter och demokrati, organised by DO in cooperation with Forum för levande historia and Institutet för mänskliga rättigheter.
