content.title: How we make it harder for criminals to use Swedish ports and sea routes for smuggling
content.description: As much of Sweden is surrounded by water, many smuggling routes pass through maritime zones. How do we strengthen our joint efforts to prevent our sea routes and ports from becoming an arena for smuggling and organised crime?
content.extendedDescription:
Drug smuggling and sales are central to organised crime in Sweden, particularly among established criminal networks with significant capacity to pose threats. Sea routes and Swedish ports are one arena for this crime, while also being a lifeline for passenger and freight transport to and from Sweden. Several authorities have cooperated for many years through various checks in port areas, but a larger joint initiative against crime has been under way since last year. It involves stronger supervision and controls, better information sharing and legislative changes.

Join a highly topical seminar on how we can jointly intensify efforts to make it harder for criminals to use sea routes and ports for criminal activity — and help make Sweden safer.
content.subject: Justice/crime

content.title: Sweden wastes the potential of 5 000 young people with neurodevelopmental conditions in every age cohort — can business afford to stand by?
content.description: While employers talk about skills shortages, thousands of young people with neurodevelopmental conditions lack effective routes into work. How do we build workplaces that can serve as a first step into working life, and what do employers need to dare to open the door?
content.extendedDescription:
Today, substantial resources go into adapting individuals to working life, but far less into developing workplaces that work for people with different ways of functioning. As a result, employers who see potential still hesitate, while young people get stuck between different systems.
A business sector that works only for some will also struggle to build the skills and resilience the future requires.
What do employers need to move from willingness to action?
Could a traineeship programme for young people with neurodevelopmental conditions — focusing as much on workplace development as on the individual — be part of the solution?
A few brief perspectives open the discussion. After that, the experiences and ideas in the room are as important as those shared from the stage.
content.subject: Business

content.title: Tomorrow's business models and leadership
content.description: Sweden must make the transition, and most people know what is needed. Yet progress often stalls. We measure, report and set targets, but change gets stuck between insight and action. Is it a reporting problem, or fundamentally a question of leadership and the courage to lead for the long term?
content.extendedDescription:
The transition requires more than targets and metrics. It needs viable business models and leaders who dare to prioritise the long term when everything around them rewards speed. This roundtable stays with precisely that challenge. You share your experience and help shape our understanding of what actually gets the transition moving.

The questions are role-based rather than industry-specific. You will meet leaders from other sectors wrestling with the same challenges. We explore what we underestimate in the world around us, which patterns in management teams obstruct the transition despite awareness of the need, and what is required to lead change more forcefully.

Here, you are a co-creator rather than an audience member. Through your and other participants' experiences and reflections, we jointly develop a clearer picture of the path from knowing to changing.
content.subject: Business
content.accessibility: Wheelchair-accessible entrance and venue

content.title: Is there a connection between social media and loneliness?
content.description: In 2023, the World Health Organization (WHO) classified loneliness as an urgent global health threat. Although social media creates new opportunities for connection and community, there are indications that being on social platforms does not always contribute to them.
content.extendedDescription:
There is increasing discussion of social media's impact on people's health and wellbeing. At the same time, involuntary loneliness is spreading through society. A new Nordic report from If shows that half of all Swedes experience involuntary loneliness to varying degrees.

The report offers deeper insights into loneliness among Swedes and other Nordic populations, including its relationship with social media use. It also highlights what parents worry about most regarding their children's future. Social media's impact on health stands out clearly.

In Almedalen, If brings together participants from business, politics, academia and civil society to discuss how loneliness and social media are connected, how to work preventively and what good examples exist of social media actually reducing loneliness.
content.subject: Health and social care
speakerTitles: Head of Advocacy and Public Opinion

content.title: Ukraine's intangible cultural heritage is being erased
content.description: Russia is systematically destroying Ukrainian cultural heritage — buildings, traditions and art forms. What responsibility do Sweden and the international community have when culture is used as a weapon of war?
content.extendedDescription:
Ukraine's cultural heritage is a target in the war. Russia is deliberately destroying museums, churches, archives and living cultural traditions, including Petrykivka painting, a Ukrainian folk art listed by UNESCO as intangible cultural heritage since 2013. The destruction is not accidental: it aims to erase Ukrainian identity and history.
This discussion brings together voices from the Ukrainian embassy, Swedish cultural heritage organisations and nonprofit associations to discuss what can actually be done: within UNESCO, in Swedish cultural policy debate and through civil society's work to document and preserve what is threatened.

The discussion is organised within Samarbetsplattformen: Sverige & Ukraina (SPSU), a project by KlinteVolontär that gives Ukrainian civil society its own voice in Sweden's democratic debate and brings Swedish and Ukrainian organisations together to strengthen long-term cooperation between the countries.
content.subject: Culture
content.organizationType: Collaboration between different types of organisation
content.accessibility: Wheelchair-accessible entrance and venue

content.title: World-leading AI in healthcare? How can Sweden take the next step?
content.description: AI has great potential to improve quality, accessibility and equity in healthcare, but its use today is fragmented and unequal. What is needed to take the next step and become a world leader in AI in Swedish healthcare?
content.extendedDescription:
Despite strong foundations and many promising initiatives, few AI solutions have achieved widespread implementation in Swedish healthcare. Meanwhile, pressure on the care system is growing, with increasing needs, resource challenges and demands for greater efficiency. Meeting these challenges requires a move from individual AI projects to more structured, coordinated and scalable use.

What is needed to scale up what works? How do we create the right conditions for national coordination, skills and implementation? And who takes responsibility for direction and delivery?

Drawing on a current overview, we bring together experts and decision-makers to discuss how Sweden can take the next step and achieve a leading position in the use of AI in healthcare.
content.subject: Innovation
content.organizationType: Collaboration between different types of organisation
content.accessibility: Wheelchair-accessible entrance and venue
speakerTitles: Regional Commissioner for Finance and Chair of the Regional Executive Board, Region Stockholm

content.title: Professional disobedience: using courage to think outside the box in transition work
content.description: A construction project navigates thousands of rules from idea to completed building. But when these rules become more important than the goal of a sustainable future, our compliance can paradoxically become our greatest risk. Do we dare to challenge the boundaries between what we are used to and what we know must be done?
content.extendedDescription:
The construction and property industry needs to act as though the situation is urgent. Liljewall and Centrum för management i byggsektorn — cmb — therefore invite you to a discussion of new climate leadership and ‘professional disobedience’: the courage to recognise when a process is going wrong and the ability to navigate gaps between legal provisions and established patterns. It means finding room to combine the best of proven methods with a willingness to try something new.

Join a discussion of leadership that dares to challenge the system in practice to build the future!

The seminar forms part of cmb's cooperation with BRG within the EU-funded project Living lab för ett klimatneutralt byggande. Read more about the project on our website below.
content.subject: Construction
content.organizationType: Collaboration between different types of organisation
speakerTitles: Head of R&D, Associate Professor of Ethnology

content.title: If electricity is the future, why is the transition so slow? What is needed to move from words to action?
content.description: What is needed to achieve our ambitious transition targets? Are Sweden and the industry ready?
content.extendedDescription: The panel begins by discussing how far Sweden has progressed in the energy transition and the electrification of society. The conversation focuses on the current situation in the public sector and business, and the targets, investments and infrastructure initiatives needed to meet growing electricity demand. Electricity grids, capacity, energy storage and smart management of energy systems are central, alongside how technology and innovation can contribute to a more stable and efficient energy system. The panel also explores future energy supply and the roles different energy sources, such as solar and nuclear power, will play in Sweden's long-term energy needs. As electrification, electric vehicles and digitalisation advance, the discussion also considers whether infrastructure is developing at the same pace as demand and the opportunities and challenges the transition presents for Sweden's competitiveness and societal development. What will the airport of the future look like with this new transition?
content.subject: Energy

content.title: How do we create conditions for constructive dialogue that advances the sustainability transition?
content.description: Environmental and sustainability challenges are often marked by disagreements, polarising conflicts and unproductive dialogue. How can we jointly achieve democratic, constructive conversations and communication methods that work in practice?
content.extendedDescription:
Join an open networking event with researchers and communicators from the Mistra Environmental Communication research programme, where you can:

- Discuss current communication challenges in environmental and sustainability issues
- Connect with people working on environmental or sustainability issues who use communication as a central tool
- Discover research insights and practical tools developed within the programme

There will be opportunities both for informal networking and for short interactive activities with environmental communication researchers.

Whatever your work in communication, decision-making, research and/or societal development, you are welcome to participate and contribute your experiences and perspectives.

Light refreshments will be provided.

content.title: Why is electrification so slow in the public sector?
content.description: Sweden's vehicle fleet is electrifying rapidly, but not everywhere. While businesses are transitioning quickly, the public sector is falling behind. Almost 9 out of 10 new company cars are plug-in vehicles. Central government, municipalities and regions barely reach half that share, and their proportion has even fallen this year.
content.extendedDescription:
Why is this? What are businesses doing that the public sector is not? How can the transition to electric cars accelerate, and will the new EU requirements in the Clean Vehicles Directive force more electric cars into the public sector?

Together with Volkswagen Finans, we examine differences between private individuals, businesses and the public sector. We take a closer look at the factors driving rapid electrification in businesses, such as focusing on total cost of ownership rather than purchase price.

The seminar also highlights structural conditions for the electric vehicle transition, from procurement rules to uncertainty about residual values and the effects of new EU requirements such as the Clean Vehicles Directive. What is needed to accelerate the transition of large public vehicle fleets?
content.subject: Sustainability

content.title: From vulnerability to strength — a new situation for Swedish cybersecurity
content.description: What political, technical and procurement decisions are needed to move from vulnerability to operational strength in Swedish cybersecurity and total defence?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden's cybersecurity is determined not only by technical capacity or political ambitions, but to a large extent by the requirements actually set when the public sector procures digital infrastructure, systems and security solutions.

European analyses show that the public sector today depends heavily on a few large, often non-European suppliers, particularly in digital infrastructure. The issue is therefore not merely cost, but how established requirements, procurement patterns and market structures affect which solutions are sought and selected.

Against this background, the seminar focuses on procurement as a strategic tool for strengthening cybersecurity, innovation and resilience — if the right requirements are set. Drawing on perspectives from business and the public sector, we discuss how Sweden can use procurement to reduce vulnerable dependencies, strengthen domestic and European markets and raise operational security.
content.subject: Security/defence
content.organizationType: Collaboration between different types of organisation

content.title: Different childhoods, different futures — what is needed to give every child a good start?
content.description: Most children in Sweden are doing well, but not all. Children whose needs are not identified in time often face several challenges. When support from society fails to arrive, the risks of poorer health, weaker school results and diminished confidence in the future increase. What do our youngest children need, and what must we change to provide it?
content.extendedDescription:
Children whose needs are not identified in time often face a combination of challenges, such as financial vulnerability, overcrowded housing and guardians outside the labour market. Sometimes a child or family member also has a disability, ill health or limited ability to benefit from public support.

When society's support comes too late or not at all, the risks of poorer health, weaker school results and diminished confidence in the future increase. This affects both the child and society as a whole.

In this exploratory seminar, we discuss preventive and early interventions. What do our youngest children need, and what must we understand, change and do differently to reach the children we fail to see in time and reverse today's trend?
content.detail: Kommun- och regionarenan (by the Kruttornet car park/Strandvägen)

content.title: The integration policy of the future
content.description: The integration debate is increasingly marked by smears and oversimplification. Meanwhile, real problems relating to work, housing, language and discrimination persist. How do we create integration policy that actually works and gives people opportunities to establish themselves and contribute?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden needs a new integration policy. In recent years, immigrants have increasingly been made scapegoats in public debate. This fuels polarisation and racism while shifting attention away from real integration problems.
Following a tour of Sweden from Skurup to Boden, Integrationsbyrån presents 31 reform proposals for better, more humane and effective integration policy. The proposals draw on conversations with people around the country, civil society experience and research into what actually strengthens integration.
The seminar addresses work, education, housing, discrimination and the role of civil society — but also what kind of society Sweden wants to be. How do we create a society in which more people can establish themselves, feel hopeful about the future and contribute their skills? And how do we move beyond an integration debate stuck in suspicion and symbolic politics?

content.title: Children and young people at the centre — how do we strengthen their influence in society?
content.description: Many young people see democracy as distant, difficult to influence and not for them, despite strong engagement. How do we make democracy more accessible, relevant and inclusive, accommodating different perspectives and taking young people's voices seriously, both locally and more broadly?
content.extendedDescription:
The event focuses on how children and young people can gain real influence over societal issues and decision-making. Interactive elements highlight different perspectives and create dialogue between generations.
The programme begins with a brief introduction to d-effect and its work to amplify young people's voices. An audience-interactive segment follows, showing interviews with people of different ages. The audience can take positions in real time and has space to discuss and reflect on different perspectives.
The event ends with a panel discussion involving young people and adult decision-makers, focusing on moving from listening to young people to actually giving them influence. The audience is invited to ask questions and contribute to the conversation.

content.title: Hybrid threats — from election interference to sabotage
content.description: Hybrid threats target the whole of society, regardless of sector. This means we all have a responsibility to detect, report and respond to them. How can hybrid threats affect our society, and how do we counter them?
content.extendedDescription:
Hybrid threats challenge the boundaries between war and peace, civilian and military, national and international. They can range from interference with democratic processes, disinformation and cyberattacks to sabotage of critical infrastructure and space-based systems.

The threats target the whole of society, regardless of sector. This means we all have a responsibility to detect, report and respond to hybrid threats. But not everything can be threatening — how should we approach such a diffuse threat landscape?

In this seminar, we follow a connected scenario from election interference to state-funded terrorism and sabotage. A panel discusses solutions for countering hybrid threats in Sweden. Among other things, a recently developed toolkit to help civilian authorities with this important work will be presented. How can different organisations act, and what does ‘managing’ hybrid threats mean?
content.subject: Security/defence

content.title: Nature-Security Nexus in the Baltic Sea Region
content.description: The Baltic region is facing times of insecurity and crisis. Ecological restoration, for example rewetting of peatlands can be integrated into the planning of national and regional resilience. A broad group of actors needs to be part of this discussion to take the next steps for nature and security.
content.extendedDescription: The Baltic region is facing times of unsecurity and crisis and is exposed to growing geopolitical tensions, once again claiming the Baltic Sea as a stage for international politics. This is mainly discussed as a defence or broader societal challenge with limited involvement of experts on ecosystems and the Baltic Sea. In recent years, aside from geopolitical significance, the Baltic is also known as one of the most environmentally vulnerable seas and its high commercial activity, through heavy shipping traffic and a significant portion of worlds commercial shipping. In addition, the Baltic is still bearing the burden of past political conflicts. In this seminar we will discuss the interlinkages between nature, security and resilience in the Baltic Sea region.
content.subject: Animals/nature

content.title: What happens when we start rewriting the rules? Is moral leadership in retreat?
content.description: Tensions are growing between national political priorities and international human rights commitments, particularly concerning refugees and other vulnerable groups.
content.extendedDescription:
Around the world, international law and multilateral cooperation are increasingly questioned. Conventions protecting refugees, children and other vulnerable groups are sometimes treated as negotiable. But these frameworks are not abstract bureaucratic tools; they are legal expressions of fundamental human values such as dignity, protection, freedom and the right to life. They rest on an international consensus that may be harder to achieve today. If we set conventions aside when they become politically inconvenient, on what basis can we hold others accountable? And what happens when norms we helped shape no longer align with national priorities?

These tensions are evident both internationally and at home. In Sweden, the Refugee Convention is being questioned in political debate, while discussion of deporting young people born and raised in the country has intensified.
content.subject: International affairs

content.title: Innovation developed in Sweden — built for the world
content.description: Europe faces a choice: compete with yesterday's technology or lead the development of the next generation of energy-efficient transport? How do we ensure that innovation developed in Sweden is not only exported globally, but also used and scaled at home?
content.extendedDescription:
How does Europe build industry amid intensifying global competition?

In this seminar, we discuss how technology developed and built in Sweden can strengthen Europe's competitiveness, reduce energy use and create new sustainable transport systems.

The discussion starts with electric hydrofoil vessels and developments in energy-efficient maritime transport, but is fundamentally about something bigger: how advanced engineering, software and sustainable production can become Sweden's next export success while creating future jobs and industrial expertise in Sweden and Europe.

The panel will also discuss the obstacles still holding back new technology in Sweden, from regulation to public procurement, and what is needed for innovative companies not only to export Swedish technology to the world but also to use and scale it at home.
content.subject: Business

content.title: Electricity shortages and growing uncertainty — can combined heat and power deliver on both fronts?
content.description: Sweden needs more fossil-free electricity for households and businesses. In a deteriorating security environment, we also need to strengthen preparedness and secure electricity supplies to our cities in crisis or war. Could combined heat and power be the answer?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden needs more fossil-free electricity and capacity here and now. New nuclear power will take time to become available. A deteriorating security environment means Sweden must strengthen preparedness and secure electricity supply in crisis and war.

Combined heat and power already plays an important role as reserve capacity and a preparedness resource. It is weather-independent and provides balancing capability. It also has unique capabilities such as black start and island operation, which can enable local electricity supply without the national transmission grid. If our transmission grid is sabotaged, combined heat and power alone can supply our cities with electricity for several months, allowing society to continue functioning. There is also considerable potential both to increase capacity and to strengthen preparedness.

What is needed from policymakers to make this happen? Sveriges Ingenjörer, E.On, Kraftringen and Stockholm Exergi jointly invite you to a seminar seeking answers.
content.subject: Energy
content.accessibility: Wheelchair-accessible toilet, wheelchair-accessible entrance and venue

content.title: What role do hunting and hunters play in society?
content.description: Everyone knows hunting is a central part of Sweden's nature conservation, food supply and rural life. Hunters contribute to wildlife management, ecological balance and community. But what other aspects are there to the importance of hunting and hunters in society, today and in the future?
content.extendedDescription:
Hunting is one of Sweden's largest popular movements and a crucial part of its food supply, nature conservation and preparedness. ‘Gilla jakt’ is a podcast on the theme ‘We are hunters — conversations about our role in society’. It will explore life as a hunter, hunting and hunters' role in society, and will be recorded at our outdoor site at 14:00 on Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday for release at 17:00.

Jägarnas Riksförbund, which produces the podcast, works to make hunting accessible, sustainable over the long term and knowledge-based. At the same time, we see how regulations, land issues and a widening gap between urban and rural areas risk making things harder for both current and future hunters. A key question is how more people, particularly young people and those without land, can participate in hunting. JRF pursues these issues with the aim of ensuring that hunting remains a natural part of a sustainable Sweden.
content.subject: Animals/nature

content.title: Beyond the crisis headlines: how is liberalism really doing?
content.description: 30 years ago, liberalism's future looked bright. Then came declining confidence in liberal democracy and growing dissatisfaction with globalisation, capitalism and individualism. What happened? Did liberalism lose its appeal when liberal democracy triumphed?
content.extendedDescription:
Thirty years ago, liberalism's future looked bright. When the Berlin Wall fell, many believed a freer, more peaceful and richer world lay ahead. What followed during the first quarter of the twenty-first century was democratic decline, falling confidence in liberal democracy and new conflicts both within and between countries. Dissatisfaction with globalisation, capitalism and individualism is growing among Western populations. While it has been a difficult quarter-century for liberal parties, much has happened in the development of liberal ideas.

What happened? Did liberalism as an ideology lose its appeal when liberal democracy triumphed? Do liberal parties have answers to today's political questions? Does an era of postliberalism await, or is liberalism's self-confidence lower than it should be?
content.subject: Democracy
content.organizationType: Collaboration between different types of organisation
content.accessibility: Hearing loop, wheelchair-accessible toilet, wheelchair-accessible entrance and venue

content.title: Hybrid threats and resilience — how do we build a strong Sweden Inc. together?
content.description: Sweden faces an increasingly complex threat landscape in which hybrid threats, cyberattacks and geopolitical uncertainty are part of everyday life. Securing a robust, functioning society requires new cooperation across boundaries between politics, business and public organisations.
content.extendedDescription:
In a rapidly changing security landscape, Sweden constantly faces new and complex threats. Meeting them requires not only strong defence, but also a business sector that takes active responsibility and works closely with public organisations.
This seminar focuses on how companies can contribute to Sweden's total defence by combining emergency preparedness with commercial viability and long-term competitiveness. Drawing on concrete examples, we discuss how new forms of cooperation can create resilient ecosystems that strengthen Sweden's preparedness in peace, crisis and ultimately war.
The conversation explores how to accelerate the security transition from strategy to action, speed up preparedness and simultaneously create growth and innovation. The goal is a more resilient Sweden Inc. built on trust, cooperation and shared responsibility.
content.subject: Democracy

content.title: Electricity is hope — what does Ukraine teach us about the importance of a resilient power system?
content.description: Sweden's electricity system is essential to a functioning society, but easily taken for granted. Experience from Ukraine shows what happens when the power system is truly tested, and what is needed for a secure and reliable electricity grid in Sweden.
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden's electricity system is one of our most critical societal functions, but also something we often take for granted. Its reliable operation today is the result of investments made to address previous crises.

In this seminar, we focus on what happens when the electricity system, and particularly the grids, are truly tested. Drawing on Ukraine's experience, where electricity grids have become a direct target in the war, we gain a concrete picture of what resilience means in practice.

Against this background, we discuss what is needed to prepare our electricity supply for today's challenges. In a new normal shaped by climate change and geopolitical uncertainty, the demands on electricity grids are changing fundamentally.

The way forward is clear. Electricity grids are essential to society and business and must now be equipped for a new era.
content.subject: Energy

content.title: Home births — from the child's perspective
content.description: There has been lively media debate about home births this year. Are they safe or not? Should they be publicly funded? What risks do home births pose to the child, and how can public funding be used to improve maternity care?
content.extendedDescription:
In this seminar, we will describe how emergency teamwork around the baby is crucial to survival without severe brain injury. We will explain what science says about the risks and benefits of home births, and why, from an ethical perspective, it may be questionable to allocate extra resources to healthy women expecting low-risk births if this reduces capacity to care for women with greater medical needs. Finally, we will present ways other than home births to develop maternity care so that women do not see giving birth at home as the safest option.

The seminar concludes with a panel debate involving invited decision-makers and representatives of medical professional associations.
content.subject: Health and social care
speakerTitles: Deputy Chair of SKR's Healthcare Delegation

content.title: The climate threat and climate policy — what do politicians want to know from researchers?
content.description: Climate change is one of the major challenges of our time. How is Sweden affected, what policies can address the climate crisis, and how effective are different policy instruments? In a time of uncertainty and rapid change, how can dialogue between science and politics be strengthened?
content.extendedDescription:
Politicians are often held to account in debates and panels, but what happens if we reverse the roles? In this seminar, Uppsala universitet gives politicians the opportunity to ask questions about climate change and policy instruments to a research panel comprising experts on both society and the environment. Possible questions include: How is Sweden affected? Which measures and policy instruments have the greatest impact? What obstacles prevent them from working effectively? How should conflicting goals be managed? The seminar aims to share scientific knowledge, strengthen dialogue between politicians and researchers, and create a platform where science and politics meet to discuss how the climate threat affects Sweden and what priorities are needed for a sustainable future.

The seminar is part of Uppsala universitet's climate days.
content.subject: Climate/environment
speakerTitles: Chair of the Cross-Party Committee on Environmental Objectives, Member of the Party Executive
Spokesperson for Environment, Defence and Foreign Policy

content.title: 3.5 years left — can insetting and auditing accelerate the transport sector's transition?
content.description: Transport must reduce emissions rapidly, and the solutions already exist. Yet they are not being chosen. Unclear accounting rules are holding back demand for fossil-free transport. Now the entire value chain is agreeing on common practice to unlock the transition.
content.extendedDescription:
Fossil-free transport is already possible through established transition solutions such as book & claim. Yet climate ambitions remain theoretical. Uncertainty about accounting, auditing and communication makes companies hesitant, and they continue buying fossil-based transport.
Transport buyers, carriers and fuel producers are now joining forces in a shared guide. It establishes clear practice for how book & claim should be accounted for and communicated so that it meets both auditors' expectations and sustainability requirements.
At the seminar, companies, industry and researchers explain the needs and obstacles. Auditors, climate experts and users examine the guide and its ability to enable real transition. Finally, the entire value chain shares what is needed to scale up and who must act next.
What has been missing is not solutions, but a shared understanding. The conditions now exist to move from ambition to impact.
content.subject: Climate/environment
content.accessibility: Hearing loop, wheelchair-accessible entrance and venue

content.title: Skills and education without geographical barriers — how do we reach the whole country?
content.description: Skills shortages affect both business competitiveness and the quality of welfare. How can higher education, distance learning and local learning centres strengthen skills supply and create opportunities for growth throughout Sweden, including far from university campuses?
content.extendedDescription:
Access to the right skills is crucial to Sweden's competitiveness, welfare and regional development. Yet many employers face major recruitment challenges, particularly in smaller municipalities and areas far from universities and university colleges. How can education become more accessible and contribute to development nationwide?

The seminar discusses current and future skills and education needs, and the solutions required for more people to access higher education regardless of where they live.

The seminar is organised by Akademi Norr and Lapplands Kommunalförbund with support from Kompetensarena Norrbotten. The project works to strengthen strategic skills supply in Norrbotten through better evidence, cooperation and support structures for municipalities and employers.
content.subject: Education
speakerTitles: Regional Development Director and Acting Head of Culture

content.title: More moving chains, affordable building projects, future buyers — how to balance the housing market
content.description: The conditions for a balanced and growing housing market are currently lacking. High prices and poor accessibility leave many people living in homes that do not meet their needs. Greater mobility and more chains of moves in the housing market are therefore needed.
content.extendedDescription:
As the population ages, the need for housing suited to older people grows. At the same time, the barrier to young people buying their first home is rising, hampering mobility in the housing market.

The panel discusses how to create more chains of moves and a better-balanced housing market through sustainable, commercially viable solutions. The conversation focuses on how smart choices throughout a property's lifecycle, from development and construction to management, sale and moving in, can improve accessibility, lower costs and use resources better.

Who is the housing customer of the future, and whom are we actually building for? The panel also explores how future-proof building concepts can create long-term value for property owners and residents and contribute to a more sustainable, functioning housing market.
content.subject: Sustainability
content.accessibility: Wheelchair-accessible toilet, wheelchair-accessible entrance and venue

content.title: The race for the future in 2036 — how can Sweden become a world leader in life sciences?
content.description: Sweden faces crucial choices for the future of its life sciences sector. Amid intensifying global competition, the decisions we make today determine how the sector can help strengthen Sweden tomorrow.
content.extendedDescription:
Life sciences is one of Sweden's most important industries of the future for health, growth and resilience. But global competition for research, investment and innovation is intensifying rapidly, while trade barriers and policy shifts are changing conditions. What is needed for Sweden to be a leading life sciences nation in 2036 — and what decisions must be made during the next parliamentary term?

At the opening of Life Science Arena, politicians and business leaders meet for a forward-looking, interactive discussion about Sweden's future. Politicians present their visions for Swedish life sciences ten years ahead, then challenge business representatives on what is required to turn those visions into reality.

The discussion covers innovation, investment, clinical trials, AI and health data, patients' access to new treatments, preparedness and Sweden's competitiveness in a new geopolitical reality.
content.subject: Innovation

content.title: Has sustainability run out of breath, or does it just need a new deep breath?
content.description: Has sustainability lost status? If success is measured primarily in growth, profitability and competitiveness, what place remains for sustainability, social responsibility and long-term value creation? What role are companies expected to play in addressing societal challenges, resilience, security and competitiveness?
content.extendedDescription:
The seminar begins with fresh findings on Swedish public views of sustainability, corporate responsibility and societal development. A discussion follows about sustainability's status in a time of geopolitical uncertainty, technological development, growing security concerns and demands for competitiveness.

Has sustainability acquired a new meaning? Which issues take priority as the world changes? What do citizens expect of companies today, and what drives corporate sustainability work?

The discussion also examines what we as a society choose to value and reward. If success is measured primarily in growth, profitability and competitiveness, what place remains for sustainability, social responsibility and long-term value creation?

A timely discussion about corporate responsibility, citizens' expectations and sustainability's importance as many societal priorities are reassessed.
content.subject: Sustainability

content.title: Who takes responsibility when systems fail? Digital resilience as a leadership issue
content.description: Sweden is digitalising faster than we are building resilience. Municipalities, regions, government agencies, businesses and civil society depend on digital systems, and no one else can guarantee delivery if those systems come under pressure or fail. We must move from digital dependence to digital resilience.
content.extendedDescription:
Hope is not a digital security strategy. Today's geopolitical situation means the likelihood of attacks on our digital systems is no longer negligible — risk and vulnerability assessments must change. An organisation providing essential services in Sweden suffers a successful cyberattack every week, and most lack a concrete plan for what happens when critical systems fail. Waiting makes no one stronger.

Netnod invites you to a panel discussion on how Sweden can move from digital dependence to digital resilience. Representatives from politics, business, the public sector and technical experts meet on stage to discuss what is actually needed for essential organisations to function when the unexpected occurs, and what action must be taken now. The discussion is open to everyone who wants to listen.
content.subject: Digitalisation

content.title: Hydropower — the crown jewel of the power system
content.description: Hydropower is the backbone of Sweden's power system. It delivers electricity, capacity, flexibility and stability for electrification while maintaining competitiveness and security of supply. How is hydropower's role evolving in an energy system facing greater security uncertainty?
content.extendedDescription:
Over an afternoon, Energiföretagen brings together key stakeholders, alongside energy companies, public authorities and political representatives, to discuss hydropower's role in Sweden's energy system.

Three seminars focus on key questions for hydropower's future: opportunities for expanding capacity and pumped storage; how to introduce modern environmental conditions for hydropower efficiently and appropriately; and hydropower's importance for electricity preparedness and total defence in a more uncertain security environment.

Schedule — Vattenkraftsarenan
14:00–14:45 — Flexibility and large-scale energy storage: think hydropower and pumped storage!
15:00–15:45 — Hydropower, aquatic environments and biodiversity: how do we find the right balance?
16:00–16:45 — Electricity preparedness in troubled times: hydropower, an unbeatable resource.

Wednesday 24 June 2026
Klosterlängan, Arena Energi, Visby

content.title: From income support to employment — how can the activity requirement make a real difference?
content.description: The activity requirement for income support could become a route to work — or an administrative dead end. What is needed for the reform to give people real steps towards employment, language skills, social connection and self-sufficiency?
content.extendedDescription:
Municipalities will have major responsibility for offering activities that improve individuals' employment prospects. At the same time, many settings where people can develop, test their capacity for work and build networks are provided by nonprofit organisations, cooperative enterprises and other public-benefit employers.

What is needed for the activity requirement to ensure quality, employment protections and lasting results? And how can municipalities, Arbetsförmedlingen and nonprofit employers cooperate so that more people move from income support to empowerment and work?

Fremia invites you to a discussion about how the activity requirement must work in practice to strengthen individuals, the labour market and civil society's role. Fremia brings together politics, municipalities, civil society and employers to discuss implementation.

The event includes a presentation of Fremia's labour market report, focused entirely on the activity requirement for income support.

content.title: NIS2 requires you to protect the room, not just the system: is your agency ready?
content.description: The EU's new cybersecurity law, NIS2, requires an all-hazards approach, including protection of the physical environment housing IT systems. Most agencies focus on firewalls and access control. But signal leakage and vulnerable equipment are rarely addressed. The law and the future demand more.
content.extendedDescription:
NIS2 entered into force in Sweden on 1 January 2025. The directive requires organisations to approach security from an all-hazards perspective. This means organisations, particularly government agencies, must not only apply digital safeguards but also protect the physical environment housing IT systems and critical equipment. In practice, this entails requirements for continuity management, protection against electromagnetic interference and signal isolation.

The discussion includes a live demonstration of what an unprepared office environment looks like from a signal perspective: which devices are visible, what is transmitting and what this means for an agency under pressure.

An open, question-led discussion held outdoors beside BLCKR's Signalskugga, a signal-blocking tent in Visby harbour. Coffee will be served.
content.subject: Digitalisation
content.accessibility: Wheelchair-accessible entrance and venue

content.title: The invisible threat — AI, OT security and espionage we do not see
content.description: Society is becoming increasingly digital and connected, and therefore more vulnerable. How can the public sector and businesses harness technology's opportunities without losing control?
content.extendedDescription:
Panel 1: Secure AI transformation in municipalities
AI creates major opportunities for the public sector, but also raises important questions about information security, responsibility and protection of digital assets. We discuss how Sweden's municipalities can take the next step in AI transformation safely and sustainably.

Panel 2: OT security and protection of critical infrastructure
Operational Technology, OT, controls everything from buildings and physical flows to critical societal functions. As these systems become connected, vulnerability increases. We highlight today's threats and discuss what organisations need to do to strengthen resilience.

Panel 3: Digital Espionage – The Invisible Threat and What We Can Do
Digital espionage often happens silently, but can have far-reaching consequences for businesses, organisations and national security. We discuss today's threat landscape and the measures needed to detect, understand and counter unseen actors.
content.subject: Business

content.title: Two different worlds of cultural policy — which will politics choose after the election?
content.description: It has been a long time since visions for Swedish cultural policy were as polarised as they are today.
content.extendedDescription:
Will cultural policy after the election leave the relatively stable track along which it has been chugging on a gentle downward slope since 1974? The politicians responsible for cultural policy will also be present to answer questions about its direction.
Last year, the think tanks Oikos and Timbro presented Tidö 2.0, a vision for the Tidö pact in the next parliamentary term.
Koalition för kulturdebatt, comprising cultural organisations, trade unions and popular education organisations, published När taket rasar in (Atlas) last year. The book celebrates 50 years of cultural policy, but also criticises contemporary policy for a lack of commitment and financial support.
Koalitionen för kulturdebatt includes organisations such as the trade unions DIK, Konstnärernas Riksorganisation and Fackförbundet Scen & Film; cultural organisations including KLYS, Folkets Hus och Parker, Ideell kulturallians, Konstfrämjandet, Riksteatern, Bildkonst Sverige and Riksförbundet Sveriges Konstföreningar; and popular education organisations including ABF, Sensus and RIO.
content.subject: Culture
content.accessibility: Wheelchair-accessible entrance and venue

content.title: The fallen of war — how do we mourn and remember those who never come home?
content.description: The war in Ukraine has claimed tens of thousands of lives. How does a society honour its fallen while war is still ongoing? Which traditions of remembrance uphold dignity?
content.extendedDescription:
Ukraine's defenders fall every day. Behind every name are families, communities and a people who must find forms of collective mourning and remembrance amid an ongoing war. Traditions of remembrance, from a minute's silence to the symbol of the empty table, play a central role in preserving dignity and cohesion.
This discussion explores Ukrainian traditions of remembrance, their historical and cultural meaning, and how we can jointly honour the fallen in ways that do not normalise war but acknowledge its real cost. The event is part of Ukraine's Day of Sorrow and Remembrance of Victims of War and includes a period of silence in memory of the fallen.

The discussion is organised within Samarbetsplattformen: Sverige & Ukraina (SPSU), a project that gives Ukrainian civil society its own voice in Sweden's democratic debate and brings Swedish and Ukrainian organisations together to strengthen long-term cooperation between the countries.
content.subject: International affairs

content.title: Sweden's nature — will it still be alive in 2050?
content.description: Nature is in a serious state; climate change and biodiversity loss are major societal problems. Sweden is subject to long-term environmental targets. Who should be responsible for nature in the future?
content.extendedDescription:
Nature is in a serious state; climate change and biodiversity loss threaten a range of important societal functions. To reverse the trend for nature, Sweden is subject to several long-term climate and other environmental targets. As the EU Nature Restoration Regulation is implemented in Sweden, we therefore ask who should be responsible for nature in 2050.

These far-reaching targets raise questions about who is actually affected by long-term environmental policy and who can help achieve the goals. This panel brings together organisations that all work closely with Swedish nature to discuss future responsibility and implementation of the legislation. Who will have access to nature in 2050? Who has restoration expertise? How can different stakeholders come together to safeguard Swedish nature in the future?

The seminar is part of Uppsala universitet's climate days.
content.subject: Climate/environment

content.title: AI data centres and energy: a Swedish business opportunity?
content.description: Data centres require electricity, capacity and fast permitting. The question is where investment will go. With the right ground rules, AI could become Sweden's greatest investment and employment opportunity.
content.extendedDescription:
AI development is moving at breakneck speed, and its use is becoming a decisive factor in Sweden's competitiveness. But AI has a physical reality: behind every model and service are data centres requiring large amounts of electricity, connection capacity in record time and a robust power system. The question is not whether this infrastructure will be built, but where. Sweden may be facing its greatest external investment opportunity ever. But the conditions must be right, or investment, skills and innovation could go elsewhere.

At this seminar, we bring together participants from several parts of the AI value chain to discuss the ground rules needed both to accelerate expansion and maximise benefits for Sweden. As Europe electrifies, seeks greater energy independence and tries to catch up in AI, energy is once again central. Designed correctly, this is an opportunity to equip Sweden with major investments in data centres and energy infrastructure and create thousands of jobs.
content.subject: Energy

content.description: Am I included in society even if I do not produce? Am I allowed space, and who decides how much? Does everyone have equal rights, or do the conditions differ?
content.extendedDescription:
Welcome to theatre with conversation:
- My everyday life is blank, or black, or full of conflicting impressions. I navigate without a map and usually get lost.
Once I thought I had found my way, because I trusted the wrong person. It did not go well.

My greatest dream is to have a completely ordinary day.

‘Wake up after a good night's sleep, say goodbye to the little ones, go to work and then home to make dinner before everyone's evening activities begin. Then a calm bedtime with happy, contented children before I get some time to myself with my partner.’

This only happens in my dreams. I am alone, afraid and vulnerable. Usually completely at others' mercy. The pain fills my whole body, and worst of all is the shame of being a failure, unwanted and rejected. My thoughts brush against the unmentionable, but hope lingers that there is help for me. Someone who understands and sees me as I am, and makes me visible again. Help me find that, and the courage to accept it. To dare to believe that I, too, am worth it.

content.title: The transition to sustainable aviation fuels — an opportunity for Sweden's and NATO's preparedness?
content.description: Civil aviation is transitioning to sustainable aviation fuels, SAF. How does this affect Sweden's and NATO's preparedness and security of supply?
content.extendedDescription:
Civil aviation is transitioning to sustainable aviation fuels, SAF. How does this affect Sweden's preparedness and Försvarsmakten's needs? The conflict in the Strait of Hormuz clearly demonstrates how global fossil fuel supply chains can quickly be disrupted. How and when could Sweden become self-sufficient in aviation fuels? What is NATO's view?

The EU has adopted ReFuelEU aviation to reduce aviation's climate impact by gradually increasing the share of sustainable aviation fuels. By 2050, 70 per cent of all aviation fuel in the EU must be sustainable (SAF), including 35 per cent eSAF (electricity-based). Sweden has unique conditions that could make it a world-leading producer of eSAF.

Currently, aircraft are only approved to use blends containing up to 50 per cent SAF, but the industry has stated its intention to reach 100% by 2030. As early as 2017, the JAS 39 Gripen made a test flight on 100 per cent SAF. How does the Swedish defence industry view these opportunities?
content.subject: Energy
speakerTitles: Head of the Energy Preparedness Department

content.title: The threat is here and now — how can Sweden strengthen defence capability and self-sufficiency?
content.description: How can Sweden rapidly increase self-sufficiency in the defence industry and strengthen defence capability? Is new legislation needed, or can we respond to the security situation faster by changing working methods within existing rules?
content.extendedDescription:
Europe's security situation has changed fundamentally. Sweden urgently needs to strengthen both its defence capability and national self-sufficiency in the defence industry. The question is no longer whether this must happen, but how quickly it can be done.

The seminar brings together representatives from business, defence and local government to discuss how Sweden can rapidly develop defence capability, its defence industry and robust infrastructure. The discussion covers establishment, permitting processes, spatial planning and cooperation between the public and private sectors.

Different perspectives are used to discuss how a regiment, a propellant factory and dual-use infrastructure can be established in practice. The question is whether legislation must change or whether there is already scope to act faster through new working methods and more efficient processes within existing rules.
content.subject: Security/defence
content.accessibility: Wheelchair-accessible entrance and venue

content.title: From action plan to reality: diagnostics as the connecting thread in cardiovascular health
content.description: Cardiovascular disease is our most widespread major disease. The government's remit for a new action plan emphasises prevention, early detection and equitable care. But success requires a clear link to healthcare. Is diagnostics the connecting thread needed to turn fine words into reality?
content.extendedDescription:
The answer is an unequivocal YES!

The action plan must not remain a paper exercise. The government emphasises prevention, early detection and equitable care, but one crucial word is missing: diagnostics. Since most care decisions start here, the field must be prioritised so that we can use its full potential to save lives and relieve pressure on healthcare.

We do not need to reinvent the wheel. Lessons from many years of investment in cancer care can help us get the direction right from the outset. We need to shift attention and resources from reactive treatment to proactive healthcare.

Join a solutions-focused discussion in Almedalen where we identify the way forward for stronger cardiovascular health. Early, equitable and innovative diagnostics is the engine that makes the vision of no premature deaths from cardiovascular disease a reality.
content.subject: Health and social care
content.accessibility: Wheelchair-accessible entrance and venue

content.title: Robust electronic communications — how do we ensure they work in crisis and war?
content.description: Electronic communications are essential to the operation of vital services. In crisis and war, systems come under pressure while dependencies and demands increase. How do we ensure not just availability, but actual functionality, even during major disruptions?
content.extendedDescription:
Electronic communications are a fundamental requirement for society to function in crisis and war. When networks and systems are affected, consequences can be immediate and extensive.

Disruptions quickly hit central functions, and dependencies between systems amplify vulnerabilities, while demands for availability, robustness and cooperation increase in a system with many mutually dependent participants. How do we ensure that electronic communications are not only built to be robust, but actually work when they are truly needed?

The seminar focuses on how electronic communications can be strengthened to sustain essential services, and what requirements are needed to ensure functionality in both the public sector and business. The discussion is held in cooperation with Krisledningspodden, with Mats Bohman as moderator.

content.title: Hybrid threats and resilience — how do we build a strong Sweden Inc. together?
content.description: Sweden faces an increasingly complex threat landscape in which hybrid threats, cyberattacks and geopolitical uncertainty are part of everyday life. Securing a robust, functioning society requires new cooperation across boundaries between politics, business and public organisations.
content.extendedDescription:
In a rapidly changing security landscape, Sweden constantly faces new and complex threats. Meeting them requires not only strong defence, but also a business sector that takes active responsibility and works closely with public organisations.

This seminar focuses on how companies can contribute to Sweden's total defence by combining emergency preparedness with commercial viability and long-term competitiveness. Drawing on concrete examples, we discuss how new forms of cooperation can create resilient ecosystems that strengthen Sweden's preparedness in peace, crisis and ultimately war.

The conversation explores how to accelerate the security transition from strategy to action, speed up preparedness and simultaneously create growth and innovation. The goal is a more resilient Sweden Inc. built on trust, cooperation and shared responsibility.

content.title: Public transport knows how we can achieve the climate targets — how do we get politicians on board?
content.description: Public transport is essential to achieving Sweden's and the EU's climate targets for 2030. Ahead of the 2026 election, we are strengthening our message and highlighting political measures needed to give us a chance of reaching the climate target. Our proposals are ready, but what do politicians say?
content.extendedDescription:
A seminar concluding with a panel debate with politicians.
Svensk Kollektivtrafik, Sveriges Bussföretag and Tågföretagen continue their joint project 4av10. The project aims to improve conditions for public transport and thereby increase its share of motorised journeys. By 2030, four in ten motorised journeys should be by public transport, compared with three in ten today.
We are doing this for road safety, accessibility and the climate on the path towards sustainable communities.

At kollektivtrafiken.se, we present the industry's policy statement with a range of short- and long-term measures. But the climate, growth and fairness also require decisions in parliament and government. Ahead of the 2026 election, we are highlighting three issues that are particularly important for a future built on sustainable travel.
content.subject: Infrastructure/transport

content.title: Migraine — an often overlooked condition affecting women: why do so few get the right treatment?
content.description: Migraine affects around 13 per cent of the population, mainly women of working age. Migraine-specific treatments exist, but requirements that only neurologists or headache specialists prescribe them create a bottleneck. The result is limited and unequal access for people with severe migraine.
content.extendedDescription:
Migraine is one of our major widespread diseases. For people with high-frequency migraine, targeted migraine-specific medicines have been developed for those with the greatest disease burden. Yet these treatments do not reach all severely affected patients.

Restricting prescribing to neurologists or headache specialists — a small specialist group responsible for a large patient population — creates bottlenecks and limited, unequal access. Patients whose condition is well managed and who could be referred back to primary care for follow-up occupy capacity, preventing or delaying access for those waiting for help.

How do we need to rethink our approach to ensure that innovations reach the right patients at the right time?

content.title: Alzheimer's care at a crossroads — can an action plan ensure the right care at the right time?
content.description: Alzheimer's disease causes considerable suffering and places pressure on healthcare. The national dementia strategy is in place, but diagnostics and treatment are advancing rapidly. Is a specific Alzheimer's action plan needed to ensure the right patient receives the right care at the right time?
content.extendedDescription: Alzheimer's disease causes considerable suffering and costs society billions each year. Research is advancing rapidly: new diagnostic tools and treatments can slow disease progression. The national dementia strategy ‘Varje dag räknas 2025–2028’ is in place, but is it sufficient to address rapid developments specifically in Alzheimer's? For patients to benefit from new opportunities, primary care must identify suspected cases early, testing capacity must expand and healthcare systems must be ready. How do we distinguish Alzheimer's from other forms of dementia or normal ageing? And how do we ensure that both regions and municipalities can meet new needs? What do patient representatives, healthcare professionals and politicians say — is it time for a national Alzheimer's action plan within the dementia strategy, to identify patients earlier and provide the right care at the right time?

content.title: Growing pains — challenges and major opportunities for Sweden's defence cities!
content.description: Defence investment and NATO membership are driving rapid growth in the defence industry's geographical hubs. How should public authorities, municipalities and businesses cooperate to enable scaling up, basing and transit amid intense pressure and a growing need for self-sufficiency and strong exports?
content.extendedDescription:
Rapid change is under way along Svenska säkerhetsstråket, including Arboga, Karlskoga and Kristinehamn, where the defence industry and defence authorities are making very substantial investments. This development is driven by increased demands for Swedish and European defence capability.

At the same time, questions arise about managing growth sustainably over the long term. How should municipalities, central government agencies and businesses cooperate to enable rapid expansion of production, new establishments and logistics flows while ensuring resilience, skills supply and societal development?

Meet leading representatives from the defence industry, defence authorities and the municipalities of Arboga, Karlskoga and Kristinehamn, working towards greater resilience and long-term, sustainable local growth.

content.title: Are we governing welfare effectively? The interplay between municipalities, regions and central government
content.description: Swedish welfare is governed at several levels. This has built our local democracy. At the same time, multilevel governance requires close interaction between central government, regions and municipalities. How can our governance model ensure both effective and equitable welfare in small and large municipalities and regions nationwide?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden's multilevel governance, involving municipalities, regions and central government, has been important in building today's welfare system and underpins local democracy. But governing welfare at several levels also requires close interaction between central government, municipalities and regions, whose needs can vary greatly across the country. There is a significant risk of inefficiency when central government dictates in detail how a municipality must perform a task.

Which issues are best resolved nationally and which locally to ensure equitable welfare nationwide?
How do we create a governance model that works for both small and large municipalities and delivers the best and most equitable welfare for every tax krona? And what is required of municipalities, regions, government and public agencies to make it work in everyday practice?

content.title: Threats and violence against social services
content.description: What happens to social services when managers, social workers and municipal politicians face direct violence? What is needed to protect public representatives from risking their lives and health while carrying out their duties, while also safeguarding open and legally sound decision-making?
content.extendedDescription:
Threats and violence against social services representatives are a structural problem affecting both legal certainty and the working environment. But are systematic, long-term organisational measures enough to bring about real change towards a zero-violence vision? What are we not doing today that we should be doing?

Threats and violence also affect individuals directly and often force personal decisions in which victims must choose between their role and job and their life, health and family. Anonymous decisions are one proposal frequently raised in the debate. How can we balance transparency in decision-making with protecting decision-makers?

Discussion leader and moderator: Lina Blombergsson, Deputy Chair, Föreningen Sverige socialchefer.

content.title: What role does energy efficiency play in a digitalised, AI-driven society?
content.description: The transition and digitalisation have created a gap between organisations that understand and want to contribute to the transition and those lacking ambition, tools or resources. Society must work towards the same goal in this effort.
content.extendedDescription:
The panel discusses how leadership needs to develop to meet the technological transition and the growing demands that digitalisation, AI and sustainability targets place on organisations today.

The focus is on the leadership required, coordination and the ability to drive change forward.
Many projects lose momentum today, not because of a lack of ambition, but because responsibility, communication and a shared overview are not maintained throughout the process.
The discussion also explores how AI and digitalisation can improve decision support and cooperation to achieve ‘Netto-=’ buildings, while organisations need to develop their working methods and leadership to fully harness technology's opportunities. How does Sweden differ from the rest of the world, and what can we learn from other countries?

content.title: Does democracy die in the heat?
content.description: Is the climate crisis a crisis of democracy? What roles do disinformation and polarisation play in our ability to make the transition? The climate crisis demands long-term decisions, while politics is often governed by short electoral terms and public opinion. How does this affect the ability to maintain ambitious climate policy?
content.extendedDescription:
The climate crisis challenges democracy's fundamental logic. Long-term, complex risks must be managed within political systems characterised by short electoral terms and strong conflicts of interest. Meanwhile, climate issues are increasingly used to undermine trust in science, the media and democratic institutions.

This discussion describes how the climate crisis can contribute to democratic decline and create space for authoritarian forces, making both climate policy and democratic decision-making more difficult.

The climate debate has also become increasingly polarised, with trust in the media and research undermined by hate, threats and organised denial.

We also discuss ways forward that can strengthen democracy's ability to manage the transition.

content.title: An entirely new playing field for entirely new nuclear power — how do we achieve something never done before?
content.description:
New nuclear power on Väröhalvön recently took a major step forward, with land secured and a nuclear technology supplier selected.
Several milestones have already been reached. What challenges remain?
content.extendedDescription:
Videberg Kraft, a brand-new energy company, is taking major steps towards doing something never done before as we begin the journey to build three modular nuclear reactors on Väröhalvön in Varbergs kommun.

Videberg Kraft has just ONE task: deliver 1500 MW of electricity to the Swedish grid.

Behind Videberg Kraft stand nine of Sweden's leading industrial companies (ABB, Alfa Laval, Boliden, Hitachi Energy, Höganäs, Saab, Stora Enso, SSAB, Volvo and Vattenfall), with the Swedish state also set to become an owner in due course.

To find out where we stand and where we are heading, join our seminar on Videberg Kraft's plans for the future. We invite you to an in-depth discussion of trade-offs, difficult decisions and practical steps that underpin how new nuclear power can be built on Väröhalvön.

Welcome to Videberg Kraft at Arena Energi.
content.subject: Energy

content.title: The future of bus services — how do we ensure sustainable procurement in public transport?
content.description: Contracted public bus services underpin many people's daily lives and businesses' skills supply and are essential to Sweden meeting its climate targets. But the system now faces a crisis: several operators are making losses. What is needed to reverse the trend?
content.extendedDescription:
Swedish bus companies operate in a pressured market with declining profitability, greater uncertainty and increasing regulatory demands. Previously stable conditions have been replaced by volatility, rising costs and higher risks.

Current contract models are identified as a central problem, with an uneven division of risk between contracting authorities and bus companies. Technical and regulatory demands are increasing while capital costs rise, particularly for vehicles. The result is wider variation in bid prices, with risk appetite carrying increasing weight. In the long run, competition is threatened as fewer operators participate in procurement under these conditions.

A new report from Sveriges Bussföretag analyses market conditions and risk allocation in publicly procured bus services and how they affect companies' ability to operate sustainably over the long term with passengers at the centre.
content.subject: Infrastructure/transport
content.accessibility: Event captioning, hearing loop

content.title: The EU's forthcoming renovation requirements — a goldmine or a climate disaster?
content.description: The EU's forthcoming renovation requirements put Sweden at a crossroads: will the renovation wave become an engine of circular innovation, or will we remain stuck in linear working methods that make the transition more expensive, slower and less sustainable?
content.extendedDescription: The EU's new Energy Performance of Buildings Directive is driving a massive transformation of Europe's building stock. Sweden, with hundreds of thousands of buildings requiring energy-efficiency improvements before 2050, faces one of its largest renovation waves ever. Yet linear working methods, complicated rules and a lack of clear incentives risk holding back the circular innovation Europe is now pursuing. Requirements for minimum standards, lifecycle calculations and renovation plans present both opportunity and risk: either we take the lead in smart energy efficiency and circular systems, or we fall behind while other countries already view their buildings as valuable material banks. This seminar brings together experts and decision-makers to discuss whether Sweden is ready for the shift and what is needed to prevent politics, industry and regulations becoming the bottleneck.
content.subject: Construction
speakerTitles: Technical Director and Head of Property Management

content.title: Is the most expensive food the food that never gets eaten?
content.description: We talk a lot about food prices but far too little about how much money we throw in the bin. Households account for half of Sweden's food waste. How can we reduce waste and spend the money on quality food from Swedish producers instead?
content.extendedDescription:
How much money is thrown in the bin? For a Swedish family, it amounts to thousands of kronor each year, and household food waste is a significant part of Sweden's total food-related climate impact.

The seminar brings together different perspectives on food waste at home. How has Coop Gotland reduced in-store food waste from 120 tonnes to almost zero, and what can households learn? What makes consumers choose distinctive local products over cheaper goods, and does that affect how much is actually eaten? And how can digital tools make weekly dinner planning easier for families?

There will be samples from Gotland food producers, canapés prepared by Evelina Collin Reuterfors from Sveriges Mästerkock and lunch by Millis Wernersson. The event is hosted by SmakShare, a Swedish recipe app helping families and couples collect their recipes in one place and plan weekly dinners more easily.
content.subject: Food

content.title: Swedish wool — local processing of a local resource
content.description: Wool is a local raw material that is not fully utilised. Much of the wool shorn annually in Sweden never enters the processing chain. A large-scale wool scouring facility opened on Gotland 10 years ago, followed by a wool spinning mill focused on industry. Has it helped?
content.extendedDescription:
Using the Gotland company Ullkontoret as an example, we describe experiences and opportunities for Swedish wool. Knowledge of wool fibre's beneficial properties, and the fact that so much wool never even reaches the first stage — collection and washing — led us to open a wool scouring facility in 2016. But most of the wool was then sent abroad for further processing. The next step was therefore to establish a spinning mill to supply Swedish industry with large batches of domestic yarn, ready for knitting and weaving machines.

Local processing of local raw materials creates resilience for future challenges, reduces transport needs and thus the CO2 footprint, and provides local jobs. A local wool value chain returns income to the place where wool is produced and strengthens that community. As long as there are sheep, wool will be shorn every year, whether we use it or not.
content.detail: Tent by the guest harbour near the Strandgatan — Kaserngatan junction
content.subject: Construction
