content.title: How can Sweden prepare people for a working life shaped by AI?
content.description: Sweden’s AI ambitions are accelerating, but the workforce is not keeping pace. A growing skills gap is slowing adoption, limiting competitiveness, and risking inequality. The key question is how to equip people, organisations, and society to turn AI into real economic and social value.
content.extendedDescription: AI is already changing how work is done across Sweden. At the same time, a crucial societal question is emerging: how do we ensure that people have the skills they need to participate, contribute and thrive in a labour market where AI is becoming part of everyday working life? Sweden has strong ambitions in AI, but many employers are already reporting skills shortages and a growing gap between rapid technological development and people’s actual readiness to keep up. Demand for AI-related competence is rising quickly, while the shift is reshaping roles, learning needs and access to opportunity. This conversation explores what is required to prepare individuals, workplaces and society for the future of work — and how Sweden can make the transition both competitive and socially sustainable.
content.subject: Digitalisation
content.accessibility: Wheelchair-accessible entrance and venue
speakerTitles: Moderator and Sr Director Marketing EMEA North

content.title: From waste targets to the classroom — put food waste on the timetable
content.description: How do we achieve the EU's food waste targets in practice? Children's eating habits are shaped at school every day, while large quantities of food are thrown away in Sweden. Putting food waste on the timetable can combine education, sustainability and behaviour change where it makes the greatest difference: in the classroom.
content.extendedDescription:
In 2025, the EU adopted binding food waste targets. Agenda 2030 calls for halving waste at the consumer level. Despite measures taken, we will not reach these targets.

One in five portions in public kitchens is thrown away. Food waste cost SEK 370 million in 2024. We urge children to conserve the planet's resources but fail to set a good example.

Real change requires a broader perspective centred on knowledge of the food system, behaviours and values. Schools are a unique setting where these three can meet and future eating habits are shaped. Learning for sustainable development, sustainable food systems and practical everyday situations can be connected here.

Everyone has a relationship with food, and therefore with food waste. By increasing understanding of food's value, we can strengthen respect for raw ingredients and take steps to reduce waste.
content.subject: Food

content.title: How do we secure skills and capacity in Sweden's defence sector?
content.description: Growing geopolitical tensions and major defence investments are creating a new situation. Defence organisations need to rapidly expand their efforts to attract, develop and retain the right skills. What is needed to secure skills supply in a new security reality?
content.extendedDescription:
EY presents insights from a Nordic study of how public and private defence organisations approach short- and long-term skills supply. The study draws on interviews with leading representatives and analysis of international trends.

The seminar explores how the defence sector meets growing skills needs during rapid expansion, technological development and tougher competition for talent. We focus on strategies to attract, develop and retain skills and on technology's role in enabling the defence of the future.

The seminar concludes with a panel discussion on which capabilities will be crucial over the next 3–5 years and what this means in practice.

The panel includes employer and employee representatives from the public and private sectors, as well as political representatives.
content.subject: Security/defence
speakerTitles: Head of National Security & Defence, Technology Strategy
Senior Vice President and Head of HR

content.title: Gambling problems — how can society better protect individuals?
content.description: Gambling addiction is a growing problem. More people are becoming trapped in games designed to create strong feelings of reward. For many, this leads to financial and relationship difficulties, stress and mental ill health, despite gambling companies' legal responsibility to protect players.
content.extendedDescription:
When someone develops gambling problems, their brain, everyday life and relationships are all affected. Many people seeking support have already accumulated large debts or lost contact with work and education. Society offers protection through gambling legislation, healthcare responsibilities and social services support, but efforts are not always coordinated or sufficient.

The seminar brings together researchers, healthcare professionals, public authorities and politicians to provide a clear picture of today's situation. They explain what research says about why gambling addiction develops, which forms of support work best and which parts of the current system need strengthening.

Together, we identify what must change for more people to receive help in time and how society can provide stronger protection for people at risk of gambling addiction.
content.subject: Research
speakerTitles: Chair of the Primary Care Committee's Public Health and Dental Care Subcommittee

content.title: AI infrastructure for Swedish competitiveness — how can public authorities and businesses feel secure?
content.description: How do we build digital infrastructure in which both public authorities and businesses are secure and independent? How can we reduce vulnerability and create the conditions needed to strengthen Swedish innovation and sovereignty?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden's future with AI is about infrastructure, energy and data centres as well as algorithms. Digital sovereignty is a prerequisite for building and operating effective, secure and energy-efficient data centres on our own terms. By controlling physical and digital infrastructure, from electricity supply and cooling to networks and storage, Sweden can strengthen innovation and retain its position as a high-tech, competitive country with scalable and sustainable AI capacity.

But do we really dare to make our future AI ecosystem dependent on infrastructure we do not control? Should Swedish energy policy and grid capacity be shaped around yesterday's IT needs when tomorrow's AI clusters require entirely different answers? And who actually sets the rules for where our most valuable data is stored — ourselves, or organisations far beyond our borders?
content.subject: Digitalisation

content.title: What has Sweden learned from four years of municipal cooperation with Ukraine?
content.description: Since 2022, Swedish municipalities have cooperated with Ukrainian counterparts during an ongoing war. What experience has been gained? What has actually worked, and what has Sweden learned about how municipal cooperation can strengthen Ukrainian democracy and resilience?
content.extendedDescription:
Since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, hundreds of Swedish municipalities and regions have established contacts with Ukrainian municipalities, districts and communities. Cooperation has taken place through SKR, Sida and direct partnerships, ranging from material support to knowledge exchange on municipal administration, democratic development and public services adapted to wartime.
But what has Sweden actually learned? Which models work during active conflict? How do Swedish municipalities manage partnerships when their counterparts are under fire, and how can these experiences shape future cooperation?

The discussion is organised within Samarbetsplattformen: Sverige & Ukraina (SPSU), a project by KlinteVolontär that gives Ukrainian civil society its own voice in Sweden's democratic debate and brings Swedish and Ukrainian organisations together to strengthen long-term cooperation between the countries.
content.subject: International affairs
content.organizationType: Collaboration between different types of organisation

content.title: If work can be done anywhere, why would anyone choose Stockholm?
content.description: The digital paradigm shift is making work increasingly independent of location. At the same time, competition for talent, companies and investment is growing. What determines which places are chosen, and what is needed to create attractive environments where people want to work, live and meet?
content.extendedDescription:
AI and technological development are changing not only working life, but also conditions for cities, offices and investment. When work can be done anywhere, new competition emerges between places. For companies, it is about where they can attract the right skills; for individuals, where they want to live; and for investors, where long-term attractiveness exists.

This places new demands on how we design cities and working environments. What makes a place relevant when physical presence can no longer be taken for granted? How is demand for offices and urban environments affected? And what is needed to create places people actually choose to spend time in?

The seminar discusses how changes in working life affect our view of place and what determines where people and companies will want to establish themselves in the future.

content.title: How free and independent are public service broadcasters and other tax-funded media?
content.description: Tax-funded media are often described as ‘free and independent’, but is that true if they also depend on tax funding? How have new challengers in the media market affected traditional media?
content.extendedDescription:
As tax-funded media face competition from new technology platforms and publishers, traditional media platforms are losing their privilege to define the issues and being challenged by an entirely new media community. What are the consequences when the tax-funded remit of Sweden's largest media organisation, public service broadcasting, is increasingly questioned and criticised for a lack of factual accuracy and impartiality?

Why have the Tidö parties avoided addressing the problems public service broadcasters are increasingly found to have? What allows SVT and SR to escape consequences for internal activism, such as the appeal concerning Swedish media reporting on Gaza, and double standards for participation in public service productions?

Opinion-maker Josefin Utas discusses these questions with public commentator Nick Alinia. Lena Malmberg (MED) moderates the discussion.
content.subject: Democracy

content.title: How do we get construction and essential energy renovations moving?
content.description: The construction sector faces a critical challenge. Despite accounting for around 11% of Sweden's GDP and being central to both growth and societal development, neither construction nor necessary energy renovations have accelerated at the required pace. The EU's new directives set clear requirements.
content.extendedDescription:
The EU's energy-efficiency requirements (EED & EPBD) concern not only climate ambitions but now also stronger preparedness and a more resilient society.
Much activity is currently stalled, while pressure to modernise, transition and renovate is growing rapidly.

The event explores why construction and energy renovations have yet to gain momentum and what obstacles, opportunities and solutions exist amid uncertainty. We discuss the new requirements, why they exist and how they contribute to both the climate transition and resilience in Sweden's building stock.

Discussions between business representatives and leading members of parliament bring different perspectives on stimulating construction and renovation. The focus is on how industry, politics and other stakeholders can jointly create the conditions to get the construction and energy renovations needed for Sweden's future under way.
content.subject: Construction

content.title: How do we create national climate infrastructure for Swedish cities and climate initiatives?
content.description: Swedish cities are to achieve climate neutrality by 2030, but often lack shared tools to collect, compare and use climate data. Without national climate infrastructure, monitoring risks becoming fragmented, duplication increasing and important climate measures being delayed.
content.extendedDescription:
How can municipalities, businesses and climate initiatives move from scattered climate calculations to shared knowledge and a faster transition? Hear how LFM30 in Malmö is developing national climate data infrastructure for cities and climate initiatives, and how pilots in several municipalities will test the collection, analysis and visualisation of climate data from construction and urban development projects for strategic climate governance.

The event takes the form of a discussion with short contributions from organisations working on climate-neutral cities, the construction sector's transition, roadmaps and digital climate data. It focuses on whether shared data, methods and tools can reduce duplication, improve comparability, provide better decision support for urban development and procurement, and contribute to climate-neutral cities. Participants are invited to join the discussion. No preparation is required.
content.subject: Sustainability
content.accessibility: Wheelchair-accessible toilet, wheelchair-accessible entrance and venue

content.title: Tomorrow's industry is being built now — but who will do the work?
content.description: Sweden is undergoing its biggest industrial transformation in generations. New investments are being made, new jobs are emerging and demand for skills is exploding. Amid this industrial boom, a crucial question arises: who will do the work?
content.extendedDescription:
Industry needs technicians, engineers, operators, data analysts, project managers and leaders as large generations retire. Competition for skills is intensifying. In this situation, Sweden cannot afford to draw on only half its talent pool.

In this discussion, we explore women, skills and the green industrial revolution, using Dalarna as a concrete example of a region where Sweden's next major growth cluster is emerging. Dalarna has global industrial companies, strong innovation and substantial skills needs in energy, steel, mining and advanced manufacturing.

We ask how to bring more women into technical professions, production and management. Do we need to broaden the image of what an industrial job is today? And how can more women of all ages come to see industry as an attractive place to grow, lead and drive change?

Tomorrow's industry is being built now. Does Sweden dare to build it using everyone's skills?
content.subject: Employment/labour market

content.title: Sweden is building resilience at record speed — could outdated thinking hold everything back?
content.description: The largest military expansion of modern times is under way, driven by the need to strengthen not only Sweden's defence capability but the resilience of society as a whole. But are we stuck in an old system?
content.extendedDescription:
The largest military expansion of modern times is under way, but the models for purchasing and building capability are not keeping pace. Investment in defence properties is expected to increase by 100 per cent within a few years, while procurement systems remain based on detailed management and control, designed for a stable world that no longer exists.

The research is clear: when pace and uncertainty increase, traditional client–supplier relationships inhibit innovation and erode trust. LUFS and LOU often allow more room than is used — the question is whether we dare to use it.

This panel brings together public-sector clients, industry and legal expertise to discuss building strategic partnerships within existing rules and what is needed to prevent outdated thinking from holding back a historic transition.
content.detail: Loops arena för impact, industri och energi
content.subject: Business

content.title: How can safety be improved in disadvantaged areas?
content.description: How can we create safe, secure and attractive environments through place development? How does the work happen in practice, and how can different organisations cooperate despite different incentives?
content.extendedDescription: Hjällbo Centrum is the heart of Hjällbo, offering a wide range of shops, services and everyday activities. The square is not only a place for commerce but also an important, lively meeting place for residents and visitors. Since 2025, it has undergone extensive renovation and become a greener, more welcoming meeting place for all generations, a centre where community continues to grow. As evidence that it meets the requirements for a safe and secure place, the square has been certified according to the principles of the BoTryggt2040 handbook. But what are the real incentives for place development? Are greater competitiveness and higher property values wholly positive for a place? Is there a risk of gentrification? Is place development a municipal matter or an investment issue for property owners? How can we measure its value? The seminar discusses different perspectives and needs in creating safe, secure and attractive places.
content.subject: Justice/crime

content.title: Self-driving buses on Gotland — the mobility of the future?
content.description: Meeting climate targets requires new solutions for sustainable, accessible transport. How can self-driving buses contribute to future mobility in Sweden and on Gotland?
content.extendedDescription:
Can self-driving buses become part of future solutions for sustainable, accessible transport? How can new technology strengthen public transport, improve accessibility and create new opportunities for residents and visitors, on Gotland and elsewhere in Sweden?

During Almedalsveckan, you can experience and explore a self-driving bus that has already operated in Linköping for several years. Come and see the technology up close and ask the experts on site questions.

Like many other places, Gotland has specific conditions, needs and challenges. Together, we want to explore how new transport opportunities can affect more parts of society than travel itself. We will look beyond legislation, funding and technology and discuss the changes we can anticipate and the functions and opportunities we want future transport to create. How are accessibility, services, meeting places and everyday life affected when new ways of travelling become possible?

content.title: Can we live healthy lives in an unhealthy society?
content.description: Stress, mental ill health and lifestyle-related diseases are increasing as inequality grows. How do societal structures affect people's health? How can economic democracy contribute to better public health?
content.extendedDescription:
More and more Swedes experience stress, mental ill health and reduced quality of life. Research also shows that economic divides, insecure living conditions and limited influence over one's daily life can affect health and wellbeing. How are societal structures, the economy and public health connected? And what reforms are needed to create a healthier, more sustainable society?
During this session, a podcast discussing these questions will be recorded on site. The conversation addresses the links between public health, economic democracy and social security, and how greater citizen influence over societal development can improve living conditions. It will also explore how healthcare policy can be reformed to become more accessible, preventive, equitable and patient-centred, with the aim of providing care that better meets people's needs nationwide.
Drawing on the social ideas of the Swedish ‘people's home’, the discussion also considers how a modern society can strengthen both physical and mental health.
content.subject: Health and social care

content.title: Why do more people with allergies not receive help in primary care?
content.description: Allergy is a widespread disease. The new national strategy emphasises that most patients should be treated in primary care. Does primary care have the resources needed for optimal treatment? What should different levels of care actually do? How do the regions govern care? And will the state provide new funding for allergies?
content.extendedDescription:
Is it finally time to address Sweden's most common widespread disease?

One in three people has an allergic disease. A national strategy and national guidelines have now been presented. The strategy emphasises, among other things, that primary care looks after most allergy patients, that access to care varies by socioeconomic status, and that there is a shortage of allergy specialists.

What happens now? Is this the moment when care for what may be Sweden's most common widespread disease takes a step forward, receives resources and becomes a priority?

What do the regions need to do to make primary care governance work, increase fairness and train more allergists? And what is the state doing?

Join an evening of knowledge about allergies, with three themes, from 17-19 in our garden.

Hot food and drinks will be available, with opportunities to mingle.
content.subject: Health and social care

content.title: From AI strategy to business value — what is needed in practice?
content.description: Why do some organisations create business value with AI while others get stuck at the pilot stage?
content.extendedDescription:
AI is high on the agenda in both politics and business, but many organisations still struggle to turn strategy and pilot projects into real use and business value.

During Almedalsveckan, Doings and Kinbergs plats 3 bring together leading voices from business, politics and AI expertise.

DISCUSSION 1. 10.15–10.35
Sweden's AI position in a global perspective

content.title: National cancer strategy — together we can move from words to action
content.description: Cancer is the leading cause of years of life lost in Sweden. But healthcare has made major progress, and mortality in Sweden is now among the lowest in the EU, partly thanks to the national cancer strategy that has guided the way. The government has updated the strategy to meet future needs.
content.extendedDescription:
The cancer strategy aims to reduce cancer risk, improve early detection, increase survival and provide the best possible quality of life during and after illness. It also emphasises the need for greater cooperation across organisations and sectors. Samverkansgruppen för svensk cancervård has been formed to coordinate this work.

Cancer care in Sweden is developing rapidly, with work under way in every area identified in the updated strategy. The strategy now provides a unifying force and a new opportunity to set priorities together. In Almedalen, we in Samverkansgruppen för svensk cancervård invite you to discuss how to move from words to action. What is the highest priority? Which partnerships need strengthening? What do the regions need from us to deliver world-class cancer care?

content.title: Time for safe care
content.description: Patients should receive timely care, and care should be safe for both patients and staff. Yet this is far from guaranteed today. Staff shortages caused by poor working conditions and heavy workloads lead to waiting lists that put both patient safety and healthcare staff's working environment at risk.
content.extendedDescription:
At the same time, effective solutions exist that need wider uptake.

In this seminar, Vårdförbundet brings together political representatives to discuss how to create sustainable, safe and accessible healthcare. Starting from voters' perspectives, we discuss the most urgent challenges and what politicians need to prioritise during the next parliamentary term to make healthcare work for those who need it most and those working in it.

The discussion focuses on real-world examples: solutions that have already shortened waiting times, improved working environments and increased patient safety. What is needed to spread them and make them the norm nationwide? And what political decisions are needed to give healthcare the right conditions?

Join a seminar shifting the focus from problems to possible ways forward — for time in care and for safe care.
content.subject: Health and social care
speakerTitles: Chair of the regional executive board

content.title: Can transparency stop Trumpism?
content.description: Regeringskollen is a database intended to promote democracy, transparency and accountability by collecting government decisions and opposition proposals in a searchable database. Many decisions are made very quickly and forgotten — we want to build a collective memory and gather the facts.
content.extendedDescription:
As citizens, we can assess a government every four years. But we often forget what it has done. Where has the government invested and where has it cut back overall? What decisions have been made in areas such as democracy, culture, education, climate and taxation? And what proposals has the opposition made in those areas?

Many decisions and proposals proceed despite criticism from consultation bodies, experts and civil society. A shift is occurring in which experts' knowledge is ignored and journalism dismissed as politics. How does this affect democracy and opportunities for accountability?

This seminar explores the work of gathering information about political proposals and decisions, the difficulties of finding the right information and why transparency matters in a democratic society.

Coffee and vegetarian breakfast rolls will be served.
content.subject: Democracy

content.title: How does the EU Pact on Migration and Asylum affect Sweden's reception of refugees?
content.description: The EU Pact on Migration and Asylum has now begun to apply throughout the EU, and migration is largely governed by European legislation. How will the change affect future reception of people seeking protection, what does the new screening involve, and how will the new reception and return centres work?
content.extendedDescription:
Join a seminar exploring the historic change as legislation on seeking protection becomes common across the EU, from Spain to Sweden. This major transition affects every part of the protection process, from applications through investigation, decisions and return. During the seminar you will learn more; during the webinar you will learn, among other things, about:
• Why the migration pact is being introduced and what it aims to achieve
• The Screening Regulation and new checks at the external border
• The new asylum process and how it differs from the current system
• How the new reception and return centres will operate
content.subject: EU
speakerTitles: Director Responsible for Implementing the EU Pact on Migration and Asylum

content.title: From protest to project — managing public opinion in urban development
content.description: More and more projects face opposition, appeals or lost momentum. This slows construction, affects investment and damages trust in planning. How can public opinion be addressed in ways that strengthen both democratic influence and feasibility, and how can earlier engagement reduce the risk of deadlock?
content.extendedDescription:
More and more projects face opposition, lose momentum or become stuck. But resistance does not necessarily mean a project is wrong; it may equally indicate inadequate engagement.

This seminar starts from two concrete cases in Uppsala illustrating both successes and setbacks in managing public opinion. They provide the basis for a panel discussion on democracy, legitimacy, feasibility and the importance of early engagement.

Experience shows that conflicts often arise when planning starts at the wrong end, with volumes and development rather than a place's conditions, qualities and potential. When people are invited in only after proposals have been formulated, the process risks becoming deadlocked.

We discuss what is needed to move from reactive management of public opinion to proactive co-creation.
content.subject: Construction
speakerTitles: Head of Urban Development Business Area

content.title: Social enterprises that make a difference exist — but how do we help more of them grow?
content.description: Across Sweden, social entrepreneurs are already tackling some of our greatest societal challenges, from exclusion to sustainable transition. They build businesses that work and do good. But what is needed for more to scale their operations and achieve greater societal impact?
content.extendedDescription:
Join a breakfast seminar on scaling businesses that both perform well and do good. During the morning, we bring together business, the public sector and civil society to share experience, identify obstacles and formulate practical solutions.

Arash Gilan offers a look ahead, followed by a panel discussion with Linda Vikström Nielsen, Head of Communications at IKEA Sverige; Annika Sten Pärson, Co-founder of The Inner Foundation; Adam Sandgren, Head of Business Development at Lunds kommun; and perspectives from social entrepreneurs in the Everyone’s Business accelerator programme.

We focus on what is missing for more social entrepreneurs to scale, how cooperation can be strengthened in practice and what we can do today. The aim is an open, forward-looking dialogue that leads to action — for society, for the future and for us all.
content.subject: Innovation

content.title: Net-zero emissions — what can Sweden learn from Denmark's CCS initiative?
content.description: Sweden has greater potential and higher ambitions for CCS than Denmark. How can effective policy implementation translate this into concrete expansion and contribute to the goal of net-zero emissions by 2045?
content.extendedDescription:
Denmark has quickly established itself as one of Europe's most advanced countries in carbon capture and storage (CCS), with concrete projects under implementation and clear frameworks for funding and responsibilities. A decisive factor has been its ability not just to adopt policy instruments but to implement them quickly and predictably in close cooperation with market participants. Meanwhile, Sweden has both greater technical potential and more far-reaching ambitions for CCS as a central tool for achieving net-zero emissions by 2045, particularly through bio-CCS.

We offer a brief overview of Swedish developments and share experience from Denmark: which policy decisions and implementation approaches have made a difference, how the value chain has been organised and which obstacles have had to be overcome. The focus is on what actually drives progress and how Sweden can turn its potential into large-scale delivery.
content.subject: Sustainability
content.accessibility: Wheelchair-accessible toilet, wheelchair-accessible entrance and venue

content.title: Can we meet without titles in a digital, performance-driven society?
content.description: How often do we meet without being defined by what we do? Almedalsveckan is built on encounters. But what happens to our conversations when titles, business cards and phones are left outside? When you cannot introduce yourself by name, profession or employer? When everything else is allowed?
content.extendedDescription:
This is not a seminar. It is not even a networking event — and if it is, it may be Almedalen's least useful one.
It is an experiment in how we meet and what happens when we stop performing and simply exist.

At the door, you encounter a few simple rules:
Put your phone in flight mode, and do not introduce yourself by name, profession or employer. No business cards. No business discussions.

Instead, we open the door to something else.

Inside, conversations without an agenda await. Hosts are present to guide and keep the room alive. Conversation cards with questions and reflections help us move beyond our usual roles towards more human encounters.

What happens when we remove titles and can meet without performance, status or expectations?

This is an experiment in what happens to our conversations — and to ourselves — when we disconnect from the outside world for a while and simply remain present together.
content.subject: Digitalisation
content.accessibility: Wheelchair-accessible entrance and venue

content.title: What would a secure and cost-effective future energy supply in Sweden look like?
content.description: How much energy will we use in the short and long term? How can Sweden secure its energy supply? What do new EU requirements mean for energy supply? How can it be made robust enough to provide essential energy services even during extreme weather, sabotage or war?
content.extendedDescription: Over recent decades, forecasts of future energy use have proved exaggerated. The government now says electricity use should double by 2050, regardless of electricity costs. This is unlikely to happen, but unclear or incorrect forecasts can lead to misguided investment. What is a reasonable long-term level? How far will new EU requirements on energy conservation and climate adaptation take us, and what difficulties arise in implementing them? What limits exist for future electricity production from nuclear and wind power? Global uncertainty affects fuel availability and prices, alongside increased opportunities to sabotage energy supply, drone weapons and extreme weather. Could local systems maintain electricity supply during temporary or prolonged outages?
content.detail: Tent by the guest harbour near the Strandgatan — Kaserngatan junction
content.subject: Construction
content.accessibility: Wheelchair-accessible toilet, wheelchair-accessible entrance and venue
speakerTitles: Doctoral Researcher in Resilient Energy Systems

content.title: What do we do when markets fail?
content.description: When market logic governs essential services, questions arise about accessibility, price and fairness. What happens when things people need — taxis, medicines, reliable trains or veterinary care — are shaped primarily by profitability rather than social responsibility?
content.extendedDescription:
What happens when market logic is applied to things people cannot do without — care for sick animals, taxis in rural areas, reliable trains, medicines or the ability to bury a loved one?
For several years, Tankesmedjan Tiden has examined markets where the promise of competition and choice has not been fully realised. Reports on veterinary care, taxis, vehicle inspections, pharmacies, railways and funerals reveal a common pattern: rising prices, growing urban–rural differences, poor accessibility and a system in which those most dependent on a service often have the least influence.
The seminar discusses the limits of markets. What happens when essential functions are governed primarily by profitability? How are ordinary people, working conditions and trust in society affected? And what political tools are needed when markets fail those who need them most?
content.subject: Economy

content.title: How can we win the global export battle?
content.description: Geopolitical chaos, accelerating technological development and trading conditions that change overnight are redrawing the playing field for Swedish export industries. What will it take for Sweden to remain a leading export nation, create jobs, attract investment and lay the foundations for future Swedish prosperity?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden's prosperity rests on exports, innovation, technological leadership and global competitiveness. But the playing field is changing rapidly. Geopolitical tensions, new trading patterns and accelerating technological development are challenging Swedish strengths in industry, transport, telecoms and energy, while competition for investment, skills and the jobs of the future intensifies.

How can Sweden maintain its position as a leading global export nation, and what decisions must be made now?

This breakfast seminar brings together representatives of business, industry and Team Sweden to discuss how Sweden can remain a leading force for innovation and the global transition, creating jobs and building a strong Sweden.

- Which export sectors are at stake, and what does this mean for Swedish jobs and GDP?
content.subject: Innovation
speakerTitles: State Secretary for Labour Market Affairs
Chair of the Committee on Finance

content.title: From vulnerability to competitiveness: what can we learn from business resilience in the north?
content.description: The green transition coincides with an ongoing hybrid conflict in northern Sweden, where total defence, robust infrastructure and security of supply are crucial for business. What can we learn from operations in the north to strengthen preparedness and competitiveness in the rest of Sweden?
content.extendedDescription:
The green transition creates major opportunities, but also new dependencies and vulnerabilities. Meanwhile, a changing security environment places greater demands on robustness, security of supply and cooperation between the public and private sectors.

In this seminar, Ramboll brings together leading players from industry, construction, transport and the public sector for a scenario-based discussion of what is needed to strengthen Sweden's preparedness and competitiveness.

The panel faces an escalating hybrid conflict in which several transport services are knocked out. How do businesses keep operating? How are business interests, social responsibility and survival prioritised when a crisis strikes? Which partnerships become crucial when systems come under pressure?
content.subject: Business
content.accessibility: Wheelchair-accessible entrance and venue
speakerTitles: Regional Head of Infrastructure in the North
Head of Public Affairs and External Communications

content.title: AI, trust and everyday life
content.description: AI is changing how we work, make decisions and interact with people. But how do we build trust, engagement and real change when technology develops faster than people's habits and behaviours?
content.extendedDescription:
AI can change a great deal: how we work, make decisions and interact with people. But one thing stays the same: trust still starts with a hello.

As technology becomes more advanced, the human dimension becomes more important, not less.

This conversation brings together Linda Vikström, Communications Director at IKEA Sverige, and Johanna Friman, brand expert at Doings. The discussion is organised by Doings and Kinbergs Plats 3. Together, they explore how trust is built when technology and ways of working change.

Drawing on IKEA's and Doings' work to bring about behavioural change in organisations, they discuss leadership, culture, trust and behaviour close to people's everyday lives.

The conversation is moderated by Marcus Wärn.

You will take away:
• How trust affects change in the AI era
• How people and behaviours determine whether change succeeds
• Perspectives from IKEA and Doings
• What leadership and communication need to do when technology develops rapidly

Brunch is served at Kinbergs Plats 3, Visby's most beautiful meeting place.

Welcome!
content.subject: Digitalisation
content.accessibility: Hearing loop, wheelchair-accessible entrance and venue

content.title: Has the region taken back control, and if so, how has this affected patients?
content.description: Following extensive changes to healthcare in Stockholm, several sources of evidence are now available to assess the results. Has the transition led to better access and equitable care, or to higher costs, reduced capacity and longer waiting lists for patients?
content.extendedDescription:
The seminar takes as its starting point two recent reports analysing the consequences of healthcare policy in Region Stockholm during the 2022–2026 electoral term. Drawing on statistics, economic analyses and patient outcomes, it examines how changes in governance, patient choice systems and operating models have affected waiting lists, costs and access.

The discussion highlights the effects on the system when established healthcare capacity is closed down faster than new capacity is built, and how these choices affect patients with substantial care needs. It concludes by discussing lessons for future decisions on healthcare organisation and how resources can be used more effectively to reduce queues and improve outcomes for patients.

The seminar ends with a panel discussion featuring representatives of both the governing administration and the opposition in Region Stockholm.
content.subject: Health and social care
speakerTitles: Professional Board Member and Former State Secretary (S)

content.title: From fossil fuels to the future: aviation's transition
content.description: Can we keep flying while reducing our climate impact? And how do geopolitical crises affect the transition?
content.extendedDescription:
What does it really take to make air travel sustainable, and what role do we ourselves play in that transition? Biofuels are often presented as a solution for long-haul flights, but how do we ensure that raw materials such as forestry and slaughterhouse waste are used without creating new problems? How do we ensure a sustainable supply chain behind the fuel?

Meanwhile, many point to the potential of electric aviation. But if electric motor technology already exists, are batteries, infrastructure or investment the real challenge?

And another important question: how do we actually view flying in the future? If flying is already accessible to relatively few people, what does making it more sustainable mean? Is it only about new technology, or also about travelling differently, less often and more consciously?

Join a conversation about fuel, technology and responsibility in aviation's transition between Elna Heimdal Nilsson, Professor of Aeronautical Sciences at Lunds universitet, and Thomas Frostberg, innovation and business journalist.
content.subject: Research
content.accessibility: Event captioned, wheelchair-accessible entrance and venue

content.title: Sustainable investment under pressure: how do we navigate the new rules?
content.description: Sustainable investment is under intense pressure as the security situation deteriorates and sustainability is dismissed as ‘woke’. Meanwhile, investors face difficult choices as geopolitical risks reshape the rules: should they stay invested and influence companies, or exclude them altogether?
content.extendedDescription:
In an increasingly conflict-ridden world, the defence and arms industries have become both more sought after and more debated. Many investors are reconsidering previous exclusions and opening up to defence investment, while others choose to reduce their exposure or entirely exclude countries such as the USA. At the same time, political initiatives, particularly in the USA, restrict consideration of ESG, diversity, equity and inclusion, and international climate commitments. This raises questions about the reliability of American companies and institutions when threats to leave shared frameworks actually materialise. Meanwhile, we are in the midst of an energy crisis. Could it reverse the trend and accelerate the transition?

The seminar focuses on how geopolitical risks should be managed in investment strategies and shareholder governance as pressure to address ESG decreases in some parts of the world but increases in others.
content.subject: Sustainability
content.accessibility: Wheelchair-accessible entrance and venue

content.title: Never again war: the path from militarism to the development of civilisation
content.description: Blind faith in military solutions risks creating serious problems for future security and welfare. Rising military expenditure takes resources away from other important areas of society. How can we build a strong movement for peace and anti-militarism?
content.extendedDescription: The post-war cry of ‘Never again war!’ has turned into an ongoing war over resources, raw materials and territory. But war is a failure. Peace, by contrast, represents the development of human civilisation. It is time to abolish war and genuinely establish human security. We know there is no empirical evidence that war can produce stability and democracy. Blind faith in military solutions risks creating serious problems for the world's future security and welfare. Rising military expenditure takes resources away from other important areas of society. Roads, railways, schools, healthcare and elderly care face cuts while billions pour into new regiments. This is unsustainable and weakens preparedness for the problems we actually face, such as those related to the climate.
content.subject: Human rights
speakerTitles: Writer and former Member of Parliament for Miljöpartiet
Social scientist and peace movement activist

content.title: Mental health among young people with diabetes
content.description: Living with type 1 diabetes affects both physical and mental health. Many young people with diabetes feel stress, worry and pressure from constantly having to manage their condition. This can lead to anxiety, low mood and feelings of exclusion, making mental health an important issue for society.
content.extendedDescription:
Living with type 1 diabetes affects not only the body but also mental health. Many young people describe stress, worry, tiredness and the feeling of always having to think about blood sugar, insulin and food. It is common to feel different, frustrated or overwhelmed at times.

Ung diabetes has therefore produced the discussion booklet ‘How are you? Practical tips for conversations about mental health and diabetes’. The booklet aims to create a sense of safety and open up important conversations about the mental wellbeing of young people with type 1 diabetes. Its goal is to reduce stigma, increase understanding and show that no one needs to carry their feelings alone.

Mental wellbeing needs more attention in diabetes care. The question ‘How are you?’ must be just as important as ‘What is your HbA1c?’ during a visit to the diabetes clinic.

Mental health is an important part of diabetes care, and talking about how you feel can make a big difference.
content.subject: Health and social care

content.title: Private capital in the service of society: opportunities and challenges in the expansion of prison and probation services
content.description: The expansion of prison and probation services is fundamentally a question of the functioning of the rule of law and long-term resilience. What role can private property owners and investors play in enabling rapid, sustainable expansion?
content.extendedDescription:
As the number of prison places is set to increase sharply, particularly in lower security categories, questions of location, delivery, security requirements, financing and timescales become critical.

How can private capital help meet capacity needs while combining commercial logic with high security requirements and clear social responsibility?

Svefa's courtyard, Fastighetshubben, at Adelsgatan 25 is the meeting place in Almedalen where the public and private sectors can meet, exchange experience and discuss property-related issues focusing on urban development, the built environment and a sustainable society. On stage, we host seminars, panel debates and networking events focusing on strategic urban development, the property market and sustainability. You can find Svefa's full Almedalen programme at www.svefa.se
content.subject: Economy
content.accessibility: Wheelchair-accessible entrance and venue
speakerTitles: Head of Urban and Property Development Business Area

content.title: From loneliness to community: what are the challenges and solutions?
content.description: Involuntary loneliness is a serious public health challenge, and the need for solutions is raised increasingly often. New meeting places are sought and new services developed. But we also need to pause and reflect: might many of the solutions already be right in front of us?
content.extendedDescription:
A range of initiatives already help people find community and new social settings. They bring people together around interests or everyday activities, taking the step from digital contact to meeting in real life.

Here, we highlight some initiatives already helping to reduce loneliness and strengthen social connections. You will encounter examples ranging from community-building apps developed by older people for older people to services for people who want to meet around shared interests.

We also explore how today's much-criticised digital platforms can actually provide an important bridge from social isolation into a social community.

Come and discover ways to build community, and try Speed-HEJ:ing, part of Hela Almedalen säger HEJ. In short sessions, you will meet randomly selected Almedalen visitors with different perspectives, experiences and opinions.
content.subject: Sustainability

content.title: The new charging economy: from challenge to business value
content.description: Electrification is happening here and now, but access to charging is deeply unequal. Technology and grants are in place. Yet too many property owners are waiting. To meet the 2030 targets, more must act now, not later.
content.extendedDescription:
What will it take for property owners, energy companies and the automotive industry to pull in the same direction? Around 70% of all vehicle emissions come from private cars. Yet most people living in apartment buildings lack access to reasonable charging facilities. This is not a technology problem or a grant problem. It is a decision-making problem.

At this breakfast seminar, we demonstrate that profitable charging is already possible, without waiting for power regulations, V2G or the next generation of technology. Everything needed is already in place.

We begin with an interactive session in which the audience shares its own views. We then take a broad look at the facts, practical experience and the questions that actually determine whether the transition gathers pace. This is followed by a panel discussion on smart charging, energy optimisation, V2G and making charging accessible to more people.

The aim is for you to leave the breakfast table with concrete next steps, not more unanswered questions.

Breakfast sandwiches and coffee from 07:45. Welcome.
content.subject: Energy
content.accessibility: Hearing loop, wheelchair-accessible entrance and venue

content.title: Values-driven non-profit schools: why does society need more providers motivated by shared values?
content.description: An increasingly complex society needs schools that do more than measure results, consciously taking responsibility for their broader educational mission and the whole picture. Values-driven non-profit schools put values, relationships and social responsibility first, helping to build trust, inclusion and sustainable social development over the long term.
content.extendedDescription:
Values-driven non-profit schools start from a clear set of values in which relationships, participation and responsibility are central. When school culture is shaped by clear values, relationships, participation and responsibility become central. Making values the primary driving force creates a long-term perspective: decisions focus on the best interests of pupils and society, even when this is difficult.

Through strong local roots, cooperation with civil society and a holistic approach to learning, values-driven non-profit schools can reach pupils who might otherwise be excluded. They contribute not only to learning but also to social cohesion, democratic education and efforts to prevent crime and exclusion.

A school system with more values-driven providers strengthens diversity, innovation and society's resilience: an investment in both today's children and tomorrow's society.
content.subject: Children/young people

content.title: How can historic environments develop sustainably in an era of climate change and transition?
content.description: Historic environments are affected by climate change, social transformation and new demands on their use. How can they be developed and managed sustainably without losing their value? This requires new approaches and knowledge that can address both preservation and change.
content.extendedDescription:
How can research help develop future approaches to historic environments? The EU currently funds several research projects exploring how cultural heritage can be managed, developed and brought into use in a rapidly changing society.

The seminar takes as its starting point three European research projects, Caleche, FuturHist and InHerit, which demonstrate different ways in which historic environments can become resources for sustainable development, innovation and new forms of management.

In a conversation between researchers and practitioners, we discuss the insights and methods emerging from the projects, how their results can inform policy and practice, and the role of research in developing the historic environment sector.

The event is aimed at decision-makers, public authorities and organisations working in the built environment, cultural heritage and urban development.
content.detail: Burmeisterska huset cultural heritage arena: sensitive renovation and World Heritage
content.subject: Climate/environment

content.title: More food in the north: how difficult can it be?
content.description: Northern Sweden has disused farmland, an increasingly favourable growing climate and untapped potential for food production. We need to increase food production here to make food preparedness more robust across Sweden, but how? What new knowledge and skills are needed?
content.extendedDescription:
Global instability is bringing a new focus on domestic food production. At the same time, the changing climate is opening up new opportunities for cultivation and food production in northern Sweden.

Agriculture in northern Sweden has long struggled with poor profitability and infrastructure, and has not been prioritised in national politics. Today, there is renewed interest in developing opportunities to produce more food in the north.

But agriculture in the north cannot be expanded by simply copying southern Sweden. In a recently published report on food production in northern Sweden, Jordbruksverket highlights the importance of coordinated efforts and greater knowledge. SLU has begun intensive work to develop a hub for increased food production in the north: production that is sustainable, resilient and profitable. How can this be ensured? What knowledge is needed?
content.subject: Food

content.title: Young people vote with their feet: from leisure to the future
content.description: Young people vote with their feet every day, but are we really listening? When some never join leisure activities or leave early, it affects their path into education and work. Why is this? How do we build systems that bring more people into communities where they develop skills for working life?
content.extendedDescription:
Young people vote with their feet every day, but are we really listening?

When children and young people choose activities, return to some settings or leave others, they tell us something important about their needs, interests and dreams. But do we use this knowledge when developing tomorrow's leisure activities?

Meanwhile, many young people remain outside leisure activities or leave them early. The consequences emerge later as reduced participation, weaker networks and fewer opportunities to develop skills that matter in education, work and society.

The seminar brings together young people, municipalities, civil society and business to discuss how we build stronger bridges between leisure and the future. How can we listen better to young people? What role does leisure play in democracy, community and hope for the future? And how can we help more young people develop, make their voices heard and find their way forward in life?

No preparation is required.
content.subject: Children/young people

content.title: Why does Sweden need a textile university?
content.description: Textiles are crucial to Europe's green transition, Sweden's competitiveness and Sweden's preparedness. The issue extends far beyond clothing and fashion. Why are textiles a strategic issue for Sweden's future, and what is a textile university?
content.extendedDescription:
Join a breakfast for anyone wanting to understand why textiles are a strategic issue for Sweden's future, and what a textile university is.

Textiles are crucial to Europe's green transition, Sweden's competitiveness and Sweden's preparedness. The issue extends far beyond clothing and fashion. Textiles are used in the automotive industry, healthcare, total defence, construction and the circular economy.

Högskolan i Borås invites you to a networking breakfast in Almedalen to discuss why Sweden needs a textile university. During the morning, you can meet representatives of the university, ask questions and discuss how research, education, innovation and industrial development can come together to strengthen Sweden's textile transition.

Högskolan i Borås has a unique environment bringing together textile design, textile technology, AI, circular flows, artistic research and business. The question is how that strength can be scaled up to meet Sweden's and Europe's needs.
content.subject: Economy

content.title: Does Sweden need anti-personnel mines?
content.description: Following the war in Ukraine, Sweden is again debating its ban on anti-personnel mines. Military benefits are weighed against humanitarian and environmental consequences. How should Sweden balance defence needs with international law and humanitarian commitments?
content.extendedDescription: This panel takes as its starting point the current Swedish debate on a possible withdrawal from the Ottawa Treaty and the reintroduction of anti-personnel mines. The debate brings together humanitarian, military, and legal perspectives, and asks how Sweden should assess the potential benefits and risks of such a policy shift. The panel will discuss what research and operational experience from past and current conflicts can tell us about the military utility of anti-personnel mines, their humanitarian consequences, and the legal implications of changing Sweden’s current position. The aim is to support a more evidence-based security policy debate. The key question is not only whether Sweden can use anti-personnel mines, but whether they would strengthen Swedish security enough to justify the documented risks for civilians, land use, infrastructure, and long-term recovery after war.
content.subject: Security/defence
content.accessibility: Wheelchair-accessible toilet, wheelchair-accessible entrance and venue

content.title: How can we secure Sweden's supply of engineers?
content.description: The need for engineers has never been greater. How can we secure technical expertise in a world of accelerating change so that Sweden can strengthen its position in global competition? Does it depend on funding, universities or the design of the education system?
content.extendedDescription:
Interest in master's programmes in engineering is greater than ever, and applications to the largest technical universities are very high.

The green and digital transitions are rapidly changing labour market needs, and industry is seeking more engineers and technical specialists. Global competition for advanced expertise is increasing.

While places at some universities remain empty, students with excellent qualifications are queuing to study at others.

How can Sweden secure its supply of engineers and technical expertise? Does the education system need to be modified, or places allocated differently between universities, to better meet society's needs?

Chalmers and KTH bring together political representatives and representatives of business, industry and academia for a panel discussion on Sweden's skills supply and competitiveness.
content.subject: Education
content.organizationType: Collaboration between different types of organisation
content.accessibility: Hearing loop, wheelchair-accessible toilet, wheelchair-accessible entrance and venue
speakerTitles: Member of the Committee on the Labour Market
Business Policy Expert, Education and Skills Supply

content.title: A well-treated patient: are data lakes and follow-up the keys to the right individual treatment?
content.description: Despite major investment in healthcare and innovative treatments, the desired results are not always achieved. Many patients do not receive the follow-up and evaluation needed for treatment to remain effective throughout. The potential of data-driven approaches and cooperation between healthcare services and patients often goes untapped.
content.extendedDescription:
How do we create future healthcare in which more people meet treatment goals, measured both by patient-reported outcome measures (PROM) and objective disease parameters, so that individuals and society gain the greatest possible benefit? Could the key be systematically recording and following up treatment outcomes, with smart data collection and use in close cooperation between patients and healthcare services creating the conditions for better long-term care and health, while giving healthcare services greater opportunities to optimise organisation, working methods and resource use?

The discussion also aims to highlight how innovation in healthcare and life sciences drives progress for the benefit of patients, care quality and society's long-term sustainability.

This event is part of Life Science Day, an initiative of the Medicon Village research park.
content.subject: Health and social care
speakerTitles: Chair of the Regional Executive Board in Region Östergötland and Deputy Chair of SKR's Healthcare Delegation
Regional councillor in Region Skåne and chair of the SKR healthcare delegation

content.title: Regional innovation systems: the foundation of Sweden's competitiveness
content.description: Sweden's competitiveness is created in regional innovation systems, where knowledge, capital and skills circulate between companies, universities and the public sector. In Skåne, research strengths underpin a strong life sciences innovation system. How can it be given the best possible conditions?
content.extendedDescription: Sweden's competitiveness is created in regional innovation systems. This is where companies, universities, test environments and the public sector meet, and where research becomes jobs, exports and solutions to societal challenges. Research on clusters and regional innovation systems shows that innovation largely emerges in geographically concentrated environments where knowledge, capital and skills circulate between participants. This is perhaps most evident in life sciences. Using concrete examples from Skåne, we show how research strengths have developed into innovation systems, how conditions for businesses have been improved, and what is needed for the systems to strengthen and grow. We also show how the European Commission's proposal for National and Regional Partnership Plans (NRPP) could support or undermine regional innovation systems across Sweden.
content.subject: Innovation

content.title: Micro- and Nanoplastics: Impact on Animals and Nature
content.description: The plastic we threw away years ago has not disappeared. It has broken down into microscopic particles — and today, these particles are found within the bodies of the species we share this planet with.
content.extendedDescription:
Together, we will explore what the latest research reveals about how micro- and nanoplastics are affecting the living systems around us — from the pets in our homes to the bees that pollinate our food, and across forests, marine life, and oceans.
 
Key insights:
	•	How plastic degrades into micro- and nanoparticles — and how electrostatic charge, combined with their small size, makes nanoplastics far more biologically active
	•	Plastic particles found in the organs and food of cats and dogs — and what this means for the animals in our care
	•	The crisis facing bee populations — and why their decline poses a direct threat to global food systems
	•	How forests function as living, interconnected systems — and how plastic particles may disrupt these systems at the cellular level, affecting photosynthesis and oxygen production
	•	What is driving the accelerating decline of marine animals and seabirds
content.subject: Animals/nature
content.accessibility: The event is captioned
speakerTitles: Electrical Engineer, musician, and active volunteer of the Creative Society

content.title: Young people's participation in democracy and social sustainability: how do we make it real?
content.description: Many young people feel that democracy is distant, difficult to influence and not for them, even though they are strongly engaged. How do we make democracy more accessible, relevant and inclusive, with room for different perspectives and young people's voices taken seriously, both locally and in a wider context?
content.extendedDescription:
Democracy begins when people meet. In D-Effect's interactive tent, we create a lively meeting place where young people, politicians and other stakeholders explore questions of democracy, influence and social sustainability.

Throughout the day, you can take part in workshops, discussions and creative activities, or sit down for a spontaneous conversation. Share perspectives, test ideas and reflect on your own role in society.

We want to challenge the idea that democracy is difficult and remote. Here, it becomes accessible, relevant and engaging for real. Through dialogue and interaction, we create space for more young people to feel that their voice matters.

As part of the EU project D-Effect, we highlight young people's perspectives from different parts of Europe and collect ideas to strengthen their influence on societal issues.

No advance registration is required. Drop by whenever it suits you.

content.title: Sweden's most important growth: marine technology and defence innovation for total defence and transition
content.description: In Blekinge, cooperation between the region, municipalities, academia, industry and central government has laid the foundations for one of Sweden's most advanced growth environments. Investment in marine technology and defence innovation has strengthened civilian industry and military capability. How can we use that strength to tackle the energy transition?
content.extendedDescription:
Region Blekinge, Karlskrona kommun and Blekinge Tekniska Högskola, together with Business Sweden, the region's business community, major industrial companies such as NKT and Saab, and authorities such as Försvarsmakten and Kustbevakningen, have cooperated in various ways to create innovation environments, meeting places and research opportunities that accelerate development.

The first discussion highlights successful examples and the most important conditions behind what we have achieved so far, focusing on Blekinge and Karlskrona.

In the second discussion, we broaden our perspective to consider the conditions for stronger total defence capabilities, from both energy supply and security perspectives, taking the Baltic Sea as our starting point.
content.subject: Employment/labour market
speakerTitles: Head of Energy Systems & Energy Storage

content.title: How do we create meeting places for business and the cultural sector?
content.description: How can the cultural sector and business come together to diversify funding for culture? What does business want, and what can the cultural sector offer? What role does the county administrative board play in regional development?
content.extendedDescription:
Join a seminar where the cultural sector and business meet, and the role of county administrative boards in regional development is clarified. Diversifying cultural funding in ways that benefit culture, business and society is a current focus for the county administrative boards of Västernorrland, Västra Götaland and Kalmar. This work takes place in cooperation with Konstnärsnämnden and the regions.

Content
- From grants to mixed funding: what is really at stake? How can we create opportunities for culture despite reduced public funding?
- Meeting places as a driving force: how do we get culture and business to actually meet? What does it take to move from dialogue to real collaboration? What does business want, and what can culture offer in return?
- Regional perspectives: what role can county administrative boards take? How can they act as neutral brokers between sectors?
content.subject: Culture
speakerTitles: Moderator and Head of the Analysis and Collaboration Department

content.title: Higher returns and impact through blended finance?
content.description: The world faces enormous investment needs in energy, infrastructure, water, health, agriculture and digitalisation. Meanwhile, asset managers are seeking new opportunities for long-term returns, diversification and measurable sustainability.
content.extendedDescription:
ISEC HållBar is back!

ISEC invites you to a panel seminar where, together with Jennie Sinclair, SPP, Fondbolagens förening, Hand in Hand and LM International, we explore one of today's most pressing questions: is blended finance the new win-win model for future investment?

The question is how these needs can be met through structures that work for institutional capital, fund management companies and private savers alike, in a solution that benefits everyone.

Blended finance is often presented as a model for reducing risk, mobilising private capital and making investment in emerging markets more commercially viable. By combining public, philanthropic and private capital, investments previously seen as too complex, illiquid or risky can be structured to create value at multiple levels.

The panel explores how the financial sector can turn global development and infrastructure needs into investable products.
content.subject: Economy

content.title: 12 000 large roofs can generate electricity: how do we turn potential into reality?
content.description: An untapped energy source lies on 12 000 Swedish roofs. Large properties can generate their own solar electricity, easing pressure on the electricity system by producing power where it is used. Why is solar power on large roofs expanding so slowly in Sweden compared with the rest of Europe?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden's large roofs are among the country's most underestimated resources. Shopping centres, apartment buildings, warehouses and sports halls can become power plants that generate electricity exactly where it is needed, while making properties active participants in the electricity system.

The potential is enormous: 12 000 large roofs could generate substantial amounts of solar electricity. The European Commission's own analysis identifies self-consumed solar power as one of Europe's greatest untapped opportunities. Yet Sweden is falling behind. Alongside Estonia and Finland, we are one of the few EU countries with strict restrictions on those wishing to generate their own electricity.

Join a conversation between key players in solar energy, energy storage and property about what is needed to unlock this potential, and how new technology can enable properties to contribute more than ever to the electricity system.
content.subject: Energy

content.title: Preparedness in spatial planning: from peacetime to a new reality
content.description: How do we plan communities that continue to function when the worst happens? Total defence considerations now need to be integrated into spatial planning, from early strategic choices to implementation.
content.extendedDescription:
Rebuilding total defence in response to a sharply deteriorating security threat environment means that preparedness considerations must now inform societal development and the physical planning of infrastructure and new construction. Come and hear an expert perspective on total defence law. This session focuses on how early decisions in spatial planning affect the options available in crisis and war. It also discusses the tools and processes different actors need to make this work in practice.

Help shape the discussion at Omställningsarenan in Sweco's courtyard during Almedalsveckan! For the fourth consecutive year, forward-looking actors from the built environment sector are coming together. No registration is required. Enjoy a relaxed atmosphere in the courtyard, hear incisive observations and take part in solution-focused discussions.

content.title: No driving licence, no job? The gap holding back Sweden's labour market
content.description: Driving licence requirements exclude young people from the labour market, while healthcare, social care and skilled trades are crying out for workers. How can we lower the barriers?
content.extendedDescription:
Unemployment, particularly among young people, is one of Sweden's major societal challenges. At the same time, several sectors face substantial recruitment needs.

Public debate often focuses on education, integration and labour market matching, but less often on the role of a driving licence. For many young people, having a driving licence has effectively become a decisive barrier to entering employment.

Sweden has one of Europe's highest rates of youth unemployment, and more than 126 000 young adults are currently out of work. Meanwhile, demand for workers is high in healthcare, services and skilled trades, where a driving licence is often a basic requirement. But young people do not have equal opportunities to obtain one. This creates a gap in the labour market: employers struggle to recruit, while many young people are excluded before they have even had a chance.

How can we lower the barriers and improve employers' access to skills? The seminar draws on current data and young people's own experiences of how a driving licence affects their chances of getting a job.
content.subject: Employment/labour market

content.title: Have we built too much bicycle parking in new housing?
content.description: Municipalities have increased bicycle parking requirements in new developments. But how should parking provision be sized now that new data on actual use is available? The issue is central to sustainable mobility, cost-effective construction and better use of space in properties.
content.extendedDescription:
Swedish municipalities have long used parking standards to encourage more sustainable travel and construction. As car parking requirements have been reduced, bicycle parking requirements have often increased. But how well do current requirements reflect actual use, and how should policy develop in light of new knowledge?
New data from 46 newly built housing projects provides a more evidence-based picture of how bicycle parking is used in practice. The results suggest that capacity and design should be based more on location, target groups and local conditions than on general standards. This raises important questions about how municipalities, developers and property owners can create solutions that both strengthen sustainable mobility and use space and resources more effectively.
The discussion explores how future requirements can become more relevant, efficient and evidence-based.

content.title: Beyond the frontline: Ukraine's defence and recovery
content.description: Beyond military defence, Ukraine must rebuild communities, support veterans and strengthen social resilience. How can recovery and reconstruction be achieved during an ongoing war? The answer will shape both Ukraine's future and Europe's long-term security.
content.extendedDescription:
Visit HUG's stand and gain insight into one of Europe's most important challenges: how Ukraine defends itself while rebuilding society. Throughout the day, we will highlight defence, resilience, veteran reintegration, rehabilitation and recovery during an ongoing war.

Meet our guests from Ukraine with firsthand experience of war, recovery and rebuilding:

• Oleksandr – Hero of Ukraine, defender of Donetsk Airport and veteran advocate
• Viktor – Veteran of the 95th Air Assault Brigade
• Ivan – Lieutenant Colonel, National Guard of Ukraine
• Oleksii – Drone Unit Commander, National Guard of Ukraine
• Oleksandr – Combat medic, tactical medicine instructor and evacuation systems specialist

We are open for dialogue, networking and knowledge-sharing with civil society, policymakers, businesses, media and the public. Drop by to exchange perspectives and learn more about the people and initiatives shaping Ukraine's future.
content.subject: International affairs

content.title: Powering Nordic AI: towards a smarter and more inclusive energy system
content.description: AI can support better forecasts, more efficient energy systems and greater flexibility. At the same time, it increases demand for energy and data and requires a high level of public trust. How can the Nordic region use AI to strengthen the energy system while driving the green transition?
content.extendedDescription:
The Nordic region is well placed to take a leading role and demonstrate how AI development and the energy transition can reinforce each other. It combines strong digital infrastructure, ambitious climate goals and a long tradition of cooperation. But this development also raises important questions about energy use, resilience and transparency, and how trust in the technology can be maintained.

This panel brings together Nordic experts to discuss how AI can contribute to a smarter, more robust energy system, and the political and technical choices required ahead. The event concludes with the award ceremony for Nordic Energy Challenge 2026, whose theme this year was ‘Powering Nordic AI’.

Curious about Nordic energy cooperation? Drop by the Norden tent for informal networking and breakfast before the event. Breakfast is served from 07.45.
