content.title: 50 years of workplace conflict: what does the employment law expert know that the rest of us miss?
content.description: Workplace conflicts are rarely just about laws; they are about leadership, responsibility and people. What can we learn from 50 years of employment disputes and working environment issues? What patterns recur when the rules of working life meet reality?
content.extendedDescription:
For five decades, Tommy Iseskog has been one of Sweden's most influential experts on employment law and the working environment. His books, analyses and training have helped generations of managers, lawyers and HR specialists understand the rules of working life. But behind the expert role is also a personal story.

How do views of responsibility, conflict and justice change after a lifetime spent dealing with the most complex workplace issues? What really happens in organisations when laws meet reality? And what has Tommy Iseskog learned after writing no fewer than 300 books, some of them novels?

We meet Tommy Iseskog in an open and personal conversation about working life, writing and the people behind the legal provisions.
It will be a fascinating story in which law meets life experience, sharp analysis blends with storytelling, and the audience meets the person behind one of the best-known voices in working life.
content.subject: Justice/crime

content.title: The working environment as a condition for artistic freedom: what challenges do artists face today?
content.description: Artists' working environments and conditions are crucial to a sustainable cultural sector. Professional artists form the creative core of the cultural and creative industries; their work is the very ‘raw material’ of cultural development.
content.extendedDescription: Artists' working environments and conditions are central to a sustainable cultural sector. As the creative core of the cultural and creative industries, professional artists provide the foundation on which all cultural development rests. Konstnärsnämnden has now surveyed artists' working environments for the second time to deepen understanding of their physical and psychosocial conditions. The seminar highlights why up-to-date, in-depth knowledge is crucial if artists are to develop, work over the long term and exercise their artistic freedom. The discussion also focuses on the political and structural measures needed to create sustainable artistic careers and strengthen the conditions on which culture depends.
content.subject: Culture

content.title: Two years of licensing requirements for sheltered accommodation
content.description: On 1 April 2024, a reform introduced licensing requirements for sheltered accommodation. Since then, around 40 women's shelters have closed their accommodation. What remains are expensive, profit-making private providers, while fewer and fewer children and women are granted protection.
content.extendedDescription:
Since April 2024, sheltered accommodation has required a licence under the Social Services Act. The legislation's original purpose was to improve quality and exclude unscrupulous providers. In practice, however, the reform has had far-reaching consequences.

Many non-profit women's shelters have been forced to close their accommodation, while private providers have gained a larger role, making profits from men's violence against women and children. At the same time, fewer children are placed in sheltered accommodation with their mothers, now that each child requires an individual placement decision.

What happens to support when quality is defined by bureaucracy rather than experience of the consequences of violence? And where do women and children go when the barriers to protection are raised?

Drawing on women's shelters' experiences, research and current analyses, we discuss the reform's actual consequences.

Has the legislation strengthened protection, or weakened it?

content.title: Who will take responsibility for making academic ATMP treatments available when industry steps back?
content.description: More academically developed cell and gene therapies are showing promising results for small patient groups, while industry withdraws from unprofitable ATMP treatments. Swedish university hospitals have the capacity, but current regulations are insufficient. Are new routes to implementation needed?
content.extendedDescription:
An increasing number of academically developed cell and gene therapies are undergoing clinical trials with promising results in diseases affecting small patient populations. At the same time, industry is discontinuing effective ATMPs for small patient populations where they are not financially or commercially viable. Swedish university hospitals have both the expertise and capacity to collaborate on production and clinical treatment, but clear routes to offering these treatments are lacking: neither commercial marketing authorisation nor the hospital exemption is a suitable way forward. Do we need to consider new routes for introducing treatments of academic origin, given how they challenge current systems?

PROGRAMME
Interview: CAR T treatment from a patient's perspective, Göran Eriksson, cancer-free after 25 years.
Panel discussion with public authorities, politicians and experts.
content.subject: Health and social care

content.title: Fewer barriers, more business owners: how do we get there?
content.description: Is Sweden a good country in which to start a business? We would like to think so, but reality tells a different story. Why are fewer people choosing to take the plunge? What happens to jobs and public services when entrepreneurship declines? Most importantly, what can we do to reverse the trend?
content.extendedDescription:
Since the turn of the millennium, the number of business owners increased by 110 000, but over the past two years it has fallen by 15 000. The business owner community is not only shrinking; it is also ageing and remains strikingly homogeneous. The share of business owners aged between 65 and 74 is growing, and only 28.9 per cent are women, one of the lowest proportions in Europe.
Conditions are tough for those who do run businesses. Företagarna's Småföretagsbarometern 2025 report shows the worst economic conditions for small businesses in 40 years. One in five business owners struggles to make ends meet. Investments are postponed or cancelled altogether.
This is not a temporary downturn we can simply wait out. Sweden is falling behind in the prosperity rankings. The growth crisis is more acute than it appears, because every krona of tax revenue must be generated before it can be redistributed. Without growing businesses, the tax base shrinks, and with it the public services we take for granted.
content.subject: Business
speakerTitles: Member of the Committee on Industry and Trade

content.title: Could unfired clay become a key material in future climate-smart construction?
content.description: The construction sector is looking for materials with low climate and environmental impacts and good indoor environmental properties. Unfired clay is one of the world's oldest building materials, but modern standardisation and industrially manufactured products are now generating renewed interest.
content.extendedDescription:
Unfired clay has been used in buildings for thousands of years, but has long been uncommon in modern construction. In recent years, standardisation, including SIS standards, and factory-made products adapted to today's building systems have brought renewed interest in the material.
The seminar explores how unfired clay can be used in modern construction, for example in plaster, mortar, blocks and finished surfaces.
We discuss the material's properties and the functions it can provide in buildings. Because the clay does not need to be fired at high temperatures, it has a low climate impact. Clay can also help regulate moisture and temperature in buildings and provide moisture and fire protection for bio-based structures.
The seminar also considers how clay-based finishes and coloured clay plasters can serve as alternatives to conventional interior finishes, and how demountable wall systems can be built using clay.

content.description: Climate change demands faster innovation and smarter systems. How is AI is enabling breakthroughs in climate modelling, energy systems and industrial efficiency?

The global transition to a low-carbon economy requires unprecedented innovation, coordination and speed. Artificial intelligence is increasingly being applied to optimise energy systems, improve climate modelling, accelerate scientific discovery and enable more efficient industrial processes. content.title: Urgently restoring personal assistance allowance: exactly SEK 400
content.description: By failing to increase personal assistance allowance in line with wage rises and other costs, successive Swedish governments are deliberately starving this vital reform of funding. How much longer can responsible providers survive?
content.extendedDescription:
SEK 347.70. That is the hourly personal assistance allowance: the amount Försäkringskassan pays, which must cover not only wages and employer contributions but also training, overheads, insurance and administration.

Over the past decade, successive Swedish governments have allowed the allowance to fall behind wage increases and inflation. For 2025–2026, collectively agreed wage rises amount to 6.4 per cent. The Tidö parties increased the allowance by 4.5 per cent over those two years. Its erosion is a fact. It cannot be news to any Member of Parliament responsible for social and financial issues that the funding no longer covers high-quality, safe personal assistance.

The funding is no longer sufficient to provide reasonable conditions for personal assistants, a good induction for new employees, or ongoing professional development and supervision. These are vital ingredients in high-quality assistance.

Are politicians killing off the reform without changing the law?

content.title: Being a Social Democrat in Danderyd: a challenge
content.description: Sweden's smallest local Social Democratic party organisation is in Danderyd. We have persuaded just over nine per cent of residents to vote for our alternative vision for our municipality's development. Low taxes and high quality: does that work in practice?
content.extendedDescription:
Jenny Åkervall, Olle Johansson and Karsten Inde are three leading Social Democrats in Danderyd. Jenny is the leader of Socialdemokraterna's group on the municipal council, Olle is new to Danderyd but has previously served, among other roles, as a municipal executive councillor in Norrköping, and Karsten is a prominent figure in sports and community associations.

Jenny, Olle and Karsten discuss with our moderator what it means to work in a traditionally centre-right context and address challenges in schools, preschool, culture and leisure, and the housing shortage. Unfortunately, Danderyd's young people lead the statistics for alcohol, tobacco and drug use. We believe Danderyd must invest much more in prevention and in strengthening schools, culture, leisure and care for older residents.

Annika Fehling opens our meeting. Annika sings Sonja Åkesson's poems. Sonja Åkesson was born 100 years ago in Buttle on Gotland. She was a strong voice for women's right to participate in society as the welfare state was being built.

content.title: Self-regulation of advertising
content.description: Self-regulation is a tool for credible, responsible advertising. As the design and distribution of advertising change, trust in advertising becomes more critical. How can self-regulation remain a relevant, effective and legitimate tool in Sweden and in relation to EU legislation?
content.extendedDescription:
Since Reklamombudsmannen was established in 2009, the advertising we encounter has changed substantially. Today, advertising is everywhere: on social media, in podcasts, in games and in public spaces. The boundaries between information, entertainment and advertising have become increasingly blurred.
Meanwhile, EU legislative work affects Sweden's advertising frameworks and rules. New demands are being placed on the interaction between EU legislation, national laws and self-regulation.
Self-regulation is a central part of society's infrastructure and a tool used in several areas, including credible and responsible advertising. But as the design and distribution of advertising change, trust in advertising becomes more crucial than ever.

content.title: Over-indebtedness among young people: a turnaround in sight?
content.description: After years of increasing over-indebtedness among people aged 18–34, a turnaround may be in sight. Forecasts suggest that the number of people in debt will fall in 2026. Yet many young people still face serious debt problems. Are we moving towards more sustainable borrowing, and what is driving the trend?
content.extendedDescription:
After several years of increasing over-indebtedness among people aged 18–34, statistics released in 2025 showed signs of a possible turnaround. Kronofogden's forecasts suggest that the number of people in debt will fall in 2026. Yet many young people still face serious debt problems.

Are we moving towards more sustainable borrowing among young people, and if so, what is driving the change? What is needed for a turnaround to happen and for the trend to continue towards fewer young people experiencing payment difficulties?

The seminar and discussion draw on the latest knowledge as we seek answers to these important questions. We also discuss why young adults take on debt, with the myth of ‘Lyxfällan’-style behaviour challenged by both experts and young people's own accounts of financial vulnerability.

The panel includes experts from KTH, Liberalerna, Kronofogden and Lendo, among others, and we also highlight young people's own perspectives.
content.subject: Economy
speakerTitles: Professor of Real Estate Law, KTH

content.title: The state's blind spot: crisis communication in a privatised urban landscape
content.description: What do we do when mobile networks are overloaded and online rumours cause panic? Public authorities' plans clash with citizens' digital everyday lives. How can we bridge the gap between government and business, and secure public screens in the urban landscape as a crisis communication channel in modern total defence?
content.extendedDescription:
Government directives require a rapid expansion of total defence capability by using civilian and private infrastructure. Yet frameworks and incentives for cooperation between the state and private actors are currently lacking. With no preparedness requirements for commercial information displays, the state is missing out on a huge untapped resource for crisis communication.
This seminar addresses the need for a new public-private social contract. When disinformation spreads and analogue or digital information flows are blocked, physical screens in squares, transport hubs and public transport can serve as a critical crisis channel for verified information. JCDecaux invites public authorities, politicians and industry representatives to discuss the legal, technical and operational challenges of building a secure and immediate way to reach citizens in public spaces, before a crisis strikes.
content.subject: Communication/information

content.title: Innovation as a force for transition: can we afford to think long term?
content.description: Major innovation initiatives are central to bringing together Sweden's innovative strength and building society's capacity and capabilities for a competitive transition over the long term. But can we afford to take a long-term view in difficult times, or will failing to do so cost us?
content.extendedDescription:
Innovation underpins Sweden's development and the future society and competitiveness we want and need.
Early results from the Impact Innovation initiative show that its five programmes are now well on their way to creating both breakthrough innovations and the conditions for society to adopt them.

At the seminar, programme directors for Net Zero Industry, ShiftSweden, SustainGov, Swedish Metals and Minerals, and Water Wise Societies discuss the strengths and weaknesses of this unique initiative that is taking the lead and showing the way. How are they working to enable an inclusive societal transition and a sustainable, competitive Sweden? How do we build a long-term perspective here and now, and what are we willing to pay for it? How can innovation make a difference as a source of learning and a resource to be shared, scaled up and used by everyone? How do we build a long-term perspective here and now, and what are we willing to pay for it?

content.title: World-class research: what investments and reforms are needed in Sweden and the EU?
content.description: What investments and reforms does Sweden need to undertake in the coming years to build strong research environments of the highest international quality? And how should we act within the EU to strengthen Europe's knowledge base and capacity for innovation?
content.extendedDescription:
In a time of geopolitical tensions, technological change and global competition, Sweden needs both to improve conditions for research at home and help shape the EU's research and innovation agenda.

This seminar brings together representatives of universities, research funders and political decision-makers to discuss how Sweden can strengthen conditions for internationally competitive research environments and take a clearer role in EU research and innovation cooperation.

The seminar is organised by Karolinska Institutet, KTH and Stockholms universitet through Universitetsalliansen Stockholm trio, in cooperation with Stockholm Science City.

The related lunch seminar ‘Knowledge and leadership in an uncertain world: how is Sweden's future being shaped?’ takes place at 12.45–13.30 in the same venue.

content.title: Standing with Ukraine: What comes next?
content.description: Russia’s aggression against Ukraine shapes ongoing discussions on peace negotiations, geopolitical escalation, and strategic choices. How can global implications explores how sustained, effective support be ensured in the context of a prolonged war?
content.extendedDescription:
Political, military and economic developments over the coming years will shape not only Ukraine's future, but also the future security and resilience of Europe. As Russia's war against Ukraine continues, critical questions remain:  What strategic choices lie ahead for Ukraine and its partners? And how can international support remain effective in a prolonged war?

Speakers:
Jessica Rosencrantz, Minister for European Union Affairs of Sweden
Svitlana Zalishchuk, Ambassador of Ukraine to Sweden
Torbjörn Becker, Director of the Stockholm Institute of Transition Economics
Maksym Horbatiuk, Head of Land Weapon Systems Service, 21st Separate Mechanized Brigade of the Armed Forces of Ukraine

content.title: Hemp for sustainable construction and increased carbon storage
content.description: Hemp can support more environmentally sound buildings and a sustainable bio-based economy. By making greater use of hemp again, with modern construction as its main market, we can radically reduce CO2 emissions.
content.extendedDescription: Hemp is a plant that people around the world have used for thousands of years. It is also an efficient carbon sink with industrial potential. Its many uses include shipping, agriculture, paper, printing, pharmaceuticals, food and construction. Hemp can radically reduce CO2 emissions by reducing the use of lime and cement, store CO2 in biomass, provide good insulation and make use of materials' hygroscopic properties to regulate the indoor climate naturally. Examples of buildings insulated with hemp include multi-storey housing for low-income residents in Paris, an environmentally adapted Marks & Spencers in England, municipal buildings in the Netherlands, Åhléns' main warehouse in Sweden and half-timbered houses among Visby's historic buildings. Hemp can help us build a more robust society: a local bio-based economy that supplies materials for homes and products while forming a logical part of an ecological cycle.

content.title: How can the Nordic region strengthen Europe's competitiveness?
content.description: As Europe falls behind in global competition, the Nordic region remains strong in industry, technology and capital. How can a more integrated Nordic region bring together companies, investors and decision-makers to create the next generation of industrial initiatives and become an engine of European growth?
content.extendedDescription:
Geopolitical tensions, technological transition and tougher global competition are changing conditions for European business. Meanwhile, the Nordic region has unique strengths: world-leading companies, strong capital markets, considerable innovative capacity and close interaction between business, research and society.
Against this backdrop, Nordic Compass has been established as a Nordic alliance of leading companies, investors and foundations aiming to strengthen the region's competitiveness.
Leading representatives of business, finance and politics discuss how the Nordic region can play a more active role in strengthening Europe's competitiveness. What investments, reforms and partnerships are needed? How can Nordic cooperation accelerate innovation, attract capital and build the industries of the future? And what role can Nordic Compass play in shaping the next chapter of Nordic growth, competitiveness and industrial development?

content.title: From preparedness plans to effective cooperation: building local robustness
content.description: Municipalities are strengthening civil preparedness, but how can ambitions translate into effective local cooperation? How do we build everyday robustness between municipalities, business and civil society?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden is investing in total defence and municipal preparedness. The next step is to strengthen local cooperation: the factor that determines how well plans work in practice.
How do we create structures in which the public sector, business and civil society work together before a crisis? How do we make community support points into active hubs? How do we build relationships that hold up under pressure? We help you succeed.
The seminar presents a practical model for integrating everyday cooperation into municipal preparedness work. It focuses on implementation, governance and long-term sustainability. The discussion offers examples of how social innovation can strengthen local resilience while increasing attractiveness and engagement.
Mötesplats Häradsbäck is an example of how the built environment can be organised as a living whole rather than separate construction projects. Properties, energy systems, activities and people are seen as parts of the same cycle.

content.title: To the Swedish mountains by fossil-free coach
content.description: Can coaches become an attractive complement to trains for climate-smart travel to the Swedish mountains? Industry players are challenging fossil fuels to a snowball fight.
content.extendedDescription:
The transition towards fossil-free operations is under way throughout the transport chain, and interest in climate-smart travel is strong. Interest in domestic holidays is also growing, and trains already offer many people a good alternative to taking the car. Yet around 9 out of 10 families drive to the Swedish mountains. Perhaps this is unsurprising: every family going on a skiing holiday knows the challenge of fitting skis, ski boots and everything else into the roof box and boot, so taking the train can feel like too great a logistical challenge. A modern, climate-smart coach can offer an appealing alternative for travelling almost door to door!

At this seminar, representatives from throughout the chain describe today's situation and future opportunities for fossil-free, sustainable coach travel to the Swedish mountains. Who knows: perhaps even Stig-Helmer Olsson will turn up to pre-book a coach trip and accommodation in the annexe?
content.subject: Visitor economy

content.title: People-centred climate adaptation: how can we protect vulnerable groups?
content.description: A changing climate brings more extreme weather and greater risks to lives, health and homes. Reducing vulnerability requires lower emissions and preventive work to strengthen preparedness. Climate adaptation is about preventing risks and protecting people, especially those hardest hit by crises.
content.extendedDescription:
Extreme weather causes more than material damage. It also affects people's health, sense of security and ability to manage everyday life, for example during heatwaves, floods and prolonged societal disruption. When society's protection falls short, already vulnerable groups are often hit hardest.

A new report from Röda Korset highlights the unequal impacts of climate change and the need to strengthen preparedness. As the Nordic region's largest insurer, If sees daily how extreme weather affects people and property. Meanwhile, important Nordic experience shows that prevention and climate adaptation can reduce risks.

During Almedalen, Röda Korset and If bring together public authorities, business and civil society to discuss how to strengthen society's resilience and better protect the most vulnerable.
content.subject: Climate/environment

content.title: Stop wasting money on unnecessary reconstruction of outdoor spaces: think sustainably
content.description: We waste millions rebuilding parks and playgrounds that could have lasted for years if we had simply maintained them. Poor maintenance becomes a convenient excuse for expensive projects. Do we want to be sustainable, or just keep wearing out what we already have?
content.extendedDescription:
Reinvestment in parks and public spaces costs society millions, often unnecessarily. Inadequate care and maintenance accelerate deterioration, making expensive reconstruction the only solution. Good maintenance, the right materials and everyday attention could have prevented many of these projects.
Sustainable management is about more than repairs and tidying up. It gives places the opportunity to develop, retain their quality and age gracefully over time. It means recognising the value and potential of what already exists instead of allowing deterioration to continue and become an argument for building anew.
At a time of financial pressure and demanding sustainability requirements, the question is clear: why invest in reconstruction when millions can be saved by caring for what we already have? Sustainable environments require a long-term approach. Better management means less, and smarter, construction.

content.title: Cultural heritage under attack!
content.description: Anundshög, one of our most iconic Viking Age archaeological sites, has been looted over the past year. This is not an isolated incident, but a growing national problem. Museums play an important role in sharing knowledge, but who is responsible for protection and preparedness?
content.extendedDescription:
Västerås museer, Gotlands Museum and many other museums meet an engaged and concerned public wanting to know what is being done to protect our shared cultural heritage.
At a time when societal preparedness is high on the agenda, protecting our shared cultural heritage has gained renewed relevance, particularly in the event of war. Ensuring that it is not damaged in peacetime should be at least as important. Quiet, systematic destruction of cultural heritage is taking place. Metal detector use is particularly serious: in practice, national coordination is lacking and responsibility for supervision is unclear. The lack of current research and investigation into heritage crime is striking. We call for:
• A national strategy and coordination against heritage crime to address ongoing looting, particularly illegal metal detecting.
• More resources for supervision, education and research into heritage crime.
content.subject: Culture

content.title: From invitation to influence: strengthening young people's impact in discussions
content.description: The ambition to include young people in discussions is growing, but practical knowledge and preparation are often lacking. Without the right support and feedback, their involvement risks becoming symbolic. How do we move from goodwill to real influence, and what happens during and after the discussion?
content.extendedDescription:
More and more people want to include a youth perspective. This is positive, but ticking a box on the agenda is not enough. Young people should not be seen as a symbolic addition, but as natural participants with the same right as everyone else to be heard, influence outcomes and contribute.
At this seminar, we present our newly developed handbook for moderators. It is for both organisers and moderators of discussions.
Inviting a young person onto a stage requires preparation. To feel comfortable as a panellist or discussion leader, young people need the right support and conditions. We share practical tips and tools for preparing young people for the stage and for creating an inclusive, respectful discussion as a moderator.
You will also gain insight into young people's own expectations: what they need before, during and after participating so they can contribute on their own terms.
content.subject: Children/young people

content.title: How do we stop labour exploitation and work-related crime in the cleaning industry?
content.description: Work-related crime in the cleaning industry harms employees, responsible businesses, municipalities and society. Unscrupulous operators exploit workers and circumvent rules. What role do the relevant authorities and procuring organisations play in avoiding contributing to its growth?
content.extendedDescription:
The seminar examines how work-related crime manifests itself in the cleaning industry and its consequences for employees, responsible businesses, municipalities and society. The sector currently faces fierce competition in which unscrupulous operators exploit vulnerable workers, circumvent rules and drive down prices in ways that distort the market.
Almega, Kommunal and Fastighets describe their joint work to combat work-related crime in the cleaning industry. We present concrete cases and best practice, and discuss the tools available, and those missing, to stop it. Alongside the social partners, decision-makers and relevant public authorities take part.

content.title: Heta stubben: what role can outdoor recreation play in strengthening Swedish total defence?
content.description: Almost half the population has dangerously poor physical fitness. According to the Defence Commission, public health is highly important to the country's resilience. Are residents total defence's weakest link, and how can organised outdoor recreation strengthen Swedish resilience and preparedness?
content.extendedDescription: Last year's Almedalen success, Heta stubben, is back. With the sea as a backdrop and the aroma of coffee from the camping stove, Friluftsfrämjandet will meet party leaders and other decision-makers on several occasions to discuss their vision for outdoor recreation. Four in five children are not active enough, and almost half of adults have dangerously poor physical fitness. The proportion of children spending time in nature daily has fallen from 78 to 49 per cent in 20 years. Seven in ten Swedes know they are responsible for preparing for a crisis, but only one in three has actually prepared or practised. Each year, Friluftsfrämjandet reaches over 100 000 children and young people through activities that strengthen fitness, navigation, endurance, knowledge and confidence in nature. How does this contribute to total defence, and could guided outdoor recreation play an even bigger role?
content.subject: Security/defence

content.title: How do we build the world's strongest knowledge environment?
content.description: Sweden needs places where research, innovation, businesses and capital come together to solve societal challenges faster. How do we build environments that attract investment, talent and new businesses, and turn knowledge into practical benefits?
content.extendedDescription:
Uppsala has an unusually concentrated knowledge environment: universities, a university hospital, public authorities, a science park, businesses and innovation support within walking distance. Here, the path from idea to application is short. The next step is to increase its international appeal, attract more capital and make room for more organisations to establish themselves.
Uppsala universitet, Uppsala kommun, Region Uppsala, Vasakronan and Akademiska Hus are joining forces through a joint declaration of intent for Uppsala Science District. Their aim is to develop the area into an internationally leading district for research, innovation and business establishment.
The seminar explores how developing the physical environment, strengthening cooperation and making long-term investments can contribute to Sweden's competitiveness and create an ecosystem where talent, capital and businesses want to be. What is needed for more Swedish knowledge environments to compete globally, and what can be learned from the cooperation developed in Uppsala?

content.title: The foundation of Sweden's economy: efficient transport for basic and export industries
content.description: Sweden's basic and export industries are the backbone of its economy. Delivery times are critical for many companies. Today, transporting goods by rail takes export companies increasingly longer than it did 20 years ago, affecting their competitiveness.
content.extendedDescription:
Europakorridoren commissioned interviews with Swedish export companies to understand how they perceive today's transport system and how they believe infrastructure needs to develop to better meet business needs. Half the interviews were with companies based in northern Sweden. The geographical range extends from Norrbotten to Småland.

The findings show that every interviewee believes shortcomings in rail infrastructure hamper their operations. The interview results are presented at the seminar, followed by a panel discussion on the consequences and what needs to be done to strengthen Sweden as an export nation.

speakerTitles: Senior Vice President of Corporate Affairs

content.title: Who owns rearmament? Sweden is investing in defence, but who owns the companies, decisions and power?
content.description: Sweden is spending SEK 175 billion on rearmament in 2026. This year's report shows that the defence sector is owned almost entirely by men. What happens to total defence, innovation and social development if half the population's skills and perspectives are not used?
content.extendedDescription:
Large public investments in defence and security raise questions extending far beyond the military. Who owns future growth? How are gender equality, innovation and social development affected when capital moves into the defence sector?
Drawing on Ownershift's new report, researchers, politicians, entrepreneurs and defence industry representatives discuss the next generation of security policy and the society we are building through today's decisions.

The panel discusses:
• Ownership in Sweden's defence industry
• Whether broader ownership can strengthen resilience and innovation
• How gender equality affects security and defence capability
• What happens when sustainability capital is redirected towards defence

Participants include Nina Larsson, Minister for Gender Equality and a former professional military officer.
content.subject: Security/defence
speakerTitles: Minister for Gender Equality and Working Life
Professor and Director of Handelshögskolan's Centre for Security and Resilience

content.title: How healthy is Swedish democracy, and how do we increase young people's participation?
content.description: We all have an important role to play in strengthening democratic society. Encounters between young and older people, and between business and politics, bring different perspectives that can together build greater trust in democracy. How can we develop the ability to act together?
content.extendedDescription:
We want to discuss this with you at the start of Almedalsveckan 2026. This pressing question takes centre stage as Novus presents its annual democracy report. The survey offers an up-to-date picture of Swedes' views of democracy and how trust in it has developed over time. Immediately after the report's release, we invite you to a practical follow-up to build the capacity to act on this crucial issue.

Join Sweden's longest conversation on democracy! Along a row of tables in Almedalsparken, we draw on insights from the report and young people's voices on democracy for a shared discussion moderated by young representatives from several organisations, including Almedalsveckans Demokratiskola. Topics include participation, trust and hope for the future.

Help us contribute to a conversation that builds understanding and responsibility in both directions.
content.subject: Democracy

content.title: How is shipping's transition progressing?
content.description: Reducing humanity's negative impact on the climate is one of today's greatest and most important challenges. It concerns every part of society, not least shipping. Changing shipping's energy use is a challenge requiring the involvement of multiple activities and actors.
content.extendedDescription: Global shipping currently accounts for around three per cent of human-caused greenhouse gas emissions, while playing a crucial role in trade and prosperity between people, countries and continents. A transition to fossil-free, sustainable energy in shipping is therefore central to society's energy transition, including through transporting new forms of energy, supporting fossil-free infrastructure and participating in circular flows that reuse resources. However, changing shipping's energy use is a complex challenge requiring cooperation between multiple actors and activities. Taking Svensk Sjöfart's Climate Roadmap, which outlines a possible path to climate neutrality by 2050, as a starting point, participants gather over breakfast for discussion, experience-sharing and networking. During the networking breakfast, three shipping companies from different parts of the sector discuss their challenges and choices.

content.title: Is now the time to end homelessness?
content.description:
So far, efforts to tackle homelessness have been small, fragmented and insufficient. But there is now momentum to end homelessness:
• A new national homelessness strategy creates new opportunities
• A new Social Services Act focuses on prevention
• A new EU plan for affordable housing
content.extendedDescription:
Homelessness is not only a social problem. It is also about ensuring enough homes for people with different financial circumstances. To solve the persistent housing problem, social and housing policy must work together, and politicians, public authorities and property owners need new ways to cooperate.

During this seminar, the panel will discuss:
How can decision-makers take responsibility for ensuring that the homelessness strategy and Social Services Act work together so that everyone experiencing homelessness gets a home?

How can decision-makers, property owners and civil society cooperate to provide more affordable housing so everyone can afford a home?

And especially: how do we seize this unique opportunity and move from words to action to end homelessness?

content.title: Digital pharmacist consultations: a possible solution for future pharmacy services
content.description: Pharmacies play an important role in access to medicines and pharmaceutical advice across the country. Yet many struggle to recruit pharmacists. How can new technology and working methods help ensure continued access to pharmaceutical expertise?
content.extendedDescription:
Are remote pharmacists part of the solution for ensuring pharmacy services throughout the country?
Alongside the seminar ‘The pharmacy of the future: how do we ensure pharmacy services across the country?’, Kronans Apotek, Apotek Hjärtat and Apoteket demonstrate how digital pharmacist consultations can work in practice. Visitors can try out how customers can receive personal advice and help with prescriptions at their local pharmacy while meeting the pharmacist digitally by video. This illustrates how digital technology can strengthen access to pharmaceutical expertise and improve conditions for pharmacy services, including where recruiting pharmacists is difficult.
Please note that this is only a demonstration of a digital pharmacist consultation. You cannot collect prescription medicines or receive pharmaceutical advice on site.

content.title: Can Sweden Lead Europe's AI Race? Infrastructure, Energy and Competitiveness
content.description: AI is creating unprecedented demand for compute capacity, energy and digital infrastructure. Can Sweden provide the conditions needed to attract investment, strengthen competitiveness and secure a leading role in Europe's AI-driven economy?
content.extendedDescription:
AI is rapidly becoming a key driver of economic growth, innovation and competitiveness. At the same time, the demand for compute capacity, digital infrastructure and reliable energy is increasing at an unprecedented pace.

Sweden has many of the strengths needed to attract large-scale AI investments, including technical expertise, strong connectivity and access to fossil-free electricity. However, global competition for investment is intensifying, raising important questions about infrastructure development, energy supply, policy frameworks and long-term competitiveness.

This discussion explores how Sweden can position itself as a leading destination for AI infrastructure, what role energy and digital infrastructure play in enabling growth, and how the eco system of actors can work together to strengthen Sweden's role in the European AI ecosystem.

Format: Breakfast and panel discussion followed by audience Q&A.
content.subject: Digitalisation

content.title: Bakers and welders, the same question: how do we secure the future skills supply?
content.description: Skills supply is one of society's major challenges today. Intensive efforts are being made everywhere to attract new employees, yet challenges persist. Why have we not made more progress?
content.extendedDescription:
Skills supply challenges affect not only day-to-day operations but also the ability to grow, develop and meet future needs. Despite major efforts to attract workers such as bakers, pastry chefs and welders, difficulties remain in encouraging more people to choose relevant courses and careers, and in some cases even ensuring that the right training is available.

In this presentation, Sveriges bagare & konditorer and Svetskommissionen share their experiences of skills challenges in their sectors. With different circumstances but similar needs and challenges, they raise questions about attractiveness, recruitment barriers and the link between education and working life.

The aim is to highlight where the challenges are greatest and open a discussion about the perspectives, partnerships and possible ways forward that politics, education and business need to consider.
content.subject: Employment/labour market
speakerTitles: CEO. Business Environment and Trends Analyst

content.title: Goodbye USA, hello world? The new investment landscape
content.description: The global economy is shifting as geopolitics, new power balances and sustainability requirements change investment patterns. US dominance is being challenged and capital is seeking new markets and technologies. How is the landscape shaped as flows are redrawn, and what role does long-term capital play?
content.extendedDescription:
We discuss global investment flows and changing economic power balances. How can capital serve as a strategic tool in an era of geopolitical uncertainty, technological transition and increasing sustainability demands?

How are investment decisions affected when traditional markets become less attractive and new regions, sectors and partnerships emerge? The focus is on how capital can contribute to the green transition, innovation and economic resilience, but also on barriers holding back investment in today's global landscape.

The discussion addresses long-term thinking, risk-sharing and the need for stable rules so that capital is willing to go where it can do the most good. How can investors balance returns and responsibility? What solutions are needed to direct capital flows towards greater sustainability? And how does the global shift affect future opportunities for Europe and Sweden?
content.subject: Economy
content.accessibility: Hearing loop, wheelchair-accessible entrance and venue

content.title: Coastguard operations: key to total defence, but without the right conditions?
content.description: Coastguard operations play an increasingly important role as total defence is rebuilt. But have the conditions really kept pace?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden's security situation has fundamentally changed. NATO membership and the rebuilding of total defence give Kustbevakningen an increasingly central and strategic role in our maritime areas. As its mission has expanded, demands on its operations have grown, while resources and staffing have not fully kept pace.
The question is therefore not only what role Kustbevakningen should play in total defence, but whether conditions are sufficient for it to fulfil its mission in practice.
How large is the gap between responsibilities and resources? What political priorities are needed to strengthen capability? How does this affect the ability to recruit, retain and develop the right skills, and therefore the employees who ultimately determine whether the mission can be delivered?
This seminar brings together representatives of the authority, politics and trade unions to discuss Kustbevakningen's role in total defence and what is needed to ensure its long-term functioning.
content.subject: Security/defence
speakerTitles: State Secretary to Minister for Civil Defence Carl-Oskar Bohlin

content.title: Stronger cooperation between civil society and business: from social value to business value
content.description: As new regulations, increasing sustainability requirements and greater emphasis on impact measurement change the conditions for cooperation, new opportunities arise to build partnerships that create value for both non-profit organisations and businesses.
content.extendedDescription:
This roundtable explores how non-profit organisations can take a more strategic approach to business partnerships to increase revenue and create greater social and business value for their partners. It focuses on developing cooperation from individual initiatives into long-term partnerships with clear benefits for both parties.

We discuss three questions together:

- How could proposed changes to tax deductibility open the door to more and larger business partnerships?

- How can partnerships build on a company's sustainability work and create both business and social value?

- How do we measure partnerships' impact, from operational benefits to tangible business results?

The roundtable begins with a presentation by our moderators introducing the topic and providing background to the questions we will discuss together.
content.subject: Business

content.title: From steel and paper to algorithms: Dalarna leads the way for Sweden's AI strategy
content.description: Sweden aims to become one of the world's ten leading AI nations. Billions are now being invested in data centres, AI infrastructure and a growing AI ecosystem in Dalarna. Could Dalarna be where Sweden's AI strategy turns from words into reality? What is needed, and who takes responsibility?
content.extendedDescription:
Dalarna is Sweden's next growth region and its new AI workshop. A strong industrial base, an exploratory public sector and rapidly growing AI infrastructure, including a European AI supercomputer, come together here. They create a unique environment where Sweden's AI strategy can move from paper to real action.

What role can a concerted regional effort play in Sweden's AI competitiveness? And how can a national strategy become tangible development in Dalarna here and now?

The seminar brings together decision-makers from politics, business and academia to discuss how AI initiatives can move from pilot to production and from vision to implementation. What must central government, regions and business do to succeed in Dalarna and Sweden? And how do we ensure that AI investment creates growth across the country?
content.subject: Digitalisation

content.title: How can we prevent children being taken abroad against their will?
content.description: Every year after the summer holidays, some classroom desks remain empty. Most children taken abroad against their will in 2022 were already known to social services, but were taken out of the country before authorities acted. Schools and social services need to identify pupils at risk before it is too late.
content.extendedDescription:
Every year after the summer holidays, some classroom desks remain empty. GAPF attempted to help bring home 47 children taken abroad against their will in 2025.

GAPF has worked with five municipalities and Stockholms universitet to produce evidence to strengthen this work. Devin Rexvid presents findings from his review of judgments under the Care of Young Persons Act (LVU), showing important qualitative differences between children exposed to honour-based violence and other children. Sara Mohammad presents the results of a survey of school staff's experiences of honour-related cases.

The study and survey form the basis of a handbook on children taken abroad against their will, intended to help professionals make better risk and protection assessments. The project is financially supported by Postkodlotteriets stiftelse and Bertil Strömbergs stiftelse.

The handbook will be distributed at the seminar.
content.subject: Human rights
speakerTitles: Researcher in Honour-based Violence and Oppression

content.title: Prevention that lasts: cooperation between municipalities and civil society across electoral terms
content.description:
When responsibility lies with the municipality, but solutions require more than the municipality alone.
How do we create preventive work that does not collapse when projects end, staff change or election results shift?
content.extendedDescription:
An open discussion on working with civil society to reach all young people, including those in the grey area, and build sustainable municipal practice.

Municipalities have a clear responsibility for early and preventive action concerning young people, safety and social sustainability. Yet many describe the same challenge: how do we reach young people outside established services before problems escalate, and sustain this work over time? During this hour, we invite municipal politicians, committee representatives and officials to join us. Political, strategic and practical perspectives meet to explore preventive work built on structures that last across electoral terms, in cooperation with civil society. The dialogue focuses on practical experience: what often falls short, what actually works and which choices are needed for continuity. Participants leave with a shared understanding of the problem, new perspectives on cooperation and ideas to take back to their municipalities.
content.subject: Children/young people

content.title: Are problems always someone else's fault? Religion, migration and responsibility
content.description: Societies facing uncertainty and change can easily be tempted to blame ‘others’. How does this affect views of migration, religion and integration? This discussion explores how shared responsibility can build trust and cohesion in a pluralist Sweden.
content.extendedDescription:
In his book Öppna era hjärtan, Simon Sorgenfrei places our culturally and religiously pluralist situation in the context of the past fifty years of Swedish history, particularly Muslim experiences in Sweden. He shows how religious expressions and experiences can shape people's identities, contributing to a more nuanced discussion of migration and encounters between religions.
This book discussion between Simon Sorgenfrei, Maha Alhaddad and Jan Eckerdal highlights religion's role in Sweden today, both as a source of conflict and as a resource and opportunity for greater trust and cohesion.
The conversation covers religious literacy, secularisation and what happens when religion is reduced to a private matter.
Musicians in Vårdklockans kyrka open and close the discussion. Refreshments are provided.

content.title: Election campaigns often talk about inclusion and participation, but what have the parties actually done?
content.description: What have decision-makers done, and what do they want to do for our members? These answers matter so that we, as voters, can make important electoral choices: which party champions our issues?
content.extendedDescription:
A question-and-answer session with politicians, a moderator and audience participation. A brief introduction to Funkisam Gotland – funktionsnedsatta i samverkan. The current situation:
• What does Funkisam Gotland do today?
• What is everyday life like for people with disabilities on Gotland?

Questions for politicians. The moderator puts prepared questions to invited politicians, for example:
• What concrete measures has your party taken over the past four years to strengthen the rights and living conditions of people with disabilities?

As an educational element, panellists are offered the chance to experience a simulated disability during part or all of the event, for example:
• Sitting in a wheelchair
• Wearing ear defenders
• Using a white cane and/or blindfold
The aim is to increase understanding of how accessibility affects participation.
Audience questions.
Questions may be asked orally or in writing.

Audience members can ask questions orally or in writing. Pre-recorded or submitted questions are warmly welcomed.

content.title: Icebreakers from a Nordic perspective: do total defence and the Arctic require new thinking on functions and technology?
content.description: The Nordic region's geopolitical position requires icebreakers, with their unique capabilities, to be considered a strategic resource. Modern technology can enable navigation in polar regions and open seas while serving winter shipping in the Bay of Bothnia. Is there political will to make this a shared Nordic issue?
content.extendedDescription: Effective icebreaking and winter shipping are matters of major importance to society and to those of us living and working in the Nordic region. Our presence in the Arctic is now more important, and we have the heritage, knowledge and ability to live in Arctic conditions. Winter shipping involves central political issues, including industrial, energy and transport policy, geopolitics and security. For example, energy carriers for icebreakers and demanding winter shipping have a 50-year time horizon, making the choice of direction highly relevant today. All the logistics involved require policy and infrastructure to align with technological development and investment across transport modes. Geopolitics encompasses security, security of supply, strategic polar research and icebreakers.

content.title: Future energy scenarios: their development and impact on spatial planning
content.description: The energy system relies on long-term planning and future energy scenarios. These have developed enormously in recent years, with ambitious assumptions and rising estimates of future demand.
content.extendedDescription:
Over the past 40 years, electricity consumption in Sweden has remained stable at around 130–140 TWh per year. Continuous energy efficiency improvements have met additional demand. But we now face a transition in which large parts of industry and transport will be electrified, and a narrative of doubling electricity use has become established. As Energimyndigheten releases new scenarios, the range of outcomes has continued to rise and widen, with further scenarios based on even more ambitious assumptions. Yet electrification has not taken off and forecasts are being pushed back. Meanwhile, factors such as the energy crisis, demographic change, faltering investment and more ambitious efficiency measures add further uncertainty.
This seminar addresses questions including: what assumptions underpin Energimyndigheten's long-term scenarios? Is the government's planned increase compatible with our energy policy goals? How should we plan energy provision in the face of current uncertainty?

content.title: Civilian evacuation in war: what lessons from Ukraine must Sweden learn?
content.description: Since 2022, Ukrainian actors have evacuated hundreds of thousands of civilians from active combat zones under fire. Sweden has not faced this reality, but needs to learn. What does it really take to save civilians when war reaches cities?
content.extendedDescription:
Since the invasion began in 2022, Ukraine's state emergency service and voluntary organisations have built one of the world's most advanced systems for civilian evacuation during active combat. White Angels units have evacuated civilians directly from the front line, including older people, sick people and families with children, under fire and amid total chaos.
Sweden strengthened its civil defence after 2022 but still lacks practical experience of large-scale civilian evacuation in war. This conversation highlights operational lessons: how do you organise evacuation under fire, how do you prioritise, and which mistakes have cost lives?

The discussion is organised within Samarbetsplattformen: Sverige & Ukraina (SPSU), an initiative of KlinteVolontär that gives Ukrainian civil society its own voice in Sweden's democratic debate and brings together Swedish and Ukrainian organisations to strengthen long-term cooperation between the countries.

content.title: Why the delay in newborn screening? A system one step behind, and what politics can do
content.description: Delayed diagnosis of cystic fibrosis can cause unnecessary suffering and poorer health for children. This matters because Sweden lacks national newborn screening for the disease, although early detection enables prompt treatment and better quality of life.
content.extendedDescription: In March 2026, Socialstyrelsen was tasked with reviewing its model for national screening programmes. This is welcome, but to make a difference the review must address a fundamental shortcoming: decisions on newborn screening for new diseases take too long. Cystic fibrosis (CF) is a clear example. Sweden screens newborns for 24 serious inherited diseases, but not CF, although most European countries do and effective treatments are available from a very early age. For a progressive disease such as CF, every month's delay can affect health and quality of life. The issue is therefore not only medical possibilities, but also how quickly society's decision-making processes can adapt as knowledge and treatment develop.

content.title: Climate, conflict and competitiveness: Europe's energy choices in a new world order
content.description: Lower climate requirements, state aid or open competition on equal terms: all are part of the debate, which also concerns becoming more resilient to geopolitical turbulence and environmental risks. How should Europe approach its future energy supply? And how should Sweden act?
content.extendedDescription:
Recent years have repeatedly shown the dangers of dependence on fossil fuel imports. The worldwide economic and industrial disruption caused by the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz illustrates this clearly.

Meanwhile, the World Economic Forum estimates that four of the ten biggest risks to the global economy over the next ten years will be environment-related. Can Europe's politicians stay the course on climate when short-term competitiveness tops the agenda? Many also agree that Sweden is well placed, but what is the path from potential to actual success?

Join a seminar taking a broad approach and asking the big questions. We begin with the global picture and work our way down to what it means for Sweden and Swedish businesses.

content.title: Policy for mental health: what does it mean?
content.description: Mental ill-health is one of Sweden's greatest public health challenges. One in three people is affected, and everyone knows someone. The disease burden and societal costs are enormous, yet in practice healthcare budgets are not increasing and care is unequal. We need a policy for mental health, but what does that mean?
content.extendedDescription:
Partnerskap för psykisk hälsa welcomes you to a lively discussion between regional politicians from different parties about raising the priority of efforts to address mental ill-health, creating a more coordinated, person-centred care pathway, and improving working conditions and the skills supply.

We cannot afford either the economic costs or the human suffering caused by mental ill-health. Real change requires long-term political responsibility and resource allocation that prioritises mental health. The National Strategy for Mental Health and Suicide Prevention is a start, but what policies are needed for real change in the regions?

In this seminar, Partnerskap för psykisk hälsa focuses on how we can contribute to long-term mental health policy: policy that makes a real difference.

Welcome!

content.title: Protected sites: national security and uncertainty
content.description: How do we create narratives about security and uncertainty in dialogue with others? What influence do storytelling and stories have on strategic and military decisions?
content.extendedDescription:
This year, a green military accommodation tent will stand on Almedalen's shore. Inside, we will perform a play connecting Gotland's past and present as a strategically important military location with fears and concerns about Gotland's and Sweden's future security.
Two signals intelligence operators are working at a temporary mobile reconnaissance station. Suddenly, one notices an anomaly on the screen. What are they seeing? And what should they do about it? Perhaps everything is about to change.
A play by Julia Hackman
Cast: Anton Cöster and Evelina Benedicks

The performance lasts 50 minutes and is staged in the tent four times a day: at 10:30, 12:45, 14:30 and 16:00. Between performances, the tent is open for visitors to step inside. Admission is free, but places are limited. To secure a place, register in advance using the web link below.

In cooperation with Kulturföreningen Roxy.

content.title: Parenthood on equal terms: how do we ensure all perspectives are included in fertility care?
content.description: Can today's fertility care meet different circumstances and needs? How do people with physical disabilities experience fertility care?
content.extendedDescription:
Although care should be based on individual psychosocial assessments, many people report being reduced to their diagnosis or disability and having their suitability as future parents questioned before an assessment has even been made. Their experiences raise questions about how well the current system recognises different life circumstances, and whether people with disabilities have equal opportunities to start a family.

In the report ‘She said: If you were my daughter, I would advise you to have an abortion’, Funktionsrätt Sverige and RFSU collect people with disabilities' experiences of fertility care.

How do we create fertility care that assesses people with disabilities on their individual circumstances rather than assumptions about them? Which perspectives do we need to understand better? And how can healthcare, public authorities and civil society work together to strengthen everyone's opportunities for parenthood?

Join a conversation about experience, knowledge and the path towards more equitable fertility care.

content.title: Tomorrow's decision-makers on Sweden's energy policy
content.description: Energy involves long-term choices for a sustainable, robust society. In an election year, young people's political perspectives are particularly important to understanding how future energy policy may take shape.
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden's energy system faces several crucial choices, and energy issues have become increasingly central to political debate, particularly in the election year. This seminar brings together representatives of political youth organisations to debate the energy system of the future. It begins with a panel of industry representatives focusing on business policy, the labour market and skills supply. These are important issues for the sector and will become increasingly vital to delivering the energy transition. Young politicians can ask questions during the opening panel.

Focusing on the energy system's role in climate, growth and local development, the discussion explores the next generation of politicians' views on responsibility, priorities and long-term thinking. The aim is to improve understanding of the energy system's complexity and contribute to constructive dialogue and debate between young decision-makers and the energy industry.
content.subject: Energy

content.title: Knowledge and leadership in an uncertain world: how is Sweden's future being shaped?
content.description: In a time of growing uncertainty, it is important to ask how our knowledge can best be used. What is needed to make the right decisions, and how do we ensure universities' expertise and leadership are actually used to shape a stronger, more resilient society?
content.extendedDescription:
Geopolitical instability, AI's rapid advance and growing skills shortages are putting Sweden under pressure. At a pivotal moment for the knowledge society, three of the country's most influential academic leaders meet to discuss power, responsibility and leadership.

The heads of Karolinska Institutet, KTH and Stockholms universitet join Anna Serner to discuss universities' role in social development and how they can strengthen Sweden's innovation, competitiveness and ability to navigate a rapidly changing world.

A conversation for anyone making decisions, investing in the future or leading in uncertain times. Organised by Stockholm Science City in cooperation with Karolinska Institutet, KTH and Stockholms universitet.

In connection with this seminar, Universitetsalliansen Stockholm trio is organising ‘World-class research: what investments and reforms are needed in Sweden and the EU?’ at 13.45–14.45.
content.subject: Research

content.title: Do older people in Sweden have weaker legal protection than animals, and why do we not talk more about it?
content.description: For almost 150 years, weekly magazines have been a natural part of everyday life. They reach a large and often overlooked audience: women in later middle age. How do you deliver public-interest journalism where the audience already is, but is rarely taken seriously?
content.extendedDescription:
For almost 150 years, the weekly magazines Allers, Allas, Hemmets Veckotidning and Året Runt have been a natural part of everyday life. Behind the short stories, recipes and crosswords, something more is happening. We use the power of lifestyle journalism to highlight issues that truly matter, and sometimes shake things up. Our widely discussed investigation Hemtjänsthaveriet revealed an uncomfortable truth: in practice, older people in Sweden have weaker legal protection than animals. How did this happen, and why do we allow it to continue?
Join a conversation about journalism that engages, challenges and makes an impact. How do you steward a cultural heritage dating from the nineteenth century while making it relevant in a digital age?
Meet editor-in-chief Åsa Liliegren and editor Maria Torshall for a conversation about the power of taking your audience seriously, combining warmth with courage, and why this kind of journalism can be crucial to driving change.

content.title: Young people's influence in construction: self-organisation, networks and activism
content.description: As a young person, it is easy to feel powerless about the direction our future is taking. Construction accounts for 22% of Sweden's domestic carbon dioxide emissions. Acting together is the only reasonable response: the acute crisis we face requires a new kind of professionalism.
content.extendedDescription:
Seminar and shared reflection.

In August, a climate election booth built by StuCAN will be displayed in central Gothenburg. Created in cooperation with Gothenburg's climate movement, it has enabled young architecture and engineering students to exert influence and practise their professions before graduating.

We have a responsibility to act not only as private individuals but also through our professional knowledge. Together, we explore how self-organisation can create change, solidarity and hope.

Throughout history, the wish to influence and make a difference without access to money or senior professional positions has forced young people to do the only thing they can: take action to gain attention. Non-profit associations with limited resources share this experience.

What can professionals learn from young architects' and engineers' engagement and activism in the environmental movement?

content.title: Mångfaldsparaden: for compassion and democracy
content.description: Do you believe everyone should have the same rights and opportunities, regardless of gender, disability, ethnicity or sexual orientation? What happens when society stands together to defend democracy and equal rights for all?
content.extendedDescription:
Welcome to what may be Almedalsveckan's most important event: Mångfaldsparaden!

The parade gives everyone who wants to defend our democracy, rights and freedoms an opportunity to unite. A chance to march together for love and for every body and soul's right to exist and live their lives.

In 2026, participants gather at 16.00 in the northern part of Almedalen for a short address by the organisers' representatives. The parade departs at 16.30 and concludes with speeches on Almedalen's stage at around 17.00.

The accessibility train joins the parade for everyone who has difficulty getting around. Those who need it can meet the train outside Gotlands Cykeluthyrning at 16.00 and ride into Almedalen for the gathering. Car drop-off is possible at the bicycle rental shop, with nearby parking for holders of disabled parking permits.

Everyone is welcome; no advance registration is required!

content.title: Prevention that lasts: cooperation between municipalities and civil society across electoral terms
content.description:
When responsibility lies with the municipality, but solutions require more than the municipality alone.
How do we create preventive work that does not collapse when projects end, staff change or election results shift?
content.extendedDescription: An open discussion on working with civil society to reach all young people, including those in the grey area, and build sustainable municipal practice. Municipalities have a clear responsibility for early and preventive action concerning young people, safety and social sustainability. Yet many describe the same challenge: how do we reach young people outside established services before problems escalate, and sustain this work over time? During this hour, we invite municipal politicians, committee representatives and officials to a discussion. Political, strategic and practical perspectives meet to explore preventive work built on structures that last across electoral terms, in cooperation with civil society. The dialogue focuses on practical experience: what often falls short, what actually works and which choices are needed for continuity. Participants leave with a shared understanding of the problem, new perspectives on cooperation and ideas to take back to their municipalities.

content.title: Is Almedalsveckan sustainable, or does it leave a hangover?
content.description: The need for lively, sustainable and visionary meeting places has never been greater. But how are Almedalsveckan and other Swedish events really doing? Are they sustainable environmentally and in terms of democracy and fairness, or does the hangover outweigh the benefits?
content.extendedDescription:
Rearmament, climate change and threats to democracy create anxiety and risk eroding hope for the future. Meeting places such as Almedalsveckan can generate visions, energy and hope as foundations for a safer, more sustainable Sweden, but how well are we succeeding? Through our movement Baksmällan, we invite sustainability and event experts, KISAM – Världens ungdomar and others to scrutinise Almedalen. Last year's focus was diversity; this year's is racism and discrimination. Findings and proposals for improvement are presented during the week's final hours.
As one of the week's final events, like a painkiller for a hangover, we get on our high horses, sum up our impressions and ask: are we reaching WHERE we want, and WHO we want? What should we continue, what should we improve, and how? Together with YOU, we sum up and develop proposals to make us even better. Join in and share your views: your voice counts!

content.title: Sweden's future in the Arctic: the need for a new research icebreaker
content.description: Sweden's only research icebreaker, Oden, is approaching the end of its technical service life. The situation is critical and a political decision is urgent. Without a successor, Sweden risks losing its internationally leading position in polar research and its influence in the Arctic.
content.extendedDescription: Sweden is a leading polar research nation, contributing to international climate and environmental research addressing major societal challenges. Through this, we have built a unique capacity to operate in the Arctic Ocean. As the Arctic security situation deteriorates, this capability has gained geopolitical importance. A Swedish polar research icebreaker is key to maintaining a presence and strengthening Sweden's and its allies' combined capacity. Procuring a new Swedish research icebreaker is necessary to maintain and develop these capabilities. It is also important for infrastructure projects relevant to Europe's digital sovereignty. Procurement is complex and time-consuming, while demand is increasing and costs risk rising. Decisions therefore need to be made soon. The seminar discusses the way forward, the risks of delay and how Sweden can secure long-term, cost-effective access to a new icebreaker.
content.subject: Research

content.title: The next technological leap is bio-based: is policy keeping up?
content.description: Sweden has the conditions to lead the transition to a circular bioeconomy: forests, agriculture, industrial expertise, strong research and companies willing to change. But biological raw materials must serve many needs, and many innovations get stuck between research, scale-up and the market.
content.extendedDescription:
The seminar focuses on the policy instruments, investments and priorities needed to strengthen Sweden's bioeconomy and create more value from biological raw materials from forests, land and water. We also examine research questions that could accelerate the transition from fossil-based to bio-based solutions.

The starting point is a report produced by Miltton Sweden for BioInnovation, analysing challenges concerning biomass availability, resource efficiency and governance, as well as future opportunities along bio-based value chains.

Drawing on the report, a panel discusses the innovation initiatives and policy agenda needed to move from analysis to concrete action.

content.title: The cancer strategy in practice: what is needed to meet growing pressure on cancer care?
content.description: Pressure on cancer care is increasing due to demographic change, new care programmes and rapid developments in areas including diagnostics. How has this changed over time, and what does it mean for Swedish cancer care?
content.extendedDescription: The seminar takes the national cancer strategy as its starting point and focuses on translating it into practical action. There are currently substantial regional differences in the quality, availability and outcomes of cancer care, and responsibilities between central government and regions are often perceived as unclear. Accelerating implementation requires shared, measurable goals, sufficient resources and national follow-up that enables comparison and learning. At the seminar, IHE presents a report commissioned by MSD on how demographic changes, national care programmes and rapid medical technology development have increased care volumes and pressure on healthcare. The discussion addresses barriers, policy instruments and how cooperation between decision-makers, professionals, patients, academia and industry can accelerate the adoption of best practice, with equity as its starting point.
