content.title: From trying to tested practice: what happens when teachers explore teaching with AI?
content.description: AI is already affecting schools, whether we want it to or not. How can AI become a tool for learning, and what questions arise along the way?
content.extendedDescription:
The research evidence on teaching with AI is limited, yet most pupils already use AI as a learning tool. Instead of waiting for research, schools can begin moving from experimentation to established practice now. In this panel discussion, Fridaskolorna and Academedia share their experiences of exploring teaching with AI in their schools.

Fridaskolorna describes its process in compulsory schools, where broad professional development has been complemented by an Innovation Hub. Within the hub, a group of educators has systematically explored AI in teaching for a year. What happens when professional curiosity leads development?

Academedia shares its professional development work and exploration of teaching with AI at 15 of its upper secondary schools. What happens when AI meets classroom reality, what different attitudes towards AI emerge, and how can we respond to create equitable conditions for pupils?
content.subject: Education
speakerTitles: Head of Schools and Organisational Development Specialist

content.title: Time to step up: how do we strengthen Sweden's exports?
content.description: Sweden is one of the world's most trade-dependent countries, but faces geopolitical tensions, trade barriers, regulatory requirements and tougher competition. Maintaining competitiveness and strengthening exports requires smarter support, simpler conditions and better opportunities for companies to grow globally.
content.extendedDescription:
In a time of intensifying geopolitics and rapidly changing trading conditions, businesses must navigate an increasingly complex world. They also face growing regulatory burdens, requirements and unequal competitive conditions. International trade is, and must remain, one of our most important engines of growth and innovation. Strengthening Swedish exports requires cooperation between business, politics and trade promotion bodies, and a clear strategy enabling Swedish companies to grow in international markets.

This discussion brings together decision-makers, entrepreneurs, experts and public authority representatives to address business's most important questions: how do we strengthen Swedish exports in a new global reality and ensure the right conditions?
content.subject: Business

content.title: We personal assistance users face several existential threats: will we be able to continue living freely?
content.description: For those of us with significant disabilities, the right to personal assistance, and therefore our freedom, is constantly threatened. Personal assistance is the only form of support that meets the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities. We are survivors, but will we be able to keep living like everyone else?
content.extendedDescription:
The 1994 personal assistance reform enabled many of us to avoid institutional living. With assistance, we could finally live like other citizens, take our place in society and participate on our own terms. But over the years, savings requirements and case law have severely restricted our freedom. Obtaining personal assistance has become increasingly difficult, and those receiving this vital support constantly worry that their assistance hours will be withdrawn.

The ability to choose a family member as an assistant and to hold dual roles as assistant, legal representative and supervisor is threatened. Who is better placed to support a person with an intellectual disability in making decisions than someone who knows them well, often a family member?

The personal assistance allowance is critically low. It must now be increased substantially, to exactly SEK 400, and then linked to a wage index. The Chair of Riksföreningen JAG gives the opening address in the JAG tent.
content.subject: Human rights

content.title: What barriers are preventing Sweden's growth as a travel and tourism destination?
content.description: Travel to the Nordic region is increasing, but more tourists choose our neighbouring countries than Sweden. Why? What are the biggest obstacles holding back Sweden's tourism industry?
content.extendedDescription:
When tourists choose to travel in Sweden, they generate a range of positive effects for our country. Tourism creates new jobs and drives place development, making Sweden more attractive to both visitors and residents.

Svensk Resebransch has surveyed travel and tourism actors at local, regional and national levels across Sweden, asking what needs to change for Sweden to grow as a tourist destination. This seminar reviews the results and presents the travel and tourism industry's priorities. To attract more international tourists, we must recognise the potential of Sweden's travel and tourism sector.

Joining us are Susanne Andersson from Visit Sweden, Maria Ros Hjelm from Svenska Turistföreningen and a representative from Skistar and Visita. We will discuss barriers and opportunities and hear concrete examples of their impact on tourism operators.
content.subject: Visitor economy

content.title: How do we future-proof large apartment housing estates?
content.description:
How do we create business models for a housing stock that is sustainable over the long term?
Sweden's apartment buildings need refurbishment, climate adaptation and stronger social conditions. This also raises a question: how can those contributing to safety and sustainable value creation share in neighbourhoods' increased value?
content.extendedDescription:
ShiftSweden's transition lab for future-proofing large apartment housing estates focuses on neighbourhoods built in the 1960s and 1970s that face major challenges concerning energy, social sustainability, finances, cultural heritage and long-term value creation. Taking the government's proposal for a new law on area-based cooperation as a starting point, we discuss the business models needed to make investment in safety, services, community, climate transition and technical refurbishment sustainable over the long term.

The event explores how property owners, businesses, civil society and public actors contributing to neighbourhood development can also share in the value they create. Hear research and discussion on translating social, environmental and economic sustainability into governance, financing and practical implementation, starting from existing buildings and place-based cooperation.
content.subject: Sustainability

content.title: When Civil Society Becomes Part of a Nation’s Defence System
content.description: In Ukraine, civil society has become an operational part of the defence ecosystem. How do civic initiatives, volunteer networks and recovery programs strengthen resilience and support those serving on the frontline?
content.extendedDescription:
Ukraine’s war has revealed how civil society can become an operational component of a nation’s defence system. Volunteer networks, civic initiatives and independent organizations play a critical role in supporting those serving on the frontline, often responding faster and more flexibly than traditional structures.

Repower’s recovery programs supporting frontline medics demonstrate how civil initiatives can strengthen the human dimension of defence by addressing psychological resilience and recovery after extreme stress.

The discussion explores how these models of civil engagement interact with formal defence structures and how they contribute to national resilience. The conversation also connects Ukraine’s experience with the Nordic perspective, including Sweden’s Total Defence doctrine and the role of civil society organizations in crisis preparedness. It invites reflection on how cooperation between state and civic initiatives can strengthen future security systems.
content.subject: International affairs

content.title: When Civil Society Becomes Part of a Nation’s Defence System
content.description: In Ukraine, civil society has become an operational part of the defence ecosystem. How do civic initiatives, volunteer networks and recovery programs strengthen resilience and support those serving on the frontline?
content.extendedDescription:
Ukraine’s war has revealed how civil society can become an operational component of a nation’s defence system. Volunteer networks, civic initiatives and independent organizations play a critical role in supporting those serving on the frontline, often responding faster and more flexibly than traditional structures.

Repower’s recovery programs supporting frontline medics demonstrate how civil initiatives can strengthen the human dimension of defence by addressing psychological resilience and recovery after extreme stress.

The discussion explores how these models of civil engagement interact with formal defence structures and how they contribute to national resilience. The conversation also connects Ukraine’s experience with the Nordic perspective, including Sweden’s Total Defence doctrine and the role of civil society organizations in crisis preparedness. It invites reflection on how cooperation between state and civic initiatives can strengthen future security systems.
content.subject: International affairs

content.title: Epilepsy: an issue that concerns us all
content.description: Over 80 000 people in Sweden, including 12 000 children and young people, live with epilepsy, a condition that can affect daily life and quality of life in many ways. Epileptic seizures vary greatly, from brief absence seizures and dizziness to major generalised seizures.
content.extendedDescription:
The diagnosis of epilepsy covers several types of seizure, but epilepsy is more than a diagnosis. Many people experience seizures infrequently, yet epilepsy can still affect large parts of their lives. Many children with epilepsy can attend mainstream school, but fatigue and learning difficulties can affect their education. Lack of understanding among those around them can lead to this being mistaken for laziness or lack of interest.

Access to appropriate care, support and follow-up is crucial to quality of life, but healthcare currently faces challenges. Unequal access to specialists and lengthy investigations can affect the chances of receiving the right diagnosis and treatment in time.

The stigma surrounding epilepsy is considerable, and the often negative responses of others, such as authorities, schools and employers, are sometimes the biggest problem. In other words, epilepsy affects more than the person with the condition: it concerns us all!

content.title: From Nordic innovation to global impact
content.description: The Nordic countries offer strong conditions for innovation, but new ideas do not automatically become successful products and services in the market. How can we better connect research, innovation and commercialisation?
content.extendedDescription:
EU competitiveness discussions identify weak commercialisation and scaling of new technology as one of Europe's biggest challenges. The Nordic countries are among the world's most innovative, but small domestic markets mean that even strong ideas often stall before reaching international scale. Does the Nordic region face similar barriers to those identified at EU level: fragmented markets, complex regulations, a shortage of venture capital and weak demand?

From a Nordic perspective, the aim is to improve conditions for innovations to scale up faster and reach international markets.

The discussion between Nordic stakeholders will identify and highlight the region's most important barriers and clarify where Nordic cooperation can add value beyond national and regional initiatives.
Small markets and big opportunities: how can the countries join forces for a more competitive Nordic region?
content.subject: Innovation

content.title: The competition for talent
content.description: Access to the right skills is crucial to growth and innovation. How do we make the Öresund region more attractive and inclusive? Sweden and Denmark need to act together to create a dynamic, inclusive labour market that attracts global talent.
content.extendedDescription:
Skills supply is one of the most important future issues for Swedish and Danish competitiveness. The Greater Copenhagen labour market region offers unique opportunities, but also clear barriers, to attracting and retaining the right skills. In a time of global competition for talent, Sweden and Denmark need to act together, not in parallel.
How can we strengthen cooperation between Sweden and Denmark to meet business needs? How can national actors, regional initiatives, municipalities and businesses cooperate more effectively?

The panel's questions align with the ongoing Cross-border Talent Bridge initiative, led by Lunds kommun in cooperation with Köpenhamns kommun, Medicon Village Innovation, Ideon Science Park, OpenTech and Medicon Valley Alliance, and co-financed by the Interreg Öresund–Kattegat–Skagerrak programme.

Moderator: Ideon Science Park.
content.subject: Employment/labour market
speakerTitles: Chair of the Municipal Executive Board

content.title: From funding gap to growth engine: how do we advance Swedish medtech?
content.description: Swedish medtech has great potential but is held back by funding gaps between validated innovation and implementation for customers and patients. What does the sector need to become a stronger engine of growth?
content.extendedDescription:
Swedish medtech has the potential to become a stronger growth engine for healthcare, exports and regional development. Yet many companies face significant funding gaps between validated innovation and implementation in healthcare.

At this seminar, Medeon Science Park, Smile Venture Hub and Invest in Skåne present findings from a preliminary study funded by Tillväxtverket. Based on interviews with startups, scaleups, established companies and investors, it examines today's funding landscape and the challenges facing companies at different stages of growth.

We also present a new report on MedTech in Skåne produced by Regional Utveckling Skåne together with Invest in Skåne.

The seminar concludes with a panel of business representatives, investors and innovation system stakeholders discussing how to strengthen Swedish medtech and improve companies' opportunities to grow, attract capital and bring innovations to healthcare and patients.
content.subject: Economy

content.title: Parent of a transgender person: the struggle to keep your child alive
content.description: What is everyday life like for the parent of a transgender person? The struggle to get schools and authorities to follow the law and the Convention on the Rights of the Child. The struggle to make daily life work. The struggle to keep your child alive.
content.extendedDescription:
When the child Jenny knew as her daughter was eleven, he showed her his diary.
‘My name is Love and I am eleven. I am a boy, but my family thinks I am a girl. They don't understand anything.’
The talk Transmamman – min berättelse is about Jenny's struggle as the parent of a transgender child.

Jenny has advocated for LGBTQI+ rights for many years. She moved to Gotland with her family after working for a year as Operations Manager at RFSL Sjuhärad. On Gotland, she has continued through involvement in RFSL Gotland, Gotland Pride and Mångfaldsparaden, which received the ‘Snällast i Almedalen’ award in 2019.
Jenny has given talks to confirmation groups, youth clinics and social services, and her talk ‘Transmamman – min berättelse’ has attracted attention in local newspapers and radio.
In 2019, Jenny received Gotlands bildningsförbund's ‘Årets Folkbildare’ award, and in 2022 she received the FPES Hero Award on the main stage at the opening of Stockholm Pride.
content.subject: Human rights

content.title: Teachers and AI: who gives them the tools when guidelines are missing?
content.description: AI has quickly become part of everyday school life, but many teachers still lack support, guidance and confidence in using it, especially with pupils. Meanwhile, differences between schools and education providers are growing. What happens to equity when development proceeds at different speeds?
content.extendedDescription:
Novus's annual survey of 530 compulsory school teachers, commissioned by Dustin, shows how quickly AI has moved from experimentation to an everyday school tool. Seven in ten teachers now use AI at work, mainly to create teaching materials and plan lessons. Just over half feel that AI improves teaching, and more feel confident with the technology than a year ago.

Yet AI is still used cautiously in teaching. Only 31 per cent of teachers have worked with AI together with pupils. Many lack time, pedagogical support and clear guidelines for safe, responsible use.

The results are presented for the first time at the seminar. The panel discusses how schools can move from uncertainty to confident AI use, and what is needed for AI to strengthen teaching without increasing inequality between pupils and schools.
content.subject: Education

content.title: When medicines change society: obesity, weight-loss treatment and the way forward
content.description: As obesity treatment changes, new questions arise about equitable access, costs, prevention and responsibility. What happens as demand rises, and how does it affect everything from healthcare and pharmacies to food, retail and consumption patterns?
content.extendedDescription:
New GLP1 medicines are revolutionising weight-loss possibilities and have already affected behaviour and consumption, particularly in the USA.

As obesity treatment changes, new questions arise about equitable access, costs, prevention and responsibility. What happens as demand rises, and how does it affect everything from healthcare and pharmacies to food, retail and consumption patterns? How do we ensure that children, young people and socioeconomically disadvantaged groups receive the support they need for prevention and treatment, and ultimately to maintain a sustainable lifestyle?

This seminar brings together perspectives from politics, public authorities, healthcare and business to discuss the way forward. How do we ensure the right patients get the right treatment? How can we afford it, and build a system that also invests in prevention and long-term outcomes? What role can, and should, pharmacies and grocery retailers play?
content.subject: Health and social care

content.title: From research to patients: how do we ensure innovation reaches patients in time?
content.description: How are research, clinical trials and patients' access to innovative treatments connected?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden has long been a strong research nation, but many patients still have to wait for new treatments already used in other countries. How well do our decision-makers understand the connection between research, clinical trials, innovation and patients' access to treatment?

The seminar presents results from a new Novus survey of national, regional and municipal politicians. It examines knowledge of how innovative treatments are introduced into Swedish healthcare, the barriers to rapid implementation and the effects on Sweden's ability to attract research and clinical trials.

Drawing on the results, we bring together politicians and other key stakeholders to discuss strengthening the entire chain, from research and clinical studies to equitable, timely patient access.

The seminar is organised by Blodcancerforum in cooperation with AbbVie, Bristol Myers Squibb (BMS), Gilead, GSK, Johnson & Johnson and Roche.

content.title: Is the EU changing innovation funding, and how will Sweden be affected?
content.description: The EU's next cohesion policy programming period may change how innovation is funded, with signs of increased national control. What does this mean for those building innovation across the country, and how is Sweden influencing developments?
content.extendedDescription:
The EU's next cohesion policy programming period is taking shape, with proposals that could change funding for innovation and regional development. New governance models are being discussed in which national priorities may carry more weight than before.

For actors working closely with businesses and innovation across the country, this could change conditions for funding, influence and working methods.

Meanwhile, negotiations are under way in which member states and other stakeholders can influence developments. But how is Sweden positioning itself? Which perspectives are we promoting, and which risk having less impact?

This seminar brings together decision-makers and actors from different parts of the system to discuss what we know about EU-level developments, what they may mean in practice and what is needed to adapt and exert influence in time.

A networking lunch is served from 1200, with limited places. The seminar starts at 1230.
content.subject: Innovation

content.title: Going to school with anxiety and a stomach ache: evidence-based social inclusion
content.description: The vision of equity and inclusion for autistic pupils in Swedish schools lacks courage, creativity and practical expertise. When schools fail to include pupils, they risk long-term exclusion. How can we create real social inclusion on a scientific basis?
content.extendedDescription:
Every day, thousands of children go to school with anxiety and stomach aches. For many pupils with autism, ADHD and other neurodevelopmental conditions, school is a place where demands exceed the conditions provided. Step by step, they lose trust not only in school and society, but also in themselves.

Despite high ambitions for equity and inclusion, courage, knowledge and practical expertise are often lacking when it comes to supporting pupils at risk of being pushed out of education. When support fails, the costs of exclusion, mental ill-health and future unemployment rise.

The seminar highlights an alarming societal problem, opens an honest discussion about our shared responsibility and points to ways forward.

The question is not whether we can afford to do more, but how long we can afford not to.

content.title: From gaps in the system to coordinated support: could a Mental Health Reform 2.0 be the way forward?
content.description: More people are seeking psychiatric care, but many do not receive help. What is needed to close the gaps between needs and services? How can we build a system that works for patients and the professionals supporting people in need?
content.extendedDescription:
Thirty years after the mental health reform, the visions of early intervention, coordinated care and secure lives remain far from fulfilled. As more children, young people and adults seek help, we see fewer inpatient beds and inadequate cooperation between psychiatric services, municipalities and emergency services. Healthcare staff, police and rescue services encounter the consequences every day: people in acute distress and a fragmented system.

The seminar brings together patient representatives, experts and politicians to discuss what is needed for functioning psychiatric care. How can we ensure early intervention for children and young people? How do we strengthen support for adults with complex needs? Which political priorities are required to build a lasting system in which more people actually have the opportunity to feel better?

Join a seminar highlighting gaps in the system and opportunities to reconnect society's safety net.
content.subject: Health and social care
speakerTitles: Chair of the Regional Executive Board

content.title: The missing link: how can more pupils succeed at school?
content.description: Too many pupils leave compulsory school without eligibility for upper secondary education. The consequences are substantial for individuals and society. Despite many initiatives, schools often struggle to provide timely, appropriate support to pupils at risk of falling behind.
content.extendedDescription:
How can schools support pupils when many begin to lose motivation, attendance and achievement? In years four to six, demands on independence and cognitive abilities increase, as does the need for support at home. Pupils who struggle to meet these demands and cannot rely on sufficient support at home often face a gap between school and home.
The intervention presented aims to fill this gap by combining individual mentoring and targeted subject support through tutoring. Mentors work closely with each pupil facing challenges, helping them establish a weekly plan covering studies and leisure and clarifying when parental support is needed.
Targeted tutoring also helps pupils catch up in core subjects. Mullsjö kommun provides a concrete example of a municipality that has adopted the model. The seminar also explores financing the initiative through a social outcomes contract.
content.subject: Children/young people

content.title: Biochar: too good to need a national policy?
content.description: Biochar is both a physical product and a carbon sink. It is made from domestic materials, increasing the value of our biological resources. Biochar improves soils and concrete and purifies water. Carbon in soil and building materials is overlooked as a means of achieving negative emissions.
content.extendedDescription:
Biochar is an established but still underused solution for long-term carbon storage. The technology can contribute to healthier soils, climate-neutral concrete, new value chains and better use of existing energy infrastructure.

Yet Sweden lacks a national policy with clear instruments and incentives to scale up production and use. This seminar discusses how biochar can become an integral part of climate action, both as a carbon sink and as a material with practical benefits for agriculture, construction and public spaces. What policy changes are needed to unlock its potential? How can municipalities, agriculture and industry cooperate to create robust regional cycles? Researchers, practitioners and decision-makers explore barriers, opportunities and concrete next steps. The seminar consists of a short introductory lecture followed by audience questions.
content.subject: Climate/environment

content.title: Essential transport in peace, crisis and war
content.description: Sweden's transport capability is crucial to business, security of supply and total defence. A deteriorating international situation demands robust freight transport, sufficient rail capacity and clear coordination to keep society functioning during disruptions, crises and heightened alert.
content.extendedDescription:
The seminar consists of opening perspectives followed by a panel discussion on strengthening Sweden's transport capability amid a deteriorating international situation. Its starting point is that functioning transport is crucial to business deliveries, society's security of supply and total defence's operational capability.

Particular attention is given to rail and freight transport during disruptions, crises and heightened alert. The discussion addresses measures to ensure long-term robustness, capacity, redundancy and coordination, and how responsibilities and priorities should be shared between public and private actors.

The event begins with a welcome, followed by a keynote and commentary, and ends with a panel discussion. It is aimed at decision-makers and actors in transport, business, security of supply and total defence. No preparation is required.
content.subject: Infrastructure/transport

content.title: How can trade associations better support their members?
content.description: Small businesses create the most new jobs. They are the largest taxpayers in 9 out of 10 municipalities. Yet many important sectors lack the resources to make their voices heard. How can we change this?
content.extendedDescription:
Many trade associations do fantastic work but often lack the time, resources or right contacts to pursue advocacy fully. This is precisely why Företagarna Branschpartner exists. We bring together associations that want to be stronger together and create direct dialogue with politicians and decision-makers. Through our networks and policy experts, we give your voice greater impact on critical issues such as the business climate, red tape, skills supply and employment law.

Thomas Byström, who leads Företagarna Branschpartner, will be present to explain this work.

SVEBRA has already joined us to maximise its influence. Would you like to do the same? During Almedalsveckan, Tuesday–Thursday, Företagarna will be at SVEBRA's Beredskapscafé. We welcome meetings with trade associations wanting closer access to decision-makers and a stronger position. Are you in Almedalen? Contact us directly to arrange a meeting and explore how we can work together to become stronger!

content.title: When AI passes the exam: who takes responsibility for patient safety?
content.description: AI and advanced technology challenge today's assessments. How do we ensure legally sound exams that assess the student, rather than AI or unauthorised aids? What is at stake for trust in academic degrees? Is patient safety at risk?
content.extendedDescription:
When AI can write essays, solve exam questions and imitate students' language, one of universities' foundations, legally sound assessment, becomes increasingly difficult to maintain. What happens when technology outpaces regulations, and how does this affect professions in which inadequate knowledge can endanger patient safety?

The seminar begins by presenting the government assignment ‘Mapping measures against cheating in distance learning’, followed by a panel debate. What is needed to ensure legally sound assessment when generative AI makes cheating easy, even in invigilated exams where legal restrictions limit checks? Can these challenges be met?

Participants explore legal, academic, regulatory, student and teacher perspectives, alongside healthcare's perspective, where inadequate knowledge can have particularly serious consequences.

content.title: Effective scrutiny of non-profit associations through bank data
content.description: Welfare fraud and hidden networks threaten the voluntary sector. When unscrupulous actors exploit the system and information-sharing falls short, old routines are not enough.
content.extendedDescription:
Non-profit associations play a crucial role in Swedish society, but this organisational form can also be misused for tax and benefit fraud and as a cover for hidden networks. Traditional checks are not always sufficient to distinguish legitimate organisations from risky ones before harm is done.

At this seminar, representatives of Ekobrottsmyndigheten and Skatteverket describe how associations can be misused and the limits of current checks. SRS Security then shows how transaction data and account analysis can complement existing methods and improve decision-making without adding to the administrative burden on well-run associations.

The panel also discusses difficult trade-offs:
- How do we strengthen scrutiny without casting suspicion on legitimate associations?
- When is a deeper investigation proportionate?
- What is needed to build trust without being naive?

content.title: Investing before the flood: how private capital creates public value
content.description: Climate change is driving increasing natural disaster damage and major societal costs. Sweden's water and wastewater infrastructure needs hundreds of billions in investment to prevent risks. Yet opportunities to use private capital for climate adaptation are limited.
content.extendedDescription: Cloudbursts, floods and billions in natural disaster damage: climate change is already here, and the bill is growing rapidly. Water and wastewater networks are an area with major investment needs and are important to Sweden's climate adaptation. Almost SEK 600 billion is needed by 2040, but current regulations limit financing through private capital. Occupational pension providers' primary task when managing capital is to generate secure returns for future pensions. A distinctive feature of occupational pension capital is its suitability for long-term investments such as infrastructure projects. What role can private capital and the insurance industry play in reducing climate-related natural disaster risks for society and individuals?
content.detail: Folkhälsodalen, in the garden behind S:t Hans café.
content.subject: Climate/environment

content.title: How can we create the next season in Earth's history, full of abundant life?
content.description: How can we create a next season in Earth's history rich in life in all its forms: nature, love, creativity and spirit? What would it mean to be human in such a future? Which dreams, ideas and questions can take us there, during the election campaign and beyond?
content.extendedDescription:
In 1962, Rachel Carson published Silent Spring, describing with both scientific rigour and poetry how humanity's destructive relationship with nature risked tipping us towards more death on Earth. Now we are there, balancing on the edge of the sixth mass extinction. How can we instead co-create a Loud Summer: a next season in Earth's history full of abundant life in all its forms?
During this event, we introduce the Loud Summer project and read aloud from our newly released anthology.
In it, 30 authors portray their dreams and ideas for a Loud Summer, a next season in Earth's history full of abundant life in all its forms, and explore humanity's potential new constructive role in the web of life.
content.subject: Sustainability

content.title: From talking about young people to building with them: how can young people participate and influence in practice?
content.description: Segregation, insecurity, crime and mental ill-health are major challenges in disadvantaged areas. Yet young people's participation often remains mere words, without structures enabling action and real influence. Building with young people strengthens democracy and prevention.
content.extendedDescription:
A discussion-based seminar with refreshments. Young people's participation and influence are often mentioned but rarely put into practice. How do we move from words to action, from talking about young people to building with them?
We share how, together with young people, we have built social and inclusive infrastructure in local communities that increases their participation and influence. We show how this strengthens democracy and participation in society while preventing challenges such as segregation, crime and mental ill-health.
Young people in disadvantaged areas describe being talked about often, but rarely talked with. The conversation focuses on designing initiatives that give young people not only a voice but also real influence and the ability to act in preventive work. Hear their journeys from participants to leaders and co-creators, and how they now make a difference for other children and young people.
content.subject: Children/young people

content.title: Tech giants under pressure?
content.description: More countries are introducing or considering age limits for social media to protect children and young people. Meanwhile, tech companies such as Meta have been found liable in court and fined billions for inadequate protection and known risks of sexual exploitation.
content.extendedDescription:
Tech giants face increasing political and legal pressure over their responsibility for children's and young people's safety online. International court rulings and regulatory initiatives reveal a growing conflict between platforms' business models and society's demands for protection.
Algorithms now control content distributed to children and young people, helping shape norms concerning women, girls, misogyny, appearance and sexuality. This includes exposure to pornographic material that normalises violence and degradation, and environments where sexualised violence can spread and intensify.
In supporting women and girls, Unizon's member support centres have long encountered the consequences of a digital environment that shapes, reinforces, spreads and normalises severe sexual violence, while responsibility for addressing these problems has largely been placed on young people themselves.
How are children and young people affected? What responsibilities do tech companies have, and which do they take? What demands can and should society make going forward?
content.subject: Digitalisation
speakerTitles: Speaker and founder of the Generation AI podcast

content.title: Cooperation is not enough: how do we make research make a difference?
content.description: There is no shortage of research, innovations or technological solutions. But why do promising initiatives often stop at pilots, despite major needs and available solutions?
content.extendedDescription:
Research should contribute to innovation and public value through interaction with the public sector, business and civil society. Yet many initiatives end as projects. Making them a reality requires shared responsibility and the courage to invest for the long term.
We often see this in prevention and societal transition: research identifies interventions with long-term effects, but costs arise here and now while benefits may accrue to other actors later. A gap then emerges between knowledge and action: projects are carried out, but implementation does not follow. Everyone sees the need, but no one drives change all the way. Can change be achieved, and if so, how?
The problem is rarely a lack of knowledge, ideas or willingness, but how we organise, finance and take responsibility for change. We discuss how a solution becomes usable, by whom and on what terms, guided by three questions: who receives the value, who pays and who must change how they work?
content.subject: Research

content.title: How can we enable more industrial projects that benefit both the climate and national security?
content.description: New technology reduces CO2 emissions and improves security of supply by producing synthetic fuels when electrified lime production, essential for high-quality steelmaking, captures unavoidable CO2 emissions. Cooperation between the private and public sectors makes this possible.
content.extendedDescription:
When energy and fuel are strategic vulnerabilities, central government, municipalities and business must cooperate to enable green investment that strengthens industrial robustness. Our neighbouring countries attract investment with faster decisions on electricity, permits and state involvement. For more investments to materialise in Sweden, we must improve our transition support systems, including Klimatklivet and Industriklivet.
In this panel discussion, private and public sector representatives discuss the need for cooperation and possible improvements. We highlight an example in which electrified lime production separates carbon dioxide from the lime reaction into a controlled stream, enabling steel production using essential lime with significantly lower CO2 emissions. These emissions instead become synthetic fuels, using electricity, hydrogen and carbon dioxide, contributing to lower emissions and greater security of supply.
content.subject: Innovation

content.title: Strengthen the law against genital mutilation
content.description: Female genital mutilation is a serious human rights violation. Despite the ban, a widely discussed court case found that mutilation of a girl's internal genital organs was not covered by the legislation. How should the law be revised to cover all forms of genital mutilation?
content.extendedDescription:
Female genital mutilation is a serious violation of girls' bodily integrity and human rights. Although it has been prohibited in Sweden since 1982, shortcomings remain in the law's wording and application.

In a widely discussed Swedish court case, a procedure on a girl's internal genital organs was found not to fall under the law and was instead handled as assault. This suggests current legislation does not cover all forms of mutilating procedures.

Why should legislation against genital mutilation be strengthened to cover all forms? How can prevention, detection and prosecution of genital mutilation affecting girls resident in Sweden be improved?

GAPF believes the legislation should be clarified to explicitly cover procedures on internal genital organs. Sweden should have zero tolerance for genital mutilation.
content.subject: Gender equality

content.title: Patient choice in primary care: dismantle or develop?
content.description: Healthcare is intensely debating independent providers' role and the future of patient choice systems. Meanwhile, we see patient choice in primary care leading to better access and strong continuity. How can we develop the current system without reducing patients' access to care?
content.extendedDescription:
Debate about private healthcare providers and patient choice has intensified on both the right and left. Yet criticism rarely concerns the quality of care delivered; instead, it focuses on governance, oversight and politicians' ability to take responsibility for the whole system. Does patient choice risk becoming a scapegoat for problems really arising from system design and follow-up?
In this seminar, Praktikertjänst presents a new report on the Act on System of Choice in primary care and brings together politicians, care providers and healthcare professionals for a nuanced discussion of future healthcare. Drawing on practical regional experience, we discuss how LOV can evolve to secure freedom of choice while strengthening access, continuity and quality. The aim is to contribute to reforms combining innovation and long-term trust.
content.subject: Health and social care
content.accessibility: Wheelchair-accessible entrance and venue
speakerTitles: Chief Medical Officer, Specialist in General Practice

content.title: The energy transition is waiting: who dares to invest?
content.description: The energy transition requires investment, but an uncertain world and financial calculations that struggle to add up create a decision-making vacuum. How can it be broken?
content.extendedDescription:
Through dialogue between politics, the energy sector, industry and finance, we seek answers to why investment is delayed and what is needed to change this.

The discussion starts from two themes:

How do you reach an investment decision for a megaproject?
• Why is reaching an investment decision on megaprojects so complex, despite their necessity for the transition?
• How must revenue models, incentives and risk allocation develop to make megaprojects investable in practice?

What can energy infrastructure developers and owners do right now?
• How can financing, guarantees and risk-sharing be structured to get capital moving when uncertainty is high?
• What can actors influence themselves, and where are political or regulatory changes required?

Join a dialogue about moving from goals to delivery despite high uncertainty.
content.subject: Energy
speakerTitles: Partner, Head of Strategy and Transaction Advisory for the Energy Sector

content.title: Can circular business models scale up in the fashion industry?
content.description: The fashion industry is producing faster and in greater quantities than ever, while textile waste grows. Can circular business models scale up in an industry built on overproduction?
content.extendedDescription:
The fashion industry is producing more clothing than ever, while textile waste rises rapidly. Fair Action's report Dressed to Waste shows that overproduction is a fundamental problem in an industry whose business models still rely on selling more garments at lower quality and prices.

Although circularity is highlighted as an important solution, many companies lack clear targets to reduce production or increase circular revenue. Meanwhile, fashion accounts for around 10 per cent of global greenhouse gas emissions, underlining the need for transition. The report shows that reducing overproduction and adopting new business models are necessary for real change.

Drawing on Dressed to Waste, the discussion explores circularity, growth and what real transition requires. Researchers, civil society and business representatives discuss circular business models, business value, overproduction and the path towards a fashion industry within planetary boundaries.
content.subject: Sustainability
speakerTitles: Doctoral Researcher in Marketing focusing on Sustainable Fashion

content.title: How do we create the right conditions for entrepreneurship that solves our biggest societal challenges?
content.description: Sweden and Europe need more companies solving today's greatest challenges, but innovation and entrepreneurship lack the conditions they need. Is ‘impact company’ a meaningful term, or does it obscure companies actually changing the world? And what policies are needed?
content.extendedDescription:
How do we build a Sweden and Europe where innovation and entrepreneurship have better conditions to solve today's greatest societal challenges? This afternoon programme explores that question, focusing on entrepreneurship, future policy and practical ideas for a more innovation-friendly society.

The stage programme has two parts. First, a panel discussion entitled ‘There are no impact companies’ explores the barriers and opportunities awaiting the next generation of impact and tech companies. Then, in Reversed Pitching, politicians pitch their best ideas and reform proposals directly to a panel of entrepreneurs, reversing the usual dynamic and placing concrete demands on politics.

After the stage programme, discussions continue at a networking event with entrepreneurs, investors, politicians and decision-makers. Register using the link below.
content.detail: Loops arena för impact, industri och energi
content.subject: Innovation

content.title: What is happening to the global playing field?
content.description: Geopolitical tensions, trade conflicts and new balances of power are changing conditions for business, investment and international cooperation. How do global developments affect Sweden and Swedish companies, and what strategic choices are required?
content.extendedDescription:
Swedish companies depend heavily on global markets for both sourcing and sales. Geopolitics, trade barriers and increasingly protectionist industrial policies in several markets make it harder to understand the actual business impact and optimise value chains.

In this discussion, Business Sweden's geopolitical advisers meet policy experts from Swedish companies. Global perspectives are combined with a closer look at US and EU industrial policy and its effects on Swedish businesses.

Main questions include:
- Which recent developments are uppermost in Swedish companies' minds?
- Will US trade policy volatility subside?
- How does EU industrial policy affect companies?
- What is the state of US–EU trade relations?
- What opportunities arise amid the current turbulence?
- What should businesses focus on going forward?
content.subject: Business

content.title: Can properties become Sweden's next preparedness resource by relieving an electricity system under pressure?
content.description: Sweden's electricity system is under pressure from power shortages, weather and increasing demands. Can properties become an active resource that reduces peaks, stores energy and strengthens preparedness? What opportunities and barriers exist, and what is needed to unlock buildings' hidden potential?
content.extendedDescription: Sweden's electricity system faces growing pressures, from power shortages and electrification to extreme weather and a greater security focus. Yet an often overlooked resource lies within our communities: buildings. Smarter controls, energy storage, reduced power demand and integration with local energy systems can enable buildings to relieve the grid when it is under greatest strain. Despite this potential, unclear regulations, weak incentives and ambiguous responsibilities are slowing progress. This seminar explores how properties can become part of Sweden's next preparedness resource, which technical and political barriers must be removed, and how industry, public authorities and decision-makers can cooperate to build a more resilient energy system. The question is no longer whether the need exists, but how quickly we dare to think differently.
content.subject: Construction
speakerTitles: Head of electrical systems and automation
Head of Digital Services Business Area
Head of the Resource-Efficient Society Department

content.title: In remand custody: when can I see Mum again?
content.description: Behind the closed doors of remand centres are children longing for home, lost and vulnerable in society and in life. Perpetrators and victims at the same time. How do you answer their questions: when can I see Mum again? Why did everything go so wrong?
content.extendedDescription:
An evening of music and conversation about guilt, vulnerability, trust, responsibility, hopelessness and hope, but also the possibility of a new beginning.

What happens behind closed doors when a remand centre chaplain meets children longing for home? Children who have committed extremely serious crimes. Children terrified of death. Deeply distrustful of adults. Children whose ability to understand consequences is not fully developed. Children who are both perpetrators and victims.
Two things recur in these conversations: longing for Mum and the hardest question, why did everything go so wrong?
How can these children learn to find their boundaries again, for themselves and for others? What can help them discover their own ‘U-turn’, the thing that gives them a second chance? And what can we do when meeting children and young people?

Olle Jonasson is one of around 180 pastoral care workers, including pastors, priests, deacons and imams, working in remand centres and prisons across Sweden. Their work is coordinated by Sveriges kristna råd under an agreement with Kriminalvården.
content.subject: Justice/crime
content.accessibility: Hearing loop, wheelchair-accessible entrance and venue

content.title: Security, energy and industry: why Östersund is growing now
content.description: As Europe's security situation changes and industry transitions, new opportunities emerge. Östersund brings together renewable energy, growing defence companies and a strategic location in northern Sweden.
content.extendedDescription:
Session 1: How do we build cities where investment and people grow together?
Historically large investments are now being made in energy, defence, industry and societal development. But investment does not automatically create attractive communities. How do we meet needs for housing, skills, infrastructure and living environments when both companies and people expect more of the places they choose? Drawing on Östersund and northern Sweden, we discuss how the public sector, energy companies, property owners and businesses can jointly create cities that remain attractive and competitive over the long term.

Session 2: Northern Sweden, more than an industrial boom
Northern Sweden plays an increasingly important role in Sweden's and Europe's competitiveness. Investment in energy, defence, innovation and industry is rapidly changing the economic and geopolitical landscape. What role do cities such as Östersund play in Sweden's next phase of growth? How do we strengthen competitiveness and resilience in a more uncertain world?
content.subject: Business
speakerTitles: Head of Finance and Governance Section
Adviser on Strategy and Total Defence

content.title: Veterinary care at any price: who is responsible, and can pet owners afford to wait?
content.description: Sweden has one of the EU's highest rates of veterinary price increases. Emergency care prices have risen by up to 50% in five years, putting considerable pressure on pet owners.
content.extendedDescription:
When the cost of saving an animal's life jeopardises household finances, both animal welfare and trust in the system are at stake. In February, Konkurrensverket found inadequate price transparency and weaker consumer protection for pet owners than for almost any other service. The government responded by instructing Konsumentverket to improve price information. In a market characterised by price rises and limited transparency, an urgent question arises: must industry actors take responsibility and regulate themselves, or is political intervention needed? What role do insurers and pet owners play in the cost spiral affecting more and more households?

Industry representatives, decision-makers, insurers and representatives of the dog community discuss how greater transparency and new forms of cooperation can become reality. By bringing together those with the power to make changes, we focus on decisions rather than analysis. One thing is certain: pet owners will soon be unable to afford to wait.
content.subject: Animals/nature
content.accessibility: Wheelchair-accessible entrance and venue

content.title: Sweden's pharmaceutical choices: how do we take the lead?
content.description: Sweden's pharmaceutical choices determine future innovation and patient access. How can we take the lead amid intensifying global competition, and which decisions are needed today?
content.extendedDescription: Sweden and Europe face a crucial choice in pharmaceutical policy. Do we continue on the current path of limited willingness to pay, rigid budget systems and the risk of declining attractiveness, or reform to strengthen life sciences competitiveness? This seminar brings together politics, public authorities, regions, industry and academia to discuss practical solutions. Drawing on current challenges, including global market changes, the panel explores value-based pricing, flexible payment models and faster access to innovation. The focus is on clear choices and concrete policy proposals. How do we ensure Sweden remains a country where patients can access new treatments and where innovation chooses to stay?
content.detail: Life Science Arena – Sweden's growth engine
content.subject: Health and social care

content.title: Vattendagen 2026: can Sweden afford not to secure its water supply?
content.description: Water is society's most fundamental resource, yet it lacks a clear political home. What do decision-makers, experts and businesses say about crisis and war, investment needs, skills supply and a coordinated water policy ahead of the 2026 election?
content.extendedDescription:
Vattendagen is organised by Vattenindustrin, Svenskt Vatten and Mötesplats Vatten in a garden at Tranhusgatan 26. Attend an individual seminar or stay all day.

Programme:

09.00–09.45 Water is our most important food: are municipalities ready for crisis and war? Svenskt Vatten on water and wastewater preparedness.

10.00–10.45 Can we afford not to invest in water and wastewater infrastructure? Investment needs of SEK 560 billion by 2040 and rising charges.

11.00–11.45 Securing future skills in the water and wastewater sector. Vattenindustrin on generational change and recruitment.

12.45–14.15 Water lunch for invited guests. Water preparedness and public-private cooperation in war and peacetime crises.

15.00–16.30 Communities are built on water: what do the parties want to do ahead of the 2026 election? Party debate on a coordinated water policy.

Vattendagen is a collaboration between Svenskt Vatten, Vattenindustrin and Mötesplats Vatten.
content.subject: Security/defence

content.title: Why is Swedish domestic aviation slowing down, and when will sustainable flying take off?
content.description: Functioning infrastructure is fundamental to enabling tourism across Sweden to thrive and grow. Yet domestic aviation is declining while rail services face problems.
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden, Norway and Finland are all large countries needing a network of different transport options. Yet our neighbours are not seeing the same decline now occurring in Sweden. Why? How do we reverse this negative trend and enable smooth travel connecting the whole country? This seminar presents an attitudes survey exploring why many people choose not to take domestic flights in Sweden. We also ask why more people do not choose fossil-free aviation fuel to reduce emissions.

We are joined by David Hild from Fly Green Fund, which offers SAF fuel, Charlotte from Norwegian on its work in Norway and Sweden, and Fredrik Kempe from Transportföretagen Flyg. The report was produced by Aura Insight for Svenska Resebranschföreningen, Transportföretagen flyg, SBTA and Svenska Regionala flygplatser.
content.subject: Visitor economy

content.title: Art as a Language of War: Making the Invisible Visible
content.description: War creates psychological experiences that are often difficult to express through policy language alone. How can art help translate complex and invisible aspects of war, trauma and resilience into a public conversation?
content.extendedDescription:
The psychological realities of war are often difficult to communicate through traditional policy discussions. Experiences such as trauma, recovery and resilience are complex and deeply human, yet they remain largely invisible within public and political discourse.
This event explores how art can function as a communication tool for translating these experiences into forms that can be understood, felt and reflected upon by a wider audience.
The installation presented within the Repower space transforms the invisible psychological pressure of war into a tangible public experience. By engaging with artistic expression, visitors are invited not only to observe but to reflect on the human dimension of war and recovery.
Drawing on Ukraine’s experience, the event demonstrates how art can open new forms of dialogue between civil society, policymakers and defence actors. It creates a space where complex themes such as resilience, trauma and recovery can be approached beyond institutional langua
content.subject: International affairs

content.title: Put jobs first: skills supply in a new era
content.description: The climate transition, digitalisation, AI development and an ageing population place new demands on labour market and education policy. Meanwhile, unemployment is high. How do we meet society's skills needs in these times? What must politics deliver in the next electoral term?
content.extendedDescription: Despite visions and discussions, governments of different political colours have failed on labour market policy: unemployment is higher than necessary, and many unemployed people do not receive the right support or have been out of work for a long time. Conditions for matching people to jobs are therefore harder than they have been for many years. TCO's skills supply policy programme and this labour market debate start from the need to move from words to action. What concrete changes are needed to reduce unemployment and increase employment, thereby strengthening the long-term skills supply? With researchers and political representatives, we seek to answer how putting jobs first can solve skills supply challenges.
content.subject: Employment/labour market

Labour Market Policy Spokesperson and Member of Parliament

content.title: How will the circular society be financed?
content.description: The transition to a more circular society, where resources are used more efficiently in circular flows, can help reduce our environmental and climate impact, lower business risks such as resource shortages and price volatility, and create value through benefits such as increased productivity.
content.extendedDescription:
This transition will bring major changes in how we live and consume, and drive substantial changes in companies' business models. One example is moving from selling capital-intensive products to charging for the function or benefit they provide: product-as-a-service. What does the transition to a circular economy mean for households and businesses? How will it be financed? What role can banks and sustainable financing solutions play?

Join a conversation about drivers, challenges and opportunities, and above all the paths and partnerships needed to make the transition to a more circular society succeed.
content.subject: Sustainability

CEO of SEB Asset Management AB and Vice Chair of the Delegation for the Circular Economy
Moderator and Head of Climate & Sustainable Finance

content.title: How can we create the next season in Earth's history, full of abundant life?
content.description: How can we create a next season in Earth's history rich in life in all its forms: nature, love, creativity and spirit? What would it mean to be human in such a future? Which dreams, ideas and questions can take us there, during the election campaign and beyond?
content.extendedDescription:
In 1962, Rachel Carson published Silent Spring, describing with both scientific rigour and poetry how humanity's destructive relationship with nature risked tipping us towards more death on Earth. Now we are there, balancing on the edge of the sixth mass extinction. How can we instead co-create a Loud Summer: a next season in Earth's history full of abundant life in all its forms?
During this event, we introduce the Loud Summer project and read aloud from our newly released anthology.
In it, 30 authors portray their dreams and ideas for a Loud Summer, a next season in Earth's history full of abundant life in all its forms, and explore humanity's potential new constructive role in the web of life.
content.subject: Sustainability
speakerTitles: CEO and Consultant, Broryd industrier AB

content.title: How can bank data change and improve checks on companies?
content.description: Background checks are now crucial to securing business relationships and protecting society. As risks, money flows and business models evolve, however, established methods increasingly need current, context-sensitive perspectives to complement them.
content.extendedDescription:
Companies may look legitimate in registry data while actually being used for financial crime or unsound arrangements. Traditional background checks do not always detect warning signs in time, and when they do, it may already be too late.

At this seminar, Ekobrottsmyndigheten and Dun & Bradstreet describe how financial crime is evolving, what today's checks detect and what they miss. SRS Security then demonstrates how bank data and account analysis can complement traditional methods and improve decisions by revealing actual activity rather than registered information alone.

The panel also discusses tougher questions:
- Where is the line between legitimate risk analysis and excessive scrutiny?
- Which is more dangerous today: too little scrutiny or too much?
- What regulatory developments are needed to strengthen checks without compromising legal safeguards?
content.detail: Cramérgatan, Uppsala universitet, Building B, main entrance, room B22
content.subject: Security/defence

content.title: How do we ensure the right pharmaceutical expertise when systems are tested by crisis and war?
content.description: Crises, war and heightened geopolitical tensions put pressure on the pharmaceutical system. How do we ensure the expertise needed to strengthen preparedness and medicine supplies? What coordination, specialist knowledge and training are required throughout the chain to withstand the next crisis?
content.extendedDescription:
Crises, geopolitical change, war near Europe's borders and recurring shortages place intense pressure on the pharmaceutical system. Sweden's pharmaceutical expertise needs to be recognised more clearly as a resource for strengthening preparedness and medicine supplies. The discussion examines future education and skills needs: how should preparedness work be designed and coordinated? What roles will pharmacists with different qualifications play in crisis and war, and are new skills needed? How can these perspectives be developed in initial, continuing and further education, and how can lifelong learning prepare professionals for changing conditions?

Representatives of academia, pharmacies, regions, authorities, total defence, politics and industry discuss in an open roundtable what is needed for Sweden to be better prepared for future pharmaceutical challenges.
content.subject: Education
content.organizationType: Collaboration between different types of organisation

content.title: Electric aviation has taken off: what happens next?
content.description: Electrifying regional aviation opens the door to systemic change. Alongside fossil-free flights, smaller aircraft and lower operating costs enable a denser route network in Sweden. Locally generated electricity gives control over aviation's energy supply and increases resilience.
content.extendedDescription:
During the spring, 30 electric aircraft flights took place on Gotland as part of the NATO exercise Aurora 2026.

These flights offer hope for an island wholly dependent on functioning transport. They open new possibilities for sustainable access to Sweden's largest island and other parts of the country.

Electrifying regional aviation opens the door to broader systemic change. Besides enabling fossil-free flights, smaller aircraft and lower operating costs allow a denser Swedish route network. Locally generated electricity also gives control over aviation's energy source and contributes to a new level of resilience.

The seminar draws on lessons from the spring's electric demonstration flights. What is now needed to take the next step, from demonstrations to scheduled services in Sweden?
content.subject: Infrastructure/transport

content.title: From exposure to reputation and impact: what do new sponsorship deduction rules mean?
content.description: Sponsorship is undergoing its biggest shift in decades. The government has now submitted a proposal to Lagrådet for tax deductibility of sponsorship as an investment intended to strengthen an organisation's reputation. This will positively affect business, sport, culture and civil society.
content.extendedDescription:
Current rules have largely treated sponsorship as exposure and advertising space. A broader view is now proposed, recognising association, reputation, relationships and long-term value creation. What could this mean for business engagement in sport, culture and social development, and for organisations dependent on these investments?

The seminar explores what this shift could mean for future sponsorship. Drawing on research into association and reputation, lessons from Gyllene Hjulet and SES Effektguide 2.0, we discuss how sponsorship can create greater business and social value, and the effects we actually want to achieve.

Cecilia Perlind from SES Sponsrings & Eventsverige joins Björn Stenvad from Rättighetsbyrån. Panel discussion with Marlene Lindholm, ICA, Camilla Winberg, Head of Partnerships at Friends, and Björn Stenvad.
content.subject: Sustainability

content.title: E-methanol: a piece of the puzzle in shipping's transition?
content.description: Shipping is central to the energy transition and the path to net-zero emissions by 2050. Electrification, efficiency and new fuels are needed. What role can e-methanol play? What are its potential and prerequisites in shipping's transition?
content.extendedDescription:
Shipping faces a crucial transition to meet the EU's net-zero emissions target by 2050. Reducing fossil fuel dependence requires a combination of electrification, energy efficiency, changed logistics and new fossil-free fuels. One of the most promising alternatives is e-methanol, an electrofuel made from fossil-free electricity, water and biogenic carbon dioxide.

E-methanol could reduce shipping's climate impact while strengthening Europe's energy security and reducing dependence on imported fossil fuels. Building domestic hydrogen and e-fuel production could create new export opportunities for Sweden, strengthen industrial competitiveness and contribute to a more robust energy system.

The seminar discusses e-methanol's role in shipping's transition, the market conditions needed to scale up production and use, and barriers and policy instruments affecting development in Sweden and the EU.
content.subject: Energy

content.title: How do we encourage more companies to participate in public procurement?
content.description: The public sector purchases SEK 1 100 billion annually, but many companies still find public procurement complicated, time-consuming and hard to navigate. How do we build a modern public market in which the best solutions want to compete?
content.extendedDescription:
Many companies avoid the public sector despite having solutions that could improve quality, innovation and efficiency. Procurement processes are often seen as complex, administrative and built for another era, risking reduced competition and making the public sector less attractive as a market.
As central government reforms procurement, much attention is given to excluding the wrong actors. This is important but insufficient. We must also discuss attracting the right actors: businesses that can improve public services, quality and resource use.
How do we create a more modern, data-driven public market in which more companies actually want to participate? How can transparency, simpler processes and AI reduce administration, strengthen competition and improve the use of taxpayers' money?
content.subject: Economy
content.organizationType: Collaboration between different types of organisation
content.accessibility: Wheelchair-accessible toilet, wheelchair-accessible entrance and venue

content.title: A narrow view of obesity medicines: when healthcare says no to productivity
content.description: Swedish healthcare and the Swedish economy face a growing productivity problem. Politicians, authorities and employers call for greater healthcare productivity, but what happens when new treatments can actually contribute to it?
content.extendedDescription:
A new generation of obesity medicines has rapidly changed the possibilities for treating excess weight and associated diseases. Yet authorities reject public subsidies, citing costs to regional budgets, although obesity is estimated to cost society over SEK 50 billion annually through sickness absence, healthcare use and lost production.
The paradox is clear: almost one in ten Swedish households already uses injectable weight-loss medicines and pays privately. Society thus signals that treatment is perceived to create considerable value, while the public system declines to invest.
Does Sweden take too narrow a view of productivity and societal economics in healthcare? What happens when effective treatments are seen as costs rather than investments?
Economists, decision-makers, healthcare representatives and pharmaceutical experts discuss obesity, productivity and future healthcare priorities.
content.subject: Health and social care

content.title: From goodwill to real impact: partnerships making a difference for children facing challenges
content.description: How can cooperation between business, the public sector and civil society create real change for children with serious illnesses and diagnoses?
content.extendedDescription:
When many actors want to take social responsibility, we need to discuss how partnerships can move beyond symbolic paperwork to create concrete, lasting and measurable impact for children and participating organisations alike.

This panel explores how partnerships can become a force for real change. Together with partners of Min Stora Dag, we examine what is needed for collaboration to engage an entire organisation and create value for everyone involved.

What happens when social sustainability is not merely decided at management level, but felt in organisational culture, employees' involvement and encounters with children and families? The discussion explores combining charity, social responsibility and strategic partnerships in initiatives that make a real difference.

Journalist Petra Nordlund McGahan moderates the seminar, made possible by Roschier – House of Many Voices.
content.subject: Children/young people
speakerTitles: Head of External Communications and PR
Head of Partnerships and Corporate Fundraising
Head of Partnerships and Corporate Fundraising

content.title: Can local economies be the answer to the climate crisis, inequality and vulnerable communities?
content.description: The globalized economic system has long been promised as a path to prosperity and efficiency — but the result has been ever increasing climate emissions, fragile supply chains and growing gaps between people. Now, a movement is growing for building new economies on a human scale.
content.extendedDescription:
On June 23, two voices from the international localization movement will come to Almedalen to share concrete solutions and inspiring examples. They will talk about their work to shed light on one of the least discussed but most influential drivers behind this development: free trade agreements and the so-called ISDS (Investor-State Dispute Settlement) mechanisms, which give multinational companies the right to sue states when political decisions threaten their expected profits. This has in practice made it more difficult for countries to pursue active climate policies, protect local markets and safeguard the interests of their citizens.

Fatima Osman Abdalla, active in Real Economy, and Henry Coleman from Local Futures — the organization founded by Right Livelihood Award recipient Helena Norberg-Hodge — meet for a conversation about economies on a human scale, beyond global corporate capitalism.
content.subject: Economy
content.organizationType: Collaboration between different types of organisation
