content.title: Healthcare on equal terms: how do we get there?
content.description: Since 1982, the Health and Medical Services Act has required care on equal terms, yet major differences remain. The causes are complex and interconnected. Fundamentally, this is an ethical issue of fairness, responsibility and priorities.
content.extendedDescription:
The law requires care on equal terms, yet substantial differences remain. How society treats its most vulnerable people, those unable to navigate the system, living far from care or unable to understand the language, reveals the values guiding it beyond legislation and election promises.

These differences are well documented. Socioeconomically disadvantaged groups use less care relative to their needs. Geographical differences persist between rural areas and cities, while digitalisation improves access for some but excludes others.

These factors reinforce one another: location determines access, socioeconomic status affects the ability to navigate the system, and resource shortages hit some groups harder.

What is needed to make the law's objective a reality? There are no simple answers, but ethical choices must be made about governance, priorities and responsibility. We discuss what it actually takes to move closer to the goal.
content.subject: Health and social care
content.accessibility: Hearing loop, wheelchair-accessible entrance and venue
speakerTitles: Regional Executive Councillor and Chair of the Regional Executive Board

content.title: From bullied pupil to headteacher: what does life teach us about school?
content.description: Many pupils still experience bullying, racism and exclusion at school. How does this affect their lives, and what responsibility does school leadership have to break these patterns and create schools where every child has an equal chance to succeed?
content.extendedDescription:
Daria Ramzi has made an unusual journey, from a childhood marked by exclusion, racism and bullying to leading two schools and becoming a prominent voice on education, the fight against bullying and people's ability to change their lives.

In her book ‘Kan jag, så kan DU! Från förorten till makthavarlistan’, she speaks openly about experiences many recognise but that rarely feature in public debate. How does growing up feeling that you do not quite belong shape a person? What happens when adults respond to bullying and abuse with silence? What does it take to break patterns and create new possibilities?

We meet Daria Ramzi for a personal conversation about leadership, courage and identity. It moves between experiences of vulnerability and her role as a school leader today: fighting bullying at school and online, and hoping for schools where more children and young people can feel their future is possible.
content.subject: Justice/crime

content.title: Less administration, more trust: using resources efficiently to achieve a shared vision
content.description: How do we create real efficiency in knowledge-intensive organisations responsible for education, research and collaboration?
content.extendedDescription:
Many organisations want to reduce administration to free energy, time and resources for their core mission. Yet experience shows that savings alone rarely create real efficiency.
What is needed? Research and practice point to engaged leadership with a shared outlook, common working methods, clear roles and responsibilities, organisational trust and learning across boundaries. But the path also presents challenges: conflicting goals, us-and-them attitudes, limited shared understanding and turbulence at boundaries within organisations.
Using current examples, the seminar explores practical approaches combining data, dialogue, gradual change and respect for an organisation's own experience. The focus is on sustainable efficiency over time and reducing administration without losing quality or important support. Ultimately, it is about achieving common goals, realising a vision and contributing to social development.
content.subject: Economy
content.accessibility: Wheelchair-accessible toilet, wheelchair-accessible entrance and venue

content.title: An energy system that lasts: how do we secure Sweden's future energy supply?
content.description: Energy needs are growing, and secure, reliable, reasonably priced energy is crucial to society, businesses and people. Geopolitical uncertainty strains the system but may also accelerate transition. How do we jointly shape sustainable energy infrastructure for Sweden?
content.extendedDescription:
Energy supply is central to the global transition. Delivering it while meeting rapidly rising energy demand requires new forms of cooperation between business and society. We begin by examining barriers affecting energy availability, including technology, regulations, investment and the constantly changing international situation. How do we balance growing electrification with capacity shortages, challenging costs, a pressing maintenance backlog and stronger robustness requirements that drive major investment needs?

We also discuss how new technology and partnerships between society and businesses can secure a stable, safe and affordable energy supply. How can new perspectives support novel energy storage solutions and alternative raw materials that strengthen the system over time?
content.subject: Energy

content.title: When AI becomes a colleague: who does what, and who is responsible?
content.description: AI has moved from a passive tool to an actor making decisions and driving workflows. This places entirely new demands on responsibility, leadership and employees' interaction with technology. How do we prepare organisations for this change, and who is responsible?
content.extendedDescription:
This panel starts from the rapid development of agentic AI systems that no longer merely support people, but can independently perform and coordinate work. As AI becomes a colleague, the allocation of tasks, responsibilities and decision-making authority changes.

We discuss redesigning work when people and AI operate side by side. Which tasks should AI perform, and which require human judgement? Who is responsible when decisions emerge from human–machine interaction? We address leadership, skills and ethics, and whether organisations can afford to delay taking these choices seriously.
We also present insights from this year's AI Jobs Barometer on AI's effects on jobs, skills requirements and the allocation of responsibility in the labour market.
content.subject: Digitalisation
speakerTitles: Author and Adviser on Leadership, Communication and Transformation

content.title: Purchasing power for sustainable timber: from ambition to demand
content.description: How can buyers and markets drive demand for sustainable, economically viable timber from forests with greater biodiversity and long-term ecosystem value? How can demand, procurement and different working methods contribute to more sustainable forestry?
content.extendedDescription:
Forestry's effects on climate, biodiversity and raw material supply are increasingly debated as timber demand grows. Yet clear market signals are often lacking for forestry methods combining long-term economic viability with higher ecological value and resilient forest production. The seminar explores how demand from construction, the public sector and other buyers can shape tomorrow's timber market.

We discuss barriers and opportunities to increase sustainable timber use, possible incentives and different actors' contributions. The focus is on markets, value chains and practical examples rather than individual solutions or certifications.

The seminar is for actors in construction, forestry, the public sector, finance and policy wanting to understand how demand can encourage more sustainable forestry and increase sustainable timber availability.
content.subject: Sustainability
content.organizationType: Collaboration between different types of organisation
content.accessibility: Wheelchair-accessible toilet, wheelchair-accessible entrance and venue

content.title: Medicines for rare diseases: time for clearer state responsibility
content.description: Patients with rare diseases are among healthcare's most vulnerable. They are few in number and their needs are often urgent and life-changing. Yet access to treatment is frequently uncertain, slow and unequal, with decision-making taking unreasonably long for patients who cannot wait.
content.extendedDescription:
There is a national ambition to improve treatment opportunities for patients with rare diseases. But ensuring access to medicines requires greater state commitment in both governance and funding. The seminar presents a report by consultancy Macanda providing a factual basis for targeted state financial support for medicines for rare conditions. Decision-makers, authorities, healthcare, patients and research-based pharmaceutical companies discuss in depth how the system can evolve so patients with rare diseases receive the medicines they need promptly, wherever they live in Sweden.

Breakfast is served on site.
content.detail: Hamnplan, location 200, Medicon Village, Life Science Day
content.subject: Health and social care
speakerTitles: Second Vice-Chair of the Primary Care Committee
Alternate Member of the Committee on Health and Welfare

content.title: Figures guiding forestry: what must future forest owners know, and where does the information come from?
content.description: Forests must meet many needs: production, recreation, carbon storage, biodiversity and preparedness. What must Swedish forest owners know to develop their forests according to their own plans and society's expectations? How do we know their decision-making information is reliable? Who is responsible for what?
content.extendedDescription:
Swedish forests provide many things, including industrial raw materials, a foundation for local economies, carbon storage and climate regulation, culture, tradition and biodiversity. Their role has broadened in recent years, and developments affect more actors nationally and internationally. Policies in an increasing number of areas target forests directly or indirectly.

How should Swedish forest owners navigate an increasingly complex world? What expectations and requirements face today's and tomorrow's owners? Where should they obtain new knowledge and reliable decision support? What must forest owners know, and where is that knowledge available? Who is responsible for ensuring it exists: landowners, market actors or the state?
content.subject: Climate/environment
speakerTitles: Professor of Forest Genetics and Plant Physiology

content.title: Are companies slowing their own transition?
content.description: A survey of Swedish companies shows that half have reduced sustainability investment over the past three years, mainly because of political uncertainty and unstable rules. But is that explanation sufficient, or do companies also bear responsibility?
content.extendedDescription:
According to a survey of UN Global Compact Sverige's members, half of responding companies have reduced sustainable investment over the past three years. Most cite political uncertainty and unstable rules as the main reasons.

It is easy to wait for clearer political signals. Harder is asking what companies themselves could do differently. Is political uncertainty sometimes used to postpone decisions that should be made anyway?

Sweco and UNGC Sverige invite you to a discussion looking not only at politics but at companies themselves. Can long-term sustainability investment be made despite uncertainty, and who is responsible for ensuring the transition maintains momentum?

Survey introduction (5–10 minutes):
Peter Pierrou, Communications Director, UNGC Sverige

Followed by a panel discussion (30–35 minutes):
content.subject: Sustainability
speakerTitles: Senior Advisor Public Affairs and Sustainability

content.title: From shop floors to resale markets and into the criminal economy: enough is enough
content.description: Shop theft increasingly forms part of organised crime, with goods systematically stolen for resale. This feeds the criminal economy while employees and customers suffer, prices rise and profitability falls. What political priorities are needed to break the chain?
content.extendedDescription:
Retail employs hundreds of thousands and provides essential infrastructure throughout Sweden. Increasing organised theft is not merely a cost for companies: it funds the criminal economy and threatens staff and customer safety.
The seminar follows a clear chain:
The current situation: what are we seeing, and why is ‘petty crime’ an inadequate description?
Shop-floor reality: consequences for staff, working conditions and safety.
Resale markets: how stolen goods are sold and why these markets enable crime rather than merely accompany it.
The way forward: tools and partnerships needed to stop the theft chain.
content.subject: Justice/crime

content.title: Democracy in the future: how can the next generation pursue civic engagement?
content.description: We see declining civic engagement among today's young people. How can we reverse this, and how can young people and adults create better opportunities for youth to influence developments? How will the next generation find ways to create a better, more democratic society?
content.extendedDescription:
Democracy networking: a meeting place to discuss democracy's future.

We present Almedalsveckans Demokratiskola, which we believe is more important than ever. Young representatives of national youth organisations, experts and decision-makers discuss leadership that lasts across generations. Young visitors from the Western Balkans share what being young in their countries is like and their views on democracy. Join an inspiring, inclusive dialogue focused on meeting one another. We believe future solutions emerge from strong relationships and the courage to share perspectives.

This gathering is an ideal start to Almedalsveckan for anyone wanting to build bridges with tomorrow's community builders. Come to network, be challenged and find inspiration. Almedalsveckans Demokratiskola provides networking and light refreshments.
content.subject: Children/young people
content.organizationType: Collaboration between different types of organisation

content.title: Unequal health: who receives help and who is left out?
content.description: Sweden is more multicultural than ever, yet health inequalities persist. When people do not feel understood, many turn away from support, resulting in poorer health and reduced trust. Cultural awareness is systematically absent from professional practice and education. What must change?
content.extendedDescription:
A moderated panel followed by open audience dialogue. It begins with a brief introduction to how inadequate intercultural awareness in people-facing professions affects health, wellbeing and trust, with concrete examples of costs to individuals and society.

The panel addresses mental health, inclusion and preventive public health work, then examines what is actually needed: from education policy and political decisions to inclusive professional interactions and practical working methods. The conversation moves between lived and practical experience and structural solutions, perspectives rarely brought together. Participants leave with concrete insights and proposals that can influence organisations and system-level decisions.
content.subject: Gender equality
content.organizationType: Collaboration between different types of organisation
speakerTitles: Counsellor and Behavioural Scientist, specialist in cultural humility
Head of Public Health and Psychiatry Section
Lawyer and Expert on Racial Justice and International Law

content.title: Is solidarity dead?
content.description: Aid budgets are shrinking and global health programmes are closing. Sweden debates who is entitled to care. Is solidarity retreating, or already dead? What is at stake when the world chooses to look away?
content.extendedDescription:
Something is changing in how we speak about and take responsibility for one another. Nationalism is gaining ground. Aid is dismissed as naive.
Countries that once led global health efforts are withdrawing, with consequences measured in closed clinics, interrupted vaccination programmes and lives not saved. We see this now in eastern Congo: an ongoing Ebola outbreak where health workers previously funded by USAID are no longer present and coordination has collapsed.
It is not only the USA. The UK, Germany and Canada are cutting back. Sweden is reducing aid and has phased out development cooperation with several countries.
Sweden's domestic debate is also affected. It is therefore relevant to ask where solidarity's boundaries lie, including in healthcare. This ethics discussion brings together different perspectives. Join us in seeking answers.
What does shrinking solidarity cost? And what are we prepared to do about it?
content.subject: International affairs
content.accessibility: Hearing loop, wheelchair-accessible entrance and venue
speakerTitles: Professor of Applied Ethics, expert adviser

content.title: Is legislation needed to create cooperation for safer, more attractive neighbourhoods?
content.description: Many places struggle with insecurity and poor coordination between actors. Can statutory area-based cooperation strengthen development, or does it risk raising new questions about responsibility, influence and financing?
content.extendedDescription: Parliament has adopted a new law on fees for area-based cooperation to give municipalities and property owners better conditions to develop safe, attractive places. But where is the boundary between public responsibility and private delivery? How is legitimacy established for mandatory cooperation, and what makes models work over time? Drawing on the current legislative proposal, we discuss responsibilities, governance and public-private cooperation. Svefa's courtyard, Fastighetshubben, is a natural meeting place where public and private actors exchange ideas and knowledge, discuss property issues and build relationships formally and informally. This year, we cooperate with Fråga Lou to offer a packed programme addressing important questions at the boundary between public and private property market actors. Welcome! Find Svefa's full Almedalen programme at www.svefa.se
content.subject: Economy

content.title: How do we find the courage for conversations that matter?
content.description: Important things are often said too late, or not at all. We frequently choose silence over discomfort, postponing, softening or avoiding conversations that matter. This affects trust, decisions and working conditions, but the price is rarely visible until it has already been paid.
content.extendedDescription:
We usually know what needs saying but avoid it for fear of conflict, discomfort or resistance. Some conversations never happen, are postponed or softened, or move to the corridor after the meeting. This roundtable stays with that issue. Share your experience and help shape how we dare to have conversations that matter: practically, simply, combining digital and physical participation.

We explore real workplace situations where people chose not to say what they thought. Together, we examine what stopped them, what could have been done differently and how to create more courage in everyday conversations.

You are a co-creator, not an audience member. Through participants' experiences and reflections, we create a shared guide to conversations we would rather avoid.

No preparation is required. The session runs twice on the same day, at 11:00 and 11:30. Choose the time that suits you.

content.title: Municipal cooperation: effective solution or expensive compromise?
content.description: Going it alone is no longer a strength. Municipalities face growing requirements, cost pressures and skills challenges. Their own organisations cannot always fulfil the municipal mission alone. Cooperation is presented as the solution, but how do we prevent it becoming an expensive compromise?
content.extendedDescription:
War nearby, stronger civil preparedness requirements and rapid AI development put municipalities under intense pressure. Finances are strained and competition for specialist skills is fierce. Delivering alone is increasingly difficult and risks creating first- and second-tier municipalities.

Cooperation is increasingly presented as the answer, but how to design it to actually strengthen capacity is far from obvious. Contractual cooperation, a joint committee, a municipal federation or a jointly owned company: each affects governance, room for action, finances and risk.

This seminar is for those making strategic decisions in a new reality. How do we build structures that work now and withstand the next crisis and technological shift? When is cooperation a real strength, and when does it risk becoming precisely the compromise we cannot afford?
content.subject: Democracy
speakerTitles: Chair of the Municipal Executive Board
Head of Coordinated Digital Infrastructure Department

content.title: Winning in AI-driven retail, whatever the future holds
content.description: AI is redrawing retail's playing field. Customer journeys are automated, business models challenged and new actors enter ecosystems. How can businesses act as initiative, interaction and commerce increasingly shift from people to machines?
content.extendedDescription:
AI is reshaping everything from how customers discover, choose and buy products to how business models, value chains and decision-making are organised. Agentic commerce and autonomous AI agents are changing power relationships, competition and customer relationships. For some, this creates growth opportunities; for others, vulnerability and loss of control.

The seminar explores how AI shapes future retail and which strategic choices matter most. Drawing on Four Futures of AI in Retail, we examine possible scenarios depending on technological maturity, regulation and market dynamics, linking them to agentic commerce, platform dynamics and shifting ecosystem power balances.

With an expert panel, we discuss the capabilities needed to succeed in AI-driven retail, whichever future materialises.
content.subject: Digitalisation

content.title: Growth in transition: who sets Sweden's direction?
content.description: What roles should central government and regional actors play in improving investment and business conditions? How do we balance growth against other important values? How do we establish lasting rules that strengthen competitiveness and hold up during transition?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden faces major choices. The need for economic growth is clear, while demands for sustainability, faster processes and clearer priorities between societal interests are increasing.

County administrative boards play a central role, particularly through permitting responsibilities and representing the state regionally. Meanwhile, companies seek better conditions, greater predictability and shorter lead times. How do these perspectives meet, and where do tensions arise?

What roles should the state and regional actors play in improving investment and business conditions? How do we balance growth against other values? How do we create lasting rules that strengthen competitiveness and withstand transition?

Business and political perspectives meet to discuss what is needed to accelerate growth throughout the country.
content.subject: Business

content.title: Step into Matoteket 2035: the lunch where tomorrow's teaching has already begun
content.description: School meals reach almost every Swedish pupil daily and offer major opportunities to strengthen learning, health, sustainable development and community. What if they had a clearer educational role? How could that enrich the school day, and which decisions would enable it?
content.extendedDescription:
In this interactive future experience, participants enter ‘Matoteket’ in 2035, an interdisciplinary learning environment where lunch and teaching form a natural part of the school day.

During 45 minutes, visitors join a simulated lunch lesson using the meal as an educational tool. The experience draws on future scenarios and policy proposals developed within Policylabbet Offentlig Måltid, a Vinnova-funded collaboration between research, the public sector and civil society within the Mission Matmiljö and PUSH innovation platforms.

It concludes with a short panel on opportunities, barriers and policy changes needed for school meals to become an established learning environment in tomorrow's schools.

Register interest using the first link below. Confirmations are sent to participants on an ongoing basis.

content.title: People have different circumstances: why we need more routes to the same professional goal
content.description: More training places are not enough unless they lead to professional skills. Better course design, more accurate matching and greater understanding of individualised learning can create more routes to the same goal without lowering standards.
content.extendedDescription:
Try this. 926 characters.

Sweden needs more people with vocational skills. But more training places are not enough unless they lead all the way to employment. When people differ in experience, learning conditions and needs for pace, structure and support, education must become better targeted.

ETG College has built a unique, industry-supported adult vocational education model with two routes to the same professional goal: regular education and accelerated learning. Both feature clear structure, progression, workplace requirements and quality assurance. Capacio contributes cognitive mapping focusing on how people absorb information, handle pace, solve problems and function in different learning environments.

Together, ETG College and Capacio show how multiple pathways, better course design and greater understanding of different learning conditions can improve matching and completion and enable more people to gain employable skills without lowering standards.
content.subject: Education

content.title: The journey to energy class A: turning costs into value-creating investments
content.description: Energy efficiency and sustainability are no longer future issues. New regulations change the playing field for property owners and demand investment, cooperation and new working methods. How can the journey towards better energy ratings be profitable?
content.extendedDescription:
Energy efficiency, sustainability and a smaller climate footprint are not just buzzwords. Regulations are arriving rapidly, increasing demands on property owners and changing the playing field. Large investments, conflicting objectives and communication problems can undermine profitability. Technology, sustainability and economics play different roles in a profitable journey towards a better energy rating. New thinking, perspectives and actors are required.

A building is designed to last around 100 years. Conditions are now changing rapidly: the green transition, rising energy prices and global instability with various threats. Building anew is not an option. How do we develop existing properties? Securing operations and finances requires new approaches, funding and skills. Several actors have made considerable progress and have solutions. How do they think, what have they done, and what results and lessons have emerged? Solutions are created together.
content.subject: Energy
content.accessibility: Wheelchair-accessible toilet, wheelchair-accessible entrance and venue

content.title: One in three Swedes is uncertain about EU membership: why?
content.description:
A democratic society welcomes participation. How does EU centralisation affect public participation? What opportunities exist to exert influence within the EU?
Which EU-related issues feel most relevant ahead of the 2026 election? What would a forthcoming constitutional amendment mean, for example?
content.extendedDescription:
According to SCB's latest survey in June 2025, 11 per cent of the electorate is ‘against’ and 23 per cent ‘uncertain about’ Swedish EU membership. These figures represent around 3 million Swedes' opposition and doubts.
Turnout in the 2024 European election fell from 55% in 2019 to 53%, indicating declining public interest in the EU as an institution. What has happened to expectations? Is today's EU what we voted on in the 1994 referendum? How can we respond to developments?

The discussion starts from three approaches to Swedish EU membership:

• Accept and embrace the EU's current development.
• Seek to influence its direction through reform.
• Leave the EU and establish corresponding cooperation along the lines of Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein.

Folkrörelsen Nej till EU (FNEU) follows up, investigates and discusses EU membership's effects in a democratic spirit without party-political affiliation.
content.subject: EU

content.title: Creating a reef on Kungliga Djurgården: a model for urban nature-based solutions
content.description: As climate change and biodiversity loss increase, nature-based solutions can become a natural part of Sweden's future societal infrastructure.
content.extendedDescription: Can nature become part of future infrastructure? After six years of research and development, LAGU shows how nature-based solutions can create habitats for fish and other species, strengthen climate adaptation and contribute to more attractive, resilient cities. Using Isbladsrevet on Djurgården and other central Stockholm waters as examples, we present practical experience of turning reused surplus stone into living habitats. The seminar discusses how municipalities, landowners and urban developers can move from pilots to large-scale application and make nature-based water infrastructure an established part of future development. A panel of politicians and experts then discusses scaling up nature-based solutions and integrating them into future urban development.
content.subject: Innovation
content.organizationType: Collaboration between different types of organisation
speakerTitles: Structural Engineer and Head of Department
Policy Area Coordinator, EU Strategy for the Baltic Sea Region 2011–2020
Head of WWF's International Baltic Sea Programme

content.title: AI is a climate blind spot: how do we make emissions visible?
content.description: AI is advancing at remarkable speed, but also increasing energy consumption and emissions. Yet established methods for calculating its climate impact are lacking and transparency is low. How can companies take responsibility for emissions they cannot measure?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden has just launched its first AI strategy, aiming to rank among the world's top 10. AI use is growing explosively, along with energy consumption and carbon dioxide emissions. Companies seeking an accurate picture of their climate impact increasingly need to calculate AI emissions. The problem is a lack of methodology and accessible data, making calculation difficult.
2050 Consulting and Klimatkollen have developed an initial methodology and a simplified, free calculator for companies to estimate emissions from their AI use. The calculator launches at this seminar, which invites small and large AI companies, politicians, finance and business representatives to discuss AI's impact, transparency in climate data and measuring something changing rapidly.

content.title: How do we build a Sweden where more businesses can start, grow and succeed?
content.description: As uncertainty, low growth and fierce competition shape Sweden's economy, the business climate becomes increasingly important. Why do some municipalities and regions succeed more than others, and what roles do political leadership, local decisions and attitudes to entrepreneurship play?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden needs more businesses starting, growing and hiring. Ultimately, however, people take the risks.

What makes someone dare to start a business, and what determines success? How can municipalities and regions create the right conditions along the way?

Drawing on real entrepreneurial experience, business and politics meet to discuss what is needed.

As uncertainty, low growth and fierce international competition shape Sweden's economy, the business climate becomes increasingly important. Some municipalities and regions are more successful at creating environments where businesses grow. What roles do political leadership, local decisions and attitudes to entrepreneurship play?

During Almedalsveckan, the entrepreneurship podcast Räkna med framgång moves from the studio to the stage for a live discussion with an audience.

content.title: Neurodevelopmental conditions at school: risk, exclusion and the teacher who noticed
content.description: Pupils with neurodevelopmental conditions are more likely than others to be pushed out of school. Inadequate support and adjustments and poor wellbeing can have far-reaching consequences, placing many at risk of destructive behaviour. How can school promote health and offer a route out of risk for these young people?
content.extendedDescription:
The seminar starts from Attention's report ‘I was not easy to like’, offering insight into the daily lives of young people aged 10 to 16 with neurodevelopmental conditions who risk destructive behaviour and exclusion, their families and the professionals around them.

We explain why school can be both protective and risky, why digital environments can be both a lifeline and a danger, why leisure and belonging matter so much, and how relatives are often forced to shoulder an unreasonable burden.

Above all, Nicole, a young woman with personal experience of being at risk, shares examples of what truly makes a difference.

The seminar ends with a panel of politicians where Nicole holds the microphone and asks the questions she would have wanted answered when she was at risk.

content.title: How do we put tomorrow's electricity system in place, for real?
content.description: Tomorrow's electricity system promises faster connections, a more efficient grid and smooth integration of electric vehicles, energy storage and renewable generation. The technology exists and solutions are known. The question is how to scale them up and make systems work in practice.
content.extendedDescription:
Energy and power available at the right time, place and price are crucial to Sweden's electrification and competitiveness. As industrial, transport and new business electrification projects are implemented, electricity demand grows. New generation is being developed while the electricity system changes fundamentally.

Renewable generation, energy storage, electric vehicles and digital controls create opportunities to use the grid more efficiently. But weather-dependent generation and increased power flows also demand greater flexibility, balancing and system integration.

This panel discusses how technology, markets and regulations must evolve to make tomorrow's electricity system work in practice. Energy sector actors, expert authorities and politicians explore the potential and way forward.

content.title: National cooperation on rural and remote healthcare and health: will you join us?
content.description: Since 2025, a national assignment has promoted knowledge of the needs, conditions, challenges and opportunities for healthcare in rural and remote areas. Cooperation can benefit residents and providers faster. Would you like to join?
content.extendedDescription: The national assignment, funded by Socialdepartementet, includes establishing a national cooperation structure. This aims to broaden and strengthen the assignment by enabling knowledge generation, dissemination and experience-sharing with actors across Sweden. It primarily supports cooperation with regions, municipalities and universities, but also national organisations and specialist centres in relevant fields. The seminar examines needs and opportunities in two areas: preparedness, and care models and skills supply. Hear why Region Gotland and Västra Götalandsregionen see this structure as key to more accessible, equitable care in everyday life and crises alike.

content.title: What reforms does Sweden need to improve life for people with rare diseases?
content.description: To strengthen care for people with rare diseases, Sweden must cooperate on diagnostics, care pathways, coordination between national and regional levels, skills supply, research and follow-up of actual treatment outcomes.
content.extendedDescription:
Work to strengthen care for people with rare diseases has made important progress in recent years. Political engagement has grown, national inquiries have been commissioned and several authorities have been tasked with improving access to care, treatment and follow-up. Yet major challenges remain. The path from innovation to actual patient benefit is often long, unequal and difficult to navigate. For patients with rare diseases, this can mean delayed diagnosis, differing care between regions and long waits for innovative treatments.

What reforms are needed? What do the parties want to see in 2026? How can responsibility, incentives and cooperation evolve to improve access to new rare-disease treatments in Sweden?
content.subject: Health and social care
speakerTitles: Regional Executive Councillor and Chair of the Health and Medical Care Committee
Vice Chair of Riksförbundet Sällsynta diagnoser and Co-opted Member of NT-rådet

content.title: How much treatment can we afford? Finding a shared path to sustainable healthcare
content.description: Primary care should be the hub of Swedish healthcare. Why is this cost-effective as medicine costs and care needs for common conditions such as obesity, diabetes and mental ill-health increase? Other societal measures are also needed for sustainable healthcare. What investments should be made?
content.extendedDescription:
Primary care should be the hub of Swedish healthcare, an excellent and resource-efficient approach from a system-wide perspective. But challenges are numerous, and primary care must take growing responsibility for meeting population needs. Treatable common conditions continue to become more prevalent, including obesity, affecting 18% of the population, diabetes and mental ill-health. Costs to individuals, society and healthcare are rising. Effective help exists, but prioritisation is increasingly difficult.
SFAM, with expertise in general practice and unique insight into the patient population, therefore wants to discuss this with experienced public health and obesity experts from Karolinska Institutet. How do society, economics and health connect, and how can we reason wisely about the way forward?
content.subject: Health and social care
speakerTitles: General Practitioner, General Practice Expert and Board Member, SFAM Gotland
Specialist in General Practice, economist, global public health, board member

content.title: How are civilians affected by persistently high levels of conflict worldwide?
content.description: Violence worldwide has increased dramatically in recent years. Many civilians die directly from violence in conflict zones, but many more suffer indirect effects. What does research say about conflict's consequences for civilians? What is the situation in Ukraine?
content.extendedDescription:
The UCDP conflict data programme at Uppsala universitet presents the global situation and discusses the effects of high conflict levels on civilians. UCDP data shows that violence worldwide has indeed increased dramatically in recent years. Our media are filled with reports of wars and threats of war. In Sweden, Russia's war against Ukraine and the war between Israel and Hamas have received particular attention. Other extremely bloody conflicts have occurred or continue in countries including Ethiopia, Sudan and Mexico without receiving the same attention.

Many civilians die directly from violence in conflict zones, but many more suffer indirect effects. The best available estimates suggest that 10–20 times as many people die from wars' indirect effects. This panel examines research on conflict's consequences for civilians in affected areas and discusses the situation on the ground in Ukraine.
content.subject: International affairs
content.accessibility: Wheelchair-accessible toilet, wheelchair-accessible entrance and venue

content.title: Choral singing as a political force
content.description: For 150 years, choral singing has played a crucial role in democratic development: in popular movements, the Baltic independence struggle, apartheid's fall in South Africa and now opposition to ICE. How can choral singing play a significant role in Swedish politics and social development today? How can singing strengthen democracy?
content.extendedDescription:
In a seminar featuring singing, we discuss choral singing, which has historically contributed to democratic development but has also been used successfully by dark forces in totalitarian states.

Today, more than half a million Swedes sing in choirs. What makes so many devote time and energy to singing together? What can settings where people listen to one another and cooperate towards a common goal mean in our polarised times?

Choral singing is now mostly discussed in terms of individual health: choir members simply feel good. How can this wellbeing spread to wider settings, to society as a whole and across policy areas? And when choral singing is prescribed, what happens to the singing itself?
content.subject: Culture
speakerTitles: Music Researcher and former Director-General of Musikverket
Singer and Artistic Director, Eric Ericson Choral Centre
Professor Emeritus of Ethnology and Music Researcher
Author and Chair of Gotlands Körförbund (moderator)

content.title: How do we ensure sound financial management in municipalities and regions?
content.description: Sweden has around 40 000 elected local politicians, about 90 per cent serving alongside work or studies. Elected representatives bear ultimate responsibility for municipal and regional finances, but are they offered sufficient training?
content.extendedDescription:
Are you an elected representative? Join a Q&A and demonstration of Kommuninvest's training platform KI-akademin for municipalities and regions. Sweden has around 40 000 elected representatives, about 90 per cent serving alongside work or studies. The sector's debt is around SEK 959 billion, giving it substantial financial responsibility. Ultimate responsibility rests with elected representatives on executive boards, committees or council preparatory bodies. Kommuninvest promotes sound financial stewardship by strengthening the sector's financial management. It offers free training to improve decision-making and dialogue between elected representatives and officials.

Immediately after the seminar and demonstration, there will be networking, coffee and pastries. Welcome!
content.subject: Economy
content.accessibility: Wheelchair-accessible entrance and venue

content.title: Forensic psychiatry under pressure: how do we meet growing future needs?
content.description: Swedish forensic psychiatric care faces an acute capacity challenge, with a shortage of 200–300 beds already projected for 2030 in a new SKR report. How do we build a system that protects society, provides the right care and gives regions sustainable conditions for delivering forensic psychiatric services?
content.extendedDescription:
The seminar focuses on increasingly urgent systemic challenges in forensic psychiatry and the need to move from analysis to action. It brings perspectives together to create solutions and clarify requirements for coordinated responsibility, from effective prevention to successful transition out of care and lasting municipal support structures.

What preventive measures are needed to reverse the trend? Who has responsibility, authority and practical ability to act? Starting from forensic psychiatry's future, the seminar opens with a review of SKR's new report, followed by a panel of politicians, healthcare and social services representatives and service-user organisations explaining what must be done now and over the longer term.
content.subject: Health and social care

content.title: How is cultural life affected by cultural policy's new direction?
content.description: Under Culture Minister Parisa Liljestrand, the Tidö government has taken clear steps towards a new direction in national cultural policy. How does this affect people's opportunities to participate in cultural life and artists' opportunities to work?
content.extendedDescription: Under Culture Minister Parisa Liljestrand, the Tidö government has taken clear steps towards a new direction in national cultural policy. Several inquiries focus on mapping and increasing private cultural funding, while culture's share of the state budget is the lowest in a decade. Debate has become increasingly ideological and polarised following this change of direction. How does it affect citizens' access to cultural life and artists' opportunities to work? We invite politicians, opinion-formers and cultural sector representatives to discuss Swedish cultural policy's future. The conversation seeks to identify dominant ideological positions, highlight key political dividing lines and show how cultural policy may change over coming decades.
content.subject: Culture
content.accessibility: Wheelchair-accessible toilet, wheelchair-accessible entrance and venue

content.title: Who represents voters in nicotine policy?
content.description: Who represents voters as the EU tightens its grip on nicotine policy? Two new surveys show how Swedish voters and politicians view snus, nicotine pouches and EU tobacco policy, and where parties risk falling out of step with their own voters ahead of the election.
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden has the EU's lowest proportion of smokers, with snus and nicotine pouches as alternatives to cigarettes. Meanwhile, the EU is pursuing a more restrictive approach, including proposed tax increases. Several member states, such as France, are banning white snus. The issue concerns not only public health but also representation, connection with voters and Sweden's freedom to act.

Two new Demoskop surveys compare public and political attitudes to tobacco, nicotine pouches and EU tobacco policy. The findings reveal where party positions align with public opinion and where clear gaps exist between voters and representatives.

EU decisions directly affect Swedish users because Sweden's snus exemption covers tobacco snus, not nicotine pouches.

The election determines Sweden's EU position. Which parties have their voters' support? Which risk falling out of step? Could nicotine policy affect party choice in September? After the presentation, contributors from politics, public opinion and public health comment on the findings.
content.subject: EU

content.title: Where is Swedish aid heading? Development, choices and consequences
content.description: Swedish aid faces choices: should it primarily reduce poverty or also serve national interests? Amid war, climate crisis and growing needs, priorities affect who receives support and Sweden's role, credibility and responsibility worldwide.
content.extendedDescription:
How is future Swedish aid shaped amid growing global crises and changing political priorities? This conversation invites in-depth dialogue on Sweden's role in international aid, bringing different perspectives on development, direction and priorities together.

It starts from choices shaping aid policy today: balancing poverty reduction with national interests, long-term development with urgent humanitarian action, and broad coverage with concentration. How do these choices affect which countries and groups receive support, and with what results?

Through open, reflective discussion, we explore the consequences of current priorities globally and for Sweden's role, credibility and responsibility internationally. The dialogue allows different voices and aims to build a more nuanced, forward-looking understanding of aid's future.
content.subject: International affairs
content.accessibility: Wheelchair-accessible entrance and venue

content.title: Healthcare's biggest headache, and the remedy
content.description: Healthcare must become more accessible, closer, better and ideally cheaper as needs keep growing. What belongs on the election agenda: digital working conditions, extra funding to support new ways of working, or better obesity care? How should Swedish healthcare be governed, organised and funded?
content.extendedDescription:
Swedish healthcare is in transition. Care should move closer to patients, more treatment should take place at home and highly specialised care should concentrate in fewer units. New patient record systems change working conditions, often provoking strong professional reactions. Meanwhile, fundamental questions grow: what role should private actors play in future care? Where should the boundary between public and private funding lie?
Is nostalgia obstructing the shift to care closer to patients? Despite broad agreement on person-centred care and substantial investment, progress is barely noticeable. What innovations do primary and inpatient care need now to connect the patient's journey, and how can they happen? What political governance is needed? Which dreams must be abandoned to move forward?
A new era for obesity care: have medicines made old advice irrelevant? How must healthcare change its working methods to help patients?
content.subject: Health and social care
content.accessibility: Wheelchair-accessible toilet, wheelchair-accessible entrance and venue
speakerTitles: Physician and Professor of Internal Medicine

content.title: Education Without Pause: How AI and Digitalization Can Strengthen Learning in Times of Crisis
content.description: Pandemics, climate crises, conflicts, and migration have shown that education is one of society’s most vulnerable systems. The question is no longer if children’s learning will be disrupted, but how we ensure that education can continue even when society is under severe pressure.
content.extendedDescription:
AI and digital tools are creating new opportunities to build flexible, resilient educational solutions that improve access to learning, support teachers, and help students continue to grow and develop, even in times of uncertainty. At the same time, this development raises important questions about pedagogy, critical thinking, and how technology can be used to strengthen rather than replace human capability and independent thought.

This seminar explores how Sweden can build the resilient education systems of the future, drawing on both Swedish experiences and lessons from Ukraine, where digitalization and AI are being used to enable continued learning during the ongoing crisis and war. The discussion brings together representatives from business, civil society, and the public sector to examine how education can become a central part of Sweden’s long-term preparedness, innovation capacity, and competitiveness.
content.subject: Education
content.organizationType: Collaboration between different types of organisation
speakerTitles: Professor, Pro-Vice-Chancellor for Digitalisation and Knowledge Exchange

content.title: The transition that matters: how can we give new nurses a stronger start in their careers?
content.description: Healthcare faces a global shortage of nurses, making the transition from education to working life particularly important. Around 20% of newly qualified nurses in Sweden consider leaving the profession early, during their first four years, and stress is a major reason.
content.extendedDescription: Many new nurses feel highly engaged at first, but can sometimes lose that engagement because of high demands, a lack of support and stress. A supportive working environment with clear leadership, reasonable staffing levels, positive peer support and well-designed induction programmes helps new nurses grow into their professional roles. These organisational conditions increase job satisfaction and contribute to better health, lower stress, higher-quality care and less sickness absence. Research also shows that socialisation programmes and brief stress-prevention interventions effectively reduce ill health among prospective and newly employed nurses, highlighting the importance of integrating evidence-based support into the transition to clinical work. Organisations that succeed in creating such environments also often have lower sickness absence and more engaged staff and nurses.
content.subject: Health and social care
speakerTitles: Member of the Riksdag's Committee on Health and Welfare

content.title: The future of district heating – flexible, efficient and resilient
content.description: District heating currently accounts for 50% of heating in Sweden. At the same time, major reinvestments in production are approaching, and uncertainty about fuel availability and costs is increasing. What does the future hold for district heating? Can it be designed to become more flexible, resource-efficient and resilient?
content.extendedDescription:
District heating has been a cornerstone of heating our towns and communities since the 1960s. It has expanded continuously and now accounts for around half of heating.
Production facilities will require reinvestment, and we are seeing growing uncertainty about fuel availability and costs.
What can we expect from tomorrow's district heating systems: more residual heat, greater flexibility, different business models, new price structures? Could flexibility, for example, make our district heating systems more resilient?
Join a discussion about the district heating systems of the future.

Help shape the discussion at Omställningsarenan in Sweco's courtyard during Almedalsveckan! For the fourth consecutive year, forward-looking organisations and people in the built environment sector are gathering here. No registration is required – we offer a relaxed courtyard setting where you can hear insightful observations and join solution-oriented conversations.
content.subject: Energy
speakerTitles: Head of Business Area Heating and Cooling

content.title: Investigating war crimes in Ukraine – how do we document them and hold Russia accountable?
content.description: Since 2022, Ukrainian and international organisations have documented thousands of war crimes. Arrest warrants have been issued. Yet most perpetrators remain at large. What stands in the way from documentation to conviction – and what can Sweden do?
content.extendedDescription:
Thousands of war crimes have been documented in Ukraine since 2022 – hospital bombings, torture, executions and deportations. The ICC has so far issued arrest warrants for six Russian individuals – including Putin, Shoigu and Gerasimov – for war crimes and crimes against humanity in Ukraine. Yet the road from documentation to conviction is long and uncertain. What prevents effective accountability?
This discussion focuses on documentation in practice: how is evidence collected during active conflict, what is required for it to stand up in international courts, and what role do Ukrainian and Swedish civil society play in advancing accountability?

The discussion is organised as part of Samarbetsplattformen: Sverige & Ukraina (SPSU) – a project by KlinteVolontär that gives Ukrainian civil society its own voice in Swedish democratic debate and brings Swedish and Ukrainian organisations together to strengthen long-term cooperation between the countries.
content.subject: Human rights
content.organizationType: Collaboration between different types of organisation

content.title: Sustainable veterinary care – a possibility or a utopia?
content.description: Soaring costs in recent years risk making pet ownership a matter of social class. This spring, Konkurrensverket's inquiry was finally published and the consultation period for the government's review of veterinary preparedness closed. How can we achieve competitive, fair and accessible hospital care?
content.extendedDescription:
But what is the next step? When will the country's worried pet owners gain access to equitable and transparent veterinary care?

We are inviting representatives of every party in the Riksdag to a panel discussion to hear their positions on proposals for open price lists, national treatment guidelines and accessible care throughout the country.
Should the major chains continue to dictate the terms of Swedish veterinary care, or are politicians prepared to set limits to safeguard animal welfare and protect pet owners against soaring care costs?

The country's 2.5 million pet owners are waiting for clear answers. Each party will now give its view on how we can return to sound veterinary care with reasonable, transparent prices and treatments of consistently equitable and high quality, regardless of the clinic. Sustainable veterinary care requires everyone to take responsibility – care providers, insurers, pet owners and politicians.

All eight parties in the Riksdag have been invited. Participants will be announced shortly.
content.subject: Animals/nature

content.title: Avtal 27 – does the Industrial Agreement deliver when the world is in turmoil?
content.description: Ahead of Avtal 27, the Swedish model is in focus. In a time of economic uncertainty and geopolitical turmoil, the Industrial Agreement's ability to deliver competitiveness, long-term stability and good wage growth is being tested. How can we jointly ensure that Sweden's collective bargaining model holds firm in an unstable world?
content.extendedDescription:
For almost three decades, the Industrial Agreement has laid the foundations for stable wage formation and stronger competitiveness in Sweden. The wage benchmark set by industry has provided predictability for businesses and employees and contributed to a well-functioning labour market. Ahead of Avtal 27, the social partners are once again coming together to shape the conditions for the coming years.

Meanwhile, the Swedish economy is undergoing a transition. Geopolitical turmoil, technological development, climate investments and new global conditions affect industry and, consequently, the entire labour market. This calls for responsibility, a long-term approach and the ability to cooperate.

This seminar brings together representatives of trade unions, employers and businesses to discuss how the Industrial Agreement can continue to contribute to stability, competitiveness and good conditions in a changing world. The discussion focuses on the choices ahead of Avtal 27 and the continued development of Sweden's labour market model.
content.subject: Education

content.title: Swedish battery research – where are we heading?
content.description: Batteries are a key technology for portable electronics, but above all for our transport sector and future energy system. They are therefore absolutely essential to the industry, prosperity, resilience, security and climate ambitions of Sweden and the EU.
content.extendedDescription:
There are major challenges – geopolitical uncertainty and global competition – but also substantial initiatives to secure a European battery value chain. Sweden can play a relatively significant role within the EU and globally, given political prioritisation and even stronger cooperation between academia, industry and wider society.

The Swedish battery research and innovation roadmap being presented represents Sweden's ecosystem along the entire battery value chain. Its ultimate purpose is to strengthen Sweden's position and competitiveness in batteries through research, development and innovation.

We will present our overall vision as well as proposals for three concrete areas of action based on six key thematic areas of need. The roadmap has a national focus, but builds on the European “Battery 2030+ R&I Roadmap” to stimulate cooperation and collaboration with European partners as effectively as possible.
content.subject: Research

content.title: From vision to reality: how can electric aviation strengthen regional growth?
content.description: The electrification of aviation creates new opportunities for regional development. Smaller aircraft, lower operating costs and fossil-free operation open up new ways to organise air services and improve accessibility. How can the public and private sectors create the conditions for electric aviation?
content.extendedDescription:
In the project Elflyget som motor för regional tillväxt, tillgänglighet och hållbarhet, four Swedish regions have analysed how electric aviation can help develop the transport system of the future. The results show that the electrification of aviation is not just a technological innovation, but a broader systemic shift involving business models, infrastructure, energy systems and public governance.

A central question is how sustainable business models can be developed. Experience from public transport, regional mobility and public–private partnerships shows that new forms of collaboration can play a decisive role.

The seminar presents the project's findings and brings regions, airports, operators, developers and investors together to discuss the next steps. How can the public and private sectors jointly create the conditions for electric aviation to become part of future regional mobility?
content.subject: Infrastructure/transport

content.title: Security in transition: how do we tackle crime against people, businesses and organisations?
content.description: Crime against businesses and organisations is a growing problem. Four in ten businesses report having experienced crime in the past year, according to Brå. How can security work evolve as threats change? And how can cooperation between the police, public authorities and business be strengthened?
content.extendedDescription:
Security and insecurity are among our greatest societal challenges. In this session, decision-makers and the organisers of SäkerhetsArenan discuss what is needed in the work ahead to keep our society safe.

Traditional security measures involving alarms, locks and cameras now need to be complemented by new approaches. Cybersecurity, identity checks, risk assessments and structured security work are becoming increasingly important in protecting operations and societal functions.

How can security work evolve to address new threats? How can cooperation between the police, public authorities and business be strengthened? And how can different security measures be combined to provide more effective protection against crime?

SäkerhetsArenan is organised by SäkerhetsBranschen, Stöldskyddsföreningen, Brandskyddsföreningen, Stiftelsen Tryggare Sverige, Almega Säkerhetsföretagen, Företagsuniversitetet and Säkerhets- och försvarsföretagen (SOFF).
content.subject: Security/defence

content.title: AI as a competitive strength – how do we build a resilient Nordic industry?
content.description: Nordic industry is under pressure from rapid AI development, geopolitical turmoil and intense global competition. How can we secure digital and industrial sovereignty, access to reliable infrastructure, and rules that both strengthen resilience and enable growth?
content.extendedDescription:
As AI becomes a cornerstone of the economy, Nordic industry risks falling behind – or becoming newly dependent on global technology giants. Securing long-term competitiveness requires robust AI ecosystems with access to secure data infrastructure, skills and capital, as well as clear rules governing how the technology is developed and used.

In this seminar, representatives of industry, politics and the technology sector discuss how the Nordic countries can move from primarily using AI to also shaping the conditions for its development, implementation and governance. We explore digital and industrial sovereignty, secure and sustainable infrastructure, the risk of new dependencies, and how regulation can support innovation instead of holding it back.

The audience will hear concrete examples of how the public sector and business can work together to build a resilient, values-driven AI-based industry that is strong in global competition.
content.subject: Digitalisation
speakerTitles: VP & Head of Research and Foresight

content.title: Different future scenarios for AI – what decisions do we need to make today?
content.description: Artificial intelligence is rapidly changing society and organisations. But its development is uncertain and could take different directions. How do different future scenarios affect business and the public sector? What decisions need to be made today to shape the future?
content.extendedDescription:
The seminar starts from four possible scenarios for AI development up to 2030: gradual growth, fundamental transformation, increased regulation and restrictions, and the concentration of AI power among a small number of actors.

These scenarios are not forecasts, but tools for strategic thinking. They help us explore the potential consequences of different development paths and how best to prepare to influence the direction ahead.

Among the topics we discuss are:
- How organisations can balance innovation and risk.
- How working life changes through the interaction between people and AI.
- What scope there is to influence which future becomes reality.

The seminar takes the form of a moderated conversation with a panel discussion and concrete reflections on strategic choices for organisations and society.
content.subject: Digitalisation
speakerTitles: Nordic Head of Organization & Workforce Transformation

content.title: Business plus the public sector: does that add up to more young people in work?
content.description: We cannot afford to lose a generation on its way into working life while employers are crying out for skills. Helping more people get their first job takes more than individual projects and goodwill. Business and civil society are on board; can we go further if the public sector dares to join them?
content.extendedDescription:
While many young people are far from entering the labour market, employers report growing skills shortages. This paradox affects growth, inclusion and confidence in the future, and no single actor can resolve it alone.

Despite substantial investment, many organisations still work in parallel rather than together. But the future labour market requires new ways of acting jointly across business, the public sector, education and civil society. The question is no longer whether we need to cooperate, but how to make cooperation the norm and build both a culture and structures that make a real difference to young people's pathways into work.
During the seminar, we will hear voices from parts of society where change is already happening, on how to move from short-term initiatives to shared long-term responsibility. We highlight good examples and discuss how they can be scaled up and spread.
content.subject: Employment/labour market
speakerTitles: Director of Local Labour Market Services

content.title: Has Sweden's medicines system reached the end of the road?
content.description: What lies ahead for Sweden's medicines system and the changes the government has announced by appointing an inquiry? Will the state assume broader and stronger responsibility for medicines and vaccines?
content.extendedDescription:
The extensive geopolitical changes, increased competition and unpredictability of recent years have put pressure on individual countries' medicines systems. Swedish healthcare is of high quality, but the number of clinical trials is declining, and access primarily to new medicines, especially orphan drugs and oncology medicines, appears to be decreasing compared with other countries. Against this background, among other factors, the government's Minister for Health and Social Affairs has stated that the system needs to change and appointed an inquiry for this purpose. In this discussion, we will hear the government's arguments for changing the system and different stakeholders' views on the needs to be addressed.

KI Science Park Lunch Talks is a collaboration between KI Science Park (KI Innovation), Bayer and Waters. It is a recurring series of discussions held twice per semester at KI Campus Solna and, on this occasion, during Almedalsveckan.

content.title: Major investment in a national test centre for digital solutions aims to future-proof Swedish industry
content.description: An investment of 300 million is now being made in a national test centre for digital solutions – to give Swedish companies a significant technological lead and shorten the path from innovation to a finished solution. The test centre's digital backbone is based on the latest capabilities in 5G, 6G and AI.
content.extendedDescription: The government's digitalisation and AI strategies highlight the need to test and apply digital solutions and AI services – innovation environments where business and public sector organisations can collaborate. A major investment in a national test centre for digital solutions, Digital Arena Sweden, is now being launched. This discussion explores its background and purpose, and how the test centre will strengthen Sweden's capacity for innovation and competitiveness by giving companies a technological lead and shortening the path from innovation to a finished solution. The initiative is led by Telia, Ericsson, RISE teknikinfrastruktur and its subsidiary AstaZero, and Future by Lund, in cooperation with a range of other organisations in business, academia and the public sector. The project is funded through the innovation and collaboration programme Avancerad Digitalisering, with support from Vinnova.
content.subject: Business

content.title: Negative emissions today for a climate-neutral society
content.description: Negative emissions are necessary for society to become climate-neutral. So why is so little being done? Approved methods already exist that could be scaled up faster with support, while creating Swedish jobs. How slowly do we want progress to be?
content.extendedDescription:
The European Commission and the IPCC highlight biochar as a method for long-term carbon storage and negative emissions, and the Swedish inquiry into climate policy pathways (SOU 2020:4) identifies biochar as central to future negative emissions. Yet Sweden lacks a national strategy – unlike Denmark. What role do we want biochar to play in Sweden's climate transition, and how can we create governance that makes a difference?
The seminar brings together three perspectives: Meva Energy shows how biogenic residual streams can be used through gasification and the co-production of bioenergy and biochar. Waila examines biochar's properties and uses, including soil improvement. Lunds kommun describes how the public sector can drive development through procurement, strategic choices and local initiatives.
We conclude with an open discussion of the barriers, opportunities and requirements for scaling up the technology that already accounts for the largest amount of negative emissions in Sweden.
content.subject: Climate/environment

content.title: From research and education to defence capability in the Arctic
content.description: In a time of growing geopolitical uncertainty, the connection between research, defence procurement and defence capability has become increasingly clear. The ability to develop, test and introduce new solutions quickly without losing sight of sustainability is crucial, particularly in an Arctic context.
content.extendedDescription:
The seminar focuses on how cooperation between academia, industry and total defence can strengthen both Sweden's defence capability and its climate transition, with a particular focus on the Arctic. This is a region with unique conditions that place demands on robustness, logistics and cooperation.

The discussion addresses Arctic test and demonstration environments, skills provision within total defence, innovation, societal resilience and security of supply, among other topics. It explores how security and sustainability interests can go hand in hand when research meets civilian and military needs in strategically critical areas.

Through examples and perspectives from different stakeholders, Luleå tekniska universitet illustrates how closer interaction between academia, industry, society and defence can contribute to both national security and long-term innovation and competitiveness.
content.detail: Norra Scen – arena för grön omställning

content.title: The limit has been reached! Provide more resources so customs officers can stop more drugs and weapons at the border
content.description: Organised crime is growing, and large quantities of drugs, weapons and illegal goods are crossing Sweden's borders. More tools are being provided, but are there enough resources?
content.extendedDescription:
Tullverket is getting more tools, but have resources kept pace? Serious organised crime poses a grave threat to society. Criminal networks are well organised and well resourced. They operate across national borders, resulting in large flows of drugs, weapons and money.
Tullverket plays a central role in stopping these flows. In recent years, the agency has gained expanded powers and more tools to combat the criminal economy. At the same time, pressure on its operations is increasing, particularly in operational work at the border. In 2025, customs seized 10 tonnes of drugs.
Staffing needs to grow in line with the agency's remit, but reinforcements have not fully kept pace with it.
What might officers encounter in the field? What is being said in the corridors of power, and what does Tullverket's management say?
How do these developments affect the ability to recruit, retain and develop the right skills among the staff who, in practice, determine whether border controls work?
content.subject: Justice/crime

content.title: How we can change society through research-based knowledge
content.description: Crises are accelerating around the world. At the same time, our knowledge is developing rapidly. Finding solutions to society's challenges requires cooperation between different stakeholders, but how can we use research-based knowledge to influence policy and change society?
content.extendedDescription: Research has long warned of the crises we now see accelerating around the world. Meanwhile, knowledge about preventing and managing societal challenges is developing rapidly. The future is here, and so are the solutions. Creating a resilient and fair society requires cooperation between different stakeholders. But how can we move beyond vague visions and empty platitudes and ensure that political decisions are truly grounded in research, knowledge and proven experience? Join a discussion in which contributions from researchers, practitioners and politicians help us explore the question: how can we change society through research-based knowledge? The seminar is part of Vetenskap & Allmänhet's arena for research and democracy. The discussion is followed by our annual networking reception and quiz, where you can compete for the title “Smartest in Almedalen”. Food and non-alcoholic drinks are provided – welcome!
content.subject: Research

content.title: Smart pills – care or control?
content.description: Tomorrow's pills could confirm that you have taken your medicine – and notify healthcare providers. Support for self-care when every dose counts. But the same technology could become surveillance. Where is the boundary?
content.extendedDescription:
In January 2026, researchers published a study of a new digital pill. It is not the first of its kind, but it solves a problem with earlier versions: existing smart pills contain non-degradable components that must pass through the body intact, risking harm to the patient with long-term use. The new pill contains components that largely dissolve in the stomach. Only a small chip passes through.
Many patients with chronic illnesses do not take their medicines as prescribed. Smart pills reduce the risk of missed medication for people for whom every missed dose could have serious consequences. But the technology raises ethical questions: who should own data about whether we take our medicines? Is there a risk that smart pills will be disproportionately targeted at vulnerable groups? And if the technology becomes safe and available to everyone, should it become standard in all future medicines? Who decides where helping a patient ends and monitoring a citizen begins?
content.subject: Health and social care

content.title: Who draws the healthcare map – politicians or companies?
content.description: Consolidation in the private health and social care sector affects how care is organised, how investments are made and how patients encounter healthcare. But how well is the political debate keeping up as the market changes?
content.extendedDescription:
Join a breakfast seminar where Grant Thornton presents its new report on privatisation, consolidation and ownership models in health and social care. This is followed by a moderated discussion with specially invited guests from the sector about the consequences of these developments – and how political decisions, regulation of private providers and governance, deliberately or otherwise, help shape the market. What is a desirable balance between small providers whose owners are close to patients or service users and larger providers with greater resources, who may be more equal counterparts for a region or municipality?

Among other issues, we discuss the clearest current trends, how governance models and regulations affect ownership, operating models and market structure, and what these developments mean for equity, quality and long-term capacity.

The discussion is followed by networking.
