content.title: Are Swedish companies equipped for tomorrow's skills needs?
content.description: The skills transition is already here, but many organisations still lack the ability to address today's capacity shortages and tomorrow's skills needs simultaneously. This goes beyond individual companies: how do we build a labour market capable of rapid adaptation and long-term skills development?
content.extendedDescription:
Drawing on fresh data from Wise in cooperation with Novus, the seminar takes a fact-based look at how Swedish organisations work to meet their skills needs today and what is required, at both company and system level, to meet future needs.

Together with our panel, we discuss:
• How short-term decisions affect organisations' ability to meet long-term skills needs.
• What trade-offs are needed between developing existing skills and recruiting new ones.
• How organisations can create structures that enable learning, mobility and continuous adaptation.

By combining data, research and perspectives from business, the social partners and politics, we develop a shared picture of the current situation and discuss the structural choices needed for Sweden to navigate the transition with both speed and staying power.

The seminar is held in cooperation with Sveriges HR-Förening and Fabege.
content.subject: Employment/labour market

content.title: How can we build an inclusive and safe local community in time?
content.description: Society's resilience takes shape in local communities. When children and young people have good conditions in which to grow up, people feel included and local stakeholders cooperate, both safety and confidence in the future are strengthened. How can we build inclusive communities over the long term that prevent exclusion and crime?
content.extendedDescription:
Many societal challenges develop over time. They are often preceded by a lack of hope for the future, poor school results, mental ill health or unsafe childhood environments. Long-term preventive work is therefore crucial.

Schools, civil society, municipalities, the police and business come together in local communities. When these actors cooperate, risks can be identified early and more children and young people can receive support to find their place in society.

A broader perspective on security is also needed. Financial stability, social cohesion and trust in society's institutions are important foundations for strengthening both inclusion and societal resilience.

Länsförsäkringar has a local presence throughout the country and sees every day how finances, health and security are connected in people's everyday lives. As an organisation with a key role in society, we want to contribute to a discussion about how long-term preventive work can strengthen inclusion, confidence in the future and security throughout Sweden.

content.title: Climate adaptation and cooperation – what is needed?
content.description: Climate change increases the risk of floods and fires. New research shows that climate adaptation is progressing slowly. Risks are underestimated, and damage is repaired rather than prevented. How can we accelerate climate adaptation?
content.extendedDescription:
Climate-related property damage is increasing in scale and cost, while many simple measures are not being taken. New research from LF Forskningsstiftelse shows that property owners underestimate risks and usually restore properties after damage rather than make adaptations that reduce the risk of further damage.
Banks and insurers have considerable opportunities to influence developments. By designing financial incentives for damage prevention and through customer communications, insurers can help steer customer behaviour in the desired direction. Banks can integrate climate risks into credit assessments, loan terms and interest-rate discounts for measures that reduce risk. Such a system of incentives could reduce costs to society and strengthen financial stability.
At the same time, clearer national frameworks, better data and a division of responsibilities that facilitates cooperation between property owners, municipalities and financial institutions are needed.
content.subject: Climate/environment
speakerTitles: State Secretary to Minister for Climate and the Environment Romina Pourmokhtari

content.title: Civil preparedness needs the security sector – when will the systems catch up?
content.description: Private security providers already underpin parts of Sweden's safety and preparedness. Yet they face slow-moving regulations and unclear roles. How can we strengthen preparedness by using the capacity, training and expertise that already exist?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden is discussing civilian service obligations, robustness and endurance. Yet the capacity already available among private security providers is not being used to its full extent. They protect essential services, secure flows, prevent incidents and contribute an operational presence throughout the country. But the systems are still characterised by lengthy permit processes, training bottlenecks and an unclear division of roles between the state and business. BYA can play a key role here, with its sector-specific training expertise, knowledge of job requirements and experience of building capabilities for a more robust society.

The seminar discusses how Sweden can move from treating the security sector as a side issue to using it as the strategic resource it already is.

SäkerhetsArenan is organised by SäkerhetsBranschen, Stöldskyddsföreningen, Brandskyddsföreningen, Stiftelsen Tryggare Sverige, Almega Säkerhetsföretagen, Företagsuniversitetet and Säkerhets- och försvarsföretagen (SOFF).

content.title: Threats to Sweden: the wider world, the Middle East and organised crime
content.description: Turbulent, uncertain, unstable, unpredictable, difficult to assess – these are some of the adjectives used to describe today's international security situation. How does this affect Sweden, and how extensive is organised crime in Sweden?
content.extendedDescription:
A discussion between three experienced experts whose perspectives draw on extensive experience in Sweden's intelligence and security services.

1.) The broad geopolitical picture. The actions of the world's leading state actors are examined and possible future outcomes analysed.
2.) The situation in the Middle East. An analysis of the current situation informed by in-depth knowledge of triggering factors, history and specific threats to Europe and Sweden.
3.) Organised crime. An account of its emergence in Sweden, the criminal economy and the consequences of the uncertain international situation.

SäkerhetsArenan is organised by SäkerhetsBranschen, Stöldskyddsföreningen, Brandskyddsföreningen, Stiftelsen Tryggare Sverige, Almega Säkerhetsföretagen, Företagsuniversitetet and Säkerhets- och försvarsföretagen (SOFF). Together, we create a shared meeting place for conversations that strengthen Sweden.

content.title: Sweden's image and the shift in security policy: perspectives on NATO membership
content.description: How does the image of Sweden, at home and abroad, change when long-standing military non-alignment is replaced by NATO membership? How is Swedish security policy affected by an increasingly uncertain international order and a deteriorating security situation?
content.extendedDescription:
Some of the chapter authors of “Är Sverige säkert nu? Perspektiv på Nato och svensk säkerhetspolitik” (edited by Linus Hagström) discuss Sweden's shift in security policy.
For two centuries, Sweden was associated with neutrality and military non-alignment – a policy that contributed significantly to the country's self-image and international identity. How has this reorientation been justified and legitimised in public? How have emotions, narratives and gender perspectives been used to understand and justify the shift in security policy? What does it mean that the feminist foreign policy was withdrawn in connection with Sweden's accession to NATO, and how can this be understood in relation to the new security policy direction? Finally, how should we view Sweden's security just over two years after joining NATO, at a time when the United States' long-term commitment to European security can increasingly be questioned, and amid a new international disorder?

content.title: New perspectives on local democracy and local energy production
content.description: Renewable electricity is crucial for jobs and welfare, but is often held back by local opposition. How are our views of energy projects formed – and how can better knowledge and more perspectives contribute to better-informed decisions?
content.extendedDescription:
Industry's transition requires more renewable electricity. Without it, investment, jobs and ultimately welfare are at risk. At the same time, energy projects face local opposition often characterised by limited participation and social misconceptions.
The ways people influence one another – through norms, conversations and local opinion – play a major role in how energy projects are perceived. Yet today's consultation processes primarily engage nearby residents, while other perspectives, particularly those of young people, are rarely heard.
Through Almedalsveckans Demokratiskola, engaged young people gain knowledge, tools and the ability to understand and influence societal issues in a democratic context. In this seminar, they contribute their perspectives and highlight both shortcomings in current processes and opportunities for more inclusive approaches.
The seminar explores how we can strengthen knowledge, broaden dialogue and make more legitimate decisions about the energy systems of the future.

content.title: Swedish nicotine innovation in the world – how do we secure competitiveness when Europe applies the brakes?
content.description: Swedish nicotine innovation contributes to smoke-free societies and a growing industry. Last year, Sweden exported nicotine pouches worth 6 billion, an increase of nearly 300% since 2022. How can we secure continued innovation, investment and jobs in Sweden's nicotine industry?
content.extendedDescription:
Swedish nicotine innovation employs over a thousand people in Sweden, with a strong presence in areas including Västra Götaland, and generates billions in Swedish export revenues. This development now faces substantial tax and regulatory proposals from the EU, while France is banning white snus entirely and placing the product in the same category as narcotics. In the longer term, this could mean reduced investment and fewer jobs in Sweden, and weaker conditions for a growing European niche in which Swedish companies currently play a leading role.

In this seminar, representatives of the industry, business and politics will discuss how Sweden can remain a leader in nicotine innovation as the EU moves towards tougher taxation and regulation. What is needed to keep nicotine industry jobs, innovation and investment in Sweden while contributing to Europe's global competitiveness?
content.subject: Innovation

content.title: The year 2040: how Sweden became a growth miracle
content.description: Sweden faces major societal changes between now and 2040. Meeting these challenges requires a long-term approach, new ideas and a shared vision of how to build Sweden's prosperity. Pension capital is a central part of the economy's backbone; how do we ensure it remains so?
content.extendedDescription:
The seminar brings together representatives of politics, academia and business for a forward-looking discussion about the forces that will shape Sweden's prosperity up to 2040. The discussion starts with demographic developments, as a growing proportion of older people and a shrinking workforce put pressure on the welfare model and call for new strategies to meet labour and skills needs. At the same time, AI and other technological leaps are transforming both the labour market and productivity, raising questions about how best to use technology to strengthen growth and security.

A central theme is the importance of a long-term approach to economic policy and the role pension capital plays as a stabilising, strategic asset for the country. How can this capital continue to contribute to investment, development and robustness in a time of rapid change? What visions and choices are needed today for Sweden to stand strong in 2040?
content.subject: Economy

content.title: How can Sweden's climate transition be fair and supported by the public?
content.description: How can the climate transition be both fast and fair – and win broad public support? Can reform proposals from researchers and civil society achieve the climate targets in a socially sustainable way, grounded in science?
content.extendedDescription:
How can Sweden transition to meet its climate targets with broad public support? Join a seminar about the report “Förslag för en folklig klimatpolitik”, where researchers and civil society present 24 reforms for a rapid, fair climate transition with public backing.

The seminar discusses how climate policy can reduce emissions while strengthening jobs, welfare and security. The discussion starts from the need to combine the climate transition with social justice. What is needed for more people to feel that the transition is possible, fair and worth taking part in?

The reform proposals were developed through interdisciplinary cooperation in the Fairtrans research programme. Their presentation is followed by panel discussions with organisations involved in Fairtrans and politicians.

The seminar is part of Uppsala universitet's climate days.

content.title: Hijabs on children – freedom or oppression?
content.description: Honour-related oppression is a widespread societal problem in which controlling women's and girls' sexuality is central. The hijab is a tool for placing responsibility for men's sexual behaviour on girls and women – and putting hijabs on children sexualises young girls' bodies.
content.extendedDescription:
Honour-related oppression is a widespread societal problem practised within religious and cultural value systems in which controlling women's and girls' sexuality is central. The hijab is a tool that sexualises young girls' bodies, deprives women of the right to decide over their own bodies, and symbolises women's and girls' responsibility for men's sexual behaviour.

This panel discussion addresses the role of the hijab in a culture of honour and its contested role in Swedish society, focusing on girls under the age of majority. We discuss the background to the hijab's role in an honour context, freedom of expression, freedom of religion and whether the hijab is compatible with schools' gender equality mission.

Devin Rexvid, a researcher on honour-related violence and oppression, opens with an introduction to the hijab's role and significance within honour culture, voluntary choice, and the consequences for girls and women who do not wear a hijab.

Can we speak of voluntary choice when discussing the hijab?

speakerTitles: Researcher in Honour-based Violence and Oppression

content.title: Mental Health as a Bridge to Integration
content.description: Mental health and integration are deeply interconnected. For displaced Ukrainians, uncertainty, war-related trauma and barriers to support can hinder participation and belonging. How can society share responsibility for creating conditions for wellbeing, inclusion and long-term integration?
content.extendedDescription:
Mental health is often treated as an individual issue, while integration is discussed as a policy challenge. But what happens when the two are inseparable? For many displaced Ukrainians in Sweden, war-related trauma, uncertainty, family separation and barriers to support affect both wellbeing and the ability to participate fully in society.
This panel explores whether mental health should be understood as a shared societal responsibility and how stronger collaboration between public institutions, civil society and local communities can contribute to both wellbeing and integration.

Discussion participants:
• Viktoriia Thander, Help Ukraine Gothenburg
• Måns Fellesson, Delmi
• Sofia Breitholtz, Reach for Change
• Alla Tangstad, displaced Ukrainian living in Sweden

Moderator:
• Anna Hammarstedt, Delmi

The conversation will highlight research findings, lived experiences and practical solutions for strengthening mental health, inclusion and and social cohesion.

content.title: From possibility to reality – how can new ways of working meet growing care needs?
content.description: Swedish healthcare is at a crossroads. An ageing population, increasing use of medicines and a shortage of healthcare staff are putting pressure on a system already working flat out. Meanwhile, technologies and solutions exist that enable earlier, more preventive and safer care at home.
content.extendedDescription:
Smart sensors and automated medication management can ease the workload of health and social care staff while helping more people manage their own care. The next generation of home-based welfare technology is already on the doorstep. It will also improve care quality through better remote care, increased prevention and continuous monitoring of health status.
But new innovations are being introduced slowly. Regulations and reimbursement models are poorly adapted to new technology, and health and social care services struggle to adopt new ways of working. The central question that must be answered is: how do we turn the potential of new technology in health and social care into reality?
Join an honest, unfiltered discussion of welfare technology as we bring the conversation often held behind the scenes in Almedalen onto a stage in Folkhälsodalen.

content.title: Knowledge or money – what determines Swedish obesity care?
content.description: On 1 June, Sweden received new national clinical guidance on obesity – but is the treatment that healthcare professionals know works reaching patients? Effective medicines are not subsidised and are not recommended, and healthcare providers are urged to wait until the disease becomes severe. Is care guided by knowledge – or by money?
content.extendedDescription:
This is an open roundtable discussion – everyone present is welcome to listen and follow the conversation around the table. We discuss what really determines Swedish obesity care in practice: knowledge and medical need, or subsidies.
The new clinical guidance raises several questions. Why, in practice, is an older medicine recommended over more effective ones? And why should care providers wait until a patient has severe obesity with complications, instead of treating the condition earlier and preventing them?
Meanwhile, Socialstyrelsen has evaluated obesity care and identified major shortcomings: few regions have an action plan, follow-up is weak, and the newer, more effective medicines are not covered by the high-cost protection scheme. Patients currently pay virtually the entire cost of medication, while regional costs have barely increased – resulting in increasingly unequal care.
What is needed to ensure that the treatment healthcare professionals know works best actually reaches patients – and who must act?

content.title: How can Sweden lead the way in the sustainable metal casting of the future?
content.description: Swedish industry faces a decisive question: how can we secure competitiveness, skills and sustainable production when the rest of the world is rapidly investing in next-generation manufacturing? Metal casting is a strategic but often invisible part of electrification, defence capability and the green transition.
content.extendedDescription:
Metal casting is a key technology for Swedish industry, from vehicles and energy to defence, electrification and advanced production. Meanwhile, international competition is intensifying. Countries that build strong testing and research environments and close cooperation with industry gain an advantage in innovation, skills provision and investment.
The seminar starts from the question of how Sweden can bring together industry, academia, research institutes and public organisations to shorten the path from research to industrial application. What is needed to make sustainable metal casting a Swedish strength? What investments, partnerships and political choices are required? And how can a regional industrial environment contribute to national competitiveness?
The discussion is not just about a new research centre, but about how Sweden can build the capability to stay at the forefront of next-generation sustainable manufacturing.

content.title: You will miss our nets when a crisis comes – household fishing and food preparedness
content.description: Everyone talks about the need for robust food preparedness, yet an inquiry is proposing a total ban on net fishing for household consumption. If we find ourselves in a serious crisis with food supplies under threat, every person with access to a boat and fishing gear will be vital.
content.extendedDescription:
Gotlands Husbehovsfiskeförening and Kullens Fiskareförening invite you to a discussion on the role of small-scale fishing in robust food preparedness in Sweden.
Coastal fishers know their waters; they know when and where to set their nets to catch fish. In a crisis, this is invaluable knowledge that society should make use of. Instead, fishing for household consumption faces a total ban, and coastal commercial fishing is struggling against industrial trawlers' high quotas and depleted fish stocks. Fish caught in our seas must become food for people, rather than being ground into fish and animal feed as they are today.
Come and listen to a discussion about the importance of small-scale fishing for our food supply, hear what politicians and public authorities think, ask questions and take the opportunity to learn more.
Welcome to our meeting point: fishing for household consumption – an important bearer of cultural traditions and essential to food supplies in a crisis.

content.title: You are thirsty, I am thirsty – water, a pressing issue for resilient spatial planning
content.description: Water is a vital resource for our society, one that we in Sweden are used to having unlimited access to. But have we failed to protect our most important resource and our most important foodstuff? New approaches and solutions for water, preparedness and resilience in the built environment are available today.
content.extendedDescription:
Water supplies are essential to our everyday lives – for drinking and hygiene, and as a resource for industry. Historically, Sweden has had good access to water. But conditions have changed. We are discovering pollutants that need to be removed, and availability is affected by a changing climate. At the same time, our existing supply systems need to be secured and developed. How do we piece together the water puzzle for the future? What do we do together, and what can each of us do to ensure secure water supplies?

Help shape the discussion at Omställningsarenan in Sweco's courtyard during Almedalsveckan! For the fourth consecutive year, forward-looking organisations and people in the built environment sector are gathering here. No registration is required – we offer a relaxed courtyard setting where you can hear insightful observations and join solution-oriented conversations. Together, we create sustainable, resilient communities. Welcome!

content.title: Obliged to say yes, required to say no – the right to a bank account versus anti-money laundering
content.description: More people risk being excluded from the financial system because of the conflict between the obligation to enter into contracts and anti-money laundering legislation. This is not only a problem for individuals – it is a societal problem.
content.extendedDescription:
Earlier this year, the government tasked Finansinspektionen with making it easier for banks to meet their obligations to provide basic banking services. The assignment highlights an issue that has become increasingly pressing as requirements for banks' anti-money laundering work have tightened.

Banks in Sweden often find themselves at the intersection of two regulatory frameworks that can pull in different directions: the Payment Services Act's requirements for access to basic banking services and the Anti-Money Laundering Act's requirements for customer due diligence and risk management. How should these interests be balanced? Where is the boundary between necessary risk management and financial exclusion? And what guidance do banks need to make legally sound and proportionate decisions?

As more people risk being excluded from the financial system, the issue becomes bigger than a matter of legal interpretation. It concerns trust, inclusion and the ability to participate fully in society.

content.title: What is required of Ukrainian trade unions on the path towards the EU?
content.description: Ukraine's path towards the EU requires far-reaching reforms – including within trade unions. The war has eroded workers' rights, fragmented the labour market and put EU harmonisation on hold. What must Ukrainian trade unions do to meet EU requirements – and what do they need to succeed?
content.extendedDescription:
Ukraine's EU candidacy requires the harmonisation of labour law, collective bargaining rights and social dialogue structures. But the war has changed the conditions: martial law has temporarily suspended labour protections, millions of workers have fled or lost their jobs, and parts of industry have been destroyed. Ukrainian trade unions are caught in this contradiction – they must be strengthened and reformed to align with the EU while operating in a country under active invasion. How can they navigate the EU's social rules when reality changes every day?
This discussion explores what moving towards the EU specifically requires of Ukrainian trade unions, what structural barriers exist, and what Sweden and European actors can contribute to support the process.

The discussion is part of Samarbetsplattformen: Sverige & Ukraina (SPSU) – a project by KlinteVolontär that gives Ukrainian civil society its own voice in Swedish democratic debate.

content.title: Knowledge without borders – with geopolitical border guards
content.description: Research cooperation with so-called difficult countries places academia in a field of tension where ethics, security, research quality and global knowledge development collide. What opportunities and risks does research cooperation involve, and how can academia act when research and geopolitics become intertwined?
content.extendedDescription:
Research cooperation with so-called difficult countries places academia in a complex field of tension where ethics, security, research quality and global knowledge development collide. International partnerships can provide access to new technology, data, infrastructure and expertise – but also entail risks such as political influence, misuse of technology and unwanted dependencies.
Yet refraining from cooperation is not without problems either. It can protect academic integrity, but risks isolating research communities, weakening dialogue and making shared solutions to global challenges harder to achieve.
In this seminar, we explore both opportunities and pitfalls and discuss how academia can navigate a world in which research and geopolitics are becoming increasingly intertwined.
• How should academia act when research and geopolitics become interwoven?
• Who is best placed to make the difficult judgements about international research cooperation?

content.title: How can research better guide decision-making during a pandemic?
content.description: A central societal question is how research can better guide decision-making during a pandemic. Experience from covid-19 showed that a gap often emerges between scientific knowledge and political decisions.
content.extendedDescription: Research can provide crucial information about the spread of infection, risks and effective measures. Knowledge must quickly be translated into clear, feasible decisions. During a pandemic, the state of knowledge changes continuously, making it difficult for decision-makers to know which measures are most effective. The challenge lies partly in time pressure and partly in uncertainty about the evidence. Political, economic and social considerations can also influence decisions, sometimes preventing research findings from having their full impact. Improving this requires stronger cooperation between researchers and decision-makers. It involves rapid knowledge transfer and structures that integrate scientific advice directly into the decision-making processes needed to manage a pandemic. Overall, the issue is about creating a system in which research not only produces knowledge but is also used effectively. This enables society to make better-informed decisions, reduce uncertainty and manage pandemics more effectively.

content.title: When children's influence declines and demands for tougher measures grow – how is young people's confidence in the future affected?
content.description: Young people describe how inequality and limited influence create mistrust. When decisions do not reflect their reality, trust in politics weakens. How can young people's confidence in the future be strengthened when children's rights receive less attention?
content.extendedDescription:
Young people describe a growing gap between their reality and political decisions. Through workshops, surveys and analysis, a youth reference group has identified areas where trust, respect and participation are lacking. The findings show a need for better feedback, clearer accountability, faster processes on issues affecting young people, and a more respectful climate of discussion.

The seminar is led by the young people themselves, who formulate the questions and set the framework based on their analyses. Politicians participate to listen, respond and reflect on how children's rights can have greater practical impact. The discussion covers participation, unequal living conditions, the role of schools, online safety and how political language affects young people's confidence in the future. The aim is to move from symbolic initiatives to real accountability that strengthens young people's trust in democracy.

content.title: The human experience of war in Ukraine
content.description: How are identity, values and resilience affected when war becomes part of everyday life? Ukraine's experience raises broader questions about the human consequences of conflict, societal resilience and how individuals and communities adapt to prolonged crisis and uncertainty.
content.extendedDescription:
PALYANYTSIA is a documentary film that explores how war transforms people, identities and values. Through the journey of two Ukrainian artists travelling across a country at war, the film offers a powerful and deeply personal perspective on resilience, humanity and the search for meaning in times of crisis.

As Russia’s war against Ukraine continues to shape millions of lives, the film raises questions that extend far beyond the battlefield: How do people preserve their humanity when confronted with destruction and uncertainty? How are identity, values and personal responsibility affected when war becomes part of everyday life? And what enables individuals and communities to remain resilient in prolonged adversity?

Through the language of art, PALYANYTSIA invites reflection on the human consequences of war and the choices each of us can make to contribute to a better future.

The screening will be introduced by Svitlana Zalishchuk, Ambassador of Ukraine to the Kingdom of Sweden.

content.title: How universities can handle pressure from competition, demography and geopolitics
content.description: How can universities deal with the pressure regarding competitiveness, demography and geopolitics?
content.extendedDescription:
In spite of considerable differences, Japan and Sweden offer interesting university sector comparisons and challenges, such as:

1. Although Sweden’s highly educated population is often considered a key to the ability to punch above its weight Japan has a higher share of young people in tertiary education.
2. While Sweden has a smaller population than Japan, the Swedish university sector as a whole is relatively strong.
3. The Japanese population is shrinking rapidly. In Sweden the number of deaths will likely outnumber births in 2026; very soon the number of potential students will decrease substantially.
 
Questions to discuss concern how the two countries’ university models can deal with the challenges:

1. Should the private sector take greater responsibility in funding higher education?
2. How can universities adapt to shrinking populations?
3. Should politicians take greater responsibility in defining research priorities for the universities?

content.title: Online sexual violence against children – how can society meet the challenge?
content.description: Children's exposure to online sexual offences is increasing and changing rapidly. At the same time, many cases go unreported. What does children's vulnerability look like today, and how can society strengthen prevention and protection for children who are affected?
content.extendedDescription:
Online sexual violence against children is a global societal problem and one of the greatest challenges of our time for children's rights. Repeated surveys by Ecpat show that in Sweden, children and young people are more likely to have experienced multiple online sexual offences than not to have done so.

Children's and young people's experiences and voices are essential to understanding their vulnerability and designing relevant, credible and effective protection and support. Through its support services, removal of abuse material and knowledge gathering, Ecpat provides unique insight into children's circumstances. Barnombudsmannen has an ongoing assignment concerning contact channels for children who have experienced, among other things, different forms of sexual abuse – how do children seek support and protection today, and how can this be improved?

How can Sweden better meet the requirements of the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child and the Council of Europe's Lanzarote Convention regarding the prevention of child sexual abuse and the provision of protection and support for children?

content.title: AI for Impact: Scaling Innovation from Sweden to the World
content.description: How AI and frontier technology leadership is driving real-world impact for children and communities globally, and what that means for partners, investors, and innovators who want to be part of it.
content.extendedDescription:
Stockholm and Sweden are a quiet powerhouse for AI and frontier tech with global reach. In this session, UNICEF's Office of Innovation shares concrete initiatives already underway, from AI-driven humanitarian tools to FemTech programs.  What does it actually take to move from local pilot to global implementation? We'll talk through the real work and where AI and emerging technologies can unlock measurable impact for the communities that need it most.


AI for global impact – from Sweden to the world

UNICEF's global Office of Innovation is based in Stockholm thanks to Sweden's support and a forward-looking technology landscape.
Join UNICEF Innovation's global leadership as they explain and answer questions about how Sweden's technology sector can contribute to a better world for all children through innovation; how investors and innovators can grow through markets that are often overlooked; how commercial value can be combined with social value; how UNICEF's investment fund works; and Swedish initiatives such as UNICEF Femtech Ventures.

content.title: A climate-friendly, secure and affordable energy supply in Sweden
content.description: Energy supplies must be secure, have a low climate impact and be affordable. This means the electricity grid must be well developed, energy storage must be available to cope with power outages, and combustion must largely be replaced by electric motors and heat pumps. What might such a scenario look like?
content.extendedDescription:
Electricity use in Sweden has remained more or less unchanged for several decades, despite GDP more than doubling and the population increasing by over 25%. Meanwhile, electricity production has risen steadily over the past 15 years. So far, demand for increased electricity use has been met through savings and efficiency improvements. The green transition is expected to require a great deal of new electricity, but electricity demand cannot keep rising indefinitely.
What are the advantages and disadvantages of solar power, wind power, bioenergy and nuclear power? What psychological and physical limits exist for new electricity generation, and what margins need to be left for the future?
What would the situation look like if, instead of focusing all our thinking on new production, we invested heavily in energy efficiency and replaced as much combustion as possible with electric motors and heat pumps? According to calculations I will present, this would considerably reduce energy needs and greatly cut greenhouse gas emissions.

content.title: Can circular solutions address water shortages?
content.description: The availability of freshwater is declining worldwide as global warming progresses. This is also happening on Öland, Gotland and in south-eastern Sweden. At the same time, rainfall is becoming more frequent, with heavy rain falling over shorter periods – rain that causes damage and usually cannot be captured.
content.extendedDescription:
Meanwhile, demand for water in agriculture, industry and society is increasing. A traditional way of addressing this is to produce drinking water from seawater. We want to highlight other solutions to this problem and a change in outlook and ambition: from “clean enough to discharge” to “as circular as possible”. Recovering resources already present in our processes and systems reduces the need to keep producing new ones. This applies particularly to rain that falls and quickly drains into the sea through drainage ditches, but also to wastewater from municipal treatment plants and industry. Circular solutions enable not only water but also input materials to be returned to the circular loop.
The seminar examines water-related challenges and solutions tested at full scale, and highlights industry's ability to lead the implementation of circular solutions.

content.title: How war changes the nature of things: People, Landscapes and Recovery
content.description: War in Ukraine changes more than lives. It transforms landscapes, ecosystems, human relationships and the way people experience the world around them. How do these changes affect mental health, resilience and society’s ability to recover during and after war?
content.extendedDescription:
The full-scale war in Ukraine has changed not only people but also the environments they inhabit. Forests have been burned and mined, coastlines militarized, and familiar sounds replaced by drones and explosions. For many Ukrainians, nature itself has become associated with danger rather than safety.
At the same time, nature remains one of the most powerful resources for psychological recovery. This creates a broader question for society: how do war, trauma and prolonged uncertainty reshape the relationship between people, places and community?

This event marks the opening of The Force of Nature, a photo exhibition created by Repower in partnership with Lumell Associates. 

Importantly, the exhibition itself does not focus on destruction, violence or loss. Instead, it highlights beauty, presence, connection and the remarkable human capacity to recover. Through photographs created during a recovery programme for Ukrainian frontline medics on Gotland, visitors encount
content.subject: International affairs

content.title: Gateway to the continent or a bottleneck?
content.description: The government recently decided that future surpluses from Öresundsbron will go towards infrastructure investments in Skåne, “in the same way as congestion charges in Stockholm and Göteborg”. But how do you negotiate with the state, and what can it lead to?
content.extendedDescription: Skåne is Sweden's gateway to the continent and Europe's route to Scandinavia. At the same time, the country's largest infrastructure bottlenecks are in Skåne. When the government recently adopted the next national transport infrastructure plan, it also decided to appoint a negotiator for Öresundsbron's surplus, in a similar way to the state's handling of congestion-charge revenues in Stockholm and Göteborg. But what is it like to negotiate transport infrastructure with the government? What should you consider, and what are the pitfalls? How do you ensure that the additional funds do not “crowd out” ordinary tax-funded infrastructure investments, so that local people do not have to pay twice for infrastructure – through congestion charges/bridge tolls and through the taxes everyone pays? What is the best way to remove the bottlenecks? Hear the answers from officials and elected representatives with experience from initiatives including Västsvenska paketet.
content.subject: Infrastructure/transport
speakerTitles: Head of Infrastructure and Public Transport

content.title: Experience heat stress!
content.description: Heat stress is a growing global occupational health and human rights issue. Textile workers in several of the world's largest producing countries regularly work in temperatures above 35 degrees, often without adequate protective measures. The consequences can include dehydration, dizziness, fainting and serious health risks.
content.extendedDescription:
What does it feel like to work in temperatures above 35 degrees, without ventilation, breaks or access to a cool space? Experience heat stress is an immersive experience in which visitors step directly into a textile worker's reality. Intense heat, authentic factory noise and workers' own accounts create a tangible physical experience. For a few minutes, visitors enter the reality that the climate crisis and conditions in the fashion industry create for many textile workers around the world. Afterwards, Fair Action invites you to discuss corporate responsibility, climate justice and what is needed for a just climate transition in the fashion industry.

Imperfect Industries will be there to share how circular business models can be created through reuse – without any new manufacturing. Their concept will be presented on site for anyone curious to learn more about how reuse can be scaled up in practice. Come and talk to us!
content.detail: The fashion industry is too hot
content.subject: Human rights

content.title: Together against cancer – when does prevention become a political responsibility?
content.description: Political decisions today can affect how many people develop cancer tomorrow. The European Code Against Cancer highlights 14 measures to reduce cancer risk, but it depends on political decisions and structural changes. How can Sweden reverse the trend as more people develop cancer?
content.extendedDescription:
While more people are living with cancer or have been treated for it, the number of new cases is increasing. A substantial proportion of cancer cases could be prevented through changes in lifestyles, the environment and societal structures. The European Code Against Cancer presents 14 recommendations to reduce and alleviate the burden of cancer – but several require political decisions and long-term investment in public health.

The seminar focuses on prevention and political responsibility. How can we reduce the number of new cases and give healthcare services better conditions for treating the cancers that do occur?

Among other topics, we discuss the cost of failing to invest in public health and cancer prevention, and the political decisions needed for Sweden to fulfil the European Code Against Cancer by shifting responsibility from individuals to society.

content.title: Who takes responsibility for the climate during refurbishment?
content.description: Tenant fit-outs and interior refurbishments are a recurring but often overlooked source of climate impact. There is considerable potential to reduce the carbon footprint through reuse, clear incentives and better evidence for decisions. How can we seize this opportunity?
content.extendedDescription:
A large part of the climate impact of the construction and property sector arises from recurring refurbishments of premises. This also presents a concrete opportunity to reduce the carbon footprint by working more systematically with reuse, long service life and climate data for interiors. HI-märkningen, Sweden's first environmental certification for premises, developed with RISE and around thirty organisations, provides a framework for setting requirements during interior design and refurbishment. Clear criteria and independent verification enable tenants, property owners and designers to reduce climate impact where decisions are actually made.
The work is now being developed further through the project “Cirkulär kontorsutveckling börjar hos hyresgästen”, focusing on generic climate data for interior products and how incentives can be changed from the earliest stages. The discussion explores how these tools can contribute to a more circular and climate-conscious construction sector.

content.title: When security is procured at the lowest price – who takes responsibility for safety?
content.description: Security is a societal issue. When purchasing and procurement are driven too strongly by the lowest price, quality, responsibility and actual effectiveness risk being overlooked. This applies to both services and technology – from guarding to alarms, cameras, drones and integrated security solutions.
content.extendedDescription:
Security is not a standard product. Real safety depends on the right skills, relevant technology, effective management and a clear chain of responsibility. Several elements often need to work together: staff, alarms, cameras, analysis, supporting systems and the ability to act when something happens.
Yet much purchasing and procurement is characterised by price pressure, silos and requirements that do not always capture the actual security outcome. This risks disadvantaging responsible providers, holding back investment and ultimately providing poorer protection for people, organisations and essential infrastructure.

SäkerhetsArenan is organised by SäkerhetsBranschen, Stöldskyddsföreningen, Brandskyddsföreningen, Tryggare Sverige, Almega Säkerhetsföretagen, Företagsuniversitetet and Säkerhets- och försvarsföretagen (SOFF). Together, we create a shared meeting place for conversations that strengthen Sweden for the future.

content.title: The battle over public art
content.description: The so-called one per cent rule means that a fixed share, usually one per cent, of a building investment is allocated to public art. In recent years, the rule and public art have become increasingly politicised, bringing the role of art in society into sharp focus.
content.extendedDescription:
In recent years, public art and the so-called one per cent rule – which allocates a fixed share, usually one per cent, of a building investment to public art – have become politicised, bringing the role of art in society into sharp focus.
The one per cent rule is currently applied by half of the country's municipalities and regions. For several years, however, proposals to abolish or change it have been put forward in many municipalities and regions. Abolishing the rule is also proposed in the much-debated policy document Tidö 2.0. Elsewhere, politicians advocate referendums on public art.
At the same time, opinion polls tell us that many people consider public art important in their local surroundings and feel that it creates safety and a pleasant environment. Because it is accessible to everyone, it is also important for achieving the national cultural policy objectives. For this discussion, we invite politicians who support and oppose the rule.

content.title: Supporting language development: talk to data, visual analytics and AI for a more coherent learning journey
content.description: Poor language skills are one of the biggest risk factors in education. How can we detect early signals before pupils fall behind? By analysing and talking to data, schools can move from late interventions to systematically supporting language development from preschool onwards.
content.extendedDescription:
In this seminar, we show how new technology and real-time data democratisation can make complex issues understandable and fundamentally change school development. It is about turning numbers and patterns into a living dialogue all the way from the classroom to the education administration.

Together with Sandra Tauberman, Head of Quality and Development at Burlövs kommun, we discuss the challenges and opportunities of “talking to your school data” using AI and generative language models.

We demonstrate how:

AI and visual real-time data can serve as an early warning system for language development and attendance.

Shared insights eliminate gaps in pupils' transitions between types of education.

Teachers receive rapid assessments of the current situation that can be used directly in lesson planning.

Cooperation at every level becomes possible when we unlock data and share the same picture in real time.
content.subject: Education
speakerTitles: CEO and Former Director of Education
Head of Quality and Development, Education and Culture Department

content.title: From innovation to competitiveness – how can Sweden become more attractive for R&D?
content.description: Global competition for investment in research, clinical trials and innovation is intensifying. How can Sweden become more attractive for R&D? And what role do the early use of new medicines and better treatment follow-up play in attracting life science investment?
content.extendedDescription:
Through the Capital of Life cluster's unique strengths in research, healthcare and innovation, Stockholm and Uppsala are well placed to be a leading life science region. Meanwhile, global competition for investment, clinical trials and skills is intensifying.

What matters is not strategies, but the ability to deliver and a clear role for the innovation chain. The ability to use new medicines early in clinical practice and follow up treatments is becoming increasingly important for turning innovation into patient benefit, keeping healthcare at the forefront and attracting investment in research and development. Ultimately, it is about being a relevant and attractive partner throughout the medicines lifecycle.

How can Stockholm and Sweden take the next step to strengthen their global position and become a first choice for investment, clinical trials and early access to new treatments?

content.title: From property financing to financing society – does our view of investment need to change?
content.description: Sweden has substantial investment needs, while financing conditions have become more challenging. Risk now encompasses not only economics, but also climate, energy and social sustainability. Meeting these challenges requires new rules and business models that reward sustainable value creation.
content.extendedDescription:
The low interest rates and abundant capital of recent decades have been replaced by higher capital costs, geopolitical uncertainties, increased sustainability requirements and growing investment needs. Sweden needs to develop cities, modernise infrastructure and energy systems, and adapt its existing property stock to climate change. The question is not whether these investments are needed, but how they will be financed and who is prepared to invest.

How should investors, banks and property owners value investments whose societal benefits are clear but whose financial returns materialise only over a long period? Meeting these challenges requires stable long-term rules, new business models and forms of investment that reward partnerships and sustainable value creation.
content.detail: Techarena, Focus stage, Site 531, Strandvägen 3, 621 55 Visby

content.title: Crime prevention through urban planning – how do we design out crime and insecurity?
content.description: The design of the physical environment has a major influence on crime and insecurity. Yet these issues are rarely considered in urban planning. How can urban planning be used to reduce crime and increase safety?
content.extendedDescription: Swedish society has changed fundamentally in recent decades, challenging the ability to create and maintain safe and secure environments. One important factor influencing crime and insecurity is the physical design of neighbourhoods, residential areas and public spaces, where conditions conducive to crime and insecurity have, to some extent, been built into many areas. Safety and security have not had a prominent place in the planning and development process. To meet the challenges facing municipalities, property owners and others, crime prevention and safety work must be integrated into that process. The seminar presents and discusses the new BoTryggt2040 standard – a handbook for safe, secure and attractive living environments – as a method to help both clients and practitioners make informed choices about designing out crime and building in safety.
content.subject: Justice/crime

content.title: The wind industry – a blight on rural areas
content.description: Wind power is often presented as a green solution, but for many people in rural areas it means something very different. Large-scale wind power changes landscapes, affects natural assets and creates conflicts where people live. What is the experience of those living near wind industry installations?
content.extendedDescription:
For people living in areas where wind power is planned, the impact starts long before any turbines are built. During project planning, many live with prolonged uncertainty: will the landscape change, will their home lose value, and how will nature and their living environment be affected? This uncertainty often creates significant psychological strain for those affected.

Once projects are built, everyday life changes noticeably. Large industrial turbines rise in formerly open landscapes, roads are built and natural environments are affected. For those living nearby, the sound of rotor blades can become a constant background presence, while flashing obstruction lights mark the installations in the night sky. For many, this creates a sense that a place once associated with home and recreation has fundamentally changed.

In this discussion, we want to highlight the human experiences behind wind power expansion – how decisions affect people living in the landscapes where projects are planned and built, and the consequences they experience.
content.subject: Climate/environment

content.title: What is needed for establishment jobs to reach their full potential?
content.description: So far, few people have obtained an establishment job, leading to some criticism of the reform. What is the criticism about? And what is needed for establishment jobs to fulfil their potential?
content.extendedDescription:
Establishment jobs resulted from an agreement signed in 2022 by the social partners Svenskt Näringsliv, LO and Unionen. The system came into use on 1 January 2024. An establishment job is a special form of full-time, fixed-term employment governed by a collective agreement. It targets both newly arrived immigrants and people who have been unemployed for a long time. Employment is limited to a maximum of two years, after which it should normally become permanent. Employees in establishment jobs must be given the opportunity to take part in education during working hours without a pay deduction.

So far, few people have obtained an establishment job. The government has therefore tasked Arbetsförmedlingen with raising awareness of the scheme among employers, jobseekers and other stakeholders, with the aim of increasing the number of jobseekers employed through it. Arbetsförmedlingen and the social partners are now working together to raise awareness and improve matching so that more employers hire newly arrived immigrants and people who have been unemployed for a long time.

content.title: The fashion industry is too hot – who takes responsibility for heat stress?
content.description: Our clothes are sewn in factories in extreme heat – often without breaks, ventilation or access to clean water. Meanwhile, Sweden is preparing for heat stress while workers in producing countries are left unprotected. Who is responsible?
content.extendedDescription:
People in fashion industry factories work every day in temperatures above 35 degrees. The consequences are serious: dizziness, collapse and, in some cases, death. Yet production continues at a rapid pace, with pressure on prices and delivery times taking priority over a safe working environment.

Meanwhile, Sweden is preparing for increased heat risks. Employers are urged to adjust working hours, ensure ventilation and allow time for recovery. But in the countries where our clothes are made, work continues as usual, even though we share the same vulnerability to heat.

Who is responsible when the climate crisis makes working conditions dangerous in the fashion industry's global production chain, and what does a just climate transition look like in practice?

A focused panel discussion brings together perspectives from civil society, medical expertise and climate science to highlight heat stress as an occupational health issue and discuss the path towards a just climate transition in the fashion industry.
content.subject: Human rights

content.title: Circularity – how hard can it be?
content.description: Europe faces a transition towards more resource-efficient ways of doing business. For several reasons, this transition has become increasingly urgent. Why is circularity both necessary and difficult? What is needed to move from principle to practice?
content.extendedDescription:
In a short time, securing access to materials and components has become a matter of both security and competitiveness. In addition, demands to reduce carbon footprints and preserve biodiversity are increasing. Working with circular principles is an effective way to meet all these challenges.
Circularity often sounds obvious: use resources more intelligently, recycle more, repair, reuse and design products to last. But for manufacturing companies, it is rarely that simple in practice.
The transition affects the entire business: product design, material choices, supply chains, servicing, spare parts, take-back, data, customer requirements, regulations and new business models. At every stage, practical questions need to be resolved. Can the product be refurbished and sold again? Do the market, logistics and profitability exist? How do new technical requirements, standards and regulations affect the ability to reuse products? What sounds simple in theory quickly becomes more complex in reality.
content.subject: Sustainability

content.title: New conditions for student housing – what do we do after the election?
content.description: The student housing market is changing. Local vacancies, shifting demographics and tougher financial calculations coincide with new opportunities from relaxed building regulations. What measures are needed? Meanwhile, new student housing is being planned under building regulations with lower accessibility requirements – find out how these are being applied in practice.
content.extendedDescription:
The student housing market is in a new situation. Changing demographics and study patterns challenge familiar assumptions about the market. In some university towns, student housing stands empty, while elsewhere there is still not enough. At the same time, high costs hamper both new construction and conversions.

How should policymakers, municipalities and market participants respond to these new conditions? What is needed to create long-term conditions for housing investment and attractive places to study? And what policies can we expect after the election, regardless of the result?

After the seminar, we invite you to an exhibition opening and ice-cream reception in the garden, focusing on the new building regulations for student housing. Are you curious about how lower accessibility requirements are being applied in practice? In our exhibition, student housing companies present concrete projects being developed under the new rules.
content.subject: Construction

content.title: From soil to jobs: how the food sector can become an engine of green growth
content.description: The need for greater domestic supply capacity and preparedness is growing rapidly, as are demands to reduce climate and environmental impact. By stepping up the green transition, Sweden can produce more food, strengthen the sector's competitiveness and resilience, and create tens of thousands of new jobs.
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden faces major challenges in food supply, preparedness, climate and competitiveness – but also major opportunities. In the report Grön uppväxling, Swedish farmers and food producers present a shared evidence base and a concrete roadmap for increasing Swedish food and beverage production while reducing climate impact and strengthening biodiversity.

The seminar discusses how Sweden can take greater responsibility for its own and Europe's food supply, the conditions needed to increase production, how tens of thousands of new jobs can be created, and how growth in agriculture and the food industry can be combined with high environmental and climate ambitions.

The discussion starts from the enormous growth potential in Sweden's primary and food production, and the political, economic and structural changes needed to enable a green scale-up.
content.subject: Business

speakerTitles: Chair of the Committee on Industry and Trade

content.title: Mental Health and Human Sustainability in Defense Systems
content.description: War places immense psychological pressure on those serving on the frontline and across defense systems. Mental health and recovery are essential for sustaining defense capacity and societal resilience. How can resilience become part of national security and preparedness?
content.extendedDescription:
This event expands the discussion by bringing practical experience from Ukraine, where the psychological impact of prolonged war on those serving on the frontline has become a critical challenge for defense systems and society.

Repower’s work is based on an innovative recovery approach developed through programs supporting frontline medical personnel exposed to the psychological pressure of war. The approach combines recovery, peer exchange and holistic practices aimed at restoring human capacity and long-term resilience.

This space creates a discussion on how mental health can be integrated into defense and preparedness strategies. Participants will reflect on resilience as a factor of national security.

It takes place in a curated space where art serves as a communication tool. A thought-provoking installation translates invisible psychological pressure into a tangible public experience and opens space for dialogue across defense, policy and civil society perspectives.
content.subject: International affairs

content.title: Creating producer responsibility for textiles – what producers need
content.description: The EU's revised Waste Directive entered into force in autumn 2025 and must be fully implemented in Sweden by 2028. This means that businesses will have to cover the costs of collecting and sorting textiles and textile waste.
content.extendedDescription:
Join a seminar on the latest developments in producer responsibility for textiles!
Work on designing Swedish producer responsibility for textiles and footwear is now at a decisive stage, as the Waste Directive must be implemented within two years. The issue is how the textile and fashion industry can transition to more sustainable and circular business models while maintaining its competitiveness. The design of Swedish producer responsibility for textiles will have consequences for both Swedish businesses and consumers.

Svensk Handel and TEKO, Sveriges Textil- och modeföretag therefore invite you to a seminar on the current state of the process. We identify the key issues ahead and highlight the potential consequences of the decisions to be made. During the seminar, a panel representing different parts of the textile value chain will discuss the issue from their perspectives.
content.subject: Business
content.accessibility: Wheelchair-accessible toilet, wheelchair-accessible entrance and venue

content.title: Concern as a driving force for a green future
content.description:
The climate crisis threatens our future – emissions are increasing when they should be falling rapidly.
Are you worried about children's future too? You are not alone! It is easy to feel powerless in the face of inadequate climate policy. How can we create a future to look forward to?
content.extendedDescription:
We talk about targets, prices at the pump and roadmaps. But something else is simmering beneath the surface: worry, anger, grief – and a growing sense of betrayal. A lack of will is not the problem: 89% of the world's population wants strong climate policy. A lack of knowledge is not the problem. What is missing is courage.

Parents know that the climate crisis concerns their children's future. Yet people continue to accept short-term thinking, denial and political games – as if time were infinite.

Rebellmammorna and Rebellpapporna say enough is enough and are creating a space in Almedalen that otherwise does not exist:
• For anger at how slowly things are moving.
• For fear about what we are losing.
• For the will to bring about real change.

When emotions are given space, they have the potential to become a powerful force.
We invite you to a conversation where the audience interacts and provides input for discussion with our panellists. This is a space where every voice is heard and every voice is needed. We have no time for more comfortable conversations.
content.subject: Climate/environment
content.accessibility: Event captioned, wheelchair-accessible entrance and venue

content.title: Sustainability risks in theory – business decisions in practice: how do we bridge the gap?
content.description: How can we make real progress on sustainability as demands for climate risk assessments, impact assessments and transition plans increase – while finance teams are expected to use the results in investment and strategic decisions?
content.extendedDescription:
At Aspia, we believe that sustainability data must be handled with the same rigour as financial data for sustainability work to be manageable and relevant to the business. This means moving from fragmented, manual data collection to integrated, standardised and quality-assured data management. But how do we get there?

Join Aspia's roundtable in Almedalen, where we bring together sustainability, finance and strategy teams to discuss:

- The challenges we face in strengthening the flow between sustainability-related and financial information.
- The role, opportunities and challenges of supporting systems.
- What is needed for a supporting system to generate the value an organisation wants.

The starting point is real experience of using supporting systems to advance organisations' sustainability work.

Format: Roundtable discussion.

Purpose: Identify shared challenges and concrete ways forward.

Refreshments: Lunch is provided.
content.subject: Sustainability

content.title: Girls and women with lipoedema receive neither a correct diagnosis nor care
content.description: 5–10 per cent of women live with the painful disease lipoedema. Research shows that they wait decades for a correct diagnosis and have to pay for their own care. Swedish healthcare is failing girls and women with lipoedema. Would you like to help change this?
content.extendedDescription:
A neglected common disease – a gender equality issue
According to researchers, one in ten women has lipoedema, a disease that is very painful and disabling for many women. Research shows that most experience a severely reduced quality of life. Despite this, healthcare services do not take this hereditary disease seriously.
There is no cure, but various treatments can relieve symptoms; however, women must pay for these themselves.
In its report, the SÖSR methods council argues that withholding multidisciplinary care, including publicly provided liposuction, from patients with lipoedema is incompatible with the spirit of the Health and Medical Services Act.
Would you like to learn more about symptoms and treatment, and what it is like to live with lipoedema?
Do you work in healthcare and want to learn how to diagnose lipoedema?
As a person with responsibility, a decision-maker or a politician, would you like to learn more about what you can do to change this situation?
What will you and your party do about the situation over the next four years?
content.subject: Health and social care

content.title: Girls and women with lipoedema receive neither a correct diagnosis nor care
content.description: 5–10 per cent of women live with the painful disease lipoedema. Research shows that they wait decades for a correct diagnosis and have to pay for their own care. Swedish healthcare is failing girls and women with lipoedema. Would you like to help change this?
content.extendedDescription:
A neglected common disease – a gender equality issue
According to researchers, one in ten women has lipoedema, a disease that is very painful and disabling for many women. Research shows that most experience a severely reduced quality of life. Despite this, healthcare services do not take this hereditary disease seriously.
There is no cure, but various treatments can relieve symptoms; however, women must pay for these themselves.
In its report, the SÖSR methods council argues that withholding multidisciplinary care, including publicly provided liposuction, from patients with lipoedema is incompatible with the spirit of the Health and Medical Services Act.
Would you like to learn more about symptoms and treatment, and what it is like to live with lipoedema?
Do you work in healthcare and want to learn how to diagnose lipoedema?
As a person with responsibility, a decision-maker or a politician, would you like to learn more about what you can do to change this situation?
What will you and your party do about the situation over the next four years?

content.title: Affordable housing in Sweden – how is it possible?
content.description: We need new solutions and affordable housing in Sweden. What alternatives exist, and can they be developed and scaled up?
content.extendedDescription:
We present different approaches already being used to provide more affordable housing for households that struggle to secure a home on their own. These are different methods that all work and help more households find a home where they can live well and stay.

Linda Lövgren from KTH presents the Kymmendö model; Cattis Carlén presents OBOS dela, a concept offering a more affordable model for buying a home; Johanna Lindroth explains how more people can gain access to suitable housing; and Helena Markgren, CEO of Skebo, presents how Skebo has developed affordable housing at scale, with 743 newly built affordable homes.

After the presentations, we discuss with our panel: how can these initiatives be scaled up, and what lessons can be learned? Where are the main barriers, and how do we overcome them? Where do policymakers need to intervene, and what is required for them to do so? Can the EU's affordable housing plan help us? What is the financing situation?
content.subject: Construction
speakerTitles: Head of the Think Tank Arena Idé and Public Commentator
Senior Strategist and Former Inquiry Expert
Public Policy Expert Responsible for Housing Development

content.title: The Fehmarn Belt tunnel is changing the Nordic region – is Sweden ready?
content.description: How can we ensure a functioning transport network as pressure increases? When the Fehmarn Belt tunnel between Denmark and Germany opens, Sweden will gain a faster, more direct connection to the continent.
content.extendedDescription:
This strengthens Nordic competitiveness and our opportunities to connect more closely with Europe.
At the same time, pressure on our own transport links is increasing, with bottlenecks on routes including Skåne–Själland and Oslo–Göteborg. Öresundsbron and the Oslo–Göteborg connection are already heavily used. So how can we ensure that the system holds up, including during crises and disruptions?

Join a panel discussion on strengthening both capacity and preparedness in our transport networks, and how cross-border cooperation can provide more robust solutions for the future.

We discuss:
• Where are the local bottlenecks or “missing links” in the transport network?
• What do the Swedish regions concerned need to meet future mobility needs?
• How can we on the Swedish side meet increased capacity requirements in the connections between Sweden and Denmark, and between Sweden and Norway?
• How can Nordic cooperation help create sustainable and resilient solutions?
content.subject: Business
content.accessibility: Hearing loop, wheelchair-accessible entrance and venue
speakerTitles: First Deputy Chair of VGR's Infrastructure and Public Transport Committee and Member of STRING's Political Forum

content.title: Who is responsible for engagement – individuals or civil society?
content.description: Civil society plays a central role in democracy, welfare and social cohesion. At the same time, forms of engagement are changing rapidly and often take the form of short-term efforts close to individuals' lives. As engagement becomes more episodic, established structures are challenged.
content.extendedDescription:
Through organised forms of engagement, civil society has created space for participation, responsibility and democratic learning over time. Membership and association life have enabled people to participate, exert influence and learn how democracy works in practice. At the same time, research shows that interest in traditional forms of engagement, such as membership, has declined, especially among younger people.
Engagement increasingly takes the form of short-term efforts close to individuals' lives rather than long-term participation. This is happening as expectations of civil society increase – to contribute to democratic participation, social cohesion and sometimes welfare provision. When giving increases but formal participation declines, collective responsibility, internal democracy and legitimate representation are challenged.
This raises crucial questions: how does engagement arise today, and whose responsibility is it to shape and sustain it? Do organisations need to change how they work to remain relevant?
content.subject: Democracy

content.title: A national museum card – the key to greater access and stronger cultural policy?
content.description: Could a shared museum card help lower barriers to culture, broaden audiences and strengthen museums' role in democracy? And what cultural policy choices arise if a museum card is to become a tool for increased
content.extendedDescription:
Sveriges Museer has received government funding to explore, with an open mind, the opportunities and challenges of a national Swedish museum card. During Kultur i Almedalen 2026, the first interim report from the feasibility study will be presented, with in-depth case studies analysing the potential effects of a museum card on accessibility, participation and museums' long-term sustainability throughout the country.

Could a shared museum card help lower barriers to culture, broaden audiences and strengthen museums' role in democracy? How would it affect the relationship between the state, regions, municipalities and civil society? And what cultural policy choices arise if a museum card is to become a tool for better achievement of objectives and equal access to culture?

Participants include Sveriges Museer's new Chair Cajsa Lagerkvist, Secretary General Gunnar Ardelius, and Jaakko Rytsölä and Perttu Rytsölä, the report authors, who have extensive experience of developing the Finnish museum card. Moderator: Sharon Jåma.
content.subject: Culture

content.title: From the frontline to the future – how is Ukrainian healthcare being rebuilt in the midst of war?
content.description: Russia's war has hit Ukraine's healthcare system hard. Yet rebuilding is taking place in the midst of active conflict. Sweden has a government mandate to support this process – but how does knowledge transfer work in practice, and what can Swedish organisations really deliver?
content.extendedDescription:
Russia's war has not only killed and injured hundreds of thousands of Ukrainians – it has systematically knocked out hospitals, ambulances, rehabilitation centres and the staff who run them. Yet rebuilding is taking place during the ongoing war: Ukrainian organisations are developing new care models adapted to wartime conditions, often without the resources that European healthcare takes for granted.
Since 2024, Sweden has had a government mandate to support the rebuilding of Ukraine's healthcare system – transferring Swedish knowledge and solutions to a country receiving them under fire. The question is no longer whether Sweden should contribute, but how: what works in practice, what do Swedish organisations fail to understand about Ukrainian conditions, and how can knowledge transfer remain effective when reality changes every day?

The discussion is part of Samarbetsplattformen: Sverige & Ukraina (SPSU) – a project by KlinteVolontär that gives Ukrainian civil society its own voice in Swedish democratic debate.
content.subject: Health and social care
content.organizationType: Collaboration between different types of organisation
