content.title: Why is a national resource centre for internationally adopted people needed?
content.description: Today, adoptees themselves often help other adoptees with questions about origins, identity and contact with authorities. This shows that society's support is insufficient. Responsibility must shift from individuals to a safe, professional and lasting structure. What do adopted people say?
content.extendedDescription:
The event takes the form of a discussion focused on the question: why is a national resource centre for internationally adopted people needed? Today, adoptees themselves often help other adoptees with questions about origins, identity, documents, rights and contact with authorities. This shows that society's support is insufficient and that responsibility must shift from individuals to a safe, professional and lasting structure.

During the discussion, we highlight the voices of internationally adopted people and examine the need for coordinated support, legal guidance and knowledge among the relevant authorities. Lawyer Lisa Gauffin Dahlin and a representative of the Chilean Consulate have been invited to contribute legal perspectives and information about how the consulate can be an important link in these matters. Participants do not need to prepare in advance.
content.subject: Human rights
content.instructions: You can submit your questions here during the event. If you have questions afterwards, you are welcome to send them to info@chileadoption.se

content.title: How can we use AI safely and in ways that build trust?
content.description: AI is fundamentally changing both the public and private sectors – but how do we manage the risks as its use increases? How can we ensure that technological development goes hand in hand with security, responsibility and regulatory compliance?
content.extendedDescription:
AI is no longer a future issue for a select few, but a tool that can be useful to everyone, albeit in different ways. This makes AI a broad societal issue in which technological development, competitiveness, democracy and trust are closely connected. As more organisations integrate AI into their operations, it also becomes essential to understand what needs to be protected, regulated and monitored.

This seminar discusses two perspectives that increasingly need to be addressed together: technical security and regulatory requirements. How are organisations affected by new rules? What risks arise when AI models are used in sensitive processes or trained on large quantities of data? And how can management teams, experts and decision-makers strike the right balance between innovation, security and responsibility? AI solutions are also often used in legacy IT environments, creating additional security challenges.
The seminar will provide insights into how security work and regulations together shape the future use of AI.
content.subject: Digitalisation
speakerTitles: Head of Regulatory and Leadership initiatives

content.title: Quantum technology is here – how can Sweden get ready?
content.description: Quantum technology is leaving the laboratory and entering the real world, with the potential to change the fundamentals of security and competitiveness. For a small country like Sweden, the question is how to join forces to compete globally. How can Sweden become quantum-ready?
content.extendedDescription:
Quantum technology is moving from research to application, while the United States, China and the EU accelerate their investments. Sweden has long had a strong, international and dynamic quantum ecosystem. Today's challenge is not only about technology, but about how we organise ourselves to achieve results.

How can we bring together research, innovation and strategic investment without fragmenting what we have already built?

On stage, actors holding different parts of the solution meet: those developing the technology, those who will use it and those shaping the conditions. What is needed to move from strong research to actual capability? Where do we get stuck today – and who takes responsibility for the next step?

The seminar is a moderated discussion in which perspectives are tested against one another, focusing on what specifically needs to happen next. It is for anyone who wants to help shape Sweden's next steps in quantum technology.

The seminar is followed by a networking lunch.

content.organizationType: Collaboration between different types of organisation

content.title: Young people's influence. Regional strength.
content.description: Young people from different parts of the country, backgrounds and age groups want to have a say. Yet there is a lack of ongoing forums where young people can influence all areas of regional responsibility. Can regional youth councils fill this gap and enable young people to exert influence?
content.extendedDescription:
Over the past three years, Sveriges ungdomsråd has worked on the Regional Youth Project, funded by Allmänna Arvsfonden, which aims to narrow the distance between young people, regional services and regional politics. Together with regions, we work to strengthen young people's participation, influence and organisation at regional level. We share challenges and lessons relating to involving a broad group of young people in decision-making through the regional youth council method.

Visit us and talk to young people from 7 different regions who have engaged in regional issues, helped establish regional youth councils and played an active part in the Regional Youth Project. Together, we look ahead: what is needed to continue strengthening young people's voices in the regions? You can also test your own knowledge of regions, share your views or perhaps take part in a mini-interview.

Young people's influence is a regional strength that we all have a responsibility to make use of.
content.subject: Children/young people

content.title: Civil society in development aid – ideological choices
content.description: Civil society has long been a central actor in Swedish development cooperation. Aid is now undergoing a shift in which political priorities, governance models and views of civil society's mission are changing. This brings ideological choices into sharp focus.
content.extendedDescription:
Civil society has long been a central actor in Swedish development cooperation. Aid is now undergoing a shift in which political priorities, governance models and views of civil society's mission are changing. This brings ideological choices into sharp focus: is civil society primarily a democratic voice, a service provider – or something else entirely?
New Swedish research examines civil society's democratic functions and growing tensions in the relationship between the state, the market and non-profit organisations. Meanwhile, civil society organisations face a changing aid policy in which expectations and rules are being redrawn. The government talks a great deal about Team Sweden; does civil society have a role in it?
This discussion brings together ideas, research and practice to explore how different ideological traditions – liberal, conservative and progressive – view civil society's role in aid today and in the future.

The seminar is part of Civilsamhällesarenan.
content.subject: Democracy

content.title: Beyond the headlines – how is successful social work done?
content.description: What happens when social services work with, for example, young people leaving crime, families escaping cycles of violence and homeless people accepting support from outreach services? The interventions are complex. What characterises social work when it goes well?
content.extendedDescription:
Susanna Alakoski, an author, social worker and long-standing contributor to social policy debate, “was utterly tired of hearing about failed social work”. She therefore posted an appeal on Facebook asking professionals to share cases where social services had made a difference. Around 500 responses quickly arrived, resulting in the anthology “Lyckade ärenden i socialtjänsten – socionomer berättar”. Its 24 contributors describe how they have changed lives and give a voice to a profession rarely heard when its efforts succeed.

Drawing on the book, Susanna Alakoski discusses what social work is and can be. The focus is on factors that enable success, including professional knowledge, compassion, cooperation, continuity and organisational conditions.

“The book does not seek to downplay criticism of social services; it simply wants to show that social work also succeeds. There is a profession and a skilled craft that sometimes work wonders,” says Susanna Alakoski.

content.title: What is needed to build new nuclear power in Sweden?
content.description: Several European countries are now investing in new nuclear power to meet energy needs and climate targets. Experience from previous reactor projects also shows that the approach taken is crucial to how efficiently expansion can be achieved. What is needed to build new nuclear power efficiently in Sweden?
content.extendedDescription:
The seminar focuses on the practical and industrial conditions for new nuclear power. In the first half, researchers from Uppsala universitet and the ANItA competence centre present new research on international experience of nuclear power expansion, new reactor technologies, global supply chains and possible sites for future reactors in Sweden. The presentations are followed by a panel discussion with the following representatives of industry, academia, public authorities and a municipality:

content.title: How do we make culture and participation a natural part of children and young people's everyday lives?
content.description: Children and young people are often described as the future, but we live here now, and the best way to face the future is together – children, young people and adults in dialogue.
content.extendedDescription: Are you curious about working with young people's influence and participation? Come and listen to, talk to and ask questions of us (KC+), young people from KulturCrew Skåne. Here you will find ideas and examples that benefit young people in practice. KulturCrew started in Skåne in 2016 and now operates in 13 counties in Sweden. The method comes from Denmark, and the aim is for children and young people's voices to be heard and taken seriously. In KulturCrew, we work together as a group and learn how to turn an idea into reality. We cooperate with the professional cultural sector across all art forms. Some questions we want to raise: how can every child's right to culture be fulfilled? Why not invest in what young people want? What is the difference between influence and participation? How do you build an association with young people in leadership roles? What are the benefits of working with youth participation and young event organisers, with a focus on culture? Who is responsible for increasing young people's participation? It is time to move beyond the planning stage and show that young people's voices count!
content.subject: Culture

content.title: The Baltic Sea as a frontier zone and energy sea – a common strategy is needed!
content.description: Europe is facing two major challenges at the same time – a security crisis and a climate crisis. The Baltic Sea is in the middle of this, where large-scale energy production and security aspects must coexist. The need for a common strategy is obvious. How can Europe best deal with the situation now?
content.extendedDescription:
Major energy investments are planned by all democratic countries around the Baltic Sea. It is an important part of Europe's energy transition. This mainly concerns plans for offshore wind power and hydrogen. At the same time, the Baltic Sea is in the most vulnerable security situation since the end of the Second World War. How can these two great needs work together? How do Wind Europe view this? How do we achieve a common strategy for the development of the Baltic Sea that safeguards both these interests? 
The decisions have been made to make Bornholm the world's first energy island. Can more islands in the Baltic Sea follow, what can we learn from Bornholm? Estonia is planning for large wind farms near Gotland, how does that fit into the picture? We provide an overview of energy trends and security developments in the Baltic Sea.

content.title: Uniform, Pride, trust – hate crime against LGBTQI people, safety and confidence in the police
content.description: Many LGBTQI people have less trust in the police and justice system than the population as a whole. Meanwhile, negative attitudes towards LGBTQI people are increasing, and hatred is taking new forms, both online and in everyday life. What is needed to strengthen safety and confidence in the police?
content.extendedDescription:
Trust in the police and justice system is an important part of a safe and democratic society. Yet RFSL's latest safety report shows that many LGBTQI people still feel less safe than the population as a whole and have lower confidence in the police and justice system. Several government agency reports also show increased negative attitudes towards LGBTQI people, growing anti-LGBTQI hostility in digital environments and continued exposure to hate crime.

The debate over police officers' ability to wear uniforms in Pride parades has brought questions of visibility, representation and trust to the fore. But what is needed for more people to feel safe in everyday life? How can hate crimes be prevented and investigated more effectively? What role do the police have in prevention, and how do we ensure that people subjected to hate crime receive equal treatment and support wherever they live in the country?

The seminar takes the form of a discussion between representatives of RFSL and Polisförbundet.
content.subject: Justice/crime

content.title: How we can strengthen Sweden's voice in the EU
content.description: The greatest opportunities to influence EU decision-making come early, before a proposal is on the table. While the national level is primarily responsible for negotiating completed proposals, several Swedish actors engage much earlier on a range of issues. How can we cooperate to maximise the benefit for Sweden?
content.extendedDescription:
Europe faces major challenges, and many signs point towards greater centralisation, making it harder to develop place-based solutions and increasing the distance from citizens. How can we achieve effective communication between regional, national and European levels? Today, Sweden's national level seeks input on EU initiatives primarily through consultations, often late in the EU decision-making process, during implementation. This can lead to misunderstandings, increased workloads and costs. Swedish regions have long made their voices heard early in EU decision-making and have built valuable networks that can provide Sweden with important information and opportunities to influence outcomes.
By improving Swedish dialogue on EU initiatives between regional and national levels, we could give Swedish positions greater impact before EU-level decisions are made. Better dialogue would also support effective implementation of EU decisions in Sweden. Let us make use of one another's strengths for a stronger Swedish voice in the EU!
content.subject: EU

content.title: Could Sweden Afford the Energy Transition? Let’s Model It Together
content.description: Sweden may be making the energy transition far more expensive than necessary. This seminar explores how decentralized EnergyNet systems, extreme efficiency and strategic sustainability planning could accelerate electrification while reducing costs, emissions and resource use.
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden and Europe are rapidly electrifying transport, industry and cities. But are we building the transition in the most affordable and sustainable way?

Previous studies indicate that a renewable-based energy system could cost around 1000 billion SEK less than one heavily dependent on new nuclear power.

Using scenarios developed in the Roadmapper platform, the seminar explores whether costs could be reduced even further through:
Decentralized EnergyNet systems with smart microgrids, local energy sharing and storage.
“Extreme efficiency” in buildings and infrastructure to reduce energy and material demand.
Using a strategic sustainability perspective developed at BTH, and examples from the upcoming BTH campus transformation project, the discussion broadens beyond energy alone so that the transition is evaluated not only by energy costs, but also by emissions, land use, material choices and social sustainability.

content.title: How we can prevent more children from becoming perpetrators – and victims at the same time
content.description: Even at an early age, we can identify children at risk of being drawn into crime. Healthcare services often see them first, at child health centres, in school health services and in child psychiatry. But what do we do with that knowledge? Prevention is overshadowed in the debate about the age of criminal responsibility – how can early signals lead to early support?
content.extendedDescription:
Long before a child becomes involved in crime, they have often already been seen by healthcare services, at a child health centre, in school health services, dental care or child and adolescent psychiatry. We see the early signs: insecurity, school absence and symptoms without a medical explanation. Yet support too rarely arrives in time.

Even at an early age, we can identify children at risk of being drawn into crime. But what do we do with that knowledge? While the debate focuses on the age of criminal responsibility and incarceration, prevention receives less attention. How can we instead build a chain of early interventions, cooperation and follow-up before a child is recruited?

The child is both perpetrator and victim. The panel brings together a remand prison chaplain, a paediatrician, psychiatry and politics to discuss how healthcare, school health services and social services can jointly reverse the trend and recognise the child's needs in time.
content.subject: Health and social care

Deputy Chair of the Committee on Health and Welfare
Chair of the Committee on Health and Welfare

content.title: Meat and the climate – what does research say, and what are policymakers doing?
content.description: To meet climate targets, wealthy countries in particular need to reduce meat consumption. Meanwhile, the political debate about whether or not we should eat meat is heated. What complex challenges and conflicts surround the role of meat in the climate transition?
content.extendedDescription:
The food sector accounts for roughly a quarter of global greenhouse gas emissions. A large share comes from meat production and consumption. Research shows that meeting national and global climate targets requires reduced meat consumption, particularly in wealthy countries. Yet meat is a charged issue in public debate. Proposals to reduce consumption often provoke strong reactions and are frequently perceived as an intrusion into people's everyday lives or a threat to agriculture. This became apparent when Livsmedelsverket recently adjusted its dietary advice to a maximum of 350 grams per week.

Why does meat provoke such strong emotions? What role should politics play in what we eat? And what might the transition to a more sustainable food system look like in practice? This discussion brings together researchers, politicians and other stakeholders to discuss meat's place in the food systems of the future – and why the debate about whether or not to eat meat is so charged.

The seminar is part of Uppsala universitet's climate days.
content.subject: Climate/environment

content.title: Public procurement – from innovation to systematic development for sustainable supply
content.description: Innovation in the public sector often happens in projects but rarely spreads further. To meet climate targets and achieve sustainable development, solutions need to scale faster. How can public procurement better help spread and use what already works?
content.extendedDescription:
Despite substantial investment, public sector innovation often occurs in time-limited projects rather than as an integral part of everyday work, limiting our ability to scale up solutions that make a real difference. Meanwhile, the need for flexible approaches driven by learning and development is growing.

Drawing on Nordic experience and cooperation, including work linked to Ignite Hero of the Year, the seminar discusses how procurement focused on sustainable supply can become a strategic tool for meeting future challenges and driving continuous innovation and improvement. It explores what being innovation-friendly means in practice, how working methods, leadership and the courage to test on a small scale can enable gradual scaling, and how cooperation and structures can help make innovation a natural part of regular processes.
content.subject: Innovation
speakerTitles: Head of Business and Organisational Development
Head of Corporate Ventures & Smart buildings

content.title: The new AI industry – how can Sweden benefit from the power-hungry players?
content.description: Sweden is attracting AI data centres – some of the world's most electricity-intensive investments. Which developments create the most value? How should electricity be used as a strategic resource as AI grows? And which “power-hungry players” will become Sweden's next engines of prosperity?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden has a strong starting position in the global AI economy. With an almost entirely fossil-free electricity system, plentiful land and competitive electricity prices, the country is attractive to AI data centres – a rapidly growing, electricity-intensive sector.

At the same time, these developments raise important questions. Data centres require large amounts of electricity and grid capacity, but their contribution to employment and local value is debated. How can we ensure that investments strengthen competitiveness and long-term societal value? And how do we design electricity systems and regulations for both industrial electrification and AI's growing demand?

As industrial policy becomes more assertive globally, Sweden faces choices. Should certain uses of electricity be prioritised – and on what grounds? Do we have the potential to become a leading hub in global AI infrastructure?

The seminar brings together perspectives from industry, the energy sector and politics to discuss electricity's strategic role in the AI era.
content.subject: Energy
speakerTitles: Head of Power System Development Department
Head of Budget & Policy to Elisabeth Svantesson

content.title: The forest industry as an engine – how can we accelerate growth and the transition?
content.description: One of Sweden's competitive advantages is its access to forests. In the long term, global demand for biomass for fossil-free products is expected to increase. Yet the challenges facing one of Swedish business's flagship sectors are greater than they have been for many years.
content.extendedDescription:
The forest sector is one of Sweden's most important export industries and a central part of both the Swedish economy and the green transition. A unique value chain has been built around the forest – from forestry and sawmills to pulp and paper mills and the transport sector – in which every link depends on the others. Industry creates the value of the forest for forest owners, and raw materials from the forest underpin industry's competitiveness.

But conditions are tougher than they have been for a long time. Meanwhile, the long-term trend clearly points in one direction: global demand for biomass and fossil-free products will increase. The question is whether Sweden is ready to take that position.

The transition from fossil to renewable resources must continue at full strength: for the climate, preparedness and Swedish competitiveness. The forest sector is one of the industries that can deliver on all three fronts, but it requires the right conditions: a functioning value chain, stable long-term rules
content.subject: Sustainability

content.title: Making integrated climate and financial data a strategic asset for the property sector
content.description: How can climate-related data be integrated into financial decisions? Despite growing requirements for climate risk and impact assessments and transition plans, a gap remains. Without reliable, connected data, sustainability risks remaining a reporting exercise rather than directing capital and reducing emissions.
content.extendedDescription:
Join an inspiring discussion offering insights and understanding of how to bridge the gap between climate data and financial information in your operations.
Aspia's climate and sustainability experts moderate the panel, where JM, Vacse and Eidra share practical experiences and perspectives on developing the connection between climate and finance.
The discussion combines concrete examples and reflections on moving from reporting to data-driven management, addressing:
- Where in organisations and processes does the connection between financial and climate-related information break down?
- Can artificial intelligence help us move from calculations to strategy and action to reduce climate impact and manage climate risks?
- How can insights from carbon accounts and climate risk assessments become relevant to financial decisions?
content.subject: Economy

content.title: We know what is coming – why are we not adapting better to climate change?
content.description: How do we make climate adaptation a natural part of planning and construction – rather than something we address when it is already too late?
content.extendedDescription:
Flooded homes. Closed schools. Businesses forced to shut their doors. These are not future scenarios – they are happening across Sweden right now.

Yet climate adaptation of the built environment is progressing too slowly. Not because we lack knowledge, but because responsibilities are poorly allocated, funding is insufficient and requirements are too weak.

The consequences are uninsurable properties and areas, disruption to essential services, and damage to infrastructure and buildings.

The next storm will not wait until we are ready.

During the seminar, Sweden Green Building Council (SGBC) highlights its report När stormen kommer, on accelerating climate adaptation of the built environment through a more reasonable allocation of responsibilities, smarter investments and tougher requirements. The seminar starts from the report's conclusions but focuses on the next step: what must the state, municipalities, public-sector clients and property owners do now, before the next cloudburst, storm or heatwave affects more people?
content.subject: Sustainability

content.title: The world's best healthcare system – why is it developing in sparsely populated areas?
content.description: In inland Västerbotten, there is one of the world's best primary healthcare systems, recognised by organisations including the WHO. Since 2025, a national assignment has focused on knowledge development, research and innovation, working with the rest of Sweden to take the next step towards even better care.
content.extendedDescription: Care models and smart working methods centred on individuals show that good, equitable care can be provided around the clock even in sparsely populated areas, despite long distances and demographic changes that leave fewer people to meet an ageing population's needs. Conditions for health and care in sparsely populated areas differ in many ways from those in urban settings. Long distances mean more care must be provided locally, primary care staff need both broad and specialised expertise, and regions, municipalities and residents must cooperate closely. Rapid technological development and access to data create new opportunities but also place greater demands on organisation, working methods and skills. How can we ensure that people, organisations and systems are equipped for this transition, so technology supports rather than complicates equitable, locally accessible care in rural and sparsely populated areas throughout Sweden?

content.title: AI and democracy – Europe’s Next Generation: Hope, Power and diversity of Democracy
content.description: Across Europe, young people are stepping into a world shaped by rapid change — from shifting democracies to digital disruption, climate anxiety and new geopolitical realities.
content.extendedDescription:
Part 1: Tech giants’ investments in AI represent the largest infrastructure shift in modern history. These developments are reshaping our societies, labour markets and information flows — and, ultimately, our democracies. Today, a handful of global actors make decisions that affect us all, yet without democratic oversight. The question is unavoidable: how can citizens influence a future that is being built by others?
This event takes an independent look at AI as a democratic and society defining issue. In an open conversation, representatives from politics, the tech sector and civil society explore who is currently setting the rules for AI, how Sweden and Europe can reclaim democratic agency, and what we should expect from our elected leaders before it is too late. The audience is invited to take an active part in the discussion.

PART 2: Discussion Diversity of Democracy in Almedalen has offered clear, strong impressions and knowledge of AI for youth. What was important?

content.title: We get the labour market we create together
content.description: Many employers are looking for staff but cannot find anyone suitable. Meanwhile, many people are out of work. Is this really a skills shortage – or are we looking in the wrong way?
content.extendedDescription:
Gotland faces a major challenge, perhaps its biggest!
Recruiting and growing as an organisation or business is becoming increasingly difficult.
We can no longer afford to have people excluded from working life and organisations unable to staff their operations and develop.
Employers now need courage and new thinking. But how easy is that?
How can we support employers? How can we make it easier to think differently, so they dare to employ people who are not “100% ready” or consider new types of roles in their businesses and organisations?

The Matcha kompetensen project, part of Gotland Forward, presents the service it has created. Uniquely, the municipality and Arbetsförmedlingen jointly offer support to employers in both private business and the public sector, tailored to the needs of each employer and workplace.

What difference can it make when employers receive support to genuinely succeed in recruitment? Will more people participate in the labour market, and will it create growth?

content.title: Can entrepreneurship address both poverty and sustainability?
content.description: How do we create economic development that reduces poverty, creates jobs and stays within planetary boundaries? How can more people – especially women, who often face less favourable economic conditions – gain the opportunity to start and run businesses?
content.extendedDescription:
Hand in Hand Sweden works globally to support people, particularly women, in starting and developing small businesses. This creates jobs, strengthens local economies and makes communities more resilient. Experience shows that entrepreneurship and access to capital are crucial to fighting poverty and enabling sustainable development.
Yet today's economic systems are often dominated by large companies, powerful institutions and production methods that are not always sustainable in the long term. How can entrepreneurs and smaller businesses drive progress towards a more sustainable economy that also includes groups often living in poverty?
Join a breakfast discussion bringing together entrepreneurs, business representatives and politicians to discuss entrepreneurship's role in a sustainable, inclusive economy. Focusing on developing economies and drawing clear parallels with Sweden, we explore how political decisions, capital and skills can create better conditions for growth.
content.subject: Business

content.title: How should we assess evidence in labour market policy?
content.description: How robust is the evidence underpinning the government's shift in labour market policy – and what happens when it turns out to rest on uncertain methodological choices? When key evaluations are questioned, the knowledge base of labour market policy comes under scrutiny.
content.extendedDescription: IFAU's impact evaluation of Rusta och matcha has had considerable influence and informed political decisions to reduce the role of independent job-matching providers. But a replication of the study using the same data, conducted by Svenskt Näringsliv, shows that its conclusions are not robust. In practice, this means political decisions may have been based on fragile evidence. A possible consequence is a reassessment of matching services, risking poorer support for jobseekers and a less effective matching system. The question is therefore not just what the findings show, but how we ensure they are reliable before translating them into policy. The panel discusses the political consequences of IFAU's report, evaluation agencies' responsibility for presenting findings in policy reports, how to ensure evaluations actually measure what we think they measure, and what is at stake for unemployed people, employers and the matching system when evidence is weak.
content.subject: Employment/labour market

content.title: From reactive to proactive health – how do we make the transition?
content.description: Sickness absence is increasing, and mental ill health is the most common reason for long-term sick leave. Yet much ill health is preventable. How can employers, healthcare services and society work more proactively to reduce sick leave and improve employee health?
content.extendedDescription:
Sickness absence and mental ill health pose growing challenges for individuals, employers and the economy. In recent years, the costs of prolonged sick leave have risen sharply, while much ill health is considered preventable through earlier intervention.
The discussion starts from how a more preventive approach can be developed at the interface between working life and healthcare.
Occupational health services have traditionally had a preventive role, but in practice interventions often begin only after problems have arisen.

The seminar explores how employers can work more proactively with employee health, the role of cooperation between private and public healthcare, and the structural barriers that exist today. It focuses on how early interventions, better use of technology and data, and new working methods can reduce sickness absence and create more sustainable workplaces.

The event takes the form of a moderated discussion.

speakerTitles: Head of HR and People Development

content.title: We face major climate change – how can we plan and build a sustainable society?
content.description: The transition concerns both concrete measures to reduce emissions from different sectors of society and the lifestyle changes needed to achieve the goal of limiting the planet's temperature increase to 1.5–2 degrees.
content.extendedDescription: We must reduce greenhouse gas emissions and stay within planetary boundaries. Fossil fuels must be replaced with renewable energy sources. Ecological sustainability means shifting agriculture, forestry and marine production to regenerative methods that preserve biodiversity. Social sustainability means a society that meets people's basic needs and gives them meaning in life. Cities must be transformed to rely on walking, cycling and public transport rather than mass car use. Existing buildings and new developments must become energy-efficient, and the materials used must not cause large climate emissions. We must move away from today's throwaway consumption towards quality, repairability and reuse. Production must therefore shift from a linear to a circular economy. Economic sustainability means moving away from a society based on growth, reducing economic inequality and making these changes possible.

content.title: What happens to a person who has survived war – and who takes responsibility for recovery?
content.description: Hundreds of thousands of Ukrainian military personnel carry traumatic experiences from the frontline. Reintegration into civilian life requires more than medical care – it requires psychological rehabilitation, social support and long-term resilience. What can Sweden contribute?
content.extendedDescription:
The war in Ukraine has created a generational problem: hundreds of thousands of soldiers carry frontline trauma that no medical treatment alone can resolve. PTSD, survivor guilt, relationship problems and difficulty returning to everyday life are well-known consequences of prolonged combat service – but in Ukraine this is happening on a scale without a modern equivalent.
This discussion brings together Ukrainian and Swedish practitioners in psychological rehabilitation, military medicine and reintegration to discuss what actually works: which methods produce results, what Ukrainian experience can teach Sweden about preparedness, and how to build long-term psychological resilience among those who have borne war's heaviest burden.

The event is part of Samarbetsplattformen: Sverige & Ukraina (SPSU), an initiative by KlinteVolontär that gives Ukrainian civil society its own voice in Swedish democratic debate and brings together Swedish and Ukrainian organisations to strengthen long-term cooperation.

content.title: The criminal economy – how do we stop the money?
content.description: Organised economic crime generates annual turnover of SEK 352 billion. To function, the money must be able to move through legitimate systems. Cooperation and information sharing have strengthened in recent years – is that enough? What is the next step towards cutting off the criminal economy?
content.extendedDescription:
Fraud against households and businesses is increasing rapidly and generates substantial capital flows that strengthen criminal networks. The financial sector is society's economic infrastructure. It can be exploited when systems fail, but is also one of the most effective tools for stopping the criminal economy.

Important steps have been taken in recent years to strengthen cooperation and information sharing between authorities and financial institutions, including through Polismyndigheten's financial intelligence centre. Restrictions on information sharing between authorities have now been eased. What difference has this made, and what is needed next? How can information sharing between financial companies, authorities and private organisations be strengthened further?

Länsförsäkringar encounters the consequences of fraud and economic crime every day. We are now bringing relevant stakeholders together to discuss responsibility, cooperation and closing gaps in the system without undermining trust in the financial system.
content.subject: Justice/crime

content.title: Sustainable development of attractive cities – how Sweden can lead the way
content.description: Sweden's cities face climate change, security threats and social challenges. How can cities develop to achieve the goal of making Sweden a leader in the sustainable development of attractive cities? What is required of the state, municipalities and business?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden's cities face major challenges. Meeting them requires the state, municipalities and business to cooperate on planning, financing and designing tomorrow's cities. Rådet för levande städer invites you to discuss how quality of life can drive the development of climate-neutral, robust and socially sustainable living environments.

The research funding call “Kommuner utformade för framtiden – klimatneutrala, robusta och socialt hållbara” is currently open as part of the cooperation within Rådet för levande städer. The discussion explores the contributions needed from the state, municipalities and business to advance the transition.

Rådet för levande städer has a government mandate to coordinate public authorities' urban development work. The national goal is for “Sweden's cities, according to their circumstances, to develop into vibrant, safe and robust living environments where people enjoy spending time. Sweden should lead the way in the sustainable development of attractive cities.”

content.title: Mice cannot get Alzheimer's
content.description: Mice cannot get Alzheimer's, yet they are the animals most commonly used to understand the disease. Questioning the use of mice in Alzheimer's research is not just about a single animal experiment, but a broader societal issue. How can we get to the bottom of it?
content.extendedDescription:
Mice are very frequently used in Alzheimer's research, although they cannot naturally develop the disease in the same way as humans. Researchers therefore modify their genes so they develop certain brain changes resembling those in humans. This creates an artificial model of the disease. Yet many treatments that worked in mice subsequently failed in human studies.
This raises an important societal question: why are animals used in research when results are often difficult to transfer to humans? The issue concerns both scientific reliability and ethics. If research models do not reflect human diseases, substantial resources risk being spent on methods that do not lead to effective treatments. Animal experiments also cause animals suffering. It is therefore important to discuss whether current research methods are the most effective and ethically defensible, or whether more resources should be invested in alternatives
content.subject: Research

content.title: Children's needs or police maps – what should determine access to organised sport?
content.description: Access to sport and association activities differs depending on where you grow up. How can more children and young people have meaningful leisure opportunities? What can national and municipal policymakers contribute?
content.extendedDescription: The sports movement actively promotes children and young people's participation in organised sport. Alongside physical activity and better health, it creates community, joy and belonging – meaningful leisure time that helps society and individuals see opportunities and have hope for the future. Idrottsklivet scales up this work, supported by annual government funding of 100 million. Its purpose is to strengthen the sports movement in areas designated as vulnerable by Polismyndigheten. But sedentary lifestyles, growing health inequalities, insecurity, ill health and crime are not determined by lines drawn on a police map. A survey by Riksidrottsförbundet shows substantial investment needs in areas outside the police list too. Its analysis identifies a further 200 areas with significant needs, home to approximately 130,000 children. #civilsamhällesarenen

content.title: From global water crisis to Gotland's transition: how do we build Europe's water resilience?
content.description: The UN now warns that many parts of the world have moved from a water crisis to what is called water bankruptcy: a situation where water systems are pushed beyond their ability to recover. On Gotland, this is already a reality – what does the global water crisis mean for Sweden in practice?
content.extendedDescription:
Meanwhile, the EU has launched its first comprehensive Water Resilience Strategy to address growing water scarcity, pollution and extreme weather in Europe. But what does the global water crisis mean for Sweden in practice?

Gotland is undertaking long-term work to address water shortages and develop new solutions for a more resilient society. What happens on the island could become an important model for how regions in Sweden and Europe can meet future water challenges.

This discussion brings together politics, research and practice to explore how local experience can connect with European policy and innovation. How can Sweden contribute to the EU's water transition? How can research and innovation become a competitive advantage in a world where water is an increasingly strategic resource? And what can the rest of the country already learn from Gotland's work?

A discussion about a transition already underway, and how local solutions can have global significance.

content.title: Attractiveness, identity and energy efficiency in properties with cultural heritage value
content.description: Renovating existing buildings is crucial to reducing society's climate and energy impact. Yet many properties have cultural and historical values requiring sensitive development. How can energy efficiency improvements strengthen rather than weaken buildings' identity and quality?
content.extendedDescription:
How can energy efficiency improvements be made in buildings of cultural and historical value without losing their identity and heritage? This question is central to the climate transition and requires cooperation between property owners, architects, energy experts and heritage specialists.

The seminar explores how cooperation between energy expertise, architecture and conservation expertise can create solutions that both reduce climate impact and improve buildings' appeal and usefulness.

Examples and experience inform a discussion of the analyses, decision-making evidence and working methods that can help property owners make sustainable decisions. The discussion also covers the expertise and documentation that can be requested in dialogue between property owners, consultants and permitting authorities.

The event is aimed at property owners, developers, public organisations and others managing and developing buildings of cultural and historical value.

content.title: Can digitalisation contribute to green fashion?
content.description: Fashion retail is undergoing a major transformation driven by companies' own ambitions to become more competitive and sustainable, consumers' growing expectations and, finally, strong political pressure reflected in the wave of EU legislation.
content.extendedDescription:
The future-proof Almedalsgarderob – digitalisation contributes to green fashion.
Achieving this requires new business models, materials and technologies. This includes using and reusing clothes for longer, as well as making use of digital opportunities.

For 10 years, Svensk Handel's Almedalsgarderob has been a meeting place for fashion enthusiasts, giving visitors the opportunity to look their best during the week by borrowing clothes from some of Sweden's leading fashion companies. To remain competitive, however, both established companies and second-hand businesses must keep pace with digital development. Come and hear how Svensk Handel ensures Swedish companies benefit from the opportunities presented by the digital and green transitions. GS1 Sweden and Högskolan i Borås will help us demonstrate the latest innovations, including next-generation QR codes and smart mirrors.

content.title: Young managers are missing, but the future cannot wait. How do we pave the way for the next generation of leaders?
content.description: Young leaders are needed more than ever. But what prevents them from becoming managers? What can established managers contribute, and what is needed from young people today? We need decisive action to create sustainable leadership at a time when the future feels more uncertain than ever.
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden and the world are experiencing growing polarisation, economic uncertainty, declining trust in institutions and a labour market changing faster than organisations can adapt. Meanwhile, we face an acute shortage of young managers. Sweden currently has a smaller proportion of young managers than the European average. This is not just a skills problem, but a societal problem.

We bring together young managers and leaders, representatives of business and other sectors to discuss what being a young manager is really like and what happens to an organisation when young people take leadership roles. What are the challenges and success factors? How can organisations be built that young people want to lead and have the opportunity to lead? What does this require of young people themselves and of organisations seeking to secure their skills supply and invest in young managers?

content.title: Values-led urban development – good neighbours as a source of societal benefit
content.description: How can we create a society with a natural place for everyone through healthcare, social care and education? What happens when values guide and underpin urban development, and when a district must accommodate 10,000 residents?
content.extendedDescription: When fully developed, Stora Sköndal will be a district where 10,000 people live, work, study and lead their lives. Its considerable natural and cultural assets provide a place accommodating different needs, focusing on inclusion, diversity and sustainability – a society with room for everyone. Urban development faces complex sustainability challenges requiring a balance between social, environmental and economic perspectives. Socially, inclusive and safe environments are needed, but segregation and inequality risk worsening without long-term planning. Society has many positive forces and initiatives, and successful cooperation makes us stronger. Environmentally, cities must reduce climate impact through energy efficiency, sustainable transport and ecosystem preservation, while urbanisation increases pressure on land and resources. Economically, major investments and affordable housing are needed, creating tensions between profitability and social sustainability.

content.title: How do we create schools where teachers and headteachers thrive – and what becomes possible then?
content.description: Many schools struggle with high staff turnover, particularly among headteachers. This raises questions about continuity and direction. Yet some schools have teachers and headteachers who thrive and stay longer. What role does wellbeing play – and what can it enable?
content.extendedDescription:
During Almedalsveckan, Frida Utbildning invites you to a seminar on wellbeing, workplace culture and organisational conditions in schools.
The discussion starts from new research based on 451 micro-reflections from 100 employees, showing how culture takes shape through everyday actions.
Researcher Martin Lackéus presents the study's design and findings. The discussion then continues with Malin Stjernman, CEO of Fridaskolorna, who offers the organisation's perspective on the findings and reflections on what can enable lasting wellbeing.
Psychologists Johannes Lundell and Per-Anders Green from Cadena Psykolog deepen the discussion with interpretations of what influences behaviour, motivation and the working environment, focusing particularly on good relationships and what research calls relational coordination.

After the seminar, the conversation continues on the terrace outside, where the audience can ask questions and talk with the panel.

content.title: How do we create long-term conditions for building housing for older people?
content.description: Sweden faces a sharp increase in its older population, particularly those over 80, while access to secure housing is declining. The sector wants to contribute, but projects are financially challenging without investment support. How can we meet the needs, with or without new support?
content.extendedDescription:
There are three reasons why Sweden faces a housing crisis for older people.

• Construction of new care homes and other housing for older people has not kept pace with needs, despite a sharp rise in the number of people over 80.

• Municipalities cannot finance the necessary investments alone. General government grants are crucial to running elder care but are neither intended nor sufficient for new construction.

• Investment support for housing for older people has been abolished.

Sweden faces a choice. Municipal investment needs are growing, the population is ageing and more older people remain in homes not adapted to tomorrow's needs. The question is not whether to act, but how. Should municipalities be left to bear the investments alone? Is it reasonable for older people to be forced to remain in homes that limit their safety and quality of life? Or must the state take greater responsibility?

This seminar discusses ways forward and solutions that work.
content.subject: Older people
speakerTitles: Head of Business Development, Residential Elder Care

content.title: How can Sweden attract the world's best startups – and enable them to stay?
content.description: Sweden competes globally for innovative companies, entrepreneurs and international talent. Yet both foreign founders and Swedish startups face barriers to establishment, residence permits and recruitment. What is needed for more people to choose to build and develop tomorrow's companies?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden competes globally for innovative startups, entrepreneurs and international talent. Yet international founders and Swedish startups face barriers to establishment, residence permits, running a business and recruitment, risking lost investment, innovation and jobs.

Commissioned by Business Sweden under the government's Work in Sweden assignment, SISP has mapped these challenges. The work has produced a policy report and a national playbook to help innovation organisations better support international startups seeking to establish themselves in Sweden and international researchers wishing to commercialise their research here. The seminar presents the playbook for the first time, followed by a discussion of the changes needed to make Sweden more attractive to international startups and talent.

content.title: What does total defence need, and how can capital support the build-up?
content.description: The international situation challenges our safety and security. Total defence needs are growing, nationally and within NATO. Politicians highlight business's role in the build-up. What role should the financial sector play, and how do we mobilise capital to strengthen Sweden's defence capability?
content.extendedDescription:
War in Europe, rising geopolitical tensions and new security threats place greater demands on societal resilience. In response, NATO has agreed to sharply increase investment in total defence, including strengthening civil defence. Meanwhile, Sweden is described as one of Europe's most capital-rich economies, with broad share ownership, strong pension funds and well-developed venture capital and bond markets.

Sweden's defence industry strategy also identifies the need for more private financing and closer cooperation between the state and business. But what investments are required to build tomorrow's total defence? How should they be financed? And what role can the financial sector and Swedish capital markets play in strengthening Sweden's security and preparedness?

The discussion addresses needs, financing and the way forward.

content.title: Time for Sweden to wake up if we are to benefit from the Fehmarn Belt link
content.description: When the Fehmarn Belt link opens, Europe's centre of gravity will move closer to Sweden. The challenge is to ensure infrastructure, business and tourism are equipped to seize the opportunities arising from greater accessibility and competition.
content.extendedDescription:
The Fehmarn Belt link is northern Europe's largest infrastructure investment. Together with other investments, such as the expansion of Copenhagen International Airport, it creates new opportunities for Swedish trade, investment, skills supply, tourism and international accessibility.

Fully benefiting from these new flows requires investment in Swedish infrastructure and transport capacity, and a clear national strategy. Although often viewed as a southern Swedish issue, it concerns the competitiveness of all Sweden and the Nordic region in a growing European corridor.

Drawing on a new scenario report, Visit Skåne and Malmö stad invite Visit Sweden and Visita to discuss how Sweden can prepare for increased flows. The focus is on destination development, tourism, accessibility, regional development and international competitiveness. Moderator Max Granström, Visit Skåne, presents the report and leads the discussion.

content.title: Back to the future – biogas as energy for preparedness
content.description: Untapped biogas production potential could provide energy for preparedness with multiple synergies: greater energy security, reduced dependence on fossil fuel imports, secure gas supplies for industry, transport and electricity generation, and greater food security while reducing climate impact.
content.extendedDescription:
Swedish biogas could be key to our energy preparedness. Small and large biogas plants can provide dispatchable, flexible backup power and island-mode operation for municipalities, and local Swedish energy for industry, agriculture and essential services. Residual streams can also become biofertiliser, improving food security. International demand is growing for robust energy systems based on renewable, local resources available during crises. Scaling up our own production can enhance Swedish competitiveness as a leader in circular energy supply.
Help shape the discussion at Omställningsarenan in Sweco's courtyard in Visby during Almedalsveckan! For the fourth consecutive year, forward-looking actors in the built environment sector gather here. content.title: Choosing upper secondary education – too early and too difficult?

Could a revised upper secondary structure with broader entry routes and gradual choices meet industry's skills needs?

Swedish industry underpins welfare, growth and our ability to remain strong in crises. Yet Industrirådet's skills analysis identifies serious challenges in every industrial sector. These threaten not only defence capability, production, innovation and competitiveness, but also the green transition.

Is today's upper secondary structure, based on early specialisation choices, one reason too few students take industry-relevant courses? Could broader entry routes and gradual choices be part of the solution? The 15-year-olds choosing their education may lack the decision-making skills the current system requires.

Could a new upper secondary structure also improve gender balance, increase the number of students completing school and help them establish themselves in the labour market? content.title: From waste to resource – making the civil engineering sector circular
content.description: Producing new materials causes far too many carbon dioxide emissions. How can we extend materials' lifespans while increasing reuse in civil engineering? What can we learn from previous generations?
content.extendedDescription: The panel begins by discussing how civil engineering can work more circularly with excavated materials, soils and organic resources. The focus is on reusing materials currently transported away or classified as waste in new projects, reducing climate impact and costs and using land more efficiently without consuming new natural resources. What role does the location of these “resource sites” play for the environment and projects? The discussion also examines how construction and civil engineering previously worked more closely with natural conditions and local resources than is often the case today, in Sweden and elsewhere. It addresses how today's built environment development affects land, agriculture and biodiversity, and the consequences for future generations. content.title: Knowledge and democracy under pressure – is the Swedish system holding up?
content.description: We live in a time when both knowledge and democracy face intense pressure worldwide. Politicians must make far-reaching decisions on climate, migration, crime and welfare, and need solid facts more than ever. But how well does Sweden's machinery for providing that knowledge work?
content.extendedDescription:
We read about legislation passed despite warnings from consultation bodies, experts and Lagrådet. What happens if confidence in the process begins to falter and decision-makers start distrusting public administration and experts generally?
New research shows that broad, independent committee inquiries have gradually been replaced by rapid, politically directed inquiries with narrow terms of reference, short deadlines and predetermined directions. The evidence base becomes thinner and independence weaker. The result is poorer laws, poorer decisions and ultimately eroded trust in both democracy and scientific experts, just when polarisation is at its worst. So what is needed to equip the system for the future, and who takes the lead: government, parliament, public authorities, researchers or civil society? What does it take for our democratic rules to endure in an ever faster-moving world? Are new institutional solutions needed, and if so, what would they look like?

content.title: How do Ukrainians preserve their culture in exile – and what can each Swedish region contribute?
content.description: Around 50,000 Ukrainians live in Sweden today, spread across the country. Access to Ukrainian literature, culture and community varies enormously between regions. How can civil society ensure Ukrainian identity and culture survive in exile, wherever people live?
content.extendedDescription:
A Ukrainian in Stockholm can find Ukrainian books, cultural programmes and a community of compatriots. A Ukrainian in Jämtland or Blekinge cannot. This unequal access to one's cultural heritage affects children most severely – those growing up without access to their language, stories and history.
Civil society has begun responding: initiatives to establish Ukrainian libraries in every Swedish region, with physical collections of literature, children's books and cultural resources, aim to give Ukrainian families a cultural anchor wherever they are in Sweden.
This discussion explores what is needed to build such infrastructure nationally: how can regions, municipalities and library institutions be engaged, and what can Ukrainian civil society in Sweden achieve on its own?

The discussion is part of Samarbetsplattformen: Sverige & Ukraina (SPSU), KlinteVolontär's project to give Ukrainian civil society a voice in Swedish debate.

content.title: Short-term politics threatens industrial jobs – Sweden risks losing its future
content.description: Sweden's pulp and paper industry faces high costs and an uncertain world. Industrial jobs are threatened when short-term symbolic policies take priority over long-term investment. How can policy create stable conditions securing industry's survival, investment and future jobs?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden's pulp and paper industry is at a critical point. The trade union Pappers sees how uncertain energy policy, weak policy instruments and a lack of stable long-term rules drive up costs, hamper investment and threaten jobs. Major redundancy announcements show that the crisis is not approaching – it is already here.

Current policy does not meet industry's needs. Active industrial policy is required to create stable, predictable conditions, a prerequisite for investment in fossil-free production and new technology in Sweden.

During the seminar, Pontus Georgsson, President of Pappers, and Jonas Algers, Industrial Policy Analyst at Katalys, present three reform proposals to strengthen competitiveness, secure investment and safeguard jobs throughout the country.

A discussion between politics, civil society and business follows, on moving from short-term measures to policies that build tomorrow's industry.

content.title: The Tidö Pact – the agreement's consequences for Swedish politics and democracy
content.description: The Tidö Agreement meant that Moderaterna, Kristdemokraterna and Liberalerna abandoned their previous refusal to cooperate with Sverigedemokraterna. Why did they change their minds? And what does the agreement mean for democracy in Sweden?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden was long an exception in Europe. A right-wing parliamentary majority refused to cooperate with a populist radical-right party, allowing a red–green minority government to govern instead. Sweden is no longer an exception. Through the Tidö Agreement, Sverigedemokraterna has been normalised.
The book “Tidöpakten. Så förändras Sverige” (Atlas, 2026) examines different explanations for what happened. Did pressure from members and voters of Moderaterna, Kristdemokraterna and Liberalerna become too strong for their leaders to resist? Or has Sverigedemokraterna changed? Is the party no longer coloured by its ideological roots, removing its pariah status?
Does the Tidö Agreement erode legal certainty and individual rights and freedoms in ways that contradict liberal democracy? What do research and established experience say about strategies established parties can use to counter the growing political strength of populist radical-right parties?

content.title: How can regional cooperation facilitate Swedish defence exports?
content.description: Sweden's defence industry needs to accelerate innovation and production to meet growing international demand while strengthening Sweden's defence capability. How can local and regional cooperation strengthen defence exports and companies' competitiveness internationally?

The seminar opens with an overview from the chairs of municipal executive boards and municipal chief executives of each municipality in Svenska säkerhetsstråket.

SOU 2026:16, “Försvarsexportinitiativet – för gemensam säkerhet”, highlights the need to strengthen Swedish defence exports and increase defence industry production. The inquiry also notes that current efforts are often fragmented and lack clear strategic coordination.

The seminar focuses on how local and regional cooperation can strengthen innovation, investment, skills provision and robust supply chains in the defence sector. It particularly discusses the role that regional initiatives and cooperation platforms, such as Svenska säkerhetsstråket and Team Sweden Defence and Security, can play in improving conditions for companies and new establishments throughout Sweden.

The event is a panel discussion with representatives of national, regional and municipal government, business and innovation organisations.

content.title: Saving and preserving kidneys – addressing the growing problem of kidney disease
content.description: Sweden faces a growing problem: chronic kidney disease is increasing, but awareness is low among both the public and primary healthcare providers. Many people remain undiagnosed for a long time and miss treatment that could slow the disease. Meanwhile, the system delays the introduction of effective new medicines.
content.extendedDescription:
The consequences are poorer quality of life for patients and substantial costs for healthcare and society. The later chronic kidney disease is detected, the greater the risk of needing dialysis or a kidney transplant to survive. Improving the situation requires earlier detection, lifestyle changes and appropriate treatment to slow progression and preserve kidney function.

The seminar launches the report “Att rädda och spara njurar – om en växande sjukdomsbörda och värdet av att bromsa kronisk njursjukdom”. It examines the disease's prevalence, medical and socioeconomic consequences, patients' circumstances, the value of treatment and the measures needed for more sustainable kidney care.

Clinical experts, patient representatives and decision-makers meet to discuss how Sweden can take a comprehensive approach to kidney health and improve patients' quality of life and prospects.

content.title: High Tech – Low Tech: how do we build the future together?
content.description: Traditional materials expertise and new digital opportunities can jointly contribute to a more sustainable built environment. New forms of cooperation emerge at the interface between high tech and low tech, through informed, evidence-based decisions and new groups of actors at new stages.

The discussion explores creativity, craftsmanship and how data can improve decision-making evidence, resource flows and climate performance throughout the value chain.

The seminar is based on learning by doing. Participants are invited to test, discuss and develop ideas together about combining technology, materials and data to meet future challenges. The focus is not only on technical solutions but also on the people, relationships and cooperation needed for a successful transition.

Working together in new combinations creates knowledge and understanding between actors from different sectors. It also builds the trust, networks and capacity for cooperation needed to develop tomorrow's sustainable society.

content.title: Sustainable urban development – creating attractive and resilient cities
content.description: Cities are changing rapidly. Under pressure from climate crises, demographic shifts and new ways of living and working, we are constantly changing. Yet urban development is too often driven by short-term priorities, fragmented responsibilities and project-by-project thinking instead of a clear strategy.
content.extendedDescription:
Today, we understand more than ever how places affect everyday life, economic development and long-term resilience. One principle remains constant: when people are the starting point, long-term value follows. Through our involvement across the value chain, from early development and construction to investment, operations and long-term ownership, we see how holistic, collaborative approaches reduce risks, strengthen resilience and create lasting value for people, cities and investors. This means integrating social, environmental and economic considerations from the outset, coordinating stakeholders around shared goals and managing development from a lifecycle perspective. But how do we create partnerships that add value, reduce risks and generate growth?

content.title: How do we create good, cost-effective living environments for an ageing population?
content.description: Sweden's population is ageing, increasing the need for secure, socially sustainable and affordable housing. Meanwhile, municipalities face high costs, growing home-care needs and loneliness among older people. Can converting apartment buildings into co-housing communities create companionship, security and lower costs?
content.extendedDescription:
Good living environments for older people are one of today's major societal issues. Traditional solutions, such as newly built sheltered housing, are often expensive, take a long time to deliver and reach a limited group. Research also shows that loneliness and a lack of social connection affect older people's health and security as much as access to formal care.

The seminar presents an alternative strategy: converting more existing apartment buildings into co-housing communities for older people. These communities can provide everyday companionship, increase security and strengthen the feeling of being needed. Their social structure can also reduce municipal home-care needs through mutual everyday support.

Using the existing housing stock can make the transition faster than building new homes. Conversion often costs less and makes it possible to keep rents affordable for more people. Co-housing can therefore become an option for a broader group of older people.

content.title: Water, wastewater and climate adaptation – how long can decisions be postponed?
content.description: Sweden talks increasingly about robustness. Yet much of its water and sewer network is ageing and was built for a different climate. Government inquiries on greater climate adaptation have clarified both investment needs and systemic risks. Political decisions are still missing.
content.extendedDescription:
Government inquiries into greater water and wastewater preparedness and climate adaptation have clarified investment needs and systemic risks. Yet the key issues of responsibility and funding have still not been advanced politically. Meanwhile, pressure is growing. Cloudbursts and floods strain municipalities and insurance systems. Drinking water supplies and stormwater management are increasingly strategic issues. Every year without decisions increases the investment backlog and vulnerability.

Most funding currently comes from municipal water and wastewater charges. Is it reasonable for households and property owners alone to bear the costs of climate adaptation and robustness? Does Sweden need a national recovery plan for water and wastewater systems as part of a broader strategy for climate adaptation and societal preparedness?

content.title: Northern Sweden's basic industries deliver – if policymakers act
content.description: Industry's operating conditions are crucial to Swedish growth. Investment continues in the north, and industry's skills needs are growing. Yet the international outlook is uncertain. Success requires the right framework conditions. What reforms should a new government implement after the election?

Ahead of the parliamentary election on 13 September, the focus must be on growth, which is crucial to Sweden's long-term prosperity. What reforms strengthen competitiveness, reduce matching problems and increase mobility towards industrial jobs in the north? What incentives encourage people to move where the jobs are? content.title: How do we secure tomorrow's drinking water when systems are put to the test?
content.description: We take water for granted until it is unavailable. Climate change, water scarcity and increased preparedness requirements place new demands on Sweden's water supply. In many places, the focus has shifted from capacity shortages to whether enough raw water exists to produce drinking water.
content.extendedDescription:
Society must manage both everyday challenges and major disruptions. How do we secure access to clean water as conditions change?

In this seminar, experts from the water sector, public services and business discuss future water supplies. The conversation starts from current issues of climate change, water scarcity, preparedness and societal vulnerability, as well as emerging solutions.

How well equipped are our systems today? What can we learn from Gotland's work on water? What role can new technologies play, and how do we create a water supply that works both in everyday life and when society is under pressure?

Topics include water preparedness, climate adaptation and societal vulnerability, and how solutions such as desalination, water reuse and mobile water treatment plants can contribute to more secure supplies.

content.title: Ban gender-segregated swimming sessions
content.description: Honour culture naturally supports gender-segregated swimming sessions: girls' and women's bodies must not be seen by any man other than a husband. Such sessions have been justified as a way to improve swimming skills among girls otherwise forbidden to swim. In practice, however, they reinforce discrimination.
content.extendedDescription:
A lecture on the consequences of gender-segregated swimming sessions and how gender segregation undermines equality, followed by a panel discussion.

Honour culture naturally supports gender-segregated swimming sessions: girls' and women's bodies must not be seen by any man other than a husband, while their brothers and husbands do as they please. Such sessions have been justified as a way to improve swimming skills among girls otherwise forbidden to swim at all. In practice, however, they reinforce discrimination.

Girls in honour cultures grow up ashamed of their bodies, and society's acceptance of this view of women's bodies confirms their families' honour norms. Some girls of compulsory school age are not allowed to attend swimming lessons but must swim at gender-segregated sessions to pass physical education.

GAPF strongly opposes gender-segregated swimming sessions. They conflict with democracy and gender equality and allow oppressive norms to grow stronger.

content.title: When AI changes the rules – is human capability our most important competitive advantage?
content.description: AI is rapidly changing what creates value in an organisation. Processes and technical capacity are becoming easier to copy. What remains is judgement, prioritisation and the ability to make people, technology and business goals work together. How do we build organisations that strengthen the human dimension in the AI era?
content.extendedDescription:
Using fresh data from Wise in cooperation with Novus, the seminar takes a fact-based look at how Swedish organisations develop human capability and what is needed to make it a genuine business strategy in an AI-driven economy.

Together with our panel, we discuss:
• Which capabilities become most crucial as change, digitalisation and AI accelerate.
• How our view of capability influences team building, leadership development and organisational design.
• What is needed to move from intuitive assessment to a more systematic and accurate approach.

Combining data, research and perspectives from business, the social partners and politics, we develop a shared picture of what making human capability a business strategy actually means, and which choices determine whether organisations fully benefit from AI.

The seminar is held in cooperation with Sveriges HR-Förening and Fabege.

content.title: As fears of crisis and war grow, mental ill health increases: outdoor recreation as a key to public health
content.description: Sweden faces its most serious security situation since the Second World War. The increased threat affects not only critical infrastructure and preparedness but also people's mental health profoundly. Psychological preparedness is a crucial component of total defence.
content.extendedDescription:
Research and experience show that prolonged worry, uncertainty and threats create psychological stress across the population. According to the WHO's latest needs assessment in Ukraine, 46 per cent of the population reports mental health problems after three years of full-scale war. Experience from the pandemic also shows how powerfully outdoor recreation can act as a protective factor during crises: nature became one of the most important sources of recovery, stability and reduced anxiety.

Sweden has a strength few countries possess: an outdoor recreation movement of 7,000 associations with two million memberships. Research shows that nature and outdoor recreation reduce stress and anxiety, among other benefits, and strengthen recovery.

These psychological mechanisms can also protect populations during crises and war. How can society make use of this movement's strength and the lessons from the pandemic about the importance of outdoor recreation?
