content.title: The neighbourhood police officer: a forgotten model for strengthening safety in vulnerable areas?
content.description: In several vulnerable areas, crime, parallel power structures and low trust in public institutions challenge the effectiveness of the rule of law. A renewed investment in neighbourhood policing could strengthen the state's local presence and increase safety and trust in everyday life.
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden faces growing challenges involving crime, insecurity and parallel power structures in vulnerable areas. This is not only about law enforcement, but the state's fundamental ability to uphold the rule of law in everyday life. When the law's effectiveness weakens, trust in society's institutions also risks eroding.

Meanwhile, local police presence has weakened over a long period through centralisation, police station closures and reduced continuous presence in communities. Several evaluations show that the goal of bringing police closer to citizens has only partly been achieved.

The seminar starts with the short documentary Polisen Ulf, following integration police officer Ulf Boström and his foot patrol work in a vulnerable area of Göteborg. After the screening, we talk with Ulf about how renewed investment in neighbourhood policing can strengthen safety and trust in vulnerable areas.

content.title: It does not happen here – or does it? Abuse of power for sex in Sweden
content.description: How does sexual corruption manifest itself in Sweden? What blind spots exist in Swedish legislation, and what should we do about them?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden is often perceived as one of the world's least corrupt and most gender-equal countries. Yet corruption in which sex is the currency occurs in Swedish public authorities, civil society organisations and companies.

Sexual corruption is the abuse of power for personal gain, with sex as the currency. Such corruption undermines trust in democratic institutions, even more than other forms of corruption. It is an old phenomenon but a new concept, now receiving attention on several fronts. Uppsala University Research Environment on Sexual Corruption (UU-RESC) studies this specific type of corruption. For two years, the UN has urged states to address corruption involving sex specifically. For the first time, sexual corruption is also highlighted in a Swedish context in the government inquiry into criminal-law measures against corruption and misconduct in public office (SOU 2025:87).

In this panel, researchers and anti-corruption experts discuss what corruption legislation is needed.

content.title: When geopolitics becomes code: cyberattacks against the Nordic region in a new security landscape
content.description: The Baltic Sea and Arctic have become central to great-power dynamics. Nordic energy production, submarine cables and digital infrastructure are strategic targets. State actors conduct grey-zone cyber operations: espionage, preparations for sabotage and influence campaigns. How do we build resilience?
content.extendedDescription:
Geopolitical tensions increasingly translate into concrete cyber activities against Nordic targets. State and state-linked actors use cyberattacks for pressure, intelligence gathering and signalling, often in the grey zone below the threshold of armed conflict. Reconnaissance, penetration testing and preparations for sabotage target critical infrastructure, while hybrid attacks such as DDoS attacks are combined with information manipulation and data leaks around political processes, elections and NATO milestones.

The seminar begins with a brief lecture by PwC's Cyber Threat Intelligence experts, outlining the Nordic region's place in today's security landscape, the geopolitical drivers of cyber operations and patterns of activity against Nordic targets.

The panel then addresses threats and trends, actors targeting the Nordic region, risk management informed by geopolitical analysis, cooperation between authorities and business, and other issues.

content.title: Sustainability through quality-assured measurement, traceability and digital product passports in the forest industry
content.description: We want to build more with wood – but how do we know it is actually sustainable? When data follows materials from forest to reuse, digital product passports can provide evidence, not just claims, about origin, processing, climate impact, quality and reusability.
content.extendedDescription:
Wood is a key material in the transition, but sustainability cannot rest on assumptions. It must be demonstrated, verified and improved. Large amounts of data are collected along the forest value chain today, but information often remains trapped in separate systems.
You will hear a presentation with examples from technology and a demonstrator. We show how traceability methods can connect data sources and establish relationships between measurements that otherwise remain isolated islands of data. We introduce ENTER, a research project developing a demonstrator for a digital value chain from forests and sawmills to building systems, construction, management and reuse, using real data and connected APIs.
Imagine a plank had eyes. What would it see along the way? The digital process declaration collects actual measurements – the product's ACTUAL values. The digital product passport brings together standards, certifications and product specifications – its REQUIRED values. Together, they provide a basis for sustainability, improvement and competitiveness.

content.title: From knowledge to action – what is needed to reduce nutrient losses from agriculture?
content.description: Agriculture around the Baltic Sea is the single largest source of phosphorus and nitrogen emissions into lakes and seas. We know which measures effectively reduce these losses into our sensitive sea, but what prevents farmers from implementing them?
content.extendedDescription:
Agriculture around the Baltic Sea is the single largest source of phosphorus and nitrogen emissions into the sea, contributing to eutrophication, algal blooms and oxygen depletion in one of the world's most sensitive inland seas. Extensive knowledge exists today about measures that effectively reduce nutrient losses from farmland, including improved nutrient balances, catch crops, structural liming, gypsum treatment, buffer strips and adapted tillage. Yet the transition is slower than environmental targets and the ecosystem require. What actually determines whether measures are implemented? Is it economics, motivation, regulations, knowledge transfer, production risks or something else?

During this panel discussion, farmers from different parts of the Baltic Sea region share their experiences of actively reducing nutrient losses. Experts then discuss barriers and opportunities for encouraging more people to take action for a cleaner sea.

content.title: The lack of rehabilitation – a loss for individuals and society
content.description: People with neurological or rheumatic diseases unnecessarily lose their ability to work. Medicines can help, but rehabilitation is often the only treatment enabling people to function in everyday life. Unfortunately, many receive no rehabilitation at all – a major loss for individuals and society.
content.extendedDescription:
We invite you to a discussion-based seminar focusing on patients' perspectives. We highlight what rehabilitation can mean for individuals' ability to live independently and for society through lower costs for benefits, personal assistance and other support.
Several reports show that access to rehabilitation is low, has declined and is unequal. The Health and Medical Services Act is clear: everyone is entitled to rehabilitation. Responsibility is shared by regions and municipalities, contributing to shortcomings and inequality.

Sweden faces skills shortages across much of the labour market. With appropriate support and rehabilitation, many people could remain employed and contribute to society and their own livelihoods.

Investment in rehabilitation pays off in several ways. Society gains higher tax revenues and lower costs for sickness compensation and personal assistance, healthcare needs decrease, and individuals' autonomy and independence increase.

content.title: Scale up – use medical technology for equitable care, shorter waiting lists and stronger competitiveness
content.description: Sweden faces societal challenges involving healthcare waiting lists, unequal care and an ageing population. At the same time, we need more growth and stronger competitiveness. Medical technology contributes solutions in these areas, but barriers prevent scaling up.

Medical technology enables early detection, safer treatments and more personalised care. For cancer patients, it is part of every step from diagnosis to rehabilitation. For healthcare services, it increases efficiency and frees up time through digital solutions, hospital care at home and self-monitoring, while strengthening patient safety. Sweden is one of Europe's leading countries for medtech patent applications. When the medical technology sector grows here, Sweden grows and strengthens Europe. When medical innovations are used in healthcare, patients, healthcare services and society benefit.

But barriers remain. What is needed to scale up the use of medical technology for more equitable care, shorter waiting lists and stronger competitiveness?

content.title: Time passes, but Alzheimer's disease remains
content.description: Alzheimer's disease should be treated like other diseases. In January 2025, the Minister for Older People and Social Security tasked Vård- och omsorgsanalys with investigating whether knowledge and experience from cancer care could strengthen health and social care for people with dementia.
content.extendedDescription:
Alzheimer's disease is not part of natural ageing. It develops when nerve cells in the brain degenerate because harmful proteins have accumulated over a long period. For those affected, and particularly their families, Alzheimer's is a cruel disease. Watching a life partner, sibling, parent or friend slowly disappear is profoundly difficult. The disease also creates many questions and uncertainties for patients and relatives. People affected by Alzheimer's want clear guidance, a care plan and access to knowledge, just as with other serious diseases.

New methods of detection and diagnosis have enabled more people to receive a diagnosis earlier in the disease's course. This also means more people may live with an Alzheimer's diagnosis for longer without developing severe symptoms. A confirmed diagnosis also improves the conditions for person-centred health and social care throughout the disease

content.title: Building vocational education that delivers employable skills
content.description: Skills shortages are well documented, yet many vocational programmes still do not lead to jobs. The problem is rarely the length of education, but how learning is organised. The question is how structure, progression and links to working life determine whether education actually becomes employable competence.
content.extendedDescription:
Skills shortages are intensely debated, but responses often focus on volume rather than how vocational education is organised to lead to jobs. Some vocational programmes do not provide participants with the skills employers actually need. The problem is rarely time, but how education is organised.

This seminar starts from a clear question: why do some vocational programmes lead to jobs while others do not? It focuses on how structure, progression and links to working life determine quality, pace and employability.

The discussion draws on a coherent model of vocational education already used in practice, showing how learning can be organised more effectively without lowering requirements, safety standards or the professional role. The perspective broadens from individual programmes to what is needed for consistent quality and scalability across larger systems.

The event is a structured discussion with concrete examples and clearly defined themes.

content.title: Finance in a new world order – resilience and adaptation in uncertain times
content.description: Geopolitical turmoil, the climate crisis and rapid technological development are shaping a new reality. How can the financial sector build resilience to uncertainty? How does a stable financial sector contribute to a more resilient society, and what leadership is needed when the future is difficult to read?
content.extendedDescription:
The global economy and geopolitical landscape are changing rapidly. Trade disputes, security tensions, the climate crisis and exponential technological development create new conditions, particularly for finance. As society's financial infrastructure, banks, insurers and asset managers play a crucial role in enabling the economy to function, businesses to invest and households to feel secure. The financial sector's resilience – its ability to withstand pressure, adapt and deliver – therefore concerns society as a whole.

The seminar begins with a macroeconomic outlook: where are we, and which scenarios should we prepare for? We then explore how the financial sector is affected, how it builds resilience and its role in society's ability to withstand disruption.

PwC brings together leading financial-sector voices to discuss changing conditions, strategic choices and the sector's growing societal responsibility.
content.subject: Economy

content.title: The right vehicle for the right task – why are we electrifying in the wrong order?
content.description: Sweden is missing its transport climate target not only because of the fuels we use, but because we drive the wrong vehicles. Swedish companies have already developed solutions. What is missing is regulation and incentives allowing energy efficiency to guide vehicle choices, not just fuel choices.
content.extendedDescription:
Clean Motion shows how matching vehicles to tasks can free up energy-system capacity and strengthen Sweden's resilience. Electrification is necessary but insufficient. Sweden will not meet its transport climate target if we keep electrifying vehicles designed for entirely different needs from their actual uses.

Much everyday urban transport involves short distances and light loads. Yet heavy vehicles are often used, causing unnecessary energy consumption thousands of times daily. The cleanest energy is energy never used, so energy efficiency must become central to transport policy.

Lightweight vehicles, preferably with integrated solar energy, can ease pressure on the electricity grid, reduce dependence on oil and imports, and contribute to a more robust society. Swedish companies have already developed solutions. A national strategy, smarter regulations and incentives enabling scale-up are now needed. The technology exists. The will exists. Political action is now required.

content.title: How do we prevent financial hardship early in life?
content.description: Financial hardship can limit families' ability to build security, health and participation in everyday life. What is needed to prevent problems early, drawing on research, health initiatives, civil society and financial knowledge, so both children and adults have stronger financial foundations?
content.extendedDescription: Financial hardship affects the whole family's everyday life. It shapes children's opportunities to participate in school, leisure activities and social life, and affects health and hope for the future. Children and parents may feel guilt and shame about finances beyond their control. In this podcast seminar, Majblomman, researchers, the insurance sector and Ung Privatekonomi discuss preventing financial hardship early in life. We start with the stories and patterns Majblomman sees in families' applications and connect them with research on the links between finances, health and living conditions. The discussion brings together experience from civil society, research, health work and education to explore what works. We examine how early intervention, financial knowledge and public financial education can reduce the risk of money problems and indebtedness later in life and help families build more sustainable finances. Finally, we highlight concrete proposals

content.title: Robots that see, act and decide – what does Sweden need to lead the next industrial wave?
content.description: Sweden has world-leading industrial companies, strong research environments and a growing robotics and AI ecosystem. But technology has outpaced governance, and industry, politicians and investors must now come together. How do we create tomorrow's manufacturing industry?
content.extendedDescription:
What is changing Swedish industry now is not a chat interface: it is robots trained in simulations, deployed in production and making decisions without a human in the loop. Autonomous systems are taking over assembly lines, logistics flows and process industries, and Sweden is in the midst of this transformation.

Yet too many initiatives remain stuck in the pilot phase. Skills are unevenly distributed. Test environments, partnerships and capital are insufficient, and questions of data, responsibility and business value in human–machine systems remain far from resolved. Who owns decisions when machines make them?

Physical AI is changing industrial production faster than policymakers can respond. Sweden risks falling behind. What is required of policy, technology and leadership for the Swedish industrial model to survive this shift and take the lead ahead of countries now automating at record speed? What does leadership require when physical AI sets a new standard?

content.description: Demand for care homes is growing rapidly. How can municipalities, property owners and other stakeholders cooperate to create enough capacity and good living environments for a growing older population while making the finances work?
content.extendedDescription: Sweden's population is ageing, and the need for residential health and social care facilities is increasing nationwide. Drawing on a new report from Stenvalvet, we discuss the challenges, opportunities and choices facing municipalities, property owners and investors. How do we ensure the right homes are built in the right places, on time and to high standards, while making the finances work? content.title: Fossil-free production in practice – how shared agreements support society's transition
content.description: The transition to a fossil-free society often meets obstacles. Laws, regulations and standards make it complicated and costly, all too often preventing it from happening.
content.extendedDescription:
Join a study visit to Arla Foods in Visby, Lundbygatan 1, and take part in a meeting where we see and discuss how the transition is made possible.
Gotland aims to lead the climate and energy transition and reach net-zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2040. Biogas Gotland and Arla Foods Visby show the way through a partnership that made the dairy Arla Group's first completely fossil-free milk-powder dairy while facilitating biogas production.

content.title: It is all on the plate – political solutions for health, climate, justice and preparedness
content.description: Sweden's food system drives emissions, ill health and inequality; farmers face pressure and many people cannot afford good food. Yet food systems can strengthen preparedness, public health and the environment – solutions exist. Political courage and decisions grounded in research and farmers' reality are now needed.
content.extendedDescription:
Today's food system harms the climate, health, biodiversity and preparedness, while not everyone has enough to eat. But it could be the opposite. Knowledge and solutions exist. Sustainable food systems can store carbon, strengthen public health and preparedness, feed people and build community. Achieving this requires political decisions and broad public support.

Format:

- Brief introduction to the current food system.
- Presentation of three concrete policy proposals.
- Presentation of guides: practical tools for transition in everyday and working life.
- Panel discussion with civil society and producer and/or research representatives.
- Open questions, inviting active participation from the audience and decision-makers.

We create a solution-oriented discussion bringing different perspectives together and giving politicians the opportunity to respond to the proposals. The focus is on how we can jointly transform the food system, moving from problems to achievable change.

content.title: Health as an engine of growth
content.description: Ill health, sickness absence and early departure from working life cause substantial production losses in Sweden. The OECD has estimated that improved health and longer life expectancy explain around half of GDP growth during the twentieth century. Yet health is often treated primarily as a cost.
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden's future growth increasingly depends on population health. An ageing population, rising chronic disease and high sickness absence put pressure on workforce size and productivity. Meanwhile, knowledge is growing about how prevention, early diagnosis, better treatment and new technologies can strengthen people's ability to work and participate in working life.
Economically, ill health is much more than a healthcare budget issue. Only around a third of its costs arise within the healthcare system itself. Most consist of lost production, reduced labour-force participation, lower productivity and social insurance costs. Improving health therefore has effects far beyond healthcare: more hours worked, higher productivity and longer working lives.
The seminar discusses how health can be understood and managed as a strategic growth factor.
content.subject: Employment/labour market

content.title: Climate risk, responsibility and property values – preparing for tomorrow: who pays for the next cloudburst?
content.description: Cloudbursts, floods and extreme weather increase costs for property owners, municipalities, water utilities, banks and insurers. Responsibilities are often unclear. How should risks, investments and costs be managed in a changing climate?
content.extendedDescription: Climate risks already affect insurance, financing, investment and property values. But who is responsible for prevention, and who should pay? Representatives of finance, insurance, water utilities and the property market discuss how climate risks change the conditions and what partnerships are needed to strengthen societal resilience. content.title: 1.3 billion Muslims lack freedom of religion – why? Is there hope for change?
content.description: Everyone has the right to freedom of thought, conscience and religion. This includes the freedom to change religion or belief, under Article 18 of the UN Declaration of Human Rights. Where is the boundary between religious freedom and political power in an open democratic society?
content.extendedDescription:
The right to change beliefs in OIC countries is violated through the application of apostasy or blasphemy laws in both criminal and civil law. We highlight examples of positive change, past and present, locally and internationally. The hour combines speeches, discussion and questions.
--
Followed by a discussion from 16:00 at the launch of “Den omstridda avhandlingen: Global politisk islam? Muslimska brödraskapet & Islamiska förbundet i Sverige.” We discuss the research and public debate that followed the dissertation. It became one of Sweden's most widely discussed academic publications in recent years and was described by Åsa Linderborg in Aftonbladet as research that “overturns an entire field of research”. Sameh Egyptson participates alongside journalists Sakine Madon and Widar Andersson.

content.title: Communities are built on water – what do the parties propose ahead of the 2026 election?
content.description: Sweden lacks a coherent water policy, although society and prosperity depend on water access. Climate change challenges both water quality and quantity. Challenges vary greatly between municipalities, and responsibility is shared among around 30 public authorities.
content.extendedDescription:
Water is an essential societal resource, and without functioning water and wastewater systems, society grinds to a halt.

Sweden's water infrastructure – pipes, waterworks and treatment plants – needs substantial investment. Yet significant funding is missing each year to meet demands arising from ageing systems, climate change, preparedness and new EU legislation. Overall, SEK 560 billion must be invested by 2040 to secure future water supplies. Households, business, welfare services, public authorities and civil society must know and trust that society is sufficiently prepared to meet everyone's requirements for robustness, resilience and reliable water and wastewater services. Although water affects everything from defence and industry to rural development and environmental policy, it lacks a clear political home. As a result, one of society's most fundamental functions risks falling through the cracks.
content.subject: Sustainability

content.title: China – a threat or opportunity for Swedish technology and industry? When global trade becomes local
content.description: Global trade is changing as production becomes more local. How does this affect the technology and automotive industries? What challenges and opportunities does it create for Swedish competitiveness in relation to China, the United States and Europe?
content.extendedDescription: Global trade faces its greatest transformation in decades. Geopolitical uncertainty, new trade barriers and an intense technological race focused strongly on time to market force companies to rethink. Globalisation is challenged by a new reality where new players emerge and supply chains change and become more local. How does this affect Swedish technology and automotive industries, which depend on both the Chinese market and global suppliers? What strategies are needed to navigate relations with China, the United States and Europe while strengthening Swedish competitiveness? Hear a unique panel discussion with leaders from major industrial companies Volvo Cars, Scania and Bosch, alongside supplier representatives through FKG and trade and investment promotion organisation Business Sweden. Moderator Lydia Capolicchio leads a discussion of concrete challenges, risks and new opportunities in this new era of global trade.

content.title: How do we ensure more reports of honour-related crime lead to prosecution?
content.description: The honour killings of Pela Atroshi in 1999 and Fadime Shahindal opened Sweden's eyes to honour-related abuse, and important legislative reforms followed. Yet very few reports lead to prosecution. Does the justice system have the knowledge and resources needed for honour-related cases?
content.extendedDescription:
During 2025, GAPF's support service had contact with over 360 people subjected to honour-related violence. Many faced serious threats. Few had police protection or other support. None were involved in ongoing investigations into honour-based oppression.

Meanwhile, Brottsförebyggande rådet's new report on honour-based oppression legislation lacks an important element: victims' perspectives. The justice system has a vital role in investigating and prosecuting honour-related crime. GAPF identifies major shortcomings in the report's conclusions and the justice system's handling of these cases.

• Why do so few reports lead to prosecution?

• Do police, prosecutors and courts have sufficient knowledge of honour-related crime?

The event is for everyone working in law enforcement – police officers, prosecutors, judges and politicians – as well as schools and social services, often the first to suspect honour-related crime.

content.title: Food or the environment – must Sweden choose?
content.description: Sweden faces a choice: how do we produce more food without compromising the environment and climate? As preparedness, costs and climate exert pressure, conflicting goals become clear. Are food and the environment at odds – and who decides what matters most?
content.extendedDescription:
Swedish food production is affected by several politically determined societal goals. Ambitious climate and environmental targets must be combined with increased food production, stronger competitiveness and improved food preparedness. Sustainable development must also encompass ecological, social and economic dimensions.
In practice, conflicting goals require trade-offs between interests and perspectives. How can these be managed so they reinforce rather than undermine one another? Do governance, regulations and priorities need reviewing in light of new knowledge, technological development and changing societal needs? How do national choices affect Swedish production, the global environment and food supply? Can ethical approaches provide guidance when societal goals conflict?
This seminar brings together politics, business and research to discuss ways forward for competitive, sustainable and robust Swedish food production.
content.subject: Food

content.title: Basketball meets the city – how a basketball court became a community plan in Stockholm
content.description: How can cities, associations and businesses jointly strengthen participation, inclusion and hope for the future among children and young people? Basketball is Stockholm's second-largest team sport and an important meeting place. What can stakeholders learn from one another to create lasting value beyond sport?
content.extendedDescription:
The seminar discusses how basketball, municipalities and other stakeholders can work together to create lasting positive effects for children and young people. Drawing on concrete experience from Stockholm, we explore how local meeting places, associations and cooperation can strengthen safety, community and social sustainability.

The discussion starts from a unique three-year partnership between Stockholms stad and Svenska Basketbollförbundet, using basketball to drive participation, strengthen communities and develop new forms of cooperation between the public sector, associations and business.

We also discuss how major international sporting events can catalyse societal development and create value long after the matches end. How can investment in sport, meeting places and cooperation contribute to a cohesive city beyond the final whistle?

content.title: Equality before the law and self-determination are fundamental human rights – do they apply to everyone?
content.description: How does self-determination work in practice for people with multiple and intellectual disabilities? What is needed for people requiring decision-making support to have their wishes respected instead of facing questioning, exclusion and discrimination?
content.extendedDescription:
The seminar starts from self-determination as a human rights issue. Article 12 of the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities establishes the right to recognition as a person before the law, to exercise legal capacity equally with others, and to receive the support needed to exercise this right.

We highlight the gap between rights and reality for people with multiple and intellectual disabilities who need support to interpret and express their wishes.
The Jag bestämmer project examines how supported decision-making works, but also why people's wishes are often questioned or disregarded by authorities, other organisations and those around them. Insufficient knowledge and negative attitudes risk leading to exclusion and IQ-based discrimination. We begin with the project's preliminary findings, then discuss the issue with a knowledgeable panel.

Jag bestämmer is an Arvsfonden project in cooperation with RFS, FUB, Hjärnkraft and Autism Sverige.

content.title: How can interaction and cooperation between higher education and working life help resolve skills shortages?
content.description: As artificial intelligence reshapes the relationship between knowledge and work, society faces a fundamental question: what should education and apprenticeship look like in the digital age?
content.extendedDescription:
Inspired by the original Bauhaus movement, which brought together art, craft and industry for a changing world, Digital Bauhaus brings together young people, experienced practitioners and entrepreneurs to collaborate on meaningful challenges in technology, sustainability and society.

The central presentation will be delivered not by its founders, but by a pupil sharing the experience from the learner's perspective. GoodInnoTech mentors will open and close the conversation, framing the broader societal questions and the vision ahead.
The next chapter is to build a wider network of pupils, educators, entrepreneurs, universities and patrons who believe the future demands a closer relationship between learning and doing.

Digital Bauhaus does not arrive at Almedalen with a completed blueprint. It arrives with evidence, questions and an invitation: to join a conversation about how we educate, create and innovate in the age of artificial intelligence.

content.title: We can detect lung cancer earlier – so why are we not doing it?
content.description: Despite clear evidence that a targeted national lung cancer screening programme could save around 500 lives annually, Sweden has not introduced one. Advanced technology that could improve diagnostics also exists. Why is implementation delayed, and what is needed for more equitable cancer care?
content.extendedDescription:
Thousands of people die from lung cancer in Sweden each year, often because the disease is detected too late.
Regional differences, fragmented procurement and a lack of national coordination create major variations in access to early diagnosis. The seminar explores why screening and modern diagnostic solutions are taking so long to introduce and what is needed for more equitable, effective cancer care throughout Sweden.
Evidence and capacity to detect lung cancer earlier and save lives already exist. Insufficient implementation is primarily a matter of governance, prioritisation and organisation. A more nationally coordinated strategy, including screening decisions and better coordinated procurement, is crucial to equal access to modern diagnostics.
The seminar is part of Swedish Medtech and Lif's joint Life Science Arena during Almedalsveckan 2026.

content.title: How great is the risk of China taking over?
content.description: Tensions between China and the United States are growing. Some say China is rising and the United States declining. Could China take over the world? How great is that risk? If it did, what would life in Sweden and Europe look like? Could the West stop China's advance?
content.extendedDescription:
China's global strategy is to start fires around the world so the United States cannot concentrate its strength on China. The United States does the opposite, trying to extinguish fires everywhere. Wars in Ukraine and the Middle East are part of the game. Persecution of dissenters within China also forms part of the CCP's global strategy to secure its domestic position while seeking world dominance. How would Swedish security, the economy and our democratic values be affected if the centre of gravity shifted eastwards?

Manyan Ng, one of Europe's leading China experts and an engaging speaker, shares his holistic, incisive and clear view of China. Manyan is a frequently consulted commentator for several media outlets. He accurately predicted developments in China's economy and global role over the past 20 years. For example, he predicted that China's economy would encounter many problems and that it was time to plan to protect investments there. A discussion of power and important strategic choices

content.title: The right to the right diagnosis at the right time
content.description: Over 80,000 people live with epilepsy in Sweden. Many are children and young people; four children are diagnosed every day. Epilepsy is Sweden's most common chronic neurological disease. Among its more severe forms are LGS (Lennox–Gastaut syndrome) and Dravet syndrome.
content.extendedDescription:
Several rare diseases include epilepsy among their symptoms. Among the more severe forms are Lennox–Gastaut syndrome (LGS) and Dravet syndrome, which affect children at an early age. LGS diagnosis currently relies mainly on clinical observations because clear tests are lacking, putting many people at risk of misdiagnosis or unnecessarily long waits.
Caring for a severely ill child entails great responsibility and can be extremely demanding, particularly with a serious disease. The situation becomes even harder when the child experiences severe seizures and a clear diagnosis takes a long time. This has several consequences for both the person affected and their relatives.

An accurate diagnosis is important for appropriate treatment, but underdiagnosis of LGS and Dravet syndrome is a significant problem. What can we do about it?

content.title: Effective dialogue between civil society and the state – how is it done?
content.description: In a functioning democracy, the state and civil society engage in dialogue. But they operate under different conditions and sometimes stand very far apart, making it difficult to meet. How can they cooperate despite different starting points?
content.extendedDescription:
The state and civil society need dialogue to produce well-supported, informed political decisions. Yet they often differ substantially, both on policy issues and on civil society's conditions, such as funding. Their reasons for attending dialogue meetings also differ: authorities and ministries want help implementing government policy, while civil society wants to advocate for change. How can both sides' needs be met? That is what this seminar discusses.

Nationellt organ för dialog och samråd mellan regeringen och det civila samhället (NOD) promotes and conducts dialogue. Drawing on our new Dialogfabriken methodology package, we make concrete how effective dialogue between civil society and the state can be created.

The seminar starts with a theoretical section on dialogue, then moves into a practical session addressing challenges and proposing solutions.

The seminar is part of Civilsamhällesarenan. #Civsamarenan

content.description: Sweden has major regional differences in access to new cardiovascular and cancer treatments. Despite national strategies, patients do not gain equitable access to innovative treatments quickly enough. How can we create clearer responsibility, better coordination and faster implementation nationwide?
content.extendedDescription:
Cardiovascular disease and cancer are Sweden's two largest major diseases and cause the most deaths. Despite significant medical advances, new treatments reach patients at different speeds depending on where they live. During the discussion, patient representatives question politicians directly to highlight the consequences of today's inequalities and opportunities for improvement. We explore how Sweden can establish clearer responsibilities, better coordination and more effective processes for introducing innovative medicines. What decisions are needed to turn strategies and action plans into reality for patients? And how does the panel intend to pursue the issue after the election?

Networking in the garden follows the panel discussion. The event is organised by Riksförbundet HjärtLung, Nätverket mot Cancer and Amgen. It is open to everyone, with no advance registration required. Welcome!

content.title: The technology exists and the trucks are running – why is hydrogen still seen as science fiction?
content.description: Hydrogen for transport is still often portrayed as a distant prospect. Yet heavy hydrogen-powered trucks already operate in Sweden, filling stations stretch from Malmö to northern Sweden, and new production facilities are being built. What is actually true about hydrogen mobility in 2026?
content.extendedDescription:
Hydrogen for transport is still often portrayed as a distant prospect, a future project that might arrive later. Yet heavy hydrogen-powered trucks already operate in Sweden, filling stations stretch from Malmö to northern Sweden, and new production facilities are being built at prices approaching those of other fossil-free alternatives.
So why do some people still seem to think hydrogen is like Santa Claus: something they enjoy discussing but do not really believe exists?
During the seminar, Hydri brings together transport, logistics and energy stakeholders to discuss real experience, business perspectives and a straightforward question: what is actually true about hydrogen mobility in 2026, and what persists as outdated beliefs, misunderstandings or outright lies?
We discuss how far development has progressed, the remaining barriers and when hydrogen becomes a business rather than just a pilot project.
The seminar concludes with a panel discussion and audience questions. Do not expect complete agreement. That makes it much more interesting.

content.title: The mobile security chain – protecting critical data in public and private organisations
content.description: When patient data, trade secrets and other sensitive information are handled in everyday work, mobile phones become central to the risk landscape. How do we ensure appropriate protection without obstructing operations?
content.extendedDescription:
Despite advanced security solutions, many breaches occur through individual employees and human error. Mobile phones have become natural work tools in both public and private sectors and therefore central to organisations' overall risk exposure.
For organisations handling patient data, personal information and other sensitive material, this increases requirements for security design and monitoring. A mobile phone can be a vulnerable entry point but also an important part of the solution when managed properly.
Reducing risks requires a coordinated approach combining hardware, software, procedures and skills development, with regulatory requirements integrated into daily work. Cybersecurity must be treated as an operational issue with clear governance and long-term planning.
Samsung Norden invites you to an experience-based discussion of how organisations can work more systematically with mobile phones as part of their security efforts, focusing on concrete choices and sustainable solutions.

content.title: Democracy under attack – how do we protect society's digital nervous system?
content.description: Democracies are eroded when their digital infrastructures fall outside democratic control. Three threats reinforce one another: market-driven institutional breakdown as infrastructure is privatised; authoritarian control as the state centralises digital systems; and loss of digital sovereignty.
content.extendedDescription:
Democracies risk erosion when critical digital infrastructures fall outside democratic control. Three interconnected threats reinforce one another: market-driven institutional breakdown as core data, identities and essential infrastructure are privatised; authoritarian technocratic control as the state centralises digital systems without sufficient transparency and accountability; and loss of sovereignty through dependence on clouds, platforms and AI under foreign jurisdiction.

The seminar explores how these forces make rule-making, the exercise of public authority, public access to information, archives and crisis preparedness vulnerable to manipulation, unclear responsibility and reduced legitimacy. We discuss how digital infrastructures can be designed to resist manipulation, remain resilient and allow decisions to be reversed, while strengthening democracy amid growing geopolitical and technological uncertainty.
content.subject: Digitalisation

content.title: How can home savings and sustainable construction help more young people get a home of their own?
content.description: How can more people have the opportunity to save for their own home while construction becomes more sustainable and climate impact decreases?
content.extendedDescription: Saving for a home has long been central to home ownership and an important foundation for social stability and financial security. Yet Sweden faces major challenges involving high barriers to entering the housing market, rising construction costs and stricter climate requirements. This discussion brings together housing policy, finance, construction and community development stakeholders to explore how new ideas about home savings can create more routes into the housing market. It focuses on connecting savings, long-term thinking and sustainable investment more closely with future housing construction, at a time when rising CO₂ costs also affect the economy. TRIQBRIQ organises the seminar to create an open meeting place for new thinking on home savings, ownership and future sustainable societal models in Sweden and the Nordic region. The discussion starts from the need for solutions that improve young people's ability to save for housing while stimulating sustainable construction and lasting responsibility.

content.title: Spatial planning in a new security and preparedness landscape – from insight to implementation
content.description: A changing international situation raises demands on how we plan, locate and develop society's most critical functions. What requirements should be integrated into planning? How should responsibility and risk be allocated? How do we ensure robustness becomes actual physical infrastructure rather than remaining an ambition?
content.extendedDescription:
Robustness and resilience cannot be added afterwards: they must be built in from the outset through land strategies, comprehensive and detailed plans, and investment and development decisions. Drawing on international experience, including Ukraine, we discuss what Sweden can and must do now and in the future to ensure society withstands crises caused by war, climate change or other systemic pressures.

content.title: What can Sweden learn about civil–military cooperation from Ukraine's frontline experience?
content.description: Ukraine has developed unique models of civil–military cooperation during four years of full-scale war. How do voluntary organisations, territorial defence and the military cooperate, and what lessons should Sweden take away?
content.extendedDescription:
During the war, Ukraine's civil defence has been shaped by necessity. Voluntary organisations, local defence groups and the regular military cooperate in ways without equivalents in peacetime European models. Territorial defence groups (DFTG) coordinate with civil society on logistics, evacuation, intelligence and humanitarian action, often without formal structures but with great effectiveness.
This discussion highlights concrete frontline experience and explores how Sweden and Europe can learn from Ukraine's model. What works? What is the human cost? And how do you build resilience in a society not yet at war?

The discussion is organised within Samarbetsplattformen: Sverige & Ukraina (SPSU), a KlinteVolontär project giving Ukrainian civil society its own voice in Swedish democratic debate and bringing Swedish and Ukrainian organisations together to strengthen long-term cooperation between the countries.

content.title: When life continues – reducing the silence after childhood cancer treatment
content.description: After childhood cancer, the goal is not just survival but quality of life. Childhood cancer care saves lives, but complications such as hearing loss can occur. Today, more than 8 in 10 children diagnosed with cancer in Sweden survive – but who takes responsibility for life afterwards?
content.extendedDescription:
The return to everyday life can be marked by late complications. Medicines are central to several treatments but can also cause permanent hearing loss. For children, this can mean lifelong difficulties at school, in relationships and later at work.

In a seminar involving the audience and making the “silence after treatment” visible, we discuss how a stronger preventive approach can reduce hearing damage: early, systematic follow-up, appropriate support and consideration of quality of life from the treatment-planning stage. Our question is simple and urgent: how do we ensure children who survive cancer also enjoy the best possible quality of life afterwards, while reducing the risk of silence after treatment?

content.title: Securing future skills in the water and wastewater sector
content.description: Sweden faces growing skills needs in the water and wastewater sector as a major generational shift coincides with increasing technical demands. Securing the water supply of the future requires efforts to make the sector more attractive and strengthen its ability to recruit.
content.extendedDescription:
The sector needs both to replace retiring staff and to attract new skills in technology, digitalisation and process development. The seminar presents the results of Vattenindustrin's 2026 skills survey, highlighting the most urgent challenges. This is followed by a panel discussion with representatives of businesses, municipalities and academia, describing the situation and the measures needed to secure the future supply of skills.

Questions addressed by the seminar
• How can we make the sector more attractive and competitive in the race for future talent?
• What skills are needed in an increasingly technical and digitalised water and wastewater system?
• How do major investment needs affect recruitment and skills requirements?
• What do businesses, municipalities, academia and industry organisations need to do together?
• How can we encourage more young people to see water and wastewater as a sector of the future where they can make a real difference?

content.title: Everyone wants to come to Örebro – how can cities attract people and businesses amid growing competition?
content.description: As cities and regions compete ever more fiercely for investment, skills and new business establishments, local attractiveness becomes increasingly important. Businesses looking to expand or establish operations weigh a range of factors in their decisions.
content.extendedDescription:
For many places, this means not only providing the right conditions here and now, but also creating long-term environments where businesses can grow, collaborate and develop. In recent years, Örebro has strengthened its position as an attractive location in Sweden, with a central geographical position, a growing business community and strong partnerships between the municipality, academia and businesses. At the same time, competition between cities and regions is increasing, both nationally and internationally.

So what actually carries most weight when businesses choose where to invest? How can Örebro continue to enhance its appeal and attract more businesses to invest, establish operations and grow here?

This discussion brings together representatives of business, the public sector and academia to explore what is needed to create an even stronger investment climate and how we can jointly position Örebro in the growing competition for the businesses of the future.

content.title: Should Sweden build carbon dioxide infrastructure for 3 million tonnes – or 30?
content.description: Sweden needs a clear carbon capture strategy specifying the capacity we should build for. The country's biogenic emissions exceed 30 million tonnes per year, but policy is based on around 3 million tonnes – a gap that risks steering the entire system in the wrong direction.
content.extendedDescription:
BioCCUS, Bioenergy Carbon Capture, Utilisation and Storage, means capturing carbon dioxide at the emission source and either storing it permanently or using it in industrial processes.

Scaling up CCUS requires a coordinated structure for capturing, handling and transporting carbon dioxide. This means solutions that work for both large and small operators, and targeted support that builds shared infrastructure rather than individual projects. Such support would make many more projects possible, particularly for operators with smaller volumes who otherwise risk being left out.

Storage and transport operators are planning for large, steady flows, requiring Sweden to design its future infrastructure for considerably larger volumes than those currently under discussion. If we build too small, we risk bottlenecks, higher costs and a market that never gets going. The central question for debate therefore remains: should Sweden build carbon dioxide infrastructure for 3 million tonnes – or 30?
content.subject: Climate/environment

content.title: How can police support for victims of crime be improved?
content.description: Despite the government's rhetoric about a paradigm shift placing victims of crime at the centre, support for victims has major shortcomings. British police have made their support for victims more effective. What can Swedish police learn from British experience?
content.extendedDescription:
A paradigm shift for Sweden: that is one way to summarise the government's justice policy. In a short time, numerous inquiries and a series of new laws and legislative proposals have been presented. Victims of crime are rarely mentioned, and when they are, it is easy to get the impression that this is primarily to justify tougher sentences. But what is the situation facing victims, and what help, support and protection do they need? At the seminar, British police describe how new systems, data-driven processes, new working methods and a change in culture have rapidly made information and support for victims more effective. The result is sharply reduced waiting times and increased trust in the police. What can Swedish police learn from British experience, and how can support for victims be improved?

SäkerhetsArenan is organised by SäkerhetsBranschen, Stöldskyddsföreningen, Brandskyddsföreningen, Stiftelsen Tryggare Sverige, Almega Säkerhetsföretagen, Företagsuniversitetet and Säkerhets- och försvarsföretagen (SOFF).

content.title: Electrifying heavy transport – why do solutions get stuck in the electricity grid?
content.description: Sweden must meet ambitious climate targets, but the electrification of heavy transport essential to society is progressing too slowly. A crucial obstacle is the behaviour of electricity grid companies: monopoly operators that control the conditions without taking responsibility for the results.
content.extendedDescription:
With lengthy processing times and enormous connection charges, electricity grid companies put obstacles in the way of transport companies seeking to lead the transition. Verdis has the will, capacity and ability to electrify waste collection in Stockholm and other municipalities right now. Yet it faces a system that holds it back rather than enables it. Why is doing the right thing so difficult? This seminar identifies who is responsible for advancing the issue and creating the right conditions, and who needs to do more.

What requirements can politicians set to make public procurement an effective tool for the transition? How can municipal politicians steer municipal companies so that they, too, contribute to climate and environmental targets? Electrifying heavy transport requires political will, smart procurement and grid owners who take their share of responsibility. Who will lead, and who will be forced to follow? The seminar begins with a networking lunch.

content.title: How club-based sport builds strong communities
content.description: Sedentary lifestyles cost society large sums, while a colder social climate creates a sense of not belonging and being unable to influence things. This is where club-based sport has an important role to play, contributing not only to greater well-being and physical health but also to increased trust between people.
content.extendedDescription:
Join us as Friskis releases figures from a unique report on how the exercise habits of more than half a million members benefit society. This includes reduced sick leave and healthcare costs, but also social capital, which is often less tangible.

More than 12,000 Friskis members have also chosen to volunteer. This makes Friskis a platform for personal development and community where young people in particular have the opportunity to grow as engaged members of society.

The panel features Carolina Klüft, Operations Director at Generation Pep, former track and field athlete and Olympic medallist; Freja Andersdotter, board member of Svensk Friidrott; and Janna Hellerup, Secretary General of Friskis&Svettis.

The seminar also highlights social sustainability, what businesses stand to gain by supporting initiatives that benefit society, and how this work can be carried out. Listen to a conversation with Björn Stenvad, CEO of Rättighetsbyrån, and Ulrika Erkenborn Rugumayo, Account Manager at Aspia.

A light breakfast will be served.
content.subject: Sustainability

content.title: The bank of the future – who will finance the next generation of entrepreneurs?
content.description: Swedish small and medium-sized businesses account for more than half of GDP and four out of five new jobs. Yet many business owners report increasing difficulty accessing capital. Has the banking system become a brake on growth for Swedish businesses? Does today's credit policy put the next generation of entrepreneurs at risk?
content.extendedDescription:
Today's banking system favours large, established companies, while growing businesses find it increasingly difficult to access capital. Specialist banks, fintech and data-driven credit models open up new opportunities for Swedish growth companies. How can we ensure that the Swedish businesses of the future have access to capital to grow, invest and create jobs? What roles should major banks, investors and new entrants play in future financing? Has the banking system become a brake on Swedish businesses? Are today's credit models still designed for an industrial society rather than entrepreneurial businesses? Does Sweden need a new banking system for entrepreneurs? How can we build a financing system that strengthens competitiveness and the Swedish businesses of the future?
In one of Almedalen's most topical economic discussions, entrepreneurs, investors, major banks and challengers meet to discuss whether today's banking system is holding back Swedish competitiveness and who will finance tomorrow's businesses.

content.title: Understanding landmines: facts behind a contested weapon
content.description: The Swedish public and political debate on anti-personnel mines often lacks technical clarity. Understanding the different types, effects, and utility of landmines is essential for judging claims about defence, humanitarian harm, and legal commitments.
content.extendedDescription: This event highlights how limited technical-military understanding can weaken public debate, political decision-making and military judgement on security policies with serious civilian consequences. In particular, it clarifies the technical details that shape the current landmine debate. Participants will learn what different mines are designed to do, how anti-personnel, anti-tank, fragmentation, blast and so-called “smart” mines differ, and why technical terms may obscure the risks involved. The event also examines how mines affect movement, infrastructure, and recovery after conflict. Through enhanced and virtual reality, participants can explore these issues concretely and experience, in a safe and controlled way, the uncertainty and restrictions faced by people in mine contaminated environments. This event is linked to the panel “Does Sweden need anti-personnel mines?” (event id: 10917). Open throughout the scheduled period; participants are welcome to drop in at any time.

content.title: Who should pay for the climate transition – the state or private capital?
content.description: The climate transition requires enormous investment, but businesses and capital markets need long-term ground rules to feel confident investing. What do long-term ground rules actually mean in practice, and how much responsibility can and should politicians take? Who should pay for the transition – the state or private capital?
content.extendedDescription:
How can we channel capital into the transition's most crucial projects despite high initial costs, long lead times and significant risks? This is a central question for both established industry and the next generation of energy, industrial and climate technology companies, where many innovations get stuck between pilot projects and large-scale implementation.
What role should the state play: regulator, investor or financial guarantor? How should banks, pension funds and other long-term investors act when climate targets, energy security and geopolitics set the parameters? And how can we balance technological neutrality, targeted initiatives and the need to scale up quickly?
At a time when the sustainability agenda is being reshaped and the focus is shifting towards resilience and competitiveness, there is a unique opportunity both to prepare Swedish industry for the future and to transform it. We discuss how to remove obstacles and mobilise long-term capital, particularly pension funds, to accelerate the transition.

content.title: The marine spatial plan sounds good, but does it apply to shipping?
content.description: Do the plans we write for the sea work in practice? Not quite, and not yet, according to new research. The ambitions are high. Sweden's marine spatial plan uses the right terminology: ecosystem approach, sustainability, coexistence. But what happens at sea paints a very different picture, for example when it comes to shipping.
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden adopted its first marine spatial plan in 2022. The plan performs well in its language (the precautionary principle, integration, adaptation) but consistently fails at an operational level. Monitoring is neither binding nor cumulative. Sectors plan in silos and largely bypass marine spatial planning.
Sweden is also working towards a shift from road to sea, which is expected to increase maritime traffic by approximately 30% by 2029. Shipping is governed by international conventions (the International Maritime Organization, IMO) that Sweden cannot override, making the marine spatial plan's ecological commitments largely aspirational. The core problem is "institutional decoupling". Authorities and sectors adopt ecosystem language because it legitimises their plans, without actually changing their practices. Sustainability becomes a word in a document rather than a constraint on decisions.

content.title: Democracy versus Destruction: How to Make Every Euro Rebuild Ukraine – Rehabilitation
content.description: Traditional aid is often too slow and bureaucratic to meet urgent local needs. Ukraine is a laboratory for democratic, technological, and rehabilitation-driven innovation that connects local needs directly with international donors, businesses, doctors, authorities and partners.
content.extendedDescription:
Ukraine’s reconstruction is Europe’s largest democracy project, yet traditional aid is often too slow to reach grassroots communities. This panel explores how Ukraine is transforming wartime challenges into innovative solutions, from municipal partnerships and digital tools to trauma rehabilitation and international medical cooperation.

* Why traditional aid mechanisms often fail local communities.
* Turning reconstruction into a participatory democratic process through technology and direct partnerships.
* Funding central governments versus empowering communities directly.
* Lessons from Ukraine’s experience in rehabilitation, resilience, and recovery. From War Trauma to Global Innovation: How Ukraine is Shaping the Future of Rehabilitation. 

This session connects war resilience, healthcare innovation, technology, and transparency, demonstrating that rebuilding is not merely charity but a citizen-driven process that can generate solutions for Ukraine, Europe, and beyond.

content.title: Public health, freedom or bans? The future of nicotine in the EU
content.description: In Sweden, smoking has been replaced by snus and nicotine pouches. The EU's review of the Tobacco Products Directive could now change the conditions. Are the new nicotine products a public health problem or part of the solution – and what position will Sweden take after the 2026 election?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden has reached the smoke-free target (fewer than five per cent smokers). Snus and nicotine pouches have played, and continue to play, a central role in Sweden's success. The EU's review of the Tobacco Products Directive could affect Sweden's ability to pursue its own nicotine policy in the future. The new products are not covered by the snus exemption. What does this mean for everyone who has stopped smoking using nicotine pouches? How will Sweden respond to new EU proposals restricting or banning new nicotine products?
Party representatives will be questioned about their positions ahead of the forthcoming EU negotiations.
How do the parties view the fundamental conflict between
- a policy of continuing to reduce smoking, in which substitute products play an important role, and
- a policy of reducing all nicotine use, meaning restricted access to substitute products?
The seminar opens with a short background on the processes surrounding the Tax Directive and Tobacco Products Directive currently being decided in the EU, and what is at stake for Sweden.

content.title: Recruitment of children and young people with disabilities into crime
content.description: Although children and young people with disabilities face a heightened risk of being recruited into crime, this group is rarely included in municipalities' crime prevention work. What consequences could this have, and how can people with disabilities be included in crime prevention efforts?
content.extendedDescription: The recruitment of children and young people into crime is a growing problem in Sweden. A report from Myndigheten för delaktighet (MFD) shows that criminal actors systematically exploit children and young people with neurodevelopmental or intellectual disabilities. Meanwhile, a new survey of municipal work, carried out by Stiftelsen Tryggare Sverige on behalf of MFD, shows that children and young people with disabilities are rarely considered in routine crime prevention work. This increases the risk of both victimisation and recruitment into crime. The seminar presents findings from the survey and highlights the need for more evidence-based and inclusive crime prevention for children and young people with disabilities. It also provides examples of working methods that can strengthen protective factors and reduce risk factors, alongside a discussion of how a disability perspective can be integrated into local crime prevention work.

content.title: Hate, threats, imprisonment – repression against human rights defenders and climate justice activists
content.description: In countries across Europe, individuals are arrested and sentenced to long prison terms after saving people from drowning at sea. Groups fighting for the climate are prosecuted for sabotage, and calls are being made to label rights activism and climate justice activism as terrorism. How did this happen?
content.extendedDescription:
The discussion describes the deterioration in the ability of human rights defenders and climate justice activists to operate in Europe and Sweden today. Companies sue organisations for millions, and individual representatives face threats and hate campaigns. Activists are accused of, and sometimes even convicted of, offences such as people smuggling, espionage, sabotage, extremism or terrorism. We highlight the problem through current cases, with some focus on prosecutions and convictions of asylum rights defenders and people saving lives in the Mediterranean. The discussion will also address situations in which individuals exercising their trade union or political rights to protest and demonstrate are portrayed as security risks and, in some cases, have lost their jobs, as well as the tightening of rules around climate justice activism.
International instruments exist to protect human rights defenders and climate justice activists. What are they, why are they needed, and how are they observed?
content.subject: Human rights

content.title: Tall timber buildings showing that sustainable architecture is possible in a dense inner-city setting
content.description: Tall timber apartment buildings offer good opportunities to develop more sustainable construction, but also present challenges associated with the conditions of a dense, high-rise inner-city environment. What are the most important issues, and what lessons can we take into the timber architecture of the future?
content.extendedDescription:
Cederhusen is a residential project completed in 2024 in Hagastaden, Stockholm. It comprises 245 apartments across two blocks with four buildings, the tallest reaching 13 storeys. With 8,798 cubic metres of Swedish-produced cross-laminated timber, it is one of the world's largest urban solid-timber projects. The project was designed by General Architecture for housing developer Folkhem.
The site was considered technically complex, making lightweight timber construction a suitable solution. The project took a long time and involved major challenges, both structural and financial. Key issues included durability, structure, fire, acoustics, wind, moisture, light, safety and climate throughout every stage.
The result is buildings that clearly demonstrate the possibilities of timber and create a living environment rooted in Stockholm, architectural history and the new district. The experience has provided valuable insights into the potential and challenges of timber architecture. The talk is given by an architect responsible for the project at General Architecture.

content.title: From words to action – which methods make a difference to the Baltic Sea's coastal environment?
content.description: Naturvårdsverket has presented its proposal for a national restoration plan under the EU Nature Restoration Regulation. The Baltic Sea needs vigorous action for both shores and waters. What makes marine restoration projects, such as shoreline protection, successful, and which partners are needed?
content.extendedDescription:
The Baltic Sea's ecosystems can strengthen biodiversity and benefit society. Many habitats, from coastal zones and underwater meadows to sheltered bays, are declining, affecting fish stocks, water quality and local assets. Naturvårdsverket's national restoration plan underlines this, which is why we aim to discuss implementation with a focus on the Baltic Sea's coastal environment.

We bring together researchers, project leaders and authorities for a forward-looking review of why biodiversity is declining, which restoration methods are used today, and how governance, increased coordination and local implementation can strengthen the coastal environment. The discussion also addresses the important indirect role of shoreline protection in preserving functioning coastal ecosystems. The session highlights ecological functions, practical experience and scalable methods, showing how stakeholders can work together to strengthen the sea's capacity to recover, restore biodiversity and create lasting value for coastal communities.

content.title: When young people are imprisoned today, who takes responsibility for their future tomorrow?
content.description: Crime has become a central issue for society, and new proposals seek tougher sentences, including for young people. At the same time, questions arise about human dignity and the future. What happens when a young person encounters the prison system, and who takes responsibility for life after the sentence?
content.extendedDescription:
As ever younger people are drawn into serious crime, demands on society's response are increasing. New proposals seek to make it possible to sentence children to prison for serious offences. This raises difficult questions about human dignity, responsibility and the future.
What happens to young people inside our prisons? And what happens when their sentence is over? Someone convicted as a child often has their whole life ahead of them. Who is responsible for the path forward?
The transition out of prison is often the most critical phase. Without support, young people risk returning to the same environments and patterns that led to the offence. Civil society plays an important role in supporting young people both during and after imprisonment, through conversation, community and practical support.
This is also about human worth, guilt and the possibility of reconciliation. What does it mean to speak of responsibility and justice while believing in people's capacity to change and make a new start? What can civil society, including the church, contribute after imprisonment? Who takes responsibility then?

content.title: Who should make the banking market work better – customers, banks or politicians?
content.description: Many people find it difficult to influence their banking terms, and competition is described as limited. There is talk of values and trust, but this is not reflected in customers switching providers. Are we content simply to complain, or who actually bears responsibility for a functioning banking market?
content.extendedDescription:
Criticism of how the banking market works is recurrent. Customers react to what they see as unjustified interest rate changes and a lack of competition. Meanwhile, banks make different choices in their treatment of customers and their role in society. This concerns trust, responsibility and values: things that ought to have an impact in a fully functioning market.
Proposals for change exist. Customers are urged to become more active and negotiate. Politicians are proposing a bank tax. Choice and transparency are increasing, yet inertia persists.
Whose responsibility is it really? Are customers too passive, are authorities failing to fulfil their duties, or do the rules stand in the way? Who has the greatest opportunity, and responsibility, to drive progress towards a better-functioning market? Or are we actually content simply to complain?
Join politicians, authorities, banks and consumer organisations for a discussion at Landshypotek Bank.

content.title: Can the economy grow within planetary boundaries – and which companies can turn this into a competitive advantage?
content.description: The research is clear: humanity has already exceeded several planetary boundaries, while global production and consumption continue to increase. So can the economy continue to grow within planetary boundaries, and if so, how?
content.extendedDescription:
The research is clear: humanity has already exceeded several planetary boundaries, while global production and consumption continue to increase. For businesses, this means a new reality in which climate, resource use and biodiversity are no longer merely sustainability issues, but direct business risks as well as new competitive advantages.

At the same time, a new business logic is emerging: studies show that companies integrating climate data, resource efficiency and governance into their core operations perform better over time, are more resilient in crises, attract capital more easily and identify new business opportunities in the transition.

Yet most companies remain in a linear business model that depletes the planet.

This panel brings together entrepreneurs, investors and business leaders to discuss how growth, capital and climate responsibility can be combined in practice, and why companies that start measuring and managing their impact also become the winners of the future.

content.title: With AI, we can analyse, manage and follow up requirements
content.description: Construction projects set requirements for execution, technology, materials and sustainability. When projects move into production, the link to the original requirements is often broken. How can AI support the management and follow-up of requirements and contribute to circularity in construction, from design and building to property management?
content.extendedDescription:
Construction projects set extensive contractual and sustainability requirements. These are incorporated into technical specifications and procurement, but when the project moves into production, the link to the original requirements is often broken. Follow-up becomes difficult and traceability is lost.
Can AI help the construction sector follow up requirements throughout a building's life cycle?
Over the past year, we have developed and tested AI assistants for requirements management that can identify, structure and follow up requirements throughout the construction and property management process, from the brief and design stages to production and management.
At the seminar, we demonstrate how AI is now being used in several related areas:
• AI assistant for requirements management
• AI guide for circular offerings
• AI guide for ESG
• Maturity model for digital sustainability management
We discuss how digital structure and AI can contribute to more effective management and follow-up of requirements and more circular processes in construction.

content.title: From idea to a force in society: how can we build confidence in the future?
content.description: At a time often dominated by social challenges and crisis headlines, we also need to talk about bright spots and the forces driving us forward. The documentary Framtiden bor hos oss portrays precisely this: the irrepressible desire to create something of your own and take control of your own future.
content.extendedDescription:
We screen the documentary "Framtiden bor hos oss", in which journalist Jan Scherman and Khalid Mohammed visit suburban neighbourhoods in Göteborg to give us that very picture: everyday life behind the headlines. Join us beyond the news reports and discouraging headlines. The screening is followed by a conversation with some of the film's participants, focusing on these questions:
Young people's motivations: what makes young people dare to commit, break new ground and create change where others see obstacles?
Entrepreneurship as a tool: how can entrepreneurship and creating something of your own provide a way forward, not only for the individual but for the entire local community? Real confidence in the future: how can we, as a society and as decision-makers, best build an environment where young people feel hope, empowerment and the ability to act? This session is for anyone looking for energy, new perspectives and practical insights from the next generation of changemakers. You can also attend just the conversation, which starts after the film at 15:15.
