content.title: The invisible road network – 75% of Sweden's roads are privately maintained
content.description: Did you know that private individuals across the country fund and maintain its longest road network? These roads are important for essential transport, food production and recreation. How should we address the challenges facing privately maintained roads? And how can we ensure their development potential is not lost?
content.extendedDescription:
1.5 million people start their morning on a privately maintained road. These roads are essential for people to reach work, school and healthcare. They are vital for getting food to the table and timber to industry. A changing climate, requirements for greater load-bearing capacity, declining engagement and eroded grants are among the challenges. How can we ensure that those responsible for privately maintained roads in the future have good conditions for developing and maintaining their roads and, ultimately, contributing to a robust society?

Through this seminar, Riksförbundet Enskilda vägar wants to highlight both the strengths and challenges of a system built on local responsibility, individual commitment and cost-effective solutions. Although privately maintained roads make up the majority of roads in Sweden, they are largely invisible in the national debate. We want to change that.
Join us to learn more about privately maintained roads and what is needed for the system to flourish. What is good for privately maintained roads is good for Sweden.
content.subject: Infrastructure/transport

content.title: The right to your own body – who takes responsibility for pupils in schools for children with intellectual disabilities?
content.description: Children and young people with intellectual disabilities face a considerably greater risk of sexual abuse than others. Yet schools often lack tools for prevention. How can we protect the most vulnerable when ambitions for teaching about bodily integrity and consent are being lowered?
content.extendedDescription:
Alarming reports reveal acute vulnerability among pupils in schools for children with intellectual disabilities: almost one in three girls has experienced sexual abuse. Despite these figures, educators report a lack of materials and methods for teaching consent, bodily integrity and relationships.

The new curriculum inquiry proposes removing these topics from schools' overarching remit. This risks ending cross-curricular work and removing headteachers' explicit responsibility. If the issue is confined to individual subjects, the continuity essential for long-term changes in attitudes will be lost.

The seminar starts from this situation and provides insight into Gymnasiebrevet, a project funded by Arvsfonden. We present work on cross-curricular materials being developed together with the target group. In a subsequent panel discussion with young people, professionals and politicians, we discuss how to create the conditions for preventing sexual abuse starting in the classroom.
content.subject: Children/young people

content.title: Sweden: a stain on the Nordic region's reputation?
content.description: Sweden ratified the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities in 2008. Yet consistent findings from UN reviews, civil society and research show that the Convention's rights are not being satisfactorily implemented in practice.
content.extendedDescription:
We see human rights being weakened around the world. The threat to the rule of law in Sweden is highly topical, with lawyers issuing public appeals. Amid all this, two of our neighbours, Iceland and Norway, decided as recently as December 2025 to strengthen the status of disability rights by incorporating the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities into national law. Finland enacted legislation when it ratified the Convention. There are further examples in Europe, such as Spain, where the Convention has been strengthened through a constitutional amendment.

Join a discussion on the state of human rights in Sweden, focusing on the status of the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities. Why is Sweden falling behind its neighbours when it comes to making the Convention Swedish law?

The seminar is organised as part of Civilsamhällesarenan.

content.title: Together for a good life for everyone – developing a place
content.description: When both individuals and places have different circumstances and opportunities, how can we create a place for everyone? Can collaboration, residents' engagement and a place's distinctive character help us shape safe, equitable environments that strengthen pride, health and confidence in the future?
content.extendedDescription:
For people to want to live and remain in Jönköpings län, sustainable and attractive living environments are needed in both urban and rural areas. In our place development work, "Together for a good life for everyone" means building collaboration, but also creating pride in and commitment to a place.
As we strive for equitable conditions for the county's residents, development based on local circumstances is central. Place development must take place at several levels and involve many stakeholders. The importance of local engagement and residents' participation is common to all of them. At regional level, we develop the county based on its combined strengths and challenges, with a strong awareness that residents' everyday lives and health vary depending on where in the county they live. At the same time, place development takes concrete form in municipalities, where local needs, resources and engagement are translated into practical development work. The discussion features examples from three of the county's municipalities of how they work with place development.

content.title: Stories from Ukrainian veterans
content.description: What can those who risk their lives to protect Europe tell us about the strength and fragility of life? Ukrainian veterans fight for their families and the future of Europe – how can they reconcile their experiences through the written word, and what can we learn from them?
content.extendedDescription:
In this seminar we meet Ukrainan veterans from the YMCA Lviv programme and hear their stories. Many are civilians who left their jobs and way of life to defend their families and country. Among them are many artists, teachers, and activists who, having participated in the war for freedom, have unique experiences and insights about life and death.
When veterans have the chance to express themselves, their experience can become a shared asset rather than a personal trauma. What opportunities does art-rehabilitation through literature offer for veterans? How does cooperation with veterans from Scandinavian countries shape the identity of the Defenders of Europe, and what opportunities does a European veterans’ network provide?

content.title: Increasing Swedish food production through innovation and industrial symbiosis – but who will handle processing?
content.description: How can resource efficiency, innovation and collaboration strengthen Swedish food production and processing? In an uncertain world, circular solutions linking industry and society create opportunities for greater preparedness, resilience and long-term supply capacity, as well as a more competitive business sector.
content.extendedDescription:
We taste Swedish canned tomatoes and listen to an exciting discussion about what is needed to take Sweden into the future and create more value from underused resources, from production to processing and from waste to resource.

Industrial symbiosis can increase our competitiveness and strengthen resilience across the business sector. We can also increase domestic food production and contribute to the production targets in the national food strategy. How many vegetables could we produce innovatively in Sweden, and how much waste heat would that require?

But how do we process what is produced, and how should these chains connect nationally, regionally and locally to ultimately reach the consumer?

08.30-09:00 – Breakfast
09.00-09.15 – Case Frövi – Ingrid Schuster, CEO, Regenergy Frövi AB
09.30-10.15 – Increasing Swedish food production through industrial symbiosis, innovatively! But who will handle processing?
content.subject: Innovation

content.title: Nordic profits: time for a harmonised fund market
content.description: A strong market for savings and investment is crucial for competitiveness and growth. The Nordic capital markets are prominent but too small and nationally focused. Differences in legal form, marketing and taxation, for example, obstruct cross-border fund trading.
content.extendedDescription:
As EU regulations are reformed and implemented, Nordic finance ministries and supervisory authorities need to collaborate. The Nordic region has the capital, expertise and trust to be a leading European market for savings and asset management, but is held back by national arrangements and a lack of coordination.

What can the Nordic countries gain by taking joint steps forward, and what needs to be done to achieve a more integrated capital market?

What is needed to create better conditions for administering, distributing and managing funds efficiently across the Nordic region? Which regulations or processes are most important to harmonise? What effect would a common market have on access to capital in Sweden and the Nordic region? How can we become a stronger collective voice in the EU while creating a more competitive offering for savers and investors?
content.subject: Economy
speakerTitles: Head of Equity Capital Markets Stockholm
Head of Planning at the Ministry of Finance

content.title: Health as a strategy, not a perk
content.description: Many employers invest in wellness allowances to reduce the negative health effects of heavy workloads. This is despite scientific studies showing that systematically implemented health processes can have major effects on productivity, work capacity and well-being.
content.extendedDescription:
The seminar highlights how systematic, management-led health processes can create real improvements in health. We address what managers and leadership teams need to know to make health part of their organisation's core strategy. We discuss the fact that dangerously low fitness levels have almost doubled over the past 30 years, contributing to reduced work capacity and increased ill health.

For health programmes to succeed, an organisation's leadership must take overall responsibility and establish an action plan with clear parameters and goals, as part of a healthy organisational culture. Under this plan, unit managers are tasked with being role models and ensuring implementation at unit level. This seminar aims to motivate managers to address health more systematically, generating effective, sustainable improvements throughout the organisation. Drawing on scientific studies and their own experience, participants suggest activities.
content.subject: Employment/labour market

content.title: Communication as critical infrastructure – being unprepared is not an option
content.description: Authorities are investing more in visibility and broad communication, but the systems intended to reach citizens in an actual crisis remain fragmented and untested. What is needed for crisis communication to work when it really matters?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden is strengthening its preparedness on many fronts. Total defence is being built up, budgets are growing and emergency stockpiles are being filled, but a crucial piece of the puzzle risks being overlooked: the communication infrastructure that must reach citizens when a crisis occurs. Authorities have become better at communicating broadly and engagingly, with campaigns that are visible and attract attention. But visibility in peacetime is not the same as functionality in a crisis. The systems that must carry crisis communication when it matters, from national warnings to local information in an individual municipality, are fragmented, untested and dependent on technology not always designed for a crisis. Radio, mobile alerts, digital platforms and public service media all have a role, but coordination of the whole is lacking and it is unclear who is responsible for ensuring the chain holds.
This is not just about technology, but about organisation, responsibility and the ability to activate prepared messages in real time.
content.subject: Digitalisation

content.title: Stable conditions for civil society funding – where are the political visions?
content.description: Civil society needs stable conditions for funding and giving. But there is no clear political vision for the long-term funding of non-profit organisations or a Swedish model for everyday philanthropy. How do politicians view sustainable funding for a strong, independent civil society?
content.extendedDescription:
Non-profit organisations create considerable value for society, from social support and international work to research, culture and activities for children and young people. To operate over the long term, they need stable, predictable funding conditions. Yet many organisations face financial uncertainty. Time-limited project funding and targeted grants from both public and private donors can restrict opportunities for long-term initiatives.

A strong civil society therefore needs a range of sustainable funding models and the ability to be an independent, sometimes uncomfortable voice in public debate. Before the 2022 election, neither tax relief on donations, public matching of donations nor simpler rules for corporate giving featured on the agenda of the parties behind the Tidö Agreement. However, interest has grown during this parliamentary term. How do the parties view civil society's future role and funding? We invite politicians to a discussion.

The seminar is part of Civilsamhällesarenan #Civsamarenan

content.title: How can we secure future skills in Sweden's vital industries?
content.description: Industries that underpin Swedish society face a skills crisis, while few people are choosing to enter them. How can we attract young people to careers in agriculture, forestry or the countryside?
content.extendedDescription:
A changing climate and increasing geopolitical tensions call for stronger Swedish preparedness. We need to produce more food with a smaller climate footprint, balance forests' role as both carbon sinks and sources of raw materials, and protect biodiversity. The need for expertise in the green industries has never been greater. Yet few people apply to the educational programmes that hold the solutions. Is this a matter of image, a gap in knowledge, or the complex conflicts between objectives that young people are expected to navigate today?

Join a breakfast discussion in which young and slightly less young people discuss the supply of skills in the green industries. We begin with a crash course in the challenges ahead, followed by a panel discussion in which tomorrow's decision-makers give their views. What is needed to encourage young people to pursue careers as, for example, agronomists, horticultural scientists or professional foresters? We finish with mingling and networking with students, decision-makers and those of us passionate about green issues.
content.subject: Employment/labour market

content.title: What is needed to reduce fatal accidents in Swedish workplaces?
content.description: Almost every week, someone dies in an accident at work. From the 1960s to the turn of the millennium, fatal accidents fell sharply in Sweden, but since 2000 progress has stalled. Why is this? What is needed to reduce fatal accidents again?
content.extendedDescription:
Nearly 50 people a year die in workplace accidents in Sweden. Most are men.
Arbetsmiljöverket's investigations into fatal accidents show that many could have been prevented with the right protective measures.
Historically, the number of fatal accidents has declined. In 1960, there were around 360 per year; by 1975, this had fallen to around 200. This is due to preventive measures, but also to fewer people working in environments with a high risk of fatal accidents.
Since 2000, this progress has stalled.
Last year, a total of 53 people died in workplace accidents, including 45 in the Swedish workforce. A notable feature of 2025 was that several women were murdered at work, partly as a result of the shooting at Risbergska skolan in Örebro.
Most fatal accidents normally occur in construction, transport and storage, manufacturing, agriculture and forestry.
In a panel discussion, we will explore what needs to be done to reduce fatal accidents in Sweden again.
content.subject: Employment/labour market

content.title: Landfills and detoxification in a circular economy – managing society's most difficult waste
content.description: Not all waste can be recycled. In a circular economy, some flows are complex, requiring long-term solutions and making detoxification crucial. How has the waste sector developed, and what exactly is a landfill – and why is it still needed?
content.extendedDescription:
Society's difficult waste requires a comprehensive approach, with its management crucial both to the climate transition and to access to important resources. How can sorting and quality-assured flows be prerequisites for effective material recycling, and why should not all waste be returned to the cycle?

Join a seminar in which we work across the value chain to highlight both opportunities and challenges in today's modern waste management, from waste to resource.

What is needed here and now to remove obstacles, create functioning markets for recycled materials and achieve Sweden's climate and environmental targets? Meet politicians, authorities and businesses for a discussion on the need for long-term conditions, efficient permitting processes and greater visibility for the enormous infrastructure required to handle difficult waste in a robust, resource-efficient waste system that benefits the climate.
content.subject: Sustainability

content.title: Smart locks for smart homes: Why cybersecurity needs to be considered
content.description: It is often assumed that cybersecurity is an important topic for businesses, public institutions and critical infrastructure. As smart homes become increasingly popular, also certain consumer IoT devices (e.g. smart locks), could become targets of cyberattacks, possibly leading to home burglaries.
content.extendedDescription:
The media regularly reports on successful cyberattacks, many of which have caused considerable damage. However, most companies and public sector organisations have put in place appropriate technologies, processes and awareness-raising measures to protect themselves against  such attacks.
On the other hand, in their private lives, almost everyone is nowadays aware that their mobile phones, tablets and computers are vulnerable to potential attacks. What many consumers do not have on their radar, is a potential security vulnerability in smart home products.
The EU Cyber Resilience Act (CRA), which shall fully apply from 11 December 2027, aims to safeguard businesses and consumers. As part of the implementation programme of the CRA, a harmonised European standard for “Essential cybersecurity requirements for smart home products with security functionalities” is currently prepared.
This topic will be covered in a lecture supported by slides, followed by a question-and-answer session.
content.subject: Security/defence

content.title: Material recycling in construction – the key to a circular economy and reduced climate impact
content.description: Construction accounts for large material flows, considerable waste volumes and a substantial share of climate impact. At the same time, a circular economy is crucial both for greater resource efficiency and stronger resilience. What obstacles exist in today's system, and why are materials not circulating to the extent needed?
content.extendedDescription:
Large-scale material recycling can provide a strong foundation for a future circular economy. In practice, however, the market is still characterised by virgin materials often being more competitive than recycled ones.

Why is this, and how can construction genuinely move from waste to resource? What obstacles in today's system hinder circularity? Is progress being slowed by insufficient demand, unclear regulations, difficult permitting processes, business risks or inadequate policy instruments?

This panel brings together politicians, the construction and property sectors, recycling operators and public bodies to discuss how building materials can be recovered in practice. The focus is on concrete solutions throughout the value chain, from procurement and permitting to business models and the allocation of responsibility. What decisions are needed now to strengthen climate benefits, increase resource efficiency and build a more resilient society?
content.subject: Sustainability

content.title: What do you know about species extinction?
content.description: Biodiversity is central to balanced ecosystems and resilience to climate change. But we are losing biodiversity at a rate 1,000 times faster than during any previous mass extinction in Earth's 4.5-billion-year history. How can we address this crisis?
content.extendedDescription:
Biodiversity can seem like an abstract concept: perhaps something that brings pandas or rainforests to mind, or EU legislation affecting Swedish forestry. But what does it actually mean to talk about the "Holocene extinction" and "biodiversity loss"?

To make this existential issue tangible, Fältbiologerna is organising an interactive quiz: "What do you know about dead animals?" Our young experts will do more than preach about creeping lady's-tresses or the three-toed woodpecker. We ask the audience questions about species on the new Swedish Red List and ask them to explain exactly why these species are threatened with extinction. Which human activities drive species extinction? What can we do about it? And what kind of planet are our decision-makers leaving to the youngest generations?

Does this sound like something for you? Test your knowledge and discover what you really know about dead animals.

content.title: When research meets the challenges facing schools
content.description: Schools must address societal challenges on a scientific basis. This is especially true today, as society and schools face one of their most complex periods in modern times, with digitalisation and AI changing how we learn and teach. Educational research is absolutely central here.
content.extendedDescription:
Digitalisation and AI bring both opportunities and challenges for teachers and pupils. Growing segregation creates schools with vastly different conditions, while increasing numbers of pupils face language challenges that require more than standard solutions. Educational research provides research-based knowledge for teachers and decision-makers at every level, including politicians.

Vetenskapsrådet works to ensure that research of the highest quality benefits all of society. At the seminar, research findings meet everyday school life. Researchers, teachers and decision-makers discuss the role of educational research in three of schools' most pressing challenges:
• How digitalisation and AI are changing the foundations of teaching and learning.
• How the consequences of segregation affect teachers' work.
• How challenges in children's and young people's reading and writing skills can be addressed.

content.title: Hope that saves lives – creating paths forward despite mental ill health
content.description: More and more people live with mental ill health, excluded from work and education. But there are approaches that break isolation and support recovery through community, structure and long-term commitment. How can political decisions and new pathways increase participation, improve quality of life and reduce costs to society?
content.extendedDescription:
How can community, structure and long-term support create paths forward when mental ill health limits opportunities to study and work?
Do people with mental ill health receive the right support in your municipality, or are there gaps along the path to work and education?

The discussion opens with a member's personal story, followed by an introduction to the Clubhouse model, an established approach to work-oriented rehabilitation found in more than 370 locations worldwide, including 20 in Sweden.

Drawing on experience and evaluations, we discuss how the model can support recovery, strengthen pathways to education and financial independence, and reduce the need for healthcare interventions. Rickard Bracken, Secretary General of Mind, shares perspectives on growing loneliness and the need for meaningful social connections, based on a recent survey.

What is needed to give more people access to effective rehabilitation, and how can proven models be scaled up?
With us, no one falls through the cracks. We show how it works.
content.subject: Employment/labour market

content.title: How can we build data-driven and AI-based services without compromising quality?
content.description: AI and automation are rapidly being integrated into business-critical processes. This creates efficiencies but raises questions about reliability, responsibility and governance. How can we ensure transparency and retain trust as decisions are increasingly made by AI?
content.extendedDescription:
AI and automation are rapidly changing how companies run and develop their businesses. AI-based solutions are becoming part of business-critical processes in finance, supply chains and customer management. This creates opportunities for efficiency, better decision support and new business models, but requires quality, transparency and accountability. How can we ensure reliable AI decisions? How can we build in governance from the start? And how can we retain customers' trust as automation increases?

The panel discussion brings together perspectives from technology, advisory services, data and research. The panel explores what it takes to scale AI in practice, from data foundations and process design to skills, governance and change management.

Participants:

• Mikael Forsberg, CEO, SAP Sverige
• Morteza Ashouri, Director & Business Leader Advisory, Azets Sverige

content.title: Mellan Rummen – phasing out fossil fuels through energy efficiency
content.description: What bottlenecks prevent scaling renewable fuels, increasing energy efficiency, treating waste as a resource, strengthening biodiversity and shifting taxation from labour to natural resources? What would we gain or lose if the transition moved 10–50–100 per cent faster?
content.extendedDescription:
We believe our times need more spaces for dialogue: places where people can think together, build relationships and practise engaging with complexity.

This form of conversation along the seafront can be seen as a kind of 'slow thought' in an age of information noise, rapid position-taking and fragmented views of reality. It is an attempt to build on shared interests, even when we do not agree with one another on everything.

Moderators (on different days): Christina Carlmark, David Björneloo, Siri Maassen, Elin Bergman, Sebastian Lindström and Mattias Axelson, with guests.

content.title: The state of digital fakery
content.description: AI hoaxes, hidden sources and coordinated campaigns. During the 2026 election year, social media moves rapidly, and journalists and the public need to distinguish real from fake just as quickly and uncover those deliberately misleading us. What have we seen so far? Who is behind it?
content.extendedDescription:
Valkollen – checking viral content during elections

AI hoaxes, hidden sources and coordinated campaigns. During the 2026 election year, social media moves rapidly, and we need to distinguish real from fake just as quickly and uncover those deliberately misleading us. But how do we do that? And what have we seen so far? Meet Valkollen's fact-checkers, researchers and experts for an up-to-date picture. Fake election posters and Vietnamese clickbait factories are already active, and digital meme warfare is raging. Have you spotted something suspicious in your feeds, or would you like to learn our techniques for monitoring this chaotic information landscape? Come to our seminar!

Valkollen is an initiative by Medieinstitutet Fojo at Linnéuniversitetet, intended to support Swedish media and inform the public in investigating digital manipulation around the 2026 election. Valkollen 2026 began in March this year with training and monitoring. See https://fojo.se/verify/valkollen/

content.title: Sweden has its antibiotic factory – but who secures the rest?
content.description: Sweden has invested in domestic antibiotic manufacturing, but preparedness concerns the entire supply chain. Today, Europe has only one fully integrated antibiotic production chain, while active ingredients are imported from Asia. What is needed for a resilient antibiotic supply in the EU?
content.extendedDescription: Sweden has taken a historic step by investing in domestic antibiotic manufacturing. This is a welcome decision and reflects a broader shift in the approach to pharmaceutical preparedness. But preparedness concerns the entire supply chain, not a single factory. Today, more than 85% of all active pharmaceutical ingredients, known as APIs, are produced in China and India. Across Europe, there is only one fully integrated penicillin production chain, from active ingredient to finished product. One factory on an entire continent. No active ingredient, no antibiotics. Meanwhile, a government inquiry into medicine shortages and preparedness is under way, and strategic autonomy has grown from a health policy issue into a security policy issue. What political and structural conditions are needed to secure a resilient antibiotic supply in Sweden and Europe? Join a discussion on responsibility, preparedness and sustainable access to antibiotics, one of healthcare's most fundamental medicines.

content.title: The manager as society's shock absorber – when did leadership become the solution to everything?
content.description: More and more workplace problems are described as leadership problems, even though they are often fundamentally psychological, relational and organisational. What will be required of tomorrow's managers when their remit expands faster than the conditions needed to fulfil it?
content.extendedDescription:
Does every manager need to be a psychologist? Not at all. But managers need to understand the people they lead and have the organisational conditions to lead in a humane, sustainable way. At a time of sky-high sick leave rates, declining interest in management roles and growing anxiety about AI in working life, the question of what leadership should actually be is becoming increasingly crucial.

In this lecture, Paulina Tranfelt, a licensed psychologist specialising in leadership and organisation, challenges today's view of leadership through three questions: what is not working in contemporary leadership? Why is it not working? And above all, how can we do things differently?

The lecture offers a psychological look ahead at what is needed to build organisational health, more humane leadership in a digitalised world, and sustainable working lives in which both managers and employees can function, develop and thrive over time.

The lecture starts at 10.15 and lasts approximately 45-50 minutes. There will be an opportunity for questions afterwards.

content.title: Sweden needs every last person – is migration policy getting in the way?
content.description: Sweden needs more people in work to secure its supply of skills. How can migration contribute to a stronger labour market? If Sweden needs every last person, how can policy make that possible?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden faces a growing dilemma: while labour shortages are severe in both welfare services and business, it has become harder for people who already work and contribute to stay. Immigrant workers are now essential to a functioning labour market, yet regulations are tightening and uncertainty is increasing.
What would migration to Sweden that strengthens the labour market look like? How can we avoid wasting skills through complicated permit procedures, insecure conditions and signals that reduce people's willingness and ability to work in Sweden? And how can we combine order and predictability with a policy that makes use of people's willingness and ability to contribute? The seminar opens with a conversation between representatives of academia and business about how current policy affects the labour market. We then speak with political representatives about their responsibilities and proposals.

content.title: Opportunities in the living city – from residents' insights to attractive living environments
content.description: An attractive city never stands still. It grows to meet the needs of residents and other stakeholders. What makes a city relevant to residents, businesses, talent and visitors? How do culture-led development and residents' own initiative contribute to a vibrant, safe and competitive city?
content.extendedDescription: How can we find new ways of working that draw on residents' energy in urban development over the long term? And how do Sweden's major cities actually compare internationally in this respect? As cities grow, new opportunities emerge to improve accessibility and develop lively meeting places and attractive living environments. The seminar focuses on opportunities for urban development driven by culture and residents. Can greater involvement from cultural life and residents improve cities' competitiveness and create better conditions for attractive, sustainable urban environments? Can we learn, find inspiration and gain insights from other major cities around the world? In this discussion, decision-makers, experts, researchers and businesses share experience and insights into how cities' qualities can be developed and remain relevant internationally in the future.

content.title: When war is already here – how can we strengthen Sweden's resilience in peacetime?
content.description: The war in Ukraine demonstrates the importance of an independent domestic defence industry, but also of civilian resilience, even in peacetime. Foreign powers launch cyberattacks daily against industry, banks and critical public infrastructure. How can preparedness in Sweden and Europe be strengthened?
content.extendedDescription:
The war in Ukraine has demonstrated the importance of domestic and European defence industries in ensuring strategic freedom of action and rapid access to critical equipment. This is especially true when several international conflicts are taking place simultaneously and established alliance structures show signs of faltering. Sweden is certainly not at war, but as Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson has pointed out, "nor is it at peace". Foreign powers launch cyberattacks daily against military and civilian industry to obtain strategic expertise and test systems' resilience. The same happens frequently to banking, electricity and telecommunications infrastructure, municipal water and wastewater facilities, healthcare and commercial businesses, for example in grocery retail.
This seminar discusses how Sweden's and Europe's military and civilian resilience can be increased, how the escalating threat to our sensitive IT infrastructure can be addressed, and, not least, the role of politics.

content.title: Parental alienation – the hippo in the nursery: an overlooked form of child abuse
content.description: Parental alienation is both scientifically documented and highly contested. Researchers and those affected describe clear and serious harm to children, while critics argue that the concept can be misused and sometimes deny its existence.
content.extendedDescription:
Parental alienation means that a child is manipulated by one parent into rejecting the other, with whom the child previously had a close relationship, without legitimate grounds for doing so. It is currently being researched as both child abuse and intimate partner violence. For children subjected to parental alienation to receive help and protection, social services, courts and others must be able to identify it and distinguish it from other forms of violence against children. At present, children subjected to parental alienation are often left to their fate with their abusers.

The seminar is led by Anna Lytsy, a journalist and author who has followed international research and knowledge development on parental alienation for more than ten years. Together with lawyer Christina Bergenstein, she wrote the book "Barn som tvingas välja bort en förälder. Föräldraalienation i Sverige: fakta, erfarenheter, rättsregler" (Norstedts Juridik, 2019 and 2023). Three parents who have lost their children through parental alienation will also be on stage.
content.subject: Children/young people

content.title: Children's rights as a compass in the climate crisis
content.description: The climate crisis is creating a growing gap between children's rights and the decisions shaping their future. A billion children already live at extremely high climate-related risk. This is a children's rights crisis, and many young people lack confidence in the future. How can children's perspectives guide the climate transition?
content.extendedDescription:
The climate crisis is not only an environmental crisis; it is a children's rights crisis. Around a billion children worldwide already live at extremely high climate-related risk, while many young people express declining confidence in the future. Climate change threatens children's rights to health, security, development and education: rights that the state is responsible for protecting under the Convention on the Rights of the Child.

Despite this, climate policy lacks a consistent children's rights perspective. Decisions are made with short time horizons, while today's children and future generations bear the consequences.

In this seminar, we explore the climate crisis as a children's rights crisis and ask: how can children's rights and future guide climate policy? What responsibility lies with politicians, businesses and adults, and what is needed for children's rights to guide practice rather than just rhetoric?

Welcome! Breakfast is served at 7:45.

content.title: When regulations hold things back, how can we secure innovation, competitiveness and patient safety?
content.description: When regulations go too far, they risk undermining their purpose. Patients must wait for medical technology that already exists, while Europe loses competitiveness. How can we strengthen patient safety without slowing innovation, access and development?
content.extendedDescription:
The implementation of regulations such as MDR and IVDR has created new problems: long lead times, certification bottlenecks and unclear application across EU countries. As a result, medical devices are delayed or disappear from the market, without clear evidence of proportionate gains in patient safety.

Meanwhile, pressure on healthcare is increasing and investors are hesitant about Sweden and Europe. The panel discussion starts from this tension: where do regulations add real value, and when do they instead become an obstacle? The focus is on unintended effects on competitiveness and how Sweden can challenge today's system, use its strength in collaboration and drive change towards faster, more proportionate processes. These should reward rapid adaptation to updated and new regulations, strengthen patient safety, innovation and competition, and deliver more sustainable and efficient healthcare.

No preparation is required.

content.title: What is needed for transparent, reliable data to become Sweden's next competitive advantage?
content.description: Is data driving the next phase of industrial development? Increasing EU requirements, global trade and AI development are making data and digitalisation strategic advantages. How can political decisions and standards strengthen competitiveness while enabling circularity and innovation in Swedish businesses?
content.extendedDescription:
As EU rules and AI change the conditions for sharing information in value chains, structured data is becoming a strategic business asset. Companies able to share, understand and use data now have a chance to move ahead, but a new study finds that 75% of Nordic companies say they are not ready.

At this seminar, politicians and businesses meet to discuss how Sweden can take a stronger leading position. The discussion starts with EU sustainability requirements, under which companies need to share standardised data such as digital product passports containing information about, for example, climate footprints and packaging materials. It will also address how to ensure that the data made available can be trusted, particularly when AI is used in decision-making.

How should responsibility actually be divided between politicians and businesses? How can companies' investments in data be turned from a requirement into business value? And what is needed to build functioning, interoperable data infrastructure?

content.title: The local energy transition – how should we build, own and finance it?
content.description: Sweden needs to expand electricity grids, local energy production, flexibility and digital infrastructure at a pace no single stakeholder can achieve alone. What needs to change to make the local energy transition investable on a larger scale, and what role can politicians play in creating long-term ground rules?
content.extendedDescription:
Municipalities are close to local needs but cannot bear all the investment risk. Capital markets seek long-term sustainable assets but often lack local roots and the capacity to deliver. Locally rooted energy companies, meanwhile, rarely have access to the capital the transition requires.

The gap between local public benefit and investment capacity remains large. Business models and ownership structures were built for a different energy system. And the question of who should take overall responsibility for local infrastructure, including electricity grids, fibre, district heating and local production, is far from resolved.

This panel discusses how municipalities, investors and locally rooted energy companies can build the infrastructure of the future together. What new partnerships and ownership models are needed? How should risk and return be shared? What needs to change to make the local energy transition investable on a larger scale, and what role can politicians play?

content.title: Does AI create a better life for residents – or just an easier working day for the organisation?
content.description: AI is now being introduced into the public sector for analysis, prioritisation and automation. As algorithms influence healthcare, services and interactions with authorities, a central question arises: does AI lead to better lives for residents, or mainly to more efficient organisations?
content.extendedDescription:
Artificial intelligence is changing how the public sector works. AI is already used for analysis, decision support and automation in everything from healthcare to public services and spatial planning.
Development is often driven by the need to make operations more efficient, address resource shortages or perhaps simply try out new technology. At the same time, the technology raises a more fundamental question: for whom is value being created?
Region Jönköpings län uses the working name Esther to personify the resident: the person its services ultimately exist to serve.
Can AI provide better access, faster service and more accurately targeted support for Esther? Or does the technology risk creating distance between Esther and the organisation? The seminar discusses how AI can be developed and used in ways that actually strengthen the resident's perspective, and how the public sector can ensure that technology serves people rather than the other way around.

content.title: A more brain-aware society and better brain health for children and young people with neurodevelopmental disabilities
content.description: Children and young people with neurodevelopmental disabilities face too many barriers in society. A lack of knowledge about the brain's needs creates inequality, stress and mental ill health. We need a brain-aware society. Research needs to be implemented in practice and in real life to benefit children and young people with neurodevelopmental disabilities.
content.extendedDescription:
More children and young people are receiving neurodevelopmental diagnoses today, while mental ill health, school absence and prolonged stress are increasing. At the same time, we know more than ever about the brain, neurodevelopmental conditions and how environments and social structures affect people's ability to function and feel well.
Yet large parts of society are still built on the idea that people function in roughly the same way.

This open discussion brings together research, lived experience and societal perspectives to explore why so many children, young people and families feel that the systems around them are not working, and what we can actually do about it.

Topics include:
Why neurodevelopmental diagnoses are increasing, mental health and prolonged stress.
School and inclusion, neurodiversity and different ways of functioning.
Early intervention and support, brain capital and the society of the future.

If we build societies that work only for some people, we risk creating unnecessary ill health, exclusion and lost potential for an entire generation.
content.subject: Children/young people

content.title: Democracy in the shadow of change – 50 decisions that have dismantled Swedish development aid
content.description: Swedish development aid is currently undergoing extensive changes. Decisions that have been implemented have undermined Sweden's international credibility and replaced democratic participation with top-down decisions ungrounded in research or the experience of organisations on the ground. What does this mean for the world's poorest people?
content.extendedDescription:
Swedish development aid is currently undergoing extensive changes. Decisions and methods have been implemented that have undermined Sweden's international credibility and replaced democratic participation with top-down decisions ungrounded in research or reality. In a short time, numerous decisions have affected priorities, working methods and relationships with civil society and the countries where Sweden operates. This development means greater political micromanagement and less room for long-term work, knowledge and local involvement. What will happen as efforts to prevent humanitarian disasters, epidemics and conflicts diminish, while China and Russia expand their presence to advance their geopolitical interests?

In this seminar, we present a review of 50 specific decisions and changes in Swedish development aid policy and discuss what is at stake for aid effectiveness, Sweden's international role and trust in policy.
content.subject: International affairs

content.title: Can Sweden afford to neglect aviation?
content.description:
Sweden is an export-dependent country with challenging geography. International and domestic connectivity is crucial for businesses, investment, skills supply and preparedness.

How can we secure aviation's contribution to Swedish competitiveness without compromising climate ambitions?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden's economy is built on international value chains, high-tech exports and a global presence. For many sectors, from life sciences and advanced industry to tourism and services, fast, reliable air connections are a prerequisite for investment and business establishments.
At the same time, Sweden is one of Europe's most sparsely populated countries, with long distances between growth regions. Aviation plays a structural role in regional development, labour market integration and the state's presence that few other modes of transport can replace. In a time of increasing geopolitical uncertainty and renewed focus on total defence, civilian aviation's importance for preparedness and redundancy has also come to the fore.

This seminar brings together decision-makers, business representatives and industry representatives to discuss:

• What role does aviation play in Sweden's long-term competitiveness?
• How does connectivity affect investment and business establishments?
• What is the state's responsibility?

content.title: Family centres: the key to parenting support and violence prevention
content.description: Family centres promote good parenting and prevent violence against children. How do staff view their conditions for violence prevention work under a new Social Services Act and expanded home-visiting programmes? How can employees' knowledge of violence against children be strengthened?
content.extendedDescription:
Since 2024, Barnafrid, the national knowledge centre on violence against children, has been tasked with supporting knowledge development in family centres. The seminar presents results from the 2026 survey, in which staff reflect on their conditions for carrying out violence prevention work.

A new workplace training programme tailored to family centre staff will also be presented. The training takes place on site and is led by a facilitator from the team's own workforce.
Barnafrid provides fact sheets, facilitator materials, presentation resources and practical case vignettes: a shared, dialogue-based approach to teaching that meets staff's wishes for high-quality learning within their teams. Launch is expected this autumn.

Barnafrid briefly describes the training and this year's survey. This is followed by a panel discussion with representatives of the board of Föreningen För Familjecentralers Främjande (FFFF).
content.subject: Children/young people

content.title: How a hard-to-love property from the 1970s was given new life through reuse
content.description: What should we do with office buildings from the 1960s and 1970s: too young to merit protection, too old to be considered modern? A completed project shows that reuse and respect for a building's original qualities can deliver both a low climate footprint and a stronger identity.
content.extendedDescription:
Office buildings from the 1960s and 1970s are demolished or rebuilt without regard for what already exists, even though reuse and preservation can deliver major climate benefits and retain unique qualities. The "hard-to-love" risks disappearing, despite possessing values we cannot recreate.
In the Vi på hörnet project in central Göteborg, Semrén & Månsson Arkitekter, together with Alecta Fastigheter and RO-Gruppen, transformed a building from the 1960s/1970s, taking its own character and period qualities as their starting point. The result: 10,000 m² of renewed office space and climate savings of 183,000 kg CO₂e.
During the discussion, we share practical lessons about reuse as a strategy, collaboration between architect, property owner and contractor, measuring climate benefits, and what is needed for circular construction to become the norm rather than the exception.
The discussion is open and requires no prior knowledge. You are welcome whether you work in construction and property or have a general interest in sustainable urban development.

content.title: Scaling up a greener food system – who will do the work?
content.description: Everyone is talking about scaling up a greener food chain. But who will do the work? Today, there is a large gap between ambitions, education and skills. This gap risks becoming a major challenge not only for the industries concerned, but for Swedish society as a whole and our food supply.
content.extendedDescription:
Green expansion has become a key phrase in discussions of Swedish food production, preparedness and transition. Fundamentally, it means increasing production, strengthening competitiveness and simultaneously meeting higher demands for sustainability and climate responsibility. But one question risks being overlooked: who will do the work?

As LRF and Livsmedelsföretagen share their perspectives, the focus turns to a growing gap between political ambitions, the education system's capacity and the industries' actual skills needs. If more people do not see the sector as a possible future, and if routes into education and employment remain unclear or non-existent, green expansion risks slowing before it has even gathered pace. Improved opportunities for adult education are crucial.

This presentation and the debate that follows therefore highlight a question both politicians and businesses must address: what conditions must be strengthened now to make the transition possible in practice?

content.title: Where did renewables go – and how do energy choices affect climate and biodiversity?
content.description: The expansion of renewable electricity generation has slowed, as has electrification. How can we reverse this trend to secure lower emissions, sufficient electricity, competitiveness and consideration for nature? What roles do efficiency, flexibility and eco-labelled electricity play in a robust energy system?
content.extendedDescription:
What happened to renewables, and how can we take the next step in the energy transition? Sweden is falling behind on electrification, transport emissions are increasing and the expansion of renewable electricity generation has slowed. How does this affect Sweden's competitiveness, climate targets and biodiversity?

This Almedalen seminar brings together businesses, politicians, electricity eco-labelling organisations and climate experts to discuss the development of the energy system. How can renewable electricity, energy efficiency and flexibility help meet demand, strengthen security of supply and reduce environmental impact?

The EU Energy Efficiency Directive requires reduced energy use by 2030. How can Sweden achieve the targets, and what effects will this have on society and businesses?

A new report on the environmental benefits of eco-labelled electricity and its significance for climate and biodiversity.
content.subject: Energy

content.title: From projects to outcomes – can outcomes-based contracts scale up prevention?
content.description: Sweden faces increasing ill health and growing welfare costs. Despite strong evidence for prevention, scaling up preventive measures is difficult. How can new governance and funding models create better conditions for long-term investment in health?
content.extendedDescription:
Despite strong evidence for prevention, Sweden struggles to move from pilot projects and temporary initiatives to long-term investment at scale. One important explanation is that today's governance and funding models often reward activities rather than achieved outcomes.
Outcomes-based contracts are attracting growing interest. By linking payments to verified outcomes, public, private and non-profit organisations can create new incentives for prevention. But which societal challenges are suited to outcomes-based funding? How can outcomes be measured credibly? And what changes are needed for prevention to become an investment rather than a cost?
Anders Ekholm from Ett Friskare Sverige opens the seminar and then moderates a discussion on how Sweden can take the next step, from projects to outcomes and from short-term interventions to long-term investment in health.
The event is part of Life Science-dagen, an initiative by Medicon Village.

content.title: Geographical divides in an election year: how is politics affected?
content.description: Geographical differences have become a growing source of polarisation around the world. Divides between urban and rural areas, but also within cities, affect political views. How is Swedish politics affected when people feel that different places offer entirely different prospects for the future?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden is changing, and differences between parts of the country are becoming increasingly apparent. In major and medium-sized cities, both economic and social divides are growing, with segregation, integration and unequal life chances shaping everyday life. Meanwhile, many people in rural and sparsely populated areas feel they are being left behind and that decisions are made far from their reality.

In this seminar, we examine polarisation between places, urban versus rural, and within places, where differences between neighbourhoods are growing in both larger and medium-sized municipalities. We also discuss what research shows about migration patterns: which areas people leave, where they move to and which values and experiences they bring with them.

Drawing on new research, researchers and politicians meet to discuss how geographical divides arise, what drives them and what consequences they have for politics, the election year and the future.

Welcome!

content.title: Can disarmament and degrowth make us safer? Turning points and systemic change in a new era
content.description: In a time of increasing military build-up, climate crisis and growing inequality, new economic and political choices arise. Can monetary and tax reform, basic income and international disarmament initiatives create both safety and security, quality of life and climate justice?
content.extendedDescription:
As military spending rises and the climate crisis deepens, discussion is growing about alternative ways to organise the economy and security. Can a society become safer through disarmament rather than military build-up? What would basic income and degrowth mean in people's everyday lives?
In this conversation, we discuss possible political turning points:
• Can international guarantees of non-aggression replace military build-up?
• How can reduced resource consumption be combined with improved quality of life and social security?
• What would an unconditional basic income mean for work, freedom and the economy?
• Can economic reforms direct investment away from exploitation and increased energy use and towards ecological transition and reduced inequality?
What do these ideas mean in practice, and what objections are there?
To prepare, we recommend the podcast "Samtal om vändpunkter" on our website, featuring in-depth discussions of these turning points. (1 of 5 seminars. Search for Partiet Vändpunkt to see all the seminars.)

content.title: Goals, uncertainty and responsibility in managing Baltic Sea fish – where have all the fish gone?
content.description: Management of our fish stocks has failed. Baltic cod has collapsed, and herring stocks are under pressure. Do we need new goals, greater caution and a broader perspective? What responsibility do policymakers, researchers and industry bear for restoring stocks?
content.extendedDescription:
The EU's Common Fisheries Policy starts from a seemingly simple idea: we should be able to catch as much fish as possible without jeopardising stocks' long-term viability. Management involves an extensive process intended to ensure sustainable fishing, with decisions based on scientific advice.

Despite this, several stocks clearly struggle to recover from historical overfishing. Baltic cod stocks have collapsed, and the situation for the Baltic Sea's most important fish species, herring, is worrying.

Our seminar examines today's management system, its shortcomings and how it may affect the developments we see in the Baltic Sea. We highlight proposals to restore fish stocks, including an ecosystem-based, holistic approach to stock management, updated goals and reduced risk-taking in fisheries management. The system needs to change: what responsibility and contribution can and should each stakeholder take?
content.subject: Animals/nature

content.title: Sweden wants to become a leading AI nation, but who is preparing young people to drive that development?
content.description: AI is changing working life faster than the education system is changing. How can we prepare young people for long working lives in an era when technology, vocational skills, responsibility, judgement and personal maturity must interact? What role does vocational education play in Sweden's future supply of skills?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden wants to become a leading AI nation, while many young people face a rapidly changing labour market and growing uncertainty about which educational choices are truly future-proof. This seminar shifts the focus from whether schools should use AI to the more fundamental question of the people Sweden needs to nurture for long working lives in which technology and human abilities must work together.

The seminar particularly highlights vocational education's role in the future supply of skills. What do employers need as technology becomes smarter? How can schools prepare young people for jobs that have yet to be fully defined? And what must policymakers enable so that education better matches a working life in which digital readiness, responsibility, judgement, teamwork and vocational skills become increasingly important? By bringing together perspectives from education, working life and society, we create a constructive discussion about confidence in the future, relevance and young people's entry into employment.
content.subject: Education

content.title: A new approach lifts Rosengård – how housing companies can strengthen disadvantaged areas
content.description: A focus on residents' influence and maintaining order has increased safety, satisfaction and pride in Rosengård, Malmö. Two years after a new approach was introduced in Rosengård, clear results are visible and have also been confirmed by a research study.
content.extendedDescription:
The approach introduced by municipal housing company MKB combines three elements: preventive support, maintaining order and improved property management. It was designed following interviews with around 700 MKB tenants in Rosengård. Their wishes were clear: more preventive measures for children and young people, and a stronger focus on order, with consequences for misconduct.

After two years, researchers Peter Esaiasson and Jacob Sohlberg at Göteborgs universitet conducted follow-up interviews showing substantial positive changes and strong support among Rosengård residents for the approach. MKB's own customer surveys point in the same direction: for example, the proportion who would recommend their neighbourhood has increased markedly.

At the seminar, MKB and the researchers from Göteborgs universitet will jointly discuss:
- How a clear focus on residents' influence has improved the area.
- Examples of stronger collective capacity.
- How responsible behaviour has become the norm in recycling buildings and shared spaces.

content.title: From need to reality: why does defence innovation get stuck in Sweden?
content.description: Needs-driven innovation has become a mantra in defence. In practice, it risks becoming both narrow and slow. When needs are defined in advance, often by major players with established methods, we risk missing the unexpected: disruptive solutions from small, agile companies.
content.extendedDescription:
Needs-driven innovation has become a mantra in defence. In practice, however, it risks becoming both narrow and slow. When needs are defined in advance, often by large organisations with established methods, we risk missing the unexpected: disruptive solutions from small, agile companies. Meanwhile, many innovative companies cannot enter the defence sector. They do not know whom to approach, how procurement works or how to connect with major prime contractors. Entry routes are unclear. How can we create a defence innovation system that is both needs-driven and open to the unexpected?

• What do we actually mean by needs-driven innovation in defence?
• When does being guided by needs become an obstacle to innovation?
• What is needed for small companies to genuinely work with the defence sector?
• How can prime contractors and startups collaborate without getting stuck in processes?
• Who takes responsibility for the interface between the public sector, prime contractors and startups?

content.title: How can the railway sector help reduce unemployment in Sweden?
content.description: Sweden faces both growing unemployment and an urgent need for technical skills. Meanwhile, the railway sector is undergoing a historic expansion, with modernisation, maintenance and sustainable transport of the future requiring more skilled professionals than ever.
content.extendedDescription:
This seminar discusses how the railway sector can become a strategic force in reducing unemployment by offering educational pathways, secure careers and routes into a growing profession of the future. How can industry, authorities, education providers and society work together to match people with opportunities and secure the skills that keep Sweden moving?

Panel 1 – Who builds Sweden? Does the skills shortage threaten implementation of the national plan? What is being done today, and what investment is needed to succeed?

Panel 2 – Railways as an industry of the future: future skills supply, innovation, digitalisation and collaboration.

Panel 3 – Railway skills supply from a total defence perspective: passenger transport, freight and total defence needs – are these interests compatible? How are measures prioritised, who funds them and how will skills be secured?

content.title: Hospital at home – can advanced cancer care move into patients' homes?
content.description: More people are living for a long time with cancer, and new treatments make care at home or close to home possible. This requires collaboration, new ways of working and clear rules on responsibility, funding and patient safety. How can hospital-at-home services develop within cancer care?
content.extendedDescription:
More patients are living for a long time with or after a cancer diagnosis. Meanwhile, new treatments, digital follow-up and medical technologies make advanced care possible at home or close to patients' homes. For many patients, this can improve quality of life and reduce the burden of repeated hospital visits.
International experience shows that treatment at home can be delivered safely when care is organised properly and multiple stakeholders collaborate. However, this development raises questions about responsibility, reimbursement systems, skills supply and collaboration between regions and municipal home healthcare.

The seminar starts from patients' vision of being treated at home when possible and in hospital when necessary. Examples from ongoing initiatives inform a discussion of the organisational and regulatory changes needed to bring future cancer care closer to patients.

content.title: Precision prevention for better health – are postcodes more important than genes?
content.description: Sweden's population is ageing, and we need to stay healthy for longer if health and social care are not to collapse. Yet health foundations are laid during childhood. Could precision prevention bring a breakthrough in more effective health promotion and disease prevention?
content.extendedDescription:
WHO says that 80% of cardiovascular disease and 40% of cancer can be prevented. Meanwhile, several risk factors are increasing in a rapidly ageing population. Healthcare spends 3% of its budget on promotion and prevention, and VAT was cut on all food on 1 April, despite evidence that a shift in food taxation could save 700 lives a year. Municipalities have no health department, yet shape the most important determinants of health.

Precision medicine has brought a breakthrough in cancer treatment. Could prevention also achieve a precision breakthrough? Should that precision target individuals, population groups or postcodes? What can municipalities do? How can different interventions reinforce one another for more effective prevention at different stages of life? Do we need a new prevention organisation and funding system, or can healthcare also deliver health promotion and primary prevention?

Hear how municipalities shape childhood conditions, what stakeholders outside healthcare can do, and about possible breakthroughs!
content.subject: Health and social care

content.title: When systems crash – will digital preparedness hold up?
content.description: Attackers are becoming increasingly sophisticated, and digital preparedness must improve. By sharing information and experience, we can jointly strengthen our resistance and move from words to action to build resilient IT infrastructure that supports society.
content.extendedDescription:
In an increasingly uncertain world, threats to society's digital infrastructure are growing. Cyberattacks are becoming more advanced and increasingly target critical functions such as energy systems, transport, commerce and public services. The question is not whether, but when, systems will face serious disruption.
Meeting these threats requires more than technology. It requires collaboration, information sharing and the ability to turn insights rapidly into concrete action. Robust, resilient IT infrastructure is essential for society to function even during crises and in the grey zone between peace and war.
How can we strengthen digital preparedness in practice? What responsibility lies with business, the public sector and politicians, and how can we jointly increase resilience?
This panel brings together businesses, authorities, politicians and academia to discuss how Sweden can move from words to action and build digital infrastructure that holds up even when systems are put to the test.
content.subject: Digitalisation

content.title: Sustainable defence companies are not built on one purchase – how can SMEs grow alongside total defence?
content.description: Sweden is undertaking a historic defence build-up, while the security situation in our region is characterised by prolonged uncertainty. This places new demands on how we build strong, resilient total defence, in which small and medium-sized enterprises play a crucial role.
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden's defence depends on small and medium-sized enterprises, both as direct suppliers and as part of larger companies' value chains. Yet many SMEs struggle to enter the market and grow within the sector. Many find it difficult to secure continuing orders after an initial purchase, creating major barriers to growth.

If Sweden is serious about strengthening its defence capability, purchasing individual solutions is not enough. The state must create better conditions for smaller companies to develop, scale up and become integrated into total defence's long-term supply chains.

The seminar discusses the concrete changes needed: faster procurement routes, more testbeds close to Försvarsmakten's operational needs, clearer pathways from initial orders to larger contracts, better financing between prototype and scale-up, and greater responsibility for established defence companies to open their value chains to Swedish SMEs.
