speakerTitles: Head of the Stockholm School of Economics Center for Security & Resilience

content.title: From bicycle storage to civil defence shelter in 100 days
content.description: Sweden's crisis preparedness is being tested in an increasingly uncertain world. Thousands of civil defence shelters exist, but many are effectively unusable today. Given the maintenance backlog, regulatory barriers and inadequate supply chains, how can shelters be made operational quickly?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden currently has around 64,000 civil defence shelters, but many have become bicycle storage rooms, storerooms and association premises.
As the international situation changes rapidly, shelters have returned to the spotlight, but awareness and confidence are low: more than half of Swedes do not know where their nearest shelter is, and 78 per cent have little confidence that shelters work.
Yet shelters are an active part of our civil defence and a tangible resource that can make a difference in a crisis. To fulfil their purpose, municipalities, authorities, property owners and businesses must collaborate. This means surveying, refurbishing and restoring shelters, securing material supplies, providing training on regulations and creating long-term maintenance plans.
How can we move from awareness to action? What is needed to open Sweden's shelters? These questions are addressed in today's seminar, where we discuss concrete steps to strengthen Sweden's preparedness.
content.subject: Security/defence
speakerTitles: Head of the Civil Protection Department

content.title: Energy preparedness now – solutions for clean energy, flexible grids and energy-positive districts
content.description: The global situation requires new approaches to reduce dependence on oil prices and strengthen energy security. Which design and system solutions can be scaled up: buildings with island operation, solar power and battery storage, waste heat recovery, balancing electricity grids or bio-CCS?
content.extendedDescription:
What concrete scenarios exist as we transition to robust, redundant and resilient energy systems? A local energy transition is under way in our cities, developing attractive places with more resilient energy supplies. Homes, blocks and neighbourhoods are moving from passive electricity customers to active parts of the energy system.
Greater sharing, digital control, electrification, solar and wind power, battery storage and waste heat recovery are creating a new, more decentralised energy landscape. These solutions provide access to cleaner energy and a vision of energy justice.
Meanwhile, today's electricity grids, historically built for a centralised, one-way system, are being challenged. Suppose this transformation were possible: what would it take?
Help shape the discussion at Omställningsarenan in Sweco's courtyard in Visby during Almedalsveckan! For the fourth consecutive year, forward-looking stakeholders in the built environment come together. You are welcome to participate.
content.subject: Energy
speakerTitles: Head of electrical systems and automation

content.title: Environmental Product Declarations for construction products: From nice to have to must have
content.description: Environmental Product Declarations (EPDs) for construction products have become increasingly prominent. With the entry into force of the revised EU Construction Products Regulation (CPR-2024), it will become mandatory for certain products to provide information on environmental impact indicators.
content.extendedDescription:
An EPD is a document that contains objective, comparable information, verified by a third party, on the environmental performance of products and services. The relevant European standard, EN 15804:2012+A2:2019, determines 13 mandatory core environmental impact indicators, with the option to include 6 additional reporting categories related to human health and land use.

In the construction sector, EPD are used to provide information on products and services, facilitating a Whole-Building Life Cycle Assessment (WBLCA).

The EU Construction Products Regulation published in 2024 (CPR-2024), regulates that for construction products for which a harmonised technical specification exists (usually a harmonised EN standard), certain environmental impact indicators must be provided. This obligation will be introduced in steps, starting with the Global Warming Potential (GWP).

This topic will be covered in a lecture supported by slides, followed by a question-and-answer session.
content.subject: Sustainability

content.title: From pilot to system – how can the state stimulate social investment?
content.description: Many of society's greatest challenges require long-term preventive measures. Yet these are difficult to finance within today's system. Testing and scaling more solutions requires risk-bearing funds repaid only if and when the interventions actually deliver results.
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden faces major societal challenges, from mental ill health and youth crime to growing needs in elderly care. We also know that early, preventive measures are often more effective than late interventions. Yet structures enabling such initiatives to be financed and scaled more widely are still missing.
The seminar discusses the state's role in strengthening Sweden's social investment ecosystem. We highlight concrete proposals, including a national knowledge centre inspired by the British Government Outcomes Lab, a government outcomes fund to co-finance results-based initiatives with municipalities and regions, and ways to mobilise more risk-tolerant capital through state actors such as Saminvest.
We also discuss how a national portal for requests for proposals can connect societal challenges, innovative solutions and investment capital more effectively.

Breakfast is served from 08.00.
content.subject: Economy
speakerTitles: Chair of the Committee on the Constitution

content.title: Climate risks and future crises – how can we prepare business and society?
content.description: Resilience is a business buzzword, but have climate risks made it into preparedness plans? Climate change can disable essential operations and critical services. How can boards and management prevent the effects of climate risks and build genuine resilience?
content.extendedDescription:
As climate change's impact becomes clearer, businesses face more and new challenges. Climate change increases the risk of extreme weather, supply-chain disruption and new requirements for businesses and other societal stakeholders. Yet many organisations remain inadequately equipped to manage climate risks within their routine governance and preparedness.

In this seminar, PwC brings together business and organisational representatives to discuss how boards and management can move from words to action. What is needed to integrate climate risks into strategy, risk management and decision-making? Who is responsible for strengthening resilience in an increasingly uncertain situation? And which reforms and priorities are needed to prepare business and society for future crises?

The audience will hear concrete perspectives on responsibility, preparedness and ways forward at a time when resilience has become crucial for competitiveness and society.
content.subject: Climate/environment

content.title: Resilience and competitiveness – how can we win both races?
content.description: Climate change, geopolitical uncertainty and supply-chain disruptions have increased the need for resilience. There is a risk that resilience is prioritised over growth, while Sweden, the Nordic region and Europe need stronger competitiveness. Which measures can build both resilient societies and a stronger economy?
content.extendedDescription:
Climate change, geopolitical uncertainty, disrupted supply chains and growing demands for robust energy supplies have made resilience a strategic issue for businesses and policymakers. Companies working in energy, industry, transport infrastructure and buildings play a crucial role in creating societies that can both withstand crises and compete globally.

Meanwhile, Sweden, the Nordic region and Europe face fierce global competition for investment, innovation and industrial development. Resilience initiatives risk becoming short-term responses to urgent crises that, at worst, inhibit innovation and growth. How can investment in energy, industry and infrastructure strengthen both resilience and growth? How can policymakers and businesses jointly create solutions that make the Nordic region more robust and competitive?
content.subject: Energy
content.accessibility: Wheelchair-accessible entrance and venue
speakerTitles: Head of the Supply Preparedness Department

content.title: Research espionage in the Nordic region – how can we protect innovation without slowing it down?
content.description: Research, technology and dual-use capabilities are strategic assets. In a heightened security situation, they must develop quickly and securely. As the EU, Sweden and the Nordic region strengthen research security, the question grows: how can we protect research from espionage without inhibiting openness, collaboration and growth?
content.extendedDescription:
Research espionage, espionage and research security have become increasingly important issues for universities, science parks, startups, investors and research-intensive companies. New technology, research data, international partnerships and dual-use capabilities can now have commercial, strategic and security-policy significance.

The EU and Sweden are strengthening work on research security, responsible internationalisation and secure innovation processes. Meanwhile, Nordic cooperation in defence, preparedness, industry and technology is deepening, including through NATO and joint Nordic initiatives.

The question is no longer whether research security is needed, but how to introduce it without unnecessary friction. When numerous collaborations, people and access rights need managing, isolated measures are insufficient. Scalable, proportionate and documented methods are needed, such as risk assessments, role analyses and background checks where relevant and permitted.
content.subject: Security/defence
content.organizationType: Collaboration between different types of organisation

content.title: EnergyNet and Energy Valley – can Skåne become a world leader in the energy systems of the future?
content.description: The electricity system must expand, but conventional grid expansion is often slow, costly and vulnerable. The question is how Sweden can create greater capacity, robustness and innovative strength faster through new local energy networks, open systems and strong regional technology ecosystems.
content.extendedDescription:
Electricity infrastructure faces a choice. The need for more capacity, robustness and rapid electrification is growing, while conventional grid expansion is often costly, slow and difficult to adapt to a more decentralised energy system. Lund is now developing EnergyNet, a new energy distribution architecture based on energy routers, open protocols and distributed control of electricity between buildings. Using the Pottugnen/Spjället pilot as a concrete example, we discuss how local meshed electricity networks can turn buildings into active nodes that produce, share, store and manage energy, taking the internet as a model.

Jonas Birgersson, "Bredbandsjesus", helped drive Sweden's internet transformation and now applies the same architectural thinking to electricity grids. Together with Dr. Marc Weiss, who helped shape Silicon Valley, we describe how EnergyNet could launch an Energy Valley in Skåne, with greater energy security, lower local energy costs, stronger robustness, growth and new skilled jobs.
content.subject: Energy
content.accessibility: Wheelchair-accessible entrance and venue

content.title: Job matching in crisis – unemployment and skills shortages divide Sweden
content.description: Sweden is divided by large differences in unemployment, with high unemployment and skills shortages in some regions and low unemployment elsewhere. How can unemployed people be given the right conditions to take jobs, municipalities secure skills and the state strengthen the labour market nationwide?
content.extendedDescription: Unemployment in Sweden is falling, but regional differences persist. Norrbotten has unemployment of 3.8 per cent, Dalarna 5.2 and Skåne 8.9 per cent, reflecting major differences in education levels, demographics and business structures. Counties with more highly educated residents and diversified labour markets fare better, while regions with larger foreign-born populations and greater dependence on individual industries face bigger challenges. Meanwhile, participation in labour market programmes is declining despite growing needs, risking deeper divides. This comes as many employers struggle to recruit the right skills, creating a growing mismatch in the labour market and reinforcing regional imbalances. What political action is needed for the state to support Sweden's municipalities and businesses and improve their conditions for recruiting skills? And how can unemployed people have better opportunities to enter the labour market?
content.subject: Employment/labour market
content.accessibility: Sign language interpretation, Wheelchair-accessible toilet, Wheelchair-accessible entrance and venue
speakerTitles: Member of Parliament and Labour Market Policy Spokesperson

content.title: AI at work: who sets the rules?
content.description: AI is changing working life rapidly, promising more productive processes and a better-matched labour market. Yet concerns include unemployment, discrimination, privacy, stress and reduced employee influence. The question is therefore increasingly important: who sets the rules for AI at work?
content.extendedDescription:
AI is entering more areas of working life, promising new ways of working, more efficient processes and better information for decisions. Yet it is often introduced before structures that give employees influence, transparency and security are in place. This increases the risks associated with AI alongside its promises: greater unemployment, discrimination, threatened privacy and increased stress.

Unionen's data shows how widespread AI use is in business, focusing on recruitment and variations in transparency and influence between workplaces. This raises questions that employers, employees and politicians must address: how can we ensure that the skills development needed for successful AI implementation exists and works?

Unionen presents new survey results from its workplace branches and members, providing insights into how well prepared employees and employers are for the transition. The question is: who sets the rules when technology changes work?
content.subject: Employment/labour market
content.accessibility: Hearing loop, wheelchair-accessible toilet, wheelchair-accessible entrance and venue

content.title: If water runs out, preparedness stops
content.description:
Water is more than a natural resource: it is fundamental to the resilience of our entire society and essential for Swedish food production to function.
How can we secure access to clean water most quickly, and what collaboration is needed to strengthen preparedness?
content.extendedDescription:
Looking at Sweden's preparedness work, we see that water and food supplies are closely linked. Livsmedelsverket describes food supply and drinking water as one of the country's most central preparedness sectors: everyone must have sufficient safe food and drinking water during crises and, ultimately, war.

For the food industry, water is a critical input, but also essential for hygiene, cleaning, cooling and robust production flows. Preparedness is therefore not just about coping with interruptions but maintaining as much normality as possible. When water supplies work, everyday life works better too: meals are served, businesses keep operating and people's security improves. This requires close collaboration between businesses, municipalities, authorities and water and wastewater operators.

Preparedness is not created in silos; it is built together. What kind of collaboration is needed, what infrastructure is already in place, and how should it be financed?
content.subject: Security/defence

content.title: Winning the AI Race: What Sweden Must Build Next
content.description: Sweden’s technical universities have built strong innovation clusters with leading companies, but in the AI era past strengths no longer suffice. Global competition is accelerating, with major investments in infrastructure, data, and talent. What decisions are needed to secure Sweden’s AI-position?
content.extendedDescription: Sweden’s technical universities have given rise to vibrant innovation clusters and world leading companies - built on a strong engineering tradition and world-class digital infrastructure. However, in the age of AI, what brought us here is not enough. Competition is intensifying rapidly. Countries and companies alike are investing at massive scale in energy, computing power, data, connectivity, and talent. The EU is stepping up, as are global investors. The risk? That Sweden loses momentum just as the playing field is being redrawn. To remain a leader, we need to strengthen the emerging AI-ecosystem in Sweden. New partnerships are required - to secure the necesarry skills and investment. This is a prerequisite for AI to truly become a superpower for Sweden, without compromising security. What must be done over the next ten years to avoid falling behind? Which investments and decisions are truly critical? And what will it take for international capital to choose Sweden?
content.subject: Digitalisation

content.title: Young people's engagement is changing – is democracy keeping up?
content.description: Young people's engagement is different from yesterday, and in 2040 it will not look like today's. Yet we still try to engage young people as though it were 1993. How can youth movements, parties, civil society and public bodies respond to young people's future civic engagement?
content.extendedDescription:
Young people's circumstances, living conditions and ways of organising change over time. Yet many democratic systems, funding models and organisations still reflect yesterday's forms of engagement.

What happens to democracy when young people engage in new ways and adults struggle to recognise and harness that engagement? Where is the balance between safeguarding traditional democratic structures and welcoming new forms of participation?

This discussion of future engagement explores how society responds to changing youth engagement and how youth movements, civil society, parties and the public sector create conditions for civic engagement in every era. Topics include:
- What will future engagement look like?
- How can systems and organisations respond to different forms of engagement over time?
- How can youth movements find purpose, a role, structures and long-term conditions as young people's engagement changes?
content.subject: Children/young people

content.title: Can a simple greeting help reduce polarisation in Sweden?
content.description: Almedalen celebrates encounters between people with different perspectives, experiences and opinions. Yet Sweden's public debate is increasingly marked by polarisation and a harsher tone. How can we safeguard dialogue and strengthen an open, respectful social climate?
content.extendedDescription:
What would happen, and what kind of society could we create, if we looked up more often and said HELLO to each other? Welcome to a HEJ walk!

When so much pulls us apart, a simple HELLO can be the beginning of something that brings us closer: a first step towards curiosity, respect and understanding other perspectives.

Almedalsveckan sees the launch of Hela Almedalen säger HEJ, a simple invitation to participants, organisations and visitors to contribute to more open, friendly conversations throughout the week. Join this cheerful HEJ walk and be part of the initiative, find inspiration and discover how you and your organisation can contribute to more encounters and conversations across boundaries.

During the walk, you will meet the initiators of Hela Sverige säger HEJ: Emma Jangö from Hej främling, Christian Altenius from Citypolarna and NSOE. Together, we say HELLO for a friendlier, more cohesive society.

Meet at the information post in Almedalsparken. Call if you cannot find us!
content.subject: Sustainability

content.title: Climate transition in rural Sweden – is it possible?
content.description: Sweden's rural areas are portrayed as bottlenecks in the climate debate. But what do people living there actually think? How can policy facilitate the transition throughout the country? What do researchers, political parties and other stakeholders say?
content.extendedDescription:
Debates about the climate transition often claim that policy penalises rural residents in particular. Claims that transition problems are especially severe in rural areas frequently justify dismantling climate policy, especially concerning climate and transport. But what do rural residents and the organisations representing them actually think? Can the transport system change in ways that also benefit rural areas? What public investment and policy instruments are needed? What do researchers, political parties and other stakeholders say?

The seminar begins with presentations by researchers and representatives of different parts of civil society, focusing on co-created climate policy for rural transitions. In the next part, political party representatives discuss the proposals presented.

The seminar is part of Uppsala universitets klimatdagar.
content.subject: Climate/environment
speakerTitles: Member of Parliament, Energy Policy Spokesperson
Member of Parliament, Climate Policy Spokesperson
Member of Parliament, Climate Policy Spokesperson

content.title: Kreativa Sverige in practice – culture, innovation and resilience
content.description: Culture and creativity play an increasing role in innovation and societal transition, while Europe accelerates through major initiatives. What paths lie ahead for the cultural and creative industries, taking the societal transition in northern Sweden as a starting point?
content.extendedDescription:
In times of crisis, uncertainty and rapid change, traditional solutions are insufficient. Culture and creativity offer new perspectives, critical thinking and the ability to make complex societal issues understandable and therefore open to change.

The Kreativa Sverige strategy has highlighted cultural and creative industries as a strategic resource for Sweden's development. Meanwhile, a European movement is growing in which culture's role in innovation and societal transition is increasingly evident, particularly through initiatives such as EIT Culture & Creativity and New European Bauhaus.

A central question remains: how can Sweden better harness the potential of cultural and creative industries?
This seminar brings together authorities, academia, regions and the cultural sector to explore the next steps.

The discussion focuses on how culture and creativity contribute to innovation, resilience and sustainable societies, and how their conditions can be strengthened regionally and nationally.
content.subject: Culture
speakerTitles: Researcher in Cultural and Creative Industries

content.title: Can measurement improve education, or do we risk measuring broader learning out of it?
content.description: Knowledge must be monitored and quality assured. But could a focus on what is measurable displace broader learning, judgement and democratic competence? How can governance encompass education's full purpose and nurture confident young people capable of action?
content.extendedDescription:
Monitoring and quality assurance are prerequisites for equitable schooling. But education is more than what appears in results. Broader learning, judgement and the ability to think independently and participate in a democratic society are equally crucial but harder to measure.

Swedish schooling has always oscillated between freedom and regulation, trust and control. The biggest school reforms in 30 years are now being implemented, with new curricula, a new grading system and increased regulation. The ambition matters. Meanwhile, the OECD highlights the importance of nurturing confident pupils who can navigate a complex world. How can we ensure that the entire mission, not just its measurable aspects, is present in encounters with children and pupils?

How can governance secure knowledge development without measuring broader learning out of education? How can we create security and trust? And what does quality in Swedish education really mean when we take the entire mission seriously in a time of climate transition and democratic retreat? These are the questions we explore.
content.subject: Education
content.accessibility: Hearing loop, wheelchair-accessible toilet, wheelchair-accessible entrance and venue
speakerTitles: Vice-Rector for Culture and Educational Development

content.title: Nordic Connector – how can we move from vision to reality?
content.description: Nordic Connector, a fixed link across Kvarken between Vasa and Umeå, would strengthen infrastructure redundancy, connect labour markets and create a new strategic east–west corridor for industry and trade. But how can we move from vision to reality?
content.extendedDescription:
In a heightened geopolitical situation, robust transport systems are crucial for security, supply and competitiveness. Connecting Sweden, Norway and Finland in the north shortens distances, expands labour markets and strengthens supply chains in an increasingly strategic region. The result is a stronger Nordic whole and a more competitive economy at a time of growing demands for security and cooperation.
Nordic Connector, a fixed link across Kvarken between Vasa and Umeå, would strengthen infrastructure redundancy, connect labour markets and create a new east–west corridor for industry and trade. But the project requires coordination, clear political priorities and new financing solutions.
How can we move from vision to reality and enable construction to begin on one of the Nordic region's most strategically significant infrastructure projects in modern times? During Almedalsveckan, we bring stakeholders together to discuss what is needed to move from idea to construction.
content.subject: Infrastructure/transport

content.title: When premises stand empty – who dares untangle the VAT problem?
content.description: Premises exist. Demand is enormous. Yet supply does not meet demand. Why? Across Sweden, sports clubs must turn away children and young people because they cannot access premises. Meanwhile, premises stand empty or are rented to others. Why? The answer is VAT.
content.extendedDescription:
Today's VAT rules make it uncertain and sometimes unprofitable for property owners to rent to organisations not conducting VAT-liable activities on the premises. The result is a system that excludes sport, culture and other parts of civil society from the premises market, despite considerable need and obvious public benefit.

For many sports clubs, finding premises has become a constant obstacle to developing their activities and, at worst, a threat to their existence. How do the rules affect property owners' ability to rent out premises, and what trade-offs are actually made in practice?

Can we create a system where anyone can rent any kind of premises, regardless of VAT status? A government inquiry argues that changes risk increasing costs. Others argue that doing nothing is considerably more expensive, through lost activities, limited growth and weaker civil society. So what is the real problem, and what will it take to solve it?
content.subject: Children/young people

content.title: Green competitiveness: making Sweden a leader in sustainable life science innovation
content.description: Sweden needs to turn sustainable pharmaceutical and medtech innovation into a competitive advantage. Stronger competitiveness requires clear incentives and simpler rules that stimulate research, development and early introduction of sustainable solutions.
content.extendedDescription: Environmentally sustainable innovation in pharmaceuticals and medical technology must shift from being seen as a costly requirement to becoming a competitive advantage. Countries investing in the climate transition become more attractive for future jobs and investment. For Sweden to lead, policies and regulations must create clear incentives for companies to invest in research, development and sustainable products, and to see Sweden as an attractive location for development, clinical trials and early introduction. Sustainable solutions require investment throughout their life cycle. Several initiatives already exist but see limited use. Standards such as PAS2090, which measures environmental impact at product level, can provide practical support. However, today's pharmaceutical substitution system does not consider sustainability. For companies to choose Sweden as an innovation environment, long-term, attractive conditions are needed to stimulate development of tomorrow's sustainable pharmaceuticals and medical technology.
content.detail: Life Science Arena – Sweden's growth engine
content.subject: Health and social care

content.title: How can Sweden secure industrial investment worth billions and jobs amid global competition?
content.description: What does Sweden need to win more investment? Sweden has global leadership in industrial innovation to defend and strengthen. Billions in investment and thousands of jobs are at stake in an increasingly fierce global contest over where investments, new operations and expansions are located.
content.extendedDescription:
Join this moderated panel discussion in Business Sweden's garden, where we explore how international companies' operations contribute to Swedish prosperity and examine global competition.

They strengthen Swedish value chains, drive research and innovation, provide capital and build Sweden's long-term competitiveness. Sweden's appeal rests on genuine strengths in stability, predictability and technological leadership, but competition from countries actively removing barriers is intensifying.

Companies evaluating Sweden encounter challenges with energy availability, permitting, skills supply and incentives. Encouraging existing operations to expand and stay is as important as attracting new ones.

The panel brings together perspectives from Team Sweden, politics, industry and Business Sweden to identify what must happen nationally, regionally and locally for Sweden to mobilise and secure the investment it deserves.
content.subject: Business
speakerTitles: Chair of the Municipal Executive Board

content.title: Demolish, remodel or develop further – how can we make the right decisions for disadvantaged areas?
content.description: How can areas facing social, economic and structural challenges be improved, and what tools are needed to create a robust, sustainable society? Many municipalities are transforming areas with low attractiveness and major management challenges. What tools and solutions are available?
content.extendedDescription:
Demolition is often suggested as an option, but is rarely the only or obvious solution. The discussion takes a broader approach to transforming disadvantaged areas, viewing demolition, renovation, densification and social measures as parts of a combined toolkit. Concrete examples inform a discussion of sound decision-making through analysis, structure and clear goals, weighing social, economic and property-economic perspectives together.

Svefa's courtyard, Fastighetshubben at Adelsgatan 25, is an Almedalen meeting place where public and private sectors can exchange experience, converse and discuss property issues, focusing on urban development, the built environment and a sustainable society. The stage hosts seminars, panel debates and networking events on strategic urban development, the property market and sustainability. Find Svefa's full Almedalen programme at www.svefa.se
content.subject: Economy

content.title: Ukraine’s Victory Alliances: Joint Actions and Commitments
content.description: Close effective cooperation between national and local authorities, international actors, civil society, cultural and educational institutions are essential to bring Ukraine's victory closer.
content.extendedDescription: Join us in exploring how we can transform dialogue into impactful actions, forging alliances to consolidate efforts to bring Ukraine's victory closer.  Carpathian Sea Democracy Week — Ukraine’s Almedalen — an international platform born in wartime in Kyiv and Truskavets but rooted in the same democratic values that define Almedalen and Gotland today: openness, accountability, transperancy. CSDW has become a bridge between Ukraine, EU, NATO members — connecting parliamentarians, ambassadors, mayors, leaders of civil society, and international partners with the belief that dialogue must lead to consolidated actions and that Ukraine’s victory is precondition for Europe’s security. Today, on Gotland — a symbol of Nordic security — we gather to transform solidarity into strategy, and strategy into concrete commitments that bring Ukraine’s victory closer. We identify concrete steps that parliaments, governments, regions, civil society can take together to have the highest impact potential.
content.detail: Cramergatan 3, space 327, Almedalensveckan, Samarbetsplatformen: Sverige och Ukraina
content.subject: International affairs

Member of Parliament, Committee on Foreign Affairs

content.title: We are building blind
content.description: The need for traceability, control and follow-up is growing. When information gets stuck between stakeholders and stages, deviations are discovered only after causing errors, delays and additional costs. Data creates value only when it is standardised, machine-readable, traceable and interoperable throughout the value chain.
content.extendedDescription:
We seem to be building blind, despite never having had more data.

Deviations are discovered late, quantities do not match and decisions rest on uncertain information. Meanwhile, demands for traceability, climate data and reporting are growing. The question is not whether information is available, but why we do not use it better.

The SBUF-funded project Från BIM till BOM – Obruten digital värdekedja brings industry stakeholders together to challenge current methods and establish a vision for a more coherent process.

How can we create information flows in which errors are immediately visible, transparency increases and we can trust what is built? And how can we ensure data strengthens productivity instead of becoming another administrative layer? These are the questions we raise.

This seminar is for those working in construction, property, design or digital development who want to help shape a more efficient, sustainable industry in an increasingly data-driven world.
content.subject: Construction

content.title: Pharmacist-supplied medicines – opportunities, responsibilities and the way forward
content.description: The Tidö Agreement announces a new category of non-prescription medicines that pharmacies may sell following individual advice from a pharmacist. The reform aims to ease pressure on healthcare and strengthen conditions for prevention and informed self-care.
content.extendedDescription:
Similar models have long been established in countries such as Norway and the United Kingdom, with documented positive results.
At the time of this seminar, the reform is at a decisive stage. We meet, regardless of the bill's position in the decision-making process, to analyse the conditions for successful implementation and the changes the reform brings to pharmacies, industry and the healthcare system.

Topics include:
How should successful introduction of pharmacist-supplied medicines be designed, and what are the critical success factors?
What does the reform require of pharmaceutical companies, pharmacies and other stakeholders to achieve its intended effect?
How can pharmacies' role in preventive healthcare be strengthened and clarified within the new category?

We welcome decision-makers, industry representatives and experts to discuss a reform with the potential to change Swedish medicine supply and self-care over the long term.
content.subject: Health and social care
speakerTitles: Chair of Parliament's Committee on Health and Welfare

content.title: Autonomous vehicles – will Europe lead or fall behind?
content.description: Autonomous vehicles are no longer a future vision: they already operate commercially in the United States and China. Europe has the potential to lead but risks falling behind, not because technology is lacking but because regulations cannot keep up. How can we ensure operations centred on safety and accessibility?
content.extendedDescription:
Waymo makes more than 450,000 trips a week in the United States and Baidu over 250,000 in China. Europe has 35 pilot projects but few commercial routes. The market is expected to reach 44 billion euros by 2030, but only if Europe moves from pilots to actual deployment.
In an on-stage conversation, Vivetha Natterjee, Head of Autonomous Product & Deployment at Bolt, shares her assessment of the technology and industry today and what Europe needs to proceed on its own terms: harmonised regulation, Vision Zero as an ethical foundation and inclusion from day one.
Mattias Goldmann from 2030-sekretariatet leads the discussion, with audience questions and participation. Key themes include regulatory challenges, where a vehicle approved in Hamburg still cannot operate in Helsinki, road safety and how autonomous vehicles can enable accessible mobility for older people, people with disabilities and rural residents. What is needed so Sweden and Europe do not miss this opportunity?
content.subject: Sustainability
content.accessibility: Hearing loop, wheelchair-accessible entrance and venue

content.title: When support and assessment do not align – how can we secure pupils' right to digital tools?
content.description: Pupils who need digital tools to support learning must be allowed to use them when their knowledge is assessed. As schools undergo reform, a crucial question is how to ensure equity means the right conditions for each pupil rather than identical conditions for everyone. What is needed for an accessible school system?
content.extendedDescription:
The event is a panel discussion bringing together perspectives on one of schools' most central questions: ensuring every pupil has the conditions to reach their full potential. Starting from concrete examples of everyday school life, the discussion highlights challenges when access to support varies. Equity means giving every pupil precisely the support they need to succeed.
The panel includes Idor Svensson, Professor of Clinical Psychology at Linnéuniversitetet, with extensive experience researching dyslexia. His perspective deepens understanding of how the right tools affect learning and participation. Eva Lundin, an educator at Solbergaskolan in Visby, also participates, bringing a close classroom perspective and experience of using digital services to create accessibility in practice. By bringing research and practice together, the seminar aims to drive a solution-oriented discussion about tomorrow's schools.
content.subject: Education

content.title: Future supply of goods – from efficient to robust flows
content.description: What happens when chips do not arrive from Asia, medicines get stuck in port or grain cannot be transported? Just-in-time no longer works. We need new solutions allowing energy, food and medicine to be produced, stored and transported securely, even in turbulent times.
content.extendedDescription:
When the pandemic struck, factories stopped. When the Suez Canal was blocked, everything was delayed. We now know global supply chains are vulnerable. The solution? More local production and smarter logistics. Think concretely: energy companies securing local energy. Food producers making and storing food regionally so shop shelves remain stocked in a crisis. Pharmaceutical companies bringing critical medicine production home. How can we plan factories, warehouses and freight terminals close to consumers? How can railways function when lorries stop? These questions are debated here.

Help shape the discussion at Omställningsarenan in Sweco's courtyard in Visby during Almedalsveckan! For the fourth consecutive year, forward-looking built-environment stakeholders gather. No registration is required: enjoy a relaxed courtyard setting with incisive observations and take part in solution-oriented discussions. Together, we create sustainable, resilient societies. Welcome!
content.subject: Infrastructure/transport
speakerTitles: Head of the Industry Business Unit
Head of the Heating Business Area,

content.title: Obesity and working life – creating sustainable solutions for health and productivity
content.description: Obesity affects health, work capacity and the economy. The disease costs society many billions of kronor annually in lost production alone. How can sustainable solutions deliver better health, stronger work capacity and increased productivity?
content.extendedDescription: Obesity is a widespread disease affecting both people's health and society's economy. It is associated with an increased risk of conditions including type 2 diabetes, serious cardiovascular disease, liver and kidney disease, certain cancers and premature death. It often leads to sick leave and reduced work capacity. Nearly a quarter of people aged 45-64 are estimated to have obesity (BMI above 30). The seminar focuses on obesity as a societal issue at the intersection of health and working life. How does it affect sick leave and work capacity? What workplace consequences arise when treatment is absent or delayed? We discuss possible co-funded treatment models, including employer funding, insurance solutions and social outcomes contracts. How can these complement public healthcare without increasing inequality? What regulatory changes could incentivise investment in treatment for better health and work capacity?
content.subject: Health and social care
speakerTitles: Head of National Market Access & Pipeline

content.title: How can we build organisations that manage technological change and care for their people?
content.description: Tomorrow's organisations and society: what skills and leadership are needed to meet AI development, global uncertainty, rapid change and increasing demands? Many people feel stressed and threatened in their profession or expertise. How can Sweden remain competitive?
content.extendedDescription:
Digitalisation, market turbulence, technological change, especially AI, demographics and more complex working lives are already changing the skills organisations need and how work must be led.

Change is rapid: how do we bring everyone along? Such extensive transformation also affects mental strain, the work environment and people's ability to sustain themselves over time.

How can we build organisations that manage technological change while caring for the people experiencing it? How can we meet different generations' needs?

What will tomorrow's organisations need, and what do we need today? How should we design them?

What kinds of organisations and leadership enable people to perform, feel well and develop over time? AI is changing our understanding of knowledge and skills.

What skills do people possess, and what knowledge capital does the organisation hold?

We hope to discuss these questions together!

Welcome!

Panels will be announced later!
content.subject: Business
content.accessibility: Hearing loop, wheelchair-accessible entrance and venue

content.title: AI in schools – who takes responsibility when development outpaces governance?
content.description: AI is changing schools faster than regulations can keep up. Clear national guidelines are lacking, but school providers must act. Scenario-based support for governance, ethics and technology has been developed. How can it help, and whose responsibility is it to lead the way?
content.extendedDescription:
AI is developing rapidly and already affects everyday school life, from learning tools and assessment to administration. Although the school system has been included in Sweden's AI strategy since February 2026, national guidelines on managing AI in schools are lacking. School providers face daily questions about ethics, law and technology choices without national support.
In this vacuum, SKR and Ifous, together with 16 other stakeholders, have developed a web-based support tool built around scenarios and three learning pathways: Governance & Leadership, Ethics & Law and Technology Procurement. The tool launches in June 2026 as an open resource. In parallel, Ifous runs the "AI i utbildning" support process, strengthening teachers' ability to select AI tools on pedagogical grounds.
The seminar demonstrates the tool and discusses responsibilities between the state, municipalities and school providers. Participants receive practical tools to take home and insights into how other municipalities address these issues. The discussion starts from real dilemmas school leaders face daily.
content.subject: Education
speakerTitles: Head of Communications and Social Impact

content.title: Can AI make regional development more accurately targeted?
content.description: Regional development often relies on statistics, analyses and forecasts based on historical data. Meanwhile, access to large datasets is growing rapidly. Can AI provide regions with better decision support and therefore more accurately targeted strategic priorities?
content.extendedDescription:
Regional development involves long-term decisions affecting labour markets, skills supply, innovation, infrastructure and business. These decisions rely heavily on statistics, analyses and forecasts describing past developments. Meanwhile, access to data is growing rapidly, from official statistics and authorities to mobility data, business data and other digital traces of societal development.
AI can analyse these datasets in new ways, providing more advanced forecasts and decision support. This raises a central question: can AI make regional development policy more data-driven and accurately targeted? Or does it risk reinforcing existing patterns and shifting the centre of decision-making from political judgements to algorithmic analysis?
How can AI be used in strategic regional development, and what opportunities and risks arise when data and advanced analysis play a greater role in how a region plans its future?
content.subject: Innovation
content.accessibility: Wheelchair-accessible entrance and venue

content.title: When customers click for sustainability – can we deliver nationwide?
content.description: More people want fossil-free deliveries, but the transition is fastest in major cities and along profitable routes. Sustainable deliveries risk becoming a big-city privilege. How can we make the transition work nationwide without compromising service, price or accessibility?
content.extendedDescription:
E-commerce and growing home delivery make transport increasingly visible to customers. Meanwhile, proposals are being discussed to scrap the target of cutting transport-sector emissions by 70 per cent by 2030 and introduce an electrification target instead. This puts even greater focus on what is actually feasible nationwide.

Conditions differ radically between urban and sparsely populated areas, and between high-volume flows and rural routes. If sustainable deliveries work only where volumes are large and alternatives plentiful, we risk a two-tier transition.

The seminar examines everyday conditions facing fuel suppliers, logistics operators and retailers with customers nationwide. We discuss what requirements, customer promises and collaboration models can actually be met, how checkout choices and communication influence demand, and what is needed to scale up more sustainable fuels. How can we design rules and business arrangements that make sustainable deliveries the norm rather than an optional extra?
content.subject: Infrastructure/transport
speakerTitles: Head of Category and Fleet Management

content.title: Trump's new pharmaceutical policy – does Sweden have a plan as the rules change?
content.description: Trump's MFN pharmaceutical policy is shaking Europe. In a new geopolitical reality, Sweden's competitiveness, patients' access to new medicines and our future resilience are at stake. How can we secure investment, innovation and faster access to new treatments as the rules change?
content.extendedDescription:
The pharmaceutical industry is one of Sweden's most important foundational industries, crucial for growth, healthcare productivity and national resilience. Meanwhile, the playing field is changing rapidly.

China is sharply increasing investment, and the United States' Most Favored Nations pricing policy has changed conditions for the global pharmaceutical industry and shaken Europe.

The consequences are already here. European research and production initiatives are being paused or relocated, investment is failing to materialise, and new medicines are not being launched or are being withdrawn in countries with heavy price pressure.

Sweden is particularly vulnerable. We have low prices, low uptake of new medicines and a model that does not fully value innovation's societal benefits. This makes us less attractive for investment, research and launches.

What is now needed to secure patients' access to new medicines and strengthen growth, resilience and Sweden's position as a leading life science nation?

Is there a plan now that the rules have changed?
content.detail: Life Science Arena – Sweden's growth engine

content.title: Resistance to knowledge – what it is, what drives it and how to counter it
content.description: Why do people cling to mistaken beliefs despite strong evidence? Resistance to knowledge is not merely ignorance or a lack of reason, but a complex interaction between psychology, politics and a changing information landscape. What drives it, and what can counter it?
content.extendedDescription: Resistance to knowledge is one of the major societal challenges of our time. Clinging to mistaken beliefs despite strong evidence can have serious consequences, for example weakening trust in democratic institutions, research and media. This can affect everything from willingness to vaccinate and climate engagement to attitudes towards elections. Resistance to knowledge is not simply ignorance or a lack of reason, but a complex interaction between group identity, distrust of established institutions, motivated reasoning and disinformation. But how does it actually work? This discussion starts from new research examining its philosophical, psychological, social and media-related drivers, consequences and remedies, and explores what is needed to counter it. The discussion is part of Vetenskap & Allmänhet's arena for research and democracy.
content.subject: Research

content.title: Digital sovereignty and digital dependence – building total defence in a digitalised society
content.description: Sweden is one of the world's most digitalised countries, but also depends on global technologies and cloud services. How are our security, robustness and freedom of action affected by cyberattacks or disruptions?
content.extendedDescription:
How can we build robust total defence in a society heavily dependent on digital infrastructure, global cloud services and strategic technologies such as AI? Sweden is one of the world's most digitalised countries, but digitalisation also creates new vulnerabilities. Cyberattacks, information influence operations and dependence on foreign platforms raise questions about cybersecurity, digital sovereignty and national freedom of action.

The seminar examines how data, AI and other strategic technologies affect future total defence and what skills, research environments and technical capabilities Sweden needs to develop to strengthen society's resilience. It also addresses collaboration between the public sector, business and academia to build secure digital systems, reduce strategic dependencies and strengthen Sweden's ability to act in an uncertain, rapidly changing world. Innovation, research and skills supply for future security are also in focus.
content.subject: Digitalisation
content.organizationType: Collaboration between different types of organisation

content.title: How can we strengthen and support municipalities' efforts against welfare crime in public procurement?
content.description: What challenges do municipalities and other public purchasing organisations face when criminal actors try to exploit public contracts and welfare systems? What measures and practical support can strengthen prevention, follow-up and collaboration?
content.extendedDescription:
Welfare crime and infiltration of public procurement by unscrupulous or criminal actors risk undermining trust in public purchasing. When taxpayers' money goes to companies whose business models involve fraud, labour-related crime or organised crime, competition is distorted, welfare service quality may deteriorate and society's resilience weakens.

How can municipalities and other public purchasing organisations use procurement to counter these risks?

A panel representing municipalities, authorities and other relevant stakeholders discusses practical experience, operational support and good examples of how procurement can help prevent and detect welfare crime. The focus is on concrete tools and forms of collaboration that strengthen municipalities' work for sound public purchasing, fair competition and effective use of public funds.
content.subject: Economy

content.title: Turning headwinds into business value: success factors for profitable electrification of heavy vehicles
content.description: Some argue that the energy transition's next major leap, electrifying public transport, boats, buses, machinery and heavy vehicles, has stalled. The pace has slowed alongside declining demand and profitability. Sometimes, the claim is that there is no business case.
content.extendedDescription:
Progress has been slower than the optimistic forecasts that dominated a few years ago. But is it premature to dismiss business models for electrifying heavy transport? Several Swedish stakeholders demonstrate the opposite.

Both private and public sectors offer examples where electric fleets provide a competitive advantage and business value. How did they achieve this? What are the success factors? Which obstacles have they encountered and overcome? And what role has policy played? The seminar examines developments from different angles and highlights key factors for overcoming barriers and daring to invest. Is it mainly about grid expansion, access to electricity and power capacity, technical solutions such as battery development and charging infrastructure, or economic viability through reasonable investment conditions, financing and business models and adapted electricity tariffs to stimulate demand? What political ground rules and policy instruments are needed?
content.subject: Energy

content.title: When land can no longer be protected – who is responsible for retreat?
content.description: Rising sea levels, erosion and flooding challenge current spatial planning. When protection is no longer sufficient or economically reasonable for society, difficult questions arise about responsibility, compensation and land use. Who decides when people, businesses and buildings must move?
content.extendedDescription: How can we plan for a society in which some places eventually can no longer be protected? Join a discussion where authorities, municipalities and the property sector explore planned retreat as a tool, the allocation of responsibility, legislation, economic consequences and timely decisions to strengthen society's long-term resilience. Svefa's courtyard, Fastighetshubben at Adelsgatan 25, is an Almedalen meeting place where public and private sectors can exchange experience, converse and discuss property issues, focusing on urban development, the built environment and a sustainable society. The stage will host seminars, panel debates and networking events on strategic urban development, the property market and sustainability. Meet property specialists from across the industry. Find Svefa's Almedalen programme at www.svefa.se

content.title: Who can influence cancer care – and on what terms?
content.description: Patient involvement is central to developing future cancer care. But whose experiences inform that development, and whose risk being absent? How can we create forms of participation that reach more people and better reflect the patient population?
content.extendedDescription:
Patient and family involvement is central to developing future cancer care. Yet experience and research show that opportunities to influence care vary. Some groups remain underrepresented in settings where care is shaped and developed.

This matters. Young adults are a small group in cancer care, but their life circumstances often differ from those of both younger children and older adults. When young people's experiences are absent, important needs also risk going unmet.

Join an inspiring seminar exploring how patient involvement can work in practice! What is needed for more people to have a say? How can we ensure patients' perspectives have an impact? And what can healthcare, research and other stakeholders gain from more voices being heard?

Concrete examples from young adults affected by cancer, healthcare, research and national development work highlight methods, lessons and opportunities for more representative patient involvement.

Breakfast will be served!

content.title: Feminism and men's violence against women – where do the parties stand?
content.description: Where do the parties stand on men's violence against women, surrogacy and abortion? How far are they willing to go to reduce women's and girls' vulnerability in pornography and prostitution?
content.extendedDescription:
An election takes place in September, with much discussion of healthcare, law and order and schools. Men's violence against women rarely receives much attention in election debates. Yet a recent Novus survey shows that 63 per cent of the population consider it important to have a women's or girls' support service near where they live. Fully 81 per cent believe children should have the right to accompany a mother experiencing violence if she is placed in protected accommodation,* despite new reforms making this harder.

This election debate focuses wholeheartedly on feminist issues, particularly men's violence against women. Topics include honour-based violence, prostitution, pornography, surrogacy, abortion, women's and girls' support services and protected accommodation.

Afterwards, there will be mingling with drinks and snacks while supplies last.

*Novus conducted the survey in week 17 of 2026 for Roks, using online interviews with a randomly recruited Swedish panel. A total of 1,003 people aged 18-84 participated.
content.subject: Gender equality
speakerTitles: Gender Equality Policy Spokesperson, Chair of S-kvinnor
Family and gender equality policy spokesperson

content.title: Culture and creativity as a transformative force in societal transition
content.description: Northern Sweden is undergoing a major societal transition. How can culture strengthen participation, attractiveness and resilience, and how can we harness the cultural and creative industries' driving forces in this transition?
content.extendedDescription:
Societal transition in northern Sweden involves major investments, but also a growing need for inclusion and participation to create sustainable living environments. Culture plays a central role in democracy, attractiveness and resilience. The seminar starts from culture's role in societal transition, drawing on experience from northern Sweden. Cultural and creative industries contribute crucial skills. The question is whether innovation systems are equipped to harness them. Addressing complex societal challenges requires better-targeted innovation support based on these industries' exploratory, cross-sectoral and boundary-crossing ways of working.

How does culture contribute to resilience and attractive communities? How must the innovation system adapt to fully harness the driving forces of cultural and creative industries?

Drawing on northern Sweden, we highlight paths towards a more inclusive innovation system regionally, nationally and in cooperation with Europe.

content.organizationType: Collaboration between different types of organisation

content.title: Less talk, more action – Skåne's green reindustrialisation creates opportunities for all of Sweden
content.description: Industrial growth is now taking place in southern Sweden, particularly Skåne, where power capacity shortages have been challenged and a sustainable system created to accommodate extensive reindustrialisation. Meanwhile, industries already producing substantial value are undergoing a green energy transition.
content.extendedDescription: Much attention in recent years has focused on reindustrialisation in the north, with energy-intensive battery storage and other flagship projects. Meanwhile, a quiet industrial transformation has taken place in the south, challenging power capacity shortages and developing a sustainable system to meet industrial demand. The collaboration platform Skånes Effektkommission has played an important role. Industrial growth is currently taking place in southern Sweden, particularly Skåne. Industries already producing substantial value are undergoing a significant green energy transition. Major industrial investments are also being made in Malmö, Lund and Landskrona, among other places. Important suppliers to Swedish manufacturing are based here, enabling industrial projects elsewhere in Sweden too. Skånes effektkommission brings municipalities, energy companies, businesses and authorities together in a shared forum to strengthen conditions for competitive business and secure energy supplies.

content.title: Innovation as defence capability: AI-enhanced processes to meet the unexpected
content.description: Försvarsmakten's need to respond to new threats requires Sweden to develop AI-enhanced innovation processes. Adapting our innovation capability to these demands strengthens the entire country's resilience. How can Sweden move from peacetime logic to smarter preparedness?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden is a world leader in innovation, but our processes are designed for peacetime. In a changing world, working harder is not enough: we must work smarter. We need AI-enhanced innovation processes in which AI is not merely part of the technology but drives the methods, functions and decision-making themselves.

The lessons from Ukraine are clear: rapidly adapting new technology is crucial. This requires a national transition making innovation integral to defence capability. By meeting the military domain's extreme demands for speed and precision, we create methods that strengthen Sweden's innovation capacity as a whole. Advances made to counter sudden threats thus become a catalyst for Swedish competitiveness and public benefit in peacetime too.

How can we build AI solutions that help us innovate more intelligently? How can solutions developed for defence strengthen Sweden as an innovation nation?

content.title: How do municipalities address national digitalisation initiatives in light of local needs?
content.description: Fewer people must deliver welfare services to more people, and digitalisation is seen as an important way forward. Municipal conditions vary, while national stakeholders offer shared solutions. How are national and local initiatives balanced in practice, and what effects are achieved?
content.extendedDescription:
With an ageing population and fewer working-age people, Sweden's municipalities and welfare services face major challenges. Digitalisation is often presented as the solution, with scalable technologies that can streamline processes and create value through new ways of working. National stakeholders such as the government, DIGG and SKR support municipalities with shared frameworks and digital solutions, but how do municipalities balance national initiatives with local needs and priorities?

The seminar starts from a master's thesis by a PwC employee who researched implementation of national digitalisation initiatives at municipal level in spring 2026. Based on in-depth interviews with representatives of 20 municipalities, the study offers a unique insight into conditions across the country. The panel brings together SKR, municipal and academic representatives to discuss the interaction between national and local digitalisation work in improving and developing welfare services.

content.title: The skills gap is growing – how can we secure the next generation of engineers?
content.description:
How can we ensure Sweden meets the growing need for engineering skills to address societal challenges:
The green transition
Defence capability
Industrial competitiveness
Jobs and welfare
content.extendedDescription:
Panel debate led by the Editor-in-Chief of Ny Teknik.
Demand for engineering skills in STEM (science, technology, engineering and mathematics) is rising rapidly as AI, digitalisation, advanced industry, electrification and cybersecurity reshape business. Meanwhile, national assessments show current educational capacity is insufficient. Just over 80,000 people currently study STEM at higher education level in Sweden, and the government aims to increase this to at least 90,000 by 2035.
Sweden thus faces a decisive technological shift in which skills requirements are changing faster than education, continuing training and the ability to attract students can keep up. Too few choose technical programmes relative to growing needs, while global competition for talent intensifies. The result is a growing gap between education and labour market needs, with direct consequences for Sweden's innovative strength, investment and long-term competitiveness.
content.subject: Business
speakerTitles: Senior Vice President and Head of HR
Executive Vice President & Head of Human Resources

content.title: From words to action – co-creation across sectors for fresh thinking and results
content.description: Sweden's distinctive strengths in trust and collaboration have contributed to its development. How can we use these strengths to address important societal challenges? A central capability is co-creation across sectors, achieving results together that no stakeholder could achieve alone.
content.extendedDescription:
The seminar for those ready to move from silos to co-creation!

During the spring, Gaia & Vocean collected ideas about co-creation across sectors. Two interactive seminars in Almedalen invite you to develop these ideas further: how can we achieve together what none of us can solve alone?

We discuss building spaces for co-creation, taking responsibility in grey areas and establishing shared ambitions. We explore what is needed to move from temporary partnerships to lasting shared responsibility.
Help shape something extending beyond organisational boundaries and individual remits: a setting for responsibility for the whole, trust and the ability to act. Leaders from civil society, municipalities, regions, authorities and business meet here. Bring your experience and be part of the solution: the future ecosystem of thinking organisations is built together! We will share the results with, among others, the Minister for Public Administration.

content.title: AI, automation and the human factor – can industry manage the transition?
content.description: Industry is becoming more automated and AI-supported. Yet our ability to interpret information, prioritise and make decisions is crucial when the unexpected happens. Requirements are now increasing faster than systems develop. How can we build systems that strengthen decision-making and reduce errors and accidents?
content.extendedDescription:
Safety work has long focused on processes, technology and compliance. As systems grow more complex, employees' roles change. Safety and quality increasingly concern how information is absorbed, prioritised and translated into decisions. This involves interaction between new technologies such as AI and cognitive capacities.

In many organisations, demands on decision-making are growing faster than organisational systems develop. This creates a gap between what employees are expected to handle and the support systems actually provide. When systems and methods do not reflect cognitive capacities, the risk of incidents, accidents and costly decisions increases.

The seminar highlights examples of how companies can strengthen safety, quality and operational capability by designing technology and systems that better support decision-making in complex, automated operations.

Drawing on research, we bring researchers and businesses together to discuss what is at stake when technology develops faster than systems and working methods.
content.subject: Business

content.title: An ADHD diagnosis: desirable to get – and to get rid of?
content.description: Sweden has one of the world's highest proportions of ADHD diagnoses. A new market is emerging for people who want their diagnosis removed. Who is responsible for removing diagnoses? Are all diagnoses needed, or should society's support systems be organised differently?
content.extendedDescription:
The number of ADHD diagnoses has multiplied over two decades. We now see the next phase: a growing group seeking reassessment of their diagnosis, and a private market offering it for 9,000 to 30,000 kronor.
An ADHD diagnosis opens doors to support and treatment that make a real difference. But when it also closes doors to education and professions, lifelong consequences arise. Who is responsible when a diagnosis is no longer relevant or perhaps was wrong from the start: the person who made it, the system that created demand, or the individual who sought help? Is removing a diagnosis a task for public healthcare? How should reassessment be prioritised relative to other care? Is there a risk that demand rather than need drives healthcare?
Some also argue that healthcare and other sectors should focus on abilities and needs rather than diagnoses. How would such a shift work? Who would gain and who would lose?
content.subject: Health and social care

content.title: Equitable crisis communication – reaching even hard-to-reach foreign-born residents
content.description: Clear, reliable information is crucial in crises. Yet important messages do not always reach everyone. Lack of trust, language barriers and different media habits mean some groups, particularly foreign-born residents, risk missing information about crises and preparedness in an increasingly uncertain world.
content.extendedDescription:
The seminar presents this year's findings from a recurring nationwide survey of more than 1,000 foreign-born residents who have lived in Sweden for 0-15 years. It provides a current picture of how different groups access public information, their trust in public institutions and barriers to reaching them. This year's focus is preparedness and crisis communication. How do people absorb information about, for example, crisis preparedness, health risks or societal disruptions? Which channels work and which do not? What is needed to ensure even hard-to-reach groups receive information they can understand, find relevant and act upon?

The presentation is followed by a panel discussion on developing more inclusive, accurately targeted crisis and preparedness communication, so we genuinely reach everyone when it matters most.

Wraps are available from 11.15 for the first 40 guests.

content.title: Low confidence in sharing health data – how does this affect new alliances in the healthcare ecosystem?
content.description: Swedish healthcare is at a crossroads. As care needs and staff shortages grow, citizens' expectations are changing. How can we secure an ecosystem that meets future needs and expectations?
content.extendedDescription: PwC and Apotek Hjärtat have investigated whether stakeholders beyond traditional healthcare providers could offer health-related services. All indications suggest the healthcare ecosystem could develop by giving other stakeholders new responsibilities. More than 1,500 citizens responded to a survey about their attitudes towards providers such as pharmacies, gyms and fitness centres and the roles these could play in the future ecosystem. An interesting finding is citizens' hesitation about sharing health data, a prerequisite for involving more stakeholders in the healthcare ecosystem. Several key stakeholders were also interviewed. Findings from the survey, interviews and document studies have been compiled in a report launched at this seminar during Almedalsveckan. We discuss the insights from this work with the aim of taking further steps in a direction.

content.title: Democratic Security Cooperation in a World of Competing Crises: Sweden and the Indo-Pacific
content.description: Sweden has a long history of cooperation and engagement in the Indo-Pacific. Developments in the Indo-Pacific are becoming more important for long-term security, trade, and international partnerships. How can we sustain cooperation across regions?
content.extendedDescription:
In this seminar ambassadors from Japan, Australia and New Zealand and a leading Swedish academic will discuss democratic security cooperation between Sweden and Indo-Pacific democracies in a global context characterised by a range of crises.
 
An important topic is how like-minded democracies can maintain cooperation despite geographic distance and differing regional priorities. They will also discuss how economic coercion, maritime security challenges, and strategic competition shape relations within the Indo-Pacific, as well as between the Indo-Pacific and Europe.
 
Another focus will be on the implications for Sweden’s security policy and its cooperation with Indo-Pacific democracies, including multilateral frameworks and NATO-related activities. The seminar highlights the need to actively maintain focus on long-term partnerships and shared security interests, and to ensure that cooperation between like-minded democracies is not sidelined when crises “in between” dominate attention.

content.title: Nordic gold at stake: trust and cohesion in today's Sweden
content.description: Sweden's high levels of trust, called "Nordic gold", have been crucial for cooperation, security and stable institutions. New research indicates declining trust in neighbours and major differences between areas. What happens when local trust erodes?
content.extendedDescription:
Swedish society is characterised by high interpersonal trust and strong confidence in its institutions. We trust one another, authorities and the functioning of systems. This has created stability, security and long-term thinking. Yet there are signs that this picture is changing.
The seminar explores Gemenskapsbarometern, Sweden's largest population survey on trust, conducted jointly by LF Forskningsstiftelse and Institutet för bostads- och urbanforskning at Uppsala universitet.
As trust is challenged and social polarisation risks increasing, understanding what strengthens or weakens community in Sweden becomes ever more important. What does research say about these developments? Is Sweden still a high-trust country? Are there differences between neighbourhoods, regions and groups? What role do media and politics play in the development of trust and social cohesion?

content.title: How can we meet the new challenges facing life sciences?
content.description: Much is happening right now. A changing geopolitical situation, preparedness efforts, disinformation and other growing threats to science make it harder to conduct essential activities such as medical research and development for quality-driven healthcare and health.
content.extendedDescription:
The 41 organisations in the think tank "Agenda för hälsa och välstånd" have identified new challenges threatening operations in academia, healthcare and business. They describe their own responses to this new reality and have agreed on ten priorities where the next government must act to secure and strengthen conditions for medical research, development and its use in Sweden.

On 23 June, join a panel discussion in which leading experts and parliamentary party spokespersons discuss what Sweden needs to meet the new life science challenges, act proactively and remain strong. The discussion draws on the think tank's new report, presented in Sveriges riksdag on 7 May. Read more at www.forskasverige.se/Agenda2026.

The seminar begins with a brief presentation followed by a panel discussion. Afterwards, join a networking lunch from 11.00.

content.title: The competition for capital – financing a competitive energy system
content.description: The energy transition requires investment of many billions, but capital hesitates when the rules change. How do political decisions and greater uncertainty affect willingness to invest? What is needed for a stable investment climate for tomorrow's energy system?
content.extendedDescription:
The energy transition requires investment of billions on a scale rarely seen before. Historically, the energy system was built through close interaction between the state and capital, but political uncertainty, geopolitical instability and new risks now challenge that model.

Long-term conditions and clear incentives are crucial for investors. Meanwhile, politicians face pressure to play an active role in developing the energy system and introduce rapid measures against high, volatile electricity prices.

Why have many investors withdrawn from the Swedish market, and how can we reverse the trend? Can politicians create sufficient investment stability while demonstrating decisive action to voters?

This panel brings together investors, energy companies and politicians to discuss financing the energy system. What role should the state play, and how can private billions contribute to a competitive energy system?
