content.title: Megaregions as a political tool – shaping Sweden's and Europe's competitiveness
content.description: Sweden is experiencing a prolonged recession while its Nordic neighbours show stronger growth and capacity for transition. How can greater cross-border integration of labour markets, innovation and infrastructure strengthen competitiveness and create sustainable growth?
content.extendedDescription:
Global competition, geopolitical uncertainty and the green transition place new demands on European regions. Meanwhile, research, including from the Kiel Institute, shows that functional megaregions can play a crucial role in competitiveness, innovation and economic development.

Starting from the Oslo–Hamburg corridor, the seminar discusses how cross-border cooperation can strengthen Sweden's position in the Nordic region and Europe. How well do current governance, investment and support systems fit functional labour markets, innovation environments and transport corridors extending across national borders? What barriers impede development, and what political decisions are needed to unlock potential?

Representatives of business, politics, transport and European institutions discuss how greater integration can strengthen competitiveness, create more robust value chains, improve skills supply and accelerate the green transition.

content.title: Electrification for European competitiveness
content.description: Europe faces geopolitical challenges in security and industry. It cannot compete using fossil-based processes because other countries control the world's fossil resources. Fossil-free electrification could therefore become an important competitive advantage for European industry.
content.extendedDescription:
The seminar focuses on how research, fossil-free electrification and skills development can strengthen Swedish and European industrial competitiveness.

How can research, education and industry jointly build competitive, fossil-free European industry?
We discuss how electrification can strengthen Swedish and European competitiveness and what conditions are needed for a successful transition. The discussion starts from Chalmers' energy research and opportunities created through collaboration between academia, industry and the energy sector.

What role do research and innovation play? How can access to the right skills be ensured? What investments and partnerships are needed for Europe to lead the global energy transition?

#EU, #industry, #electrification, #innovation, #research, #education

content.title: How We See Each Other: Brand America and Transatlantic Opportunity
content.description: How do changing attitudes toward the United States affect Sweden’s economic development, competitiveness, and international partnerships? This issue examines how public perception influences trade, investment, technology cooperation, and growth in an increasingly uncertain geopolitical environment.
content.extendedDescription:
This event examines how changing public perceptions of the United States influence Sweden’s economic development, competitiveness, and international partnerships. As geopolitical uncertainty increases, public opinion can affect trade, investment, technology cooperation, and the willingness of businesses, governments, and institutions to engage across borders. The discussion will explore the relationship between perception and economic reality, and how trust between countries can shape opportunities for growth and innovation.

The session will draw on recent research on Swedish attitudes toward the United States, as well as data on the transatlantic economic relationship and emerging areas of cooperation. Particular attention will be given to technology, industrial competitiveness, investment, and innovation policy. Participants will discuss how Sweden and the United States can strengthen collaboration in strategic sectors and translate economic ties into long-term prosperity.

content.title: New roles for business support organisations and investors – are they needed when the next unicorn is vibe-coded?
content.description: AI is reshaping the conditions for starting and running businesses. What makes a business idea sustainable over the long term when anyone can suddenly build services? How must Sweden's innovation system adapt to remain relevant as AI agents change the playing field?
content.extendedDescription:
The shift from AI assistant to AI agent creates entirely new demands on leadership, governance and business models, and on those supporting companies. Swedish SMEs lag substantially behind larger companies in AI adoption, creating gaps that will be difficult to close. Meanwhile, startups move from idea to product at record speed, with fewer employees and lower costs, using agentic AI and tools such as Claude Code. Two parallel realities emerge: those accelerating and building anew with AI as their engine, and those stopping at small incremental efficiencies.

How can Sweden's innovation system, including business support organisations and investors, support companies through this paradigm shift? What role should innovation stakeholders take, and what do companies need?

The seminar challenges the innovation system's self-image and discusses the roles business support organisations and investors need to take as the playing field changes in real time.

content.title: The menopause effect: the billions lost in healthcare and at work
content.description: Although most women experience menopausal symptoms at some point, organisations lack strategic planning and workplace health measures to address them. Greater knowledge can give more women better health, enable continued full participation in working life and improve well-being.
content.extendedDescription:
Although most women experience menopausal symptoms at some point, the issue is almost absent from organisations' strategic planning and workplace health efforts. Lack of knowledge also leads to women being mistreated or dismissed, contributing, alongside other factors, to higher sick leave rates among women over 45 than among men.

Making menopause a strategic workplace health issue can help retain invaluable expertise and drive future growth and health.

Join a conversation between medical experts, business and society. During Almedalsveckan 2026, we challenge stigma and advance work on hormonal health, other treatments and menopause. We discuss current research and practical solutions that strengthen women's health and minimise hidden production losses currently costing Swedish companies billions through sick leave and reduced work performance.

The discussion continues in smaller conversations with experts. More speakers will be announced.

content.title: The cancer strategy has been adopted – but how do we measure its success?
content.description: The new national cancer strategy sets goals for greater survival, better quality of life and more equitable care. But how do we know whether it actually improves patient outcomes? Which indicators are needed to track developments in cancer care?
content.extendedDescription:
The national cancer strategy sets goals to improve prevention, earlier detection, more effective treatment and quality of life for people living with or after cancer.
To make a real difference, monitoring must reflect what matters most to patients and society. Cancer care is often measured using process indicators, such as adherence to care guidelines, rather than outcomes such as survival, quality of life and equitable access to innovation.
As cancer care moves towards more personalised diagnosis and treatment, a central question arises: what do we actually need to measure to ensure the strategy delivers real patient benefit?
The seminar brings stakeholders from across cancer care together to discuss translating the strategy's goals into concrete, meaningful indicators.

content.title: Can life science investment create growth and resilience? Sweden and Germany as examples
content.description: In a time of growing geopolitical tensions, demographic challenges and strained public finances, investment in innovation is increasingly central to long-term growth and economic stability. Life sciences play a central role but risk losing ground.
content.extendedDescription:
Life sciences, among the most research-intensive and knowledge-driven sectors, play a particularly important role, not only in public health but also in competitiveness, productivity and public finances.

Yet Europe, Germany and Sweden risk losing ground in the global innovation race. Strengthening national and European resilience requires strategic initiatives supporting research, innovation and effective healthcare systems. The Swedish–German innovation partnership offers a unique platform to advance this work and create tangible value for both the economy and society.

Join a breakfast seminar with interactive dialogue, bringing leading political and business representatives and other experts together to discuss how innovation investment can strengthen growth, competitiveness and financial sustainability in Sweden, Germany and Europe.

Breakfast will be served.

content.title: The blue investment grant – how could it support clean water throughout Sweden?
content.description: 240,000 properties still lack approved wastewater treatment. Phosphorus leaks into lakes and the Baltic Sea while the pace of action stagnates. The blue investment grant could reverse this trend, but how should support be designed to encourage more property owners to act?
content.extendedDescription:
Representatives of MRV and Villaägarnas riksförbund present, together with the audience, the initiative Det blå investeringsbidraget: a concrete proposal for making approved wastewater treatment financially accessible to property owners nationwide.

Sweden has 419,000 kilometres of shoreline and bears full responsibility for its own lakes and watercourses. Yet almost a quarter of a million properties lack approved treatment.

Technology is not the problem. Financial incentives are missing. For individual property owners, the investment feels unaffordable without support. Meanwhile, municipal water and wastewater finances face investment needs of 31 billion kronor annually: every property treating its own wastewater is one the municipality need not connect by pipeline.

The proposed blue investment grant would be included in the green technology tax deduction framework and could provide the boost needed to finally increase the pace of action.

Coffee, sandwiches and drinks will be served.
content.subject: Climate/environment

content.title: The school system fails the most vulnerable, but some independent schools make a difference. What makes the system dysfunctional?
content.description: Special education for pupils with mobility difficulties is lacking, limiting their physical and intellectual development. Schools are responsible for everyone's right to movement, yet habilitation services direct provision for this group. Why? People with mobility disabilities can develop and have a lifelong right to grow.
content.extendedDescription:
Part of Almega Utbildning's "Forum för svensk skola".

Sweden has special education approaches for deaf and blind people and those with intellectual disabilities, but not for people with mobility disabilities. Yet disability is almost always represented by a wheelchair. Consequently, thousands of children and young people with mobility disabilities:

• Encounter schools lacking knowledge of how motor limitations affect learning.
• Receive interventions directed by regional habilitation services rather than schools' educational remit.
• Must learn abstractly what others learn through their bodies.
• Fall into gaps between responsible organisations.

Independent schools can work more flexibly and individually. They often show greater ability to meet these pupils' needs. Yet there is still no nationally recognised pedagogy to draw on.

• Introductory presentation: a headteacher's perspective.
• Civil society voices: Neuroförbundet, RBU and Hjärnfonden participate.
• Political panel: reflection and dialogue on what the parties want to do.

content.title: How do singing, music and culture contribute to resilience and democracy?
content.description: Art, literature, singing and music can challenge established world orders. They are a political force, another language in our turbulent world. They can support peaceful protest and healing. How does culture contribute to change and the shaping of a democratic society?
content.extendedDescription:
Tonight, we sing together about democracy, courage and hope, for the world's sake.
For centuries, culture has been used to stand up to injustice and abuses of power. Early this year, we saw a protest movement of songs spread across the United States as equal human worth was threatened by an indecent migration policy.
Tonight, we want to express "singing resistance". We sing for everyone worldwide who is forbidden to gather, silenced and denied opportunities for expression.
Culture is about resilience, survival and healing. It shapes our democratic society peacefully.
Music and stories protect not only our inner lives but also what risks being threatened: our language, history and identity.
In times of unrest and war, music is our strongest resource. It unites us in a collective peace movement across boundaries.
Let us sing tonight and raise the roof of Vårdklockans kyrka!

content.title: How can tax rules promote reuse in the property sector?
content.description: Reuse and circular construction are central to the climate transition, but current tax and VAT systems often work against them. How do tax rules affect property owners' incentives, and how can they change to encourage sustainable investment?
content.extendedDescription:
From an income tax perspective, rules on deductions for scrapped assets limit opportunities for reuse. If parts of a building are retained, the owner must continue depreciating tax values no longer recognised in the accounts. Changing the rules would improve cash flow and release capital for sustainability measures.

VAT also creates obstacles. Valuing reused building components is often complex, potentially resulting in output VAT without a corresponding deduction entitlement. For stakeholders with limited deduction rights, reuse therefore becomes an actual cost.

Property tax compounds the problem. Investment in environmental and energy improvements can raise the assessed value and thus the ongoing tax burden.

The consequences are clear: current tax rules can effectively favour demolition over reuse.
The seminar discusses the measures needed to make reuse the obvious choice.

content.title: Source to Sea and the Catchment Approach – voices from around the Baltic Sea
content.description: Scaling up Swedish measures and implementing the EU Water Framework Directive can cut nutrient emissions to the Baltic Sea and restore freshwater ecosystems. But progress is too slow—what can Sweden learn from neighbouring countries’ source‑to‑sea projects?
content.extendedDescription:
The Baltic Sea's ecosystems are threatened by eutrophication, environmental toxins and many freshwater and coastal ecosystems in the catchment area have been destroyed by physical impacts. 
A number of large national projects focusing on scaling up action work and implementing the EU's Water Framework Directive and reducing the impact on the Baltic Sea have been started in our neighboring countries. In the seminar, experts from Finland and Estonia together with Swedish experts will reflect on and discuss the following questions:
- Which strategies and approaches are successful for scaling up the remediation work? 
- What are the challenges to succeed in scaling up action on a national level?
- How do we organize learning and exchange of experience between the Baltic Sea countries?
- What are the next steps for the Swedish work protecting and restoring the Baltic Sea?

content.title: Governance under pressure: data, cloud services and cybersecurity in the public sector
content.description: Cyber threats and geopolitical tensions put pressure on the public sector, while new regulations impose rigorous requirements. How can we protect citizens' data and national security without stopping necessary digital modernisation? The balancing act has never been harder.
content.extendedDescription:
Data is both a strategic asset and a vulnerability. The public sector faces a complex choice: how can we modernise systems and harness cloud services and AI while complying with rapidly changing regulations and facing escalating threats?
This seminar explores the challenge of data governance in an uncertain world. We discuss building operational resilience and ensuring continuity without stalling innovation.
The session addresses:
• Navigating regulation: implementing NIS2, DORA and the AI Act in practice.
• Secure modernisation: strategies for moving to the cloud and using AI without compromising sovereignty and security.
• Cyber resilience: protecting critical infrastructure as the boundary between technology and national security blurs.
Join a discussion on securing Sweden's digital future through proactive data governance.

content.title: Strategic or naive – how should Sweden navigate defence and conflict prevention?
content.description: As global security becomes unstable, political priorities favour defence over aid and diplomacy. Meanwhile, humanitarian needs are exploding amid more conflicts, a rapidly worsening climate crisis and displacement. What does security actually mean, and how can we build it?
content.extendedDescription:
Aid is declining when humanitarian needs have never been greater. Military spending is rising instead. Security is increasingly defined in terms of defence, while research shows that long-term stability is built through investment in democracy, human rights and conflict prevention. What role do Sweden's aid and foreign policies play in today's security situation? Questions include:
• Is prioritising prevention politically possible without appearing naive in today's world?
• What is the cost of focusing solely on defence and reducing investment in preventing conflicts, pandemics and climate-related disasters?
• How should we shape future security policy, diplomacy and aid as the global map of power changes?
• What role should Sweden take?
Join an in-depth discussion of what Swedish policy needs to genuinely contribute to a safer, more stable world.

content.title: Without the Internet of Things, Sweden stops
content.description: Sweden already depends on connected data flows. Healthcare is digitalising, cities are becoming smarter and digital technology, including artificial intelligence, increasingly shapes national security and preparedness. None of this works without robust Internet of Things infrastructure.
content.extendedDescription:
The Internet of Things, or sensor-based infrastructure, has become a quiet prerequisite for welfare, security and competitiveness. Sweden depends on it functioning. Yet connected systems and services are still treated as separate IT projects rather than critical societal infrastructure.

The public sector is expected to take extensive responsibility for essential functions, data management and continuity amid rapid technological change. The panel addresses three questions:

• What does it mean to view IoT as critical societal infrastructure?
• Why has this become a neglected issue, despite IoT infrastructure being crucial to Sweden's resilience, digital transition and growth?
• How can the public sector take responsibility when technology advances faster than regulation and procurement?

The seminar brings together the public sector, academia and business.

Coffee and sandwiches will be served from 09:30.

content.title: Now it concerns us – human rights in Sweden today
content.description: How can we strengthen respect for rights in Sweden, learn from European experience and contribute to future development of standards? How can we ensure human rights are more than fine words and instead essential building blocks of a living democracy?
content.extendedDescription:
For a long time, human rights and international conventions mainly inspired engagement concerning countries other than Sweden. Developments in Sweden and several other European countries in recent years mean that, in many areas, we have approached the boundaries set by our international commitments to the UN, EU and Council of Europe. The risk of human rights violations is increasing, particularly when decisions are made quickly with less regard for objections from experts and consultation bodies. Human rights protections, including the right not to be discriminated against, risk being sidelined.

States' respect for international commitments is fundamental to a rules-based world order. Fundamental freedoms and rights sustain democracy and underpin dignified lives and societal stability.

Come to listen and ask questions at a round-table discussion at Torget för mänskliga rättigheter och demokrati.

content.title: From flexibility to storage – does energy need a new financing model?
content.description: Sweden is rapidly expanding electricity generation to meet its 2045 climate and energy targets. Demand for flexibility and battery storage is also growing: solutions that ease and stabilise the grid, smooth peaks in power demand and make renewable energy available when needed. But how will it all be paid for?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden is rapidly expanding electricity generation to meet its 2045 climate and energy targets. Demand for flexibility and battery storage is also growing: solutions that ease and stabilise the grid, smooth peaks in power demand and make renewable energy available when needed.

Scaling up requires capital. But many investors and lenders remain more familiar with traditional energy assets. Flexibility and storage often involve multiple revenue streams, new contracts and a rapidly evolving market, demanding new approaches to assessing, pricing and packaging risk.

This panel discusses unlocking more capital for energy storage and flexibility. Are new financing and contractual models needed to make more projects investable? How should risk be shared? What incentives are needed, and what role can politicians play in creating long-term ground rules? Are there international examples to learn from?

content.title: Resilience in Sweden's municipalities and regions – in war and peace
content.description: A changing world increases Sweden's need for resilience. Military capability and self-sufficiency are often highlighted, but what access to transport, energy and culture can we expect across the country in a crisis? How prepared are we for threats to society's foundation: democracy?
content.extendedDescription:
Growing global tensions have forced the EU to focus more on Europe's competitiveness and security. Much concerns reducing dependencies and increasing self-sufficiency. Yet the war in Ukraine has demonstrated the importance of strong public services during crises. Alongside military functions, people need to heat their homes, reach work and healthcare, and access culture that makes life worth living and builds understanding and resilience.
The EU's changing focus is expected to affect regional work. We know resilience grows from below through place-specific solutions. Is this sufficiently reflected in Sweden's regional development remit?
Societal resilience is central to free and fair elections, which require a democracy that earns citizens' trust and engagement. What internal and external threats face democracy as Sweden goes to the polls this autumn?

content.title: Home first – how can children avoid placement in care?
content.description: More children are being placed in foster families or residential care homes. Placements may be necessary but often have major consequences for children and very high costs for society. Yet experience shows that early, coordinated support can enable more children to grow up with their families.
content.extendedDescription:
How can society improve timely family support so more children can grow up at home with their own families?
The seminar presents Hemma först in Rättviks kommun. Through early, intensive and coordinated support for families in vulnerable circumstances, it aims to enable more children to remain at home and avoid foster or residential care placements.
We examine the model's structure, methods and organisational changes needed for more preventive social services. The seminar also explores the effects of a more family-strengthening approach on children's lives and municipalities' long-term costs.
The initiative is financed through a social outcomes contract, with an external investor enabling the intervention upfront. The municipality repays only if and as agreed results are achieved. This allows important preventive initiatives without the municipality bearing the full financial risk.

content.title: AI and health data – are we finally moving from vision to reality in cancer care?
content.description: AI and advanced data analysis can support earlier detection, more accurate treatment decisions and better follow-up in cancer care. But fragmented IT systems, unclear regulations and limited data sharing currently impede progress. How can we create more data-driven cancer care?
content.extendedDescription:
Cancer is one of today's greatest public health challenges, with cases expected to rise as the population ages. Meanwhile, new diagnostic methods, treatments and data-driven tools are developing rapidly. For patients to benefit, healthcare must use health data more effectively, securely and systematically than today.
Sweden has strong foundations in national registries, digital maturity and research. Yet major barriers remain to sharing, analysing and using health data in clinical practice, quality monitoring and research. Poor interoperability, unclear regulations and fragmented IT systems prevent the full potential of AI and advanced data analysis from being realised.
The seminar discusses how AI and better use of health data can support earlier detection, more personalised diagnosis and better treatment decisions, and how Sweden can benefit from initiatives such as the European Health Data Space.

content.title: What is needed for regions to succeed in building world-leading life science clusters?
content.description: Sweden wants to lead in life sciences, but is losing ground in introducing new medicines. Rapidly bringing innovation into healthcare determines our international strength. Can research clusters flourish without leading clinical development?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden's metropolitan regions want to build world-leading life science clusters. Success requires a willingness to lead development, not merely follow it. The introduction of new medicines is slowing faster in Sweden than in comparable countries. Reversing the trend requires better conditions for rapidly implementing new therapies.

An innovation cluster is only as strong as its ability to turn innovation into clinical benefit and attractiveness. Some regions want to lead, but national support is not always sufficient. Sweden could establish a unique ecosystem of testbeds. Earlier introduction of medicines gives patients faster access to breakthroughs while making clinical trials more attractive.

Is it a strength that some regions lead the way, or are better national conditions needed throughout the country? How can we secure international competitiveness?

The seminar is a collaboration between BMS, Roche and Takeda.

content.title: Strategic purchasing for resilience – public procurement in the NATO era
content.description: What happens to public procurement when supply preparedness, protective security and NATO cooperation become everyday concerns for municipalities, regions and government agencies?
content.extendedDescription:
What requirements and expectations come with NATO membership, and how are public contracting authorities, entities and suppliers on the civilian side affected? How can Sweden secure critical goods and services during crises and war?

This seminar discusses public procurement's strategic role in total defence. Supplying public operations with goods and services is crucial for essential functions such as healthcare, social care and schools, even under extreme conditions. Access to medicines, food and energy must be secured, and public purchasing is central to Sweden's preparedness.

The seminar examines the requirements NATO membership, including host nation support, places on public organisations, how the civilian side is affected and why collaboration with business is essential for stronger total defence. We also discuss the most important measures for success.

content.title: Resilience creates competitiveness – a shared direction for resilient cities of the future
content.description: When climate crises, geopolitics and disruption become everyday realities, urban resilience is crucial to competitiveness. Resilience-focused urban development means fewer interruptions, higher gross regional product and more secure investments. How can we collaborate more systemically around shared visions to succeed?
content.extendedDescription:
Experience from Europe and the Nordic region shows that resilience is not only about managing crises. It also creates long-term growth, stability and attractiveness. Yet investment in resilience is too often treated as a cost rather than a strategic investment in the future.

The discussion draws on Ramboll's Nordic expertise and The Nordic Way report, based on round tables in Stockholm, Oslo, Copenhagen and Helsinki with 103 leaders from the public sector, property development, infrastructure, water and energy. We discuss how cities can strengthen competitiveness by encouraging stakeholders to collaborate at system level, increasing resilience to different disruptions and addressing complex societal challenges.

How can clear visions and partnerships mobilise public and private stakeholders for tomorrow's city?
Join this discussion led by Anette Seger, CEO of Ramboll Sweden.

content.title: How can we continue successfully combating financial crime?
content.description: In recent years, society has taken decisive measures against organised and financial crime, with results. However, major challenges remain, and further action across society is needed to continue curbing crime.
content.extendedDescription:
Measures taken by politicians, police, banks and other authorities in recent years against organised and financial crime, including legislative changes, increased resources, stronger cooperation and new security solutions, have had positive effects. For example, profits from telephone fraud have fallen substantially and shootings have decreased sharply. Yet the criminal economy continues to grow. A report from Expertgruppen för studier i offentlig ekonomi concluded early this year that the criminal economy turns over 352 billion kronor annually.

How can we best continue countering organised and financial crime and the criminal economy? What additional measures are needed, and in which areas? How can banks contribute further? How can practical cooperation and information sharing between authorities and business become even more effective?

content.title: From AI to Impact: Securing Competitive and Equitable Growth
content.description: Sweden faces slowing productivity, shortage of talent, and rising global competition. How can AI drive real growth—by building trust, ensuring security, scaling adoption, and embedding AI across sectors to boost productivity and inclusive value creation?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden faces a structural growth challenge marked by slowing productivity, demographic pressure, and intensifying global competition. While AI is often framed as a risk or compliance issue, its core economic potential—boosting productivity and value creation—remains underexplored. This panel starts from a clear premise: AI delivers national impact only when trust, security, and scale are in place.
 
Building on Sweden’s national AI strategy, the discussion focuses on moving from vision to execution—embedding AI in core processes, investing in shared capabilities like data, platforms, and skills, and aligning innovation with regulation without slowing progress. Rather than replacing jobs, AI can augment human capability, speed decision-making, and scale expertise across sectors.
 
Drawing on global examples, the panel explores how to unlock equitable growth by ensuring AI benefits reach SMEs, public services, and all regions.

content.title: Advanced healthcare at home – an important provider making a difference
content.description: Advanced home healthcare has evolved from palliative care towards increasingly advanced treatment at home for several patient groups. It steps in when hospital care is needed but enables care in patients' own homes instead. The service faces challenges requiring matching resources.
content.extendedDescription:
The lecture describes how advanced home healthcare is organised, providing skilled care in patients' homes and access to its own inpatient services. Many enrolled patients have oncological or haematological diseases and undergo long-term treatment.

Inpatient beds have declined over time while the population has grown, making more advanced treatment at home necessary. Multidisciplinary teams provide holistic care addressing medical and psychosocial needs. The lecture highlights the challenges and how this form of care can reach more patients, improve quality of life and enable more efficient use of limited healthcare resources. More people need to know the service exists and what it offers.

The seminar ends with a panel including representatives of patient associations and acute hospital projects.

How can we create a system sized for future needs rather than yesterday's organisation?

content.title: Small sums, major consequences – preventing young people from being drawn into money laundering
content.description: Children and young people in Sweden increasingly face attempts to recruit them as money mules. The phenomenon is difficult to detect, occurs in children's own digital channels and relies on young people often not knowing that forwarding the money makes them offenders themselves.
content.extendedDescription:
Children and young people are increasingly recruited as money mules, for example through Swish. Criminal networks reach them directly through social media, games and chats, often with simple, quick tasks that seem harmless but lead directly into money laundering. Many children do not understand that they themselves can become criminal suspects, while parents often overestimate their insight into their children's finances and digital behaviour. This growing problem shows how organised crime finds new routes through young people and how society urgently needs stronger knowledge and protection.

The seminar discusses new findings on the frequency of contact attempts by strangers, risk awareness among young people and adults, and the potential gap between parents' perceptions and children's reality. It addresses how boundaries and routines can reduce exploitation risks, and how adults can prevent children from entering situations where small sums have enormous consequences.

content.title: How innovative may schools be – where should exploration happen if not in schools?
content.description: School practice rests on research, proven experience and clear governing documents. Yet pupils' circumstances, society's needs and forms of knowledge are changing rapidly. This creates tension but also room for action. What responsibility do schools have to develop?
content.extendedDescription:
During Almedalsveckan, Frida Utbildning invites you to a panel on one of schools' most pressing questions: what responsibility and scope for action do schools have to develop in a time of change?

Schools must create good conditions for children's and young people's learning and futures amid rapid societal change. They therefore need both to safeguard proven approaches and explore what is not yet finished, fully understood or regulated.

How much can and should schools themselves explore new methods, tools and forms of learning?
Can we wait for ready-made answers, or must the profession help shape them?

We welcome everyone engaged in school development to pause and think together. We want to share perspectives, listen to different experiences and deepen our collective understanding of schools' responsibilities and scope for action when answers are uncertain but responsibility cannot wait.

content.title: Can a foundation training year ensure access to dentists nationwide?
content.description: Swedish dental care is high quality, but much of the country, particularly the north, lacks staff. Many newly qualified dentists also find the transition from education to clinical work substantial. Could a foundation training year be part of the solution?
content.extendedDescription:
Dental care in Sweden faces challenges affecting skills supply, patient safety and equitable access. Dentists are unevenly distributed geographically, with pronounced shortages in sparsely populated areas and smaller towns. Patients' chances of receiving timely care therefore vary across the country. Many providers also struggle to recruit and retain dentists, reinforcing the imbalance.
The seminar presents the report "Bastjänstgöringsår för tandläkare", produced by Praktikertjänst and Ramboll. Could a foundation training year help address national skills shortages while strengthening new graduates' clinical skills? What would make it attractive to students and employers?
The seminar brings together dental care stakeholders to discuss the report, including outlines of how a foundation training year could be designed.

content.title: How innovative may schools be – AI with courage and reflection
content.description: Artificial intelligence already affects how we work, learn and communicate. For schools, it brings significant opportunities and crucial pedagogical, ethical and democratic questions. How can schools approach AI responsibly without becoming passive?
content.extendedDescription:
During Almedalsveckan, Frida Utbildning invites you to a panel on one of schools' most pressing questions: what responsibility and scope for action do schools have to develop in a time of change?

Schools must create good conditions for children's and young people's learning and futures amid rapid societal change. They therefore need both to safeguard proven approaches and explore what is not yet finished, fully understood or regulated.

How can we balance the courage to experiment with taking time to understand the consequences?
What must children and young people know, understand and critically assess in a world where AI is part of everyday life?

We welcome everyone engaged in school development to pause and think together. We want to share perspectives, listen to different experiences and deepen our collective understanding of schools' responsibilities and scope for action when answers are uncertain but responsibility cannot wait.

content.title: Shared ground rules for preparedness – translating political ambitions into operational capability
content.description: Essential services are expected to continue during crises and war. Yet shared, practical ground rules defining this are lacking. How can political ambitions become operational capability, and what is needed to connect responsibility, requirements and implementation?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden's total defence depends on public services and businesses functioning even during crises and war. Yet current work is marked by unclear requirements, uneven application and a lack of shared measures of preparedness capability, with concrete consequences for planning, procurement and implementation.

Clearer structures for responsibility, requirements and methods are needed, along with a better connection between political ambitions and operational reality. Shared frameworks offer one approach, with standardisation among several tools. But these frameworks work only when consistently applied across organisational boundaries.

The seminar discusses translating preparedness ambitions into operational capability. What is needed to clarify requirements and connect responsibility with implementation? The discussion is organised with Krisledningspodden and moderated by Mats Bohman.

content.title: How can Sweden prepare for self-driving vehicles?
content.description: Automated vehicles could make transport safer and more sustainable. But the technology needs more than intelligent vehicles: it needs an intelligent system. How can we create the clarity and predictability required for safe, sustainable introduction?
content.extendedDescription:
From 2027, the EU opens type approval for mass-produced, fully automated vehicles. This could make Europe attractive to commercial operators that have mainly invested in the United States and China. Encouraging them to invest in Sweden requires a balance between clear frameworks and flexible learning. We also share responsibility for ensuring the technology contributes to a safer, more accessible and resource-efficient society.

Join a seminar on the national Transformationskartan! Initiated by Transportstyrelsen under the strategic innovation programme Drive Sweden, the project aims to establish a shared vision and action plan for fully automated transport in Sweden. We discuss how a neutral collaboration platform can accelerate knowledge sharing, improve Sweden's competitiveness and ensure we keep pace with rapid technological development.

content.title: Can collaboration and technology solve the teacher shortage?
content.description: Securing teacher supply while maintaining quality, equity and accessibility matters for schools and is crucial to Sweden's competitiveness. Today's system cannot meet needs nationwide. New ways of working that use modern technology are therefore needed.
content.extendedDescription:
Through close collaboration with municipalities and other universities, Luleå tekniska universitet has developed models making teacher education accessible throughout northern Sweden and, in practice, nationwide. University collaboration has also strengthened provision in smaller subjects and built strong research environments.

Meanwhile, new technologies can ease teachers' workloads, support pupils' learning and provide more tailored, interactive teaching support. How can we combine next-generation technologies with new approaches to teacher supply without losing sight of teachers' vital role and the importance of classrooms?

Effective teacher education is crucial for effective schools here and now, but the consequences reach much further. This is where we secure Sweden's future competitiveness and ability to address societal challenges, particularly in STEM.

content.title: Data between the committee and the construction site: Sweden's next productivity boost
content.description: With the right data linking political committees and construction sites, we can build a more productive Sweden. Political ambitions do not always reach those building society, and lessons from completed projects rarely reach decision-makers. How can AI close the gap and release billions?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden's built-environment sector loses more than 100 billion kronor annually, with much determined in the gap between the committee and the construction site. This is the stage between political ambition and breaking ground, when tender documents, estimates and bids lock in project finances. Major decisions are made here, and major mistakes hidden. Political vision and technical reality speak different languages, and knowledge from completed projects rarely returns to decision-makers.

Brickanta and Verumatic have built two sides of the same bridge. Verumatic is an AI-driven platform analysing municipal political data and making it traceable. Brickanta is the agentic AI operating system that reads tender documents, learns from previous projects and gives built-environment professionals the conditions to build society.

This panel discusses how the data connects in practice: tracing political decisions into construction and bringing lessons from completed projects back to the committee.

content.title: When one in five parents struggles with mental health – who supports the families?
content.description: One in five parents in Sweden experiences mental ill health, but few receive timely support. Almost half want practical help, yet only 10% of municipalities offer it. How can early, coordinated interventions reach families at risk of falling through the cracks?
content.extendedDescription:
One in five parents in Sweden experiences mental ill health, but too few receive timely support. Almost half want practical help such as support at home, respite and assistance with daily routines, yet only 10% of municipalities offer it. Group-based support is also widely lacking despite parents wanting it to share experiences and reduce isolation.

The seminar brings together politicians, authorities, civil society and professionals in social services, psychiatry and parenting support.
MFoF presents the report Stärkt föräldraskapsstöd till föräldrar med psykisk ohälsa eller kognitiva svårigheter; Bräcke diakoni shares experience from TrUSt and Homestart; NSPH highlights the target group's needs.

The round table discusses how coordinated support can reach parents in time, civil society's role when welfare provision falls short, and accessible interventions for the most vulnerable, including parents new to Sweden.

The proposals are summarised in a panel discussion.

content.title: Construction boom, concrete shortage and preparedness – new conditions for material supply
content.description: Construction faces material shortages and vulnerable supply chains, while concrete is increasingly prioritised for total defence expansion and critical infrastructure. Climate, security and availability must be weighed against each other. How can we build when concrete supply is no longer assured?
content.extendedDescription:
A changing world, with security concerns, vulnerable supply chains and new wartime preparedness requirements, fundamentally affects construction planning and delivery. Meanwhile, construction and property must transition to lower climate impacts and more efficient resource use. Concrete, long taken for granted in infrastructure and essential buildings, has therefore become a strategic resource requiring trade-offs between availability, climate threats and wartime preparedness.
When material availability can no longer be assumed, perspectives must broaden. Circular material flows, reuse, new structural principles, alternative construction methods and hybrid solutions can contribute to both total defence and climate benefits, but bring new risks and trade-offs.
This open discussion explores how construction can strengthen resilience through better analysis, early choices and interdisciplinary collaboration between clients, industry, authorities and technical consultants.

content.title: From words to action – co-creation across sectors for fresh thinking and results
content.description: Sweden's distinctive strengths in trust and collaboration have contributed to its development. How can we use these strengths to address important societal challenges? A central capability is co-creation across sectors, achieving results together that no stakeholder could achieve alone.
content.extendedDescription:
The seminar for anyone who wants to move from silos to co-creation!

During the spring, Gaia & Vocean have gathered ideas about co-creation across sectors. At two interactive seminars in Almedalen, you are invited to develop these ideas further: how can we achieve together what none of us can solve alone?

We discuss, among other things, how to build spaces for co-creation, take responsibility in grey areas and establish shared ambitions. We explore what it takes to move from temporary partnerships to lasting, shared responsibility.
Help shape something that reaches beyond organisational boundaries and individual mandates. A setting that makes room for responsibility for the whole, trust and the ability to act. Leaders from civil society, municipalities, regions, public agencies and business will meet here. Bring your experience and be part of the solution – we build tomorrow's ecosystem of thinking organisations together! We will share the results with, among others, the Minister for Public Administration.

content.description: Gothenburg and West Sweden have become a dynamic arena for innovation focused on sustainable growth. By discussing topics such as electrification, AI and entrepreneurship, as well as the mobility of the future, we can strengthen Sweden's competitiveness in global markets.
content.extendedDescription:
In a short time, Gothenburg and West Sweden have established themselves as one of the Nordic region's most exciting innovation clusters, with strong growth in areas such as mobility, deep tech and AI. Leading figures from business, startups, investment, politics and innovation systems will gather here for moderated discussions. Together, we discuss how regional innovation can strengthen Sweden's national competitiveness in an increasingly global and competitive world.

content.title: Are AI and entrepreneurship Sweden's next growth engine?
content.description: AI is already changing how companies create value, how new business models emerge and how new companies are formed. Meanwhile, a global race for talent, investment and innovation in AI is under way. Sweden is well placed to take a leading position – but what will it take?
content.extendedDescription:
AI is already changing how companies create value, develop products and reach their customers. But AI is also changing the very conditions for entrepreneurship. What previously required large teams, substantial capital and long development cycles can now be achieved by small, agile companies using AI. New business models are emerging, barriers to innovation are falling and the opportunities to build global companies from a local base are greater than ever.

History shows that regions that succeed early in combining new technology with strong entrepreneurship often become tomorrow's growth engines. The question is whether Sweden and cities such as Gothenburg are ready to take that position in the AI era. Competition is fierce. Cities and regions across the Nordic countries and Europe are investing to attract companies, skills and capital.

Has AI Gothenburg cracked the code for creating these conditions?
- In less than 4 weeks, more than 100 AI companies have applied to be part of the initiative!
What are the ingredients needed?

content.title: Which food should be saved, and why – how do we reduce food waste sustainably?
content.description: In 2025, the EU adopted binding food waste targets. The focus often falls on reducing waste in retail and households. Yet every year, a hundred million meals are wasted in public-sector kitchens, along with up to 1 million tonnes of crops in fields. Given growing public health problems and overconsumption, which wasted food should we eat?
content.extendedDescription: Ätbart is a non-profit association that publishes annual food bank reports. In them, we highlight the fallacy in the idea that everything produced should be eaten to reduce food waste, and in its supposed environmental benefits. Reducing all waste indiscriminately through retail clearance sales or charitable donations does not necessarily lead to resource efficiency. Donations are an increasingly common way to reduce waste – but do they solve any problems, and what are their long-term consequences for social policy, the environment, the climate and public health? In this year's report, presented in a short lecture for event participants, Ätbart describes the problem of food losses in fields and serving waste in public-sector kitchens. The report gives examples of how the recently adopted legally binding food waste targets for large-scale catering can be achieved partly through redistribution as takeaway meals. It also presents good examples of partnerships between farms and local associations providing food support. A warm welcome!
content.subject: Food

content.title: AI in practice – how do Swedish companies create business value, competitiveness and trust?
content.description: AI is often highlighted as crucial to Sweden's future competitiveness. But how do Swedish organisations move from AI strategies and pilot projects to tangible impact in customer interactions, decision-making and service development? And how can this development also strengthen responsibility, skills and lasting trust?
content.extendedDescription:
In a short time, AI has gone from a question for the future to a crucial issue for business, working life and society. For Swedish organisations, the next step is no longer about testing the technology – it is about creating real value in their operations.

This development is about more than efficiency and innovation. It also raises broader questions about responsibility, skills and trust. How do organisations prioritise different AI investments? How do they ensure that these investments actually have an impact? And how do they build leadership, culture and self-leadership at a time when AI is rapidly changing roles, responsibilities and expectations?

At this seminar, organised by Svenska Spel and Google, perspectives from business and politics meet in a discussion about how AI. The discussion also looks ahead. Which choices will be crucial in the coming years? What will distinguish organisations that succeed from those that fall behind? And what do politicians, businesses and organisations need to do now for Sweden to remain at the forefront?
content.subject: Digitalisation

content.title: How well equipped are schools to support children and young people in crisis and grief?
content.description: Every year, thousands of children and young people experience crises, grief and difficult life events. For many, school becomes the most important place for security, structure and a functioning everyday life. Yet many schools lack the support, knowledge and conditions to help them.
content.extendedDescription:
Schools can make a decisive difference for children experiencing crisis and grief and prevent future mental ill health if they have the knowledge and conditions needed. But what is the reality today?

How do you talk about what has happened?
How do you support the child – and the class?
How do you engage with relatives and other adults?
And how do staff look after one another when the difficult situation affects them too?

When crisis and grief affect a child, they also affect the school. Support needs to be equitable across the country so that neither schools nor children are left alone in difficult situations. With support from Folkhälsomyndigheten, Ericastiftelsen has developed initiatives to strengthen schools' preparedness and expertise in crisis support and suicide prevention.

The seminar discusses what schools need to support children experiencing crisis and grief, both immediately and in the longer term. And what is needed to prevent children and young people from falling through the cracks when life becomes difficult.

content.title: Ukrainian veterans' perspectives – new knowledge for reintegration and societal development
content.description: Since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, hundreds of thousands of Ukrainians have served in the war. Veterans are a highly respected and influential group in society. How do their wartime experiences affect their views on key societal issues?
content.extendedDescription:
The seminar draws on a new survey of Ukrainian veterans' attitudes to issues including democracy, gender equality, social inclusion and trust. The study is a collaboration between Försvarshögskolan and Folke Bernadotteakademin. The results show that differences between veterans and civilians are often smaller than expected, but that specific experiences – particularly war injuries and the transition to civilian life – are especially significant in shaping attitudes.
The seminar discusses how these insights can inform reintegration policy, focusing on psychosocial support, gender equality and trust in democratic institutions. Ukraine is a democracy fighting a full-scale, prolonged defensive war on its own territory, making its experiences unique in modern times. At the same time, there are reasons to compare these experiences with other conflicts and draw lessons for the future.

content.title: The global humanitarian system in crisis and reform: how do we do more with less, and do it better?
content.description: The world faces record humanitarian needs while funding falls and millions go without support. This has put the global humanitarian system under intense pressure, leading to difficult priorities and extensive ongoing reforms. How should Swedish aid develop in this new context?
content.extendedDescription:
Humanitarian needs are at a record high. More than 120 armed conflicts are ongoing, 123 million people are displaced and 305 million need urgent support. Meanwhile, major donors are reducing their support and the UN faces a deep funding crisis. At this critical moment, we are forced to rethink and find new approaches.

Against this backdrop, a new design for the humanitarian system has taken shape – The Humanitarian Reset – with clearer recognition of local actors' role, a stronger focus on anticipatory action and higher demands for cost efficiency. Meanwhile, major shifts are taking place in development aid globally and within the EU. How Sweden and the Swedish organisations and expertise involved in aid respond to this paradigm shift, addressing its challenges and opportunities, will determine the future of aid. How do we do more with less without compromising humanitarian principles?

Sweden is in an election year, and several political parties promise further reform and a new aid agenda. How should Swedish aid develop in this new context, and how does it compare with other donors and the EU?
content.subject: International affairs
speakerTitles: Head for the Nordic and Baltic Countries

content.title: Cross-bloc cooperation or deadlock? The future of Swedish CCUS – carbon capture and storage
content.description: CCUS can give Sweden a new industrial future through carbon capture and storage – but policy is lagging behind. How do we build a national strategy and cross-bloc consensus that lasts, strengthens competitiveness and matches our neighbours' investments?
content.extendedDescription:
CCUS – carbon capture, utilisation and storage – has the potential to become both a new Swedish industry of the future and a crucial tool for achieving climate targets. Yet Sweden lacks a coherent national strategy and a long-term policy framework. In an unsettled world, investments risk being postponed if policy is perceived as short-sighted.
Several of our neighbours are now making substantial investments in carbon capture and storage, creating both competition and new opportunities for Nordic cooperation. For Sweden, this is about more than climate: it concerns industrial development, new value chains, exports and future jobs.

The seminar brings together politics and industry to discuss how broad, cross-bloc support for CCUS can be built and sustained across electoral terms. How do we create stable conditions for investment? What does it take to move from individual facilities to a new industry? And can Sweden take the next step from pioneer to a leading nation in carbon capture and storage?

content.title: How much truth can we handle? How do we recognise when a lie becomes the truth?
content.description: In politics, the same facts are used to reach different conclusions while disinformation and distrust spread. A crisis of truth emerges. Red lines are there not to be crossed, but when facts are ignored, they are crossed anyway. What happens to democracy, the state and its citizens when we become loose with the truth?
content.extendedDescription:
In a polarised debate, truth risks becoming a tool rather than common ground – but where is the line between interpretation and stretching the truth? What happens to democracy when we ourselves share uncertain information and contribute to this shift?

• How are crises of truth exposed, and how can we best counter disinformation, fake news, conspiracy theories and growing distrust of institutions that produce knowledge?
• What happens when people, who may already be in vulnerable situations, also lose confidence in public agencies and the institutions that underpin society?
• How can trust in society best be built over time?
• Where are our own 'red' lines in relation to what is happening?

The Christian tradition has a strong ideal of truth. 'The truth will set you free' (the Gospel of John). But what does that expression mean in a public debate where facts are interpreted, simplified and sometimes distorted? What is the difference between truth and interpretation? What responsibility do we all bear?

content.title: Molecules as resilience – what role do the chemical and process industries play in preparedness?
content.description: More than ninety per cent of the products we use every day depend on the chemical and process industries. These industries currently rely heavily on imported raw materials from fossil sources. This makes Sweden and Europe vulnerable to geopolitical crises and disruptions in global supply chains.
content.extendedDescription:
Transformed chemical and process industries using a greater share of domestic bio-based and circular raw materials could become a cornerstone of secure supplies and stronger defence capabilities in Sweden and Europe. The benefits are clear, but how do we achieve domestic supply chains independent of fossil resources while maintaining competitiveness? In this seminar, we outline the path towards resilient, strong and green chemical and process industries and the obstacles that industry, politics and the market must overcome together.

Together with industry representatives, defence experts and politicians, we explore the role the Swedish chemical and process industries play, and could play, in Sweden's preparedness for crisis or conflict. What needs to be done, and who needs to act, to create more robust chemical and process industries that can support Sweden's and Europe's defence capabilities?

content.title: The transport sector: a backbone of total defence
content.description: Which interests need to coexist and work together for greater resilience? How does the transport sector function, and how can robust infrastructure be secured as a strategic security issue in everyday life, in a crisis and, in the worst case, in war?
content.extendedDescription:
This concerns the principles that need to be considered in transport, including people's lives and health; the functioning of society, for example food and business transport; commuting; the environment and economic assets; and national sovereignty, transit and host nation support.
Sweden must never come to a standstill. To fully succeed, public agencies and business now need to deepen their cooperation.

The seminar will focus on three perspectives on the principles that need to be considered in transport:
• Normal conditions: What must already be in place when we build and plan infrastructure to meet several interests at once?
• The crisis perspective: What must work from each actor's perspective when the system is severely tested?
• Prioritisation in an actual crisis: What is the order of priorities? How do we balance different interests and ensure shared priorities in a real emergency?

The seminar will also be streamed online; this page will be updated with a link.

content.title: From grassroots movement to personal brand – what happens to the collective 'we'?
content.description: Many civil society movements have grown out of shared commitment. Yet today, organisations often build their visibility on strong personal brands and well-known figures. What happens to the collective 'we' when movements increasingly revolve around individuals? Is it a gain or a loss?
content.extendedDescription:
Today there is a tension between grassroots engagement and personal branding.

Traditional popular movements are based on membership. They start from democratic structures and have a shared vision. Digital platform algorithms are designed the other way round. Faces and personal stories are favoured over the collective.
When the focus shifts to the personal brand (influencers, charismatic leaders), the movement risks becoming centred on one person. The 'we' is replaced by a vertical relationship between a 'star' and an audience. Engagement arises but is vulnerable. When the person falls, the cause often falls too.

Instead of co-creating a movement, we risk becoming consumers of someone's brand. Our role is to be 'followers', rather than a shared voice. But are 'personal brands' entirely bad?

How can a future balance be struck in which the 'we' is not weakened – and can actually be strengthened by personal 'brands'?
Has the balance already tipped, and if so, what is needed for the future?

content.title: Sweden and Ukraine – how can universities keep functioning during acute crises?
content.description: Universities play an important role in peacetime, but what role do universities play during a societal crisis? Ukraine's universities have suffered under Russia's war of aggression, yet continue to operate. How can we support Ukraine and learn from their experiences?
content.extendedDescription: In peacetime, universities uphold democracy and culture, produce and disseminate knowledge about nature and society, advance health and quality of life, drive innovation, supply the labor market with educated workers, and much more. What becomes of the university's role when war or a profound societal crisis happens? Ukraine's universities are operating under extremely difficult conditions. The past winter has been especially difficult, and today the war has lasted longer than the Second World War. We will hear accounts of what the challenges of everyday life look like at Ukrainian universities. Many students and researchers are becoming soldiers, finances are strained, and conducting field research can be life-threatening. At the same time, Ukrainian universities are managing to continue their work. How can we offer Ukrainian researchers and universities partnerships that are mutually beneficial? Can we learn from the Ukrainian experience while offering concrete support here and now?
content.subject: Security/defence

content.title: E-cigarettes under scrutiny – from niche product to regulated market: what do we know today?
content.description: E-cigarettes have been available in Sweden for more than 15 years and are now used by hundreds of thousands of adults. Meanwhile, the debate centres on questions about health, product safety, young people's use and strict regulation. What does the market look like today, and what do we really know about the products?
content.extendedDescription:
Over the past fifteen years, e-cigarettes have developed from a niche product into an established and growing part of the Swedish nicotine market. Meanwhile, regulation has become more extensive, with increasing requirements for product safety, ingredient declarations and traceability.

But the debate about e-cigarettes is still marked by many questions. How is e-liquid manufactured? How do today's safety checks work? What does use among adults and young people look like? How does today's market differ from the one that emerged in the 2010s? How does a market function when small local businesses operate alongside multinational giants?

The discussion examines this development from manufacturers', retailers' and consumers' perspectives. It focuses on changes in the market, product safety, quality requirements, common misconceptions about e-cigarettes and the challenges and opportunities ahead.

The aim is to provide a fact-based picture of a product category relevant to both public health and the future of nicotine policy.
content.subject: Innovation

content.title: Municipal IT and operational systems based on open source for greater digital sovereignty
content.description: Today, Sweden's municipalities depend more or less entirely on systems from American tech giants in their day-to-day operations. But what happens if those companies cannot be relied on, and what alternatives exist for municipalities that want greater independence and less lock-in?
content.extendedDescription:
American software suppliers have long dominated the Swedish market, not least in Sweden's municipalities. Much of their day-to-day work depends on services and platforms over which the municipalities themselves have limited control. This makes the question increasingly pressing: what happens if these companies can no longer provide the services we depend on, change their terms unilaterally or are affected by geopolitical decisions?
This discussion explores whether municipalities have an alternative route to greater digital sovereignty through solutions such as open source and open technical standards. Are there concrete examples of organisations that have chosen this path? What are the lessons, and is it even possible?

Help shape the discussion at Omställningsarenan in Sweco's courtyard during Almedalsveckan! No registration is required – we offer a relaxed courtyard setting where you can hear incisive observations and take part in solution-focused discussions.

content.title: From healthcare to working life – the path back through collaboration
content.description: We often speak of people as patients, on sick leave or dependent. But what happens if we instead see people as assets and future colleagues? New approaches bringing healthcare and employment services together are already being tested on Gotland – but they remain the exception rather than the norm.
content.extendedDescription:
Questions we ask in the seminar:

Why do people get stuck in systems despite labour shortages?
Do our structures prevent more people from finding work?
Is healthcare part of the solution – or part of the problem?

During the seminar, we will describe two different projects in which the employment unit and healthcare services on Gotland address these questions together, and what happens when shared perspectives and greater understanding allow us to develop a new view of patients and people experiencing exclusion.
We want to dare to challenge our own view of the 'problem' and achieve new results through shared commitment.

IPS Gotland is a project in which psychiatric services and the employment unit work to implement IPS for people with substance use disorders.

Jobbvägen Södra Gotland is part of the ESF project Gotland Forward. Employment coaches and the psychosocial team at the health centre in Hemse work as colleagues to find new ways to make a difference.

content.title: Support that safeguards legal rights for deaf and hard-of-hearing people with intellectual disabilities
content.description: Deaf and hard-of-hearing people with intellectual disabilities are a particularly vulnerable group who often miss out on support and assistance in sign language because of gaps in knowledge and accessibility. What happens when support and assistance fail to materialise? What is needed to provide help and support that safeguards their legal rights?
content.extendedDescription: People who are deaf or hard of hearing and also have a mild to moderate intellectual disability are a group about whom society knows very little. This is even more the case when they are victims of crime and different forms of violence. How well are this group's legal rights protected today? Sweden has 290 municipalities, all of which interpret, assess and provide support in different ways. Stöd på dina villkor is a project funded by Allmänna arvsfonden and run by Nationell kvinnojour och stöd på teckenspråk. The project began after several people with intellectual disabilities contacted the organisation's sign-language support line. Over three years, the project has collected, documented and developed methods for support work that can contribute to greater security and understanding for deaf and hard-of-hearing crime victims with intellectual disabilities. The discussion will explore these issues in greater depth through the project's work and present the results of its mapping of legal safeguards.
content.subject: Human rights

content.title: How do public agencies and companies ensure joint crisis preparedness in an uncertain world?
content.description: Sweden's preparedness is being tested: the state bears responsibility, but private actors own some of the critical infrastructure. Responding to an uncertain world requires a shift from efficiency-optimised 'Just-in-Time' to security-driven 'Just-in-Case'. How do we work together when the market meets the requirements of total defence?
content.extendedDescription:
In a new normal marked by geopolitical unrest and growing threats to our infrastructure, isolated preparedness plans are no longer enough. Swedish resilience depends on seamless interaction between the public and private sectors. But what does cooperation look like in practice when supply chains are under pressure and national security requirements are weighed against market logic? We bring together leading figures from business's most critical sectors (energy, food, finance and telecoms) and public-agency experts to discuss the way forward for Sweden's total defence.
We discuss:
• From efficiency to robustness: How do we adapt logistics and business models to a 'Just-in-Case' mindset?
• Allocation of responsibility: Where does a company's responsibility end and the state's begin when a crisis strikes?
• Vulnerabilities at the interface: How do we eliminate critical weaknesses between public governance and private operation?
Join a discussion about future crisis preparedness and concrete solutions for a safer Sweden.
content.subject: Democracy
speakerTitles: Head of the Personal Banking Market, Sweden

content.title: How do we enable constructive dialogue on the environment and sustainability?
content.description: Challenges such as the energy transition and the climate crisis require constructive dialogue to resolve. Yet trust in research is faltering, facts are questioned and polarising narratives clash. How can we work together to achieve constructive discussions and communication methods that work in practice?
content.extendedDescription:
Environmental and climate crises are accompanied by disagreements, polarising conflicts and unproductive dialogue. When these crises intensify public debate, it becomes harder to create constructive discussions that lead to practical solutions.

In a co-creative panel discussion, researchers and communicators invite a conversation about how we can navigate these disagreements and create conditions for different perspectives to meet. How can democratic dialogue and participation be strengthened on issues relating to climate and energy? How can discussions about the environment and sustainability contribute to progress rather than polarising conflicts?

The panel discussion exchanges ideas about dialogue-based environmental communication, drawing on visitors', researchers' and communicators' own experiences. Together, we discuss how environmental and sustainability issues are discussed during and outside Almedalsveckan, and how those discussions could take place.

The panel discussion is organised by the Mistra Environmental Communication research programme.
