content.title: Menstrual health, empowerment and economic development
content.description: Menstruation is still surrounded by stigma, taboos and a lack of knowledge. When it is not treated as a societal issue, girls risk missing school and women being excluded from working life. Breaking taboos is about more than dignity and rights: it is about development, the economy and gender equality.
content.extendedDescription:
When girls can attend school and women can work, both household incomes and entire communities are strengthened. What happens to a society's productivity when girls and women are forced to be absent simply because they lack the means to manage their periods safely? How does access to water and toilets affect women's participation in the labour market? What responsibility do male decision-makers have to advance this issue?

The breakfast seminar focuses on why menstruation is still surrounded by stigma and its consequences for girls' education, women's labour-market opportunities and societies' economic development. We also discuss how investment in water, sanitation, knowledge and education can contribute to better menstrual health and more equal societies.
Together with participants from business and politics, we explore how menstruation can be elevated from a private concern to a question of rights, gender equality and sustainable development. What political changes are needed to increase investment?
content.subject: Gender equality
speakerTitles: Member of Parliament and Chair of S-kvinnor
Senior Consultant in Trade and Development

content.title: How can public procurement drive reuse in the construction sector?
content.description: Extensive renovation needs risk increasing the construction sector's climate impact. At the same time, there are demands for lower emissions and circular material flows. How can reuse be scaled up, and what role can public procurement play in enabling this development?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden faces extensive renovation of apartment buildings from the 1960s, 70s and 80s. These investments involve large material flows that, using traditional approaches, risk causing substantial climate impact. Meanwhile, the construction sector and municipal housing companies have ambitious goals for lower emissions, greater resource efficiency and more circular material flows.

Reusing construction products is highlighted as an important part of the solution, as it can reduce the need for newly manufactured materials and thus climate impact. But making reuse an integral part of construction and renovation processes requires changes to working methods, business models and regulations.

Drawing on experience from research, innovation and practical projects, the discussion explores the opportunities and obstacles to scaling up reuse in construction and renovation projects. Where are we today, and what is needed to take the next step? And what does it take for public procurement to serve as a tool in this development?
content.subject: Construction
speakerTitles: Head of Projects and Property Development

content.title: The Stockholm of the future – strategies for even more urban life, experiences and innovation
content.description: Long-term urban development requires both courage and new thinking, especially in changing times. What opportunities are offered by existing built structures and the blue-green assets that characterise Stockholm? And how can urban planning continue to drive the realisation of visions?
content.extendedDescription:
Stockholm has always been a city of development and change. Over the past 25 years, it has grown by 250 000 new residents in 100 000 new homes, with new workplaces, public services, attractive public spaces and infrastructure, particularly through expanded public transport. All of this is rooted in long-term plans spanning many decades, which the city and everyone involved have been good at bringing to life.

What could Stockholm look like in the 2060s – what opportunities does our future offer? Work is currently under way to shape that future in a new comprehensive plan. Which of today's known conditions are given space alongside what is still unknown and unplanned? And how do we use urban development in our everyday lives to create an even more attractive city to live in?

Meet representatives from the city and the sector who share their vision of the future. They also show how the city is developing today through urban development that adds value, making Stockholm an even better city for everyone.

content.title: AI, You and I: The Reinvention of Industry - How Are We Building the Next Industrial Era?
content.description: Artificial intelligence is transforming how industries design, produce and innovate. The shift requires new skills, processes, and governance. How can industry, policymakers and innovation ecosystems collaborate to ensure the AI-driven industrial transition is inclusive and sustainable?
content.extendedDescription:
The shift toward AI-driven industry is not simply about adopting new tools. It requires rethinking industrial systems, supply chains, workforce skills and research collaboration.
The 2026 series of Engaging India at Almedalen examines how artificial intelligence is influencing identity, industrial transformation and planetary transition. In this seminar businesses, policymakers and innovators from Sweden and India share insights on building the next AI-enabled industrial era responsibly and sustainably.

content.title: Osteoporosis – a neglected investment
content.description: On unequal care, growing waiting lists and why better care matters from a societal perspective. Despite affecting so many people, the disease remains both underdiagnosed and undertreated. How can we improve care and reduce unnecessary suffering?
content.extendedDescription:
Osteoporosis is one of our major common diseases and causes more than 100 000 fractures every year in Sweden. It primarily affects older people, more often women, and leads to considerable pain, poorer quality of life, disability and increased mortality. For society, this places a substantial burden on healthcare and social care.
Waiting times for assessment vary greatly between regions. Many patients are not identified after their first fracture, which often leads to repeated, frequently preventable fractures and resulting increases in costs and care needs.
Clear national guidelines and effective treatment strategies are available today and have been shown to reduce the risk of further fractures. Despite this, only a small proportion of patients receive adequate secondary prevention within a year of a fracture.
Join a discussion about how osteoporosis care can become more equitable, preventive and sustainable in the long term, and why this should be seen as an investment rather than a cost.

content.title: What do Swedes think about climate and biodiversity policy?
content.description: Political decisions are needed to meet climate and biodiversity targets, yet environmental policy is being weakened today in the belief that the public does not support more ambitious measures. But what does research say about Swedes' views on environmental policy measures? What conclusions do politicians draw from the findings?
content.extendedDescription:
Research shows that more policy measures are needed to meet environmental targets for climate and biodiversity. Yet parts of environmental policy have recently been weakened on the grounds that public support is lacking. But what do we actually know about Swedes' attitudes to more concrete environmental policy proposals? The answer matters because attitudes have a major bearing on political feasibility.

The seminar draws on the findings of a new scientific report, 'Svenska folkets attityder till styrmedel för klimat och biologisk mångfald' (Swedish public attitudes to policy instruments for climate and biodiversity). The report is based on a survey in which around 2000 Swedes expressed their views on 30 specific policy measures relating to climate and biodiversity. The survey also examined Swedes' concerns and priorities in environmental policy, and whether attitudes differ between social groups.

The report will be presented at the seminar, followed by a panel discussion with representatives of parliamentary parties.

The seminar is part of Uppsala universitet's climate days.

content.title: Humanoid Robotics: Is Sweden Ready for Physical AI?
content.description: Humanoid robots are leaving the labs and entering workplaces, manufacturing and everyday life. Global investments are accelerating. For Sweden – with its strong industrial base and automation heritage – the question is urgent: how do we prepare our society and industry for the new era of physical AI
content.extendedDescription:
Humanoid robots are advancing rapidly from research prototypes to commercial products. Companies worldwide are investing billions to bring humanoids into manufacturing, logistics, healthcare and services. For Sweden, with its robotics heritage and world-leading industry, this is both an opportunity and a challenge.
 
The session combines a keynote, a live humanoid robot demonstration and a panel discussion. The keynote examines the technologies driving progress, the global momentum behind the field, and the key engineering and deployment challenges that remain. A moderated panel then brings together researchers in humanoid robotics and production automation alongside industry representatives to explore: Are industry and society ready for humanoids? What can we realistically expect in the near term? And what must Sweden do to punch above its weight and put itself on the map in physical AI and humanoid robotics?

content.title: The weakest link: how does inadequate infrastructure threaten industry and Sweden's competitiveness?
content.description: Is Sweden's transport infrastructure equipped to meet both industry's needs and the new security situation's demands for robustness, redundancy and preparedness? When business competitiveness, society's ability to maintain supplies and the needs of total defence converge in the same transport system, new perspectives are required.
content.extendedDescription:
When transport stops: is Swedish infrastructure built for the new security situation?
Infrastructure is no longer just about costs per kilometre and logistics – it is a matter of national resilience, business-critical robustness and regional survival. In a changed international environment, the Swedish transport system faces entirely new demands. Yet we often still plan and make decisions in silos.
This seminar takes a wider view, analysing the transport system as an interconnected whole, with a focus on the strategic E12 corridor and Västerbotniabanan.
The overall perspective that is often forgotten: from Helsinki to the nearest Atlantic port, the fastest and most strategic route follows the E12 corridor – through Finland, across Kvarken and on through Västerbotten to Mo i Rana. This makes E12 a key corridor for both civilian and military transport in northern Europe.
Main themes:
• The strategic east-west corridor and local growth
• Preparedness, supplies and industrial vulnerability
• From vulnerability to systems thinking

content.title: From obstacle to enabler – the public sector's role in securing future food supplies
content.description: Swedish farmers face economic, climate-related and structural challenges, while playing a central role in food supplies, preparedness and public health. How can the public sector break down silos and proactively contribute to a more resilient food system?
content.extendedDescription:
Swedish farmers are in a perfect storm of high costs, low profitability, extreme weather, generational transitions and a growing regulatory burden. At the same time, their role is crucial to the country's food supply, especially in an era marked by geopolitical uncertainty, climate change and public health challenges. The challenges are both systemic and complex.
What role does the public sector need to play in a system-wide transition that secures Sweden's future food supply and overcomes today's fragmented governance?

To explore this, we invite Anna Olofsson, Director General of Jordbruksverket, and Helene Hellmark Knutsson, County Governor of Västerbottens län, to a strategic discussion. We discuss what systems leadership means in practice and what shifts are needed for the public sector to move from silos to collaboration with producers, consumers and other societal actors, thereby strengthening a more resilient, healthy and sustainable food system.

content.title: Forest policy – how smaller family forest owners are affected
content.description: The debate about forests has been heated in recent years. Forestry companies are usually pitted against environmental organisations in a polarising way. But how are Sweden's family forest owners affected by current policy and by the parties' proposals ahead of the election?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden has 300 000 forest owners. They are often overlooked in the debate about national forest policy, where active forestry is set against a conservation perspective. As EU legislation is to be implemented in Sweden and a comprehensive forestry inquiry presents a range of national proposals, questions about economic conditions, usage rights, compensation and public-agency responsibilities become highly significant for individual forest owners. Many parties say they care about forest owners' profitability. But how do their different proposals affect family forest owners – and their finances?
Landshypotek Bank and Föreningen Skogen have asked the parliamentary parties about their forest policies and invited all of them to this seminar. The starting point is a discussion from the family forest owner's perspective.
The discussion aims to clarify what is needed from policy to provide long-term sustainability, willingness to invest and economic empowerment for the country's 300 000 family forest owners.

content.title: Large-scale flexibility and energy storage – think hydropower and pumped storage
content.description: Sweden's electricity needs are expected to rise sharply as electrification gathers pace. At some times we may face a shortage of power, and at others we may have large electricity surpluses. How does this fit together, and how can investments in hydropower and pumped storage help meet future needs?
content.extendedDescription:
The electrification of industry, transport and society is expected to bring rapidly growing electricity demand. At the same time, an electricity system more dependent on weather places greater demands on flexibility, power capacity and system stability.

Hydropower already plays a central role by providing power capacity, flexibility, ancillary services and large-scale energy storage when the electricity system needs them. Meanwhile, opportunities to strengthen hydropower's capabilities further are being explored through upgrades to existing facilities, capacity increases and investments in pumped storage. Several projects are already under way, and some have been completed. Studies show great potential, but also significant challenges.

The seminar brings together energy companies, public agencies, industry and political representatives to discuss the role hydropower can play in strengthening the capacity balance and flexibility of the electricity system. Which investments are possible, what have we learned so far, and what matters for making further progress?

content.title: War, crises and climate: is Nordic energy cooperation enough?
content.description: War, energy crises and climate-related disruptions are putting energy systems under pressure. In the Nordic region, energy markets and infrastructure are closely interconnected across borders, and Sweden plays a central role. How can Nordic cooperation strengthen energy security and preparedness?
content.extendedDescription:
Energy security has become a central issue in an era marked by war, geopolitical uncertainty and recurring energy crises. Cyber and military attacks in recent years have shown how vulnerable energy systems can be – but also how crucial close Nordic cooperation is. For Sweden, a central actor in the Nordic electricity system, this raises questions about how cooperation can develop to strengthen energy security in the region.

Integrated energy markets and shared solutions have given the Nordic region a strong starting point, but how robust is energy cooperation when the energy system comes under pressure?

Nordisk Energiforskning and Nordiska ministerrådet have mapped energy security in the Nordic region in the report Mapping Energy Security in the Nordics. During the event, we discuss what the findings mean for the Nordic region: what are our shared challenges, what opportunities exist – and how can energy cooperation strengthen Nordic energy security and resilience?

content.title: The Veteran – an Essential  Resource for the Reconstruction of a War-Torn Society
content.description: Millions of Ukrainian soldiers are returning from the war with experiences and support needs. Providing psychosocial support and using their skills is crucial for successful reintegration and Ukraine’s future. What are the roles of policy, civil society, and Sweden in veteran support?
content.extendedDescription:
The number of Ukrainian veterans now counts in millions and continues to grow every day. Soldiers returning home from the front carry with them a backpack filled with experiences and memories from the relentless reality of war, together with the many skills and areas of knowledge they had as members of society before Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022. Successfully reintegrating Ukrainian veterans—providing adequate psycosocial support while also making use of each individual’s competencies and motivation—has therefore become a highly prioritized societal issue, which many consider decisive for Ukraine’s survival as a nation.
What are the key factors for successfully integrating Ukrainian veterans? How is veteran support organized at the political level, and what different roles do civil society actors play? What can Swedish veteran policy—through government agencies and non-profit veteran and family organizations—learn from Ukraine’s work with veterans, and vice versa?

content.title: How Sweden can become the EU's hub for circular industry with AI and digital product passports
content.description: Starting in 2027, the EU requires digital product passports. Together with the AI transition, these could drive circular value chains and strengthen Sweden's competitiveness. But are we ready – and which standards, incentives and actors are needed to enable both small and large companies to keep up?
content.extendedDescription:
The EU will soon introduce digital product passports for products with a substantial environmental and resource impact. The rollout starts with batteries, followed by textiles, furniture and more product categories. For many companies, this entails an extensive transition. Data on materials, climate impact and product lifecycles must be traceable throughout the value chain and shared between different actors and IT systems. For policymakers, this is an opportunity to strengthen transparency, resource efficiency and competitiveness in Swedish industry.

Meanwhile, a rapid AI transition is under way, in which structured, reliable and traceable data are the prerequisite for AI's full potential.

Many are now asking: How can regulatory compliance and AI transformation create synergies that strengthen Swedish competitiveness? Which standards, actors and incentives are needed to enable circular resource flows? How can policymakers create conditions that allow companies of all sizes to participate?
content.subject: Sustainability
speakerTitles: Head of Standards and Chair of the DPP EU Standard

content.title: What actually is palliative care? On living life close to death
content.description: Palliative care often raises questions and fears. Many people immediately think of death. The focus is on living the life that remains to the fullest. Palliative care takes a holistic view of the person and aims to promote quality of life, reduce suffering and enable a meaningful life.
content.extendedDescription:
The event is a lecture in which we explain palliative care simply and clearly. We see value in clarifying what palliative care is and what it involves, as misunderstandings currently create fear. We want to show how palliative care supports life at its most fragile and is not about giving up. Reports show that access to palliative care in Sweden is unequal and that unclear perceptions and fears may be part of the explanation.
The lecture draws on research and relates to Socialstyrelsen's updated definitions and guidelines. Palliative care is provided for conditions that may lead to death within days, months or years, and therefore needs to be integrated into other healthcare and social care.
There is a great need for knowledge. We hope the lecture will dispel myths, spark curiosity and provide an understanding of what palliative care is and why it concerns us all.

content.title: Who takes responsibility for cleaning up the atmosphere with carbon credits – companies, the state or the EU?
content.description: Carbon credits (CDR, Carbon Dioxide Removals) are shifting from a climate tool to a strategic market issue. Companies buy credits to strengthen their climate plans, investors demand net-zero strategies and the EU is building a new regulatory framework for certifying negative emissions.
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden is testing reverse auctions to purchase permanent negative emissions – but without a long-term plan for what happens afterwards. The result is a rapidly growing but fragmented market in which three actors are trying to take the lead:

Companies – net emitters:
They have current and historical emissions. They want to use carbon credits and CDRs to strengthen competitiveness, win business and invest in new technology – but need clear rules and quality assurance.

The state:
It is testing auctions and pilot programmes, but has not yet defined the role Sweden should play in the European CDR market.

The EU:
It is developing certification frameworks and discussing joint purchasing programmes, which could reshape the entire market and affect opportunities for Swedish companies.

The big question is therefore:
Who should take the lead in building a credible and competitive market for negative emissions – companies, the state or the EU – and what is the next step in its development?

content.title: Sweden lacks safe rest areas for commercial transport – a systemic failure that threatens the entire transport chain
content.description:
Sweden's lorry drivers perform a critical societal function – without them, Sweden stops.
Yet there is a major shortage of secure lorry parking for commercial transport, both in Sweden and across Europe. The problem is not a lack of awareness, but a lack of responsibility, incentives and implementation.
content.extendedDescription:
Resilient transport infrastructure is crucial to Sweden's supply chain and preparedness. Despite broad agreement on the need for more and better rest areas, too little is happening. Responsibilities are unclear, incentives are weak and implementation stalls.
This seminar moves from describing the problem to addressing responsibility. We identify why progress has stalled and what is needed to produce concrete solutions.
We bring together actors from the entire chain: business, politics and people with first-hand experience from the road. Together, we discuss what a functioning model for future rest areas could look like, with clear responsibilities, relevant requirements and feasible solutions.

• What is preventing the expansion of safe rest areas in Sweden?
• How do today's shortcomings affect transport capacity and delivery reliability?
• What concrete requirements should be placed on the state, municipalities and business?
• What does it take to create a transport sector that can cope with both everyday conditions and crises?
• Are we willing to pay for social responsibility?

content.title: Civil defence and urban design – how do we build attractive and resilient living environments?
content.description: How can we build attractive environments that combine sustainable development with preparedness for crisis and war? New approaches to designed environments at neighbourhood level, with local resilience and public spaces that can be mobilised for critical societal functions. What strengthens our social and civil capabilities in the built environment?
content.extendedDescription:
With greater pressure on total defence, the built environment sector needs to rethink urban design. This involves aspects of the physical environment: evacuation routes, shelters, multifunctional spaces, building conversion, energy supply and alternative modes of transport. Our social capital, neighbourhood cooperation and local expertise are also very important. Can the transition to circular cities strengthen civil defence capabilities?
For the 4th consecutive year, join discussions at Omställningsarenan in Sweco's courtyard in Visby, with leading representatives of the built environment sector, the public sector and urban design. In an era of increased vulnerability, we jointly frame the big questions and the strategies required.
No registration is required – we offer a relaxed courtyard setting where you can hear incisive observations and take part in solution-focused discussions. Together, we create sustainable, resilient communities. Welcome!

content.title: The other side of the medal – insecure living conditions, financial stress and an uncertain future
content.description: Behind medals and high rankings, elite athletes struggle financially. They dedicate their lives to representing Sweden at the highest level, but when their careers end, the future is often uncertain. Sickness benefits and pensions are parts of the social security system that many take for granted, yet they fall short for elite athletes.
content.extendedDescription:
Contrary to what many believe, most people competing for medals for Sweden face finances that do not add up. Half struggle to make ends meet – and more than 200 elite athletes have quit in four years. Two in three Paralympians are considering quitting for financial reasons. Four in ten applicants for SOK's scholarship live below the minimum subsistence level.

What can the social partners do to improve elite athletes' living conditions? What can be resolved through collective agreements, and what requires changes to legislation and regulations? Are there lessons to learn from the cultural sector?

Elite athletes' lives are shaped by training periods, competitions and irregular incomes. They rarely fit into a social insurance system designed to support people in long-term employment. This disadvantages elite athletes, whose careers have peaks and troughs in income and workload. They lack sufficient protection in the event of injury, illness or parental leave. When their careers end, their pensions are often negligible.
content.subject: Employment/labour market
speakerTitles: Head of Operational Support and Development

content.title: Security and cooperation in the Baltic Sea – how can marine data strengthen defence and society?
content.description: Activities at sea generate large amounts of data that help to identify risks, protect infrastructure, and improve environmental monitoring. Data sharing raises questions about security, confidentiality, and governance. How can we strengthen security and cooperation among actors through data sharing?
content.extendedDescription:
The development of sensors, autonomous systems, and offshore infrastructure is generating large volumes of data collected by both public and private actors. These technologies often have dual-use applications and can support environmental and security-related monitoring as well as operational activities. In Sweden, however, this potential remains largely underutilized. One reason is that issues related to data access, ownership, and use remain unclear. At the same time, international experiences suggest that improved secure data sharing can create opportunities for collaboration between civilian and security stakeholders.

The seminar will be conducted in English and is organized within the framework of two research projects. Mistra Co-Creating Better Blue (C2B2), which explores how collaboration can strengthen ocean governance, and SAFEWIN, funded by Formas, which examines how dual-use technologies can contribute to secure data sharing and the protection of energy infrastructure.

content.organizationType: Collaboration between different types of organisation

content.title: How do we create meaningful participation for young people – in actions as well as words?
content.description: In an era of complex societal challenges, young people's participation is crucial. As trust in democracy and societal institutions is challenged, we need to create meaningful influence and draw on young people's perspectives to develop sustainable solutions for the future.
content.extendedDescription:
How can municipalities and other actors work more systematically to strengthen young people's influence – especially for those currently furthest from decision-making?

The seminar shares experiences from Solidarity4All, a project that strengthens people's capacity to participate. Together with partners, we have developed concrete approaches to increase young people's influence in practice.

We explore what it takes to move from ambition to real change and how lasting structures for influence can be built over time.

Reaching young people who are often overlooked requires new forms of collaboration. We highlight how civil society and public services can together create better conditions for inclusive influence and stronger democratic trust.

The panel discusses obstacles, success factors and methods that have delivered results.

The seminar is for anyone working in a municipality, civil society or otherwise engaging with young people who wants to develop structures that make a real difference. Ice cream is available!
content.subject: Children/young people

content.title: 15 000 new jobs and better public health – is it possible?
content.description: Poor eating habits affect both individuals and society through poorer health and productivity. What if a reform could help more people eat better while creating thousands of entry-level jobs? It already exists in Europe. It is now high time for Sweden to introduce smart meal benefits too.
content.extendedDescription:
Did you know that three in ten employees cannot afford to eat lunch every day?
This is concerning because unhealthy eating habits are the second-largest risk factor for disease after tobacco. Research also shows that poor lunch habits have major consequences over time for everything from quality of life to sickness absence and productivity growth.
Rising food prices have also made meals a source of stress for many households. The government's temporary reduction in food VAT is a welcome step in the right direction, but what if there were a more cost-effective, long-term reform that could do everything from improving public health to strengthening the Swedish economy?
That reform already exists in several European countries – and has proved effective both in creating jobs and in revitalising the restaurant industry.
Join a seminar where experts and decision-makers discuss how tax-free and tax-deductible meal benefits can make a real difference – for individuals and society as a whole.
content.subject: Economy
speakerTitles: PhD in Economics or Business Administration
Member of Parliament, Party Group Leader on a Committee

content.title: When uncertainty slows sustainable procurement – how can guidance on equivalent labels help?
content.description: How can procurement regulations be used and developed to strengthen sustainable development through public purchasing? And how can greater clarity about equivalent labels make it easier to use sustainability labels in procurement?
content.extendedDescription:
Public procurement amounts to around SEK 1 000 billion annually and is one of society's most powerful tools for driving a sustainable transition. Yet the field is marked by legal uncertainty, particularly around the concept of 'equivalent labels'. Although legislation clearly states that equivalent labels must be accepted, both the EU procurement directives and Swedish legislation lack a clear, consistent definition.

In practice, this ambiguity sometimes leads procuring organisations to refrain from setting ambitious sustainability requirements, while also creating a risk that labels are accepted without actually meeting equivalent requirements.

Against this backdrop, the need for both legal clarification and practical guidance is growing. How can equivalence be assessed in practice? The seminar presents a new legal report analysing the concept and providing guidance on how organisations can act. We also share municipal examples and experiences.

content.title: How do we strengthen Sweden's medical preparedness in an era of crisis and war?
content.description: Sweden's security situation is changing, and demands on societal preparedness are growing. What role can medical research, education, collaboration and innovation play in strengthening the country's ability to handle future crises and conflicts? How can universities best contribute to medical preparedness?
content.extendedDescription:
As geopolitical tensions rise and the focus on total defence grows, questions arise about how Sweden can strengthen its medical preparedness for future crises, disasters and ultimately war. What skills and resources are needed, and how can knowledge be put into practice more quickly? What role should medical research and education environments play in stronger total defence?

The discussion draws on Karolinska Institutet's strategic initiative on medical preparedness, bringing together research, education, innovation and cross-sector collaboration. It combines expertise in areas including health crises, disaster medicine, defence-related medicine and research into human performance and resilience in extreme environments.

The aim is to open up new perspectives and partnerships on one of the most pressing societal issues of our time. How should universities, public agencies, healthcare services and other societal actors work together to strengthen Sweden's ability to prevent, manage and learn from crises?

content.title: Preparedness and geopolitics make cancer care and cancer research a security issue
content.description: In a new security-policy environment, cancer care, medicines, medical technology and health data become part of society's critical infrastructure. How do we ensure robust care, research and clinical trials even in crisis and war – and how does life science strengthen Sweden's resilience?
content.extendedDescription:
As competitiveness becomes increasingly linked to security policy, cancer care, research and innovation need to be seen as part of society's critical infrastructure. Vulnerable supply chains, dependence on advanced medical technology and increasing cyber threats mean that diagnostics, medicines, radiotherapy and health data must be integrated into Sweden's civil preparedness.

At the same time, questions arise about how research and clinical trials can continue even when healthcare resources are under pressure. How do we ensure patients retain access to new treatments and Sweden maintains its international position in life science?
The seminar discusses how cancer care can be integrated into national preparedness and total defence planning.

Scenario-based panel discussions examine cancer care as critical societal infrastructure, medicines supply and medical technology as strategic resources, and how research, data resources and international partnerships can strengthen the system's resilience.

content.title: Essential self-care – how university hospitals are leading the transition from hospital to home
content.description: As advanced care moves into the home, person-centred systems are needed to ensure high-quality care. University hospitals need legally sound models for self-care. How can chief nursing officers, heads of administration, patients and relatives together lead a safe transition from hospital to home?
content.extendedDescription: The transformation of healthcare means that increasingly highly specialised care is moving from university hospitals to patients' homes. Maintaining high-quality care and patient safety requires a shift to genuinely person-centred systems, drawing on patients' own resources through safe and well-founded self-care. But as the boundaries between inpatient care, Hospital at Home and patients' own responsibility shift, complex challenges arise. How do we create legally sound models in which information requirements, consent and the allocation of responsibility are based on each individual's unique circumstances and needs? The seminar places CNO/CMO leadership at the heart of this quality-driven transition. We explore how chief nursing officers and heads of administration at management level must lead the development of future self-care together with patients and relatives. We discuss how to move from parallel care structures to coherent, person-centred processes that strengthen patient empowerment and build quality all the way home.

content.title: Heta stubben: a boost for outdoor recreation through investment in nature and physical activity – the perfect recipe for sustainability?
content.description: Naturvårdsverket proposes doubling funding for organised outdoor recreation and substantially increasing funding for the management of valuable natural areas. Folkhälsomyndigheten wants a national initiative to increase physical activity, with outdoor recreation playing an important role. Is this the perfect recipe for sustainability?
content.extendedDescription:
Last year's Almedalen success, Heta stubben, is back. With the sea as a backdrop and the smell of coffee brewing on a camping stove, Friluftsfrämjandet will meet party leaders and other decision-makers on different occasions to discuss their vision for outdoor recreation. 94 per cent of Swedes believe that outdoor recreation benefits health and well-being. How can outdoor recreation have as natural a place in societal development as it does in our hearts? How can more people be encouraged to be active in nature?
Four in five children get too little physical activity, and half of adults have dangerously poor fitness. The proportion of children spending time in nature every day has fallen from 80 to 50 per cent in 20 years, and we see a growing fear of nature. While the evidence for nature's health benefits has become robust, the management of our most valuable natural areas has been severely neglected following major funding cuts.
Investment in physical activity and accessible nature delivers very strong returns.
See you under the large tree, with the sea as a backdrop.

content.title: Data centres, the electricity grid and public benefit – how should Sweden prioritise when capacity is insufficient?
content.description: Data centre and AI infrastructure development is now moving faster than most other electricity-intensive parts of the economy. Projects enter planning processes early, with very large requests for power capacity and relatively short lead times.
content.extendedDescription:
Electricity grid capacity is already under strain in many parts of the country, and electricity demand is also rising as industry, transport, housing and essential services are electrified.

Meanwhile, the growing link between digital infrastructure and the energy system makes questions of security, preparedness and societal resilience increasingly important. Data centres are no longer solely about business policy or new facilities – they are also about control over data, AI capacity and energy supply.

When all of society's interests want to connect to the grid, but capacity is insufficient, who should set priorities, and on what grounds?

As a grid company, we see the development in real time: rapidly growing queues in which data centres account for a large share, changing customer profiles and rising expectations from both business and society. Grid companies neither can nor should take on the role of political 'prioritiser' between different societal needs. Where and how do politics enter the electricity system?

content.title: What happens if business gets to steer total defence planning?
content.description: Total defence involves everyone – not least business, which supplies most of the goods and services needed. But companies are often brought into total defence planning late. What happens if the perspective is reversed and companies' needs and solutions become the starting point instead?
content.extendedDescription:
The national adviser for stronger public-private cooperation in total defence is tasked with driving closer cooperation between the public sector and business. Could one approach be to reverse the perspective and start from companies' situations?

At the seminar, national adviser Charlotte Petri Gornitzka highlights several examples together with representatives of four companies:
- At the high-level Merkurius course, organised by the adviser together with ICA and others, companies' perspectives dominated the questions. What lessons were learned?
- Volvo does not wait for an invitation from the public sector, but invites others to total defence workshops centred on its own factories. What happens then?
- Tetra Pak actively participates in work to develop a standard for business preparedness. How can this work strengthen total defence?
- Heidelberg Materials produces cement – a potentially critical resource in wartime. How does the company view its role in Sweden's total defence?

content.title: AI, You & I: When AI Thinks Like Us, Who Shapes Intelligence and Human Identity?
content.description: Artificial intelligence is increasingly capable of reasoning, creating and making decisions. As AI systems shape information, institutions and economies, this raises crucial questions about human identity, agency and who controls the intelligence influencing societies and global governance.
content.extendedDescription:
Artificial intelligence is evolving from a tool into a collaborator capable of generating knowledge, influencing decisions and shaping social systems. As AI becomes embedded in institutions, economies and everyday life, it challenges long-held assumptions about human identity, agency and control over knowledge.
Engaging India @ Almedalen brings together leaders from Sweden & India to explore global challenges through dialogue between policy, industry and academia. The 2026 series examines artificial intelligence through the lens of identity, industry and planetary transition.
This seminar explores how AI may redefine what it means to be human while also reshaping global power structures. Who shapes the intelligence that will influence societies, democratic institutions and international relations? And how can societies ensure that the development of AI reflects shared human values?

content.title: Electricity preparedness in uncertain times – hydropower as a unique resource
content.description: Energy supply is a central part of total defence. Hydropower has unique capabilities for Sweden's electricity preparedness, but these risk being lost during environmental permitting. How do we ensure that hydropower's preparedness capabilities are developed rather than dismantled?
content.extendedDescription:
Europe's security situation has changed rapidly. Experience from Ukraine shows how vulnerable energy infrastructure is and how crucial robust electricity generation is to society's resilience.

Hydropower accounts for a substantial share of Sweden's electricity generation and has unique capabilities needed during severe disruptions and war. It is dispatchable, has large energy stores in reservoirs and is geographically distributed across the country, often near population centres. Hydropower's contribution to preparedness is often taken for granted and may be jeopardised during permit reviews.
Meanwhile, some preparedness capabilities have been designed out or forgotten because they have not been needed for a long time.

The seminar brings together energy companies, public agencies and political representatives to discuss hydropower's strategic importance for electricity preparedness and total defence. How can lost capabilities be restored, and how can we ensure important facilities are not eliminated during environmental reviews?

content.title: Unequal gynaecological cancer care – who takes responsibility for equal access to testing and treatment?
content.description: Gynaecological cancer affects 3000 women and causes around 1200 deaths annually. This overlooked cancer group receives limited research resources and has modest survival rates. Waiting times for diagnosis and treatment are often long, access to molecular testing is unequal and few patients participate in clinical trials, hampering progress.
content.extendedDescription:
Gynaecological cancer includes cancer of the ovaries, endometrium, cervix or vulva, with ovarian and endometrial cancer being the most common. Early detection is crucial to improving survival, but little progress has been made in the past decade. Treatment is mainly surgical, with limited access to precision medicines, although development is accelerating.
Waiting times for diagnosis and treatment vary greatly between regions. The proportion of patients meeting the time targets in standardised care pathways (SVF) is far below the goal. Access to molecular testing and clinical trials is also uneven. Few are offered trial participation, with major regional differences. Inequality is exacerbated by a lack of organisation of care into appropriate levels in some regions, affecting access to specialised care and expertise. Developments in precision medicine place new demands on healthcare, requiring well-developed testing to analyse tumours' genetic characteristics. This is crucial to providing the right treatment to the right patient, regardless of where they live.

content.title: How do we measure sustainable business beyond growth?
content.description: Our economic system still rewards what can be counted in money – not always what truly counts. As long as business success is measured in growth, both people and the planet risk becoming expendable resources. But what if growth is no longer the goal?
content.extendedDescription:
The seminar challenges the metrics guiding today's business decisions and the idea that more is always better. Starting from concepts such as degrowth, decoupling and true cost, we explore what happens when the economy must operate within planetary and social boundaries.

What happens if success is measured in impact or resilience rather than revenue? In actual benefit rather than volume? In lives saved, calories produced per unit of energy used, actual equality or perceived fairness – rather than growth?

What do new goals and KPIs look like in practice? Efficiency measures aligned with planetary boundaries, absolute resource limits following the logic of CSRD – or entirely new ways to measure value creation?

Are today's standardised ESRS sufficient, or are tailored measures needed for an economy that can no longer afford to grow at the expense of its own future?

This is a discussion for anyone who suspects that the sustainable transition is failing not for lack of ambition, but because we are still measuring the wrong things.

content.title: When children are victims of crime – how can their rights throughout the process be strengthened?
content.description: 57% of all children have experienced some form of violence. Yet society often fails to provide the right support in time. This makes child victims of crime one of our most vulnerable and overlooked groups. How can public agencies jointly create safer, more coherent systems for children affected by crime?
content.extendedDescription:
In Sweden, 57% of all children have experienced some form of violence while growing up. Society often fails to provide the right support in time. This makes child victims of crime one of our most vulnerable and also most overlooked groups. Yet public debate today tends to focus on gang crime and less on children who themselves experience crime.
Children exposed to violence encounter several parts of society – social services, police, prosecutors, healthcare and sometimes Barnahus centres. This seminar brings together Socialstyrelsen, Polismyndigheten, Åklagarmyndigheten and Barnafrid to discuss how children's rights can be strengthened throughout the process, from early detection, reporting and investigations to ongoing support.
Keeping the child at the centre, we highlight key challenges – such as parallel investigations, long waits, varying support measures and inadequate participation – and examine what these mean for the child.

content.title: When the tone becomes harsher – does democracy work in digital debate?
content.description: Digital debate has become harsher. Civil society employees now face personal attacks, threats and invasions of privacy in digital channels – often anonymous and without boundaries. What does this mean for the working environment, willingness to join the debate and, ultimately, democracy?
content.extendedDescription:
Digital debate has changed. In associations, trade unions, interest organisations and other parts of civil society, employees now face an increasingly harsh tone in digital channels: hostile language, personal attacks, invasions of privacy and daily life in which the boundary between work and private life is blurred. Sometimes this is anonymous, sometimes not. Sometimes there is an underlying agenda, sometimes not.

But what does this really mean for the working environment? For well-being? For the working environment? For willingness to keep participating in public debate? And what needs to be done so that those sustaining democratic debate can do their jobs without being worn down?

Join a discussion about democratic debate. Taking the working environment as our starting point, we highlight experiences of civil society employees working in digital channels every day, and of public figures encountering an increasingly harsh tone in emails, comment sections and social media.

content.title: What happens when municipal housing companies sell their homes?
content.description: When municipalities sell municipal housing, the housing market changes fundamentally. This often leads to higher rents, reduced tenant influence and greater insecurity. The municipality also loses its most important tool for influencing the housing market, including rents, housing availability and social sustainability.
content.extendedDescription: Parts of the municipal housing stock in Örebro, Gävle and Eskilstuna have been sold to private property companies in successive rounds. These sales have consistently prompted dissatisfaction and protests among affected tenants and Hyresgästföreningen. Hyresgästföreningen Region Aros-Gävle/ Mitt, with help from Mats Wingborg, has therefore produced the report 'vad händer när allmännyttan säljer sina bostäder?' (What happens when municipal housing companies sell their homes?), published on Bostad2030. It will be presented, followed by a panel discussion asking, for example: What happens to people's everyday lives – what kind of security is lost when municipal housing is sold? What happens to the municipality's responsibility and opportunities – are there situations where selling is actually defensible? And what does this mean for future housing policy – how can we meet housing needs without a strong municipal housing sector? What is needed to reverse the trend? What role should municipal housing play in future? You are welcome to come and share your opinion!

content.title: Following the money – what is banks' role in combating welfare crime?
content.description: The criminal economy turns over SEK 352 billion a year, and welfare crime is a growing part of it. Banks have unique insight into transactions, patterns and anomalies that can signal abuse of welfare systems early. What is banks' role in combating welfare crime?
content.extendedDescription:
Banks' role in combating welfare crime involves stopping the flows of the criminal economy. Their central position in the financial system allows banks to detect unusual transaction patterns, suspicious arrangements and structures linked to systematic abuse of welfare systems early – things that might otherwise remain invisible to individual public agencies.

However, effective work requires more than traditional regulatory compliance. As crime becomes more sophisticated, banks' role in prevention and detection grows. Realising this potential requires closer cooperation with the public sector, clear structures for information sharing and a shared understanding of how welfare crime is organised and financed. Technology, data analysis and shared risk assessments become central tools.

The panel discussion examines banks' societal role, obstacles in current regulations and how stronger cooperation can protect welfare systems.
content.subject: Economy

content.title: Climate adaptation and digital services – AI and data-driven decisions for a more resilient society
content.description: As extreme weather such as flooding, storms and drought increases, banks, insurers and property owners face growing climate risks. Digital solutions, data-driven decisions and AI can help predict, quantify and reduce risks, both physically and financially.
content.extendedDescription:
In a changing climate, we see more frequent and intense extreme weather events, such as torrential rain, flooding and wildfires, as well as long-term changes such as extended dry periods and rising sea levels. This creates growing climate risks for banks, insurers and property owners, at both asset and portfolio level.
At the same time, digital solutions, data analysis and AI create new opportunities to understand, anticipate and manage these risks. Combining data, climate scenarios and analysis can reveal, quantify and in some cases prevent risks, both physically and financially.
The discussion brings together perspectives on managing climate risks in a changing climate. It focuses on how data, experience and digital tools can support better-informed decisions and greater preparedness in banking, insurance and property, as well as municipal planning.

Help shape the discussion and join conversations at Omställningsarenan in Sweco's courtyard during Almedalsveckan!

Managing Director for Google Cloud Nordics

content.title: Quality, knowledge and greater well-being in nursing care through quality registries
content.description: Behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia (BPSD) reduce well-being and affect almost everyone with a cognitive disorder or dementia at some point during their illness. Can person-centred care interventions, multidisciplinary teamwork and a structured approach improve the person's well-being?
content.extendedDescription:
BPSD-registret is a national quality registry intended to ensure the quality of care for people with cognitive disorders or dementia.
Through person-centred care, BPSD-registret contributes to greater well-being and quality of life by reducing the person's behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia, BPSD.
Regular, ongoing recording allows results to be monitored at individual level and aggregated at unit, municipal, county and national level. Individual results are used to improve each person's well-being. Aggregated data are used in research and improvement work to ensure quality and develop care and services. BPSD-registret also contributes to better multidisciplinary teamwork and opportunities for learning and reflection, increasing knowledge and care quality.

Across Sweden, services in this field use BPSD-registret to improve both care quality and staff knowledge.
Come and visit us!

content.title: Culture – a key to innovation
content.description: Culture and creative skills play an increasingly important role in innovation and societal transformation. How does culture drive development, and how can cross-sector collaboration help address complex societal challenges and strengthen the sustainable, competitive societies of the future?
content.extendedDescription:
The discussion draws on Region Jönköpings län's regional development strategy, which highlights innovation, collaboration and sustainability as central to the county's development. Meanwhile, a clear shift is visible, not least within the EU, where culture is increasingly seen as an enabler of innovation, sustainable development and societal transformation. But what is needed to enable this, and is culture a key to innovation?
How can culture-driven societal development and creative approaches strengthen innovation capacity, create new partnerships and contribute to solutions to complex societal challenges? Perspectives from culture, business, the public sector and the European level inform a discussion on how cultural values, artistic processes and creative skills can contribute to future societal development. An opening presentation offers insight into Piteå Science Park's work on culture-driven societal development and its use of art and culture as tools for engagement, learning, innovation and systemic change.

content.title: How to design capacity charges that work
content.description: Capacity charges are intended to shift electricity use away from periods of heavy grid load, freeing up capacity and keeping costs down. But the current model is now being challenged politically. How can charges be designed to be effective, fair and understandable for customers?
content.extendedDescription:
Capacity charges are intended to shift electricity use away from periods when the grid is heavily loaded. The aim is to enable greater electrification without extensive grid expansion, thereby lowering the total cost for electricity customers. During the spring, the current design of the charges has been heavily criticised in public debate. Energy Minister Ebba Busch has therefore tasked Energimarknadsinspektionen with developing a new proposal.
Two Energiforsk projects have analysed how capacity tariffs can be designed. UniFlex has developed an hourly capacity charge based on forecasts, charged only when expected grid load is high. At other times the charge is zero, so it does not, for example, deter electric vehicle charging when electricity prices are low.
K-flex starts from the growing importance of demand flexibility and energy storage. Enabling customers to help limit the need for grid expansion requires economic incentives that are clear in both time and location, and tools to counter local overload.

content.title: Sweden is lagging behind: time to introduce advanced practice nurses throughout the care pathway
content.description: The WHO's 2025 report states that advanced practice nurses (AVS) are crucial to strengthening healthcare. The WHO urges all countries to introduce regulations enabling AVS to improve care quality and accessibility. Sweden is lagging behind in this area.
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden still lacks national regulation and lags behind many comparable countries. AVS roles are already established in Denmark, Norway and Iceland, with clear education and competence requirements aligned with international standards.

The 2020–2022 pandemic exposed significant shortcomings in Sweden, particularly in municipal healthcare. Several inquiries therefore recommend introducing AVS in municipal healthcare to strengthen medical expertise, improve staffing and skills provision, and ensure care at the right level. Specialist healthcare, which is becoming increasingly advanced, also has substantial needs for expanded expertise. AVS in surgical care have demonstrated good synergies and teamwork, as well as improved quality for patients. Nationella Vårdkompetensrådet also supports introducing AVS to improve continuity and expertise throughout the care pathway, benefiting patients, staff and society. Why, then, is Sweden taking so long?

content.title: The US has the billions, China the data – Can Small Giants save Swedish AI?
content.description: The US pours in endless venture capital and China has endless data. In Europe, we build regulations. Sweden will never win the AI war on the superpowers' terms. But what if our limitations are our greatest strength? How do we secure Swedish competitiveness by playing a completely different game?
content.extendedDescription:
Panel discussion, morning coffee & a classic Swedish breakfast sandwich ("frukostmacka").

While tech giants burn billions on supercomputers, AI is rewriting the rules of entrepreneurship. Today, a team of 1-3 people in Visby or Malmö, backed by AI agents, can do what used to take 500 employees in Silicon Valley.

We call them "Small Giants" – extremely capital-lean, resourceful companies that outmaneuver the giants through speed and creativity, rather than brute force.

We throw the old VC-hungry "unicorn" model in the trash to discuss how Swedish entrepreneurs can build global companies from day one.

In the panel we discuss: 
• Why Europe's AI strategy often misses the mark. 
• From Unicorn to Small Giant: Lowering the barrier to building global companies. 
• AI-native ways of working: How agents crush resource-rich competitors. 
• What Sweden's government and ecosystem must do now to accelerate these Small Giants.

content.title: With AI we can produce more than ever – but are we creating more value?
content.description: AI enables us to produce more than ever – but is real value increasing at the same pace? When output grows faster than judgement, quality, trust and confidence are at stake. What role does communication play, and what leadership is needed for AI to create business value rather than just more content?
content.extendedDescription:
More and more organisations are embedding AI in processes and daily work. But its effects become visible first in marketing and communications. Here, AI strategy is tested in real time and choices are exposed: what is automated, what requires human judgement and what actually creates value?

Despite high ambitions, many still see limited business impact. Have we become better at producing, but not at deciding what is good? And what happens to brands when everything can be generated but fewer people take responsibility for quality, relevance and trust? The discussion is not about AI as technology, but about what AI reveals about how we lead, prioritise and build our organisations. The focus shifts from what AI can do to what organisations can actually use, understand and evaluate.

A moderated panel discussion for marketing and communications directors, brand managers and leaders navigating the shift between technology, business and customer relationships.

content.title: Why should we protect children?
content.description: Increasingly young children are being recruited into criminal acts and serious violent offences. Debates and measures have focused on more police, more policing tools, harsher sentences and lowering the age for imprisonment. How can society build resilience beyond measures focused on sentencing?
content.extendedDescription: The discussion centres on young people's vulnerability. Meet researchers and practitioners discussing society's preventive work to create safe settings and counter exclusion, youth crime and recruitment into gangs. We ask researchers at Svenska Kriminalpolitiska laboratoriet about the effects of policy reforms, and researchers and practitioners how knowledge of successful collaboration and intervention models can be shared and used more widely. During the seminar, we will also consider the risks when researchers and practitioners feel political decisions conflict with science and proven experience. How do we promote safer environments for children and young people as part of crime prevention and enforcement? What new knowledge can strengthen society's preparedness, sustainability and resilience? And who needs access to it? What are the challenges when more actors and professions need to work together?

content.title: Why are companies overlooking one of the world's largest minority groups?
content.description: People with disabilities make up one of the world's largest minority groups, yet remain invisible in much business communication and strategy. How can business value, representation and inclusion create benefits for both society and business?
content.extendedDescription:
People with disabilities make up one of the world's largest minority groups. Around 16 per cent of the global population lives with some form of disability, and the group represents significant economic and social influence. Globally, its combined disposable income is estimated at almost USD 2 trillion annually. Yet people with disabilities remain heavily underrepresented in corporate strategies, marketing and communications.

In Sweden, around 12 per cent of the working-age population has a disability, while the employment rate is considerably lower among people with reduced work capacity.

During the seminar, American researcher Edward Timke presents current research on disability in communication and visibility in society. This is followed by a discussion about business value, inclusion, representation and how companies and society can together contribute to real change.

content.title: Information preparedness and communication in crisis and war
content.description: Who ensures communication and information in crisis and war? How do essential societal actors reach people when it matters most? How does the emergency alert chain work, and who picks up on what is happening? What can we expect in terms of psychological influence operations?
content.extendedDescription:
Communication is the most important thing under challenging conditions. In this session, essential societal actors discuss systematic security work, information preparedness and communication in crisis and war.

In an era marked by hybrid influence operations, cyber threats and uncertainty in our neighbourhood, what international developments do security companies need to prepare for to ensure security provision for companies and critical services?

SVT's total defence mission is to ensure the public can access news, public information and important announcements in everyday life, during crises, heightened alert and war. They share experiences of building resilience, securing information provision and strengthening public preparedness.

SOS Alarm discusses how the emergency alert chain works, what can go wrong and experiences from Ukraine.

content.title: The state, capital or citizens – who should fund civil society?
content.description: In public debate, civil society often appears dependent on public grants. But most resources come from the public and other private actors. What role should civil society play, and how should funding responsibility be shared between citizens, capital and the public sector?
content.extendedDescription:
A broad, independent civil society is a prerequisite for democracy, openness and free debate. It provides a platform for people to engage, take a stand or contribute. But who should help fund non-profit organisations without limiting their independence, while enabling stable, long-term operations?

Civil society encompasses everything from new initiatives and networks to faith communities, popular movements and associations with histories spanning centuries. Millions of Swedes volunteer here every week, supported by a few hundred thousand employees. So how should this diverse landscape of organisations fund itself without jeopardising independence? Does the method matter? Do the state and municipalities have a responsibility, or should citizens fund civil society? What should companies' role be? A discussion based on the report 'Staten, kapitalet och medborgaren – vem finansierar civilsamhället?' (The state, capital and citizens – who funds civil society?).
content.subject: Democracy
speakerTitles: Head of Ideas and Legal Counsel
Acting Secretary General and Chief of Staff

content.title: Physiological optimisation – how does the human body cope with war?
content.description: How do we strengthen human capabilities in extreme, high-risk environments? Cold, sleep deprivation and stress strain the body and mind. With the right knowledge, we can reduce injuries, strengthen resilience and create sustainable operational capability without compromising long-term health or the return to civilian life.
content.extendedDescription:
This seminar brings together perspectives from research, defence and industry to examine human capabilities and vulnerabilities in war and serious crises. How are performance, decision-making and recovery affected when people operate in environments involving extreme cold, heavy physical demands, infection risks, advanced technical systems and repeated traumatic events?
The discussion takes a holistic view of the human dimension, from physiological and cognitive limitations to immune function and mental health over time. Particular attention is given to prevention and support for PTSD and increased suicide risk following deployment.

The seminar highlights how knowledge can be applied in practice: in requirements profiles, training, equipment and operational approaches, as well as long-term support before, during and after service. A central question is how responsibility can be shared between the state, employers and business to ensure that people working in extreme environments receive appropriate protection, support and follow-up.
content.subject: Research
speakerTitles: Orthopaedic Surgeon, Aviation and Diving Physician, Doctor of Aviation Medicine, Medical Adviser

content.title: Gaza and Sweden's responsibility
content.description: During the genocide in Gaza, society has been shattered, and the ongoing humanitarian catastrophe will have consequences for generations. Sweden has a responsibility. What should the government do, and what opportunities do we have to influence events? What is the situation in Gaza, and what efforts are being made on the ground?
content.extendedDescription:
Israel's attacks have devastated homes, hospitals, roads, farmland and public infrastructure in Gaza. The population lacks access to basic necessities, and displacement, indiscriminate killing and the obstruction of humanitarian aid continue despite the ceasefire agreement.

Israel's actions and the international community's inability to stop the genocide have also shaken the international legal order. The UN Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide obliges states to prevent and punish acts of genocide. States are also required to act to end the unlawful situation created by Israel's occupation.

The Swedish government has faced massive criticism from human rights organisations and broad public opinion demanding effective political, economic and diplomatic measures from Sweden. What should the government do, and what opportunities do we have to influence events? What is the situation in Gaza now, and what efforts are being made on the ground to alleviate suffering?
content.subject: International affairs
speakerTitles: Head of Policy and Advocacy Work, with Particular Responsibility for Armed Conflict and Human Rights Issues

content.title: AI, Talent and Innovation: Can Sweden stay competitive without India?
content.description: As AI transforms the global economy, countries are competing for talent, innovation and technological leadership at an unprecedented scale. For Sweden, this raises new questions about how international partnerships will shape future competitiveness — and what role India could play.
content.extendedDescription:
AI is rapidly reshaping economies, industries and global power structures. As competition for talent, technology and innovation accelerates, countries like Sweden — with strong research and innovation ecosystems — face growing pressure to strengthen their international position.

At the same time, India is emerging as a global AI powerhouse through major investments in digital infrastructure, entrepreneurship, research and technology talent. This creates new opportunities — but also strategic questions — for countries seeking to remain competitive.

Following recent initiatives launched during the Indian Prime Minister’s visit to Gothenburg, this panel explores how collaboration between Sweden and India could contribute to future research, innovation and industrial development.

The discussion will examine opportunities in research collaboration, talent exchange and industrial innovation — and how Sweden should position itself in a rapidly changing global AI landscape.

content.title: The lottery for people with lung disease – which postcode wins access to adequate care and new technology?
content.description: COPD (chronic obstructive pulmonary disease) is a stigmatised condition affecting hundreds of thousands of Swedes. Despite new medical innovations, access to these technologies varies widely. Standardised care pathways ensuring equitable, evidence-based care are lacking.
content.extendedDescription:
COPD (chronic obstructive pulmonary disease) is a stigmatised condition affecting hundreds of thousands of Swedes. Although new medical innovations improve quality of life and reduce patients' need for healthcare visits, access to these technologies varies considerably across our 21 regions. At the same time, standardised care pathways are lacking, despite being an important component in ensuring equitable, evidence-based care for people living with COPD, regardless of where in the country they live. This challenge requires strategic collaboration and fresh thinking.

How can we ensure that everyone living with lung disease, regardless of background or place of residence, has equitable access to the best possible treatment?

During the debate, we bring together healthcare decision-makers and stakeholders, politicians and companies to highlight challenges and opportunities associated with introducing innovative technology and national care pathways in COPD care.

content.title: What can we learn from Ukraine for our own resilience and societal development?
content.description: During the ongoing war, Ukraine has demonstrated an impressive ability to maintain essential services, rebuild what has been destroyed and develop new innovations. Its experiences cover both protecting essential infrastructure and new material flows. What can we learn from its agility?
content.extendedDescription:
How do our cities function when the power fails, water runs out and roads are clogged with abandoned cars? Sweden can learn important lessons from Ukraine, which has increased its resilience and preparedness despite ongoing war. This involves expertise in rebuilding and renewal, but also unleashing and harnessing people's capacity to innovate. Placemaking in cities and parks has proved highly important for residents' mental strength and adaptability. What can we achieve by acting on these lessons? Which solutions for energy, mobility and material flows are relevant? What could work in a Swedish context?
Meet our panel with extensive experience from Ukraine.

content.title: When AI determines the future, how does Sweden take the lead?
content.description: Skills, infrastructure and green energy give Sweden a strong starting point in AI. A well-balanced regulatory framework for the AI market can become a competitive advantage, but requires wider adoption and greater investment. What is needed for Sweden to move from cautious user to leading AI nation?
content.extendedDescription:
AI, data, critical digital infrastructure and cybersecurity have become strategic resources, not only for innovation and growth but also for national security, sovereignty and resilience.

Sweden has strong digital foundations and a national AI strategy aiming to become one of the world's top 10 AI countries and the world leader in using AI in public administration. Yet EY's global AI Sentiment Index 2026 shows Sweden lagging behind: only 37 per cent of Swedes feel comfortable with AI, compared with 49 per cent globally, only 15% use AI daily at work and 6 in 10 lack AI training.
The gap is therefore less about technology and more about trust, skills and practical application in business, politics, the public sector and academia.

During the seminar, we discuss how Sweden can strengthen its competitiveness and international position through responsible governance, broad skills development and safe, accelerated AI adoption.
content.subject: Digitalisation
