content.title: Many funding calls – but does the system fit together? Funding for a sustainable built environment
content.description: Municipalities and regions face major societal challenges, but the funding landscape is often complex and fragmented. How can EU programmes, national investments and regional initiatives work together more effectively to drive real transformation in cities and regions?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden has a strong innovation and funding system for sustainable societal development, but the system is also divided among many actors, programmes and funding calls. This creates opportunities, but also challenges for municipalities and regions needing to work over the long term on climate transition, digitalisation, housing provision, infrastructure and attractive living environments.

As a new EU programming period takes shape and national innovation initiatives develop, there is an important opportunity to discuss making funding more coherent. How can EU programmes, government agencies, regional initiatives and strategic innovation programmes pull in the same direction?

The event is a panel discussion with representatives from a municipality, national agencies and innovation programmes. It focuses on how research, development and innovation funding can be better coordinated and provide stronger conditions for real transformation in Sweden's cities and regions.
content.subject: Sustainability
speakerTitles: Chair of Rådet för levande städer
Innovation Strategist for Environment and Urban Planning
Director of Environment and Urban Development

content.title: Exercise on prescription – a natural part of today's prostate cancer treatment and rehabilitation?
content.description: Receiving a prostate cancer diagnosis and undergoing treatment often affect both the body and energy levels. Particularly during hormone therapy, side effects such as reduced muscle mass, increased body fat, fatigue and osteoporosis can make people feel weaker over time. Regular exercise makes a difference.
content.extendedDescription:
Regular physical activity can help counteract adverse effects of prostate cancer treatment and contribute to better quality of life.

Research and healthcare rehabilitation recommendations indicate that exercise is not merely 'good to do' – it can actively contribute to recovery. A combination of aerobic and strength training is often particularly valuable for maintaining strength, balance and endurance. For many, a simple start may be enough: regular walks, lighter strength exercises at home and gradually increasing intensity.

In this discussion, we explore examples where exercise has made a major difference to individual patients in concrete projects in which Prostatacancerförbundet has made high-intensity training available to men undergoing prostate cancer treatment in region Skåne. Meanwhile, exciting research into the subject is under way at Gymnastik och idrottshögskolan, GIH, in Stockholm.

You can stay after the event to speak with the participants.

speakerTitles: Senior Lecturer in Sports Science, Specialising in Exercise Science
Medical Director, PhD, Senior Consultant Physician

content.title: From vision to reality – how do we make animal-free research the norm?
content.description: Increasing numbers of researchers, public agencies and societal actors express a desire to reduce and ultimately replace the use of animals in research. Yet millions of animals are still used globally in biomedical research every year.
content.extendedDescription:
The event is a panel debate bringing together researchers and other actors in the research system to discuss how to accelerate the transition to animal-free research methods. The discussion starts with how the vision of animal-free research can be put into practice and what is needed for animal-free methods to become the norm more widely.

The panel will highlight both opportunities and obstacles. Despite rapid development of new methods, such as advanced cell models, organ-on-chip technology and AI-based models, large numbers of laboratory animals are still used in research. Why is the transition so slow? Which structures in the research system need to change? And how can researchers, funders, public agencies and other actors work together to accelerate progress?

The panel will discuss research culture, funding, validation and implementation of new methods, and the role politics and society can play in driving change.

content.title: How do we accelerate the circular transition? Business solutions for a sustainable future
content.description: Sweden has ambitious climate and environmental goals. National targets and EU requirements are driving a green transition in which waste is increasingly seen as a resource. Meanwhile, business is now being given greater responsibility for efficient recycling and circular material flows.
content.extendedDescription:
The government has recently reformed waste legislation to create better conditions for recycling. But legislation on paper is one thing; functioning systems in practice are another. How does this affect companies' opportunities to invest and develop new circular solutions? And which parts of the regulatory framework need further simplification to achieve ambitious climate and environmental goals?

Join a seminar presenting concrete examples of circular solutions that work in practice. We discuss opportunities and ways to strengthen cooperation throughout the value chain, and address challenges still slowing the transition.

What is needed here and now to remove further barriers, create functioning markets for recycled materials and meet Sweden's commitments? Meet representatives of politics, public agencies and business for a discussion about a long-term framework and how to achieve a circular economy that delivers both climate benefits and competitiveness.
content.subject: Sustainability
speakerTitles: feedstock trader & analyst in HVO value chain

content.title: Orphan medicines in the election – from promises to solutions
content.description: Inadequate access to orphan medicines has serious consequences for patients with rare conditions. Ahead of the election, the question comes to a head: how can political ambitions become concrete reforms that ensure equitable care and strengthen Sweden as a research nation?
content.extendedDescription:
Access to orphan medicines is central, often life-changing, for people with rare conditions. During the spring, debate about access to orphan medicines and Sweden's role as a research nation has intensified. New US pharmaceutical policy is changing the landscape, access to orphan medicines remains low by international standards, and Sweden faces challenges in life science.

The election takes place in September. Voters often rank healthcare among the most important political issues. Kommissionen för innovativa särläkemedel is now taking a new approach, launching its own election manifesto with reform proposals for the coming electoral term.

How can the trend be reversed? What changes are needed in the short and long term? And what are politicians prepared to do? Patients, relatives, experts and business representatives meet politicians in one of Almedalen's most important discussions.

content.title: Energy production and defence – Gotland leads the way
content.description: Many societal interests collide on Gotland. A strong defence is needed for obvious reasons, while energy supplies must function both under normal conditions and during heightened alert. Region Gotland presents its roadmap for how the island can operate in island mode if cut off.
content.extendedDescription:
Gotland has four major national interests.
1. Försvarsmakten has re-established its presence and is expected to double its operations. 2. Heidelberg Materials in Slite will soon be the country's only cement production site. 3. Heidelberg must become fossil-free through a CCS facility, as its products form part of many industries' value chains. 4. The ferry services, procured by the state, must also become fossil-free.

All four interests are energy-intensive.

Meanwhile, Försvarsmakten is now blocking almost all new local energy production, even though total defence requires substantial local electricity and fuel supplies to remain operational over time.

Region Gotland presents its roadmap for reconciling energy production and defence. Länsstyrelsen presents the FRAMAT project, which works on coexistence. National and international energy experts comment. Political representatives reflect on how the next government needs to act to resolve this.

content.title: Equitable menopause care: why do not all women receive the treatment they need?
content.description: Access to menopause care and treatment in Sweden is currently unequal. Differences in access to gynaecologists, primary care knowledge and medicines mean many women do not receive the care they need, with consequences for both health and working life.
content.extendedDescription:
Although menopause affects a large part of the population, care is marked by significant inequalities. Access to specialist expertise varies between regions, and primary care knowledge is uneven, meaning many women do not receive the right diagnosis or treatment in time. The consequences are extensive. Women risk poorer quality of life, increased sickness absence and reduced work capacity. Particularly vulnerable groups, such as women with neurodevelopmental disabilities, are more likely to experience severe symptoms and inadequate support. Meanwhile, recurring shortages of important medicines further impede equitable treatment.
What role can national policy play in reducing these differences? How can governance, follow-up and medicines supply be developed to ensure all women have access to adequate care? Join medical experts and decision-makers for a discussion about the path towards more equitable menopause care.

content.title: Endless possibilities for future infrastructure – how can the sector step up?
content.description: Sweden has a great need for resilient infrastructure. It needs to be built promptly, sustainably and cost-effectively. If technology, methods and expertise are available, how can the sector cooperate to deliver value faster? Could openness, considered risk-taking and courage be the answer?
content.extendedDescription:
There are major opportunities to build infrastructure in modern ways. Technology has advanced rapidly, new methods are available and with them comes the opportunity to build infrastructure more cheaply, quickly and resiliently. Yet despite rapid technological development, our sector has not managed to implement it at the pace society needs. We have a chance to catch up, eliminate the maintenance backlog, increase preparedness and build a sustainable society. Today, outdated regulations and a lack of broad agreements stand in the way. We risk locking ourselves into old technology. Collaboration and an innovative approach now offer an opportunity to get more infrastructure for the money. So what do we need to do?
In this discussion, decision-makers from public agencies and business meet to consider how we can deliver future infrastructure sooner.

Help shape the discussion at Omställningsarenan in Sweco's courtyard during Almedalsveckan!

Deputy CEO of Skanska Sverige, Civil Engineering Business Stream

content.title: Insider threat prevention and background checks against organised crime
content.description: Insider threats and improper influence are societal problems with serious consequences and links to organised crime. They are spreading and infiltrating companies. At a time when confidence matters more than ever, we want a society built on trust. How can we strengthen our organisations?
content.extendedDescription:
This seminar focuses on one of organisations' most underestimated risks: threats arising from within, and how work to create safer workplaces becomes a crucial part of the solution.

The human factor is both one of an organisation's greatest vulnerabilities and its greatest assets. Managing this complexity requires more than checks, policies and technical safeguards: it takes conscious leadership, an open culture and the right knowledge.

Internal culture – security culture – is increasingly important for strengthening protection against criminal infiltration. Employers face difficult trade-offs: where is the boundary between security, privacy and social responsibility?

In this session, experts discuss identity and background checks, risk assessment and leadership to develop safe workplaces.

SäkerhetsArenan is organised by SäkerhetsBranschen, Stöldskyddsföreningen, Brandskyddsföreningen, Tryggare Sverige, Säkerhetsföretagen, Företagsuniversitetet and SOFF.

content.title: How can educational research become relevant and accessible in schools and teacher education?
content.description: Relevant, accessible research is needed for education to rest on a scientific foundation. One approach is practice-based research in Sweden. Yet challenges remain in ensuring high scientific quality, relevance and accessibility in schools and teacher education programmes.
content.extendedDescription:
The seminar presents a search engine for educational research developed within ULF (Utbildning, Lärande, Forskning). It enables users to search, filter and find research according to their needs, helping improve access to educational research for schools and teacher education programmes. It brings together around 600 publications, approximately 150 of them peer-reviewed, and will be connected to DiVA, providing access to a much larger research base.

The national ULF agreement creates long-term conditions for practice-based research through collaboration between school authorities and higher education institutions. Shared structures and approaches develop knowledge of high relevance and quality for schools' and teacher education programmes' needs.

The seminar addresses scientific quality and relevance, and how the search engine can contribute to greater access to research and increased engagement in educational research.

content.title: Leadership on the Front Line – Governing a Region Under War
content.description: How do you lead a region on the front line, partly occupied, under constant attack and hosting Europe’s largest nuclear power plant? How do civilian and military leaders cooperate to protect people, services, and stability in such conditions?
content.extendedDescription:
What does it mean to lead a region under constant threat, where parts of the territory are occupied, where civilians live under repeated attacks, and where Europe’s largest nuclear power plant remains at the center of global security concerns?
In this session, the regional leader of Zaporizhzhia will share first-hand insights into governing under wartime conditions. The discussion will address the challenges of maintaining public services, supporting civilians, and making critical decisions while operating close to an active front line.
The conversation will also include military representatives responsible for defending the region. Together, we will explore how civilian leadership and military command work in parallel, how responsibilities are coordinated, and what this cooperation looks like in practice.
This session offers a unique perspective on resilience, crisis leadership, and the reality of managing a European region in the midst of war.
There will be much room for questions.

content.title: Strengthen language and communication in the workplace
content.description: Communication has always been a workplace challenge. This is even clearer now that more people in Sweden's labour market have Swedish neither as their first nor strongest language. Language is a working-environment issue. How is your workplace doing? How could it do better?
content.extendedDescription:
Language and communication are fundamental to a healthy workplace. Language is the key to individual participation and development. Effective communication is essential for an efficient, safe and inclusive workplace. Language support and development therefore need to be an integral part of working-environment efforts.

When employees lack the necessary language skills, insecurity, misunderstandings and ultimately exclusion from working life can result. This makes language both a working-environment issue and, ultimately, a public health issue.

How can we promote workplaces that develop language skills, where language and communication are a shared concern at individual, group and organisational level? This is one of the most important societal issues of our time and the future.

content.title: From skills shortages to competitiveness – how do we secure the future?
content.description: Sweden's technology industry is changing rapidly, with skills determining innovation, growth and global competitiveness. When needs grow faster than the supply of suitable skills, recruitment is not enough. We also need to improve how we educate, attract, develop and retain people.
content.extendedDescription:
At a breakfast panel, Rejlers and Siemens Energy bring together perspectives from Östergötland, a region with strong roots in technology-based industry, rapid growth and increasing skills needs, particularly in STEM. Future jobs exist, but where are the people? Place also matters increasingly: what makes people move here, stay and build their lives here?

Siemens Energy, this year's recipient of Industrins jämställdhetspris, operates in a buoyant international market and needs to recruit 1 000 people over the next few years. With around 600 employees in R&D alone, the question is: how can momentum be maintained?

Rejlers contributes the consulting sector's perspective on developing technical expertise and matching it to industry's needs. Linköpings kommun, Teknikföretagen, Linköpings universitet and Future Place Leadership address business establishments, education, skills provision and what makes people choose a place.

The focus is on moving from skills shortages to long-term competitiveness outside metropolitan regions.

content.title: How do we develop our environments without losing architectural and cultural heritage values?
content.description: Visby and the visible and hidden layers of its cultural environment. How is a city shaped by its history, and how does each generation rewrite it? As Swedish city centres change, we face the same question: how do we develop our shared environments without losing the values that make them significant?
content.extendedDescription:
Visby's squares and public spaces contain both visible and hidden layers of stories. During this guided city walk, organised by Gotlands Museum and Tengbom, we explore how the city's cultural environment has changed over the centuries and how different generations have left their mark on urban space.

Among our stops is Donners plats, where we discuss how historical traces have developed, been reinterpreted and sometimes replaced as new needs and functions emerged. Change and additions to the urban environment are not new phenomena, but a process that has continued from the Middle Ages to today.

Through conversations while walking, we explore how cultural environments can remain vibrant and relevant while preserving their historic values. The walk invites reflection on how we understand, use and develop our shared environments, and which stories we choose to pass on to the future.

content.title: Students as total defence innovators – education's role in driving innovation in total defence
content.description: In a more serious security situation, Sweden needs more innovators for total defence. How can higher education institutions and students contribute expertise, ideas and prototypes that complement industry and total defence? Which models work, and how can they spread between institutions and regions?
content.extendedDescription:
13:00-13:15 Introduction to the event – Anna Nyman, MCF, and Vice-Chancellor Emeritus Johan Schnürer, Chair of the CTF Steering Group.

A moderated discussion in which Linköpings universitet demonstrates how students make concrete contributions to total defence innovation. The starting point is the InDefense pilot project, in which students from several project courses worked on real challenges from Flygvapnets Experimentkontor in autumn 2025, together with FHS, Försvarsmakten and LiU Innovation. The results included prototypes demonstrated at a military exercise, two continuing degree projects and a project progressing towards company formation.

We also look ahead to Pilot 2 in autumn 2026, with more courses, broader regional involvement, a wider range of needs owners including both civilian and military actors, and a permanent interdisciplinary course from autumn 2027. The goal is a model that can spread to higher education institutions nationwide. The panel discusses what is needed for student innovation to deliver benefits: real challenges, integration into existing courses and the right conditions.
content.subject: Research
speakerTitles: Strategic Coordinator Innovation for Civil Defence

content.title: Who staffs Sweden's security services? Skills provision, wage formation and the state's responsibility as an employer
content.description: Sweden is strengthening its defences, but skills provision risks becoming the major bottleneck. How can the state recruit, develop and retain staff in the police, armed forces, customs and coast guard when competition for workers increases and security requirements tighten?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden is strengthening its defence, expanding the police and placing higher demands on agencies responsible for border protection and preparedness. Yet many organisations report difficulties recruiting, developing and retaining the right expertise. In professions where skills develop through education, experience and long-term knowledge transfer, staff shortages can directly affect society's security and resilience.

The discussion starts from how the state can secure long-term staffing and skills in the police, armed forces, customs and coast guard. We discuss the challenges, how state employer policy affects the ability to attract and retain qualified staff, and the role of wage formation, working conditions and career paths in operational capability.

The seminar is a panel discussion with representatives from politics, research and the professions concerned.

content.title: A digital twin of yourself: the foundation for a new health ecosystem
content.description: What would it be like to have access to all accumulated knowledge about the human body in a way that is relevant to you and your health right now? This is being developed through a so-called digital twin. How can it replace animal experiments and make society as a whole healthier?
content.extendedDescription:
Researchers at Linköpings universitet have developed a new, globally unique technology: a digital twin of the human body. It can compile all conceivable knowledge both about you specifically and about human health in general. Such knowledge can come from clinical trials, cell experiments, activity trackers, online forums and more. This twin can be used to replace animal experiments. It can also be used by various societal actors, such as the food industry, schools, sports clubs, healthcare, elderly care and occupational health services.
These new possibilities underpin a new excellence cluster, M4-HEALTH, comprising researchers from 14 universities and higher education institutions and supported by 100+ companies, public agencies, associations and others. At this event, you will hear from some of these actors and learn more about how to obtain your own twin, and how it can help move both your life and society as a whole in a healthier direction.

content.title: Does Swedish politics need more evidence?
content.description: Many knowledge organisations feel that the evidence they produce does not sufficiently inform decision-making in their fields. What is evidence, how does it relate to politics, and what does bringing evidence into political organisations entail?
content.extendedDescription:
Over an afternoon (14.00-16.00), we will examine the concept of evidence in relation to decision-making, governance and implementation in Swedish politics. The two-hour discussion is divided into three parts, with plenty of time for questions and networking between them. The aim is a nuanced dialogue about how more knowledge-driven decision-making can contribute to more precisely targeted, legally sound and effective policy interventions.

In this first discussion, the heads of the EBA and Delmi secretariats meet an investigative journalist to discuss what bringing evidence into political organisations means, why it matters (if it matters), what happens when political decisions are not based on research, the role of the media and how knowledge organisations can communicate knowledge and make it heard. The discussion draws on development aid and migration policy.

content.title: How can we stop children being recruited into gangs?
content.description: 93% of the children were already known to public services – how do we stop gang recruitment? How can society prevent children and young people from being exploited and recruited by criminal networks, and how can early intervention and stronger collaboration bring about real change?
content.extendedDescription:
93% of the children were known to the police, social services or schools before they were recruited.
How can society stop young people being recruited into criminal networks?

The seminar brings together police, civil society and other key actors to discuss how we can jointly prevent children and young people from being drawn into gang crime. Statistics show that 93% of children recruited into gangs were already known to public services, and that 80% still live at home and are recruited in their local area. The risk factors are therefore well known, as is much of the knowledge required – but how do we turn it into early, targeted interventions?
The seminar examines how adults can work more preventively, how collaboration between different actors can be strengthened and how we can create more alternatives for young people at risk. What are we still missing? And how can we start seeing early intervention as an investment in children's futures, instead of bearing the much greater costs when things have already gone too far?

content.title: ADHD costs society billions – how do we enable functioning everyday lives, work and quality of life?
content.description: ADHD diagnoses are rising rapidly in Sweden, while many families feel support arrives late. Research and public agencies highlight systemic shortcomings. What drives this development, where do gaps arise, and how can support work earlier and better in practice?
content.extendedDescription:
ADHD diagnoses are rising rapidly in Sweden, particularly among children and young people. Meanwhile, healthcare, schools and families describe a system where support often arrives late and many needs are only identified once problems have become extensive.

The seminar focuses particularly on three areas:
• research and systems perspectives
• schools and early intervention
• women and ADHD

Research from Karolinska Institutet points to a need to shift the focus from diagnosis to functioning and earlier support. Meanwhile, Socialstyrelsen highlights significant shortcomings and variations in care.

The discussion examines why diagnoses are increasing, the gaps between research, schools, healthcare and everyday life, and the consequences of late interventions, from schooling to working life.

The seminar is a moderated panel discussion bringing together perspectives from research, healthcare, schools, working life and users. The focus is on solutions, concrete experiences and changes needed to make everyday life work better in practice.

No preparation is required.

content.title: Ethics is practice – when technology develops faster than reflection
content.description: Technology is never neutral. AI systems are shaped by people's priorities, blind spots and worldviews. How can we use design to make ethical questions visible and create organisations and decisions where ethics is more than a policy on paper – something actually practised?
content.extendedDescription:
Technology is often developed without a holistic view of how the systems around us affect people socially, organisationally and democratically. What future are we actually building? What do we want to preserve, strengthen or avoid? How do we ensure technological development leads to societies people actually want to live in?

ETHICS IS PRACTICE is a workshop on how AI and digitalisation affect people's judgement, relationships and decisions. We explore why ethics must become part of practice, not just policy documents.

Through reflection, concrete examples and shared exercises using Ethical Impact Canvas, we explore how organisations, designers, decision-makers and the public sector can work more consciously with perspectives, inclusion and human consequences when developing technology and services.

The aim is not consensus. It is to create a safe space for new perspectives, inspiration and practical knowledge.

content.title: Research and infrastructure for security in northern Sweden
content.description: Northern Sweden is gaining strategic importance for energy, raw materials and security. This requires strong total defence, with research, innovation and skills strengthening societal resilience. The region's unique environments also make it an important testbed for new technology.
content.extendedDescription:
Northern Sweden has growing strategic importance for energy, raw materials, the climate transition and security. This places greater demands on robust total defence, with knowledge, innovation and societal resilience as important components.

Research helps us understand and address complex threats, from cyberattacks to supply-chain disruptions. Research infrastructure also serves as test environments where new solutions can be developed and tested under realistic conditions. Northern Sweden's unique circumstances make the region an important testbed.

Universities play a central role by educating skilled people, conducting relevant research and fostering collaboration between academia, business and public actors. Investment in research and infrastructure therefore strengthens not just the region, but Sweden's total defence and resilience as a whole. The seminar examines how these elements can develop together.

content.title: Strengthen language and communication in the workplace
content.description: Communication has always been a workplace challenge. This is even clearer now that more people in Sweden's labour market have Swedish neither as their first nor strongest language. Language is a working-environment issue. How is your workplace doing? How could it do better?
content.extendedDescription:
Language and communication are fundamental to a healthy workplace. Language is the key to individual participation and development. Effective communication is essential for an efficient, safe and inclusive workplace. Language support and development therefore need to be an integral part of working-environment efforts.

When employees lack the necessary language skills, insecurity, misunderstandings and ultimately exclusion from working life can result. This makes language both a working-environment issue and, ultimately, a public health issue.

How can we promote workplaces that develop language skills, where language and communication are a shared concern at individual, group and organisational level? This is one of the most important societal issues of our time and the future.

Tip! This session is a walk & talk. (We wait for participants at the meeting point for 15 minutes.) We walk together and explore how to strengthen language and communication at your workplace.

content.title: Sällsynta Almedalen – voices on living with rare conditions
content.description: In Sweden, 500 000 people live with rare conditions. What do their everyday lives, joys and sorrows look like, what challenges exist in healthcare and society, and why does the 'rare' matter? What do politicians say about rare conditions?

Perhaps Almedalen's most important discussion? Rare voices will be heard at an open event celebrating the very idea of Almedalen's democratic arena. Come and listen, ask questions and learn more. We will also remember all those with rare conditions who are no longer with us. For many reasons, this could be Almedalsveckan's most important discussion, and it is open to everyone.

content.title: A holistic health ecosystem through digital twins – a digital copy of yourself
content.description: What if you had a digital twin of yourself that could help you understand how to optimise exercise, diet and treatment? What if all societal actors used this twin and worked together to move society as a whole in a healthier direction?
content.extendedDescription:
25 years of research at Linköpings universitet have produced a new, globally unique technology: a digital twin of the human body. It looks like you on the outside and can simulate and show what happens inside your body when you do different things, such as exercising, eating or taking medicine. If you become ill, you can ask your twin what has happened and what you can do. You can connect with other people and life stories similar to yours and see what they did to improve. These stories also come with explanatory models of why they improved.
This globally unique technology underpins a new excellence cluster, M4-HEALTH, a new model for health. M4-HEALTH comprises researchers from 14 Swedish universities and higher education institutions, is supported by 100+ companies and involves public agencies, voluntary organisations and others. You will hear about this technology and how it can affect research, the food industry, healthcare providers, occupational health, elderly care and more.

content.title: Changes unseen in a hundred years – China, Russia and the new aid landscape
content.description: As Western donors withdraw, they create a vacuum that authoritarian actors quickly fill. Both China and Russia are expanding their presence as global development actors. What roles can and should Sweden and the EU play in a more fragmented development landscape?
content.extendedDescription:
China's global influence is increasing while Western aid actors cut their assistance. Like other aid actors, China is keen to support initiatives aligned with its own priorities and interests. Meanwhile, Russian actors have established themselves as key partners in several African countries through a transactional strategy combining military services, access to natural resources and political support. This model differs clearly from traditional Western aid, which is often linked to democracy, institutional development and long-term societal goals.

Join a discussion about what China's and Russia's global ambitions and influence mean for Western and Swedish aid, and for attitudes and values in recipient countries in areas such as gender equality, sustainable development, democracy and human rights.

content.title: How will Sweden cope with a crisis when our own medical technology is not even used in healthcare today?
content.description: Sweden has no shortage of medical technology solutions – quite the opposite. But too many remain pilot projects or never reach widespread use in healthcare. This is an everyday problem. In a crisis, it becomes a risk.
content.extendedDescription:
Meanwhile, we talk increasingly about preparedness, robustness and resilience. But preparedness is not built during a crisis; it is built on what already works. If we cannot implement and scale medical technology in peacetime, how will we do so when it really matters?

What political decisions are needed to change this, and who takes responsibility? Medtech4Health invites you to a panel discussion about the concrete steps Sweden needs to move from innovation to use, strengthening healthcare, preparedness and competitiveness.

The discussion draws on Medtech4Health's election platform and focuses on:
- What prevents implementation and scaling today
- How responsibility, funding and regulations can work together better
- What is needed to strengthen healthcare's ability to implement change
- How medical technology can become an integral part of Sweden

The seminar brings together political representatives and key actors from healthcare, business and academia for a pointed discussion about the way forward.

content.title: Is public transport ready for self-driving vehicles, and what role should it play in their development?
content.description: Autonomous transport is entering real traffic. The question is not whether it is coming, but who shapes it. Shared travel will be crucial to public benefit. Integration into public transport is key. What initiatives do public transport actors need to take to steer development?
content.extendedDescription:
Public transport faces major challenges today: rising costs, difficulty providing adequate access in smaller towns, driver shortages and increased competition from cars and new mobility services, while demands for accessibility, climate benefits and efficient resource use keep growing.

The question is whether autonomous vehicles will worsen these problems or become part of the solution. As the technology moves from pilots to commercial operation, regions and public transport authorities face a crucial choice. Should they wait, or actively steer development towards shared, resource-efficient mobility services that strengthen public transport?

This session focuses on that choice. How can autonomous mobility services be integrated into public transport? What does the sector need to move from testing technology to changing the system?
And what role must public transport actors play to steer development in the right direction?

content.title: How can AI make our public-service processes more efficient? What can we learn from Norway?
content.description: How can AI improve the efficiency of public-service processes? Digitalisation of core welfare processes is accelerating, but the gap between pilots and production, and between technology and real operational value, determines whether AI becomes a powerful tool or more unfulfilled potential.
content.extendedDescription:
AI has the potential to revolutionise welfare provision, but the path from promising experiments to full-scale implementation is often obstructed. Why do so many projects get stuck in the pilot phase? What is needed for AI to deliver measurable efficiency in society's core processes? During the seminar, we look towards Norway, which has made considerable progress integrating AI into the public sector. We analyse success factors and pitfalls and discuss how Sweden can use these lessons to get started sooner. Discussion themes:
• From the lab to reality: How do we scale AI solutions to make a difference in everyday life for both citizens and employees?
• Norwegian experiences: What concrete results have been achieved in Norway, and what can we copy?
• Governance and leadership: How do we lead an organisation through a technological shift where value often arises at the intersection of IT and core operations?
Join an exchange of experience on closing the gap between technology and value.

content.title: A new assessment from school professionals – how are pupils doing in today's schools?
content.description: How are pupils doing in today's schools, and what do those who meet them every day see? Schools face major challenges such as mental ill health, absenteeism and social unrest. This is a societal issue. Student health services and school staff have unique insight into pupils' everyday lives and well-being.
content.extendedDescription:
During the seminar, Elevhälsan.se presents results from Elevhälsobarometern 2026, a national survey in which student health teams, school leaders and teachers describe pupils' well-being, the challenges shaping their work and the needs they identify in prevention.

The results are placed in a wider context through current research and the ongoing inquiry into student health services.

Participants from organisations, public agencies and business share perspectives on how schools and society can together help strengthen pupils' health and security.

The seminar provides an up-to-date picture while highlighting the roles different actors, including business, can play in strengthening young people's well-being and futures.

How has pupils' well-being changed, according to school professionals?
Which challenges are most prominent in schools' daily work?

content.title: Too little specialised housing for older people despite growing needs – reforms for more construction and choice
content.description: Housing can contribute to security, health and quality of life. Yet more older people find themselves staying in their homes involuntarily, experiencing loneliness, receiving more support at home and relying more on relatives. Putting people at the centre can increase care housing, but structural and financial barriers must first be removed.
content.extendedDescription:
Being able to adapt your housing to your life circumstances. Experiencing security, community and quality of life. As you grow older, you should be able to choose to remain at home, move to supported senior housing or move to care housing. But the reality is the opposite for many older people. Self-determination declines, at the cost of greater insecurity and loneliness. How did this happen? And how do we change it?
The report 'Från hinder till hem' (From barriers to homes) offers a unique examination of today's system, a patchwork of rules and conflicting funding conditions. It answers questions such as: How can more care housing and supported senior housing be built? What are the different actors' responsibilities, risks, financing and powers? How should the system for land, care payments, procurement and occupancy be organised?
Our reform agenda enables the right homes to be built in the right places, with the right conditions for care, the working environment, security and long-term operation. It is a model for greater self-determination, improved quality of life and better public finances.

content.title: More treatment options – a prerequisite for personalised care and investment in life science
content.description: Just over 30% of primary care doctors prescribe a different medicine each week from the one they consider most suitable, because of prescribing controls. More treatment options can enable more personalised asthma and COPD care. What risks arise from restricted treatment choices, and what is the impact on life science?
content.extendedDescription: A recent market survey of 893 primary care doctors shows that most view recommended medicine lists as helpful. However, just over 30% report prescribing a different medicine each week from the one they consider most appropriate, because of prescribing controls. Recommended lists must ensure patients with asthma and COPD have access to several treatment options and therefore more personalised care and well-controlled disease. Join a seminar where patients, experts and decision-makers discuss the risk of Sweden entering a monopoly-like situation if regions do not actively prioritise diversity in treatment options. Such a development would not only restrict patients' choices and affect care quality, but also reduce life science companies' willingness to invest and conduct research here, potentially weakening Sweden's position as a leading innovation nation over time.

content.title: Many of us stand behind the call – Russia out of Ukraine!
content.description: More than four years ago, on 24 February 2022, Russia launched a full-scale invasion of neighbouring Ukraine in violation of international law. Ukraine's population faces constant attacks every day. Ukraine needs all the support it can get in its struggle for peace, freedom and independence.
content.extendedDescription:
We invite everyone to join a demonstration independent of political parties and organisations to show that Sweden stands behind Ukraine's struggle for freedom, peace and independence! Together with civil society organisations, we gather around a shared demand – Russia out of Ukraine!

For just over four years, Ukraine has endured an inhumane assault, with constant drone and missile attacks. The Ukrainian population faces continuous suffering and oppression. Meanwhile, the Ukrainian army is fighting heroically against an occupying power and has succeeded in stopping Russia's initial plan to occupy all of Ukraine.

Today, Ukraine's eastern border is not only a boundary with an aggressive neighbour, but a boundary between democratic Europe and imperialist Russia. Ukraine is fighting for a democratic Europe today. We must therefore give Ukraine all the support it needs in its struggle. For Ukraine! For Europe! And for Sweden! Slava Ukraini!

content.title: Healthcare cannot do everything – who should decide, and how do we talk about it?
content.description: Healthcare has limited resources, both staff and money, and cannot meet every citizen's needs or wishes. Who should take responsibility for deciding what publicly funded healthcare should include, and how should we talk to citizens about those limits?
content.extendedDescription:
Politicians are accused of being unable to set limits on healthcare; the knowledge-based management system and public agencies produce guidelines seen as driving resource use; and professionals try to do the best for their patients, while we know healthcare resources are limited. How do we navigate this difficult equation?

In Västra Götalandsregionen, politicians have decided to work systematically on priority-setting across different areas of care, testing models to address growing expectations of healthcare provision from different quarters. Could this provide a starting point for better dialogue with citizens about what they should be able to expect from healthcare given resource constraints? At the seminar, representatives of regional politics, healthcare management, public agencies, the national knowledge-based management structure and the medical profession discuss who is responsible for deciding healthcare's limits and how to talk about them with citizens.

content.title: Circular value creation: transforming buildings and reuse along the value chain
content.description: A shift is under way in how we value what is already built. Inventories of cultural heritage values, material resources and climate investments, and avoiding waste, are becoming central to a circular economy. Meanwhile, the value chain is changing around guarantees, take-back schemes and logistics for circular product flows.
content.extendedDescription: Which actors manage value where, upstream and downstream in the value chain? What characterises an architecture of transformation, where buildings and construction products are designed for longer lives, flexibility, disassembly and modification? EU requirements for digital product passports will soon be introduced, and the Ecodesign Directive raises repairability requirements. Inventories can collect information on existing materials digitally, linked through ReUseApp as reuse data directly in BIM models. Data on reused materials becomes searchable, comparable and traceable to better manage the value of what already exists. For the fourth consecutive year, forward-looking actors in the built environment sector gather at Omställningsarenan, Sweco's courtyard, during Almedalsveckan! This moderated roundtable in fishbowl format is organised with Tarkett. A group representing different perspectives on the value chain shares incisive observations in a solution-focused discussion about circular value creation for buildings and the construction product value chain.

content.title: Northern Europe’s Security Landscape – Strengthening Cooperation in an Evolving Defence Alliance
content.description: Northern Europe’s security environment is changing due to Russia’s war against Ukraine and uncertainty over transatlantic engagement. Stronger Nordic-Baltic cooperation could enhance collective defence, while ensuring cohesion, resilience and effective burden-sharing across the defence alliance.
content.extendedDescription:
Northern Europe is becoming increasingly central to NATO’s deterrence and defence posture. This seminar brings together representatives from NATO, the defence sector and the security policy community to discuss how regional cooperation can strengthen collective defence and resilience.

The discussion will explore how cooperation across defence, security, industry, innovation and civil preparedness can support NATO’s strategic objectives in the Nordic-Baltic region. Particular attention will be given to partnerships with Ukraine and other key partners, and their contribution to European and transatlantic security.

The seminar will also address challenges linked to deeper integration, including risks of fragmentation, duplication and political divergence. Participants will discuss how these risks can be managed while enhancing deterrence, defence capabilities and societal resilience. The event concludes with audience questions.

content.title:
Can Sweden afford to ignore women's health?
Growth, innovation and health – overlooked billions
content.description: Delayed diagnoses, lower quality of life, lost working years, missed business opportunities. Despite women making up half the population, major disparities remain in research, innovation, diagnostics and care. The consequences affect not only individuals but also productivity, the labour market and the economy.
content.extendedDescription:
Internationally, recognition is growing that women's health is not only a healthcare issue but also one of innovation, competitiveness and economic development. Meanwhile, research shows that many diseases disproportionately affecting women remain underrepresented in research, diagnostics and innovation. International analyses also indicate significant economic gains from narrowing the health gap between women and men.
Are innovations lacking, or the ability to implement them? Who is responsible for turning research into patient benefits, growth, jobs and exports?
A challenging discussion about women's health as the next major issue for growth, innovation, implementation and policy. Patient perspectives, startups, the pharmaceutical industry, the regional innovation system and politics come together to discuss what is needed to move from insight to action.
The seminar takes the form of a moderated conversation and panel, followed by audience questions if time permits.
content.subject: Health and social care
speakerTitles: Moderator, Member of the Government's Life Science Council and Chair of the Board

content.title: Doctors save lives – is our naivety playing into criminals' hands?
content.description: Criminal actors build their business on a vulnerable link: positions of trust. In the public sector and private business, people are lured or threatened into enabling different types of crime. How do we protect ourselves against criminal enablers, and how can we stop improper influence?
content.extendedDescription:
Journalist Lasse Wierup's book 'Maffiapakten' paints a frightening picture of how more criminal networks are targeting companies and public agencies in pursuit of easy money. Lawyers and doctors, as well as auditors, business leaders, bank staff and public employees, then become involved as enablers of organised crime. The results can include false certificates, improper decisions, information leaks, fraud and damage to both the economy and public trust.

Have we become too naive? For example, we often picture doctors wearing white coats and saving lives, rather than prescribing narcotics or issuing false medical certificates for payment or under pressure.

But what exactly is an enabler? Why does someone become one? How do we detect one? Above all, how can we protect ourselves, one another and our organisations against attempts to recruit enablers and exert improper influence?

content.title: Everyone talks about prevention – why is it not happening in practice?
content.description: Schools have a clear duty to work preventively, from mental health and fundamental values to ANDTS (alcohol, drugs, doping, tobacco and gambling) and safety. Yet research, public-agency reports and surveys show that prevention is often squeezed out of schools' daily work.
content.extendedDescription:
Several reports from Skolinspektionen and Skolverket show shortcomings in schools' preventive work relating to safety, a calm learning environment and degrading treatment.
Current ANDTS data from school professionals confirms this. In a new survey, 80 per cent say schools do not do enough prevention, while 76 per cent say pupils rarely or never get to discuss alcohol in lessons. Many also identify concrete barriers: 68 per cent cite a lack of time and 64 per cent a lack of materials.
This reveals a clear pattern: the willingness is there, but the conditions are not.
The seminar discusses why preventive work, which everyone agrees is crucial, still struggles to have an impact in practice, and what is needed to strengthen it.

Sample questions:

Why does prevention have insufficient impact in schools' daily work?
Which conditions are currently missing?
What is needed to move from ambition to practice?

content.title: The next generation of cross-party action for energy security, competitiveness and independence
content.description: There are clear synergies between a robust, decentralised energy system and total defence capabilities. Research and dialogue with public agencies have turned conflicting goals towards opportunities for dual use and resilience. NATO neighbours lead the way. Once difficult questions have answers, politics remains. But what kind?
content.extendedDescription:
Region Blekinge and Region Gotland invite you to a solution-focused seminar followed by a panel discussion, aiming to spark curiosity among a new generation of national and local politicians about solutions and ways forward for Sweden's energy security, competitiveness and strategic independence in an uncertain world.
• We invite experts from projects, academia and public agencies (Elevated launch, FHS, SEI and others).
• We invite youth politicians from across the political spectrum alongside members of parliament and municipal and regional politicians.
• How do we develop policy for continued investment in synergies between wind power, subsea cables and defence interests in Sweden?
• What do politicians need to translate existing knowledge, experience and solutions into concrete action for more electricity generation and defence benefits?
• Particular focus on complex conflicts between wind power and defence interests, and perspectives on coexistence and synergies.

content.title: From innovation to real benefit – how life science, tech and defence can strengthen Sweden's preparedness
content.description: In a time of geopolitical unrest and an approaching election, stronger preparedness and greater competitiveness are highly relevant. Sweden has strong research, high innovation capacity and world-leading companies in tech, life science and defence. But we need to improve how we implement innovations. What is required?
content.extendedDescription:
We need better conditions for effectively implementing innovations in practice, where they deliver concrete benefits, to increase preparedness and strengthen competitiveness.

The seminar and panel discussion bring together a broad panel from tech, life science and defence, alongside public agencies, politicians and decision-makers, to discuss:
• how to implement innovations more effectively to strengthen Sweden's preparedness capabilities
• concrete measures that can shorten the path from innovation to practical application: legislation, processes, governance, funding models, skills and responsibility
• decisions needed from politicians and decision-makers
• how this also strengthens Sweden's competitiveness

Welcome to Novartis Innovationsträdgård in Almedalen!
We look forward to an important, solution-focused discussion with representatives from tech, life science, defence, research, public agencies, decision-making and politics.

content.title: From strategy to results – how can Sweden strengthen its position as a life science nation?
content.description: Life science is a Swedish strength, but the system is fragmented and implementation of the life science strategy is insufficient. Long-term investment, clearer priorities, coordination and implementation capacity are needed to secure Sweden's position as a leading life science nation.
content.extendedDescription:
Swedish life science policy needs to step up to realise the full potential of one of our most important future industries. The national strategy has been updated, but implementation remains insufficient. Responsibilities are unclear, and there is a lack of long-term investment, shared priorities, action plans with timelines and resources, structured follow-up, problem-solving capacity and the ability to drive forceful, coordinated change. Meanwhile, other countries are making long-term, coordinated investments in this field.

For Sweden to retain its position as a successful, competitive life science nation, clearer direction, greater mobilisation and stronger implementation are required.

In the seminar, politicians, healthcare, academia and business discuss who takes responsibility for driving work forward and which models best strengthen governance, coordination and implementation to move Swedish life science from strategy to results.

content.title: Glaucoma care in transition – those who live should be able to see
content.description: Glaucoma is a common disease affecting hundreds of thousands of patients and is the leading cause of irreversible blindness. For patients, this means a dramatic decline in quality of life, while the burden and costs for healthcare keep increasing. New treatment methods can prevent this!
content.extendedDescription: In an educational seminar, we will hear both the glaucoma surgeon's and the patient's perspectives, and explore the opportunities offered by fully implementing medical technology and benefiting from its positive effects. In this case, that means not only reducing the risk of patients with glaucoma becoming visually impaired or even blind, but also easing pressure on healthcare and substantially reducing the costs of glaucoma care overall. In a chronic disease where patients cannot regain lost sight, all attempts to halt or delay progression are clearly beneficial. Not least because quality of life is enormously affected for the unfortunate patients who become severely ill, often unnecessarily. We also know that a very large share of the burden and costs falls on these severely ill patients. We therefore cannot afford NOT to treat patients earlier – and patients, surgeons, health economists and healthcare representatives agree on this.

content.title: How can policy strengthen schools' work against violence towards children?
content.description: Children living with violence are in every classroom, but far too few are identified. Schools have a clear mandate but often lack the conditions to act. What political measures are needed to change this?
content.extendedDescription:
At least 210 000 children in Sweden are estimated to live with domestic violence – around one in ten. The consequences are serious: increased risk of mental ill health, difficulties at school and poorer life chances.

Yet few of these children access society's support services. Only a small proportion tell school staff, and schools account for a very limited share of child welfare reports, despite being where children spend most time outside the home.

Teachers' and school leaders' experiences point not to a lack of willingness but to inadequate conditions: uncertainty about signs of violence, fear of making mistakes and insufficient support in difficult situations.

The panel discussion starts from these problems, bringing together parliamentary parties' education policy representatives to discuss political measures that could strengthen schools' ability to identify and act on suspicions that a child lives with violence at home.

content.title: Decision-making in an uncertain world: which futures must we prepare society for?
content.description: Major systems involving climate, conflict, energy, technology and geopolitics are changing faster than ever. Much of what affects us lies beyond our control. How do we nevertheless make decisions, and how can scenarios help build resilience and robust strategies?
content.extendedDescription:
Society often plans for one risk at a time. But disruptions are interconnected: wars and conflicts affect energy, the economy and goods flows. AI and other technological changes create new dependencies. Natural disasters, disease outbreaks and food crises cause humanitarian suffering.

The seminar explores how exploratory scenarios, stress tests, no-regrets measures and critical examination of our assumptions can support decisions under uncertainty. Perspectives from energy, humanitarian work, security and leadership in complex systems come together to discuss what is needed for robust decision-making processes in an uncertain world.

The starting point is a compound sequence in which disrupted energy supplies, humanitarian pressures and security-policy demands simultaneously confront Swedish actors with difficult choices. What assumptions underpin today's decisions? Which risks are we missing? And how can essential societal actors strengthen their ability to manage deep uncertainty and compound societal risks?

content.title: How do we reach net zero by 2045? Sweden first with a shared climate ambition for healthcare and life science
content.description: The healthcare sector accounts for around five per cent of global climate emissions. At the same time, care must remain high-quality and strengthen Sweden's life science competitiveness. How can the sector transition to net zero by 2045 without jeopardising patient safety, innovation or access to effect
content.extendedDescription: Sweden has high ambitions for both climate and medical quality. A public-private partnership bringing together actors across the healthcare value chain around a shared climate ambition – net-zero emissions by 2045 – was established in 2026. Healthcare, pharmaceutical companies, medical technology companies, pharmacies and other parts of life science depend on one another. Collaboration is therefore needed to reduce both direct and indirect emissions. The partnership prioritises actions delivering the greatest climate benefits, such as prevention, early diagnosis and effective treatment that reduces the need for resource-intensive care. It also focuses on innovation, circular material flows, reuse, reduced waste and climate-smart logistics. More resource-efficient working methods also strengthen robustness and competitiveness. We present the initiative and how more actors can join.

content.title: When does power stop serving and start demanding obedience? How do I wrestle with my own desire for power as a leader?
content.description: Wrestling with a desire for power as a leader is probably common, but we do not talk openly about it. What warning signs help us avoid an unhealthy desire for power? When does it become destructive? What ethical boundaries and strategies exist? How can a desire for power become a positive driving force?
content.extendedDescription:
The classic question is as uncomfortable as it is relevant: how does power corrupt me?
Where is the line between legitimate authority and a destructive desire for power? How do we recognise when our own leadership turns into control, prestige and a need for validation? What warning signs help us avoid this?

Theologically, power is delegated and subject to accountability. The biblical tradition includes both criticism of kings and prophetic scrutiny. No ruler stands above truth or righteousness. What does this mean when strength is often rewarded over self-examination and religion is even used as a tool for gaining power?

Power changes things! Not only societies, but us as individuals. It provides room for action, influence and responsibility while testing judgement, character and self-image.
How do we use power as leaders and decision-makers so that desires for power become positive drivers and a tool for creating change and empowering more people?

content.title: Welfare crime – a growing societal problem requiring shared responsibility
content.description: Welfare crime is a serious threat to our shared welfare systems. When public funds are misused or obtained through irregularities, resources are drained from schools, healthcare and social care. For municipalities and regions, this means financial losses and reduced trust in the public sector.
content.extendedDescription:
How extensive is welfare crime in municipalities and regions today, what methods are used and how is it developing over time? Effective prevention requires knowledge of the scale of the problem and an understanding of risks and vulnerabilities within one's own organisation.

This seminar examines the development of welfare crime in municipalities and regions. You will receive an up-to-date picture of how it appears in practice and which areas are particularly vulnerable. We also highlight auditing's role in revealing risks, examining governance and controls, and contributing to more systematic prevention. Concrete examples from municipalities and regions provide experience of how organisations can strengthen their work against welfare crime before harm occurs.

The seminar is aimed at elected representatives, managers, auditors and others wishing to strengthen their work to protect welfare and ensure public resources are used properly.

content.title: Who decides over the landscape during the energy transition?
content.description: The energy transition must happen, and it needs space. Invisible harmful emissions are replaced by energy infrastructure visible in landscapes where people live and work. Municipalities and regions increasingly need to demonstrate local leadership, authority and the ability to make courageous decisions.
content.extendedDescription:
Energikontoren Sverige, together with #Krafttag i Väst – ElSA, invites you to this seminar, drawing on current research on regional energy planning and highlighting regions' role in managing conflicts between climate, industry, natural values and local acceptance. We also focus on municipalities' crucial role, where their planning monopoly and local decision-making powers must translate into actions that drive the transition.
Using examples from Dalarna, Energikontoret i Östergötland's energy planning work, the SpeedLocal research project on social acceptance and Fyrbodals kommunalförbund's politically adopted direction, we discuss how strategic planning can become concrete municipal action, and what is needed to dare to prioritise conflicting interests.
The discussion is moderated by Tomas Kåberger, Chair of Energikontoren Sverige.
The seminar offers:
• Insights, perspectives and examples of municipalities' role as enablers of energy expansion.

content.description: What can we do together that no actor can achieve alone? Today's and tomorrow's cancer challenges require collaboration between research, healthcare, business, civil society and patients. Unexpected partnerships can deliver faster innovation, more effective prevention and better support for everyone with cancer.

An inspiring, interactive session focusing on unexpected collaborations between organisations and sectors. content.title: Total defence starts in everyday life – what role does cooperation between social partners play?
content.description: Sweden's security situation affects all central government operations. Total defence is built not only through plans and structures but through daily life in government workplaces. How is robustness created in the central government sector, and how does the Swedish model contribute to the functioning of total defence?
content.extendedDescription:
The current international situation affects conditions for the central government sector. Security, information influence operations and preparedness place new demands on organisations. Against this backdrop, local social partners must be able to engage in informed dialogue and cooperate on operational issues relating to security and preparedness. Karin Lönnheden of Myndigheten för psykologiskt försvar describes today's reality and tomorrow's security requirements. Drawing on the report 'Öppenhet och säkerhet inom statliga myndigheter' (Openness and security in government agencies), produced by Centrum för totalförsvar och samhällets säkerhet at Försvarshögskolan, the discussion continues with local and central social partners.
Questions include:
What does the changed security situation mean for government operations in practice?
How are managers, employees and relations between social partners affected by heightened preparedness?
Why are trust and dialogue crucial to total defence too?
How can local social partners contribute to the state's collective resilience?

content.title: Healthcare crisis or transformation? Parkinson's patient numbers expected to double by 2040 – how do we ensure equitable care?
content.description: Parkinson's is the fastest-growing neurological disease. 22 000 people live with the diagnosis, and many more are affected. Every hour counts. Timely, appropriate care determines functioning and quality of life. Technology and guidelines exist; political will and organisational structures are now needed. Who takes responsibility and leads the way?
content.extendedDescription:
Parkinson's is a disease in which every hour without appropriate care can permanently impair functioning and quality of life. Despite medical advances, place of residence often determines the care received. Socialstyrelsen's 2025 evaluation shows we are far from achieving equitable care: only 60% see their neurologist once a year, despite guidelines recommending two annual visits, and regional differences are substantial. Resource shortages affect follow-up, assessment, care interventions and quality of life.

We need to move from passive waiting to active follow-up and action based on need. Achieving Socialstyrelsen's goals requires a structured care pathway that identifies patients' medical needs in time. The seminar discusses innovative methods and proactive triage that can improve Parkinson's care, use healthcare resources more efficiently, shorten waiting lists and provide care according to patients' needs rather than fixed schedules. The right care at the right time saves society's resources.

content.title: Is Sweden ready for breakthrough technology?
content.description: Global competition in breakthrough technology is intensifying, prompting a historic Swedish investment in research and innovation. Investment in excellence clusters aims to secure international competitiveness and build a resilient society. But is Sweden ready for radically groundbreaking technology?
content.extendedDescription:
In a critical geopolitical situation, breakthrough technology is crucial. Excellence clusters bring together the country's leading researchers and industry's most forward-looking leaders to move Sweden towards international technological leadership. The clusters are intended to fundamentally change how we solve problems and break new ground in pursuit of future research and innovation breakthroughs.
The initiative is jointly run by Vetenskapsrådet and Vinnova. The first call closed a few weeks ago. We are now entering a new phase: establishment.
Does Sweden have the conditions and capacity to take on new, groundbreaking technology? How should we cooperate and think to ensure new solutions and breakthroughs have an impact on everyday life? What happens when new technology meets people and society?
The seminar explores these questions with representatives of business, academia and the public sector. You will also get a preview of strong technology areas in the recently closed call.

content.title: Hydropower, aquatic environments and biodiversity – how do we find the right balance?
content.description: The national plan for modern environmental conditions (NAP) aims to improve aquatic environments without unnecessarily weakening hydropower's role in the climate transition, competitiveness and electricity preparedness. How do we balance aquatic environments, hydropower, biodiversity and local interests in practice?
content.extendedDescription:
The national plan for modern environmental conditions (NAP) requires Sweden's hydropower plants to undergo permit reviews to improve river environments and preserve valuable species and habitats. This is a very extensive process expected to take 20 years. At the same time, hydropower is crucial to the green transition, competitiveness and electricity preparedness.

Policymakers have made clear that NAP should be implemented without affecting hydropower's electricity generation, balancing capability and electricity preparedness more than necessary to comply with EU law. But how do we achieve this in practice? How do we weigh energy and climate benefits against natural environments and biodiversity? What do we do when national interests and local needs conflict?

The seminar brings together energy companies, public agencies, civil society and political representatives to discuss implementing NAP proportionately and sustainably from a socioeconomic perspective, safeguarding both environmental goals and the energy system's needs.

content.title: From north to south – regional strengths and differences in total defence development
content.description: Work to strengthen Sweden's total defence has progressed and is now rooted in society. Yet differences in conditions and implementation remain between civil defence areas, sectors and companies. What does this mean for our resilience, and what is needed for more robust development?
content.extendedDescription:
Innovation, technological development, adaptability, leadership and cooperation are among the most crucial building blocks of strong civil and military defence. The seminar brings together representatives of business, the public sector and politics to discuss strengthening Sweden's preparedness.

Drawing on Totalförsvarsrapporten, based on insights from business decision-makers, we highlight measurable progress driving development. We also reveal differences between civil defence areas and companies.

The discussion focuses on preparedness work in practice, what works and the conditions needed to maintain momentum. Through good examples and dialogue, we aim to reflect ongoing developments and challenge areas where the pace must increase.

Säkerhetsarenan brings together leading actors in safety, security and preparedness to highlight important perspectives and discuss ways forward. It is a meeting place for discussions that help strengthen Sweden.

content.title: Humans as masters of creation or relatives among other beings – different perspectives and consequences?
content.description: How do we experience our relationship with the rest of the planet? Are humans in charge, or are we all equally important and interconnected? What does it mean that our experiences differ? How does Svenska kyrkan view this from biblical and human perspectives? What do the performing arts think, and what do you think?
content.extendedDescription:
A warm welcome to an open public conversation with guests from Visby Stift and the performing arts collective Tellus°. The gathering begins with a special version of Tellus°#3: Sympoiesis, a physical performance that premiered in February at Naturhistoriska Museet in Gothenburg. The performance then transitions into the conversation, both taking place inside Visby Domkyrka.
Tellus°#3: Sympoiesis is a physical, multidisciplinary artwork in which voice, movement, music and video portray humanity's attempt to reconnect with the living world it has never really left. We journey out of the Anthropocene – a popular way of viewing our human-dominated and sometimes ruthless era – and glimpse the Chthulucene, a very different and at least equally true account of our world. Shaped by ancient mechanisms and collaborations between life and matter, constantly evolving symbioses and relationships between life, time and rhythm. Natural laws and phenomena that seem undeterred by restrictive norms, structures and behaviours.

content.title: From genetic data to treatment: how do we build equitable cancer care nationwide?
content.description: Precision diagnostics shifts the focus from cancer's location in the body to the tumour's genetic profile. But advanced testing requires specialist expertise and structures for interpreting large datasets. How do we ensure equitable access to the right testing and treatment throughout the country?
content.extendedDescription:
A Molecular Tumour Board (MTB) is a central function in modern cancer care, where multidisciplinary expert teams interpret complex genetic information to select the right treatment for the right patient. But access to both advanced genetic testing and MTB expertise varies across the country. This risks reinforcing inequalities in cancer care and hindering implementation of precision medicine in clinical practice. How do we ensure every patient has access to the right diagnostics, interpretation and treatment, regardless of where they live?

The seminar focuses on the strategic choice facing Sweden:
• How do we make MTB a national concern adapted to regional needs?
• What investments are needed in infrastructure, expertise and data management?
• How do we ensure innovation translates into actual patient benefits for everyone, not just some?

The discussion brings together decision-makers, healthcare providers and experts to identify concrete ways forward.
